title: Bridging Structure and Semantics: Knowledge Graph Verification via Triple-to-Text Alignment
description:
arXiv:2611.07780v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Semantic accuracy is an important dimension of knowledge graph quality. Graph-based scoring methods exploit relational structure, while textual representations allow classifiers to draw on knowledge encoded by pre-trained language models (PLMs). We present GenVer, a generative verifier that scores triples using both their serialized form and generated natural language representations (NLRs). A triple-text alignment procedure selects training pairs for a sequence-to-sequence generator; a BERT-based classifier then combines features from each triple and its generated NLR. On four FactFB variants, constructed from FB15k using perturbed negative triples, GenVer obtains the highest classification accuracy among the evaluated baselines, ranging from 88.56% to 91.52%. The experiments suggest that generated representations can help triple classification, while the case analysis also exposes semantic drift and high-confidence errors.

title: Guidance Is a Field, Not a Scalar: Interval-Integrated Classifier-Free Guidance for One-Step Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.07566v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One-step generators built on MeanFlow synthesize a video in a single function evaluation, yet inherit a rigid treatment of classifier-free guidance (CFG): the guidance scale is frozen during training or, at best, exposed as a single scalar. This conflicts with mounting evidence that the optimal guidance is not a constant but a field that varies with the noise level, with spatial content, and, for video, with frame position. Every existing remedy presupposes a multi-step sampler along which guidance can be re-scheduled--an assumption one-step models violate by construction. We resolve this tension through a single observation: because the MeanFlow target is an integral over a noise interval, an arbitrary guidance field can be absorbed into the target itself and compiled into one evaluation. We formalize this as the interval-integrated CFG identity, prove that the compiled guidance carries no schedule-discretization error and can thus match or exceed any finite multi-step sampler, and instantiate it as AGAVE, which equips the average-velocity field with a learnable temporal schedule, a free motion-saliency spatial modulation, and a frame-position asymmetry. Adding fewer than ten scalars at zero inference cost, AGAVE surpasses all one-step baselines on VBench, UCF-101 and MSR-VTT while matching multi-step guided sampling. Project repository: https://github.com/YMlinfeng/AGAVE.

title: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time
description:
arXiv:2611.07025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.

title: Depth or Description? When a One-Step Latent Score Replaces Lookahead in Proactive Information Acquisition
description:
arXiv:2611.07155v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A proactive agent must decide what to ask before it acts. Exact lookahead values combinations of questions but is expensive and leans on a fitted model; a one-step score is cheap but can miss them. Our main finding: the need for depth often lies in how the hidden cause is described. A one-step score on the label can be blind to an interaction among answers. A score on a suitable latent cause is not, and where that latent encodes the decision it replaces most of depth at a fraction of the search. Described differently, the same problem can defeat the score while exact values do not move, so keep the latent small and check it against exact values. Probabilities learned from one language model's answers do not carry to another unless planning allows for both; those read from tokens are worth only a few labels.

title: Responsible GenAI Use During Active Armed Conflict: Evidence from Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms
description:
arXiv:2611.07874v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Armed conflict can increase the value of Generative AI (GenAI) while undermining the conditions required for its responsible use. Yet the perspectives of community-based humanitarian responders working under these conditions remain underrepresented in responsible AI research. We examine GenAI use in Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs), a community-led humanitarian network, through an exploratory survey of 89 respondents and 15 semi-structured interviews with GenAI users and non-users. War reconfigures GenAI's role, making it most useful where its outputs are hardest to verify. ERR responders turned to GenAI when conflict made human expertise difficult or dangerous to reach. However, participants cautioned that GenAI could not independently establish rapidly changing local conditions, and that relying on its outputs could lead to harmful decisions when human verification was difficult. Risks arose before GenAI was used. For some volunteers, carrying a phone or accessing the internet could expose them to danger. Others were concerned that sharing sensitive beneficiary or operational information with GenAI could put people at risk. Participants feared that AI-assisted reports could undermine their credibility with donors, whose funding sustains the food and medical aid ERRs provide. Access to GenAI was uneven, and volunteers using it sometimes relied on colleagues with relevant expertise or local knowledge to verify its results. Our findings show that responsible use of GenAI during conflict depends not only on model performance or individual adoption, but also on whether responders can safely access these tools, verify their outputs against local conditions, and recognize when limiting or avoiding GenAI is the more responsible choice.

title: Training-Free Predictive Spatio-Temporal Token Pruning for Few-Step Autoregressive Video Diffusion
description:
arXiv:2611.07551v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Few-step autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk and have made efficient video generation practical. However, further accelerating these models toward real-time generation remains challenging, as few-step distillation leaves little cross-step redundancy for existing training-free caching methods to exploit. We revisit this regime and identify two token-level redundancy patterns: cross-frame redundancy from static content shared across adjacent frames, and cross-step redundancy from tokens that converge early during denoising. Crucially, we find that early clean estimates along the model's own denoising trajectory provide an effective online signal for locating both patterns, requiring no retraining, auxiliary predictor, or reference video. Based on these findings, we propose PreSTP (Predictive Spatio-Temporal Token Pruning), a training-free framework that constructs a unified token-wise redundancy mask from cross-frame similarity and cross-step convergence. Tokens marked as redundant skip subsequent computation under a consistent last-computed-value restoration rule, and a content-adaptive mask reuse strategy further reduces dense probing cost. On 5-second generation, PreSTP achieves 1.52x-3.20x speedups and a better efficiency-fidelity trade-off than coarse-grained caching baselines such as TeaCache and FlowCache. On 30-second generation, it reaches up to 1.96x speedup while improving VBench-Long and suppressing long-horizon drift. Notably, it continues to reduce inference cost even in the extreme one-step regime, where cross-step redundancy vanishes entirely and coarse step-wise caching is no longer applicable.

title: Persistent Retrieval for Conversational Agents: A Study of Retrieval Efficiency
description:
arXiv:2611.07899v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conversational agents can retrieve information directly or delegate retrieval to a subagent. This design choice affects how retrieval history is maintained, what context each model call receives, and what information must be re-retrieved in follow-up questions. We compare three designs: skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent that generates a findings response, and our persistent retrieval subagent, which maintains retrieval history across turns and returns retrieved evidence directly to the main agent. Our approach also allows the main agent to request corrections from the same subagent.
  We evaluate the three designs on enterprise questions posed independently, within shared conversations, and as dependent follow-ups. Across five multi-turn settings, our approach uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens and incurs 45.0% lower estimated API cost than skill-based retrieval, while reducing average response time by 9.1%. Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it reduces response time by 15.6 seconds per question, while using 65.1% more tokens and incurring 29.1% higher estimated API cost.
  Our approach shifts the retrieval subagent from producing synthesized responses to maintaining retrieval state and supplying evidence that the main agent can directly evaluate and use for answer generation.

title: GEKey: Learning Geodesic Eccentric 3D Keypoints via Self-Supervision
description:
arXiv:2611.07677v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Point clouds represent 3D object geometry as sets of spatial coordinates. A fundamental task in their analysis is keypoint detection, i.e., identifying a sparse subset of points that captures the most salient features. While supervised methods rely on manual annotations, unsupervised approaches leverage intrinsic geometric properties to localize keypoints without human input. We introduce GEKey, a self-supervised framework that uses the geodesic eccentricity transform, an SE(3)-invariant geometric measure, to identify instance-specific salient points. These points serve as pseudo-labels to train a model that aligns its predictions with the object's intrinsic structure. GEKey is simple, efficient, and robust, preserving intra-class variation by balancing instance-specific and category-level structure. Extensive experiments on ShapeNetCoreV2, KeypointNet, CAPE, ITOP, and DeformingThings4D show state-of-the-art performance in both keypoint detection and alignment, with strong resilience to noise, downsampling, deformations, and real-world conditions. The code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/Pierreoo/GEKey.

title: I'm building an open-source messenger for developers: This is what I have learned so far
description:
Talking code in a regular chat app is frustrating. Snippets turn into walls of text. Pull request links get buried. And worst of all, people paste database URLs and API keys into chat, where they stay in the history forever.

So I started building Ack, an open-source messenger for developers.

What Ack does

Code blocks and diffs that look like they belong in an editor
Repo-linked rooms, so pull requests and CI results show up in the conversation

Secret vaults: the secret is encrypted in your browser and deleted after the recipient reveals it
Search that only finds people who have joined Ack, with an invite link for everyone else

Where it is today

Working now: sign in with GitHub, search for people who have joined Ack, send an invite link to anyone who hasn't, and chat one on one. Messages are stored in Appwrite and sync between devices. When a friend joins through your invite link, your chat opens automatically.

Still in progress: locking each conversation so only its two participants can read it, and making the secret vault delete the secret on the server, not just in the browser. Until both are done, please don't put real passwords or keys into Ack. Treat it as a test.

Using sample data for now: the pull request cards and the Reviews inbox. Real GitHub connections through a GitHub App come next.

Not built yet: voice and video calls and pair programming. They're designed, and they're switched off behind feature flags until they work for real.

Try it: https://project-ack.vercel.app
Repo: https://github.com/kingenious0/ACK

How I'm building it

I'm not a hand-coder, and I'm upfront about that. I research the idea, write a spec, hand it to an AI coding IDE, build in small phases, test each phase, and review what the AI produced. The stack is Vite, React 19, TypeScript, Appwrite for sign-in and the database, and Vercel for hosting. I have been doing this for about 2 years now and it is really helping me.

Three things I learned

1. A display name is not a username.
My first version guessed a person's GitHub handle from their display name, and the link led to a GitHub 404. Display name and login handle are different fields. The fix was to fetch the real profile from GitHub's API after sign-in and store GitHub's numeric user ID, which never changes.

2. Don't search all of GitHub.
I first let anyone message any GitHub username. That means messages can pile up for someone who never agreed to join, and a stranger can spam them. Now search only looks at people who have joined Ack. If someone isn't there, you get an invite link, and nothing is stored for them until they sign up.

3. Be honest about security from day one.
I removed "end-to-end encrypted" from the app because it wasn't true yet. Saying less and being right builds more trust than a big claim.

What's next

Real-time sync, connecting GitHub repos through a GitHub App so pull requests and CI results appear in chat, and then calls.

Thanks for reading. If you try Ack, tell me what breaks.

title: MAC-v2: Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels
description:
arXiv:2611.07245v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study whether \emph{long-horizon model-based value expansion} can serve as an effective framework in pixel-based offline reinforcement learning (RL). Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels is substantially harder than state-based environments, as the agent must learn both the representation and its dynamics, and errors from either can accumulate recursively over imagined trajectories. We introduce MAC-v2, which enables long-horizon model-based expansion from pixels by training a reconstruction-free latent world model with action chunking. By learning representations from prediction and control objectives, MAC-v2 does not need to encode control-irrelevant visual details that can hinder the dynamics prediction. Action chunking further mitigates the prediction error by reducing the number of recursive model predictions required for value expansion. Across diverse visual benchmarks including visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10, MAC-v2 achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines. Our analyses show that long-horizon model-based value expansion is critical for the performance of MAC-v2, and that both action chunking and latent learning objectives are essential for reliable long-horizon latent imagination.

title: AI Automation Cost: Why $0.12 Per Run Can Become $12,000 at Scale
description:
Originally published on Soluma AI.

One of our workflows cost about $0.12 per prospect across a 500 run test. That is either trivial or a $12,000 decision, depending entirely on the multiplier behind it.

One of the most useful lessons we learned about AI cost started with a number that looked almost too small to care about: $0.12. That was roughly what one of our AI workflows was costing to research a prospect. Twelve cents. For a workflow doing real research, that sounded perfectly reasonable, and at small volume it was.

Then we did the obvious calculation we probably should all do much earlier when building AI systems. What happens at 100,000 runs? The answer is $12,000. Suddenly, a fraction of a dollar is no longer a technical detail. It is an operating decision.

That led us to look much more carefully at what the $0.12 actually contained. The workflow was not making one simple AI request. It was carrying out six separate buyer searches, processing the findings and performing a final analysis. The interesting question was never which AI model is cheapest. It was what one completed piece of work actually costs, where that money goes, and how much can be removed before the work gets worse.

How much does AI automation actually cost per run?

There is no universally good AI automation cost per run. The useful number is the cost of producing one acceptable completed job, including model usage, tool calls, search or retrieval, external APIs, retries and other resources required by the workflow. A $0.12 workflow may be economical at 500 runs and material at 100,000. The cost only makes sense when it is viewed alongside volume, quality and the commercial value of the output.

Quick takeaways

  1. 1Tiny unit costs become real budgets at volume: $0.12 per run becomes $12,000 across 100,000 runs.
  2. 2Model price is only part of the cost. Search, retrieval, tools, retries and workflow design create a cost floor that changing models does not remove.
  3. 3Cheaper output is not automatically better economics. If saving a few cents reduces research quality, the cheaper workflow may create less business value.
  4. 4Measure before you optimise. Establish a quality baseline, calculate the full cost per acceptable job, then change one part of the workflow at a time.

The $0.12 problem: tiny number, real money

Here is what the same workflow looks like at different volumes. Nothing changed technically between the first row and the last. Only the multiplier changed.

RUNS COST AT $0.12 PER RUN
100 $12
500 $60
1,000 $120
10,000 $1,200
50,000 $6,000
100,000 $12,000

This is one of the easiest things to miss while prototyping. During development you might test ten rows, twenty, fifty, so a workflow can feel almost free. Then someone adds a Run All button, and that button changes the economics completely. If 100,000 eligible records sit behind it, a twelve cent workflow has turned one click into roughly $12,000 of authorised usage.

The question is not whether $0.12 is cheap. It is how many times you are about to spend $0.12.

Model cost and workflow cost are not the same thing

A common way to estimate AI cost is to read the model pricing page: input tokens cost X, output tokens cost Y, multiply and you have your number. That works for a single model request. It becomes incomplete once the model sits inside a larger workflow.

  • web searches and retrieval
  • external APIs and database operations
  • multiple model calls and reasoning steps
  • validation calls and secondary models
  • retries and failed attempts

OpenAI, for example, currently prices its web search tool at $10 per 1,000 calls, or $0.01 per search call, with search content tokens additionally billed at the selected model rates. That mattered in our workflow. Each prospect required six buyer searches, so six search calls alone contributed six cents before any analysis. That is half of a $0.12 run in tool call fees.

This is what we mean by a structural cost floor. If the workflow genuinely requires those six searches, switching to a cheaper analysis model does not make that six cent layer disappear.

Our 500 run test changed what we wanted to optimise

Before scaling further we ran the workflow across approximately 500 prospects, roughly $60 in operating cost. We were not testing cost alone. We wanted to know whether the searches produced useful evidence, whether the buyer questions were realistic, whether the final analysis retained the right context, whether outputs were consistent enough to use downstream, and where failures happened.

If we had optimised for price before establishing a quality baseline, we would have had no reliable way to tell whether a cheaper version was still doing the same job. We did test cheaper configurations. The cost went down and so did the quality. That told us some of the spend was not waste. It was buying information the workflow needed.

Cost per run can still hide the real number

Even after calculating cost per run, there is another level worth measuring: cost per acceptable completed job. Suppose a workflow costs $0.12 every time it starts. If only 90 percent of outputs meet the acceptance standard, you did not pay twelve cents for every usable result. You paid more.

Cost per acceptable completed job = total workflow cost divided by accepted outputs.

ACCEPTANCE RATE EFFECTIVE COST PER ACCEPTED RESULT
100% $0.120
95% $0.126
90% $0.133
80% $0.150

This is why an apparently cheaper configuration can lose its advantage quickly if it creates more failures, retries or unusable outputs. The business is not buying API calls. It is buying completed work.

The cheapest model does not necessarily create the cheapest system

Model choice obviously matters, and current model line ups reflect that trade off between frontier capability, balanced cost and high volume workloads. But a cheaper model only saves money on the work that model is responsible for. It does not reduce search calls, external API fees, duplicate retrieval, unnecessary workflow stages, poor retry logic, or calls that should never have happened.

OPTIMISATION LAYER WHAT YOU CHANGE TYPICAL EXAMPLES
Model optimisation How expensive each model operation is Smaller model, lower reasoning effort, shorter output, prompt caching
Architecture optimisation How much work the system performs Fewer calls, reused results, conditional research, deterministic processing, controlled retries

Both matter, but the second becomes increasingly important as volume rises. If your system performs eight paid actions where four would produce the same result, changing models treats the symptom while the workflow keeps doing unnecessary work.

The better question: what is the lowest cost that preserves the job?

There is a dangerous version of AI optimisation that looks excellent on a spreadsheet. Version A costs $0.12. Version B costs $0.08. Success. Except Version B misses more evidence, produces weaker classifications, requires more human checking or sends poorer output into the next stage. The four cent saving is real. So is the quality loss.

For prospect research that influences who a business contacts and what it says to them, four cents is an absurd place to compromise when the downstream opportunity is worth hundreds or thousands of dollars. A better target is the lowest cost at which the workflow still performs its job to the required standard.

What we are optimising next

Our approximately $0.12 figure is the baseline, not the finish line. The working target we are testing towards is around $0.08 per run while maintaining the same output quality. That is not a market benchmark. Another workflow could reasonably cost $0.01, $0.40 or $4 depending on what it does.

VOLUME $0.12 PER RUN $0.08 PER RUN POTENTIAL SAVING
500 $60 $40 $20
10,000 $1,200 $800 $400
50,000 $6,000 $4,000 $2,000
100,000 $12,000 $8,000 $4,000

At 500 runs the difference is $20 and easy to dismiss. At 100,000 runs the exact same engineering improvement is worth $4,000. That is why we test small but design with the larger volume in mind.

Where should you look for AI cost savings first?

1. Establish the quality baseline

Take a representative sample and run the version you currently trust. Define what a good output means before changing anything. Accuracy alone may not be enough. Depending on the task you may also care about evidence quality, completeness, consistency, format compliance, latency or human review time.

2. Break the run into cost components

Do not leave yourself with one number called AI cost. Separate model input, model output, tool calls, retrieval and search, external APIs, retries, failures and infrastructure. Now you know what is actually worth optimising.

3. Find the structural floor

Ask which costs remain even if you changed the model tomorrow. In our case, six paid buyer searches immediately exposed a meaningful part of the floor, which changes where engineering effort should go.

4. Remove duplicated work before reducing intelligence

Could a result already collected in step two be reused in step five? Is static context being repeatedly sent? Could deterministic code handle filtering, joining, ranking, deduplication or validation instead of another model call? Current OpenAI guidance recommends bounded programmatic processing for predictable operations rather than forcing every intermediate step through a model.

5. Use cheaper models where the task genuinely allows it

Classification does not need the same model as final synthesis, and extraction does not need the same reasoning level as strategic analysis. Current guidance recommends evaluating model tiers and reasoning levels against representative tasks. The key word is evaluating. Do not downgrade and assume equivalence. Test it.

6. Make prompts leaner, not merely shorter

A shorter prompt only helps if it still contains the instructions that affect the result. Remove repeated instructions, irrelevant tools and unnecessary examples, while retaining guidance that corrects measured quality gaps. The goal is not prompt minimalism. It is removing instructions that are not earning their cost.

7. Use caching where repeated context makes it worthwhile

If large parts of the prompt stay identical across runs, prompt caching can reduce the cost of reprocessing the same input. Measure actual cache hits. A feature being available does not mean your workflow is structured to benefit from it.

8. Consider batch processing where the workload fits

For asynchronous work that does not need an immediate response, the OpenAI Batch API currently offers a 50 percent discount within a 24 hour completion window. That can be meaningful at volume, though tool heavy workflows should be tested for compatibility rather than moved wholesale.

9. Control retries and stopping conditions

Retries are useful when something genuinely failed. They are expensive when nobody told the system when to stop. Define what counts as success, recoverable failure, permanent failure and stop. This matters even more when the workflow can run without anyone watching.

What the Run All button really means

A button labelled Run All Empty Rows looks operational. Financially it is closer to: authorise every eligible row to consume the resources required to finish. Two hundred rows at $0.12 is about $24. Ten thousand is about $1,200. One hundred thousand is about $12,000.

This is not an argument against automation. It is an argument for attaching economics to automation. Before enabling large autonomous queues, a production system should know how many records are eligible, the expected cost per record, the likely failure rate, the maximum acceptable spend and how execution can be stopped.

Four numbers we now want before scaling an AI workflow

  1. 1Cost per acceptable completed job, not just the model request or the tokens.
  2. 2Structural cost floor, meaning the costs inherent in the current architecture.
  3. 3Expected volume, because a unit cost without volume is almost meaningless.
  4. 4Value of the output, because cost must be judged against the value created.

A four cent saving on an internal classification task could matter enormously across millions of runs. A four cent saving on high value B2B research may matter far less than preserving the quality of the research.

What people often misunderstand about AI cost optimisation

The biggest misunderstanding is treating optimisation as a race towards the cheapest possible model. Sometimes the model is the problem and sometimes it is not. The useful question is which part of this workflow is expensive without improving the final result. That could be a model, a redundant search, duplicated context, excessive reasoning, a needless intermediate summary, poor retry logic or a human review step caused by unreliable output upstream.

Removing useful intelligence is cost cutting. Removing unnecessary work is optimisation. They are not the same thing.

When cost optimisation may not be worth doing yet

If a workflow runs 200 times per year and costs a few dollars in total, spending days redesigning it to save two cents per run is poor economics. Likewise, if a workflow is still changing dramatically, premature cost engineering may optimise architecture that disappears next week. Prove the job works, measure it, understand the cost, then optimise what survives.

High volume repeatable workflows are different. At 100,000 runs, a one cent reduction is worth $1,000 and a four cent reduction is worth $4,000. Now the engineering conversation changes.

Questions to ask before scaling an AI workflow

  • What does one acceptable completed job cost?
  • Which part of that cost comes from models, and which from tools, search, APIs or retrieval?
  • What is the unavoidable cost floor?
  • What percentage of runs produce acceptable outputs, and what happens when something fails?
  • Can the workflow retry indefinitely?
  • Is repeated information being fetched or processed more than once?
  • Could simpler steps use cheaper models or deterministic code?
  • How much quality can change before the optimisation stops being worthwhile?
  • What is the expected monthly or annual volume, and what is a successful output worth commercially?

If those answers are unknown, Run All is still partly a guess.

How should businesses think about value, not just API price?

An AI workflow is economically useful when the value of the work it produces comfortably exceeds the cost of producing and operating it. Model pricing makes it easy to become obsessed with decimal places. If high quality research costs twelve cents and materially improves a high value sales process, twelve cents may be excellent economics. If a workflow performs a low value task ten million times, twelve cents may be completely unacceptable.

The lesson from twelve cents

The important thing we learned was not that our workflow costs $0.12. That number will change. Models change, pricing changes and the architecture will change. The more useful lesson is how we now think about scaling: we test before we multiply, we establish what good output looks like, we measure where the money is actually going, then we optimise the system without quietly removing the things that made it useful.

An AI demo only has to work. A production AI system has to work repeatedly, economically and at the quality the business actually needs. That is how we approach the systems we build with clients at Soluma: start with the business problem, test the workflow under real conditions, measure the economics, then improve the architecture before volume magnifies every unnecessary decision.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good cost per run for AI automation?

There is no universal good cost per run. A useful target depends on task complexity, volume, success rate and the value of the finished output. The correct comparison is between cost and business value, not between your workflow and an arbitrary industry average.

How do I calculate the real cost of an AI workflow?

Add model token costs, tool and search fees, external APIs, retrieval, retries, failed runs and other operating resources, then divide total spend by the number of acceptable completed outputs. This gives a more useful figure than model cost alone.

Are web search calls charged separately from model tokens?

Yes, for OpenAI's current web search tool. OpenAI lists web search at $10 per 1,000 calls, with search content tokens additionally billed at the selected model rates.

Is using a cheaper AI model always the best way to reduce cost?

No. A cheaper model helps only if it maintains the required quality and reliability. Workflow architecture, duplicate calls, unnecessary retrieval, retries and excessive context can sometimes offer better savings without weakening the result.

When should I start optimising AI costs?

Start measuring costs during testing, but make major optimisation decisions after you have a reliable quality baseline. Otherwise you risk reducing cost without knowing whether you also reduced the value of the output.

How do I stop an AI automation from creating a surprise bill?

Set clear run limits, budget thresholds, stopping conditions, retry limits and cost monitoring before allowing large autonomous queues. Forecast expected spend by multiplying eligible volume by measured cost per acceptable completed task.

What is the difference between cost per run and cost per completed task?

Cost per run measures one execution attempt. Cost per completed task measures what you actually spent to obtain a usable result after accounting for failures, rejected outputs and retries. For business decisions, the second number is usually more useful.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Form Guided Exploration
description:
arXiv:2611.07066v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Discovering cooperative behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is challenging due to the combinatorial complexity of joint state-action spaces, which hinders the emergence of coordinated behaviors from trial-and-error alone. Intrinsic rewards are often used to aid discovery, but naively combining them with team objectives can distort the learning signal, compromising task performance. In this paper, we propose EFXPLORER, a constrained exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance. We solve the resulting problem using an epigraph reformulation that introduces adaptive exploration budgets. This approach separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility. To further encourage diverse and temporally extended exploration, we incorporate a successor distance-based intrinsic reward that captures long-horizon dependencies. Empirically, our method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across SMAX, VMAS, and MPE benchmark suites.

title: Remotion alternatives: what to use instead, depending on why you're leaving
description:
People search for a Remotion alternative for four different reasons, and the right answer changes with each one. Here are the real options, with repo facts and license terms checked on 3 November 2026.

Disclosure first: I build ReelMint, and ReelMint is built on Remotion. Our render pipeline is Remotion underneath, so I am not selling you a way out of it. What I can offer is a map of why people look for a Remotion alternative and what exists for each reason, including the cases where the honest answer is a different tool, or Remotion itself.

Everything with a date below was checked on 3 November 2026 against the live repository, license page or pricing page. Where I could not check something, I say so. For the Python and math side of this question, I won't repeat myself: see Remotion vs Manim and the Manim alternatives roundup.

Why people look for a Remotion alternative

Four reasons cover nearly every case I have seen, and they point to different tools:

  • License. Remotion is free for some users and paid for others, and a company that grows past the free tier needs a plan.
  • No React. Remotion videos are React components. If your team writes Python, Go or plain TypeScript, that is a tax on every video.
  • Need a GUI. You want to drag a clip, fix a typo in a title and re-export, without opening a code editor.
  • Need an agent or an API. You want Claude Code, Cursor or a backend job to produce videos, ideally without owning a render farm.

Speed and render cost sometimes make a fifth reason. I have not benchmarked any of these tools against each other, so I won't rank them on it. Measure on your own hardware with your own scene.

Is Remotion free for commercial use?

Often yes, not always. As of 3 November 2026, the LICENSE.md in the Remotion repository says you are eligible for the free license if you are "an individual", "a for-profit organization with up to 3 employees", "a non-profit or not-for-profit organization", or "evaluating whether Remotion is a good fit, and are not yet using it in a commercial way". It adds that "a company license is required for for-profit organizations of a certain size".

Remotion's own pricing page, read the same day, words it as "individuals and companies up to three people" for free, and a Company License for "collaborations and companies of 4+ people". It lists two paid tracks: Remotion for Creators at $25 per month per seat, and Remotion for Automators at $0.01 per render with a $100 per month minimum. The LICENSE.md also says the license will change slightly in Remotion 5.0. Read the current terms at remotion.dev/docs/license before you commit a team. I am not a lawyer, and this is a pointer, not advice.

Remotion alternatives by reason

If the problem is the license: a Remotion open source alternative

Two code-first tools are MIT licensed. Motion Canvas is a TypeScript animation tool with a browser editor for previewing and syncing to audio. We compared Motion Canvas with Remotion head-to-head. On 3 November 2026 the motion-canvas/motion-canvas repository showed 19.6k stars, an MIT license, was not archived, and its latest commit was 2 July 2026. Revideo describes itself as a rendering engine for creating videos in code, with a headless render API and a React player for previews. Its repository (now at midrender/revideo) showed 4.2k stars, an MIT license, and a latest commit on 15 July 2026.

Both use a generator-function style: you write scenes as TypeScript that yields animations in order, instead of React components keyed to a frame number. That is a different mental model, not a drop-in replacement. Porting a large Remotion project means rewriting it, so this route suits new projects more than migrations. Commit dates are not a health report. Check each project's open issues before building a business on it.

A different way to read the license problem: for a lot of teams, paying is fine. Remotion's terms exist to fund the project, and the paid tracks above are priced per seat or per render. Compare that against the engineering cost of switching before you assume free is cheaper.

What is the best Remotion alternative that doesn't need React?

It depends on what you are making. For TypeScript without React, Motion Canvas and Revideo are the closest code-first options. For a declarative, no-code-framework approach, Editly assembles a video from a JSON5 spec or a small JavaScript API on top of ffmpeg. Its repository showed 5.6k stars, an MIT license and a latest commit on 12 May 2025, so it is stable rather than fast-moving. For Python and math content, Manim, covered in the posts linked above.

If you want no framework at all, scripting ffmpeg directly is always available. It handles cuts, overlays, subtitles and concatenation well, and it gets painful the moment you want animated layout, because ffmpeg has no layout engine.

If you need a GUI: timeline editors and template APIs

Code-first tools make a poor fit when a non-developer must edit the result. There are two honest families. The first is template-based video APIs such as JSON2Video and Creatomate: you design a template, then fill it with data over an API. JSON2Video's pricing page listed, on 3 November 2026, a $49.95 one-time pack of 7,200 credits described as up to 120 minutes of rendered video, and a free entry tier of 600 credits. Creatomate listed a monthly Essential plan with 2,000 credits and a 50-credit trial. I did not read the full fine print of either, so confirm what a credit buys for your resolution before you budget.

The second family is After Effects with Lottie export. Lottie is a playback format for vector animation, not a general video renderer, so it fits UI motion and small loops, not a 60-second narrated explainer. The airbnb/lottie-web player showed 32.3k stars and an MIT license on 3 November 2026. Theatre.js (Apache-2.0, 12.8k stars) is a motion design editor for the web rather than a video encoder, and its latest commit was 14 August 2024, so treat it as a tool for animating in the browser, not an off-the-shelf video pipeline.

If you need an agent or an API: keep Remotion, change who drives it

Here the answer is often not to leave Remotion at all. Remotion's docs have a page on prompting videos with coding agents, naming Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code and OpenCode, with an install step of npx remotion skills add. A coding agent can write Remotion compositions today.

What an agent loop still lacks is a persistent project: scenes you can read back, patch one at a time, preview and re-render without regenerating the whole file. That is the gap ReelMint fills. It keeps Remotion rendering underneath, exposes 130+ MCP tools at https://studio.reelmint.io/api/mcp that Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Cursor can drive, and keeps every generated scene editable in a visual editor. It runs on your own provider keys (BYOK) and has a free tier. If you want the wiring, see connecting Claude Code to a video pipeline and what MCP video generation is.

Comparison list: language, license, last commit, output

All figures from GitHub's API and each project's own pages on 3 November 2026. "Last commit" is the repository's most recent push date.

  • Remotion: TypeScript and React. Source-available with a company license above the free tier (terms above). 70.3k stars, latest commit 3 Nov 2026. Output: video and images, any dimensions.
  • Motion Canvas: TypeScript, generator scenes. MIT. 19.6k stars, latest commit 2 Jul 2026. Output: video through its editor and render pipeline.
  • Revideo: TypeScript, generator scenes, headless render API. MIT. 4.2k stars, latest commit 15 Jul 2026.
  • Editly: JSON5 or JavaScript on ffmpeg. MIT. 5.6k stars, latest commit 12 May 2025. Output: video or GIF at any dimensions, including 9:16.
  • Manim Community: Python. MIT. 42.2k stars, latest commit 2 Nov 2026. Output: landscape by default, math-focused.
  • Theatre.js: TypeScript, in-browser editor. Apache-2.0. 12.8k stars, latest commit 14 Aug 2024. A motion editor, not a video encoder.
  • JSON2Video and Creatomate: hosted template APIs, usage-priced, closed source.
  • ReelMint: MCP server and visual editor on a Remotion render pipeline. Free tier, BYOK. YouTube Shorts publishing is available; Instagram Reels publishing is pending Meta App Review.

Which Remotion alternative is right for you?

  • License is the blocker and you write TypeScript: try Motion Canvas or Revideo on a small project before committing.
  • You do not want React and you assemble clips: Editly, or ffmpeg directly.
  • Non-developers need to edit the output: a template API, or a tool with a visual editor.
  • You want vector UI motion rather than video: Lottie.
  • You want an AI agent to produce vertical Shorts you can still edit: ReelMint, or Remotion plus a coding agent if you are happy owning the React project.
  • Your content is math: Manim, per the posts linked at the top.

Can an AI agent drive Remotion?

Yes. Remotion documents the workflow itself, and I covered a hands-on version in Claude Code and Remotion for motion graphics. The limit is not whether the agent can write the code but whether the result stays maintainable: a one-shot generated composition is hard to patch scene by scene. A persistent, tool-driven project helps there, which is the job of an MCP server rather than a prompt.

When Remotion is still the right call

Stay on Remotion if you already write React, your team is within the free license or happy with the paid one, and you want full frame-level control. It has the largest community of the code-first tools above by star count, and its latest commit was the day I wrote this. Nothing on the alternatives list gives you its component model and web ecosystem together. And if you only want a finished Short, with no code ownership, ReelMint is the wrong pick for some people: a template API or an editor-first tool will get a non-technical user there with less setup. Our fit is developers who want an agent in the loop and an editable result. Start from the code explainer Shorts maker or the pricing page and judge for yourself.

Originally published on reelmint.io.

title: Coverage Hides Churn: Auditing and Preserving Conformal Decisions as VLM Label Registries Grow
description:
arXiv:2611.07502v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language classifiers can learn new labels from text alone, so the label lists they serve keep growing. We show that this growth silently changes conformal decisions about old labels. Common softmax-based conformal scores compare each label with an average over all labels; adding labels changes that average, and with it the score of every old label, even when the model, the image, and the old calibration data stay the same. Recalibrating after the update keeps the coverage guarantee, yet across eleven settings it changes at least one old decision on 53-90% of new images. Coverage cannot reveal this, because it checks only the true label: in five controlled settings that keep the old calibration, so that only the normalizer changes, old-class coverage moves by at most 0.01 while 60-67% of images change. We propose a lifecycle audit that measures these changes alongside coverage and set size, and a simple fix, PrefixCP: each class keeps the label registry that existed when it was added. Its old decisions then never change, each class keeps exact class-conditional coverage under exchangeability, and one prefix scan computes all historical normalizers at once. PrefixCP recovers 40.9-58.5% of the set-size gap between never updating the reference and recalibrating, which gives smaller sets but changes old decisions.

title: A button on the lock screen must not open a chat: an unlock trampoline on Android
description:
QuickDial puts a small chat button next to a normal phone call, so you can jump from the call to a chat with that number without saving it. Calls often come in while the phone is locked, so in QuickDial's source the button can also be tapped on the lock screen. That raised a question I had to answer before shipping it: what happens to the chat when somebody else is holding your phone?

The answer had to be "nothing opens until the phone is unlocked". This post is about the small, invisible activity that enforces that.

Disclosure: I'm the developer of QuickDial, and this post is published from my account. It was written and published by an AI agent working on my behalf. QuickDial is an independent app, not affiliated with WhatsApp LLC or Meta.

The risk

A chat screen shows message history, names, photos and documents. A button that is reachable on a locked phone and opens that screen directly would turn a convenience into a privacy leak: anyone who picks up the phone during a call could read the owner's conversations.

So the rule is simple to state:

  • The button may be visible on the lock screen.
  • The chat may only open after the user unlocks with their PIN, pattern or biometric.
  • If the unlock is cancelled or fails, nothing opens. Not the chat, not the app, not a half-loaded screen.

Decide at the call site

The service that handles the tap checks the keyguard first. If the phone is unlocked, the chat intent starts as usual. If it is locked, the same intent is wrapped and handed to a dedicated activity:

private fun startBehindUnlock(next: Intent) {
    val keyguard = getSystemService(Context.KEYGUARD_SERVICE) as KeyguardManager
    startActivity(
        if (keyguard.isKeyguardLocked) {
            UnlockThenOpenActivity.wrap(this, next)
        } else {
            next.addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK)
        },
    )
}

Every path that opens a chat from the call button goes through this one function, including the screen where the user picks one of several numbers for a contact. One choke point means one place to get right.

The trampoline

UnlockThenOpenActivity has no layout of its own. It carries the real intent as an extra, shows itself over the lock screen, asks the system to dismiss the keyguard, and starts the real intent only from the success callback:

class UnlockThenOpenActivity : Activity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        val next = nextIntent(intent) ?: run { finish(); return }

        val keyguard = getSystemService(Context.KEYGUARD_SERVICE) as KeyguardManager
        if (!keyguard.isKeyguardLocked) { launch(next); return }

        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.O_MR1) setShowWhenLocked(true)
        keyguard.requestDismissKeyguard(this, object : KeyguardManager.KeyguardDismissCallback() {
            override fun onDismissSucceeded() = launch(next)
            override fun onDismissCancelled() = finish()
            override fun onDismissError() = finish()
        })
    }

    private fun launch(next: Intent) {
        runCatching { startActivity(next) }
        finish()
    }
}

A few details carry the weight here:

The real intent is started in exactly one place. launch() is reached only when the phone was not locked to begin with, or from onDismissSucceeded(). Cancelled and error both call finish() and nothing else. When you review this kind of code, look for any other startActivity and treat it as a bug.

It re-checks the lock. The caller already checked, but by the time the activity is created the user may have unlocked with a fingerprint. Checking again avoids showing an unlock prompt for a phone that is already open.

requestDismissKeyguard lets the system own the unlock. The app never sees the PIN or the biometric. It shows the standard prompt, and the callback reports the result. Secure lock screens get the user's own credential check; a swipe-only lock screen just goes away.

It finishes on every path. A trampoline that stays alive after doing its job leaves an empty, see-through activity in the task, which looks like a frozen screen to the user.

The manifest entry matters as much as the code 

<activity
    android:name=".ui.unlock.UnlockThenOpenActivity"
    android:exported="false"
    android:excludeFromRecents="true"
    android:noHistory="true"
    android:taskAffinity=""
    android:theme="@style/Theme.QuickDialCallBridge.Chooser" />
  • exported="false": no other app can send an intent to it and use it as a way to open arbitrary intents over the lock screen. This is the most important line in the file. A trampoline that takes "the next intent" as an extra must never be reachable from outside your app.
  • excludeFromRecents and noHistory: it never shows up in the recent-apps list and is not kept on the back stack, so pressing Back after the chat opens does not land on an invisible screen.
  • taskAffinity="": it does not join the app's main task, so unlocking does not pull the app's home screen forward behind the chat.
  • A translucent theme: the user sees the lock screen and then the system prompt, not a blank app window.

Reading the wrapped intent

Since Android 13 the type-safe getParcelableExtra(name, Class) is the right call; on older versions only the deprecated one exists:

private fun nextIntent(intent: Intent?): Intent? =
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.TIRAMISU) {
        intent?.getParcelableExtra(EXTRA_NEXT, Intent::class.java)
    } else {
        @Suppress("DEPRECATION")
        intent?.getParcelableExtra(EXTRA_NEXT)
    }

A missing extra finishes the activity at once. "Nothing to open" is a normal outcome, not a crash.

Version notes

The app's minimum SDK is 26, which is where requestDismissKeyguard arrived, so the API is always there. setShowWhenLocked arrived one release later, in 8.1 (API 27). On 8.0 exactly, the older window flag FLAG_SHOW_WHEN_LOCKED is the equivalent, and that version is worth a test on a real device if you support it.

Test it like an attacker would

Things I check by hand on a locked phone:

  1. Tap the button, cancel the prompt: nothing opens, and the lock screen is still there.
  2. Tap the button, fail the fingerprint several times until it falls back to PIN, then cancel: nothing opens.
  3. Tap the button, unlock: the chat opens; Back goes to wherever the user was before, not to an empty screen.
  4. Open Recents afterwards: no blank entry.
  5. Phone already unlocked: no prompt at all, the chat opens straight away.

Takeaways

  • Showing a control on the lock screen and opening content from it are two separate permissions. Grant the first, gate the second.
  • Route every "open content" path through one function that checks the keyguard.
  • Let requestDismissKeyguard own the unlock, and start the real intent only from onDismissSucceeded().
  • A trampoline that forwards an intent must be exported="false".
  • Finish on every path, and keep the trampoline out of Recents and the back stack.

QuickDial is on Google Play as "QuickDial: Direct Chat & Call": https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ashwar.quickdialbridge&utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=2026-w45-unlock. It works with WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business; independent app, not affiliated with WhatsApp LLC or Meta.

title: AraEngage: Interpretable Linguistic Correlates of Engagement in Arabic Facebook News
description:
arXiv:2611.07926v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Engagement features developed for English are routinely applied to Arabic, but unvocalized Arabic changes what a lexical feature measures. We introduce AraEngage, a query-defined sample of 10,000 public Arabic Facebook news posts from 2,451 pages in 57 countries (2023-2024) that pairs engagement counts with interpretable linguistic features. We use it to examine which interpretable Arabic indicators are associated with follower-normalized engagement, and how far those associations can be trusted given publisher context, the definition of engagement, and lexical ambiguity. Religious expressions, message length, sentence length, and lexical density are the leading correlates in a Random Forest model ($R^2$ = 0.38 on a post-level split) interpreted with SHAP. Unlike English news, positive sentiment is associated with higher engagement in this Arabic news sample. Message length shows a length paradox: unadjusted raw engagement is highest for long posts, whereas the model's attributions for follower-normalized engagement favor short posts. A linguistic audit identifies why standard lexicon features are fragile in unvocalized Arabic: imperative lists contain homographs such as the form read as "express!" that is also the frequent preposition "via", hedge lists conflate the possibility marker qad + imperfect ("may") with the emphatic qad + perfect ("has indeed"), and religious lists mix devotional formulas with place names in political news. These are plausible sources of measurement error that may attenuate the near-zero associations of imperatives and hedges. All findings are observational associations with operationalized indicators. We release the derived linguistic features, engagement counts, refined lexicons, and analysis code; raw posts are not redistributed, in line with CrowdTangle terms.

title: Pourquoi du et le Finder affichent des tailles de dossier différentes
description:
Lancez du -sh sur un dossier et comparez avec la taille affichée par le Finder : les deux valeurs divergent souvent, parfois de plusieurs gigaoctets. Aucune des deux n'est fausse. Elles répondent à des questions différentes : quelle est la longueur des fichiers, et quelle place ils occupent sur le disque. Quand le disque est plein, seule la seconde compte, et la calculer correctement demande plus que d'additionner st_size.

Les règles ci-dessous sont celles que suit l'écran Disk de l'application de bureau osFoundry. Son scanner est une courte fonction Rust au-dessus de std::fs, et la même logique tient en une quarantaine de lignes de Python. Tous les chiffres viennent d'un dossier de test sur un volume APFS avec des blocs d'allocation de 4 Ko.

Compter les blocs, pas les octets

st_size est la longueur du fichier. st_blocks est le nombre d'unités de 512 octets que le système de fichiers lui a allouées, quelle que soit la taille de bloc réelle du volume. Le scanner de l'application utilise par défaut la seconde :

fn allocated_bytes(meta: &fs::Metadata, apparent: bool) -> u64 {
    if apparent {
        return meta.len();
    }
    #[cfg(unix)]
    {
        use std::os::unix::fs::MetadataExt;
        meta.blocks().saturating_mul(512)
    }
    #[cfg(not(unix))]
    {
        meta.len()
    }
}

Trois fichiers du dossier de test montrent pourquoi :

Fichier st_size st_blocks × 512
small.txt (2 octets de texte) 2 4,096
sparse.img (tronqué à 1 Gio, jamais écrit) 1,073,741,824 0
big.bin (200 Mio de données) 209,715,200 209,715,200

Un tout petit fichier occupe quand même un bloc entier : un dossier de 100 000 petits fichiers pèse donc plusieurs centaines de mégaoctets de plus sur le disque que son nombre d'octets. Un fichier creux (sparse) est l'inverse : disques de machines virtuelles, fichiers de bases de données et certains téléchargements réservent une grande longueur et n'utilisent des blocs que pour les parties écrites. Le du de macOS compte les blocs ; du -A affiche la taille apparente. La case Apparent size de l'application fait la même bascule.

Ne pas suivre les liens, ne pas quitter le volume

Un scanner qui suit les liens symboliques peut compter deux fois le même dossier, ou tourner indéfiniment sur un lien qui pointe vers son propre parent. Celui qui entre dans un disque monté ajoute les fichiers d'un autre disque au total de celui-ci. L'application lit chaque entrée avec symlink_metadata, qui décrit le lien et non sa cible, et compare les identifiants de périphérique avec ceux du dossier de départ du scan :

if child_meta.file_type().is_symlink() || !same_device(root_meta, &child_meta) {
    continue;
}

same_device compare st_dev, ce qui est la même vérification que du -x ou find -xdev.

Liens physiques et clones

Les liens physiques (hard links) sont un seul fichier avec plusieurs noms. Dans le dossier de test, ln big.bin hard.bin fait afficher à ls -l deux fichiers de 200 Mio, mais du ne compte les données qu'une fois, car il mémorise chaque paire (st_dev, st_ino) déjà vue dès que st_nlink dépasse 1. Tout scanner qui additionne des blocs devrait faire de même. Les sauvegardes Time Machine sur disques HFS+ et certains gestionnaires de paquets s'appuient beaucoup sur les liens physiques.

Les clones APFS sont plus délicats. cp -c big.bin clone.bin (ou Dupliquer dans le Finder) crée un second fichier qui partage les blocs de l'original jusqu'à ce que l'un des deux change. Chaque fichier a son propre inode, son propre st_blocks et un compteur de liens égal à 1, donc du compte 400 Mio pour la paire. Mesuré avec df avant et après, le clone a consommé 0 Ko d'espace libre, alors qu'un cp normal du même fichier en a consommé 204 984 Ko. Aucun champ POSIX n'indique ce partage : un total fondé sur les blocs surestime donc ce que libère la suppression d'un clone. Pour des dossiers pleins de projets dupliqués ou de photothèques, comparer df avant et après est la seule vérification fiable.

Une version Python

Les mêmes règles, avec la seule bibliothèque standard :

import os
import stat
import sys

def usage(root):
    root_dev = os.lstat(root).st_dev
    seen = set()
    allocated = apparent = 0
    skipped = 0
    stack = [root]
    while stack:
        path = stack.pop()
        try:
            entries = list(os.scandir(path))
        except OSError:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        for e in entries:
            try:
                st = e.stat(follow_symlinks=False)
            except OSError:
                skipped += 1
                continue
            if stat.S_ISLNK(st.st_mode) or st.st_dev != root_dev:
                continue
            if stat.S_ISDIR(st.st_mode):
                stack.append(e.path)
                continue
            if st.st_nlink > 1:
                key = (st.st_dev, st.st_ino)
                if key in seen:
                    continue
                seen.add(key)
            allocated += st.st_blocks * 512
            apparent += st.st_size
    return allocated, apparent, skipped

if __name__ == "__main__":
    alloc, appar, skipped = usage(sys.argv[1])
    print(f"on disk  {alloc / 2**30:8.2f} GiB")
    print(f"apparent {appar / 2**30:8.2f} GiB")
    if skipped:
        print(f"skipped  {skipped} unreadable entries")

Sur le dossier de test, le script affiche 0,39 Gio sur le disque et 1,39 Gio en taille apparente, ce qui correspond à du -sk (409 604 Ko) et à du -sAk. Sur une arborescence de sources de 14 Gio, il concorde avec du -sk à deux décimales près. Gardez le compte des entrées ignorées : sur macOS, les dossiers protégés par les autorisations de confidentialité (Mail, Messages, Safari) sont illisibles sans l'accès complet au disque, et un total qui les omet en silence paraît plus complet qu'il ne l'est.

L'application garde le résultat assez petit pour être dessiné. Chaque dossier conserve ses 36 plus gros enfants et le reste est additionné dans un seul nœud « Other items » ; ouvrir un dossier node_modules de mille paquets affiche donc 36 cases et une de plus pour tout le reste, pas mille fragments.

Supprimer sans risque

Le vrai risque d'un outil de disque se trouve à l'étape de suppression. L'application déplace les éléments vers la corbeille du système avec le crate trash plutôt que de les supprimer par unlink, et vérifie chaque chemin avant de déplacer quoi que ce soit :

if !target.starts_with(&root) || target == root || home.as_ref() == Some(&target) {
    return Err("Cannot move a scan root or home folder to Trash".into());
}
if mount_points
    .iter()
    .any(|mount| target == *mount || target.parent() == Some(mount.as_path()))
{
    return Err("Cannot move a volume or its top-level items to Trash".into());
}

Les chemins sont d'abord canonisés, de sorte que .. ou un lien symbolique ne peut pas glisser une cible en dehors du dossier analysé. Une sélection où un dossier coché en contient un autre est aussi refusée : une fois le parent dans la corbeille, le chemin de l'enfant n'existe plus et le lot échouerait à mi-parcours.

L'application de bureau est gratuite sur la page de téléchargement d'osFoundry.

title: Test your prompts like code: a Node.js prompt test sheet for AI students
description:
Most students learning generative AI write a prompt, try it twice and move on. Developers test. Here is a weekend project that turns prompt testing into code: a tiny Node.js script that runs one prompt over a list of test inputs and checks each answer against simple rules.

It doesn't depend on any one AI provider. You plug in whichever API you have access to.

What you will build

  • cases.json: 10 test inputs, each with rules the answer must pass
  • test.mjs: sends each input with your prompt, checks the rules, prints a pass/fail table

Step 1: the test cases 

[
  { "input": "Library closes at 6 pm on Saturday from next week.",
    "mustInclude": ["6 pm", "Saturday"], "maxWords": 25 },
  { "input": "Fee deadline for semester 5 is extended to 20 November.",
    "mustInclude": ["20 November"], "maxWords": 25 }
]

The prompt's job here: summarise a college notice in one short sentence without losing dates and times. Write at least 10 cases, including awkward ones (two dates, Hindi-English mixed text, an empty notice).

Step 2: the checker 

// test.mjs  (Node 18+; .mjs so import and top-level await work)
import fs from "node:fs";

const PROMPT = "Summarise this college notice in one sentence. Keep every date and time exactly as written.";
const cases = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("cases.json", "utf8"));

async function ask(text) {
  // Replace with your provider's API call. It must return the model's reply as a string.
  throw new Error("connect your AI API here");
}

function check(answer, c) {
  const problems = [];
  for (const word of c.mustInclude || []) {
    if (!answer.includes(word)) problems.push(`missing "${word}"`);
  }
  const words = answer.trim().split(/\s+/).length;
  if (c.maxWords && words > c.maxWords) problems.push(`${words} words`);
  return problems;
}

let passed = 0;
for (const c of cases) {
  const answer = await ask(`${PROMPT}\n\nNotice: ${c.input}`);
  const problems = check(answer, c);
  if (problems.length === 0) passed++;
  console.log(problems.length ? "FAIL" : "PASS", "|", c.input.slice(0, 40), "|", problems.join(", "));
}
console.log(`${passed}/${cases.length} passed`);

Keep your API key in an environment variable, never in the file, and never commit it to GitHub.

Step 3: improve the prompt, not the tests

Run it, look at the failures, change one thing in PROMPT, run again. Write down each change and the new score. After three or four rounds you will have a short, honest record like "v1 7/10, v2 9/10 (added 'keep dates exactly')". That record is a far better interview story than "I know ChatGPT".

Ideas to extend it

  • Run each case 3 times, because AI answers vary.
  • Add a mustNotInclude rule to catch made-up details.
  • Save results to a CSV and compare two models.

I put this together for students at Dzimark Training in Mohali, where the AI programmes cover prompt engineering, AI agents and AI-powered full-stack work. If you are in the Tricity and want the structured version, the course outline is on the Dzimark Training AI programmes page.

title: I wanted backups on a VPS I rent, not another Dropbox subscription
description:
Most people need a backup. The usual choices feel bad: a monthly fee to keep files on someone else's computers, "pro" backup software with schedules that are easy to set up wrong, or a USB drive you forget until the day you need it.

I wanted something in the middle — a small always-on computer I rent (a VPS), almost no setup, and defaults that back up the folders I'd miss. That's OpenBackup.

What you get

  • Automatic backups of Documents, Pictures, Videos, Music, Desktop (and folders you add)
  • Only changed pieces of files are uploaded, so daily runs stay light
  • History — restore yesterday's version, or last week's
  • A dashboard in the browser to see devices and download a file or folder as a ZIP
  • An optional desktop app if you prefer buttons over a terminal
  • Optional encryption, so even the server can't read the files (you keep a recovery code)
  • Agents for Windows, macOS and Linux

It does not try to clone your whole OS install. It backs up your files. System folders, trash, caches, node_modules, build output and huge VM images are skipped on purpose.

Android is not ready yet.

Install in four steps

1. Put the server on a VPS (Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 is easiest):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/foisalislambd/openbackup/main/scripts/install-server.sh | sudo sh

It prints a web address like http://YOUR_IP:18200 plus a sign-in email and password. Open that, sign in, change the password. Prefer reading the script first if you don't like piping to sh — it's in the repo at scripts/install-server.sh.

2. Create a connection code in the dashboard under Devices. It looks like ABCD-EFGH-JKLM, works once, expires in 24 hours.

3. Connect each computer

  • Windows: download the desktop installer from Releases
  • Mac / Linux: 
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/foisalislambd/openbackup/main/scripts/install-agent.sh | sh
openbackup connect --server http://YOUR_IP:18200 --code ABCD-EFGH-JKLM

Use HTTPS for real use — the install-server docs cover that.

4. Check

openbackup status
openbackup doctor

Then restore one file while nothing is broken, so you know how when you need it.

Everyday commands (optional)

The background service keeps working without you. Handy when you want control:

openbackup backup
openbackup folders
openbackup folders add ~/Projects
openbackup pause --for 2h
openbackup find "tax return"
openbackup restore --path Documents/report.docx --to .

Encryption 

openbackup encrypt

You'll get a recovery code. Write it down somewhere safe that is not only on that same computer. Lose the code and those encrypted backups can't be opened. There is no "reset password" on the server side — that's the point.

Status and license

Server, agent, dashboard and desktop app work end to end. Current release is v0.2.9. Until 1.0, treat minor versions as able to change the wire protocol — upgrade the server before the agents. MIT. Repo: github.com/foisalislambd/openbackup.

Disk on the VPS matters more than CPU. The README's tip is that many people run this on a roughly €4–6/month plan. prices change; pick a plan with enough disk for your photos and video.

If you try it, I'd like to hear where the defaults were wrong for your machine, and whether the connection-code flow felt clear. Issues and discussions are open on GitHub.

— foisal

title: How do Transformers Perform Low-Level Control In-Context?
description:
arXiv:2611.07291v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One of the remarkable abilities of Transformer-based neural networks is in-context learning. This motivates us to think about "in-context" control. Can we control a system knowing only (1) that it belongs to a particular family of systems and (2) some data on system evolution (provided as the context trajectory) but no specific parameter information? Specifically, we investigate the ability of Transformer-models to perform "in-context" control of unstable, nonlinear dynamical systems, where context consists only of the unforced system dynamics. We leverage a multi-head, GPT-2-style architecture, and we evaluate performance for two classical nonlinear systems -- the cartpole system and the two-link acrobot system, where the system parameters are unknown to the Transformer. We consider a setting where trajectories from an expert controller are available at training time but not at inference time. Here, we identify training techniques that are essential to train Transformers to perform low-level control. Through an analysis over checkpoints, we show that in-context control is possible, and the learned policy performance generally improves as context increases. Furthermore, the Transformer models can generalize to stabilize systems that are out-of-distribution.
