title: Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI
description:
arXiv:2611.07048v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evolution has shaped intelligence for billions of years. Artificial intelligence (AI) now raises a striking possibility: intelligence may begin to direct its own evolution. As AI agents become capable of modifying and evaluating their own behavior, how quickly could they improve, and how can that improvement remain safe? We develop a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed evolution following environmental change. Darwinian evolution relies on natural selection, Lamarckian evolution adds inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution allows agents to generate and evaluate behavioral variants and choose how extensively to search. When learning is sufficiently effective, these mechanisms exhibit progressively faster adaptation. Generating more variants accelerates adaptation, while optimal search effort depends on learning ability, problem difficulty, and experimentation costs. However, an agent's ability to direct its improvement does not ensure that improvements are evaluated against the intended objective. When the evaluation target is misspecified, additional search accelerates convergence toward the wrong behavior, even as measured performance improves. In recursive self-improvement, such errors may persist across generations, posing challenges for AI safety. Independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development. The central challenge is not simply to accelerate the evolution of intelligence, but to preserve humanity's ability to guide its direction, limit its speed, and intervene when necessary.

title: MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.07689v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction.
  We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone.
  We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at https://github.com/J1zz/mcp_hallu.

title: The Citrix XenServer Vulnerability Nobody Can Fully Explain Yet
description:
The Citrix XenServer Vulnerability Nobody Can Fully Explain Yet

The Citrix XenServer vulnerability disclosed November 3, 2026 lets an unauthenticated attacker on the management network compromise the host itself, according to Citrix's own bulletin. What Citrix hasn't published is how. No root-cause analysis, no technical mechanism, no exploit detail, just the outcome and a patch. For a flaw this severe, that gap is as newsworthy as the vulnerability itself.

Jump to the identifier confusion nobody has resolved if you want the strangest part first.

What Citrix Actually Disclosed

Cloud Software Group's bulletin CTX697256, published November 3, 2026, covers nine CVEs across XenServer 8.4 and XenServer 9. The headline issue, according to GBHackers' reporting, is CVE-2026-98432: "an unauthenticated attacker on the management network may compromise the host and/or any running Workload Balancing (WLB) or Conversion Manager appliances." A second flaw, CVE-2026-102703, may let a privileged user inside a guest virtual machine compromise the host, the exact boundary virtualization exists to hold.

Cyberpress's analysis is careful to separate the two by precondition: CVE-2026-98432 requires only management-network reachability and no credentials at all, while CVE-2026-102703 requires an attacker who already has elevated access inside a guest. The bulletin, per multiple outlets, "does not map individual identifiers to each outcome," so matching the remaining seven CVEs, which cover PXE network-boot compromise and guest Secure Boot bypass, to specific mechanisms isn't currently possible from public information.

The Identifier Confusion Nobody Has Resolved

Here's where the story gets genuinely strange. GBHackers reports that "CVE-2026-98432 shares the same identifier as a Linux kernel IPv4 TCP use-after-free vulnerability, which has a CVSS score of 9.8," a completely different technical description than Citrix's own management-network compromise narrative. SecurityOnline's advisory independently describes CVE-2026-98432 as "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," the Linux kernel description, not Citrix's.

Citrix itself has not indicated whether the two descriptions refer to the same underlying bug or are simply colliding identifiers, and GBHackers states plainly that "administrators should not assume a connection." That's an unusually direct editorial caution for a vulnerability disclosure, and it tells you something about how little public technical detail actually exists here: enough trackers are filling the gap with an unrelated CVE's description that distinguishing fact from identifier confusion is itself part of the job right now.

Even the Severity Rating Isn't Settled

Brandefense's patch ranking and GBHackers both note that Citrix rates the bulletin Critical, while Hong Kong's HKCERT rated it only Medium risk, listing denial of service and security restriction bypass as the impacts rather than full host compromise. Two credible sources, reading the same bulletin, arrived at materially different severity assessments. Neither is necessarily wrong; they may be weighting the unauthenticated-but-network-restricted precondition differently. But it means the "how bad is this, really" question doesn't currently have a single answer, only competing ones.

What's Actually Confirmed, Separate From the Noise

Strip out the identifier confusion and the severity disagreement, and the confirmed facts are narrower than the headlines suggest. No outlet, including Citrix's own bulletin, confirms active exploitation or a public proof-of-concept. Mallory's incident tracker states the bulletin "does not confirm active exploitation or identify an associated malware campaign." Exposure to the headline flaw depends specifically on management-network reachability, not unrestricted internet exposure, a meaningful limiting factor that several outlets flag explicitly rather than letting the Critical label stand unqualified.

What This Means for Anyone Running XenServer or Similar Hypervisors

Our verdict: patch now regardless of the unresolved identifier confusion or the severity disagreement, because an unauthenticated path to host compromise, even one gated by management-network access, is not something to wait on while vendors and trackers sort out the details. But don't let a Critical label substitute for understanding your own exposure: if your management network is genuinely isolated from anything an attacker could reach, your actual risk looks very different than the headline score implies.

  • Patch management-plane hosts first, per GBHackers' own recommendation, and update Workload Balancing to 2026.1.1 or later and Conversion Manager to 2026.2.0 if you run either.
  • Audit management-network isolation specifically, since Mallory's tracker is explicit that exposure "depends on management-network reachability, not unrestricted internet access." If that network is flat or reachable from general infrastructure, your real exposure is higher than the precondition suggests.
  • Treat CVE-2026-102703, the guest-to-host flaw, as the one that matters most in multi-tenant or hosting environments, where a guest administrator is, by definition, someone outside your own trust boundary. GBHackers calls this risk "highest in multi-tenant and hosting environments, where guest administrators may not be fully trusted," which is exactly the scenario a hosting provider can't simply patch around with network segmentation alone.

FAQ

What does the Citrix XenServer vulnerability CVE-2026-98432 actually let an attacker do?

According to Citrix's own bulletin, an unauthenticated attacker with access to the management network may be able to compromise a XenServer host, as well as any running Workload Balancing or Conversion Manager appliances. Citrix has not published a technical root-cause analysis or exploit details, and the bulletin does not confirm active exploitation in the wild.

Is CVE-2026-98432 the same vulnerability as a Linux kernel IPv4 bug with the same identifier?

That's unresolved. Some trackers have described CVE-2026-98432 using the technical details of an unrelated Linux kernel IPv4 use-after-free vulnerability that happens to share the same identifier. Citrix has not confirmed whether the two are related, and security researchers have explicitly cautioned against assuming a connection between them.

Does CVE-2026-102703 let a guest virtual machine attacker break out to the host?

Yes, under a specific precondition. Citrix's bulletin states that a privileged user inside a guest virtual machine may be able to compromise the underlying host. This requires the attacker to already hold elevated privileges within the guest; it is not an unauthenticated flaw like CVE-2026-98432, but it directly breaks the isolation boundary virtualization is meant to provide.

What We Checked Before Publishing

We pulled Citrix's own bulletin as reported directly by GBHackers and Cyberpress, cross-referenced the severity disagreement against Brandefense's and HKCERT's independent assessments, and confirmed the CVE identifier confusion across both GBHackers and SecurityOnline's independent advisories. We were not able to find a public technical root-cause explanation from Citrix itself for either headline CVE, and we've reported that absence directly rather than filling the gap with a tracker's unconfirmed description.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud: every Cube runs its own kernel behind a per-cube jailer sandbox, so there's no shared management-network API standing between one customer's VM and every other tenant's host-level access. That doesn't mean a Firecracker-based hypervisor can't have its own version of this bug class.

It means the specific failure mode here, an unauthenticated path from management network to host, and a guest-privileged path from VM to host, is exactly the two directions isolation architecture has to hold against, every time, not just when a CVE forces the question. More debugging stories at debugly.dev.

title: The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Models, and Systems of Record
description:
arXiv:2611.06989v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration harnesses, and systems of record. Finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period. The business question (what did this order, claim, or case cost in AI?) cannot be answered from billing data, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain even as it adds AI token and requester attribution. We formalize this grain mismatch, derive seven requirements, and propose the Two-Ledger Model: a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence; a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time; period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice, and the unexplained residual identifies shadow AI. Costs are reported per order, claim, or outcome with agentic cost metrics. A simulation with known ground truth shows the spine sustaining cost coverage above 99% as trace propagation falls to zero, the reconciliation residual recovering planted unmetered spend within 0.24 percentage points while flagging provider billing errors, and mid-flight gating cutting p99 transaction cost by up to 61% at a 2-4% false-pause rate. We propose the attribution ledger as an invocation-grain FOCUS profile for standardization.

title: TACT-KV: Tri-Axis Cosine Transform for Compressing Volumetric KV Caches in Medical VLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.07593v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) applied to 3D medical scans face a structural memory wall. A single CT or MRI volume produces tens of thousands of vision tokens, and the resulting key-value (KV) cache scales linearly with both batch and context. Existing KV compression methods operate on the cache's feature or token statistics, or apply 1D and 2D transforms, leaving the three-axis spatial structure in the cache unexploited. We propose TACT-KV (Tri-Axis Cosine Transform), a calibration-free KV compression method that exploits strong spatial correlations in visual KV states along all three anatomical axes of 3D scans. This correlation concentrates the KV cache energy under a frequency-domain transform. TACT-KV applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform to the KV cache, allocates a per-layer bit budget across frequency bins via reverse water-filling (more bits to high-energy components), and quantizes each bin with a fixed scalar codebook. We derive a close-form relation: the distortion reduction from adaptive bit allocation is dominated by the spectral concentration of the transformed cache. Across six medical VLMs and two 3D CT benchmarks, TACT-KV achieves the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs in our main comparison. The same advantage reproduces on four general-purpose VLMs evaluated on video tasks, indicating that the benefit of exploiting three-axis structure generalizes beyond medical imaging. At equal high-bandwidth memory (HBM), TACT-KV scales the decoding batch size on a single GPU by up to $8\times$.

title: Sell the same key twice, or take money and deliver nothing: the bug every key store must make impossible
description:
A digital-goods store can fail in exactly two ways that really matter:

  1. It sells the same license key to two people. One of them gets an "already redeemed" error, a refund request and a chargeback.
  2. It takes someone's money and assigns no key at all. That's worse.

At Increddy, a storefront for game and software keys, preventing both is the whole job. Here's the problem as a puzzle. Try solving it before you scroll.

The puzzle

  • A customer pays. Your backend receives order.placed.
  • Your payment provider sends payment.captured.
  • Either event can arrive more than once, because providers retry by design.
  • They don't always arrive in the order you expect.
  • Each order must end up with exactly one key. Not zero. Not two.

What's your design?

The answer most people reach first

"Reserve a key when order.placed fires."

It works in every test you'll write. Then one busy weekend a webhook retries, the handler runs twice, and a customer gets two keys. Or the event never shows up, and they get nothing.

Retries aren't an edge case. They're the normal case. A system that only works when every webhook arrives exactly once works in staging and breaks in production.

The second answer (still wrong)

"Fine, check whether the order already has a key before reserving one."

if (!order.hasKey) {
  assignKey(order)   // two handlers can both get here
}

This is the bug that gets past code review. Two handlers can both run the check, both see "no key", and both write. Check-then-write has a race right in the gap between the check and the write.

What we actually built

One: make the write itself idempotent. Idempotency lives at the data layer, not in an if statement. A second attempt to reserve a key for an order that already has one is a no-op, however many handlers race to do it.

Two: two independent triggers. order.placed is the primary path. payment.captured is a fully independent safety net. Since the write is idempotent, both can fire, both can retry, and the result is still exactly one key.

Three: a sweep for whatever slips through. Some cases fall through both triggers, like a captured payment where no order event ever fires. So a job runs every 15 minutes, finds payments captured more than 5 minutes ago with no key assigned, and fixes them.

That job isn't a patch. Every event-driven system has a tail of cases that need a sweep, not a trigger. It's cheaper to build that in on day one than to find out you need it from a support ticket.

The decision that surprises everyone

There's one more piece, and it runs against every inventory instinct you have: Increddy lets customers buy products that are sold out.

It's on purpose, and why it's the right call for a key store is in the full write-up on our blog.

The rule to steal

Make the state transition idempotent ("this order has a key"), not the event that triggers it. Treat reconciliation as part of the design, not a fix after the first incident.

Want the whole picture? The key engine was one module in a full backend rebuild under a live storefront. Read the Increddy case study on kryeo.com →

We're Kryeo. We build order-fulfillment logic like this as part of our Medusa development work.

title: DelegateEval: Evaluating Platforms for Personal External Service Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.07508v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents that work for an individual over time may also help that individual serve external clients. We define a personal external service agent as an agent authorized and continuously managed by a specific individual to accept client requests, deliver work, and provide ongoing support using that person's knowledge, experience, professional methods, and service boundaries. Such agents could allow individuals to serve more clients with less direct involvement and generate economic value at scale. We propose DelegateEval, a platform-level evaluation framework for agent systems that may combine large language models, reusable skills, protocols such as MCP, and executable tool environments. It covers eight dimensions: ease of creation, service discovery and matching, delivery quality, expertise inheritance, service continuity, learning and improvement, reliability and governance, and efficiency and value. These dimensions assess whether a platform enables people with different backgrounds to turn their expertise into ongoing services that deliver verifiable work, develop capabilities through experience, and remain economically feasible. We present the framework and an experimental design. Complete datasets, executable environments, a unified scoring protocol, and cross-model results remain to be developed and empirically validated.

title: Vercel Daemons is now in public beta
description:
Vercel Daemons is now in public beta, allowing you to run long-running processes that pull and execute work from Vercel Queues, databases, or third-party systems without requiring an HTTP server:

  • Consumers using Vercel Queues poll mode, Celery, BullMQ, RabbitMQ, or Kafka.

  • Temporal or Cadence workers that long-poll their task queues.

  • Self-hosted CI runners for GitHub Actions, GitLab, or CircleCI that poll for jobs without requiring inbound connections.

Daemons run containers on Fluid compute and deploy alongside your app in the same project. Vercel builds your image and maintains the instance count you configure in each region, restarting instances that exit or crash.

Get started by packaging your application and dependencies in a Dockerfile or Containerfile, then adding a daemons entry to one configuration file at your project root. This example uses worker/Dockerfile to run one Celery worker in iad1 (Washington, D.C.):

Set any connection details your worker needs in your project's production environment variables, then deploy to production. Vercel starts the configured instances, and their output appears in your project's Logs. CPU and memory metrics are available with Observability Plus.

Learn more in the Vercel Daemons documentation and read the complete guide.

title: November 03, 2026
description:
API Gateway

Feature

Call Google Cloud APIs from streaming gateways

Streaming gateways can now call Google Cloud APIs such as aiplatform.googleapis.com. A gateway with an effectiveStreamingMode of EFFECTIVE_STREAMING_MODE_ENABLED authenticates to backends whose host ends in .googleapis.com or .vertexai.goog with an access token for the gateway's service account. Other backends still receive an ID token. An existing streaming gateway switches when API Gateway next rolls out a gateway update, or immediately when you update it to a new API config.

For more information, see Securing backend services.

title: A trip to China is 311 trips, not 44,473 — and four of the six line items are constants
description:
I expected the expensive part of building a travel-cost dataset to be the flights. It turned out to be the opposite: the flights were the only part that needed real modelling, because everything else collapsed into a constant.

The table

44,473 priced routes. 88 origin countries. 311 Chinese destinations. Each row itemises six things — flights, accommodation, food, local transport, attractions, fixed costs (visa, insurance, eSIM, card fees) — and the six sum exactly to the stored total.

The first thing I did after loading it was check whether that "exactly" was true:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS bad
FROM cost_routes
WHERE flight_low + hotel_low + food_low + local_low + acts_low + fixed_low <> total_low;
-- 0

Good. The totals are derived, not typed in.

Then the interesting query

I picked Beijing, because it has 143 origin cities — the deepest slice in the set — and asked how many distinct values each line takes:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS routes,
       COUNT(DISTINCT flight_low)  AS flight_values,
       COUNT(DISTINCT hotel_low)   AS hotel_values,
       COUNT(DISTINCT food_low)    AS food_values,
       COUNT(DISTINCT local_low)   AS local_values,
       COUNT(DISTINCT acts_low)    AS acts_values
FROM cost_routes WHERE dest_slug = 'beijing';

routes 143 | flight 126 | hotel 1 | food 1 | local 1 | acts 1

Four of the six take one value. Not a tight range — one integer, shared by a route starting in Seoul and a route starting in Buenos Aires.

Line Distinct values across 143 origins Value
Accommodation, 9 nights 1 $540
Food and drink, 10 days 1 $430
Local transport 1 $120
Attractions and activities 1 $300
Fixed costs 7 $63–$203
Flights 126 $183–$1,117

That is not a coincidence of Beijing. Run the same count grouped by destination:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS destinations,
       SUM(CASE WHEN hv = 1 AND fv = 1 AND lv = 1 AND av = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS all_constant
FROM (
  SELECT dest_slug,
         COUNT(DISTINCT hotel_low) hv,
         COUNT(DISTINCT food_low)  fv,
         COUNT(DISTINCT local_low) lv,
         COUNT(DISTINCT acts_low)  av
  FROM cost_routes GROUP BY dest_slug
);
-- 311 destinations, 311 all_constant

All of them. 311 destinations, and not one has a hotel band that varies by origin.

Why that is the correct model, not a shortcut

It would be easy to read this as laziness — "they just didn't compute per-origin hotel prices". The opposite is true: the on-the-ground cost genuinely belongs to the destination.

Every input to those four lines is a property of the city:

  • Accommodation from the star mix and the depth of compliant supply. A city with few registered hotels has less to choose from, so the room you actually book costs more.
  • Food from restaurant density. A dense market prices lower, a thin one prices higher.
  • Activities from the 5A/4A count, because a 5A ticket is dearer than a 4A one.
  • Local transport from the size of the built-up area.

None of these change because your flight departed from a different continent. Storing them per-route would mean 143 copies of the same six numbers, and 143 chances to drift out of sync.

Where the 39% goes

Averaged across the whole set:

Line Average Share
Flights $602 39%
Accommodation $329 21%
Food $291 19%
Attractions $157 10%
Fixed costs $90 6%
Local transport $82 5%
Total $1,550

The flight is the largest single line and the only one with real spread. On Beijing it runs $183 from Seoul (951 km) to $1,117 from Buenos Aires (19,266 km) — a 6.1× range on one line item, which produces the entire $934 gap between a $1,636 trip and a $2,570 one.

The second variable is your passport

Fixed costs are the only other origin-dependent line, and they take 7 values: $63 for visa-free passports, tiered fees up to $163, and $203 for the United States. An American passport adds $140 against a visa-free one — the second-biggest origin effect in the model, and still under a sixth of the widest flight spread.

What I'd carry to another dataset

The check that paid for itself was asking how many distinct values each field takes after grouping by the entity it should vary within. One value where you expected hundreds tells you the field belongs to a different entity than you assumed. In this case four fields belong to the destination, one to the origin, and one to the passport — three different owners inside what looked like a single flat route table.

The routes are browsable at sinostay — Beijing from Seoul and from Buenos Aires are /cost/145.html and /cost/3313.html.

title: A quick way to compare screen sizes and resolutions side by side
description:
When I'm designing for multiple devices, the part that slows me down most is the boring arithmetic: is a 6.1" phone really smaller than a 6.7" one? How much narrower is a 13" laptop than a 15.6" one? How do pixel densities compare once you stop trusting the "inches" number?

I've been using Screen Size Comparison for this. You pick two devices and it shows their physical dimensions, diagonal, and resolution next to each other, so you can eyeball the difference instead of converting units in your head.

A few things that surprised me:

  • Diagonal inches hide aspect ratio. A 16:9 and a 3:2 panel with the same diagonal have noticeably different width and height, which matters as soon as you're planning layout breakpoints.
  • Bigger diagonal doesn't always mean more pixels. Resolution and PPI are separate numbers; a low-density big screen can look worse than a dense small one.
  • Ratios are easier to reason about than absolute sizes. Once you know that two screens are within a few percent of each other in width, the "which is wider" question mostly goes away.

It's free and needs no account. If you keep a device matrix in your design system, it's a handy reference to link next to it.

What's your usual workflow for picking breakpoints across devices?

title: One Lamport Can Break Consensus: Solana’s Integer Inflation
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

Once an epoch, every Solana validator computes how many lamports of inflation to mint, adds them to the chain’s capitalization, and folds the result into its bank hash. Today that calculation runs in floating point, with a powf in the middle of it.

SIMD-0607, written by engineers from both Anza and Firedancer, replaces every floating-point step with integer arithmetic specified down to the order of its divisions. Agave merged the implementation on 30 October behind a feature gate. We copied the specification’s Rust into a test harness to check its claims and to measure the problem it fixes. Two mathematically identical float formulas for the same reward disagreed by one lamport in 62 of 60,000 epochs. The integer path cannot disagree with itself.

Why one lamport is a consensus failure

Capitalization is part of the state every validator hashes. If two clients compute the same epoch’s reward and land one lamport apart, their capitalizations differ, their bank hashes differ, and the network has a disagreement no vote can fix. The proposal’s motivation is exactly that: these values “must be computed identically by all validator clients, without relying on IEEE-754 behavior or platform math-library functions such as powf.”

Basic float operations are deterministic. Exponentiation is not specified to the last bit, and the inflation rate is 0.08 × (1 − taper)^year. To see how much that matters, we computed the legacy epoch reward two ways that are equal on paper, (1 − taper).powf(year) and exp(year × ln(1 − taper)), for 6,000 epochs in each of five slot-time regimes and both tapers:

Capitalization 10¹⁸ lamports — 62 of 60,000 rewards differ

Capitalization 6.2 × 10¹⁷ lamports — 47 of 60,000 rewards differ

Size of every difference — 1 lamport

About one epoch in a thousand, the truncation that turns a float reward into lamports lands on the other side of an integer. That is not a claim that Agave and Firedancer compute different rewards today. It is the reason neither should depend on how a math library rounds the last bit.

The integer schedule

Rates are integers over RATE_SCALE = 10^15, so 8% is 80_000_000_000_000. Decay factors are integers over 2^64, a finer scale because a factor very close to one is multiplied by itself across hundreds of millions of slots. The per-slot factor is derived, not tabulated: a 32-term series for the logarithm of the taper and a cubic approximation of the exponential, then a binary exponentiation whose order and flooring are fixed:

fn decay_per_slot(ns: u128, taper_num: u32, taper_den: u32) -> Option<u128> {
    // -ln(1 - taper) = ln(taper_den / (taper_den - taper_num)), scaled by 2^64
    let annual_exponent =
        approximate_logarithm(taper_den, taper_den.checked_sub(taper_num)?)?;
    let slot_exponent = annual_exponent.checked_mul(ns)? / YEAR_NS;
    approximate_exponential(slot_exponent) // 2^64 * exp(-x), cubic
}

fn pow_decay_floor(mut base: u128, mut n: u64) -> u128 {
    let mut result = DECAY_SCALE;
    while n > 0 {
        if n & 1 != 0 { result = mul_decay_floor(result, base); }
        n >>= 1;
        if n > 0 { base = mul_decay_floor(base, base); }
    }
    result
}

// rate   = max(TERMINAL_RATE, floor(anchor_rate * decay / 2^64))
// annual = floor(capitalization * rate / 10^15)
// reward = floor(annual * slots_in_epoch * ns_per_slot / YEAR_NS)

Every step floors, every multiplication is checked, and an overflow is an error the validator must turn into a panic. The specification forbids wrapping, saturating or substituting a value, and it forbids falling back to floating point.

Its numbers, reproduced to the lamport

The proposal publishes how far the integer schedule drifts from the floating-point one: the largest difference in a single epoch’s reward over 6,000 epochs, at a capitalization of 10¹⁸ lamports, across the 400, 350, 300, 250 and 200 ms slot regimes. Running its functions verbatim against its stated float baseline:

15% taper, largest difference — 5,923 lamports (spec: 5,923)

30% taper, largest difference — 1,061 lamports (spec: 1,061)

Where the 15% worst case falls — 350 ms, epoch 1,282

Where the 30% worst case falls — 400 ms, epoch 509

32-term logarithm vs 200 terms — identical, both tapers

Both drift figures match exactly. So does the claim that 32 terms of the logarithm series are enough: for the 15% and 30% tapers, the 32-term sum and a 200-term sum are the same integer, to the last of 2⁶⁴ units. The drift is the price of the change, at most a few thousand lamports of an epoch’s reward. A relative difference below 7 × 10⁻¹¹ buys a reward every client computes identically.

Overflow, and why it panics

With 128-bit intermediates, the reward arithmetic stays valid up to a capitalization of about 18.4 trillion SOL, a thousand times beyond the 18.4 billion SOL a 64-bit lamport count can hold at all. The checks that can fail in practice are the invalid inputs: a zero slot duration, or a taper of 100% or more, return an error before any arithmetic.

The panic rule is deliberate. A validator that cannot compute the reward exactly as specified is safer stopped than running on a number the rest of the cluster did not compute. That is the same reasoning as the proposal itself, applied to its own failure path.

The activation order with SIMD-0550

SIMD-0550 doubles the yearly disinflation from 15% to 30%. Its original design kept issuance continuous by recomputing the stored initial rate at activation, initial = anchor / (1 − 0.30)^year, with powf. Our earlier post on SIMD-0550 described that design. An amendment merged on 29 October replaced it: SIMD-0607 must activate first or at the same boundary, the anchor is computed with the integer 15% schedule including its terminal clamp, and the 30% integer taper applies from the activation slot. Agave rekeyed the SIMD-0550 gate in the 4.4.0 release.

Anchor rate, activation at year 6 (illustrative) — 3.0172%

Rate zero slots after activation — 3.0172%

Rate one year later — 2.1120%

Naive governor formula, 0.08 × 0.70⁶ — 1.5% (terminal floor)

The anchor works: at zero elapsed slots the decay factor is exactly 2⁶⁴, so the rate does not move. The trap is for anyone reading the stored governor. After activation it reports initial = 0.08 and taper = 0.30, and the textbook formula built from those two numbers, which measures decay from genesis, lands on the 1.5% floor while the chain is minting at about 3%. Forward curves should start from getInflationRate, not from getInflationGovernor.

Where it stands

Agave’s implementation, #16355, merged on 30 October behind the remove_runtime_float_ops gate. Neither that gate nor SIMD-0550’s has been activated on mainnet. When SIMD-0607 does activate at the boundary into epoch E+1, rewards earned in epoch E are still paid with the legacy calculation, and the integer path starts with rewards earned in E+1.

What this does not show

We ran the specification’s code, not Agave’s implementation of it, and compared against the float baseline the specification states rather than against a running validator. The two float paths in section 01 are a test of sensitivity, not a measurement of any client. The year-6 activation in section 05 is illustrative, at constant 400 ms slots; the real anchor depends on the slot-time history up to the activation slot.

Integer Inflation: Questions People Actually Ask

Why does Solana want to remove floating point from inflation?

Inflation rewards are added to capitalization, which is part of the bank hash. If two validator clients compute an epoch’s reward one lamport apart, their bank hashes differ. Floating-point exponentiation depends on the math library, and mathematically identical float formulas can round to different lamport amounts. SIMD-0607 specifies the whole calculation in integers so every client gets the same number.

How large is the difference between the integer and floating-point schedules?

At most 5,923 lamports per epoch for the 15% taper and 1,061 for the 30% taper, over 6,000 epochs and five slot-time regimes at a capitalization of 10^18 lamports, a relative difference below 7.03 × 10^-11. We reproduced both figures exactly from the specification’s code.

What does SIMD-0607 have to do with SIMD-0550?

SIMD-0550 doubles the disinflation rate from 15% to 30% a year. Since an amendment merged on 29 October 2026, it must activate after or together with SIMD-0607: the anchor rate at activation is computed with the integer 15% schedule, and the 30% integer taper applies from there. The stored inflation governor keeps initial 0.08 and switches taper to 0.30.

Can I compute Solana’s inflation rate from getInflationGovernor?

Not after SIMD-0550 activates. The governor will report initial 0.08 and taper 0.30, but the rate decays from the activation anchor, not from genesis, so initial × (1 − taper)^years gives the wrong answer. Read getInflationRate, which the node computes.

Is SIMD-0607 active on mainnet?

Not as of 30 October 2026. Agave merged the implementation that day behind the remove_runtime_float_ops feature gate, which has not been activated on mainnet.

The one-line version

Floating point lets two correct implementations disagree by a lamport about once in a thousand epochs; SIMD-0607 trades a few thousand lamports of drift per epoch for a reward every client computes identically, and SIMD-0550 now waits for it.

The faster disinflation itself is in Solana’s inflation will decay twice as fast, how those rewards reach stake accounts is in when staking rewards arrive, and why two independent clients matter at all is in which client built each block.

Sources: SIMD-0607 as amended at commit 2934dbeb; the SIMD-0550 amendment; Agave #16355 (commit 9bcf93e368) and #16499. Measurements are from the specification’s functions run in our own harness.

title: Proving What AI Generates: Running Formally Verified Lean 4 Inside Clojure Services
description:
TL;DR:

  • Unit tests only check sample points; formal verification in Lean 4 mathematically guarantees logic for all inputs.
  • The new Ansatz Lean/JVM SDK (org.replikativ/ansatz-lean-jvm:0.2.615) lets you compile Lean into an intermediate artifact (.leanjvm) and interpret it directly on standard OpenJDK 17+ with zero native C/JNI dependencies.
  • This article demonstrates how an AI coding agent can write financial ledger invariants, self-correct via Lean compiler proofs, and deploy proved code into a Clojure service.

Credit & Attribution: This workflow builds on the breakthrough work by the Simmis team introducing the Ansatz Lean/JVM SDK (org.replikativ/ansatz-lean-jvm). The financial settlement walkthrough below illustrates these mechanics applied to autonomous agent engineering.

The LLM Reliability Wall in Production

Every engineering team deploying autonomous AI coding agents eventually runs into the LLM Reliability Wall.

An agent prompted to generate an account transfer or settlement routine writes clean code in seconds. It even produces dozens of passing unit tests. But unit tests only sample finite scenarios. In financial ledgers, the bug that triggers insolvency is never the one tested by a handful of mock transactions—it lurks in the untested corner case where an overdraft limit, a currency conversion edge, and a zero-sum constraint collide.

For decades, formal methods offered the mathematical antidote: prove that code satisfies invariants for all possible inputs using proof assistants like Lean 4. But Lean code was traditionally an island:

  • Native binaries required brittle JNI or Panama bridges.
  • Memory models clashed: Lean frees memory via reference counting, while the JVM uses a garbage collector. Cycles across the boundary leak memory.
  • Deployed servers required the full native Lean toolchain installed.

The release of the Ansatz Lean/JVM SDK (org.replikativ/ansatz-lean-jvm:0.2.615) changes this equation. It provides a pure JVM intermediate-representation (IR) interpreter that runs proved Lean functions directly on stock OpenJDK 17+.

This unlocks an autonomous ground-truth loop: agents synthesize formally verified invariants in Lean, prove them against the Lean compiler, and deploy them directly into production Clojure and Java microservices.

The Architecture: Build-Time Proofs, Run-Time JVM 

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   BUILD & PROOF STAGE                  │
│               (Linux x86-64 / CI / Docker)             │
│                                                        │
│  AI Agent writes:                                      │
│  • Settlement logic                                    │
│  • Invariant theorems (Conservation & Solvency)        │
│                                                        │
│                     ▼                                  │
│         Lean 4.33.1 Toolchain Check                    │
│    [ Fails: Agent self-corrects proof ]                │
│    [ Passes: Proof erased, IR compiled ]               │
│                     ▼                                  │
│            ledger.leanjvm Artifact                     │
│          + SHA-256 Manifest Fingerprint                │
└────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                         │
                         ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   PRODUCTION STAGE                     │
│              (Any OpenJDK 17+ Environment)             │
│                                                        │
│  Clojure / JVM Microservice                            │
│  • Loads ledger.leanjvm into pure Java Interpreter     │
│  • Zero native C / JNI / platform dependencies         │
│  • Managed 100% by JVM Garbage Collector               │
│  • Enforces instruction budgets (default: 2M ops)      │
│  • Exposes bidirectional host callbacks (IO)           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The division of labor is clean:

  1. At build time, native Lean compiles the source, checks the proofs, and strips them away. The compiler packages the intermediate code, types, and layouts into a portable .leanjvm artifact.
  2. At run time, standard Clojure services interpret the intermediate representation. The production container needs no Lean toolchain.

The Domain: A Conservation-of-Value Financial Settlement

Consider an account settlement function. The business requires two non-negotiable invariants:

  1. Solvency: No account may be debited below its configured floor (zero).
  2. Conservation of Value: The total amount debited must equal the total amount credited. No money appears or vanishes.

Let's see how an autonomous agent interacts with this system.

1. The Agent Self-Correction Loop

When an AI agent is instructed to write settlement logic, it often generates subtle bugs. Here is what happens when Lean's type checker acts as the agent's supervisor.

Round 1: The Agent Hallucinates an Edge Case

The agent drafts an initial version in Ledger.lean:

namespace Ledger

def transfer (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) : (Nat × Nat) :=
  -- Naive transfer: subtracts without checking if balance < amount
  (fromBal - amount, toBal + amount)

theorem transfer_conserves_value (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) :
  let (f, t) := transfer fromBal toBal amount
  f + t = fromBal + toBal := by
  unfold transfer
  -- Proof attempt fails when amount > fromBal due to Nat underflow truncation!

In Lean, natural numbers (Nat) truncate subtraction at zero (3 - 5 = 0). Because of this, fromBal - amount breaks conservation of value whenever amount > fromBal!

The Lean compiler rejects the code:

error: unsolved goals
case h
fromBal toBal amount : Nat
⊢ (fromBal - amount) + (toBal + amount) = fromBal + toBal

The agent cannot hallucinate or hand-wave this failure away. The build stops cold.

Round 2: Self-Correction with Machine-Checked Solvency

The agent reads the compiler error, realizes Nat subtraction truncates at zero, and refines the logic to guard the transfer:

namespace Ledger

def settleTransfer (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) : (Nat × Nat) :=
  if amount ≤ fromBal then
    (fromBal - amount, toBal + amount)
  else
    (fromBal, toBal) -- Rejected transfer preserves balances unchanged

/-- Theorem: Transfers strictly conserve total capital. -/
theorem settle_conserves_value (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) :
  let (f, t) := settleTransfer fromBal toBal amount
  f + t = fromBal + toBal := by
  unfold settleTransfer
  split
  · rename_i h
    omega
  · rfl

/-- Theorem: The sender account never drops below zero (solvency guarantee). -/
theorem settle_preserves_solvency (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) :
  let (f, _) := settleTransfer fromBal toBal amount
  f ≤ fromBal := by
  unfold settleTransfer
  split
  · rename_i h
    omega
  · rfl

end Ledger

Both proofs pass. Lean guarantees that no transaction can ever violate solvency or fabricate currency, across all infinite combinations of Nat.

2. Compiling the Verified Artifact

During the CI build (currently supported on Linux x86-64 with prlimit, or via Docker), the agent triggers artifact preparation:

java -cp "$SDK_CLASSPATH" ansatz.lean.jvm.LeanPreparation \
  --source ./ledger \
  --sysroot "$LEAN_SYSROOT" \
  --producer-bundle "$PRODUCER_BUNDLE" \
  --cache "$COMPILER_CACHE" \
  --root-module Ledger \
  --entry Ledger.settleTransfer \
  --output ./ledger.leanjvm

This generates ledger.leanjvm and prints its SHA-256 fingerprint:
sha256:d8a2...3f10

3. Running Inside Clojure at the REPL

In the production service, add the SDK dependency to deps.edn:

{:deps {org.replikativ/ansatz-lean-jvm {:mvn/version "0.2.615"}}}

Load the artifact and invoke the formally proved function directly from the Clojure REPL:

(ns ledger.core
  (:require [ansatz.lean.jvm :as lean]
            [clojure.java.io :as io]))

(defn run-settlement []
  (with-open [runtime (lean/open)
              input   (io/input-stream "ledger.leanjvm")
              project (lean/load-artifact runtime input (System/getenv "EXPECTED_MANIFEST_SHA256"))]
    (let [settle (lean/function project "Ledger.settleTransfer")]
      ;; 1. Valid transfer: $500 from Acc1 ($10,000) to Acc2 ($1,000)
      ;; 2. Overdraft attempt: $15,000 from Acc1 ($10,000) to Acc2 ($1,000)
      {:valid-transfer     (settle 10000 1000 500)
       :overdraft-rejected (settle 10000 1000 15000)})))

;; (run-settlement)
;; => {:valid-transfer     [9500N 1500N]
;;     :overdraft-rejected [10000N 1000N]}

Key runtime observations:

  • Clojure passes standard numbers and receives back persistent vectors containing java.math.BigInteger instances.
  • Zero JNI code or platform native bridges.
  • Memory management is 100% handled by the JVM garbage collector.

4. Inversion of Control: Lean Calling Clojure

Real business operations require dynamic runtime data—like querying fee tiers from a database or configuration file.

Lean declares the external callback:

namespace Ledger

@[extern "ansatz_jvm_account_fee"]
opaque getAccountFee : String → IO Nat

def settleWithFee (fromBal toBal amount : Nat) (tier : String) : IO (Nat × Nat) := do
  let feeRate ← getAccountFee tier
  let fee := (amount * feeRate) / 1000
  let totalDebit := amount + fee
  if totalDebit ≤ fromBal then
    pure (fromBal - totalDebit, toBal + amount)
  else
    pure (fromBal, toBal)

end Ledger

In Clojure, supply the implementation under the declaration's name when loading the artifact:

(def host-bindings
  {"Ledger.getAccountFee"
   {:implementation-id "fees/v1"
    :effect :io
    :fn (fn [tier]
          (case tier
            "vip"      0N     ;; Zero fee
            "standard" 15N    ;; 1.5% fee
            50N))}})          ;; Default 5.0%

(with-open [runtime (lean/open)
              input   (io/input-stream "ledger.leanjvm")
              project (lean/load-artifact runtime input 
                                          (System/getenv "EXPECTED_MANIFEST_SHA256")
                                          host-bindings)]
  ;; IO functions return an IOResult object carrying values or errors
  (let [result (lean/call project "Ledger.settleWithFee" 10000 1000 2000 "standard")]
    (if (.isOk result)
      (.getValue result)
      (throw (ex-info "Lean IO Error" {:cause (.getError result)})))))
;; => [7970N 3000N]  ; Total debit: 2000 + 30 fee = 2030

Mathematical proofs that parameterize over host inputs remain sound, even when values are resolved dynamically by host Clojure code.

5. Architectural Differentiator: Forkable Execution State

Why run Lean through a pure JVM interpreter instead of compiling hot machine code?

The Simmis team highlighted an architectural breakthrough: execution state forkability.

Because Lean's entire execution state (call frames, heap objects, and registers) is stored as standard JVM heap objects, the engine can clone that state mid-computation. Pausing an engine allows branching it into two independent engines that proceed down separate computational paths.

Note: While the core Ansatz engine implements state forking internally today, the public SDK does not expose fork handles yet. It represents groundwork for upcoming releases.

For future AI reasoning pipelines, this capability enables:

  • Counterfactual Branching: An agent pauses a complex financial settlement, branches the execution into two what-if paths (e.g., assessing different liquidity routing strategies), and compares the outcomes.
  • Rollback without Transaction Resets: Discarding a failed branch requires only dropping the cloned JVM object, with zero external database rollback needed.

6. Safety & Operational Guardrails

When executing autonomous agent code in production, defensive constraints are mandatory:

Guardrail Enforcement Mechanism
Infinite Recursion / DOS Invocations run under strict instruction budgets (default: 2,000,000 steps) and wall-clock timeouts (default: 5.0s).
Tampered / Stale Artifacts Artifact loading strictly validates the build-time SHA-256 manifest hash before execution.
Error Isolation Out-of-budget calls fail cleanly with ProjectFailed. The service restarts the engine via project.restart(), discarding corrupted state while preserving verified code handles.
Language Constraints The current release enforces closed, first-order signatures across host boundaries and caps project modules at 128 (beyond Lean's Init).

Conclusion

The conversation around AI coding agents has focused primarily on generating code and generating unit tests. But in high-consequence domains like finance, tests cannot establish absolute correctness.

By uniting Lean 4's proof assistant with the JVM's operational maturity, tools like Ansatz establish a practical verification bridge:

  1. Agents specify and prove invariants rather than guessing implementations.
  2. The compiler enforces ground truth, rejecting flawed edge cases with actionable counter-examples.
  3. The runtime executes natively on standard JVMs, eliminating native operational overhead.

The future of autonomous systems isn't just agents that code faster—it's agents that prove their work before hitting production.

Further Reading

  • Primary Source: Simmis: Lean on the JVM: proved functions for Java and Clojure
  • SDK Artifact: org.replikativ/ansatz-lean-jvm on Clojars
  • Lean 4 Guide: Functional Programming in Lean by David Thrane Christiansen

title: Compression Through a Context Lens: Evaluating Adaptation, Quantization, and Distillation in Arabic Legal LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.07988v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model compression can facilitate the deployment of large language models in resource-constrained legal settings, but its effects on domain-specific performance may depend on the evaluation protocol. We investigate this issue using ArabLegalEval, a Saudi Arabic legal benchmark, under both with-context and no-context evaluation. The former provides supporting legal passages, while the latter assesses performance without external context. Removing the context produces accuracy gaps of up to 27 percentage points for the base model. We examine three stages: domain adaptation, quantization, and knowledge distillation across FANAR-9B, JAIS-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B. Four-bit quantization reduces model memory by 64-71%, with changes in no-context MCQ accuracy ranging from -3.2 to +1.6 percentage points. Distillation produces more variable results, with accuracy generally declining as student size decreases. A Qwen2.5-7B student distilled from FANAR achieves 76.6% no-context accuracy, compared with 77.2% for its teacher. Our findings suggest that no-context evaluation provides a useful complement to context-supported testing when assessing the effects of adaptation and compression on Arabic legal language models.

title: VINO: Revisiting 3D Representation Learning with Volume Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.07176v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised learning has given rise to vision foundation models that learn general-purpose image representations transferable across downstream tasks, yet representation learning for 3D scenes has not achieved comparable success. Motivated by this, we identify key limitations of current 3D representation learning approaches and revisit their core design choices. We first replace the commonly used hierarchical PTv3 backbone with the Volume Transformer, a ViT-like architecture for 3D scenes. We then redesign two core objectives of modern approaches built around student-teacher networks: matching representations across views and predicting masked content from visible context. For the first objective, we separate the roles of teacher and student: the teacher provides clean, consistent targets while the student learns invariance to stronger perturbations. For the second objective, we prevent the student from accessing the masked geometry and instead require it to infer missing representations from visible context only. Finally, we redesign 2D-to-3D knowledge distillation, replacing direct regression of view-dependent image features with view-consistent supervision. Together, these changes form VINO, a framework that learns semantic representations of 3D scenes without labels. VINO substantially improves dense linear probing across indoor and outdoor benchmarks and transfers strongly to out-of-domain settings.

title: Recursive Sparse Attention: Million-Token Length Extrapolation at Logarithmic Cost
description:
arXiv:2611.07232v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: At context lengths of about 1M tokens, dense attention is costly in prefill and decoding, and training typically relies on long documents, which become scarcer as the target length increases. Most sparse attention methods score all preceding blocks or tokens, so their selection cost per query is $O(L)$ at context length $L$; hierarchical selection reduces it to $O(\log L)$, but prior trainable hierarchical methods report accuracy only within their training length. We propose RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), which builds a tree over the KV cache in which each node summarizes its subtree with one key and one mean-pooled value. The keys come from one pooler per layer, shared by all levels and distilled from dense attention. Each level above the tokens selects at most $k$ candidates, so each query has $O(\log L)$ selection cost and reads $O(\log L)$ entries; the summaries of unselected candidates share one softmax with the exact tokens. Each entry's RoPE position is its index among the candidates of its level, so at any length every relative distance stays within the range seen during training. Initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62B tokens at the original model's 32K training length, RecSA outperforms all baselines on RULER at every length from 131K to 2M; at 1M, it scores 60.5, compared with 40.0 for the best baseline, Dense + DCA. With our optimized kernels, RecSA is faster than dense attention in end-to-end prefill and decoding from 64K to 2M; at 524K on one H200 GPU, it accelerates prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x.

title: AI Agents Are Trading Real Money Now — Here Is the Verified Record, Not the Hype
description:
Forget the screenshots. On-chain and venue data from November 2026 shows what AI agents, vaults, and apps actually did with real money — and 17 of 18 advertised claims still can't be checked.

AI agents trading real money is no longer a demo. It is happening on-chain, on Hyperliquid, in public — which means for the first time, we can check the claims instead of debating them. And the verified record, published 2 November 2026 from public chain and venue data, is much more interesting than either the hype or the dismissal.

Here is what it actually shows.

Prediction-market agents: small profit, before costs

Across 312 active AI agents registered on-chain, trading ROI over 90 days was +9.2% — before what they pay for AI predictions. Among agents with enough activity to judge (159 with at least 10 trades), median ROI was +1.6%. The most efficient agents — the 15 making at least $100 per trade — averaged +11.6%, while the least efficient, just 2 agents, averaged −11.5%. Prediction accuracy averaged 60.4%, 10.4 points above chance. On Polymarket, the top AI agents made $1,500–$1,700 in profit over 90 days — enough to show the approach works, not enough to retire on. The best agents were not necessarily the smartest models; they were the ones that traded least often, and wasted least on prediction costs.

AI-labelled vaults: a mixed bag, honestly measured

Of 6 Hyperliquid vaults whose leaders say they are AI-run, 3 beat Bitcoin over the same dates, 2 lost money, and 1 fell more than 30% from a peak. The best stories and the worst drawdowns live in the same table. That is what real trading looks like: not a uniform win, but a spread of outcomes with a real downside. The vaults that survived were not the ones that promised most, but the ones that lost least when they were wrong.

AI trading apps: users mostly lost a little

Across 8 AI trading apps on Hyperliquid, 1,365 users traded $21.0M in 30 days (3 Oct – 1 Nov 2026). In 4 of the 8 apps, users lost money overall, and in most apps fewer than half the users were in profit. The apps are easy to use, the marketing is loud, and the median user still ends the month slightly down. That is the gap between a good demo and a good trade.

AI models with real money: mostly lost

In Nof1's Alpha Arena, where leading models traded real crypto perps, 2 of 6 finished Season 1 with a profit; in Season 1.5, only 5 of 32 accounts did. The best single result was Qwen3 Max at +20.3%; the worst was GPT-5 at −63.4%. And 11.3% of all starting money went to trading fees — 3.7 times the combined profit of the accounts that finished up. Fees are the quiet winner of every AI trading contest.

And the advertised claims?

Of 18 public performance claims checked, 17 had no record anyone else could verify, and 6 were backtests or hypotheticals by the product's own description. A claim without evidence may be true, but it is not a fact. And in trading, the difference between a fact and a story is the difference between a strategy and a sales pitch.

The verdict

The verdict is neither “AI trading works” nor “AI trading is a scam.” It is: some agents make small money, most models lose, fees take a real cut, and nearly every advertised claim is still unverifiable. If the record does not exist, the claim does not either.

That is the same discipline BuildIT Index applies to backtests: recompute from raw data, beat the baselines, survive the folds. The tools change; the standard does not.

If the record does not exist, the claim does not either.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past results do not predict future returns.

title: Run the Fence Before You Ship the Paragraph: An Executable-Example Gate for Model-Drafted Docs
description:
A model may draft the prose of a documentation page, but it may not own the example that proves the prose. That single rule converts doc generation from a trust argument into a build step with an exit code, and it holds even when the drafting model is free, fast, and only loosely supervised. Everything below is a working gate built on that rule: prose is model-draftable, executed code is the evidence, and any example that cannot run becomes a named human's problem.

The failure mode this targets is not bad writing. Documentation pages usually rot at the example rather than the sentence: a flag gets renamed, a response field moves, a command silently starts printing a warning that breaks a copy-paste pipeline. Prose drifts slowly and reads plausibly the whole way down, while a broken fence fails loudly the moment somebody executes it. So the gate asks the cheap, objective question first — does this block still run? — and lets that answer decide how much draft text is allowed to survive.

Step 1: Declare the ownership boundary before drafting

Write the boundary down as a one-line policy, because models follow explicit scopes far more reliably than implicit ones. The model owns sentences that describe behaviour, rationale, and trade-offs; the human owns every fenced example and every sentence whose only support is a failing fence. This split matters because it maps to different verification costs: prose is reviewed by reading, examples are reviewed by executing.

A page therefore has two artifacts with two owners. The prose artifact can be regenerated as often as you like, and the example artifact changes only when a human accepts a new execution result. Keep that distinction visible in your repo layout, so reviewers never have to guess which part of a diff they are approving.

Step 2: Extract and execute every fence

The gate itself is deliberately boring: walk the docs tree, pull out fenced blocks, run the ones that have a runner, and emit a JSON report. Info strings carry control flags, so a block written as `python noexec is parsed but never executed.

`python

!/usr/bin/env python3

"""tools/fence_gate.py - execute every runnable fence under a docs tree."""
from future import annotations

import json
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

RUNNERS = {
"python": (".py", ["python3", "{file}"]),
"py": (".py", ["python3", "{file}"]),
"bash": (".sh", ["bash", "{file}"]),
"sh": (".sh", ["bash", "{file}"]),
"js": (".mjs", ["node", "{file}"]),
"javascript": (".mjs", ["node", "{file}"]),
}

@dataclass
class Fence:
doc: str
line: int
lang: str
flags: list[str]
body: str
status: str = "skipped" # passed | failed | skipped | unowned
detail: str = ""

def parse_fences(doc: Path) -> list[Fence]:
fences: list[Fence] = []
inside, start, info, body = False, 0, "", []
for lineno, line in enumerate(doc.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines(), start=1):
stripped = line.strip()
if not inside and stripped.startswith(""):
inside, start, info, body = True, lineno, stripped[3:].strip(), []
continue
if inside and stripped.startswith(""):
words = info.split()
lang = words[0].lower() if words else ""
fences.append(Fence(str(doc), start, lang, words[1:], "\n".join(body)))
inside = False
continue
if inside:
body.append(line)
return fences

def run_fence(fence: Fence, timeout: int = 20) -> None:
if "noexec" in fence.flags:
fence.status, fence.detail = "unowned", "marked noexec: needs a named owner"
return
runner = RUNNERS.get(fence.lang)
if runner is None:
fence.status, fence.detail = "skipped", f"no runner for {fence.lang!r}"
return
suffix, argv_tpl = runner
exe = shutil.which(argv_tpl[0])
if exe is None:
fence.status, fence.detail = "skipped", f"{argv_tpl[0]} not installed"
return
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
path = Path(tmp) / f"fence{suffix}"
path.write_text(fence.body, encoding="utf-8")
argv = [exe if a == argv_tpl[0] else a.replace("{file}", str(path)) for a in argv_tpl]
try:
proc = subprocess.run(argv, cwd=tmp, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
fence.status, fence.detail = "failed", f"timeout after {timeout}s"
return
fence.status = "passed" if proc.returncode == 0 else "failed"
if proc.returncode != 0:
tail = proc.stderr.strip().splitlines()
fence.detail = tail[-1][:200] if tail else f"exit {proc.returncode}"

def main(root: str, out: str) -> int:
results: list[Fence] = []
for doc in sorted(Path(root).rglob("*.md")):
for fence in parse_fences(doc):
run_fence(fence)
results.append(fence)
Path(out).write_text(json.dumps([f.dict for f in results], indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
bad = [f for f in results if f.status in {"failed", "unowned"}]
for f in bad:
print(f"{f.status:8} {f.doc}:{f.line} [{f.lang}] {f.detail}")
return 1 if bad else 0

if name == "main":
raise SystemExit(main(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "docs",
sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else "fence-report.json"))
`

Run it as python3 tools/fence_gate.py docs fence-report.json. The non-zero exit on failure is the whole point: the gate is a test, not a report you read when convenient. Treat a red gate exactly like a red unit test suite.

Step 3: Turn gate results into a routing decision

Four outcomes are enough to cover real docs, and each one maps to a different owner. Encode the mapping once so nobody relitigates it in review.

Gate result Who owns the paragraph above the fence Ship the draft?
passed Model draft allowed Yes, review as prose
failed Named human in owners.yml No — revert to last shipped text
skipped (no runner installed) Named human in owners.yml Yes, marked unverified in front matter
unowned (noexec) Named human must claim the block No, until claimed

The skipped row is where most teams quietly cheat. A missing language runtime is an environment fact, not a documentation fact, so the honest response is to keep the example, label it unverified, and assign a person — not to delete it and pretend the page is fully checked.

Step 4: Route failures to a name, not a channel

Ownership that lives in a shared inbox is ownership that nobody holds. Keep a small map from doc path to a person, and let the gate generate the work items directly from the JSON report.

`yaml

docs/owners.yml - routing targets for fences the gate cannot clear

"guide/install.md": "@avery"
"guide/webhooks.md": "@ops-docs"
"reference/cli.md": "@avery"
default: "@docs-oncall"
`

`bash
jq -r '.[] | select(.status == "failed" or .status == "unowned")
| "- [ ] `\(.doc):\(.line)` [\(.status)] — \(.detail)"' \
fence-report.json > fence-issues.md
`

That fence-issues.md is the human queue, and it is intentionally short. A page with nine broken examples produces nine checkboxes with file and line numbers, which is a far better review artifact than a paragraph explaining that the docs "may be slightly outdated".

Step 5: Let the free model draft inside the evidence boundary

This is where I actually use MonkeyCode: its free model access handles the prose pass, and the free server option runs the fence sweep on a schedule so drift shows up even when my laptop is closed. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Availability and limits are operator-supplied and change over time, so verify them against the product's current documentation before you build a pipeline around them.

The drafting prompt gets two inputs — the current page and the fence report — and one hard constraint: it may only describe commands, flags, or output shapes that appear in a passed fence. Anything else must be written as an open question addressed to the owner in owners.yml. In practice the model becomes a rewriter of verified material rather than an author of plausible material, and the questions it emits are often the most useful part of the diff.

Schedule the sweep however your environment already schedules jobs, for example 0 6 * * 1 python3 tools/fence_gate.py docs fence-report.json for a Monday morning pass. If you run it on the free server, the command does not change — only the machine that executes it does, which is exactly what you want from a gate.

Limitations and who should skip this

The gate only proves that a block exits zero, never that it demonstrates the right thing; a fence can pass while teaching an obsolete workflow. Examples that need credentials, network access, or destructive side effects will either fail or need a sandbox you maintain, and flaky ones will teach your team to ignore red builds. Languages without a cheap local runner produce skipped rows forever unless somebody writes a runner.

Skip this approach if your docs are mostly conceptual, if you have no CI or scheduled jobs to hang it on, or if nobody is willing to be the name in owners.yml. A gate with no owner is just a slower way to generate unflagged warnings. Start with one high-traffic page, run the gate for two weeks, and only then decide whether the prose pass is worth automating across the tree.

If you try it, the smallest useful version is Step 2 plus a single owner entry — that combination already tells you which half of your documentation is actually verified.
