title: Nodejs Queue Handoff: Publish Durable Alerts So Offline Users Get Notified
description:
Nodejs Queue Handoff: Publish Durable Alerts So Offline Users Get Notified

Short answer: In a Nodejs application, queue the notification before trying to publish it; offline users still get notified because the durable inbox, rather than the live connection, owns delivery.

The important trade-off is simple: presence should be allowed to expire, while a notification should remain durable until the application records that it was delivered or acknowledged. Treating both as the same realtime message is how a shared workspace quietly loses the person who was offline when a comment arrived. Queue the notification as application state first, then attempt the live delivery; the live channel is an optimization, not the record of truth.

I design this boundary around an incident pattern rather than a transport demo. A collaborator edits a document, another collaborator is disconnected for 90 seconds, and the product must still show that mention later. A presence badge that says “online” after the lease expired is stale data. A mention that disappears because a socket was absent is a delivery bug. Those are different failures and deserve different storage and retry rules. In Nodejs, the event loop changes how the worker is scheduled, but it does not change this ownership decision.

That is the boundary.

Keep it boring.

The failure worth designing around is the gap between two acknowledgements. The application commits a notification intent, a worker claims it, and the live transport accepts the envelope. Before the worker can mark the row delivered, its process is restarted, the network path times out, or the connection disappears. On restart, the pending row is visible again. A design that assumes the first acceptance was final either loses the item or sends it twice; a design with a stable notification ID lets the client and server collapse the second attempt into the same user-visible event. This is why the queue record needs an ownership lease, why the consumer needs deduplication, and why “the socket was connected” is not an audit trail. The extra state is operational work, but it is work that can be inspected and repaired.

What should survive the disconnect?

The durable record needs an idempotency key, recipient, event type, a reference to the workspace object, creation time, and a delivery state. It does not need to preserve a socket. The queue worker can read that record after a reconnect, while the presence service can independently observe a heartbeat and replace the badge with “offline” when its lease ends.

That split also makes the user-visible contract honest. “Alex is online” is a current observation with a bounded freshness window. “Alex mentioned you in a document” is an application event with retention and read semantics. A transient connection can carry either signal, but it should not own either meaning.

The first trap is enqueueing only after a publish call succeeds. A broker or websocket gateway can accept a message and the process can still fail before the database transaction that records the notification commits. The opposite ordering has a different cost: a worker may publish twice after a timeout. At-least-once work plus an idempotent consumer is the defensible default here; exactly-once delivery is not a property I would infer from a successful network write.

How should a Nodejs queue publish alerts when users go offline?

The queue-first path gives the application a recoverable fact before it asks a connection to do something best-effort. In a real implementation, the comment transaction and notification intent should be committed together, or an outbox row should be committed in the same transaction. A separate worker claims pending rows, publishes a small envelope, and advances the row only after a defined acknowledgement. If the recipient has no active session, the worker leaves the item pending for inbox retrieval or a later live session.

Here is the critical part of that path in Go. The interfaces are deliberately generic because the contract matters more than a particular queue or realtime product.

package notify

import (
    "context"
    "time"
)

type Notification struct {
    ID        string
    Recipient string
    Workspace string
    Kind      string
    ObjectID  string
    CreatedAt time.Time
}

// Store and LiveTransport are adapters around durable storage and a live channel.
type Store interface {
    ClaimPending(ctx context.Context, limit int) ([]Notification, error)
    MarkDelivered(ctx context.Context, id string, at time.Time) error
    Release(ctx context.Context, id string, reason string) error
}

type LiveTransport interface {
    Publish(ctx context.Context, n Notification) error
}

func DeliverBatch(ctx context.Context, store Store, live LiveTransport, limit int) error {
    items, err := store.ClaimPending(ctx, limit)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    for _, item := range items {
        err := live.Publish(ctx, item)
        if err != nil {
            if releaseErr := store.Release(ctx, item.ID, err.Error()); releaseErr != nil {
                return releaseErr
            }
            continue
        }
        if err := store.MarkDelivered(ctx, item.ID, time.Now().UTC()); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return nil
}

The worker must claim with a lease or equivalent ownership token. Otherwise two workers can process the same row concurrently. The receiver must also deduplicate by ID, because the publish acknowledgement and the delivery-state update are separate operations. A retry after the first succeeds can therefore produce a duplicate attempt, even though the user should see one notification.

This code intentionally does not mark a notification read. Delivery means the application handed the envelope to the live transport or made it available through the inbox contract. Read state belongs to an explicit user action, and it should not be guessed from a websocket acknowledgement.

What does an offline user actually receive?

An offline user needs a second path: on session establishment, fetch the unread durable notifications for that user and workspace, order them by the application timestamp, and then subscribe to new events. The ordering boundary matters. If the initial fetch and subscription are arranged carelessly, an event can land between them and be omitted from the client view. A cursor, sequence number, or transactional snapshot gives the reconnect path a point from which to resume.

Presence does not belong in that backlog. The client can request current presence after authentication and then listen for changes; it should not replay ten-minute-old heartbeats as though they were current. A useful rule is that a presence lease is valid only until its expiry plus a deliberately small clock-skew allowance. The exact interval is a product decision tied to network conditions and the cost of showing stale availability, not a universal constant.

For a shared workspace, I would keep the notification payload narrow: notification ID, workspace ID, event kind, object ID, and a revision or timestamp. The client can fetch authorized details rather than trusting arbitrary text embedded in a broadcast. Authorization is checked again on fetch, because a recipient’s access to a document can change while a notification is waiting.

Which failure should page the on-call engineer?

A dashboard showing “connected clients” is a weak answer. It can be green while the durable backlog grows, or red while every notification is being recovered through inbox reads. I want signals that expose the user contract: age of the oldest pending notification, retry counts by reason, claim lease expirations, duplicate suppression, reconnect fetch latency, and the proportion of live publishes followed by a valid acknowledgement. The alert question is blunt: what page fired, and which user-visible promise is currently at risk?

Keep the incident boundary explicit. A temporary live-channel outage should increase pending age and retries; it should not erase notifications. A storage failure should block creation of the durable intent and may need a higher-severity response because the system no longer knows what it owes. A presence stream failure should degrade the badge to an unknown or stale state rather than manufacture online users.

Testing should exercise the gaps between operations, not just the happy path. Insert failures after the durable write, after claim, after live publish, and before the delivery-state update. Reconnect a client between its initial inbox read and subscription. Send the same notification twice. Revoke workspace access while an item is pending. Those cases reveal whether the design has a recovery contract or merely a successful demo.

Where this advice stops applying

Queue-first delivery is the wrong shape for data that has no value after the connection closes, such as a typing indicator or a rapidly changing cursor. It is also insufficient for urgent external escalation, where a separate policy may require provider-specific acknowledgement, rate limits, and human escalation. For ordinary in-app mentions, task assignments, and review activity, durable intent plus a live hint is a reasonable boundary.

The decision is therefore not “which realtime transport is fastest?” It is “which state must remain true when nobody is connected?” Presence answers: very little, and only for a bounded lease. Notifications answer: enough to reconstruct an unread inbox. Once that distinction is encoded in storage, queue retries, reconnect reads, and observability all become easier to reason about.

Sources

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket

title: $D^2$-OPD: Separating Direction and Distance in Extrapolative On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.07241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model to match a teacher's next-token distributions on student-generated prefixes. Extrapolative OPD further extends the teacher's log-probability shift relative to a reference policy to construct stronger learning targets. However, existing methods couple extrapolation direction and distance, allowing the magnitude of the teacher's shift to dictate how far the target moves. We propose $D^2$-OPD, decoupling these two factors: a per-prefix hard KL constraint bounds the target's distance from the teacher, while an adaptive combination of the teacher's post-training shift and the initial student--teacher gap determines the extrapolation direction. We optimize the student toward this target using forward KL, providing learning signals even for low-probability tokens. We evaluate three settings: where standard OPD performs well, where it struggles with base-model initialization, and where no teacher reference is available. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, $D^2$-OPD attains the highest score in all three settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points. Ablations validate the contributions of each component.

title: From Backtest to Funded Account: The Validation Checklist Prop Traders Need Before Paying
description:
Challenge fees are $200–$1,000+ per attempt, and ~90% of attempts fail. This checklist — run before you pay, not after — is the cheapest money in prop trading.

A prop challenge fee is $200–$1,000+ per attempt, depending on account size. About 90% of attempts fail. That means the average trader pays several fees before ever seeing a funded account — or never does. The cheapest money in prop trading is the validation you run before you pay, not after.

Here is the checklist, in order. Skip a step and you are paying to discover what that step would have told you.

1. Recompute from raw predictions

If your strategy's numbers come from a claimed-accuracy column, a vendor's screenshot, or a backtest you cannot reproduce from raw data, stop. Recompute accuracy from the raw predictions yourself. If the recomputed number is much lower than the claimed one, you just saved a challenge fee.

2. Beat the dumb baselines

Always-bullish and no-change, on the same data. If your model cannot beat both, it adds nothing — it is riding the base rate of up-moves. On a bare CSV with no price history, those two baselines are the honest ones.

3. Check walk-forward folds, not the average

A single overall accuracy hides decay. Demand fold-by-fold results, earliest to latest. A model decaying from 80% to 56% across folds is a dying edge with a flattering average — and it will die faster under challenge pressure.

4. Count the trials and correct for them

How many configurations did you try before this one? If the answer is “hundreds” and no multiple-testing correction was applied, the headline number is partly luck. Apply a Bonferroni-style correction, or at least discount the result honestly.

5. Model costs and slippage

Backtest with realistic spread, slippage, commissions, and taxes. A strategy whose edge survives only at zero friction does not survive.

6. Backtest against the firm's exact rules

Daily drawdown from intraday peaks (5% at FTMO), total drawdown (10%), profit target (10% phase 1, 5% phase 2), minimum trading days. Run the strategy through those constraints historically. If it breaches the daily cap in backtest, it will breach it live — with a fee attached.

7. Size for the worst streak, not the average

Set risk per trade at 0.5–1%, so a normal four-loss streak stays inside the daily cap. Then set a personal daily stop below the firm's cap (stop at 3% down, not 5%).

8. Forward-test on paper first

Two to four weeks of live paper trading under the same rules. Backtesting tells you if a strategy could have worked; forward testing tells you if it actually functions — with real data flow, real fills, and real psychology.

9. Only then, pay

One challenge, sized to the account you can afford to lose the fee on, with the validated strategy and the validated risk parameters.

Most traders do this list backwards: pay first, discover the failures with money. The traders who pass are usually the ones who did the boring work first. Validation is not the opposite of ambition. It is the cheapest form of it.

BuildIT Index runs steps 1–5 mechanically on any prediction file: recompute accuracy, beat baselines, check folds, count trials, model costs, return a verdict with an exit code.

Validation is not the opposite of ambition. It is the cheapest form of it.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past results do not predict future returns.

title: Open source AI shorts generators: the repos worth running in 2026
description:
Most open source AI shorts generators fall into two families: faceless stock-footage pipelines and long-video clippers. Here are five on GitHub with the facts I checked today, what each one does and doesn't do, and where they fall down for code content.

Full disclosure first: I build ReelMint, a closed-source video studio for developers making vertical Shorts, so I have a stake here. This post is for someone who typed "open source ai shorts generator" into a search box and wants to know which repos are real, what they need to run, and whether any of them fit technical content. Stars, licences and last-commit dates below come from the GitHub API on 3 November 2026. Feature details come from each repo's README on the same day. I did not install or benchmark any of them, so I describe what they claim to do, not how well they do it.

What an open source AI shorts generator does (and doesn't)

The category splits into two families, and mixing them up is the most common mistake in search results.

  • Topic to video (faceless pipelines). You give a topic. An LLM writes a script, a TTS engine reads it, stock footage is matched to the sentences, captions are burned in, and an MP4 comes out.
  • Long video to clips. You give a podcast or a YouTube URL. Whisper transcribes it, an LLM picks highlight moments, and the tool crops them to 9:16.

What both families leave to you: editing a finished result, keeping a consistent brand look across videos, and judging whether the content is any good. Most also leave the publishing step half-built, and that last point matters more than it looks (see the YouTube policy section below).

The repos worth running (verified)

All figures below were read from https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo> on 3 November 2026. Star counts move daily, so treat them as a snapshot.

MoneyPrinterTurbo (harry0703/MoneyPrinterTurbo): MIT, Python, about 137,900 stars, last push 2 Nov 2026. It takes a topic or keyword and generates the script, matches stock footage, adds voiceover, subtitles and background music, and renders an HD video. The README lists a web UI and an API, Docker support (docker compose -f docker-compose.release.yml up, UI on port 8501), and LLM options including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and DeepSeek. Edge TTS needs no key; other voice providers need their own. The README says the minimum is 4 CPU cores and 4 GB RAM with no GPU. It lists publishing to TikTok, Instagram and YouTube Shorts as a feature but gives no setup details, so check that part yourself before relying on it.

OpenShorts (mutonby/openshorts): MIT, Python, about 7,400 stars, last push 2 Nov 2026. This is the long-video family: it detects moments, reframes with face tracking, adds subtitles and can dub. It also has an AI actor tool and a title and thumbnail tool. Self-hosting is docker compose up --build, then you enter keys in Settings. The README names Gemini as required for the AI features, fal.ai for the AI actor shorts, ElevenLabs for voice and dubbing, and Upload-Post for social posting (TikTok, Reels, YouTube Shorts). It ships an MCP server, at localhost:8000/mcp when self-hosted. There is also a hosted version; the README lists a free plan of 20 minutes a month with a watermark and paid plans from $12 a month.

ShortGPT (RayVentura/ShortGPT): MIT, Python, about 8,100 stars, last push 10 Feb 2025. The repo describes itself as an experimental framework for YouTube Shorts and TikTok channel automation, covering script, voiceover, footage, captions and rendering. I am not calling it abandoned. I am reporting that the last push was in February 2025, and that the README says documentation is still coming. The README does not list required keys, though it names OpenAI, ElevenLabs and Pexels as technologies used.

AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator (SamurAIGPT/AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator): MIT, Python, about 5,700 stars, last push 3 Nov 2026. It is a long-video clipper pitched as an open source alternative to Opus Clip. Give it a YouTube URL and it uses Whisper, an LLM for highlights, and automatic cropping to produce ranked 9:16 clips. API mode needs a MUAPI_API_KEY; local mode needs an OpenAI or Gemini key plus ffmpeg. The README does not mention uploading to YouTube. It also promotes a hosted per-clip API from the same ecosystem.

MoneyPrinterV2 (FujiwaraChoki/MoneyPrinterV2): AGPL-3.0, Python, about 32,300 stars, last push 15 Sep 2026. It bundles several automations, including a scheduled YouTube Shorts automator, a Twitter bot and affiliate tooling, configured through config.json and requiring Python 3.12. The AGPL licence matters if you plan to run a modified version as a service. I could not confirm the upload credentials it needs from the README.

Comparison list

  • MoneyPrinterTurbo: topic to video, MIT, key for an LLM (Edge TTS free), stock footage, active as of 2 Nov 2026.
  • OpenShorts: long video to clips plus extras, MIT, Gemini required, optional fal.ai, ElevenLabs and Upload-Post keys, has an MCP server, active as of 2 Nov 2026.
  • ShortGPT: topic to video framework, MIT, last push Feb 2025, documentation incomplete.
  • AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator: long video to clips, MIT, one API key (MuAPI, or OpenAI/Gemini in local mode), no upload described.
  • MoneyPrinterV2: multi-automation toolkit, AGPL-3.0, config-file driven, last push 15 Sep 2026.

I also looked for n8n and Make templates that wrap these steps. I did not verify any specific template well enough to list it, so I left them out rather than guess.

Automating YouTube Shorts: what YouTube's policy actually says

Developers asking about "youtube shorts automation" usually worry about getting a channel flagged. The relevant text is YouTube's channel monetization policies page, support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392, which I read on 3 November 2026. A July 2025 update on that page renamed the policy from "repetitious content" to "inauthentic content".

What I took from it, in my own words. Automation and AI are not banned. The page says that if you use automated tools or templates, the final product still has to show your creative vision and give viewers educational or entertainment value. The things it names as a problem are content that looks made from a template, and AI content made with generic or unoriginal templates that gives the impression of mass production. Channels whose videos are interchangeable are described as not eligible to monetize. Note the scope: this is about eligibility for the YouTube Partner Program. Content that breaks the Community Guidelines is a separate matter and can be removed. I found no numeric threshold, such as a maximum number of uploads per day, and I won't invent one.

The practical reading for a pipeline: a script written by an LLM from a bare keyword, stock clips, a default voice and the same layout on every video is the pattern the page describes. A video built from your own repo, your own terminal output and your own explanation is not interchangeable with the next channel's. That is a judgement about the content, which no repo can make for you.

Where open-source pipelines fall down for technical content

The topic-to-video family matches stock footage to sentences. Ask it for a video about a Postgres index and you get b-roll of servers and someone typing, not the query plan. There is no step where a real code snippet, a terminal session or a chart is rendered as the visual. The long-video family has the opposite problem: it needs a long recording to exist already, and it crops talking heads, not syntax-highlighted code that must stay legible at 9:16.

Three more gaps show up for developers specifically. First, editing: when scene four has the wrong variable name, you re-run the pipeline or open the MP4 in a separate editor. Second, consistency: nothing carries a code theme, font or colour palette from one video to the next. Third, accuracy: an LLM writing narration over stock footage has nothing checking that the code on screen is the code being described, because no code is on screen. Our own take on the editing problem is in editable AI Shorts generators, and the content side is in YouTube Shorts for developers.

Where ReelMint fits (and that it isn't open source)

ReelMint is not open source. It is a hosted product; you cannot read or self-host the code. What it is: a Remotion-based render pipeline where every generated scene is editable in a visual editor, with code cards, terminal cards and chart animations as scene types. It is driven by an MCP server that Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Cursor can connect to, with 130+ MCP tools. It is BYOK, meaning you bring your own OpenAI, Anthropic, ElevenLabs and similar keys, and there is a free tier. It publishes to YouTube Shorts. Instagram Reels publishing is pending Meta App Review, so I am not counting it.

On time, the only number I will stand behind: on the MCP path, a 60 to 90 second reel took me 45 to 60 minutes elapsed, of which 10 to 20 minutes were hands-on. That is one person, the person who built it, so a newcomer will be slower.

When ReelMint is not the right pick

  • You need to read or modify the source, or run everything offline on your own hardware. Use MoneyPrinterTurbo or OpenShorts.
  • You have a long recording and want clips from it. Use OpenShorts or AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator. That is not what we do.
  • You want zero-cost faceless channel output from a keyword and do not care about technical accuracy. A stock-footage pipeline is closer to that job.
  • You need a proof or equation animation. That is Manim territory, not ours.

Is there a free open source AI shorts generator?

Yes. MoneyPrinterTurbo, OpenShorts, ShortGPT and AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator are all MIT licensed per the GitHub API on 3 November 2026, and MoneyPrinterV2 is AGPL-3.0. Free to use does not mean free to run: most need at least one LLM key, and some need voice, video or posting keys, billed by those providers.

Can I automate YouTube Shorts with an API?

Partly. OpenShorts documents a REST API and an MCP server, and MoneyPrinterTurbo documents API docs at port 8080 in its Docker setup. Both can generate clips programmatically. Uploading is a separate step handled by YouTube's own APIs or a service like Upload-Post, which OpenShorts uses. I did not test any of these end to end, so verify the upload path before building on it.

Will YouTube penalise auto-generated Shorts?

YouTube's policy page does not ban automation or AI. It says the final video still has to show your creative vision and have educational or entertainment value, and it describes template-made, mass-produced, interchangeable content as ineligible for monetization. It reads as a monetization policy, not a ban on uploading. I found no stated upload-volume threshold.

If your content is technical, the easier route to non-interchangeable videos is to put real code and real output on screen. You can try that with the code explainer Shorts maker on the free tier.

Originally published on reelmint.io.

title: Product photo to video with AI: from 1–10 shop photos to 5-second clips that keep the label (real outputs inside)
description:
Most product pages on Shopify or Etsy still have only photos. A 5-second clip of the product spinning, splashing or being worn shows the back, the scale and the finish better than another still, and you no longer need a shoot to make one. This post walks through how we turn product photos into short clips in RefVid: what kind of AI model keeps the label intact, which photos to give it, which shots to make first, and how to write the prompt. Every image below is a frame from a real output, next to the photos it came from. The full guide, with every template and the current prices, is on our product photo to video page.


A frame from a 5-second clip made from one side-view photo of AERO 1, an invented running shoe, on Kling 4. Prompt: "the shoe on a wet rock by a mountain stream at sunrise, the camera moving slowly along it". Not edited.

Image-to-video vs reference-to-video

There are two ways to turn a product photo into a video, and the difference decides whether your label survives.

  • Image-to-video animates the photo itself as the first frame. Once the camera moves away from that frame, the model has to invent the product, so it drifts: the logo warps, the stitching changes, the colour shifts.
  • Reference-to-video treats your photos as a description of the product and builds every frame around it. The shape and label hold through the whole clip, and a second and third clip match the first, which matters when a listing or an ad set needs several videos of one item.


One of the three AERO 1 photos behind the next two clips: a plain background, even light, the label readable.



Two scenes from the same three photos, the same shoe in both (Kling 3.0 Omni in RefVid).

RefVid is reference-to-video: you save the product once from its photos, and every clip in any scene starts from that saved product.

Step 1: give it the right photos

One sharp photo is enough to start: your main product-page angle, on a plain background, with the label readable and the colours accurate. If that is all you have, RefVid can draw three more angles from it with the same shape, colours and label text, so the video model sees more than one side.

With three to five photos the result gets steadier: add a side, the back and a close-up of the label. You can save 1 to 10 photos per product. If the photos are already on your shop page, paste the product link instead of uploading; RefVid reads the photos from Shopify stores, Amazon listings and shop pages that describe the product in structured data.

Leave out photos with price stickers, props that are not part of the product, or phone-screenshot clutter. A screenshot of a listing brings the status bar and the app's buttons into the video, so crop it first:


Adding a photo in the studio. When a photo has a phone screenshot's shape, the studio offers Crop; the model sees the cropped photo.

Step 2: make the clips that sell first

Start with the clips that sell, not the ones that impress. A turntable spin shows the back on a product page. An unboxing shows what arrives. Someone holding the product and talking works as a TikTok or Reels ad. A lifestyle shot on a shelf or a desk shows scale and use.

Each of these exists in RefVid as a template that opens the studio with the shots, length and shape already written, so your photos are all you add. A few of the 27 product templates:

Template What you get Length and shape
360 turntable Your product spins slowly through a full turn on a white studio turntable 5 s, square 1:1
Unboxing Hands open a kraft box, lift the product out, turn the label to the camera, with paper sounds 10 s, vertical 9:16
Water splash The product drops into clear water in slow motion and settles upright 5 s, vertical 9:16
Perfume reveal Mist and one puff of spray in warm backlight, then light through the glass onto the label 5 s, vertical 9:16
Jewelry on hand A hand wearing your ring or bracelet turns slowly in warm window light 5 s, square 1:1
Tech reveal A line of light traces your device in the dark, then the camera arcs around it 5 s, wide 16:9

Three of them, each with a reference photo and a frame from its real example clip. The products are AI-made samples; the prompts are the templates' own, word for word, with {1} where your product's name goes.

360 turntable: AERO 1, from 3 photos.

{1} on a round white turntable in a photo studio, rotating slowly through a full 360 degrees, light grey seamless background, soft even studio light, locked-off camera, sharp focus on every detail.



Every side faces the camera once as it turns, so photograph the front, both sides and the back at the same height; the back is the side a listing rarely shows, so include it, above all if it carries a label. 5 seconds, square, silent, on Kling 3.0 Omni: the cheapest of the three to make, and the template RefVid's paying customers make most. 360 turntable template.

Perfume reveal: NOIR 07, from 3 photos.

{1} stands on glossy black glass wrapped in slowly drifting soft mist; a single fine puff of perfume spray bursts from the top and catches a warm golden backlight, then the mist clears and a beam of light passes through the glass, ending on the label sharp and centred. Low-key, luxurious, slow push-in.



Shoot the bottle straight on with the label square to the lens and no glare: the clip ends on that label. 5 seconds, 9:16, with sound, on Kling 4. Perfume reveal template.

Jewelry on hand: HALO, from 4 photos.

Close-up: a woman's hand with a soft natural manicure, wearing {1}, rests on cream silk and turns slowly toward the camera, {1} catching small sparkles in warm window light. Shallow depth of field, gentle slow push-in, elegant and natural.



No hand model needed. Show the piece from the angle a wearer sees, plus the band and the setting; a photo of it on a finger helps the size look right. 5 seconds, square, with sound. Jewelry on hand template.

Step 3: let the photos describe the product, the prompt describe the rest

The prompt should cover the place, one motion, the camera move, the light and the last frame. Use the product's saved name instead of describing it again: a second description in words competes with the photos and is the most common reason a label changes. Two prompts that work:

AERO 1 slowly rotates on a round white plinth in a minimal studio, static camera at shoe height, soft key light, sharp focus

A hand lifts AERO 1 out of a kraft box on a wooden table and turns it toward the camera, soft daylight


Made from the three AERO 1 photos with a prompt close to the first one. Short, concrete prompts beat long lists of adjectives.

Pick the shape for where it goes

Square 1:1 for product pages, vertical 9:16 for TikTok, Reels and Shorts, wide 16:9 for your own site. Clips run 3 to 30 seconds on Kling 4 (up to 15 on Kling 3.0 Omni), can have sound, and one clip can hold up to three subjects, such as the product and the person holding it.



The same prompt and the same three photos, made vertical for social and square for a product page.

If the clip is going into paid placements rather than a product page, it is built in three beats: something that stops the eye, the product doing the one thing you sell, and a last frame on the label. We wrote that up in making a video ad of your own product from photos, with three ad formats from the same photos to test against each other.

Check every clip before it goes live

Watch each clip at full size. The label and logo should read the same as on the real item; small print is the part most likely to change, so keep the takes where it holds. Check the colours against the photo, and never show features or accessories the product does not have.

What it costs

New accounts start with free credits and no card: they cover a first 5-second clip on Kling 3.0 Omni (Vidu Q2 in some regions), and every clip, free or paid, has no watermark and may be used commercially. After that, clips are priced in credits by the second. A 5-second silent clip on Kling 3.0 Omni, such as the 360 turntable, is 155 credits; the same 5 seconds on Kling 4 at 720p, with sound, is 290. Here is what each way of paying buys, from the RefVid pricing page:

How you pay Price 5-second Kling 3.0 Omni clips, like the turntable 5-second Kling 4 clips
One video, no plan $2.99 up to 5 s, $4.99 up to 10 s, $6.99 up to 15 s 1 1
Credit pack, one time $9.90 for 1,500 credits (also $19.90 for 3,200, $49.90 for 8,500) 9 5
Basic plan $10 a month, or $96 a year, for 2,000 credits a month 12 a month 6 a month

Credits never expire: unused plan credits roll over and pack credits stay. Failed videos give their credits back, and unused pack credits are refunded in full within 14 days.

The full product photo to video guide lists all the templates with their lengths and shapes, and answers the questions shop owners ask us most, like whether one photo is enough and how to get a 360-degree spin.

— Louis Chi, RefVid

title: ISC Stormcast For Friday, November 6th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10168, (Fri, Nov 6th)
PromptOps: Iterative Prompt Optimization for LLM-as-a-Judge Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.07123v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for evaluating the behavior of chatbots and other AI systems. In deployment, however, their agreement with the intended human evaluation policy may degrade as user interactions and score distributions change. Existing automatic prompt optimization methods are primarily studied as one-shot procedures on static development sets and therefore provide limited guidance for maintaining LLM judges over time. We frame this problem as judge drift and introduce PromptOps, a closedloop framework for monitoring and iteratively recalibrating LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaaJ) systems. PromptOps separates four operational decisions: when to optimize, which optimization procedure to apply, which feedback records to use, and how to update the judge prompt. We instantiate the framework with five prompt optimization methods: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. Our experiments demonstrate that iterative prompt optimization can recalibrate LLM judges and recover performance after controlled shifts in the referencescore distribution. However, effective maintenance is inherently contextdependent: neither optimization algorithm choice nor update timing generalizes universally across settings. These findings establish prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an inherently iterative maintenance problem and demonstrate that PromptOps provides a practical abstraction for studying and implementing this process.

title: Beyond the Keyword: A Human-Annotated Benchmark for Arabic Anxiety-Related Discourse
description:
arXiv:2611.07949v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Keyword retrieval returns expressions of personal anxiety together with many other uses of anxiety-related language. We present a benchmark of 1,000 Arabic Twitter/X posts retrieved with the keyword qalaq ("anxiety/worry") and annotated for six discourse functions. Two native Arabic-speaking annotators labeled every post independently, reaching 51.1% raw agreement (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.378$). We then reviewed all 489 disagreements and all 511 agreements under the same guidelines. The review changed 120 of the agreed labels (23.5%), which shows that agreements need auditing as well as disagreements. The final labels form a consensus reference; on a random sample of 200 posts, an additional annotator agreed with it on 60.5% of posts ($\kappa = 0.517$). Against this reference, Fanar-C-2-27B reaches 79.8% accuracy and macro-F1 0.784 ($\kappa = 0.749$). Its errors concentrate in the residual category (41.1% of errors; precision 0.905, recall 0.447), whose definition is internally inconsistent in the executed prompt, so the low recall cannot be attributed to the model alone. Sociopolitical Anxiety (27.1%) outnumbers Personal Emotional Expression (22.0%); these are assignment proportions in the sample, not estimates of prevalence or retrieval precision. We release the guidelines, a residual-subtype scheme, a fixed data split, label provenance, and evaluation code.

title: You Write the Code. React Renders the UI. But What Happens Between Your Code and the Magic?
description:
To understand the magic, you first need to understand what a React element is.

So, a React element is, by definition, a lightweight description of a UI node.

A React element looks like this:

{
  type: "h1",
  props: {
    children: "Hello, World!"
  }
}

It’s a description of the UI, where it describes which elements to render, what content they contain, and, if there are more props, more details about that UI.

The JSX code is first converted into React elements.

But a React element does not, by itself, represent an actual browser DOM node.

Now the question comes to mind:

How does React create DOM elements, and why does it need to introduce React elements?

In a JSX component, you describe only the desired UI. But React needs a description of those elements.

For that reason, it processes that UI using its rendering machinery and creates React elements.

Now React creates the DOM elements from those React elements and inserts them into the document during the commit process. After the commit, you see the magic on the screen.

To understand the commit process, we need to understand many concepts. One of them is the Fiber tree, which we will discuss in the next post.

title: Native is a floor, not a ceiling
description:
With AI, a polished look costs nothing. Native brings what can’t be drawn, and it moves with the system, one step ahead of what imitates it.

An AI assistant helped me write this. The ideas, the experience and the final edit are mine.

In June 2025, Apple introduced Liquid Glass, the new material of iOS 26. In its WWDC session on UIKit, the company put it plainly: “Your apps get this new appearance as soon as you recompile with the new SDK.” Bars, sheets, popovers and controls: most of what comes from the system frameworks changed at once, without a designer touching it.

Apps that drew their own controls got nothing. The next day, the Flutter team replied on GitHub that it was not developing Apple’s new design in its Cupertino library, the one that imitates iOS, for now. Its documentation presents drawing your own controls as a benefit: a Flutter app “looks and feels the same on all versions of the OS, even if the OS changed the implementations of its controls.” When iOS 26 shipped on September 15, 2025, that promise of stability had turned into a visible lag. The team has since moved its libraries out of the core framework to move faster, and says work is underway on Liquid Glass, but as of November 5, 2026, the issue is still open.

I worked with that choice for a long time, for the same reasons. Drawing your own controls means owning your rendering, on every version of the system. The price is that lag at every change. As long as a polished look took work, the price was worth paying: that work is what set an app apart.

AI changes the math. A polished look now takes one prompt, and generated interfaces converge in visual appearance and layout. I wrote elsewhere about why everything ends up looking alike, what people call slop; there I called apparent quality the floor, and AI now hands it to everyone. Native is a floor of another kind, the one an image doesn’t give you. Native components don’t make an app beautiful. They keep it from looking fake, and they move with the system.

AI draws the picture of native

Since October, I have been asking several AI models to design app screens, for a study I will publish soon. They imitate the system, under certain conditions, and only what can be seen.

The first condition is naming the device. Ask for a mobile app without saying which, and you get a generic screen that doesn’t really follow either iPhone or Android. Write “iPhone”, and the switches do have the shape of iOS switches. Add the instruction to follow the platform’s current conventions, and they fix a few more things that have a name: the green of the switches, the back chevron. But a year after iOS 26 shipped, the iOS they draw is still mostly the old one. The floating tab bar and the sheets detached from the edges, the iOS 26 design, only show up with that instruction, and rarely.

My explanation: an AI learns from what already exists, and the old iOS had years to fill the web. The system, meanwhile, moves every year, a little and sometimes a lot. On iOS, a native app follows by recompiling; an imitation stays stuck on the day it was copied. It’s the counterfeit copying last year’s collection, when the fashion house has already moved on to the next one.

A study published this spring points the same way. Researchers had three AI design tools generate 138 mobile screens, without mentioning iOS or Android. The models have learned “the visual syntax of contemporary mobile interfaces”, they write: navigation conventions are almost always there. But that success, in their words, “appears to be pattern-driven rather than principle-driven”, and they report a significant gap between visual and functional usability: help, error prevention and error recovery are often missing.

What the image doesn’t show

Imitating is already a lot. But the floor is mostly behavior. The back gesture that works everywhere. The share sheet everyone recognizes. The confirmation that, on iOS 26, grows out of the button that opened it. The sheet that rises from the bottom and that you dismiss with a swipe. A screenshot shows, at best, the picture of it.

Apple says it in the branding page of its guidelines: when you use components people already know, the experience feels “immediately reliable and familiar”. A familiar control does what you expect it to.

In 1998, with desktop software, John Satzinger and Lorne Olfman showed that commands that change from one application to the next make users take more actions, while a different visual appearance tends to make them more accurate. What matters is that the way you act stays the same.

It’s like the grammar of a language: everyone shares the same one, and nobody calls it slop. Slop is the stock phrase you’ve read a hundred times.

UIKit controls also come with built-in accessibility, and system components with text that scales to the size the user picked and a layout that flips for Arabic or Hebrew. On Android, the Compose documentation says that “most accessibility support is provided with little or no additional work” by its components, Material included. A control redrawn by hand has to rebuild all of that, and nothing guarantees it will: Kate Owens, at Deque, describes a custom slider that VoiceOver “skipped over entirely and never focused”.

Louie Mantia, a former Apple icon designer and a sharp critic of Liquid Glass, put it this way in 2025, about icons: “Everyone can look decent without actually being decent.” A generated mockup can draw an alert that looks like the iOS one without saying that the iOS one should be used. Rebuilt by hand, however faithfully, it only gives the app the picture of the floor.

The more apps get built from generated mockups, the more of them will look native without being native. That’s why, in my view, native matters more today than it did yesterday. The risk lies in the copied mockup: when an AI writes the code of a native project, it can call the real components. It can also produce native slop: the real components, all left at their defaults, and nothing of the brand around them. It works and it follows the system, but it looks like every other app.

On iPhone, the difference shows

You might think users see none of this. The only controlled experiment I found that pits a native app against its cross-platform version says they do see a difference, on iPhone, as soon as they can compare.

In 2014, Esteban Angulo and Xavier Ferré had thirty-seven people test two versions of the same app, fourteen of them on iPhone. One was native, the other built with Titanium, a cross-platform tool. Asked which version best matched their idea of an app for their phone, iPhone users picked the native one 86% to 7%. On Android, the gap was much smaller: 52% to 39%.

On iPhone, the seven people who had tried the cross-platform version first found it typical of iOS; among the seven who tried it after the native one, only four did. The gap mostly shows by comparison. But the cross-platform version also displayed native components, and a different team had designed it: the study can’t tell what made the difference. Nor does it say what it’s worth in ratings or sales, and a study of nearly 12,000 Android apps concludes that native and hybrid apps (web apps in a native shell) do equally well in ratings.

The ceiling is elsewhere

Native fixes the fake, not the alike. Standing out from other apps is still the brand’s job, and the floor doesn’t prevent it. In 2019, on UX Collective, Reza Bigdeli, an Android developer, answered designers who find standard components “cheap”. His advice: follow the platform’s guidelines, and keep creativity for the web. I follow him on the floor; for the rest, an app can have a strong identity without leaving its platform’s conventions.

Apple itself doesn’t reward a single style. In 2023, its Design Awards honored Flighty and Duolingo the same year. Flighty won in the Interaction category, which rewards interfaces “perfectly tailored to their platform”. Its founder, Ryan Jones, wanted the app to work so well that it would feel “almost boringly obvious”. Duolingo, on the other hand, is a highly stylized interface, which Apple still praises for its “best-in-class design” and “easy-to-follow UI”.

For Apple, “even a highly stylized interface can be approachable if it maintains familiar behaviors and patterns.” A WWDC26 session describes an app in two layers: bars and controls rely on what people already know, the content carries the brand, and the whole rests on a “baseline of platform familiarity”. That boundary is what a generated mockup doesn’t show.

Where to spend the effort

What comes from the system: navigation, back, sharing, confirmations, sheets, controls, text size. You don’t redraw them by default: Apple advises keeping custom work for the places where it has the “biggest impact”, and warns that a utility control remade by hand can make an app look less native, or even dated. Specify them by name, so nobody rebuilds them as a picture.

What comes from the brand: the content, the typography of headings (which should also follow the size the user picked), illustration, the tone of the copy, the moments where the app surprises. That’s where the identity budget gets spent. Apple even warns against too much brand: a brand color used everywhere dilutes its impact.

When the mockup comes from an AI, name the device and its current conventions in the prompt, then review that split first. Anything that looks like a system control should at least behave like one, and the safest bet is that it is one. The rest can be as free as you like: that’s where an app stops looking like the others.

Cover image: Apple’s design kits for iOS 27, the system components every app gets. Image: Apple Developer.

Mathieu Poli is Head of Frontend Engineering at GoodBarber and writes about frontend engineering, product design and AI.

Native is a floor, not a ceiling was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Your AI Is Only as Reliable as Its Data: Designing an AI-Ready Data Architecture
description:
An AI model can be powerful, your infrastructure can scale, and your application can have a clean architecture.

But if the model receives outdated records, incomplete documents, inconsistent features, or data the user isn't authorized to access, the system can still produce unreliable results.

This is one of the reasons enterprise AI projects often struggle after the proof of concept.

The bottleneck isn't always model performance. It's the data architecture surrounding the model.

Traditional analytics platforms are designed to help people understand data through dashboards and reports. AI systems have a different requirement: they need data that is fresh, trusted, contextual, traceable, and permissioned at the moment of inference.

At SotaTek, we approach AI-ready data architecture as a foundation for production AI, connecting enterprise sources, data pipelines, governance, AI serving, and feedback into one operating system.

Let's look at how to design that foundation.

1. An AI-Ready Data Platform Is Different From an Analytics Stack

A traditional analytics architecture typically moves data from operational systems into a warehouse, transforms it, and makes it available to BI tools.

An AI application consumes data differently.

It may need structured customer records, PDF contracts, product images, transaction events, support tickets, or IoT sensor data in the same workflow.

The data also needs to carry enough context for a machine to interpret it correctly.

Consider the difference:

Dimension Traditional analytics AI-ready data architecture
Main consumer Analysts and dashboards Models, agents, applications
Data types Mostly structured tables Tables, documents, images, audio, events
Freshness Daily or hourly batches Use-case-dependent, from batch to near real time
Metadata Documentation for people Machine-readable metadata
Quality Periodic audits Automated pipeline checks
Access control Table and report level Row, column, and document level
Lineage Useful for reporting Needed to trace model outputs
Feedback Limited Corrections and outcomes return to the data layer

There are four questions an AI-ready platform should answer for every dataset:

  • Fresh: Is the information current enough for this workflow?
  • Trusted: Is it reliable, and can its origin be traced?
  • Contextual: Does it include the schema, definitions, and ownership needed to interpret it?
  • Permissioned: Can this user access it, including when the AI retrieves it?

A dataset doesn't need to be perfect before AI can use it. It needs to meet the requirements of the workflow it supports.

2. The Six Layers of an AI-Ready Data Architecture

There is no single universal layer model. The following six-layer architecture is a practical way to understand how data moves from enterprise systems into AI applications.

+--------------------------------------+
|  6. Consumption & Feedback           |
|  Model APIs | Agents | Apps | BI      |
+--------------------------------------+
                    |
+--------------------------------------+
|  5. AI Serving                       |
|  Feature Store | Embeddings | RAG     |
+--------------------------------------+
                    |
+--------------------------------------+
|  4. Governance & Metadata            |
|  Catalog | Lineage | Policies        |
+--------------------------------------+
                    |
+--------------------------------------+
|  3. Storage & Processing             |
|  Warehouse | Lakehouse | Object Store|
+--------------------------------------+
                    |
+--------------------------------------+
|  2. Ingestion & Integration          |
|  Batch ELT | CDC | Event Streaming   |
+--------------------------------------+
                    |
+--------------------------------------+
|  1. Source Systems                   |
|  ERP | CRM | Apps | IoT | Documents   |
+--------------------------------------+

Each layer solves a different engineering problem.

Layer 1: Source Systems

This is where enterprise data originates.

Typical sources include:

  • ERP and CRM platforms
  • Transactional databases
  • Internal applications
  • IoT devices and sensors
  • Documents, PDFs, and emails
  • Images, audio, and video
  • Logs and event streams

The first task is not to ingest everything.

Identify which sources are required for the target AI workflow, who owns them, and what access restrictions apply.

Layer 2: Ingestion and Integration

This layer moves data from source systems into the platform.

The ingestion strategy should match the freshness requirement.

Pattern Suitable use case
Batch ELT Historical reporting and periodic model training
Change Data Capture (CDC) Synchronizing operational database changes
Event streaming Workflows that must react to events quickly

For example, a customer support assistant may only need policy documents refreshed every few hours.

A fraud detection system may need transaction events within seconds.

Streaming every dataset is not automatically better. It introduces infrastructure, monitoring, and operational complexity. Use it when the workflow actually needs low-latency updates.

A simplified CDC flow:

Operational Database
        |
        v
  Change Log / CDC
        |
        v
   Ingestion Service
        |
        v
    Data Platform
        |
        v
   Downstream Consumers

The ingestion layer should also detect schema changes and prevent unexpected source modifications from silently breaking downstream consumers.

Layer 3: Storage and Processing

AI workloads often need both structured and unstructured data.

A lakehouse is one possible architecture for managing these data types within a governed platform.

A common organization pattern is the medallion architecture:

Bronze
  |
  | Raw source data
  v
Silver
  |
  | Cleaned and conformed data
  v
Gold
  |
  | Business-ready datasets
  v
AI / Analytics Consumers
  • Bronze: Preserve raw source data.
  • Silver: Clean, validate, deduplicate, and standardize.
  • Gold: Prepare data for specific business and AI workloads.

Keeping the raw layer matters. When transformation logic changes, teams may need to rebuild features, reprocess records, or re-embed documents.

For storage, open table formats such as Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Apache Hudi can help support different processing engines without tying the entire architecture to one proprietary format.

The important decision is to choose storage based on workload requirements, not simply because a particular technology is popular.

Layer 4: Governance and Metadata

Governance should not be a document created after the data pipeline is finished.

It should be part of the data path.

This layer manages:

  • Data catalog and ownership
  • Schema definitions
  • Data lineage
  • Data contracts
  • Quality expectations
  • Access policies
  • Sensitive-data classification
  • Data observability

A data contract makes expectations between producers and consumers explicit.

For example:

dataset: customer_profile

owner: customer-platform

schema:
  customer_id:
    type: string
    required: true

  email:
    type: string
    required: false
    classification: personal_data

  updated_at:
    type: timestamp
    required: true

quality:
  unique_key: customer_id
  freshness_sla: 15m
  null_threshold:
    customer_id: 0

This is an illustrative contract, not a framework-specific configuration.

If an upstream service changes a field or stops sending required values, validation should detect the issue before it reaches model training or inference.

Lineage is equally important.

When an AI system produces an answer or prediction, teams should be able to trace the relevant data sources and transformations behind it.

Layer 5: AI Serving

This is where data becomes usable by AI models.

The serving architecture differs depending on the workload.

For traditional machine learning, a feature store can help maintain consistency between training and inference features.

For generative AI, the architecture may include document parsing, chunking, embeddings, vector indexes, and retrieval services.

A simplified RAG ingestion and query flow:

Document Sources
      |
      v
Parsing & Extraction
      |
      v
Chunking + Metadata
      |
      v
Embedding Generation
      |
      v
Vector Index
      |
      v
User Query
      |
      v
Retrieval + Filtering
      |
      v
Relevant Context
      |
      v
LLM

The vector database is only one component of this architecture.

It does not automatically solve document quality, metadata, freshness, authorization, or source traceability.

Those responsibilities need to be handled across the data and serving layers.

Layer 6: Consumption and Feedback

The final layer delivers data and AI capabilities to applications, agents, APIs, and users.

But the flow should not stop when a model returns a response.

Capture relevant outcomes:

  • What data was retrieved?
  • Which model and prompt versions were used?
  • Was the result accepted or corrected?
  • Did the user complete the intended workflow?
  • Did a human reviewer override the output?

Human corrections and confirmed business outcomes can become valuable inputs for evaluation and future improvements.

This creates a feedback loop:

Data Sources
     |
     v
AI Processing
     |
     v
Model Output
     |
     v
User / Business Workflow
     |
     v
Feedback & Evaluation
     |
     v
Updated Data / Features
     |
     +----------> AI Processing

3. Permission-Aware Retrieval Is a Security Requirement

One of the easiest mistakes in enterprise RAG is treating retrieval as a search problem only.

Imagine an organization with three departments:

  • Finance
  • Human Resources
  • Engineering

All three departments share one document platform, but they do not have permission to access the same documents.

A naive retrieval system may search across the entire index and send the top matching chunks to the LLM.

Even if the model is instructed not to reveal confidential information, the unauthorized information has already entered its context.

The correct approach is to enforce permissions during retrieval.

A simplified example:

def retrieve_context(query, user):
    filters = {
        "tenant_id": user.tenant_id,
        "allowed_roles": {
            "$in": user.roles
        }
    }

    documents = vector_store.search(
        query=query,
        filters=filters,
        top_k=8,
    )

    return documents

This example illustrates the filtering concept. Actual implementations must enforce authorization in a trusted server-side layer, use the identity and policy model of the organization, and account for document-level permissions and permission changes.

The principle is straightforward:

Access control must follow the data into the retrieval layer.

A RAG system should never become an alternative route around the permissions already enforced by enterprise applications.

4. Choose the Architecture Pattern Based on the Actual Constraint

Warehouse, lakehouse, data mesh, and data fabric are not interchangeable labels for the same platform.

Each addresses a different architectural constraint.

Pattern Best suited for Main trade-off
Cloud data warehouse Structured, BI-heavy workloads Less flexible for unstructured data
Lakehouse Mixed data, ML, and analytics Requires disciplined data engineering
Data mesh Multiple domains with distributed ownership Higher coordination complexity
Data fabric Data spread across systems and clouds Depends heavily on metadata quality

A practical starting rule:

  • If your first AI use case mainly uses structured tables owned by one team, a warehouse plus a vector index may be sufficient.
  • If PDFs, support tickets, images, and tables all matter, consider a lakehouse.
  • If domain ownership is slowing down delivery, introduce data products and mesh-style ownership.
  • If data must remain distributed across multiple systems, a fabric-style metadata and integration layer may help.

These patterns can coexist. An enterprise might use a lakehouse for storage, domain ownership for data products, and a fabric-style catalog for discovery.

The goal is not to adopt every architecture pattern. It is to solve the constraint that is currently blocking the AI use case.

5. Build a Thin Slice Before Building an Enterprise-Wide Platform

Trying to make every dataset AI-ready before launching the first use case is an expensive mistake.

Start with one workflow and build only the data foundation it needs.

A practical implementation sequence:

Step 1: Pick one use case and define readiness

Identify the workflow, business owner, required data, freshness target, quality threshold, and access requirements.

Step 2: Inventory and score the data

List the sources, owners, formats, quality issues, and sensitivity levels.

Evaluate each source against four dimensions:

  • Freshness
  • Trustworthiness
  • Context
  • Permissions

The output should be a prioritized gap list, not a company-wide data-cleanup project.

Step 3: Build a thin platform slice

Set up ingestion for the selected sources, a bronze-to-gold transformation path, a catalog entry, lineage, and automated data tests.

Avoid implementing layers that the first use case does not need.

Step 4: Add AI serving and evaluate

Create features or embeddings, implement permission-aware retrieval where required, and test against a representative evaluation dataset.

Use real data from the selected workflow rather than relying exclusively on small synthetic samples.

Step 5: Operate and expand

Monitor freshness, quality, drift, and cost. Capture user corrections and business outcomes.

Once the first workflow is reliable, reuse the same foundation for the next use case.

6. Common Engineering Mistakes

Several architecture decisions can create problems that only become visible after deployment.

Buying the platform before defining the use case

Technology selection should follow data requirements, latency, governance, and operational constraints.

Treating the vector database as the entire architecture

A vector index cannot fix incorrect source records, missing metadata, or broken access policies.

Cleaning every dataset before starting

Enterprise-wide data cleanup delays value. Start with the sources required by the first workflow and expand incrementally.

Ignoring unstructured data

Contracts, manuals, emails, images, and support tickets may contain important context that isn't represented in relational tables.

Leaving datasets without an owner

Every important dataset needs someone accountable for quality, freshness, and access.

Treating governance as a final approval gate

If governance happens only after development, teams may create unmanaged data copies to avoid delays. Put quality checks, classification, and access enforcement into the pipeline itself.

Final Thoughts

An AI-ready data architecture is not simply a bigger data warehouse or a vector database connected to an LLM.

It is a platform that delivers fresh, trusted, contextual, and permissioned data to AI systems, with governance and traceability built into the data flow.

The six layers provide a practical foundation:

Sources → Ingestion → Storage → Governance → AI Serving → Consumption & Feedback

Start with one workflow. Identify its data requirements. Build a thin slice. Measure its reliability. Then expand the architecture based on what the next use case actually needs.

At SotaTek, we approach this foundation as part of production AI engineering, connecting data readiness, architecture design, AI integration, and MLOps rather than treating data preparation as a separate preliminary task.

For a deeper breakdown of the six architectural layers, design principles, and five-step implementation plan, read our AI-Ready Data Architecture guide.

title: Which Objects Stay? Learning Hierarchical Persistence Beliefs for Lifelong Open-Vocabulary Object Maps
description:
arXiv:2611.07662v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Lifelong object maps must estimate whether an object remains at its previously observed location after it leaves view. Existing persistence filters rely on class-based survival priors, making them difficult to apply reliably in open-vocabulary settings. We introduce HiPer, a hierarchical persistence filter that derives persistence beliefs directly from data rather than semantic categories. For a new object, HiPer retrieves visually and geometrically similar training instances and estimates an initial survival rate from their observed histories, without requiring class labels. This estimate initializes a conjugate Beta belief over the object's survival probability, which is updated in closed form using detections and missed observations under Rosen's persistence-filter framework. When an object is re-identified at a new location, its persistence belief is transferred with the object, enabling the map to learn object-specific mobility over time. Experiments on 120 held-out simulated sequences show that HiPer consistently achieves the best performance among competing methods. Retrieval-based priors outperform CLIP-derived label priors, and object-specific online learning provides further gains. Results on 47 held-out 3RScan environments demonstrate that the proposed retrieval-based prior also outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in real-world settings.
