title: Beyond K/V Caches: Cross-Model State Handoff in Hybrid Linear-Attention LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.08133v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Production deployments often use different models to balance cost and quality through cascading, routing, and switching models during long conversations. Context accumulates across turns. Each switch requires the target to repeat prefill over this context. Existing methods transfer full-attention (FA) K/V caches across models. Hybrid linear-attention models also retain recurrent states (REC) and convolution histories (Conv). The interaction between Conv and REC complicates cross-model state transfer. Conv perturbations can change keys and values in recurrent layers and alter REC updates. Conv histories are overwritten, but changes in REC can still affect later outputs. More accurate REC reconstruction need not improve continuation. Building on this, we propose Hybrid State Transfer (HST) for all three state types. It uses structured REC maps and preserves history order during Conv alignment. We calibrate the adapters using the frozen target's outputs during continuation. FA cache map updates are merged offline. Across five benchmarks, Qwen3.5 4B$\rightarrow$27B and 9B$\rightarrow$27B achieve mean task retentions of 89.88% and 94.11%, respectively. With source caches already available, separate timing on synthetic 16K inputs yields handoff body speedups of $21.66\times$ and $21.91\times$.

title: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-Model Transfer
description:
arXiv:2611.06976v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-model Transfer (PACT), a form of latent communication between language models, combines a larger model's prompt representations with a smaller model's efficient generation, offering a promising way to balance capability and inference cost. However, existing systems provide limited support for independently evaluating large-small model collaboration, and improved task performance alone does not establish whether the receiver benefits from the sender's information. We introduce PLatour, an open-source PACT framework that connects frozen models through lightweight, zero-initialized linear bridges trained directly with task rewards and supports hybrid-attention architectures. PLatour significantly outperforms open-source baselines on generation tasks and surpasses Mostik's reported results on shared mathematics and coding benchmarks using a substantially smaller sender. However, controlled experiments show that the gains on some tasks can be reproduced by uninformative sender signals, self-communication, or receiver-only training. We find that trainable bridges can act as parameter-efficient adaptation mechanisms without exploiting useful sender information. We therefore propose PACT-Check to quantify how much of a trained PACT system's gain genuinely comes from communication. Finally, we discuss the opportunities and challenges of PACT systems. Code is available at https://github.com/zhenyi4/platour.

title: Your Free Server's Local Disk Is Not a Database: Five Persistence Myths and a Restart Probe
description:
You deployed it. It worked. Then the instance restarted overnight.

Now your chat endpoint answers as if the conversation never happened. Was that disk supposed to hold your state?

This is a myth-busting FAQ about persistence on small, free-hosted apps. It ships with a restart probe you can run in about ten minutes. All code below is a template; I am not publishing measured results for your host.

The five myths I keep hearing

Myth 1: "If I write it to disk, it is persisted"

The claim. fs.writeFile is durable, so a local JSON file is fine storage.

Why it feels true. It survives your process crashing. That is real.

What to check. Does the instance keep its disk across a restart? Across a rebuild? Those are different events. Ask your host explicitly, and reread the storage docs.

Corrected model. Local disk is scratch space with a marketing problem. Treat it as a cache you cannot trust.

Myth 2: "A restart and a redeploy are the same thing"

The claim. If the disk survived last time, it will survive next time.

Why it feels true. You restarted the service and your files were still there.

What to check. A redeploy often builds a fresh image on a fresh machine. A restart may reuse the old one. Your test must name which event it exercised.

Corrected model. Restart, redeploy, and resize are three separate experiments. Run all three, or stop claiming durability.

Myth 3: "My in-memory cache will just refill"

The claim. Losing a warm cache is fine, because the cache warms itself.

Why it feels true. In steady traffic, yes, it does.

What to check. What happens on the first request after a cold start, with five hundred users arriving at once? That is a thundering herd, not a cache miss.

Corrected model. A cold cache is a load event. Budget for it, or gate the refill.

Myth 4: "Session state can live in a local file until we get a DB"

The claim. A sessions.json on disk is a fine interim solution.

Why it feels true. On a single instance, it is trivially simple and fast.

What to check. Restart the box while a user is mid-conversation. If the session vanishes, users see a forgotten session and a fresh greeting. They blame the model.

Corrected model. Local-file sessions are a single-instance lock-in. Fine for a demo, dishonest as a default.

Myth 5: "My local logs are an audit trail"

The claim. I log every prompt and response to app.log, so I can debug later.

Why it feels true. The file exists, and it grows.

What to check. Restart, then look for the file. If it is gone, your audit trail had a lifetime measured in uptime.

Corrected model. A log on ephemeral disk is a debugging aid for the current boot, nothing more.

Corrected mental model: three tiers of state

Stop asking "is it stored?" Start asking "where does it live, and what kills it?"

Tier Survives process crash Survives restart Survives rebuild Right home for
Process memory No No No Hot caches, connection pools
Instance-local disk Usually Sometimes Rarely Temp files, build output, scratch
Attached volume Usually Usually Depends on config Single-writer scratch
External store Yes Yes Yes Sessions, prompt journals, ledgers

The rule I use: anything a user would notice missing goes in the bottom row. Everything else may live above it.

Artifact: a restart probe in forty lines

Here is the probe. Standard library only, no dependencies.

# restart_probe.py
import json, os, sys, time, uuid

STATE = os.environ.get("PROBE_STATE", "./probe_state")
LEDGER = os.environ["PROBE_LEDGER"]  # MUST live outside this instance
MARKER = os.path.join(STATE, "marker.json")


def write_phase():
    os.makedirs(STATE, exist_ok=True)
    rec = {"token": uuid.uuid4().hex, "written_at": time.time()}
    with open(MARKER, "w") as f:
        json.dump(rec, f)
    with open(LEDGER, "a") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps({"phase": "write", **rec}) + "\n")
    print("wrote token=%s" % rec["token"])


def verify_phase():
    want = None
    with open(LEDGER) as f:
        for line in f:
            rec = json.loads(line)
            if rec["phase"] == "write":
                want = rec["token"]
    if want is None:
        sys.exit("no write recorded in ledger")
    try:
        with open(MARKER) as f:
            got = json.load(f)["token"]
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print("MISSING: expected %s, marker gone" % want)
        return 1
    if got == want:
        print("SURVIVED: %s" % want)
        return 0
    print("DRIFT: expected %s, found %s" % (want, got))
    return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(write_phase() if sys.argv[1] == "write" else verify_phase())

The one rule that makes or breaks this test. PROBE_LEDGER must point outside the instance. Put it on your laptop, in paste buffer output you capture, or in any store that does not die with the box. A ledger on the same disk proves nothing.

Run protocol

  1. Write phase: PROBE_LEDGER=$HOME/probe.jsonl python restart_probe.py write.
  2. Restart the service only. Verify.
  3. Redeploy or rebuild. Verify again.
  4. If your host suspends idle instances, let it idle, wake it, verify a third time.

Three runs, three answers. Now you know which event eats your files. Do not guess.

The model part: your prompt journal is state too

If your app calls a model, the only record of what the model saw is the journal you wrote. Lose it, and you cannot explain a bad answer later.

So extend the probe. Log a prompt hash and a response hash per call, to the same external ledger.

import hashlib

def journal(ledger_path, prompt, response):
    row = {
        "prompt_sha256": hashlib.sha256(prompt.encode()).hexdigest(),
        "response_sha256": hashlib.sha256(response.encode()).hexdigest(),
        "ts": time.time(),
    }
    with open(ledger_path, "a") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(row) + "\n")

Hashes keep the ledger small and avoid storing user text. You lose readability, and you gain the ability to prove a call happened. That trade is usually the right one for a prototype.

Why hash instead of skip? Because "the model gave a weird answer" is unfalsifiable without a record. Twelve hours after a restart, your log is gone and so is your argument.

Where a free server and free models fit

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

This probe is cheap to run and cheaper to run repeatedly. That is where a free server option and free model access genuinely help: you can host the tiny probe app, drive it with real model calls, and repeat the restart cycle without a paid round trip each time.

The workflow that makes sense:

  • Host the probe app on a free server, and keep the ledger off that server.
  • Drive it with real prompts through free model access, so the journal has traffic in it.
  • Restart, rebuild, and wake it. Compare runs.
  • Only then decide what belongs in durable storage.

What this does not give you: any promise about durability, uptime, or retention. Availability of a free tier says nothing about persistence. That is exactly why you probe.

If you want to run this loop yourself, the free server option on MonkeyCode is enough to start, as long as you bring your own off-box ledger.

Limits, and who should skip this

  • The probe tests restart behavior, not crash-during-write. Use a real database for atomicity questions.
  • It cannot tell you about partial writes, fsync semantics, or replication lag.
  • One instance tells you nothing about multi-instance races. Two writers on one file will teach you the hard way.
  • If your platform already gives you managed durable storage with documented guarantees, skip the probe. Read the docs instead.
  • If your data is regulated, this toy ledger is not a compliance control. Talk to someone qualified.

The question to ask before the next deploy

Not "where did I write it?" Ask "what kills this, and have I watched it die?"

Run the probe once. If it prints MISSING, you just saved yourself a confusing support ticket. If it prints SURVIVED, you now have evidence instead of a feeling.

title: Wide View Synthesis from Overlapping Perspective Cameras in Autonomous Driving
description:
arXiv:2611.07081v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-perspective-camera systems are widely adopted since they provide broad visual coverage for autonomous driving, motivating the synthesis of a unified wide view from spatially separated observations. In this work, we formulate wide view synthesis (WVS), which aims to synthesize a geometrically consistent wide view at a specified virtual viewpoint from multiple perspective cameras. Unlike conventional image stitching, WVS requires reasoning about 3D geometry and visibility to handle depth-dependent parallax and occlusions arising from spatially separated camera centers. While vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-fidelity view synthesis, its reliance on per-scene optimization limits its applicability to driving scenes. Furthermore, WVS introduces additional challenges, *e.g.*, peripheral stretching under perspective projection and photometric inconsistencies across cameras. To address these challenges, we propose **Wide-View Gaussian Splatting (WV-GS)**, a feed-forward Gaussian-splatting framework that synthesizes wide views without per-scene optimization. Specifically, we introduce Piecewise Perspective Rendering (PPR) to mitigate peripheral stretching through local perspective projections sharing a common camera center, and Spatial Affine Photometric Modeling (SAPM) to account for camera-dependent photometric variations during training. We further introduce **WideDrive**, a synthetic benchmark providing dense ground-truth wide views and adapt a LiDAR-projected sparse-reference protocol to real-world datasets. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of WV-GS for WVS. Dataset and code will be publicly released.

title: Automatic keyphrase extraction and annotation: modern theoretical approaches and practical solutions for text and speech
description:
arXiv:2611.08006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The exponential growth of textual and audiovisual information has made the task of automatic keyphrase extraction (KE) increasingly significant. This article provides a comprehensive analysis of contemporary theoretical approaches and practical solutions for KE across both text and speech modalities. The primary contribution of this work is its systematic synthesis of these often-disparate research strands into a unified analytical framework, highlighting the evolution of the field from statistical methods towards large language models (LLMs) and end-to-end speech processing. We examine the stages of KE, the characteristics of keyphrases in written and spoken language, and terminological nuances. Various methods for automatic KE are discussed and analyzed in detail: statistical, hybrid, machine learning-based, and structural. The review dedicates substantial attention to emerging paradigms, including keyphrase generation using LLMs, and provides a detailed overview of methodologies and challenges in automatic corpus annotation. Furthermore, we specifically analyze current directions and inherent difficulties in KE for spoken language, comparing transcript based and end-to-end acoustic approaches. This synthesis leads us to conclude that the field is moving towards a more integrated, context-aware paradigm. Future progress will depend on addressing key challenges such as data scarcity for low-resource languages, effective multimodal fusion, and the nuanced evaluation of generative KE systems.

title: ReviewMap: Mapping Evaluative Acts and Automation Boundaries in Peer-Review Comments
description:
arXiv:2611.07489v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Peer-review comments check what a paper does and judge why it matters, but no existing scheme distinguishes these two evaluative acts. We argue that making these acts explicit and measuring how reliably LLMs identify them is a prerequisite for responsible LLM-assisted review analysis: humans need to inspect review judgments and their grounds. This defines a more honest mission for NLP in peer review than full automation. We present ReviewMap, a framework that classifies each comment as assessment of claims and scholarly standards or calibration of contribution value and venue fit, with finer-grained attributes applied conditionally by act type. Applied to 500 ICLR~2026 papers through multi-model LLM consensus, the act layer proves reliably automatable under the operational guideline (inter-model $\kappa \geq 0.75$), supported by five-human validation on 470 development comments, while the attribute layer requires human oversight, defining a measured automation boundary. At the corpus level, 17% of reviewer-paper instances contain no panel-coded calibration, and the panel-coded calibration share is nearly $3\times$ as high in Strengths as in Weaknesses. This boundary informs three affordances: a review guideline that operationalizes the assessment-then-calibration workflow for reviewers, a per-comment rebuttal strategy scaffold for authors, and a discussion-phase dashboard for area chairs.

title: TileQuant: Tile as the Precision-Allocation Unit for LLM Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization
description:
arXiv:2611.07217v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces large language model (LLM) deployment costs, but preserving quality requires accounting for uneven weight sensitivity. Uniform PTQ uses one weight bit-width, importance-aware PTQ adjusts scales or reconstructs weights within that width, and column-wise mixed precision retains selected columns at higher precision. However, sensitivity varies within columns, so whole-column retention also protects less sensitive weights, while runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead. We therefore introduce TileQuant, a training-free framework that assigns precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. Offline calibration provides input-activation-aware scoring from forward statistics for lower calibration cost and gradient-informed scoring from loss sensitivity for stronger quality preservation. Within each projection's retention budget, the highest-scoring tiles remain at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit. The resulting map guides reconstruction into compact weight buffers, which the kernel reuses for native integer and 16-bit computation with local accumulation to reduce memory traffic. Experiments show that TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering, it preserves quality and surpasses quantized and original models on multiple tasks. These results support selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution. The implementation is: https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TileQuant

title: Machine Learning for Live-Birth Prediction After IVF/ICSI From Structured Clinical Data: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Critical Appraisal
description:
arXiv:2611.07124v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine-learning models predicting live birth after in vitro fertilisation (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) from routine clinical data report performance from near chance to near perfect. We systematically reviewed these models under PRISMA 2020, searching OpenAlex, Scopus and Web of Science to 22 October 2026, appraised them with PROBAST+AI and TRIPOD+AI, and pooled their discrimination with random-effects meta-analysis on the logit scale. We define what fixes the meaning of a model's output (decision point, endpoint, unit of analysis, data source) and map the 48 included studies by model family, decision point and validation design. Models evaluated only internally pooled to an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.814, against 0.756 (95% prediction interval 0.546-0.889) for models evaluated on a later period or another centre, and 0.764 for studies not at high risk of bias; neither difference was significant, and heterogeneity was extreme. Models whose decision point was not stated pooled to 0.910, the only significant moderator in meta-regression. Against logistic regression fitted to the same data, the best machine-learning model gained a pooled 0.056 AUC (95% CI 0.017-0.090). Of 48 studies, 47 were at high or unclear risk of bias, only four assessed the calibration slope, and no model has evidence of clinical impact. The certainty of the pooled evidence is low to very low; the gains that survive validation came from staging predictions to decision points and local calibration, not deeper architectures. We provide a TRIPOD+AI-mapped checklist, a benchmark specification and a research agenda.

title: Structured Machine Theory of Mind from Agent Trajectories
description:
arXiv:2611.07208v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Predictive models of human behavior trained on large-scale trajectory data optimize for statistical accuracy without representing the mental states that causally generate behavior. Such models support prediction but not principled intervention: they cannot answer how an agent's behavior would change if its beliefs or preferences were different. We introduce Structured Machine Theory of Mind (SMToM), a framework that attributes explicit, independently supervised belief and desire representations from observed trajectories within a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) causal structure. The central architectural element is a goal head that consumes only the predicted mental-state channels and a current-trajectory embedding; counterfactual intervention on beliefs and desires is a direct operation. We instantiate SMToM on a controlled pedestrian navigation domain where ground-truth mental states are known by construction, enabling evaluation of attribution accuracy, local channel interventions, and trajectory-level counterfactual diagnostics. The resulting model, BDIBottleneck, improves over trajectory-only and unsupervised-context neural baselines. It is also competitive with a matched auxiliary-supervised context baseline while providing an editable mental-state interface that the unbottlenecked baseline lacks. Counterfactual experiments on desires confirm that substituting an agent's inferred preferences with a different activity type coherently shifts predicted destinations toward relevant locations. Counterfactual experiments on beliefs confirm that marking a location as unavailable in the agent's belief state reduces its predicted probability as a destination, though in a complex way. These results demonstrate, in a controlled navigation setting, that explicit BDI-structured supervision is a viable foundation for interpretable and counterfactual analysis of longitudinal trajectory data.

title: One Solana Slot, Multiple Banks: Fork-Aware Geyser Indexing
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

Your Geyser plugin buffers account updates by slot and writes a slot to the analytics tables when the slot is rooted. For as long as a slot meant one bank, that was correct. In October, Agave’s accounts database finished a migration whose stated purpose is to let “multiple banks with the same slot” exist side by side.

A bank is one replay of one block. When a node replays a slot twice, both replays stream their account writes and transactions to every Geyser plugin as they execute, and only one of them is ever finalized. The interface has been naming the bank behind each update since version 4.3.0. An indexer that keys by slot alone merges the two, and the abandoned bank’s data reaches the finalized table.

Here is where the second bank comes from, what a plugin is and is not told, what a slot-keyed indexer commits wrongly, and the bank-keyed buffer that fixes it, with tests that show both.

A slot is not a bank

A slot is a position in time: the window one leader has to produce a block. A bank is a node’s execution of a specific block at that position, with its own account changes, its own transaction results and its own ID. The Solana SDK says it plainly: a BankId “is unique even if the slot number of two different slots is the same”.

Agave’s accounts database used to assume the opposite inside its write cache, the in-memory layer that holds a bank’s account writes until its slot is rooted and flushed. Between late September and the end of October, one Agave engineer moved it from slot keys to bank keys:

BankId becomes its own type (#15620) — 2 Oct

Ancestors carry (slot, bank ID) (#15857) — 8 Oct

Write cache rekeyed by bank ID (#16102) — 20 Oct

Roots added by bank (#16262) — 23 Oct

Purge by bank ID (#16360) — 27 Oct

Flush and freeze by bank ID (#16447, #16459) — 28 Oct

Slot-to-bank map removed (#16497) — 28 Oct

Purge deferred to bank drop (#16508) — 31 Oct

The two highlighted changes say what the series is for. #16360 switched purging to bank IDs “so multiple banks with the same slot can exist in the write cache”. #16497 removed the last lookup by slot, after which the cache “no longer asserts one bank per slot: banks at the same slot each keep their own cache, and removing a bank removes only its own cache.” Before the series, the old bank’s cache had to be purged inline before the slot could be created again. #16508 moved that purge to the background and measured it falling from about 2 milliseconds to about 100 microseconds.

Where the second bank comes from

Three paths in Agave’s replay stage clear a bank and let the same slot be replayed into a new one.

  • Switching to the cluster’s version of a block. A leader can produce more than one version of a block for its slot. Under Alpenglow, live on mainnet since 21 October, votor tells replay when the version the cluster certified differs from the one the node replayed. Replay repairs the cluster’s version, then clears its own bank for that slot and every descendant and replays again. The same slots come back with new bank IDs.
  • Fast leader handover. The first slot of a leader’s four-slot window may start on an optimistic parent, before the previous leader’s last block is settled. If the leader then switches parents, the block carries an UpdateParent marker, and replay clears the in-progress bank and recreates it from the marker’s position in the block.
  • The leader’s own optimistic bank. On the producing side, the same handover clears the bank the leader started building and replaces it.

The second and third paths are fast leader handover, and replay’s restart path checks the FastLeaderHandover11111111111111111111111111 feature, which has not been activated on mainnet. The first needs only a leader that produced two versions of a block, which is rare, but the path is live today. The write-cache series is what lets these replays happen without the old bank’s cache being torn down first.

What a Geyser plugin is told, and what it is not

Since agave-geyser-plugin-interface 4.3.0, the callbacks that carry data name the bank they came from. In version 6.0.0, the current one on 31 October:

update_account_for_bank — slot + bank ID, every write

notify_transaction_for_bank — slot + bank ID, every transaction

update_bank_status · Rooted — bank ID + parent, once per rooted slot

update_slot_status · Dead — slot only, no bank ID

notify_entry_update_parent — cleared bank ID, entry plugins only

bank cleared to switch block versions — no callback at all

Three things in that table decide how an indexer has to be built.

Discards are mostly silent. The only notice of a cleared bank is the UpdateParent entry notification, and the plugin manager sends it only to plugins that enable entry notifications, which most account indexers do not. A bank cleared to switch block versions produces nothing at all. By the time either happens, the bank’s writes and transactions have already been delivered.

Finality is per bank, and ordered. When votor roots a block, the RPC tracker sorts the newly rooted chain by slot and reports each slot once, with its bank ID and with the previous root as its parent. The chain arrives contiguous: a slot between a rooted slot and its reported parent was never rooted. And a bank’s Rooted arrives after its data. Account writes are delivered synchronously while the bank replays, before it can freeze. Transactions travel through a separate service, but the root notification waits on that service’s declared work before it is processed.

Old plugins are blind. The slot-only callbacks were deprecated in 4.3.0, and each new bank-aware method’s default implementation forwards to its old counterpart, dropping the bank ID on the way. A plugin that still implements only update_account keeps compiling and keeps receiving data, with no way to tell two banks of one slot apart.

What a slot-keyed indexer commits

To see the failure without a validator, we fed the event sequence these paths produce to two small indexers in Rust. One buffers by slot and commits a slot when it is rooted. The other buffers by slot and bank ID. Slot 104 is replayed twice: bank 5 executes transactions a and b, writing account X to 70 and account Y to 1, and is then cleared. Bank 6 executes transaction c, writing X to 90, and is rooted.

// bank 5: the version that is abandoned
ix.transaction(104, 5, sig(0xa));
ix.account(104, 5, w(X, 70, 2));
ix.transaction(104, 5, sig(0xb));
ix.account(104, 5, w(Y, 1, 3));
// bank 6: the version the cluster finalizes
ix.transaction(104, 6, sig(0xc));
ix.account(104, 6, w(X, 90, 4));
ix.rooted(104, 103, 6);

// slot-keyed: Y = 1 is "finalized", slot 104 has 3 transactions
// bank-keyed: no Y, slot 104 has 1 transaction (c), X = 90

The slot-keyed indexer commits a value for Y that never existed on the finalized chain, and counts three transactions in a block that has one. Volume, fee and activity tables built on it are inflated by exactly the abandoned bank’s work.

It does get X right, and only by luck. Both banks wrote X, and the higher write_version happened to belong to bank 6, because the clearing paths remove the old bank before the new one replays. Swap the arrival order and a third test shows the slot-keyed indexer committing the abandoned value. Nothing in the interface promises that order, and the write-cache series exists to make same-slot banks cheaper to keep around.

Key by bank, commit on the rooted bank

The fix is a different buffer key and one rule at root time:

pub struct BankKeyed {
    pending: BTreeMap<(Slot, BankId), Pending>,
    pub finalized: Finalized,
}

impl BankKeyed {
    // update_account_for_bank / notify_transaction_for_bank
    pub fn account(&mut self, slot: Slot, bank_id: BankId, w: AccountWrite) {
        self.pending.entry((slot, bank_id)).or_default().write(w);
    }

    // update_bank_status(slot, parent, Rooted, bank_id): one call per newly
    // rooted slot, in slot order, parent = the previous root. Every bank
    // buffered in (parent, slot] is decided now: keep the rooted one.
    pub fn rooted(&mut self, slot: Slot, parent: Slot, bank_id: BankId) {
        let decided: Vec<_> = self
            .pending
            .range((parent + 1, BankId::MIN)..=(slot, BankId::MAX))
            .map(|(key, _)| *key)
            .collect();
        for key in decided {
            let p = self.pending.remove(&key).expect("key was just listed");
            if key == (slot, bank_id) {
                p.commit(slot, &mut self.finalized);
            }
        }
    }
}

The range does two jobs. It drops other banks at the rooted slot, the same-slot case, and it drops banks at slots the chain skipped, an ordinary abandoned fork, because a slot between a root and its reported parent will never be rooted. Banks above the rooted slot stay buffered until their own turn. Handling notify_entry_update_parent is optional: it lets a cleared bank’s buffer go early, but correctness rests on the rooted bank ID, the one signal every plugin receives.

Six tests pin both behaviours down. Two show the slot-keyed indexer committing the abandoned bank’s data, one of them through arrival order alone. The others show the bank-keyed buffer handling the same-slot case, an abandoned fork at a skipped slot, descendants of the root that must stay buffered, and the early discard. Inside a bank, the highest write_version per account is its final state, and that rule is still correct. It just has to be applied per bank, not per slot.

What this does not show

The tests replay event sequences derived from Agave’s source. They are not a captured Geyser stream from a validator, and we have not measured how often a mainnet node clears a bank today. With fast leader handover inactive, only the block-version switch can do it on mainnet, and that needs a leader to have produced two versions of a block.

The ordering guarantees in section 03 come from reading the notification paths, not from a fault-injection test. And a Dead status still names only a slot. A plugin that must react to a dead bank, rather than simply never committing it, cannot tell from that call which of a slot’s banks died.

Same-Slot Banks: Questions People Actually Ask

Can two Solana banks have the same slot?

Yes. A bank is one replay of one block, and Agave gives every bank a unique bank ID even when two banks share a slot. Under Alpenglow a node replaces its bank for a slot when the cluster settles on a different version of that block, and fast leader handover adds a second way once its feature activates.

Does Geyser tell a plugin which bank an update came from?

Since agave-geyser-plugin-interface 4.3.0, yes: update_account_for_bank, notify_transaction_for_bank and update_bank_status all carry a bank_id. The older slot-only callbacks are deprecated, and the default bank-aware methods forward to them without the bank ID.

How does an indexer know which bank was finalized?

Agave reports every newly rooted slot through update_bank_status with SlotStatus::Rooted and the rooted bank’s ID, in slot order, with the previous root as the parent. Commit only that bank, and discard every other bank buffered between the parent and the rooted slot.

Is buffering by slot until the slot is rooted enough?

No. A slot-keyed buffer merges every bank that ever replayed the slot, so accounts written only by an abandoned bank and transactions executed only in it reach the finalized table. Key the buffer by slot and bank ID.

Does Agave notify a plugin when it discards a bank?

Not in general. A bank cleared by fast leader handover produces an UpdateParent entry notification, but only to plugins that enable entry notifications. A bank cleared to switch to the cluster’s version of a block produces no notification at all. The rooted bank ID is the only signal every plugin gets.

The one-line version

A slot can have more than one bank, Geyser streams all of them, and only the bank named in the Rooted status is the finalized one. Key the buffer by slot and bank ID, and implement the _for_bank callbacks.

The pipeline this buffer belongs in is the subject of ingesting the Solana firehose with Rust, and the certificates that decide which bank is rooted are in Alpenglow finality in numbers. What a block says about its own producer is in which client built each block.

Sources: Agave master at commit 5817ebe009, the merge of #16508: replay_stage.rs, update_parent.rs, optimistically_confirmed_bank_tracker.rs, entry_notifier.rs and transaction_status_service.rs; pull requests #16360, #16497 and #16508; the GeyserPlugin trait in agave-geyser-plugin-interface 6.0.0; and solana_clock::BankId. The feature account FastLeaderHandover11111111111111111111111111 does not exist on mainnet.

title: Solana Geo Leader Schedule: Location Pays, Splitting Doesn’t
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

Under Alpenglow’s fast leader handover, the gap between two leaders is mostly the time a block takes to cross from one to the next. Today’s schedule picks leaders at random, so that crossing is often an ocean. SIMD-0675 proposes to reorder the schedule so that leaders near each other go one after another.

In review, Dean Little raised the obvious worry: that the reordering “appears to incentivize sybils”, letting validators use geography, “or even just a self-attestation of geography”, to line up their leader rotations “with better-than-random odds”. Two days later, the author of the proposal’s parameter analysis answered that splitting stake barely moves the odds, 7.146% to 7.147% in one example, because “the majority of the ‘upside’ for extractors (compared to random) is already given by the schedule design.”

We rebuilt the reordering in Rust from the specification to check both statements. The reviewer is right about splitting: it changes nothing, not even one window. But the second half of the sentence is the finding. The upside the schedule hands out depends on where an operator’s stake sits, and an honest operator in the right region gets back-to-back windows five to seven times as often as today, without splitting or lying about anything.

Bins, radii and runs

The base schedule is computed exactly as today, one stake-weighted random leader per four-slot window. SIMD-0675 then walks it in order and drops each leader into a bin:

  • Radius. Every validator has a radius, the smallest distance around it that holds STAKE_FLOOR (10%) of all stake. Dense places get small radii, isolated ones large radii. Locations are self-reported, through SIMD-0674.
  • Bins. A leader joins a random open bin whose anchor is within the larger of the two radii, or opens a new bin if none is.
  • Runs. When a bin holds RUN_LENGTH leaders, it is shuffled and written out as a block of consecutive windows. The proposal says 3; reviewers have argued for 7.

Every validator keeps exactly the windows it would have had. Only their order changes. With 200 ms slots, a run of three windows is 2.4 seconds of block production from one area of the map.

for &l in base {
    let near: Vec<usize> = (0..bins.len())
        .filter(|&i| {
            let a = bins[i].anchor;
            dist2(&vs[l], &vs[a]) <= r[a].max(r[l])
        })
        .collect();
    let bi = if near.is_empty() {
        bins.push(Bin { anchor: l, members: vec![l] });
        bins.len() - 1
    } else {
        let i = near[rng.roll(near.len())]; // one roll per join
        bins[i].members.push(l);
        i
    };
    if bins[bi].members.len() == run_length {
        let mut b = bins.remove(bi);
        rng.shuffle(&mut b.members); // Fisher-Yates
        out.extend(b.members);
    }
}
// end of epoch: shuffle the open bins, shuffle each one, append

The model, and a check against the proposal

Our implementation follows the specification’s pseudocode line for line: the radius, the nearness test, one random draw per join, Fisher-Yates within a run and a shuffled flush at the end of the epoch. Two simplifications are deliberate. The random generator is SplitMix64 rather than the specified ChaCha20, which changes which schedule comes out but not its statistics. And the network is stylized: about 800 validators with lognormal stake across 19 metros. Asia holds 10.4% of stake, the figure in the parameter analysis published on solana.com; the European and North American split and the metro mix are our assumptions. Latency between leaders uses the analysis’ estimate, 1.5 times the great-circle distance at 200 km per millisecond. Each scenario is 108,000 windows, an epoch, averaged over five seeds.

Mean handover, random schedule (SIMD’s figure) — 37.3 ms (36.2)

RUN_LENGTH 3 — 18.2 ms (17.0)

RUN_LENGTH 7 — 11.6 ms (10.8)

The proposal’s simulation, on the real stake distribution of epoch 1038 and measured round-trip times, is in brackets. Our stylized network lands within about a millisecond at every run length, which is close enough to trust it for the question it was built for: who gets consecutive windows.

Splitting stake changes nothing

We gave one operator 3% of stake as one validator in Frankfurt, then as six validators of 0.5% each in the same place. The two schedules were identical, window for window, at every run length.

That is not a statistical tie, it is structural. The base schedule gives the six the same windows the one would have had. The radius of a location is computed from all the stake there, so it is the same. And a bin only ever asks about locations and radii, never identities. Sybils at one address are invisible to the reorder, which is the reviewer’s 7.146% to 7.147% taken to its limit.

Splitting across regions is worse than useless for an extractor. The same 3% spread over Frankfurt, Ashburn and Singapore led two windows in a row 4.2% of the time at RUN_LENGTH 3, against 7.6% for the operator that stayed in one place.

Location changes a lot

Consecutive windows under one operator are the precondition for multi-block MEV: two windows are eight slots in which one party orders every transaction. We measured how often an operator’s window is followed by another of its own, under today’s random schedule and under the reorder. Columns are random, then RUN_LENGTH 3, then 7.

1% operator, Frankfurt — 1.06% → 2.56% → 3.31%

1% operator, Tokyo — 1.06% → 5.31% → 7.66%

3% operator, Frankfurt — 3.15% → 7.56% → 9.22%

3% operator, Tokyo — 3.15% → 15.10% → 19.10%

3% split over three regions — 3.15% → 4.18% → 4.90%

Under random, the chance is the operator’s stake share, wherever it sits. Under the reorder, a run is filled from nearby stake, so the chance tracks the operator’s share of its region instead. Three percent of all stake is a modest slice of Europe and a large slice of Asia, the smallest region that still forms bins of its own at a 10% floor. The same operator in Tokyo gets back-to-back windows 4.8 times as often as today at RUN_LENGTH 3, and 6.1 times at 7, twice what it would get in Frankfurt.

Nobody lied and nobody split stake. This is the schedule working as designed, and it is the reviewer’s point stated with a location attached: the upside comes from the design, and the design pays most to the largest operator in the smallest self-contained region. The solana.com analysis already notes that Asia sits just above the floor, at 10.4%, “with very little margin”. Our numbers say the margin is also where consecutive control is cheapest.

And lying about it

The attack the proposal’s authors model is a validator that declares an isolated location, so that no one else joins its bins. The solana.com analysis uses the most isolated point it could find, in the South Pacific, and reports that at RUN_LENGTH 7 lying is worth 0.28 extra consecutive windows to a validator with 4.07% of stake, the largest today, and 1.69 to one with 10%.

4.07% operator, back-to-back, truthful in Frankfurt — 4.23% → 10.13% → 12.15%

4.07% operator, back-to-back, declares South Pacific — 4.23% → 32.34% → 41.59%

10% operator, back-to-back, truthful in Frankfurt — 10.05% → 21.72% → 25.98%

10% operator, back-to-back, declares South Pacific — 10.05% → 65.11% → 83.19%

Measured the analysis’ way, as the expected run remaining from one of the liar’s windows, our model puts the gain from lying, against the same operator in Frankfurt, at 0.58 windows for the 4.07% validator and 2.43 for the 10% one, both at RUN_LENGTH 7. That is higher than the analysis’ figures, which come from the real map, where a few validators in Argentina and Australia can still reach the isolated point. The direction is the same: lying pays a little below the floor and a lot at it, which is why STAKE_FLOOR is pinned at 10%.

The proposal’s own location-fibbing table shows lying rarely improves a validator’s latency. It was never meant to. The reason to lie is the run, not the handover.

What it means for the parameters

RUN_LENGTH moves every number above. Going from 3 to 7 buys 6.6 milliseconds of mean handover in our model and raises back-to-back control for every operator we measured. The proposal’s authors prefer 3 for exactly this reason; the analysis finds a knee at 7 and calls 3 “the conservative choice”. Reviewers suggested handling Sybils outside the protocol, by raising the validator admission ticket or by detecting misreported locations, and the authors agreed that detection is probably possible.

Neither remedy touches the effect in section 04. A ticket prices the number of validators, and the location-driven gain needs only one. Detection catches false locations, and the Tokyo operator’s location is true. If the concern is consecutive control by honest operators, the levers are the run length and the floor, and the floor is already pressed against Asia’s share.

What this does not show

The network is stylized, so the exact percentages belong to it; the mechanism, that consecutive control tracks local rather than global share, does not depend on the split we chose. Back-to-back windows are a precondition for multi-block MEV, not a measure of its value, which the analysis also stresses. The random generator differs from the specified one. And SIMD-0675 and SIMD-0674 are open proposals, last amended on 22 October, so the constants may still change.

Geo-Aware Leader Schedule: Questions People Actually Ask

What is Solana’s geo-aware leader schedule?

SIMD-0675, an open proposal, keeps today’s stake-weighted random leader schedule and then reorders it: leaders that are geographically close are grouped into runs of RUN_LENGTH consecutive leader windows, so the handover between them is short. Every validator keeps exactly as many windows as before.

Does splitting stake into several validators help under SIMD-0675?

Not at one location. The reorder sees a validator’s location and stake, not its identity, so six validators in one city with a combined stake behave exactly like one. In our model they produced identical schedules, window for window.

Where does the geo-aware schedule give an operator more consecutive windows?

Where its share of the local stake is large. A run is filled from nearby stake, so an operator’s chance of leading two windows in a row tracks its share of its region. In our model a 3% operator in Tokyo got back-to-back windows 15% of the time at RUN_LENGTH 3, against 3% under today’s random schedule and 7.6% in Frankfurt.

Can a validator lie about its location to get consecutive leader slots?

Yes, and the proposal’s parameter analysis measures it: a validator that declares an isolated location ends up alone in its bins. The analysis puts the gain at 0.28 extra consecutive windows for a 4.07% validator at RUN_LENGTH 7, rising sharply once the liar holds STAKE_FLOOR, 10% of stake, which is why STAKE_FLOOR sits at 10%.

Is SIMD-0675 live on mainnet?

No. As of 26 October 2026 it is an open proposal, as is SIMD-0674, the location registration it depends on. Its parameters, especially RUN_LENGTH, are still being debated between 3 and 7.

The one-line version

SIMD-0675 halves handover latency and does not reward Sybils, but it turns local stake share into consecutive leader windows, and the smallest region that forms its own bins is where a large operator gains the most.

The consensus this schedule feeds is in Alpenglow finality in numbers, the admission ticket reviewers proposed raising is in the 2,000 validator seats, and the stake-weighted QoS that follows the leader is in stake-weighted QoS, with the formula.

Sources: SIMD-0675 and SIMD-0674 as amended on 22 October 2026, with their review threads to 26 October; the parameter analysis on solana.com, by Umberto Natale, 14 October 2026. Results are from our Rust model of the reorder, described in section 02.

description:

title: Robust Ranking of Port Impacts from Impending Tropical Cyclones: A Two-Stage Recommendation System
description:
arXiv:2611.07296v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a tropical cyclone (TC) threatens several ports, preparedness planning depends on anticipating which ports are likely to be affected and where disruptions may last longest. Limited historical observations at individual ports and uncertainty in landfall location make these relative impacts difficult to estimate. We use a two-stage recommendation framework that first selects candidate ports based on their proximity to the expected landfall location and then ranks them by their estimated number of impact days. Using AIS-derived impact days for 37 ports and 31 TCs in the Gulf of Mexico study region, we compare three ways of representing port--cyclone interactions: pairwise feature interactions, tree-based feature combinations, and explicit feature crosses combined with learned embeddings. In tests on Hurricanes Nicole and Ian, the retrieval stage consistently identifies all observed affected ports under landfall uncertainty. Among the ranking models, Wide & Deep Learning achieves the closest agreement with the observed port rankings. Its mean ranking agreement exceeds that of the distance-based baseline by 85.5% for Nicole and 55.5% for Ian and is less sensitive to uncertainty in the landfall location. These rankings could help port authorities prioritize post-cyclone inspections and allocate recovery resources across ports threatened by the same event.

title: Householder Motion Embedding: Noise Modulation for Motion-Controllable Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.07294v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models for video generation have achieved remarkable success, yet precise motion control under explicit user guidance remains challenging. Recent noise-warping methods introduce temporal correlations by warping the noise according to the user-provided motion signal. However, standard spatial warping generally disrupts the noise's i.i.d. Gaussian structure, requiring distribution correction, such as Jacobian-based correction, but at a substantial computational overhead. We propose Householder Motion Embedding (HME), which encodes the motion signal into the noise through a sequence of Householder reflections that together form an orthogonal transformation applied to each location's channel vector. HME exactly preserves the spatial Gaussian structure within each frame while introducing cross-frame correlations that promote temporally consistent video. HME is agnostic to the network architecture and integrates directly into standard video diffusion fine-tuning pipelines. Experiments on different scenarios show that HME matches or outperforms the state of the art, while achieving a 2.7x speedup over noise warping. These results demonstrate that channel-space Householder transformations offer a principled and efficient alternative to noise warping for motion-controllable video generation.

title: I got tired of pasting API keys into every coding agent, so I built a local router
description:
You open Cursor and paste an OpenAI key. Then Claude Code wants Anthropic. OpenCode wants something else. Switch models for a week and you're editing three config files and hoping you didn't leave a key in a screenshot.

I wanted one address on my own machine that every OpenAI-compatible client could talk to, with the provider keys staying on disk. That's WowRouter.

What it actually is

WowRouter is a local AI router. It listens only on this computer:

What Address
Web panel http://127.0.0.1:8787
OpenAI-compatible API http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1

You add provider keys in the panel, turn models on, create a router key (shown once, starts with sk-airoute-), and point Cursor or any OpenAI client at that base URL with the router key.

A public model id looks like openai/gpt-4o-mini. You can also set the model to auto (or auto/cheap, auto/fast, auto/coding) and let the router pick among the chat models you turned on. Named combos use ids like fallback/daily and fall through when a model fails.

Provider keys are encrypted with a local secret. Router keys are stored as hashes — the panel cannot show a router key again after you leave the create screen. The server rejects a listen address that isn't loopback (127.0.0.1, localhost, or ::1).

Install

Node.js 20 or newer:

npm install -g wowrouter
wowrouter

npm install -g airoute is the same program. Desktop builds for Windows, macOS and Linux are attached to each GitHub release. Docker works too, still bound to this computer:

docker run -d --name wowrouter \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8787:8787 \
  -v wowrouter:/data \
  foisalislambd/wowrouter:latest

First setup

  1. Open the panel.
  2. Providers — save an API key (GitHub Enterprise Copilot uses Sign in with GitHub; Copilot Web asks for a bearer token). Rows marked Unsupported have no stable API.
  3. Turn on the models you want. A model that is off is not offered to clients.
  4. API keys — create a router key.
  5. In Cursor (or any OpenAI client): base URL http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1, API key = that router key.

Chat calls need three things at once: a saved provider key, the model switched on, and a router key on the request. Password / OIDC on the panel are off by default. Leave them off on your own computer. Turn one on before you publish the port (for example from Docker on a VPS).

Some providers ship with an empty model list. Load models on that provider's page fills it from the provider.

What's in the panel

Overview, Providers, Routing (auto presets and named fallbacks), API keys, Playground, Activity (each gateway call with request/response), Clients (copy-paste setup plus a confirmed one-click writer for Claude Code, OpenCode and Codex), Usage (calls by model, 14-day chart, estimated cost), Memory (optional notes prepended to chat), and Settings.

Closing the browser tab does not stop the router.

Stack and license

Go server and SQLite, React panel, native desktop wrapper, npm CLI that launches the server. MIT. Current release is v1.5.5. Repo: github.com/foisalislambd/wowrouter.

Honest limits

  • It's young. The repo started in October 2026. I'm one person.
  • Some providers are marked Unsupported. Decision models use POST /v1/systemone, not chat completions.
  • If you expose the port past loopback without a panel password or OIDC, that's on you — the README is clear about locking it first.
  • I have not counted how many providers the catalog currently lists; open the Providers page after install rather than trusting a number from a blog post.

If you try it and something breaks, open an issue on the repo. If your setup is "three agents, five keys, one laptop", I'd like to know whether one local endpoint actually helped.

— foisal

title: Latency-Aware Adaptive Best-of-$N$
description:
arXiv:2611.07453v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language model responses by spending additional computation at inference time, and the right amount of compute depends on the prompt. Adaptive TTC methods allocate compute based on signals of response quality such as observed rewards, often by stopping once the signal exceeds a fixed threshold, and generally measure cost by the number of generations or tokens. But in online serving, latency is also a cost: it grows with server load, so a method using a fixed threshold spends too little compute when generation is fast and too much when it is slow. For Best-of-$N$ sampling, a widely used TTC method, we propose a two-stage adaptive algorithm that draws an initial batch, then uses the observed rewards and the batch's latency to decide whether to draw a second batch and at what size by comparing expected improvement against predicted cost: it draws one when the first batch's best reward is below a threshold that decreases with the first batch's latency, without explicitly measuring server load. We map each reward to its value under the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the prompt's reward distribution, so the same tradeoff parameters can be reused across tasks; a regression fitted offline on other prompts predicts a distribution for the CDF value of the first batch's best reward, giving the expected improvement in closed form. We evaluate the method by simulation on a preference-based alignment benchmark, measuring generations-equivalent cost: generations plus latency, converted to generations. The method reaches Best-of-$N$'s reward at lower generations-equivalent cost, and conditioning on the measured first-batch latency saves at least as much of that cost as fixed-threshold (latency-unaware) baselines, and more when latency is highly variable, when it grows with batch size, and when the second batch's latency is highly predictable from the first's.

title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
description:
arXiv:2611.07854v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autoregressive approaches with large language models, such as long chain-of-thought reasoning, have become the default for new AI applications because they reach higher accuracy on a wide range of tasks. In production, however, they give inconsistent answers, require parsing of outputs, and add cost and latency. Decision models address this: given a question and a set of options supplied by the user, they return a probability distribution over the options without autoregressive decoding. We present Drex, a family of four open decision models with 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B with 3B active (v2.0), and 27B (Max) parameters. Each request consists of a state (a document, record, or agent context, optionally with images) and questions about it, each asking for a choice among options, a yes/no judgment, or a score on an ordered scale. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), plus vision tuning for Max. Ablations show that RLAF improves accuracy and that consistency losses improve robustness to option order. On Decision Index 0.4.1, Max sets a new state of the art among the decision models we compare (67.52 on the public suite vs. 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0). On Decision Bench v4, it is statistically tied with d3-turbo and GPT-6 Sol and trails Claude Opus 5.5 by 1.6 points, and it has the highest accuracy among decision models on DecideBench. Max answers a typical request in 183 ms, against about 2.0 s for GPT-6 Sol and 3.5 s for Claude Opus 5.5, and its outputs are stable under option reordering. All four models are open source: https://github.com/nace-ai/drex-decision-models

title: Circe: Training-Free LLM Self-Evaluation via Component Interaction Consistency
description:
arXiv:2611.07948v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, evaluating the correctness of their responses is crucial for reliable use. However, such evaluation is challenging because reference answers are rarely available in practice. Existing reference-free methods mainly rely on output signals, which may assign high scores to incorrect responses and thus do not necessarily reflect correctness. This motivates exploring the model's internal computation for complementary correctness signals. Recent studies exploit internal states, but they mainly analyze hidden-state trajectories across layers, which record only the combined updates of attention and feed-forward networks (FFNs) and overlook how these components interact. We therefore propose Circe, a training-free self-evaluation method that assesses a response using both internal and external signals, without reference answers or repeated sampling. For internal signals, we first introduce component interaction consistency (CIC), which measures the directional alignment between attention updates in earlier layers and attention-induced FFN output changes in later layers. We further incorporate representation geometry (RG) to characterize normalized displacement and angular changes along layerwise hidden-state trajectories. For the external signal, we convert the mean negative log-likelihood of generated tokens into a bounded likelihood confidence (LC) score. Finally, we fuse CIC, RG, and LC into a unified correctness score. Experiments on five LLMs and six benchmarks across four domains show that our method distinguishes correct from incorrect responses more effectively than existing baselines, and generalizes to multilingual, multimodal, and open-world settings.

title: Redacting Personal Data: A Speed and Accuracy Comparison of Regex, Presidio and Hybrid Designs
description:
arXiv:2611.07633v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many enterprise projects now pass free text to large language models (LLMs), and that text often contains personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, phone numbers, email addresses, home addresses and dates of birth. Once a prompt is sent, this data is copied into provider systems, application logs and observability traces. Redacting PII before the call is an obvious control, yet teams seldom have numbers on what it costs in latency or what it lets through. This paper compares four redaction designs that any LLM pipeline can adopt: a pure regular-expression (regex) redactor, Microsoft Presidio running on a spaCy model, a hybrid in which Presidio finds only person names while regex handles structured identifiers, and a fast hybrid that calls spaCy's named-entity component directly. All four share a known-entity rule, which removes the person the system already knows it is handling, and a consistent placeholder scheme, so the LLM can still tell one person from another after redaction. We evaluate the designs on a sample workflow, which we call ProfileAssist, that turns resumes into structured profiles, using 100 synthetic resumes (523 characters on average, with 900 PII values and 600 business terms that must survive). Regex ran at a 0.20 ms median but caught only 88.9% of PII, because it cannot find names that are not known in advance, such as the references listed in a resume. Presidio, hybrid and fast hybrid each caught 100% of PII and kept 100% of business terms, at median latencies of 37.59 ms, 30.23 ms and 13.48 ms. Measured against a 9,120 ms median LLM call, even the slowest option adds only 0.41% to the request. We therefore recommend the fast hybrid as a default for LLM pipelines that handle personal data, with regex kept as a safety net rather than as the only control.

title: SAVeR$^2$: Reasoning-based Safety Alignment for Large Reasoning Models via Verifiable Rewards
description:
arXiv:2611.07482v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved impressive performance via explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet this process introduces critical safety risks. We formalize LRM safety objectives as requiring non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency, and explicit intent identification. We argue that existing alignment methods suffer from poor adversarial generalization, a significant ``safety tax'' on reasoning, and unfaithful coarse-grained rewards, primarily due to their neglect of the LRM's intrinsic reasoning capabilities for safety. To address these, we propose \textbf{SAVeR$^2$}, a novel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{A}lignment method via \textbf{R}ewards with \textbf{R}easoning capability. SAVeR$^2$ decomposes the safety objective into four fine-grained verifiable reward signals and utilizes a difficulty-aware data selection strategy to stabilize training. Crucially, we introduce a reasoning-preserving gradient projection mechanism that analytically resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients, effectively eliminating the safety tax. Extensive experiments on models ranging from 1.5B to 671B demonstrate that SAVeR$^2$ achieves superior safety performance and significantly lower over-refusal rates across multiple benchmarks without compromising general reasoning capabilities.

title: Open-weight models take 56% of token volume, Astra doubles Fable 5.1 spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — September 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from June, July, and August.

September 2026 summary

The September index reports on AI Gateway data collected through August 2026.

  • Open-weight models ran the majority of gateway tokens for the first time, up from 7% in December to 56% in August.

  • The average token costs less than half what it did five months ago. Price per token fell 23.2% in August, the third straight monthly drop, and the median team paid 7.6% less.

  • Fable 5, Anthropic's most capable model, lost two-thirds of its share of gateway spend in one month. Opus 5, at half the price, tripled its share. Anthropic kept 64% of all spend.

  • Gemini 3 Flash has lost 95% of its share of gateway tokens since May, and more than three-quarters of the volume it lost went to models from other labs.

Latest Index updates

The monthly report covers data through August. We add notable developments here between editions.

  • September 17: OpenAI launched Astra on September 3, and it took a third of OpenAI's spend within two days and twice Fable 5.1's share of gateway spend. Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend in its first twelve days while Fable 5.1, launched two days earlier at the same price, took 3.7%.

  • September 18: Jev is now the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history. Within its first 24 hours, it was being used by nearly 13% of paid teams, 2x as many as the GPT-5.6 family and over 6x as many as Fable 5.1.

Open-weight models take a majority of token volume for the first time

In August, open-weight models ran 56% of all tokens on AI Gateway, marking the first month they took the majority of volume.

In December 2025, they processed fewer than one in ten tokens, and only eight months later, they ran more token volume than all closed-weight models combined.

Though the frontier kept the majority of spend, open-weight dollar share is accelerating. As open-weight models become more capable, customers are moving more production workloads over to them.

Growth in open-weight model adoption helped push the average price per token across the gateway down 23.2% in August, its third consecutive monthly drop and the steepest since April. Among teams running more than ten million tokens in both months, the median team paid 7.6% less per token, more than double July's 2.9% decline.

Teams can now get more inference from the same budget and reserve frontier models only for the tasks that justify the premium.

Frontier plateaus as Fable spend goes to Opus 5

Production workloads that justify a frontier model don't always need the most expensive one. They need one that’s good enough.

Fable is the most capable model Anthropic sells. Opus is the tier below it and costs roughly half of Fable’s price per token. When the US export control on Fable 5 was lifted and its access restored on July 1, its gateway spend share surged to 13.2%. At the end of that same month, Opus 5 came online.

In August, Fable 5’s share of gateway spend fell to 4.9%, and Opus 5's share rose to 22.5%. Nine in ten of the teams that ran Fable cut their usage, and more of them moved their workloads to Opus 5 than any other model. Fable’s extra capability wasn’t worth double the price.

Teams left Fable, Anthropic's most expensive and capable model, but the lab retained the lion’s share of gateway spend because those workloads stepped down to Opus 5, not a different lab.

Anthropic has taken at least 61 cents of every dollar spent through AI Gateway every month since December, and 64 cents in August. Its models have held the top two spots by spend every month since December, even as the models in those spots changed.

Customer loyalty follows the model profile, not the lab

Lab loyalty doesn’t follow brand, it follows model profile, and consistency wins.

When a new model preserves what users valued in its predecessor, the lab retains its customers. When it doesn’t, those customers fill the need through other providers.

When Claude Opus 5 launched, it gained almost twice what Fable lost, because it handled the same workloads at half the price. And within five days of Z.ai launching GLM-5.3-Flash, it was running three times GLM-5.2's daily volume.

Google struggled to retain customers with its new models. Because the new offerings didn’t provide a relative advantage on capability or price, a majority of Gemini 3 Flash’s workloads moved to OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek.

About half of the volume that left Gemini 3 Flash went to cheaper models, led by GPT-5.6 Luna, which costs less than half as much per token. Most of the other half went to higher-priced models, led by Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, which cost roughly nine and three times as much as Gemini 3 Flash, respectively.

The flight to better-fit models meant that over the same period, Google’s share of gateway token volume fell from 30% to 5%, with Gemini 3 Flash accounting for 22 of the 25 percentage points lost.

Special report: Astra took a third of OpenAI spend within 48 hours and outpaced Fable 5.1 two to one at launch

GPT-6 Astra launched on the AI Gateway on September 3 at the same price as Fable 5.1 and two and a half times the price of GPT-5.6 Sol. Two days later, it accounted for one in every three dollars spent on OpenAI models through the gateway. Its share of spend has held, hovering between 28% and 39% since.

Within OpenAI’s model lineup, Astra and Sol processed 27% of OpenAI’s tokens but accounted for 71% of its spending from September 4 through 16. Luna and Nano processed more than twice as many tokens for about one-ninth as much spending.

Anthropic launched Fable 5.1 on September 1, two days before Astra. Over each model's first twelve days on the gateway, Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend, more than twice Fable 5.1's share of 3.7%, and was used by twice as many teams.

OpenAI’s cheaper models carry its volume, while Astra’s early lead over Fable shows it can also attract teams at the highest price point. Together, they let OpenAI compete with other frontier labs for both scale and premium spend.

Stay tuned for more in next month's report.

Also in August’s data

  • Google's Nano Banana took the lead in image spend for the first time, at 50% to GPT Image's 44%, even as GPT Image took back the lead in images generated, 46% to 39%.

  • Google's Veo rose to second in video spend, at 20%, up from 15% in July. Seedance remained in first on both videos generated and video spend.

  • The share of videos generated by xAI’s Grok Imagine has more than halved since June, from 42% to 31% to 19%.

Previous AI Gateway Production Index reports

  • May 2026

  • June 2026

  • July 2026

  • August 2026

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through August 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input, and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated using labs’ published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Statements about where volume moved compare changes among the same teams. They do not trace individual tokens between models.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, which is broader than the definition used in earlier reports.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution
description:
arXiv:2611.07624v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select, analyze, mutate, and gate, achieving the best performance.

title: TraCE: Trajectory-Aware Concepts for Explainable Video Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.07009v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video understanding models often rely on motion, yet their explanations can obscure which motion sources support a prediction. We identify motion-source under-specification as a limitation of existing video XAI: region-centric explanations can be source-ambiguous, while motion vocabularies restricted to single-person pose sequences are source-incomplete. We propose TraCE (Trajectory-Aware Concepts for Explainable Video Understanding), a concept-based framework that discovers source-flexible motion concepts by clustering optical-flow trajectories from training videos. These concepts represent dynamic evidence from people, objects, and interactions, while object and scene concepts account for static context. The resulting typed trajectory/object/scene interface supports class prediction for action recognition and question-conditioned concept matching for video question answering (VQA). We evaluate TraCE across five random seeds on six benchmarks: NTU RGB+D Mutual, Chiral SSv2, UCF-101, KTH, TOMATO, and STAR. Relative to non-interpretable baselines, TraCE maintains competitive task performance, with an average accuracy drop of 1.0 points for action recognition and a nominal gain of 0.4 points for VQA. Motion perturbation and concept-removal tests provide complementary evidence of directional semantic alignment and decision faithfulness, while sample-level interventions illustrate targeted model debugging. Our project page is available at https://leewooil.github.io/TraCE_project_page/.

title: PSGAgent: Enhancing MLLMs' Dynamic Visual Perception for Panoptic Scene Graph Generation via Agentic Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.07408v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Panoptic Scene Graph generation (PSG) requires holistic yet fine-grained reasoning over complex relations among objects. However, current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) applied to PSG suffer from a perception bottleneck: they function as static observers limited by fixed-resolution views. As a result, models often overlook critical relations involving small or peripheral objects and struggle to differentiate ambiguous predicates in complex scenes. To address these limitations, we propose PSGAgent, an agentic framework that enhances visual perception for PSG through a think-act-observe loop. PSGAgent allows MLLMs to dynamically refine their visual perception using two tools: a Region Zoom-In Tool for local exploration of small or boundary relations and a Visual Highlight Tool for relation-focused segmentation that filters out irrelevant contextual noise. To optimize decision-making, we construct a two-stage training pipeline. First, we create a high-quality, error-aware Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (M-CoT) dataset that provides robust supervision for cold-start learning. Then, we design a novel hierarchical reward mechanism integrated with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) to enable strategic and adaptive tool usage. Extensive experiments on the PSG benchmark show that PSGAgent achieves SOTA performance, demonstrating strong capability in both holistic and fine-grained scene understanding.

title: Finite-Time Convergence and Regret Guarantees for Neural Reinforcement Learning in POMDPs
description:
arXiv:2611.07069v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) is computationally challenging due to the curse of long-range dependence on history. Fortunately, recent studies have shown that a range of POMDPs that satisfy the filter stability assumption can be well approximated by a superstate Markov Decision Process (MDP) based on a truncated history in a finite-memory window, with a value gap that decays with the window length. However, existing finite-time convergence analyses on such superstate MDP surrogates are either limited to over-simplified linear function approximation or rely on an i.i.d. sampling oracle that is violated by POMDP trajectories, both of which severely limit the applicability of these theoretical results in practice. This motivates us to bridge the gap by investigating RL in POMDPs with nonlinear neural value function approximation. Our main contributions are threefold: i) We first establish a new finite-state MDP point-wise approximation error bound, which lays the foundation for our RL algorithm design and analysis in POMDPs; ii) By applying Temporal-Difference (TD) learning to POMDP-generated superstate transitions and targeting the Bellman fixed point of the superstate MDP, we prove a finite-time critic error bound with nonlinear neural value function approximation; and iii) By combining the neural critic function approximation error bound with the policy mirror descent framework, we obtain a finite-time sublinear regret against the optimal POMDP value. To the best of our knowledge, such a finite-time sublinear regret based on neural function approximation is the first in the literature for finite-memory POMDPs. Our numerical experiments also verify our theoretical results.

title: When Bigger Becomes Brittle: Why Compression Hurts More as Language Models Scale
description:
arXiv:2611.07891v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantization and pruning reduce the cost of deploying language models, but their effects are usually reported as benchmark scores. Such scores record only the loss that remains at the output. Inside the model, compression damages some components more than others, and the rest of the network can partly compensate. The observed loss therefore reflects both the damage and this compensation, which benchmark scores cannot separate. How the two combine, and whether their balance changes with model size, remains unclear. We study this compensation for in-context retrieval, a capability carried by a small, identifiable set of attention heads. To separate the two, the expected loss from ablating these heads is decomposed exactly into the part restored by the rest of the network, attributed to the components responsible, and the part that reaches the output. This decomposition is then compared across model sizes. For damage of comparable size, smaller models restore most of the loss, whereas larger models retain most of it, because the compensating responses offset less of it as models grow. Compressing the heads produces the same pattern. Compression that is nearly harmless in small models can therefore be costly in large ones.
