title: Energy Measurement and Optimization of TinyML in Resource-Constrained Embedded Systems: A Systematic Mapping Study
description:
arXiv:2611.07264v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has increased the volume of data generated at the network edge, where many devices operate under severe memory, processing, and energy constraints. In this context, Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) enables machine learning (ML) tasks to be executed on microcontrollers, smart sensors, and other resource-constrained platforms. However, the literature remains heterogeneous regarding the algorithms evaluated, energy-measurement methods, reported metrics, influencing factors, and optimization strategies. This study presents a systematic mapping of energy-aware TinyML research. It identifies the main models and learning approaches, classifies energy-evaluation methodologies and metrics, examines the technical factors affecting energy consumption, and organizes the reported optimization techniques into a structured taxonomy. The findings highlight the frequent use of convolutional and lightweight architectures, direct measurements and analytical estimations, and factors related to model architecture, hardware, communication, numerical precision, and input characteristics. The optimization strategies were grouped into model compression, hardware-aware design, system and communication optimization, and data and processing optimization. The results also reveal limited standardization in experimental platforms, measurement procedures, and reporting practices, limiting reproducibility and direct comparison across studies. This mapping provides an updated overview of the field and guidance for developing and evaluating more energy-efficient TinyML solutions.

title: TRACEMARK: Editor-Aware Watermarking for User Attribution in Text-Guided Image Editing
description:
arXiv:2611.07632v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An image editing service records which user requests each edit, but the edited image itself does not contain this account information. Once the image is downloaded and shared, the service cannot identify the requesting user from the image alone. Embedding a user-specific watermark could enable such attribution, but semantic editing may erase the signal. We propose Tracemark, an editor-aware watermarking framework for identifying users from edited images. A shared encoder embeds a user-specific signal before editing, and a shared detector recovers the user by comparing features of the edited image with learned reference vectors. Both components are trained jointly through an editor with fixed parameters. User identification errors encourage the encoder to produce watermarks that survive editing, while fidelity losses limit changes to the input image and intended edit. Each image domain and editing instruction uses a separately trained model shared across registered users. Experiments on three image domains show that editor-aware training improves user recovery with both reference-vector matching and binary watermark decoding. Separately trained models reach 87.5% mean identification accuracy among 500 users. When tested with a different editor without retraining, the watermark modules still recover user information. These results demonstrate that learning watermarks through the editing process enables user attribution without modifying the editor.

title: Inheritance in Java, Polymorphism
description:
What is Inheritance?

Inheritance is an OOP concept in Java that allows one class to acquire the properties and methods of another class.

It helps us reuse existing code instead of writing the same code again.

Why Do We Need Inheritance?

Consider a simple example.

We have two classes: Animal and Dog.

Both animals and dogs can eat. Instead of writing the eat() method separately in both classes, we can create it inside the Animal class and allow the Dog class to inherit it.

This avoids code duplication and improves code reusability.

How to Implement Inheritance?

In Java, we use the extends keyword to inherit one class from another.

class Animal {

    void eat() {
        System.out.println("Eating...");
    }

}

class Dog extends Animal {

    void bark() {
        System.out.println("Barking...");
    }

}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Dog dog = new Dog();

        dog.eat();
        dog.bark();

    }
}

Output:

Eating...
Barking...

Here:

  • Animal is the parent class (superclass).
  • Dog is the child class (subclass).
  • extends is used to establish inheritance.

The Dog class can access the eat() method from the Animal class without creating it again.

Types of Inheritance in Java

  • Single Inheritance
  • Multilevel Inheritance
  • Hierarchical Inheritance
  • Hybrid Inheritance

1) Single Inheritance

One child class inherits from one parent class.

class Animal { }

class Dog extends Animal { }

2) Multilevel Inheritance

A class inherits from another child class, forming a chain.

class Animal { }

class Dog extends Animal { }

class Puppy extends Dog { }

Here, Puppy inherits from Dog, and indirectly from Animal.

3) Hierarchical Inheritance

Multiple child classes inherit from the same parent class.

class Animal { }

class Dog extends Animal { }

class Cat extends Animal { }

Both Dog and Cat inherit from Animal.

4) Hybrid Inheritance

Hybrid inheritance is a combination of two or more types of inheritance.

Java doesn't support hybrid inheritance through classes alone because it doesn't support multiple inheritance through classes.

However, we can achieve hybrid inheritance using interfaces.

Example:

class Animal {

    void eat() {
        System.out.println("Eating...");
    }

}

interface Pet {

    void play();

}

class Dog extends Animal implements Pet {

    public void play() {
        System.out.println("Playing...");
    }

}

class Puppy extends Dog { }

Here:

  • Dog extends Animal and implements Pet.
  • Puppy extends Dog.
  • This combines hierarchical/multiple inheritance concepts through classes and interfaces.

Note: Java doesn't support multiple inheritance through classes. A class cannot extend two classes at the same time. This avoids ambiguity when parent classes contain methods with the same signature.

However, Java supports multiple inheritance of type through interfaces.

Method Overloading in Java

Method overloading means creating multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists.

We can change:

  • Number of parameters.
  • Type of parameters.
  • Order of parameter types.

Example:

class Calculator {

    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }

    double add(double a, double b) {
        return a + b;
    }

}

Here, all three methods have the same name but different parameters.

Compile-Time Polymorphism

Method overloading is also called compile-time polymorphism because the compiler determines which overloaded method to call based on the arguments.

Let's take another example from Java itself.

System.out.println("Java");
System.out.println(100);
System.out.println(10.5);
System.out.println(100L);

All these statements use the same println() method name.

But how does Java print different data types?

The PrintStream class provides multiple overloaded versions of println() for different argument types, such as String, int, double, long and Object.

The compiler selects the appropriate overloaded method based on the argument type.

That's method overloading in action!

Method Overriding in Inheritance

Method overriding happens when a child class provides its own implementation of a method already available in the parent class.

class Animal {

    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal makes sound");
    }

}

class Dog extends Animal {

    @Override
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }

}

Here, the Dog class overrides the sound() method of the Animal class.

Runtime Polymorphism

Method overriding is also called runtime polymorphism because the method implementation is selected at runtime based on the actual object.

Example:

Animal animal = new Dog();

animal.sound();

Output:

Dog barks

Even though the reference type is Animal, the actual object is Dog.

So Java executes the overridden method from the Dog class.

Method Overloading vs Method Overriding

Method Overloading Method Overriding
Same method name, different parameters Same method signature
Usually happens within the same class Happens between parent and child classes
Compile-time polymorphism Runtime polymorphism
Inheritance is not required Inheritance is required

The super Keyword

The super keyword is used to refer to the immediate parent class.

It is commonly used to:

  • Access parent class variables.
  • Call parent class methods.
  • Call parent class constructors using super().

Example:

class Animal {

    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal Sound");
    }

}

class Dog extends Animal {

    void sound() {

        super.sound();

        System.out.println("Dog Barks");

    }

}

Here, super.sound() calls the parent class method.

The Object Class in Java

This is an important concept in Java inheritance.

In Java, the Object class is the root superclass of all classes.

It belongs to the java.lang package.

If we create a class without extending any other class, Java implicitly makes it a subclass of Object.

For example:

class Student {

    String name = "John";

}

Internally, it is equivalent to:

class Student extends Object {

    String name = "John";

}

This means every Java class inherits methods from the Object class.

Some commonly used methods are:

  • toString()
  • equals()
  • hashCode()
  • getClass()

How Does toString() Work?

The toString() method belongs to the Object class.

Whenever we print an object using System.out.println(), Java calls its toString() method to get a String representation of that object.

Let's understand with an example.

1) Printing a String Object

String name = "Java";

System.out.println(name);

Output:

Java

Why does it print Java?

Because the String class overrides the toString() method inherited from the Object class.

Its implementation returns the actual string value.

2) Printing a Normal Object

class Student {

    String name = "John";

}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student student = new Student();

        System.out.println(student);

    }
}

Output (example):

Student@5acf9800

Why does this happen?

The Student class hasn't overridden the toString() method.

So Java uses the inherited toString() implementation from the Object class.

The default implementation returns a String containing the class name, @, and the hexadecimal representation of the object's hash code.

3) Overriding toString()

We can override toString() to get a meaningful representation of our object.

class Student {

    String name = "John";

    @Override
    public String toString() {

        return name;

    }

}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student student = new Student();

        System.out.println(student);

    }
}

Output:

John

Now, instead of printing the default object representation, Java prints the value returned by our overridden toString() method.

Important Points

  • Inheritance helps us reuse existing code.
  • We use the extends keyword for class inheritance.
  • Java supports single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance through classes.
  • Hybrid inheritance can be achieved using classes and interfaces.
  • Java doesn't support multiple inheritance through classes.
  • The super keyword refers to the immediate parent class.
  • Method overloading is compile-time polymorphism.
  • Method overriding is runtime polymorphism.
  • The Object class is the root superclass of all Java classes.
  • Every Java class inherits methods from the Object class.
  • toString() returns a String representation of an object.
  • We can override toString() to provide our own object representation.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute, allowing connectors to reach providers with IP allowlists, such as Salesforce and Snowflake.

With Secure Compute routing enabled, Connect’s provider requests use the selected network’s dedicated static IP addresses instead of Connect’s shared IPs. Requests to obtain and refresh access tokens follow that route; your app’s direct API routing is unchanged by this setting. title: Why Converted PDF Tables Break in Excel and Word (And How to Fix '=SUM() = 0')
description:
Every developer, financial analyst, or accountant who has ever tried to extract data from a PDF invoice or bank statement has run into this infuriating scenario:

You convert the PDF table into an Excel spreadsheet or Word document. The grid looks visually acceptable. You highlight the total column, type =SUM(E2:E50), press Enter... and Excel returns 0.

Or worse: numbers with commas turn into dates, negative numbers in accounting parentheses like (1,250.00) get treated as plain text, and multi-line descriptions spill across three independent rows, throwing every debit and credit out of alignment.

Why does converting PDF tables into editable documents fail so consistently, and what is the underlying engineering fix?

1. The Architectural Illusion: PDFs Have No Concept of "Tables"

In HTML, a table is a rigid semantic hierarchy: <table> contains <tr>, which contains <td>.

In the Adobe PDF specification (ISO 32000), tables do not exist.

A PDF is essentially a visual canvas program written in PostScript-derived display commands. When you see a financial table in a PDF, the file actually contains:

  1. Isolated vector stroke instructions (m for move-to, l for line-to, s for stroke) that draw black lines on the page.
  2. Floating text operators (BT, Tf, Td, Tj, ET) that place character glyphs at absolute two-dimensional coordinate positions $(x, y)$. 
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| VISUAL PERCEPTION (A Clean 3-Column Table)                  |
| Date        | Description            | Amount               |
| 2026-11-01  | Cloud Hosting Server   | $1,450.00            |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                              vs
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| PDF INTERNAL DATA STREAM (Raw Coordinate Paints)            |
| 0.5 w  72.0 450.0 m  520.0 450.0 l S  (Draws top horizontal)|
| 72.0 440.0 Td (2026-11-01) Tj          (Paints string at x,y) |
| 160.0 440.0 Td (Cloud Hosting) Tj      (Paints string at x,y) |
| 450.0 440.0 Td ($1,450.00) Tj          (Paints string at x,y) |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Because the PDF file itself has no concept of rows, columns, or cell boundaries, any converter must reverse-engineer and hallucinate the table structure entirely from geometric coordinates. When that reverse-engineering fails, your spreadsheet breaks.

2. The 3 Silent Killers in Converted Financial Data

A. The CHAR(160) Non-Breaking Space Trap

This is the single most common cause of =SUM() = 0.

When converters extract horizontal text streams, coordinate gaps between words and numbers are often translated into non-breaking spaces (  or Unicode U+00A0 / ASCII 160) rather than standard ASCII whitespace (CHAR(32)).

To human eyes, 1450.00 and 1450.00 look identical. But to Excel's calculation engine, any cell containing CHAR(160) is strictly classified as a Text String, not a Number. Excel silently ignores text strings inside =SUM(), yielding a grand total of zero without throwing a single error.

B. Accounting Parentheses vs Negative Signs

Financial statements frequently represent negative values using parentheses: (1,450.00) instead of -1,450.00. Naive regex parsers and basic OCR tools either strip the opening parenthesis, misinterpret the brackets as text characters, or drop the negative multiplier altogether, turning debits into credits.

C. Multi-Line Description Drift

If a transaction description wraps over two lines:

  • Line 1: Invoice #9824 - Annual Enterprise
  • Line 2: Software Subscription Renewal

Naive converters interpret each line as a distinct table row. As a result, the numeric amount ($4,800.00) is assigned to Line 1, while Line 2 creates an empty ghost row beneath it, shifting subsequent transactions out of sync with their timestamps.

3. How to Clean Broken Tables in Excel (The Quick Fix)

If you are currently stuck with an Excel sheet where formulas return zero, run these three quick remediation steps:

  1. Purge Non-Breaking Spaces: In a helper column, clean the numeric values using: 
   =VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(CLEAN(A1), CHAR(160), ""))
  1. Convert Text-Formatted Numbers via Text-to-Columns: Select your amount column > Go to the Data tab > Click Text to Columns > Click Finish. This forces Excel to re-evaluate the cell formatting from raw text to floating-point numbers.
  2. Verify with =ISNUMBER(): Before building pivot tables or financial reports, enter =ISNUMBER(E2). If it returns FALSE, the cell still contains hidden typographic artifacts.

4. How Modern Reconstruction Engines Solve Table Extraction

To extract complex tables, bank statements, and invoices without manual data cleaning, modern layout-aware engines use a multi-pass geometric pipeline:

  1. Vertical Projection Profiling: Instead of looking for borders, the engine casts vertical rays down the page to locate whitespace gutters—the natural empty channels between columns that exist even in borderless financial statements.
  2. Horizontal Baseline Clustering: Text tokens are grouped into discrete row buckets based on typographical font baselines, allowing multi-line descriptions within the same vertical envelope to be unified into a single cell.
  3. OpenXML Native AST Generation: When exporting to Word or Excel, the engine outputs genuine <w:tbl>, <w:tr>, and <w:tc> structural trees rather than floating text frames.

Summary

Tables in PDFs are an optical illusion. Understanding the difference between coordinate-based PDF paints and semantic document trees is essential for anyone building or managing document automation pipelines.

At PDF Retype, we engineered dedicated layout reconstruction tools to eliminate broken columns and non-breaking space errors:

  • Try our free Extract Table from PDF tool to pull clean tabular data into Word and Excel without formula corruption.
  • For complete scanned documents with tables and stamps, check out Scanned PDF to Word with TrueLayout.

Disclosure: I am the founder of PDF Retype (https://pdfretype.com), an independent, zero-registration document engineering platform designed to solve real-world document formatting, OCR, and table conversion failures.

title: Robust Stream Classification using Time Neutralising Decision Trees
description:
arXiv:2611.06991v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data Streams are characterised as a potentially infinite source of data subject to non-stationarity. This non-stationarity, also called Concept Drift, often results in deployed predictive models having to be perpetually retrained as the underlying data generating process of the stream changes over time. Drift Detectors are a class of methods used to identify these changes, triggering these retraining procedures. Historically, Stream Learning has operated under the assumption that instances are only seen once, and cannot be stored for later use. Contemporary work relaxes this assumption, yet drift detection and simple resetting procedures are still ubiquitous.
  Building on related work which has shown that traditional Batch Learning algorithms often outperform Stream Learning algorithms when instances can be stored, we introduce Time Neutralising Trees (TNT), a Decision Tree architecture that enables robust stream classification in settings with Concept Drift. During training, TNT will filter out ("neutralise") old training samples that are no longer relevant given the current context of the stream. If those instances become relevant again, TNT will then re-include them. We evaluate TNT, and related algorithms on 24 real and semi-real classification data streams from the USP DS repository. Results show strong evidence that TNT achieves best-in-class performance on a wide-range of data streams with varying concept drift types.

title: Stress Testing Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Against Covert Misalignment
description:
arXiv:2611.07586v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As LLM agents advance rapidly in autonomy, the risk of hidden objectives that bypass safety constraints becomes increasingly plausible. Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring offers a key control mechanism by reading the agent's reasoning and flagging misalignment before it materializes into action, yet its reliability depends on the realism of the red-team it is stress-tested against. Existing red-teaming efforts rely on shared templates, such as casting a side task as a prerequisite, which treat the side objective as an exogenous insertion and leave task-specific, contextually grounded evasions underexplored. We therefore ask: How robust is CoT monitoring against agents that strategically conceal misalignment? To answer this, we introduce TraceMRT, an automated Trace-level Monitor Red-Teaming framework that reframes the side task as a coherent sub-goal of the primary task and searches trace-shaping strategies whose induced trajectories complete the misaligned objective while reading as natural execution. Through black-box attacks on state-of-the-art monitors such as GPT-5.2 and Claude-4.5, we reveal substantial vulnerabilities even in top models. To counter these vulnerabilities, we propose a Bayesian Trajectory Monitoring framework, integrating global context and local segment evidence to detect covert misalignment. Empirically, our method significantly consolidates monitor robustness with 0.91 AUC and 0.74 TPR@FPR=0.05.

title: React accesible: estados claros en formularios
description:
React accesible: estados claros en formularios

Un formulario puede verse limpio y aun así ser dificil de usar. El problema suele aparecer cuando algo cambia: el botón está enviando, el email no es válido, o el servidor responde tarde. En esos momentos, el diseño visual, React y la accesibilidad dejan de ser temas separados. El estado de la interfaz es el producto.

En este artículo comparto un patrón pequeño para construir formularios más claros. Sirve para un registro, una recuperación de contraseña o una validación con correo de usar y tirar durante pruebas. La idea no es añadir una librería enorme, sino hacer que cada estado tenga una señal visible, comprensible y anunciable.

El estado también es parte del diseño

Un formulario de registro normalmente tiene al menos estos estados:

  • idle: todavía no hay una acción.
  • submitting: se está procesando el envío.
  • success: la operación terminó bien.
  • error: el usuario puede corregir algo o reintentar.

Si el botón solo cambia de color, una persona que usa teclado o lector de pantalla puede no entender qué ocurrió. Y si el mensaje aparece debajo de un campo sin una relación semántica, el error queda visualmente bonito pero poco util.

También conviene separar los errores de validación de los errores del servidor. “Escribe un email válido” pide una corrección local. “No pudimos enviar el enlace” pide esperar o intentar otra vez. Mezclarlos genera fricción y hace que el usuario no sabe cual es el siguiente paso.

Un modelo pequeño de estados

En React, un objeto de estado explícito suele ser suficiente:

const [status, setStatus] = useState("idle");
const [message, setMessage] = useState("");

async function handleSubmit(event) {
  event.preventDefault();
  const email = new FormData(event.currentTarget).get("email");

  if (!email || !email.includes("@")) {
    setStatus("error");
    setMessage("Escribe un email válido.");
    return;
  }

  setStatus("submitting");
  setMessage("");

  try {
    await submitEmail(email);
    setStatus("success");
    setMessage("Revisa tu bandeja para continuar.");
  } catch {
    setStatus("error");
    setMessage("No pudimos enviar el enlace. Inténtalo de nuevo.");
  }
}

La ventaja está en que la interfaz no depende de muchos booleanos que pueden entrar en conflicto. isLoading, hasError y isDone pueden terminar activos a la vez; un estado único hace la transición más facil de razonar.

Para pruebas de flujos, mantengo además un identificador del escenario y una bandeja controlada. Una cuenta de correo desechable, como la que puede gestionarse en separar correos por contexto, ayuda a que dos ejecuciones no mezclen sus mensajes. No es una excusa para descuidar la seguridad: nunca debe usarse para datos sensibles.

Mensajes que ayudan sin mover el layout

Un error que aparece y desaparece puede empujar todo el formulario. Ese salto desconcierta, sobre todo en móvil. Reserva espacio para el mensaje o usa una estructura que mantenga estable la altura del bloque. El CSS puede ser sencillo:

.field-message {
  min-height: 1.5rem;
  color: #b42318;
  font-size: 0.9rem;
}

.form-status[aria-live="polite"] {
  min-height: 1.5rem;
}

El texto debe describir una acción concreta. “Error” no dice nada; “Revisa el dominio del email” sí. Evita esconder el problema solo con rojo. Añade texto, conserva un contraste suficiente y marca el campo con aria-invalid cuando corresponda.

Un componente React legible

El mensaje de estado global puede usar role="status" y aria-live="polite". Así, un lector de pantalla recibe la confirmación sin ser interrumpido de forma agresiva:

<form onSubmit={handleSubmit} noValidate>
  <label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
  <input
    id="email"
    name="email"
    type="email"
    aria-invalid={status === "error"}
    aria-describedby="email-message"
  />
  <p id="email-message" className="field-message">
    {status === "error" ? message : ""}
  </p>

  <button type="submit" disabled={status === "submitting"}>
    {status === "submitting" ? "Enviando…" : "Continuar"}
  </button>

  <p className="form-status" role="status" aria-live="polite">
    {status === "success" ? message : ""}
  </p>
</form>

No conviene desactivar el botón para siempre después de un error. El usuario necesita una salida clara para reintentar. Durante la carga, en cambio, sí es razonable bloquear el doble envío y mostrar una señal de progreso.

Para interfaces con agentes o pasos automáticos, los manifiestos mínimos antes de ejecutar ofrecen una idea útil: declarar qué está permitido antes de actuar. En el frontend, eso se traduce en enseñar qué acción está ocurriendo y qué resultado se espera.

Accesibilidad y revisión visual

Mi lista de revisión es corta:

  1. Navegar el formulario solo con teclado.
  2. Comprobar que el foco no desaparece tras el envío.
  3. Leer cada error en voz alta con un lector de pantalla.
  4. Probar zoom y una pantalla estrecha.
  5. Revisar contraste, foco visible y orden de lectura.
  6. Confirmar que el mensaje no depende solo del color.

También pruebo una red lenta. Si el estado de carga no aparece, el formulario parece roto. A veces un pequeño retraso controlado revela problemas que una conexión local oculta; es una prueba simple pero muy valiosa.

En búsquedas sobre tempmailso, tempail mail o tamp mail com, el contexto importa: una interfaz debe explicar si el email es de prueba, temporal o real. No hay que prometer privacidad que el sistema no ofrece, ni mandar al usuario a un estado sin salida.

Preguntas rápidas

¿Debo validar el email en cada tecla?

No siempre. Validar al salir del campo o al enviar suele ser menos ruidoso. En campos complejos, una ayuda temprana puede ser útil, pero no conviertas cada pulsación en un mensaje de error.

¿Qué hago si el servidor tarda mucho?

Mantén el estado submitting, explica que la operación sigue en curso y define un límite razonable. Si se supera, ofrece reintentar sin borrar los datos escritos.

¿Dónde encaja tempmailso en este patrón?

Para pruebas aisladas puede servir una cuenta de correo desechable, siempre con datos no sensibles y una política clara de expiración. El componente React debe seguir tratando la respuesta como no confiable y mostrar estados verificables.

Cierre

La accesibilidad de un formulario no se arregla al final con un atributo suelto. Empieza modelando estados claros, continúa con mensajes accionables y termina probando teclado, lector de pantalla y red lenta. El resultado suele ser una interfaz más amable para todos, además de más fácil de depurar y mantener.

title: ElevenLabs on AI Gateway
description:
Vercel and ElevenLabs are partnering to bring 14 ElevenLabs models to AI Gateway. To celebrate the launch, all ElevenLabs models are 50% off on AI Gateway for the first 14 days, through November 9th.

AI Gateway supports six different types of ElevenLabs audio models:

  • Speech to text: Transcribe recordings or caption live audio as people speak.

  • Streaming text to speech: Start playing audio while a language model is still writing its reply, so users don't have to wait for the full answer.

  • Realtime voice agents: Let users talk to your app and listen to it respond out loud in a single live session. Useful for support lines, tutors, and in-app assistants.

  • Music: Describe a track in plain text and get back a finished song or instrumental at the length you need.

  • Sound effects: Generate game and interface sounds, or ambience that loops cleanly, from a short description.

  • Multi-voice dialogue: Voice a whole conversation in one call, with a different voice for each speaker.

All of these audio models are accessible through a single gateway API key. Your app or agent can transcribe what a user says, reason over it with your choice of hundreds of models, then answer in an ElevenLabs voice. You can also create soundtracks with generated music and sound effects.

Every request lands in the same usage, cost, and trace views as your other AI Gateway traffic.

Model types

AI Gateway gives you access to 14 ElevenLabs models, spanning speech to text, realtime voice, and music.

Speech and transcription

Scribe v2 Realtime turns a user's speech into text while they are still talking. A language model of your choice then writes the answer. Eleven Flash v2.5, a low-latency ElevenLabs voice model, reads that answer aloud as it streams in, so the user hears the reply begin before the model finishes writing it.

Because each step is its own model, you can swap the transcription, language, or speech model without touching the rest of the pipeline.

In the example below, a user asks whether they’ll make a connecting flight. The text model combines flight status and gate distance to answer, then the speech model delivers the response.

Realtime voice agents

Eleven Realtime v1 Max and Eleven Realtime v1 Mini run the whole spoken conversation in one model, which suits conversations where users expect natural back-and-forth, like a support call or an in-app assistant. Both models take the user's audio in and speak a reply back over a single WebSocket session, so there's no separate transcription or speech step to wire up.

Eleven Realtime hears “Can I change the delivery address for my order?” and responds “I can help with that. What’s your order number?” over one WebSocket session.

In the browser, connect with the useRealtime hook from @ai-sdk/react, which handles the WebSocket connection, microphone capture, and audio playback. In the hook's sessionConfig, set an ElevenLabs voice ID and turnDetection: { type: 'semantic-vad' }. These models support semantic voice activity detection (VAD) to decide when the user has finished speaking, but they don't support server-vad. The realtime guide walks through the full browser setup.

Music and sound effects

Music v2.5 and Music v2 compose original music from a text description. Name a genre, a mood, or the instruments you want, and the model returns a finished track at the length you ask for, with or without vocals. For more control, you can lay out a song section by section and give each section its own style and length.

Sound Effects v2 works the same way for shorter sounds, such as footsteps, a door slamming, or rain that loops under a game level.

All three models use generateSpeech, with text describing the sound you want instead of words to read aloud. This example requests a 30-second track:

Multi-voice dialogue

Eleven v4, Eleven v4 Turbo, and Eleven v3 perform a script with several speakers in a single request. You assign a voice to each line, and each change of voice starts a new turn. A two-host podcast or a scene with a full cast comes back as one continuous recording, so there are no separate clips to stitch together.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

The AI Gateway audio docs have examples across the ElevenLabs models. Browse all audio models on AI Gateway, and try ElevenLabs at 50% off until November 9th.

title: The Intrusion Pathway: How Non-Evidential Context Degrades Language Model Performance
description:
arXiv:2611.07778v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models lose accuracy when a prompt contains non-evidential context: irrelevant statements from unrelated domains, or random off-distribution tokens, with no competing answer and no semantic overlap with the query. Such noise pervades retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and long-context deployments, yet the failure has lacked a mechanistic account. We trace the corruption to the Intrusion Pathway, which starts with MLPs enriching both query-subject and irrelevant-token representations, parroting heads carry prefix-token content to the prediction position, and relational readers largely avoid unrelated sources. Nevertheless, preserved subject enrichment and selective reading do not prevent intrusion in the broader computation. We then localize part of this interference to a sparse set of attention heads, which we call intrusion heads. Their prefix-derived writes promote distractor-related content, while their reduced support for the correct answer arises primarily from weaker non-prefix contributions rather than direct suppression by the prefix. The same heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely weight-disjoint from the heads that integrate relevant contextual evidence, enabling a class-conditional intervention. Replacing the corrupted last-token residual with its clean counterpart, an oracle probe that requires a matched clean forward pass, recovers 97.6% on average of the distractor-induced drop across four downstream tasks. A deployable mask level knockout of about ten heads, roughly 1% of the model's attention heads, recovers 57% at bounded cost to helpful context.

title: making procedural sky based on realtime weather data using feTurbulence
description:
Creating dynamic, environment-aware UI elements adds a layer of polish to web applications. By combining React, realtime weather APIs, and SVG filters, we can build a procedural sky that automatically reflects the user's local time of day and cloud cover.

Here is a breakdown of how to build a realtime procedural sky without relying on heavy WebGL libraries or prompting the user for intrusive location permissions.

  1. Privacy-Friendly Location & Weather Fetching

Browsers have a native Geolocation API, but triggering a location permission popup immediately upon page load is a terrible user experience. Instead, we can approximate the user's location using their IP address. It's less precise than GPS, but perfectly adequate for fetching general weather data like cloud cover.

Using ipapi.co, we fetch the rough latitude and longitude, then pass those coordinates to the free Open-Meteo API to retrieve the current cloud_cover percentage. To prevent rate-limiting and unnecessary network requests, this data is cached in localStorage for one hour.

// Fetching rough location via IP (No permission popup required)
const ipRes = await fetch("https://ipapi.co/json/");
const ipData = await ipRes.json();

const latitude = ipData.latitude || 19.076;
const longitude = ipData.longitude || 72.8777;

// Fetching cloud cover based on coordinates
const weatherUrl = `https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=${latitude}&longitude=${longitude}&current=cloud_cover`;
const weatherRes = await fetch(weatherUrl);
const weatherData = await weatherRes.json();

const cloudDensity = weatherData.current.cloud_cover;
  1. Painting the Sky Gradient

The background sky is driven by the user's local time. By extracting the current hour (new Date().getHours()), we can map it to an array of predefined CSS gradients.

Night hours return pure black or deep navy, early mornings transition through sunrise colors, and midday hours use bright blues.

const skyGradientByHour = [
  // ... other hours
  { hour: 6, gradient: `linear-gradient(180deg, #000000 0%, #00274C 50%, #83270080 100%)` }, // Sunrise
  { hour: 12, gradient: `linear-gradient(180deg, #004381 0%, #FFFFFF 100%)` }, // Noon
  { hour: 18, gradient: `linear-gradient(180deg, #004381 0%, #B78A78 100%)` }, // Sunset
  // ...
];

const getSkyGradient = (timeOfDay) => {
  const match = skyGradientByHour.find(sky => sky.hour === timeOfDay);
  return match?.gradient || "#000000";
};
  1. Sculpting Clouds with CSS and feTurbulence

The most complex part is rendering the clouds. Instead of using static PNGs or expensive canvas rendering, we can use CSS box-shadow coupled with SVG filters to generate organic, fluffy shapes.

First, we generate a massive, comma-separated box-shadow string. Each shadow acts as a single cloud "blob," scattered randomly across the viewport using vw and vh units. The number of blobs is dictated by the cloudDensity fetched from the weather API (capped to maintain performance).

To make these perfect circles look like actual clouds, we apply an SVG filter. generates fractal noise, and uses that noise to warp and distort the smooth edges of our box shadows into organic, chaotic cloud formations.

import { useMemo } from "react";

const CloudSheet = ({ cloudDensity, timeOfDay }) => {
  const isSunsetOrSunrise = (timeOfDay >= 6 && timeOfDay <= 9) || (timeOfDay >= 18 && timeOfDay <= 20);

  const memoizeShadows = useMemo(() => {
    const safeDensity = Math.min(cloudDensity, 30); // Cap density for performance

    // Generate scattered box-shadows based on density
    let shadows = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < safeDensity; ++i) {
      // Random position (vw/vh), size (vmin), and color tint based on time of day
      shadows.push(`${rn(1, 100)}vw ${rn(1, 100)}vh ${rn(20, 40)}vmin ${rn(1, 20)}vmin ${isSunsetOrSunrise ? rs("#0385FF00", "#53ACFF", "#CCE6FF") : rs("#0385FF00", "#53ACFF", "#CCE6FF", "#FFFFFF")}`);
    }
    return shadows.join(",");
  }, [cloudDensity, isSunsetOrSunrise]);

  return (
    <div className="bg-transparent absolute w-screen h-screen z-30">
      {/* SVG Filter for Cloud Distortion */}
      <svg width="0" height="0" className="absolute">
        <filter id="cloud-filter" x="-50%" y="-50%" width="200%" height="200%">
          <feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency=".01" numOctaves="10" result="noise" />
          <feDisplacementMap in="SourceGraphic" in2="noise" scale="180" />
        </filter>
      </svg>

      {/* The base element that holds the shadows and applies the filter */}
      <div
        className="fixed -top-1 -left-1 w-1 h-1 bg-white rounded-full filter-[url(#cloud-filter)]"
        style={{
          boxShadow: memoizeShadows,
          transform: "translateZ(0)", // Force hardware acceleration
        }}
      />
    </div>
  );
};

By combining these three layers—IP-based weather data, time-mapped gradients, and SVG-distorted box shadows—you get a responsive, performant procedural sky that accurately reflects the physical world outside your user's window.

title: Auditing 687 React & Tailwind Files for "Vibecoded" UI Tells (and Catching Two False-Positive Traps)
description:
When I ran the first version of my static UI linter against OpenCode-App (536 .tsx files on my machine), two things broke immediately:

  1. Code blocks and syntax themes triggered false positives. Scanning raw file strings flagged <pre><code> documentation blocks for sample href="#" tags and terminal ANSI color maps for indigo tokens.
  2. Global weight subtraction punished large repos. Subtracting raw rule weights without normalizing for file count gave a 536-file desktop app a 68/100 (Grade C) when 99.1% of its files had zero findings (only 2 dialog components used indigo utilities and 3 routes had an em-dash).

After masking out comments, <pre>, <code>, and <svg> blocks while preserving exact \n line numbers, and normalizing cosmetic penalties by sqrt(4 / filesScanned), I published uislop (npx uislop) to catch 16 deterministic "vibecoded UI" tells across React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Tailwind, and HTML.

npx uislop ./src

Real benchmark across 687 UI files 

Target            : W.prince/Princeportfolio (129 UI files) vs Vibecoded SaaS Landing
Files scanned     : 129 UI files · 47 findings across 3/6 categories
Human-Craft Score : 65/100 (Grade C) · Vibecode Index: 35/100
Palette Entropy   : 50/297 chromatic tokens in indigo/violet/purple (16.8%)

REAL CORPUS BENCHMARK (687 UI files across 4 repositories)
  rajesh-portfolio (21 UI files)          100/100 (Grade A) ·  0 findings ·  0.0% indigo
  OpenCode-App (536 UI files)              97/100 (Grade A) ·  6 findings · 13.0% indigo
  W.prince/Princeportfolio (129 UI files)  65/100 (Grade C) · 47 findings · 16.8% indigo
  vibecoded-landing.tsx (1 UI file)         0/100 (Grade F) · 24 findings · 95.2% indigo

What the 16 rules catch

  • Palette & Gradient Defaulting (UIS001-UIS004): bg-clip-text text-transparent bg-gradient-to-* headings, from-indigo-500 via-purple-500 to-pink-500 gradients, files where indigo/violet/purple exceed 35% of all chromatic Tailwind utilities, and blur-3xl rounded-full opacity-20 background orbs.
  • Icon & Eyebrow Clichés (UIS005-UIS007): Importing 3+ of Sparkles, Zap, Rocket, Shield, Brain, Wand2 from lucide-react, <Sparkles> + animate-ping hero pills above <h1>, and repeated bg-indigo-500/10 rounded-xl p-3 squircle icon boxes.
  • Layout Monotony (UIS008-UIS009): Stacked grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-3 sections and backdrop-blur + hover:-translate-y-1 glass cards.
  • AI Copywriting (UIS010-UIS011): "Supercharge your", "Unleash the power of", "Built for modern teams", "Next-Generation", and em-dash splices in UI text.
  • Fake Social Proof (UIS012-UIS014): "Sarah Chen", "Alex Rivera", "Acme Corp", "TechFlow", pravatar.cc, and LLM-memorized Unsplash portrait IDs (photo-1534528741775-53994a69daeb).
  • Hollow Wiring (UIS015-UIS016): Dead <a href="#"> links and onClick={() => {}} / console.log handlers.

Code and CLI are MIT-licensed at https://github.com/princejain756/uislop (and on npm at https://www.npmjs.com/package/uislop).

title: I built an app with ChatGPT or Claude. How do I put it online, with a database and logins?
description:
Connect the AI you built the app with to LIIVO, then tell it to "Deploy to LIIVO". Your AI puts the app online with its own link, sets up the database and user logins the app needs, and you never open a terminal. It is free to try, and 15 EUR a month to keep an app online all the time.

The rest of this post walks through it step by step, including what it costs and what can trip you up.

Why does my app only work on my computer?

When ChatGPT or Claude builds an app, it usually runs inside the chat preview or on your own computer. It looks finished, but nobody else can open it. To share it, the app needs a home on the internet: a link people can visit, a place to keep its data, and a way for people to sign in. That home is what people mean by "hosting".

LIIVO is that home, and it is built for people who don't write code. You keep using the AI you already have. LIIVO puts what it builds online and keeps it running.

What do I need before I start?

You need three things, and none of them is a LIIVO sign-up form.

  • A computer. The setup happens in the Claude or ChatGPT desktop app. Once your app is live, anyone can use it on a phone.
  • A ChatGPT or Claude account. A paid AI plan works best. Free AI plans have tighter usage limits, and on Claude's free plan you can build in the regular chat but not in Claude's Code mode.
  • An idea, or the app your AI already made. A booking page, a tracker for the family chores, a small shop. Whatever you were going to describe anyway.

You don't create a LIIVO account first. When you connect your AI, it sends you to a sign-in screen. You sign in with Google, Apple or email, and that sign-in is your LIIVO account.

How do I connect ChatGPT or Claude to LIIVO?

Your AI talks to LIIVO through one address: https://my.liivo.ai/mcp. You paste it into your AI's settings once.

In Claude (desktop app): open Connectors from the chat box, choose to add a custom connector, name it LIIVO and paste the address. Claude opens your browser so you can sign in, then sends you back to the chat.

In ChatGPT (desktop app): open the ChatGPT menu and choose Settings. Under Integrations, click Plugins, open the MCPs tab, click Add and then Add MCP server. Set the name to LIIVO, the type to Streamable HTTP and the URL to https://my.liivo.ai/mcp, leave the token fields empty and click Save. Then start a new chat so the connection is picked up.

If you get stuck, LIIVO's connect page shows each step with pictures.

How do I actually put my app online?

Tell your AI what you want, the way you would tell a friend, and end with "Deploy to LIIVO". For example:

Make a simple booking page for my yoga class. People pick a time, enter their name and email, and get a confirmation. I want to see all bookings in a list. Deploy to LIIVO.

Your AI writes the app and sends it to LIIVO, and LIIVO puts it online. A few minutes later you get a link you can open, send to people, or put on your Instagram.

If the app already exists in a chat, say "Put the app we just made on LIIVO so other people can use it." If something goes wrong, tell your AI what you see. It can read what happened and try again. And if your app was built somewhere else and you have its code, open that code in Claude or ChatGPT and ask it to deploy the app to LIIVO.

Can my app have a database and user logins?

Yes. LIIVO has the pieces most real apps need, ready for your AI to wire up: databases, logins, file storage, email, visitor stats and video. You don't pick them from a menu. You describe what the app should do, and your AI chooses.

Let people create an account and log in, and save each person's bookings so they can see them next time. Deploy to LIIVO.

Each app gets its own space. Its logins, its data and its keys are not shared with any other app on LIIVO, so if something breaks somewhere else, your app keeps running.

What does it cost, including the AI?

There are two separate bills, and it helps to see both.

The first is your AI plan. That stays with ChatGPT or Claude, and LIIVO charges nothing for the AI. There is no fee per prompt and no second bill for the same thing.

The second is LIIVO, for keeping your app online.

Free Creator
Price 0 EUR 15 EUR a month, excl. VAT
Card needed No Yes, billed from day one
Tokens 100, once 40 every day
Good for Trying it and building a first app Keeping an app online around the clock

Tokens are how LIIVO counts the time your app's pieces are running. Each running piece uses some tokens every day, typically between 10 and 100, so the 100 free tokens last days rather than months. They are a one-time start, not a monthly allowance. On the free plan, an app that runs out is paused, not deleted.

Creator is 15 EUR a month with 40 tokens a day, and you can cancel with one click; your plan stays active to the end of the period you paid for. There is no free trial of Creator. If you want your app on your own web address, like a name you bought, that needs the Professional plan at 69 EUR a month. Most people start with the link LIIVO gives them.

What happens if I want to leave later?

You keep your app. You can export the app and its data whenever you want and move it somewhere else, with no export fee. Every piece LIIVO runs is open code that anyone can run, which is why the move is possible.

Your app and the data it stores run in Sweden, in Stockholm, on Swedish-owned servers.

Is my app ready for real people?

Before you send the link to everyone, ask your AI to check it with you. Can a stranger sign up without your help? What happens if someone types something odd into a form? Does it work on a phone? LIIVO has a short list of prompts for this, Is your app ready for real users, and you can paste them straight into your chat.

Where do I start?

Open liivo.ai/connect on your computer, connect the AI you already use, and ask it for the smallest version of your idea. When it says the app is live, open the link on your phone. That is the moment it stops being a chat and becomes something people can use.

title: Java OOMKilled in Kubernetes: Find the Memory Pool with NMT
description:
“Pile of Laptop & Desktop RAM Memory Modules” by Wilbysuffolk, CC BY-SA 4.0

A Java pod that restarts with OOMKilled is a frustrating problem, because the JVM often leaves no stack trace and no OutOfMemoryError. The kernel simply ends the process. This guide is for engineers who run Java services on Kubernetes and need to answer one question: which memory pool grew? We will use Native Memory Tracking (NMT) and jcmd to find out, then map the result to a fix.

Why Java OOMKilled is not a Java OutOfMemoryError

Two different things get confused. A Java OutOfMemoryError is thrown by the JVM when it cannot satisfy an allocation inside its own limits, for example when the heap is full. OOMKilled means the container as a whole used more memory than its Kubernetes limit. The Kubernetes documentation explains that memory limits are enforced by the kernel with out-of-memory kills, and that this enforcement is reactive: a container can briefly exceed the limit, and it is killed when the kernel detects memory pressure.

The container’s memory is more than the Java heap. It also includes class metadata, thread stacks, JIT-compiled code, GC data structures, direct buffers and memory from native libraries. A pod can be killed while the heap graph looks healthy. That is why heap dumps alone often do not explain it.

Confirm that it really was an OOM kill

Start by checking the termination reason. The Kubernetes memory tutorial shows that a killed container reports reason: OOMKilled and exitCode: 137, which is 128 + 9 (SIGKILL).

kubectl get pod my-app-7d9f -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated}'
kubectl describe pod my-app-7d9f | grep -A6 "Last State"

Replace my-app-7d9f with your pod name. If the reason is something else (for example an error exit from your own code), this guide does not apply.

Do the budget arithmetic first

Before measuring, add up what the JVM is allowed to use. The java command reference gives these facts:

  • -XX:MaxRAMPercentage defaults to 25 percent, and the RAM it is a percentage of is limited by container constraints.
  • The default maximum code cache is 240 MB (48 MB without tiered compilation).
  • The default thread stack size on Linux/x64 is 1024 KB.
  • Metaspace is not limited by default (-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize), and direct buffer size is chosen automatically unless you set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize.

Take a hypothetical pod with a 1024Mi limit whose JVM runs with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75, so the maximum heap is 768Mi. If the service has 200 threads on Linux/x64, their stacks can reserve up to 200 x 1 MB = 200 MB. Only the stack pages a thread actually touches count toward the container, so real use is usually lower, but in the worst case heap plus stacks is 968 MB. That leaves 56 MB of the 1024Mi limit for metaspace, code cache, GC structures, direct buffers and everything else. A budget this tight can explain a kill without any leak at all.

The JVM Container Memory Calculator does this addition for you with your own heap, metaspace, thread and direct memory inputs.

Enable Native Memory Tracking

NMT is off by default. According to the java command reference, -XX:NativeMemoryTracking accepts off, summary and detail. The Java troubleshooting guide states that enabling NMT costs a 5-10 percent performance drop, so turn it on in a test or canary environment first. It cannot be switched on in a running JVM; it needs a restart.

env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: "-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary"

This sets the flag through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, which the JVM reads at startup, so you do not have to edit the image. Use detail only when summary points to a category and you need call sites.

Read the NMT summary with jcmd

Run jcmd inside the container. In many images the Java process is PID 1. jcmd ships with the JDK, so JRE-only or distroless images may not include it; in that case use an image variant that has the JDK tools, or an ephemeral debug container with a JDK that shares the pod’s process namespace. Run jcmd as the same user as the Java process, or it cannot attach.

kubectl exec my-app-7d9f -- jcmd 1 VM.native_memory

The output lists the total reserved and committed memory, then one block per category. The categories documented by Oracle include Java Heap, Class, Thread, Code, GC, Compiler, Internal, Symbol and Native Memory Tracking itself. The page notes that the list may change between releases. Focus on committed values, since committed memory is what counts against the container.

One limit matters here: NMT does not track allocations made by non-JVM native code, such as a JNI library. If the NMT total is far below what the container reports, suspect native libraries rather than the JVM.

Compare against a baseline

A single snapshot rarely shows growth. Take a baseline after warm-up, wait while the problem develops, then diff.

kubectl exec my-app-7d9f -- jcmd 1 VM.native_memory baseline
# ...wait until memory has grown...
kubectl exec my-app-7d9f -- jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary.diff

The diff prints each category with a plus or minus delta. The category with the largest positive delta is your suspect. If you need allocation sites, restart with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=detail and use detail.diff the same way.

Match the growing pool to a fix

Growing category Typical cause What to try
Java Heap Heap max is too large for the limit, or real object growth Lower -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, or take a heap dump with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError (disabled by default) and -XX:HeapDumpPath
Thread Too many threads, each with a stack Cap thread pools; reduce -Xss only if the code allows it
Class Metaspace growth from class loading, for example repeated redeploys or dynamic proxies Find the class loader leak; set -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize to fail early with a clear error
Code Code cache filling toward its maximum Check -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize against your budget
GC Collector structures that scale with heap size Reduce heap, or leave more headroom
Nothing in NMT, but container grows Direct buffers or native code outside NMT Set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize; review JNI or native libraries

Setting -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize or -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize does not remove a leak, but it turns a silent kernel kill into a Java OutOfMemoryError with a message, which is much easier to diagnose.

Set limits that leave headroom

Once you know the pools, size the container with a margin. A reasonable pattern is to set the heap as a percentage and leave the rest explicitly for non-heap memory:

resources:
  requests:
    memory: "1536Mi"
  limits:
    memory: "1536Mi"
env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m"

Line by line: the request equals the limit so the scheduler reserves what the pod can use; MaxRAMPercentage=60 gives a heap cap of about 921Mi (0.60 x 1536Mi); the metaspace and direct memory caps are bounded explicitly. These values are an illustration, not a recommendation. Replace them with the committed sizes you measured with NMT. Note that Mi is a binary unit; 1536M would be a different, smaller amount.

Key takeaways

  • Java OOMKilled means the whole container exceeded its limit; it is not the same as a Java OutOfMemoryError.
  • Confirm with reason: OOMKilled and exit code 137 before investigating.
  • Add up heap, stacks, code cache, metaspace and direct memory first; many kills are budget mistakes.
  • Enable -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary (5-10 percent overhead, restart needed), take a baseline, then run summary.diff.
  • NMT does not see memory allocated by non-JVM native code.
  • Cap metaspace and direct memory so failures are explicit and diagnosable.

Conclusion

Treat a Java OOMKilled as an accounting problem. Work out the budget, measure which pool grows with NMT diffs, and then either fix the growth or give the container honest headroom. Repeat the diff after each change to confirm that the growing category is the one you fixed.

Related reading

  • OpsHubs ops calculators and tools
