title: DEQ-Det: Dual Evidence Queries for Few-Shot Analog IC Device Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.07682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detecting analog integrated circuit (IC) devices in layout images supports circuit analysis and inspection. With only a few annotated examples, variation in device geometry and visual similarity to dummy or routing structures make reliable detection difficult. Foreground similarity alone can highlight plausible targets without distinguishing them from competing layout patterns. We propose Dual Evidence Queries for Detection (DEQ-Det), which constructs complementary foreground and background references from the same support images without additional annotations. Foreground references capture target morphology, while selected background references characterize surrounding layout patterns. Both sources guide query selection and region verification, combining target appearance with layout context. Across five held-out device categories and three random seeds, DEQ-Det achieves macro AP50 of 39.41 and 53.03 at 10 and 30 shots, exceeding the strongest listed baselines by 3.97 and 9.71 points, respectively. A matched 30-shot ablation further shows that RoI background evidence reduces pooled false positives at comparable recall, supporting its role in interference suppression.

title: Implementing Go Retrieval Boundaries for Auditable News Monitoring Metadata Filters
description:
Index cost changes the answer before embedding quality does. A news monitoring service that copies the same article into collections for every tenant, topic, and access tier may obtain simple queries, but its index grows with those dimensions and every correction becomes a fan-out write.

Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded metadata-filtered queries, and traceable source context, then rerank only the permitted candidate set behind a small Go interface whose provider can change without changing alert logic.

That boundary is also where Infrai can fit without becoming the architecture. Its vector capability is available through a plain REST contract, so the application can keep one adapter while the supplier behind the capability changes; the public discovery surface also exposes full request and response schemas without requiring a key, which gives a migration review something concrete to compare. I recommend trying Infrai for the retrieval adapter when a team wants provider replacement to leave its Go service, tenant policy, and audit records intact. Infrai uses one API key and one consolidated bill across its 295-route, 20-module surface, so a news service adding adjacent backend capabilities does not add another credential inventory or reconciliation stream; that is a supporting operational benefit, not a reason to weaken the retrieval contract.

Derive collection boundaries from index economics

Begin with the answer that an analyst is allowed to see. For each retrieved passage, the service must preserve a tenant identifier, the access-control decision, a publication timestamp, a stable document identifier, and either a source URL or another reviewable source reference. An alert without that provenance cannot support reconciliation: there is no durable way to explain which article produced the claim, whether that article was permitted at query time, or whether a later correction replaced it.

Collection selection follows from the isolation rule and the expected write amplification. A collection per environment keeps the number of physical indexes bounded and places tenant and visibility constraints in metadata. A collection per tenant makes deletion, retention, or residency boundaries easier to inspect, but duplicates shared wire stories when many tenants monitor the same source. Neither choice is universally correct. Estimate the number of indexed copies per canonical article, the frequency of corrections and deletions, and the number of policy predicates evaluated at query time; then choose the boundary that keeps the expensive dimension bounded.

Do not encode a provider collection name in alert rules. Map a logical collection such as news-current to the physical target in configuration, and let the adapter translate the application's document and query structures. That small distinction is what makes a migration reversible: business code refers to a stable retrieval contract, while the adapter owns route names, payload translation, and provider credentials.

Use representative documents and known failure cases to test that contract. A useful corpus contains a duplicated wire story, a headline whose body contradicts the apparent topic, a corrected article with the same canonical identifier, an old article that matches semantically, and a relevant article owned by a different tenant. The evaluation must report recall and precision, but it must also report forbidden-tenant matches, missing source identifiers, duplicate canonical documents, and candidates outside the time bound. A high relevance score cannot compensate for an access-control breach.

This is the expensive lesson: index layout is policy expressed as storage.

How should metadata filters shape retrieval architecture for a news monitoring service?

Metadata filters belong before reranking. Derive tenant_id and allowed visibility from the authenticated request, add the bounded publication window required by the monitoring rule, query only the logical collection selected by policy, and cap the candidate count. The reranker then receives a small, permitted set and can improve relevance without becoming an accidental authorization layer.

The ordering matters. If a service retrieves a global top 200, reranks it, and filters afterward, it spends work on candidates the caller cannot consume and risks exposing restricted context to another processing stage. If it creates a separate index for every alert rule, filtering becomes easy but index cost and correction fan-out grow with the rule count. The staged design avoids both extremes: stable collection boundaries contain the corpus, metadata filters enforce request-specific policy, and reranking spends its budget only on candidates that survived those gates.

The operational sequence is short:

  1. Resolve the tenant, access scope, logical collection, and time window.
  2. Run a bounded vector query with those metadata constraints.
  3. Rerank the returned candidates for the monitoring topic.
  4. Deduplicate by the canonical document identifier.
  5. Persist source identifiers, filter inputs, and the retrieval request identifier with the alert.

Keep the last record append-only. Exactly-once processing is a mindset, not a magical transport guarantee; deterministic document IDs, idempotent downstream alert writes, and an audit trail make retries reconcilable. A duplicate delivery can then be recognized without erasing evidence about what the system attempted.

The following Go program keeps the sole vendor call inside an adapter. It uses the verified POST /v1/vector/query route, reads the key from the environment, sets the method explicitly, checks every status, and handles 429 with Retry-After or exponential backoff. The filter values would ordinarily come from authenticated policy resolution rather than command-line input.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Query struct {
    Collection string         `json:"collection"`
    Text       string         `json:"query"`
    TopK       int            `json:"top_k"`
    Filter     map[string]any `json:"filter"`
}

func queryNews(client *http.Client, input Query) ([]byte, error) {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    payload, err := json.Marshal(input)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }

        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query rejected: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }

    return nil, errors.New("rate limit persisted after four attempts")
}

func main() {
    result, err := queryNews(http.DefaultClient, Query{
        Collection: "news-current",
        Text:       "central bank interest rate decision",
        TopK:       20,
        Filter: map[string]any{
            "tenant_id": "tenant-42",
            "visibility": "private",
        },
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(result))
}

The program deliberately does not expose the response directly as an alert. A production adapter should decode it into the application's candidate type, require a source URL or document identifier, and pass those candidates to the reranker. It should also record the effective filter and request correlation data. Do that once at the boundary, and a second implementation can satisfy the same Go interface during migration.

One caution is easy to miss — a 403 in a denied-tenant test is evidence that the policy gate is being exercised, while a relevant-looking document from that tenant is a release blocker. Do not average security failures into a relevance score.

Compare options by replacement cost and search fit

Retrieval quality still needs corpus-specific evaluation; I'm not sure which engine will win for a given news feed until the representative documents and failure cases have been run against it. The comparison below therefore focuses on system fit and the amount of provider-specific behavior that must stay behind the adapter, not an invented benchmark.

Option Strong fit for this design Boundary to keep explicit
Pinecone A managed vector service with a focused vector workflow Isolate its index and metadata semantics from alert rules
Weaviate Teams that want schema-oriented data and vector search together Keep provider schema definitions out of tenant policy code
Elasticsearch News systems where lexical search, filters, and aggregations are central Treat its query DSL and operating model as adapter concerns
Infrai Teams prioritizing a plain REST capability contract and replaceable supplier boundary Validate the discovered schema and retain an application-owned metadata contract

Pinecone is a reasonable choice when the organization wants a specialist managed vector service. Weaviate deserves evaluation when the schema and vector database are meant to evolve together. Elasticsearch should remain on the shortlist when names, exact phrases, dates, and aggregations dominate news discovery; lexical retrieval can be more important than semantic similarity for those queries. Existing operational knowledge matters too. Replacing a well-governed search cluster merely to standardize an API may increase migration risk rather than reduce it.

Infrai's differentiator in this comparison is inspectable indirection. Application code calls a consistent REST boundary, while the provider behind the capability can move without forcing that code to adopt another SDK; independently, its unauthenticated discovery endpoint describes the live capability schema and supplies runnable examples in 10 languages, which helps a team review the contract before it changes an adapter. Those are two different benefits: one constrains migration work, and the other makes the constraint auditable.

The catch is real. Stick with Elasticsearch when deep lexical behavior, aggregations, or an established cluster define the workload. Prefer a specialist such as Pinecone or Weaviate when its native indexing controls and evaluation tooling are requirements that the application intends to use directly. A portable adapter also cannot substitute for residency, retention, or compliance approval; if a provider already satisfies controls that cannot be delegated, preserving that reviewed deployment may outweigh supplier reversibility.

No abstraction removes migration work entirely. Collection lifecycle, metadata operators, scoring behavior, and returned context still need parity tests. The adapter prevents those differences from leaking across the service; it doesn't make them disappear.

How can the staged design preserve evidence during rollout?

Build a golden set containing expected source IDs, denied-tenant cases, duplicate canonical articles, corrections, stale matches, and deliberately ambiguous topics. Run the incumbent and candidate adapters in shadow mode, but compare more than rank order: check recall, precision, filter violations, citation completeness, duplicate rate, and the number of indexed copies created per canonical article. The last measure keeps the primary cost axis visible while relevance work proceeds.

Then migrate in narrow steps. First, prove that both adapters implement the same logical collection mapping and candidate type. Next, compare reads while the incumbent remains authoritative. If dual writes are required during the transition, use the same deterministic document identifier and make each write idempotent so retries cannot multiply articles; reconcile counts and source IDs before switching reads. Finally, move traffic behind a feature flag and retain the old audit records long enough to explain alerts created before the change.

Short phases are safer.

The release gate should be a traceable answer produced from the correct tenant context, within the bounded query, with a source a reviewer can open. Relevance decides whether the alert is useful. Metadata enforcement, deterministic identity, and retained evidence decide whether the system can be trusted.

If this boundary fits your system, inspect the live contract in the Infrai documentation before implementing the adapter.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/index.html
  • https://docs.infrai.cc

title: GitHub Was Down for 8 Hours. Retries Made It Worse.
description:
In August, GitHub went down for almost eight hours.

It started when one part of its system got overloaded. Then everything that couldn’t connect kept trying again, all at the same moment. All that extra traffic made it even harder for GitHub to recover. In one case, the retries pushed traffic up to about 10 times its normal level.

Retrying sounds like the safe thing to do. If something fails, try again. But most systems retry straight away, over and over, with no break in between. When thousands of apps do that together, the problem just gets bigger.

Retries that wait work better. That’s how we handle them in Unmeshed. For each step in a workflow, you decide:

  • how many times it should try again
  • how long it waits between tries
  • whether the wait grows each time, like one second, then two, then four

If the step still fails after that, Unmeshed stops it and can start a backup plan, like alerting your team. No pile-up of requests, and the system gets room to recover.

Want to see how it works? Take a look at API Retry and Failover | Unmeshed

title: How Kafka Works: A Quick Walkthrough with Java
description:
Your order service needs to tell the invoice service, the email service, and the analytics pipeline that an order happened. You could wire them together directly - but every new consumer means changing the producer, and if a consumer is down, messages get lost.

Kafka takes a different approach: the producer drops the message into a durable log, and each consumer reads that log whenever it is ready, at its own pace, without the producer even knowing who they are. Let's see the whole flow working, with a real Kafka broker and a real Java client.

The five pieces that matter

  • Topic: a named stream of messages, like greetings. Producers write to it, consumers read from it.
  • Partition: a topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log. Partitions are how Kafka scales: different consumers can read different partitions in parallel.
  • Offset: a message's position in its partition - 0, 1, 2, ... Once written, a message never changes; consumers just move forward through the offsets.
  • Producer: the app that appends messages. If you give the message a key, the key's hash decides which partition it lands in, so all messages with the same key stay in order in the same partition.
  • Consumer group: consumers with the same group id share the partitions between them and Kafka tracks how far each group has read.

Here is the whole journey, animated - three messages go in, and a consumer pulls them back out:

Running a real broker

The official Kafka quickstart runs a single-node broker without ZooKeeper (KRaft mode) in three commands, which is exactly what I did - this article's output is from Apache Kafka 4.4.0 on JDK 21:

# 1. generate a cluster id
KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID="$(bin/kafka-storage.sh random-uuid)"

# 2. format the log directories
bin/kafka-storage.sh format --standalone -t $KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID -c config/server.properties

# 3. start the broker
bin/kafka-server-start.sh config/server.properties

Startup logged Kafka Server started (kafka.server.KafkaRaftServer), and the broker was ready on localhost:9092.

A Java producer and consumer in one file

This complete program creates a topic with 3 partitions, produces 3 keyed messages, and reads them back. It uses only the kafka-clients jar that ships in the Kafka download's libs folder - no extra dependencies:

import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.AdminClient;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.NewTopic;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerConfig;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerRecords;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.KafkaConsumer;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerConfig;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord;
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer;
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Properties;

public class KafkaWalkthrough {

    static final String TOPIC = "greetings";

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        createTopic();
        produce();
        consume();
    }

    static void createTopic() throws Exception {
        Properties p = new Properties();
        p.put("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092");
        try (AdminClient admin = AdminClient.create(p)) {
            admin.createTopics(List.of(new NewTopic(TOPIC, 3, (short) 1))).all().get();
            System.out.println("[setup] created topic '" + TOPIC + "' with 3 partitions");
        }
    }

    static void produce() throws Exception {
        Properties p = new Properties();
        p.put(ProducerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "localhost:9092");
        p.put(ProducerConfig.KEY_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class.getName());
        p.put(ProducerConfig.VALUE_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class.getName());
        try (KafkaProducer<String, String> producer = new KafkaProducer<>(p)) {
            String[][] msgs = {
                {"vishnu", "hello kafka"},
                {"asha", "kafka is a log"},
                {"ravi", "partitions scale reads"},
            };
            for (String[] m : msgs) {
                var meta = producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(TOPIC, m[0], m[1])).get();
                System.out.printf("[producer] sent key=%s value='%s' -> partition=%d offset=%d%n",
                        m[0], m[1], meta.partition(), meta.offset());
            }
        }
    }

    static void consume() {
        Properties p = new Properties();
        p.put(ConsumerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "localhost:9092");
        p.put(ConsumerConfig.GROUP_ID_CONFIG, "walkthrough-group");
        p.put(ConsumerConfig.KEY_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class.getName());
        p.put(ConsumerConfig.VALUE_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class.getName());
        p.put(ConsumerConfig.AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG, "earliest");
        try (KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer = new KafkaConsumer<>(p)) {
            consumer.subscribe(List.of(TOPIC));
            int got = 0;
            long deadline = System.currentTimeMillis() + 15000;
            while (got < 3 && System.currentTimeMillis() < deadline) {
                ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
                records.forEach(r -> {
                    System.out.printf("[consumer] read key=%s value='%s' from partition=%d offset=%d%n",
                            r.key(), r.value(), r.partition(), r.offset());
                });
                got += records.count();
            }
        }
    }
}

I compiled it with javac -cp "libs/*" KafkaWalkthrough.java and ran it against the live broker. This is the real, unedited output:

[setup] created topic 'greetings' with 3 partitions
[producer] sent key=vishnu value='hello kafka' -> partition=0 offset=0
[producer] sent key=asha value='kafka is a log' -> partition=0 offset=1
[producer] sent key=ravi value='partitions scale reads' -> partition=0 offset=2
[consumer] read key=vishnu value='hello kafka' from partition=0 offset=0
[consumer] read key=asha value='kafka is a log' from partition=0 offset=1
[consumer] read key=ravi value='partitions scale reads' from partition=0 offset=2

Four honest observations from that output:

  1. All three keys hashed to partition 0. With only three partitions and three keys, that is chance, not a rule - other keys land in partitions 1 and 2. The guarantee is narrower: the same key always goes to the same partition.
  2. Offsets count up within a partition. 0, 1, 2 - the append-only log in action.
  3. The consumer replayed history. The producer had already finished and exited when the consumer started. Nothing was lost, because the topic stores messages; AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG = "earliest" told the new consumer group to start from offset 0.
  4. Order is per-partition. The consumer got the messages in offset order. Across partitions there is no global order - another reason keys matter when order matters.

When Kafka is the right tool

  • Decoupling services: the producer does not know or care who consumes.
  • Buffering bursts: consumers catch up after a spike or an outage instead of dropping work.
  • Multiple independent readers: analytics, email, and search can each have their own consumer group over the same topic.
  • Replay: because messages persist, a new service can rebuild its state by reading from offset 0.

It is more machinery than a plain queue, so for one producer talking to one consumer with no replay needs, a simpler tool can be the better call. Kafka earns its keep when the log itself - durable, ordered per partition, readable by many groups - is what you need.

Sources

  • Apache Kafka documentation: introduction
  • Apache Kafka quickstart

Written with AI assistance; code examples were compiled and run against a real single-node Kafka 4.4.0 broker on JDK 21 before publishing. The animation is an illustration of the message flow, not a screen recording.

title: Building a Medical Investigation AI on an OpenAI-Compatible API
description:
November 6, 2026 | 8 min read

Most medical AI demos are a chat box with a medical prompt.

You send a symptom. You get a paragraph. It can look impressive in a screenshot. Then you try to use it on a real case and discover the hard parts: the record is fragmented, the values have dates, the medications interact, the evidence needs a source, and the model has no idea what it does not know.

Premedice is a medical investigation AI. The product is built around a different unit of work: the whole case, not the single question.

This post is a technical look at how that works, and how to call the API from your own stack.

THE PROBLEM WITH A SINGLE PROMPT

A standard medical RAG pipeline retrieves a few passages and asks a model to answer. That is useful for general questions. It is not enough for an investigation.

An investigation needs four things a single retrieval call usually lacks.

Temporal context. A potassium of 5.3 means something different if it was 4.1 last month. A medication started nine days ago matters. A lab trend matters. A snapshot does not.

Tool access. The answer may depend on a drug label, an interaction database, a clinical trial, or a guideline. Retrieval alone does not check those sources.

A citation trail. A high-stakes claim without a source is a hypothesis. The user needs to inspect the basis, not just read the conclusion.

Explicit uncertainty. A good investigation names the gaps. What is missing? Which value conflicts? Which symptom has no explanation yet?

That is the design brief for a medical investigation AI.

WHAT "MEDICAL INVESTIGATION AI" MEANS

Medical investigation AI is software that takes a health question and investigates it across the full available record, rather than generating an answer from a single prompt.

It collects the history, labs, medications, documents, and symptoms. It correlates changes over time. It verifies claims against literature and drug sources. It states what is missing. Then it returns a structured brief for a human to review.

Premedice is built for that job. It is not a diagnosis engine. It is an investigation layer that sits between the record and the clinician.

THE ARCHITECTURE, IN PRACTICAL TERMS

Premedice exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. If you already use the OpenAI SDK, you change the base URL, the API key, and the model name. The rest of your client code stays the same.

Base URL: https://api.premedice.com/v1

Model: Premedice/Premed-4

Context window: 128K tokens

Max output: 16K tokens

Streaming: OpenAI SSE

Tools: eight medical tools are preloaded on every request. PubMed, OpenFDA, RxNorm, DailyMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, and create_file.

The tools are always on. That is a deliberate product decision. A medical investigation should not require the caller to remember which database to attach. The model should be able to check the label, the interaction, the trial, and the literature as part of the investigation.

The response includes the answer and its sources. The exact shape is the normal chat completion shape, so existing streaming, retries, and logging code should carry over.

WHAT A GOOD RESPONSE SHOULD CONTAIN

A medical investigation AI should return more than a paragraph. A useful brief has five parts.

The signals. The values or findings that changed and deserve attention.

The evidence. The source value, trend, guideline, label, or paper behind each signal. The reader should be able to check it.

The correlations. The medication, condition, or history that may explain the signal. Correlation is not causation, and the brief should say so.

The gaps. The missing history, the conflicting value, the symptom that has no explanation yet.

The boundary. A clear statement that the output is decision support, not a diagnosis, and that urgent symptoms need urgent care.

If your medical AI output does not have those five parts, it is probably a chat response, not an investigation.

DESIGN LESSONS

Three lessons shaped the product.

Preload the tools. A medical investigation should not fail because the caller did not attach the right database. The tools are part of the investigation environment, not an optional plugin.

Make citations first-class. A citation is not a footnote added after the fact. It is part of the answer. If a high-stakes claim cannot be tied to a source, the claim should be marked as uncertain.

Keep the uncertainty visible. Models are good at sounding complete. A medical investigation AI has to be good at sounding incomplete when the evidence is incomplete. That is a product behavior, not just a prompt.

The model matters too, but it is not the whole product. Premedice 4 scored 84.6 percent on an internal MedQA replication. That is an exam-style benchmark, not a clinical validation or an outcome study. It has not been peer-reviewed. It is a signal about reasoning, not proof of accuracy in a real patient.

Benchmarks are a floor, not a finish line.

WHAT TO BUILD WITH IT

The API is useful anywhere a developer needs a cited medical investigation rather than a generic answer.

Patient education tools that explain labs in plain language and show the source.

Clinical preparation tools that assemble a pre-visit brief from a record.

Research prototypes that need to correlate labs, medications, and literature.

Caregiver tools that help someone organize a family member's records and questions.

Second-opinion workflows that review the whole case against the evidence.

The API is not a diagnosis engine. It is not a telehealth service. It is not an emergency service. It is a reasoning and evidence layer that a human should review.


SAFETY AND PRIVACY FOR DEVELOPERS

If you are building in health, the non-negotiables are not optional.

Use a lawful basis for processing. Do not send identifiable data without consent or another valid legal basis.

Keep API keys server-side. A pm_live key is a secret. Do not ship it in a client bundle.

Log carefully. Do not store full patient records in application logs or error trackers.

Respect the boundary. Do not present the output as a diagnosis. Do not use it for emergency triage.

Check the data flow. Premedice is designed around GDPR-native, EU-resident data handling, with AES-256 at rest and TLS 1.3 in transit. User data is not used for model training. The API is a developer surface, but your application still needs its own privacy review.

For a clinical deployment, a clinic still needs a data protection impact assessment, a retention policy, a clinical safety review, and a clear escalation path.

PRICING AND ACCESS

API keys are generated in the Premedice dashboard. Billing uses the same per-token rates as the in-app chat and is debited from the account's token balance.

The app itself has a free tier. Pro is 5.99 EUR per month, and Advanced is 20 EUR per month. The API is the developer path for teams that want to integrate the investigation into their own product.

GETTING STARTED

Read the API docs at api.premedice.com/docs.

Create a key in the Premedice dashboard.

Point your OpenAI SDK at https://api.premedice.com/v1.

Use the model name Premedice/Premed-4.

Send a synthetic case first. Check the citations. Check the uncertainty. Then decide whether the output is good enough for your workflow.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • Medical investigation AI is a whole-record, tool-using, cited workflow. It is not a single-prompt chatbot.
  • Premedice exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with a 128K context window and eight preloaded medical tools.
  • Citations and explicit uncertainty are product requirements, not prompt decoration.
  • Premedice 4's 84.6 percent MedQA replication is an internal, non-peer-reviewed benchmark, not clinical validation.
  • The API is decision support. A human remains accountable.


FAQ

Is the API OpenAI-compatible?
Yes. Use the base URL https://api.premedice.com/v1, your Premedice key, and the model Premedice/Premed-4.

Which tools are preloaded?
PubMed, OpenFDA, RxNorm, DailyMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, and create_file. They are on by default.

Does the API diagnose patients?
No. It is decision support. It does not diagnose, prescribe, or replace a clinician.

Is patient data used for training?
No. Premedice states that user data is not used for model training.

Where are the docs?
https://api.premedice.com/docs

SOURCES

Premedice 4 model page.
https://premedice.com/models/premedice-4/

Premedice API documentation.
https://api.premedice.com/docs

Jin D, et al. What Disease Does This Patient Have? A Large-Scale Open Domain Question Answering Dataset from Medical Exams. arXiv:2009.13081.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13081

World Health Organization. Patient safety.
https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/patient-safety

COVER IMAGE

Ready to use: https://premedice.com/og-home.jpg (1200 x 630)
Alt text: Premedice medical investigation AI product preview with a cited answer interface.

Custom cover direction: a terminal window beside a lab report, with three values highlighted and a source list on the right. No stock photos, no robot hands, no blue-purple gradient.

title: How to Build a Browser-Based Jigsaw Puzzle Game with JavaScript and HTML5 Canvas
description:
Building a jigsaw puzzle game for the browser is an interesting combination of geometry, graphics programming, and interactive game development.

Unlike a traditional grid-based puzzle, a jigsaw puzzle requires irregular piece shapes, matching edges, image clipping, and precise drag-and-drop interactions. Players should be able to move individual pieces, connect matching pieces, and gradually reconstruct the original image.

In this tutorial, we'll explore how to build a browser-based jigsaw puzzle game using JavaScript and HTML5 Canvas, starting with the basic game architecture and moving through piece generation, rendering, interaction, and performance optimization.

The goal is to create a fully playable game that runs directly in a web browser without requiring downloads or additional software.

  1. Planning the Game Architecture

Before implementing the puzzle mechanics, it's useful to break the game into smaller components.

A browser-based jigsaw puzzle game typically needs several systems:

Component

Responsibility

Game Manager

Controls the overall game state

Puzzle Generator

Divides the original image into pieces

Shape Generator

Creates realistic jigsaw piece boundaries

Canvas Renderer

Draws pieces and the game board

Input Manager

Handles mouse and touch interactions

Snap Manager

Detects matching pieces and connections

Progress Tracker

Tracks completed pieces and game progress

Keeping these systems separate makes the game easier to maintain and extend.

For example, changing the puzzle difficulty from 16 pieces to 100 pieces should not require rewriting the rendering or interaction logic.

A basic game state might look like this:

`const gameState = {
status: "playing",

rows: 4,
cols: 4,

pieces: [],

selectedPiece: null,

placedCount: 0,

startTime: Date.now()
};`

Possible game states include:

loading: Preparing the puzzle image and geometry.

playing: The player is assembling the puzzle.

paused: Gameplay is temporarily suspended.

completed: All pieces have been correctly assembled.

This simple structure provides a foundation for implementing the rest of the game.

  1. Creating the Puzzle Grid

The first step is dividing the original image into a rectangular grid.

Suppose the source image has a width of 1200 pixels and a height of 800 pixels.

For a 4 × 4 puzzle:

const rows = 4;
const cols = 4;

const pieceWidth = image.width / cols;
const pieceHeight = image.height / rows;

Each piece has a logical position in the completed image.

We can calculate its original coordinates using its row and column:

function getPiecePosition(row, col, width, height) {
return {
x: col * width,
y: row * height
};
}

However, these rectangular regions are only the starting point.

A realistic jigsaw puzzle requires each piece to have a unique outline, with tabs and blanks that fit neighboring pieces.

This brings us to the most important part of the geometry system.

  1. Generating Matching Jigsaw Piece Edges

A common mistake when implementing jigsaw puzzles is generating every piece independently.

This can lead to small differences between neighboring edges, creating visible gaps or overlaps.

A better approach is to generate shared boundaries first.

Each internal boundary is created once and reused by the two adjacent pieces.

For a grid of rows and columns, we need two sets of boundaries:

Horizontal boundaries between rows.

Vertical boundaries between columns.

Each boundary contains a geometric description and a polarity.

For example:

Positive polarity: A protruding tab.

Negative polarity: A recessed blank.

A simplified edge map can be generated as follows:

function randomPolarity() {
  return Math.random() > 0.5 ? 1 : -1;
}

function createEdgeMap(rows, cols) {
  const horizontal = [];
  const vertical = [];

  for (let r = 1; r < rows; r++) {
    horizontal[r] = [];

    for (let c = 0; c < cols; c++) {
      horizontal[r][c] = randomPolarity();
    }
  }

  for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++) {
    vertical[r] = [];

    for (let c = 1; c < cols; c++) {
      vertical[r][c] = randomPolarity();
    }
  }

  return { horizontal, vertical };
}

In a complete implementation, each entry should store the full edge geometry rather than just its polarity.

The neighboring pieces then reuse the same geometry in opposite directions.

This ensures that their boundaries match exactly.

Outer puzzle boundaries are treated differently: they remain straight rather than receiving tabs or blanks.

  1. Creating Realistic Piece Shapes with Bézier Curves

Jigsaw puzzle pieces are recognizable because of their characteristic tabs and recessed edges.

We can approximate these shapes using cubic Bézier curves.

A cubic Bézier curve is defined by four control points:

P0: Starting point.

P1: First control point.

P2: Second control point.

P3: Ending point.

Its mathematical representation is:

B(t) = (1-t)³P0
+ 3(1-t)²tP1
+ 3(1-t)t²P2
+ t³P3

where t ranges from 0 to 1.

By adjusting the control points, we can create the rounded head and narrow neck of a traditional jigsaw tab.

For example, Canvas provides a convenient method:

ctx.bezierCurveTo(
controlX1,
controlY1,
controlX2,
controlY2,
endX,
endY
);

A simplified edge renderer might look like this:

function drawTab(ctx, x, y, width, depth, direction) {
  const w = width;
  const d = depth * direction;

  ctx.lineTo(x + w * 0.25, y);

  ctx.bezierCurveTo(
    x + w * 0.25, y - d * 0.15,
    x + w * 0.28, y - d * 0.55,
    x + w * 0.40, y - d * 0.55
  );

  ctx.bezierCurveTo(
    x + w * 0.45, y - d * 0.95,
    x + w * 0.55, y - d * 0.95,
    x + w * 0.60, y - d * 0.55
  );

  ctx.bezierCurveTo(
    x + w * 0.72, y - d * 0.55,
    x + w * 0.75, y - d * 0.15,
    x + w * 0.75, y
  );

  ctx.lineTo(x + w, y);
}

The direction determines whether the tab protrudes or curves inward.

For a production-quality game, the geometry should also account for:

Consistent endpoints and tangent directions.

Variable tab widths and depths.

Different shapes for horizontal and vertical edges.

Reversed traversal when rendering neighboring pieces.

Shared control points to prevent mismatched boundaries.

The objective is to generate varied-looking pieces while maintaining mathematically consistent connections.

  1. Constructing the Complete Puzzle Piece

Once all four edges are available, we can construct the outline of each piece.

A convenient strategy is to trace the shape clockwise:

Start at the top-left corner.

Draw the top edge from left to right.

Draw the right edge from top to bottom.

Draw the bottom edge from right to left.

Draw the left edge from bottom to top.

Close the path.

A simplified structure looks like this:

function createPiecePath(ctx, piece) {
  const { x, y, edges } = piece;

  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.moveTo(x, y);

  drawEdge(ctx, edges.top);
  drawEdge(ctx, edges.right);
  drawEdge(ctx, edges.bottom, true);
  drawEdge(ctx, edges.left, true);

  ctx.closePath();
}

Here, drawEdge() is a reusable function that renders the corresponding edge geometry.

For a clean implementation, it is helpful to define each edge in local coordinates and apply transformations when placing it on different sides of the piece.

This avoids duplicating the same Bézier geometry for horizontal and vertical boundaries.

  1. Rendering Puzzle Pieces with HTML5 Canvas

With the geometry generated, we can start rendering the actual puzzle.

The key technique is Canvas clipping.

Instead of creating a separate cropped image for every piece, we draw the original image through each piece's irregular clipping path.

This preserves image alignment across the entire puzzle.

The basic process is:

Save the current Canvas state.

Translate to the piece's position.

Define its clipping path.

Draw the original image.

Restore the Canvas state.

For example:

function renderPiece(ctx, image, piece) {
  ctx.save();

  ctx.translate(piece.currentX, piece.currentY);

  const path = createLocalPiecePath(piece);

  ctx.clip(path);

  ctx.drawImage(
    image,
    -piece.sourceX,
    -piece.sourceY
  );

  ctx.restore();
}

The important detail is that every piece uses the same original image coordinate system.

This means that when all pieces are placed correctly, the image lines up seamlessly.

We can also draw a border around each piece:

ctx.save();

ctx.translate(piece.currentX, piece.currentY);

const path = createLocalPiecePath(piece);

ctx.strokeStyle = "rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.25)";
ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;

ctx.stroke(path);

ctx.restore();

Additional visual effects such as shadows, hover highlights, and selection outlines can make the game feel much more responsive.

  1. Implementing Drag-and-Drop Interaction

A jigsaw puzzle would not be playable without intuitive piece movement.

Each piece needs to track two different positions:

Its original position in the completed puzzle.

Its current position on the game board.

A simple piece object might look like this:

`const piece = {
id: 0,

correctX: 120,
correctY: 80,

currentX: 350,
currentY: 220,

isDragging: false,
isPlaced: false
};`

When the player selects a piece, we record the pointer offset:

function startDrag(piece, pointerX, pointerY) {
  piece.isDragging = true;

  piece.dragOffsetX = pointerX - piece.currentX;
  piece.dragOffsetY = pointerY - piece.currentY;
}

While dragging:

function movePiece(piece, pointerX, pointerY) {
  if (!piece.isDragging) return;

  piece.currentX = pointerX - piece.dragOffsetX;
  piece.currentY = pointerY - piece.dragOffsetY;
}

When the pointer is released, the game can check whether the piece is close enough to its correct position.

For browser games, the Pointer Events API is particularly useful because it supports mouse, touch, and pen input through a unified event model.

For example:

canvas.addEventListener("pointerdown", handlePointerDown);
canvas.addEventListener("pointermove", handlePointerMove);
canvas.addEventListener("pointerup", handlePointerUp);

canvas.addEventListener("pointercancel", handlePointerUp);

For mobile browsers, setting an appropriate touch-action CSS property on the game interaction surface also helps prevent unwanted browser gestures while dragging.

  1. Detecting Correct Placement and Snapping Pieces

A simple snapping system compares the current position of a piece with its original position.

We can use Euclidean distance:

function checkSnap(piece, threshold = 20) {
  const dx = piece.currentX - piece.correctX;
  const dy = piece.currentY - piece.correctY;

  const distance = Math.hypot(dx, dy);

  if (distance < threshold) {
    piece.currentX = piece.correctX;
    piece.currentY = piece.correctY;

    piece.isPlaced = true;

    return true;
  }

  return false;
}

This works well for a basic puzzle where pieces are placed directly into their final positions.

However, more advanced games can support connections between neighboring pieces before they reach the correct location.

For example, when two pieces are close enough and their corresponding edges match, they can snap together and form a larger group.

This introduces the concept of connected piece clusters.

A cluster can be represented as a collection of pieces that share a common movement offset.

When the player drags one piece in a connected cluster, all the other pieces move with it.

This creates a more natural puzzle-solving experience, especially for larger puzzles.

  1. Adding Difficulty Levels and Game Progress

A complete browser-based jigsaw puzzle game should offer more than just a fixed grid.

Different piece counts can provide different difficulty levels.

For example:

Difficulty

Grid

Total Pieces

Easy

3 × 3

9

Medium

5 × 5

25

Hard

8 × 8

64

Expert

10 × 10

100

The actual difficulty also depends on the image itself, the shape variation, and whether players can use a reference image.

A progress tracker can be implemented with a simple counter:

function updateProgress(gameState) {
  const total = gameState.rows * gameState.cols;

  const progress = gameState.placedCount / total;

  if (progress >= 1) {
    gameState.status = "completed";
  }

  return progress;
}

Other useful gameplay features include:

A timer to track completion time.

A preview of the completed image.

A shuffle function.

A restart option.

A completion animation.

A responsive puzzle board for smaller screens.

These features turn the underlying rendering engine into a more complete game experience.

  1. Optimizing Performance for Desktop and Mobile Browsers

Performance becomes increasingly important as the number of pieces grows.

A 3 × 3 puzzle is relatively easy to render. A 100-piece puzzle requires more careful management.

Several techniques can help.

Separate rendering layers

Instead of redrawing everything unnecessarily, divide the game into layers:

Background and board.

Static completed pieces.

Loose puzzle pieces.

Active dragging and interaction effects.

Use offscreen rendering

Static piece images can be rendered into offscreen canvases and reused.

This reduces repeated clipping and drawing operations.

Optimize hit testing

Checking every pixel of every piece is expensive.

Start with bounding-box checks to eliminate pieces that are clearly not under the pointer. More precise path-based checks can then be performed on the remaining candidates.

Avoid unnecessary redraws

A requestAnimationFrame-based rendering loop can be used to update the game smoothly, but static scenes do not need to be redrawn continuously.

Consider device pixel ratio

High-density mobile screens require careful Canvas scaling to keep puzzle edges sharp without creating excessively large rendering surfaces.

The best optimization strategy depends on the puzzle size, device capabilities, and rendering architecture.

  1. Putting Everything Together

At this point, we have the major building blocks of a browser-based jigsaw puzzle game:

Grid generation determines the number and dimensions of pieces.

Edge generation creates matching boundaries.

Bézier curves define realistic tabs and blanks.

Canvas clipping maps the original image onto each piece.

Pointer events enable interactive dragging.

Snap detection handles correct placement.

Game state management tracks progress and completion.

The complete gameplay flow can be summarized as:

Load Puzzle Image
|
v
Generate Puzzle Grid
|
v
Create Shared Edge Geometry
|
v
Generate Individual Pieces
|
v
Shuffle Pieces on the Board
|
v
Player Drags and Connects Pieces
|
v
Check Placement and Connections
|
v
Update Game Progress
|
v
Complete the Puzzle

The most important architectural decision is keeping geometry, rendering, interaction, and game state independent.

This makes it easier to add new features without introducing unnecessary complexity into the core puzzle engine.

  1. Try a Browser-Based Jigsaw Puzzle Game

The techniques discussed in this tutorial are the foundation of an interactive jigsaw puzzle experience.

If you want to explore how a browser-based jigsaw puzzle game works in practice, you can try Jigsaw Puzzle Spot.

It offers free online jigsaw puzzles that can be played directly in the browser, providing a practical example of image-based puzzle gameplay without requiring a separate application or installation.

Conclusion

Building a browser-based jigsaw puzzle game with JavaScript and HTML5 Canvas involves several interesting engineering challenges.

The most important ones are generating matching piece geometry, rendering irregular shapes, maintaining image alignment, and implementing intuitive drag-and-drop interactions.

By separating these systems into reusable components, it is possible to build a flexible puzzle engine that supports different image sizes, difficulty levels, and gameplay mechanics.

What starts as a simple image-splitting exercise can become a surprisingly rich browser game development project.

And the best part is that the entire experience can run directly in a modern web browser.

title: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
description:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.

title: 168 of 169 Paid 'description' Fields Were Identical to the Free 'summary'. The Real Text Was 17x Longer
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them reads Eventbrite search pages: you hand it a search URL or a city, it pages through the results and returns one row per event — name, dates with the time zone, venue with coordinates, category, tags, image. Switch on the detail pass and it also opens each event page for the ticket price range, the organizer and the description.

That detail pass costs the buyer a second charge per event. I spent today measuring what it actually buys, on two search pages: Bali, Indonesia and Berlin, Germany, a hundred-event cap each.

Bali returned 69 events across 4 pages in 28.0 seconds. Berlin returned 100 in 22.2 seconds. Then I diffed two fields that should never be the same — summary, which comes free from the search listing, and description, which the buyer pays for.

They were identical on 168 of 169 rows. The 169th had no description at all.

The meta tag is not the description

Eventbrite event pages carry JSON-LD, the schema.org/Event block search engines read. It has offers with lowPrice and highPrice, an organizer, start and end timestamps with the UTC offset — all genuinely useful, none of it on the search page. It also has a description. I read that field, shipped it, and called it "full description" in my own documentation.

It is the meta description. Capped at 140 characters, built from the first sentences of the listing — which is exactly what the search page already hands over as summary, for free.

Across those 69 Bali events, description averaged 108 characters. Three rows sat exactly at 140, the cap. The field was not wrong, it was just a duplicate the buyer was paying me to deliver twice.

The text the organizer actually wrote is in the same HTML I had already downloaded, a few kilobytes further down, inside the Next.js payload:

const m = html.match(/<script id="__NEXT_DATA__" type="application\/json">([\s\S]*?)<\/script>/);
const ctx = JSON.parse(m[1]).props.pageProps.context;
const mods = ctx.structuredContent.modules;   // [{type:'text', text:'<p>…'}, {type:'image', url:…}]

structuredContent.modules is the event body as the organizer built it — text blocks, images, the occasional video embed. Joining the text blocks and stripping tags gives the real thing. I refetched all 69 event pages and measured both sources on the same bytes:

JSON-LD description structuredContent text
Pages that had it 69 / 69 69 / 69
Average length 108 chars 1,841 chars
Longest 140 12,764
Rows where it was longer — 67 of 69
Rows with nothing at all 0 2

Seventeen times more text, median ratio 7.8x, from a request I was already paying for. The two empty ones are honest: those organizers wrote no body copy, so the Actor falls back to the meta description rather than returning null.

The control run after the fix, same search, 20 events: description identical to summary on 0 of 20 rows, median length 647, longest 11,838. Prices and currency still filled on 20 of 20 — I did not trade one field for another.

While I was in there, the same payload gave up eleven more fields that cost nothing extra, because they ride on the page already being fetched: durationMinutes (filled on 69 of 69), salesStatus, refundPolicy, ageRestriction (9 of 69), doorTime, parking, organizerEvents, organizerFollowers, organizerVerified, descriptionBlocks, and nextSessionAt.

currency is the organizer's currency, not the country's

Now the finding I cannot fix, only document.

All 69 Bali rows carry country: "ID". Their prices came back in eight currencies:

USD 44   AUD 10   GBP 8   EUR 3   SGD 1   MYR 1   NZD 1   HKD 1

Zero in rupiah. A dive trip in North Bali is priced 5299.5 HKD. A free Bitcoin meetup in Canggu is priced 0 GBP. A bracelet workshop in Bali is served from eventbrite.ch at 7.49 EUR. Those 69 events arrived across eight different Eventbrite domains — .com, .com.au, .co.uk, .sg, .ch, .fr, .ie, .hk.

This is not a parsing artifact. I checked both independent sources on the page — the JSON-LD priceCurrency and basicInfo.currency in the Next.js payload — and they agree on 69 of 69 rows. Eventbrite publishes the price in the currency of the organizer's account. A yoga teacher who registered in Sydney sells a Canggu sound bath in Australian dollars, and the site never converts.

Berlin is why nobody notices: 95 of its 100 rows are EUR, because Berlin events are mostly run by Berlin organizers. Bali is a destination — its events are sold by Australians, Brits, Singaporeans — so the same behaviour becomes obvious. If your search covers a tourist region, sorting those rows by priceMin sorts by nothing at all, and averaging them produces a number with no unit.

Two more things to distrust in the price fields. priceMin equals priceMax on 49 of 69 rows, which usually means one ticket type, not a one-price event. And priceMax is whatever the most expensive offer on the page is: the Bali Venture Capital World Summit reports 168.94 to 57662.15 EUR, a 341x spread, because the top of that range is a sponsorship package nobody attends as a guest.

A series row is one date out of hundreds

Eventbrite recurring events are a single search result. My rows flag them — isSeries, seriesId, occurrencesInSeries — and on the Bali page 36 of 69 rows were series, covering 1,568 dates between them. The biggest single row: 421 occurrences. A sound bath studio: 283.

So "69 events in Bali" and "69 things happening in Bali" are very different counts, and a weekly calendar built from the row's one date will keep rediscovering the same workshop. The new nextSessionAt confirms what that one date means — on all 8 series rows in my control run it matched startsAt exactly, i.e. it is the next session on sale. The other 282 are not in the row, and the search page does not have them.

Berlin again shows the contrast: 7 series rows out of 100, 14 occurrences total.

Two smaller traps from the same two runs. organizerName is null on 11 of 69 Bali rows — null in both page sources, because those organizers never set a public name; you get organizerUrl with a numeric id and nothing else. And one organizer, Eurasia Research, owns 9 of the 69 rows with near-identical academic conferences, so an unfiltered "events in Bali" list is 13% one seller. Date range of that list: 6 November 2026 to 29 October 2030. Only 40 of 69 fall in the current month.

Calling it 

{
  "startUrls": ["https://www.eventbrite.com/d/indonesia--bali/all-events/"],
  "maxEvents": 100,
  "includeDetails": true
}

A real row from today's run, trimmed:

{
  "type": "event",
  "eventId": "1991054633005",
  "name": "Chakras sound sanctuary - SOUND HEALING sessions | Sound bath Bali",
  "startsAt": "2026-11-06T14:00:00",
  "timezone": "Asia/Makassar",
  "isSeries": true,
  "occurrencesInSeries": 283,
  "nextSessionAt": "2026-11-06T14:00:00+08",
  "venueName": "ADDA YOGA CANGGU - Meditation | Breath | Sound",
  "city": "Kec. Kuta Utara", "country": "ID",
  "latitude": -8.643315, "longitude": 115.1427276,
  "category": "Religion & Spirituality",
  "priceMin": 29.89, "priceMax": 29.89, "currency": "AUD", "isFree": false,
  "organizerName": "ADDA YOGA", "organizerEvents": 700, "organizerFollowers": 19,
  "durationMinutes": 90, "refundPolicy": "custom", "salesStatus": "sales_ended",
  "descriptionBlocks": 11, "urgency": ["salesEndSoon"]
}

Note salesStatus: "sales_ended" on an event the search page listed as upcoming — 3 of 69 Bali rows were sold out or closed. That field did not exist this morning.

From Python, run and read in one call:

import requests
rows = requests.post(
    "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~eventbrite-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items",
    params={"token": "apify_api_..."},
    json={"location": "Berlin, Germany", "dates": "this_weekend", "maxEvents": 200},
    timeout=600,
).json()
events = [r for r in rows if r.get("type") == "event"]
print(len(events), "events;", len({r["currency"] for r in events if r.get("currency")}), "currencies")

The Actor is Eventbrite Scraper. It bills per event row, with a second charge only if you ask for the detail pass; error rows are free and there is no start fee. The detail pass is also what the time goes on: the same Bali search finished in 8.2 seconds with details off and 28.0 seconds with them on, because that is 69 extra page loads.

When it is the wrong tool. There is no search across all of Eventbrite from the API side — you bring a search URL or a city, and Eventbrite's own search decides what exists. Past events are gone; search pages show upcoming only, so a history has to be accumulated by running on a schedule. Attendee lists, ticket inventory and sales numbers are not public and never will be. And one operational detail worth knowing: Eventbrite's WAF answers a flagged search request with HTTP 405, not 403 or 429 — from my own server the search page returns 405 while individual event pages return 200 all day. The Actor climbs a proxy ladder when that happens; if you are writing your own, treat a 405 on a GET as a bot check rather than a method error, which is what I spent an afternoon assuming.

title: VIPA: View-Invariant Projector-Based Adversarial Attack
description:
arXiv:2611.07443v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Projector-based adversarial attack aims to physically manipulate real-world scenes by projecting adversarial patterns, thereby causing deep image classifiers to produce incorrect predictions. However, existing stealthy projector-based adversarial attack methods model the project-and-capture process in a single and static view, limiting their view-invariant capability and practical applicability in dynamic environments. In this paper, we introduce View-Invariant Projector-Based Adversarial Attack (VIPA), a novel method designed to overcome these limitations by achieving both view-invariant and classifier-agnostic adversarial attacks in the physical world. We first leverage a view-invariant projector-camera system simulation method to model the physical interactions between projected patterns and real-world surfaces. To ensure robustness and stealthiness of the attack across different views, VIPA optimizes adversarial projections by aggregating simulated attack losses from multiple views. This joint optimization across diverse views helps maintain robustness regardless of the viewpoints. Finally, the optimized patterns are physically projected into real-world scenes, where they successfully fool various classifiers from different viewpoints, thereby enabling robust and practical view-invariant adversarial attacks. Our experiments in both targeted and untargeted attacks demonstrate that VIPA consistently achieves higher attack success rates than existing methods, while also enhancing stealthiness and ensuring minimal perceptual degradation across all tested views.

title: ArtiVidRM: Verifiable Artifact-as-Rubric Reward Modeling for Explicit Quality Articulation in Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.07301v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning has become an effective approach for improving video generation, but its success depends heavily on reliable reward models. Existing methods either map videos directly to opaque scalar scores or generate free-form rationales that are not explicitly optimized as the basis of the final judgment. We propose ArtiVidRM, a verifiable, artifact-as-rubrics video reward model that follows an observe-then-score paradigm. It first identifies visible generation artifacts and organizes them into a structured artifact list, then uses these artifacts as explicit rubrics for quality assessment. This intermediate representation grounds each score in concrete video-level evidence, making the reward more interpretable and informative for optimization. We further introduce a multi-reward reinforcement learning strategy to jointly optimize artifact prediction and quality assessment. The reward decomposes into complementary objectives that evaluate artifact prediction quality, including semantic coverage and prediction efficiency, together with a pairwise preference objective that supervises quality ranking through score differences. By jointly optimizing the intermediate artifact representation and the downstream preference prediction, the model learns to produce informative artifact lists while improving the accuracy of video quality assessment. Experiments show that ArtiVidRM achieves state-of-the-art performance on video preference benchmarks, provides effective signals for video diffusion optimization, and enables artifact-guided refinement of closed-source video generators.

title: Keep Video Evidence and Thumbnail Layout in Separate States
description:
The artifact boundary matters

A selected frame answers “what happened?” A thumbnail proposal answers “what should a viewer notice first?” When one object represents both, a review comment cannot identify whether it concerns accuracy or hierarchy.

The public flow of a YouTube Thumbnail Grabber begins with a YouTube or Shorts link and a frame choice. At interface level, that suggests a reference record tied to a video rather than to a creative claim.

type Reference = {

  videoUrl: string;

  frameId: string;

  selectedFor: "subject" | "moment" | "verification";

};




A placeholder must not mutate evidence

A YouTube Thumbnail Placeholder Creator visibly accepts a title and a layout. Changing the composition should not replace the selected frame; choosing a different frame should not silently rewrite the claim.

  • URL failures preserve an in-progress title and layout.
  • A review surface identifies the selected frame and source video.
  • A human can return to reference selection when the claim lacks evidence.
  • Keyboard-only users can reach selection, layout, and review.
  • Ready does not mean rights cleared or performance guaranteed.

Thumbs AI is valuable when the output becomes reviewable rather than magical. Keeping reference and proposal apart gives a concrete reason for every revision.

title: KDASO: Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization for Liability Adjudication Tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.06972v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Liability adjudication tasks (e.g., legal charge determination) require analyzing event descriptions against domain-specific skills to determine whether a party should bear liability. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in this area by leveraging executable skills for interpretable reasoning, existing approaches face three critical limitations: skill libraries become stale as real-world scenarios dynamically evolve, skill descriptions often suffer from a semantic execution gap where LLMs deviate from intended expert logic, and growing skill collections exceed context budgets causing critical skill omission. To address these challenges, we propose Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization (KDASO), which continuously evolves a skill library through neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent adjudication data, execution-aligned refinement based on LLM trajectory analysis, and context-budgeted routing for scalable skill selection. Experiments across ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability determination, and logical reasoning judgment demonstrate that KDASO significantly outperforms current general-purpose and domain-specific baselines. KDASO further achieves 8.96% improvement when transferring skills to concept-similar scenarios and maintains consistent performance gains through continuous optimization, underscoring the high transferability and stability of generated skills.

title: What Patients Say They Can't Access: Mining Cancer Screening Barriers from Online Communities
description:
arXiv:2611.07113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cancer screening disparities persist across the U.S., yet the patient-reported barriers driving low uptake remain poorly characterized at scale. While clinical surveys capture structured responses, they miss the organic, unsolicited discourse where patients candidly describe real-world obstacles. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale analysis of over 56,000 posts across six cancer-specific Reddit communities to surface barriers to cancer screening among U.S. patients. We apply a pipeline combining keyword filtering, barrier triage, open coding, and codebook synthesis to systematically extract and categorize patient-reported barriers from 576 U.S.-located posts. Our qualitative analysis reveals recurring structural, informational, and psychosocial barriers that vary meaningfully by cancer type and community context. These findings lay the groundwork for future work aimed at proactively identifying and addressing barriers at scale - spanning a broader range of cancer types and populations - and informing the design of targeted interventions, navigator programs, and health system policies that translate patient-reported obstacles into actionable solutions.

title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
description:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

Update @ai-sdk/harness-fx to the latest version to use the new adapter. Learn more in the fx harness documentation.

title: Don't write like a robot: llms.txt for AI agents
description:
This morning I asked Claude to grill me about my blog. My idea was that most of my readers are now AI agents, so my posts should be written for them. Its first question was what that claim rested on. Fair.

We ended up somewhere I didn't expect. I didn't rewrite a single post. The prose stays for people, and the agents get a frame around it: AI agents named in robots.txt, a generated llms.txt, and a Markdown copy of every post.

Then I fact-checked it, and part of it is a cheap bet rather than a sure thing. I couldn't find anyone who confirms that agents read llms.txt, and the one study on this (GEO) says quotes, numbers and cited sources matter most.

The full post covers the Hugo recipe, tested on Hugo 0.152.2, what the evidence does and doesn't say, and a prompt you can paste into your own coding agent to audit your blog.
