title: Go Tenant Password Reset Email: Template Evidence and Retention in 2026
description:
A property manager needs a password reset email whose required fields help a tenant recover access while leaving an auditable record of the instruction. Start with one application-owned recovery template and a separate audit record. The bill contains message transport, retained content, event storage, and investigation work; for the content term alone, keeping 2 identical full bodies consumes twice the body storage of keeping 1, before compression or storage overhead. That arithmetic is a design illustration, not a measured operating cost. Remove the duplicate body before considering a more elaborate template system.

TL;DR: A password reset email should identify the service and the requested action, contain a controlled recovery link, explain its validity and single-use behavior, and tell an unrecognized requester how to obtain help. These are proposed application requirements, not a universal list of fields mandated by an email standard. Keep the template version and delivery events as evidence; exclude the usable recovery secret from that evidence. For a property-management compliance notice, establish separately what the applicable rule accepts as service or receipt.

Keep secrets separate.

What fields belong in a tenant password reset email?

Treat the email as an instruction to the tenant, while treating the audit record as evidence about the instruction. Mixing those responsibilities encourages a tempting mistake: retaining a complete rendered email because it is convenient to inspect, even though its recovery link carries authority to change an account credential. A record that helps investigate a complaint should not become a second place from which somebody can initiate account recovery.

For an application implemented in Go, the following is a template acceptance checklist. It defines the behavior the application must implement before the wording can truthfully promise it; it does not claim that a particular set of visible fields establishes security by itself.

Template element Proposed content Acceptance boundary
Service identity The property-management service name and a clear recovery subject Identify the account service without including a unit number or tenancy dispute details.
Request explanation A statement that an account password reset was requested Do not imply that the request authenticates the person who submitted it.
Recovery action A clearly labeled link to the application's controlled recovery destination Keep the destination under application control and review the rendered target as well as its label.
Validity The application's actual expiration condition Publish wording only when the backend enforces the same condition.
Single-use instruction A statement that a successful reset consumes the recovery authorization Make consumption an application invariant, not merely template text.
Unexpected-request guidance A brief explanation of what to do if the tenant did not request recovery Ensure the guidance matches the application's actual account behavior.
Help route An established way to reach the service's support function Do not ask the tenant to reply with a password or recovery secret.

No password belongs in this template. Nor does the underlying compliance notice: the recovery message should enable access to the account where the notice can be handled through its own workflow. That separation preserves a useful distinction between a recovery request, a completed password change, and the later handling of a notice. They are three different application events.

The supplied validity statement deserves particular care. A template saying that a link expires cannot enforce expiration, and a single-use sentence cannot arbitrate two concurrent redemption attempts; the backend must decide which attempt consumes the authorization and reject subsequent consumption. An exactly-once mindset is useful here because it forces the invariant into a durable state transition. It should not become a promise of exactly-once email delivery.

Own the template and the evidence contract together

Template ownership is the primary decision. Give the application team responsibility for the recovery action, supported variables, version identifier, and retention boundary; require the party responsible for compliance language to review wording that describes notice obligations. This is a proposed division of responsibility, not a claim that one organizational arrangement satisfies every property-management rule.

A useful example record identifies a tenant account, a notice reference, a recovery-request identifier, a template version, a rendering locale, and the transport attempt identifier. Choose the account reference rather than a street address when the address adds no investigative value. The compliance notice should have its own record and its own evidence requirements. Link the records through an internal reference instead of copying the notice into the recovery email.

Version the words.

If a template can change without a retained version, an investigator may know that an email was submitted but be unable to establish what the tenant was told about expiration or support. Keep an immutable reviewed template artifact and its variable schema, then record which artifact a rendering used. Separate approved edits to explanatory language from changes to destinations or security promises, because those changes require different review expertise. A deployment that changes token behavior must include a check that the associated language still describes the resulting behavior.

This boundary also determines whether an external template editor is appropriate: require an exportable, reviewable version and a reliable way to associate that exact version with an attempt. If those conditions cannot be met, retain rendering ownership in the application. The trade-off is additional release responsibility for the application team in exchange for a simpler account of which words were authorized.

Reconcile delivery events without claiming proof of receipt

RFC 6376 describes DomainKeys Identified Mail, including the relationship between a signing domain, message headers, and a message body. Its signing-domain identifier is not an assertion that the signer is the author. A valid signature is therefore useful evidence within its defined scope; it does not establish that a tenant opened a recovery email, controlled the intended account, or received legally sufficient service of a compliance notice.

Those limits matter.

Use distinct application states for a recovery request, a submission attempt, a reported transport outcome, and a completed reset. Preserve the provenance and interpretation of each event. Do not relabel an intermediate transport event as tenant receipt merely because a reporting interface calls it delivery, and do not infer notice acknowledgment from successful account recovery. The relevant property-management requirement must determine what additional evidence is necessary. This article does not establish a jurisdiction's service rules or retention period.

An idempotent submission policy should attach retry attempts to one logical recovery request, while preserving each attempt as a separate audit event. Repeated ingestion of the same event should leave the interpreted state unchanged. That preserves reconciliation without erasing the attempt history, which is the difference between suppressing a duplicate state transition and pretending a retry never occurred. Record the event identity and its source so an operator can explain the distinction later.

Before release, exercise expiration, repeated redemption, concurrent redemption, a retry after an ambiguous submission outcome, and a repeated event notification. Inspect the generated email as well as the state transitions. Operational monitoring should distinguish submission failures from missing or delayed outcome events, and logs should reference the recovery request without recording its usable link. These are acceptance tests and operating rules for the proposed design, not reported performance results.

Retain the explanation and retire the secret

The storage change follows from the ownership choice: retain one immutable template artifact per version, retain the permitted nonsecret rendering inputs and event history per request, and avoid retaining a second complete body containing the recovery authorization. This reduces the duplicated-body term identified at the start. It does not establish that storage dominates the total bill; transport volume and investigation labor need their own measurements. Do not trade away evidence merely to improve an unmeasured cost estimate.

A template hash can help identify an artifact, but a hash alone cannot reconstruct its text. Likewise, a redacted rendering can explain the visible instructions while failing to reproduce the exact bytes of the original signed message. Decide whether either limitation is acceptable before adopting the retention policy. If exact-message evidence is required, that requirement needs a separate design for access control, secret lifetime, and retention review.

For this design, deliberately stop keeping usable recovery URLs in ordinary audit records, stop duplicating full bodies across routine logs, and stop retaining raw recipient details once the approved retention purpose ends. Keep the versioned explanatory text and permitted event references for the period established by the applicable policy. The cost appears during an investigation: a redacted record cannot reproduce the original usable link, and deleting recipient details can prevent later independent reconstruction of the destination. Accept those losses explicitly, with the compliance owner, before deletion begins.

References

RFC 6376 supplies the technical basis for the discussion of signing identity and the limits of message-signature evidence. The field checklist, ownership boundaries, tests, and retention choices above are proposed application controls; the RFC does not prescribe password reset email content or establish legal proof of service.

Further reading

  • RFC 6376, DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), especially signing identity, signature scope, and security considerations: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6376

title: Motion Canvas vs Remotion: which one should you build video with?
description:
Generator functions and signals on one side, React components and frames on the other. A head-to-head on the axes that decide it, with the same small scene sketched in both.

Motion Canvas vs Remotion is a question that comes up when you want to write video as code and have narrowed it to two TypeScript options. Full disclosure: I build ReelMint, which is built on Remotion, so I have a stake. I checked both projects' repositories, docs and licenses on November 3, 2026, and I mark below what I did not run myself. Short version: Motion Canvas is an animation tool with its own timeline model and editor, Remotion is React rendered frame by frame to video. They overlap less than the search results suggest.

What each one is

Motion Canvas is, in its own docs' words, a tool for building animations in code. You write scenes as generator functions and the animation plays as you yield instructions. It works with TypeScript or JavaScript, the guide recommends TypeScript, and the quickstart scaffolds a project with npm init @motion-canvas@latest. Its GitHub repository is MIT licensed.

Remotion is a framework for making video with React. A video is a component that reads the current frame and returns markup, and Remotion renders it by stepping through frames and encoding the result. Anything the browser can draw is available: HTML, CSS, SVG, canvas, npm packages.

Mental model: generator functions and signals versus components and frames

In Motion Canvas you describe a sequence of events. You add nodes to the view, hold references to them with createRef, and yield* tweens one after another. To run things at once you wrap them in all(). Values that change over time live in signals created with createSignal, and a text node can take a function so the label updates whenever the signal does. The scene reads like a script: do this, then this, then these two together.

In Remotion nothing persists between frames. Each frame is a pure function of useCurrentFrame(), and you express motion as math on the frame number, usually with interpolate() or spring(). There is no sequence of events to write; there is a picture for every frame number. If you know React this is familiar. If you think in timelines, the Motion Canvas model will feel closer to how you plan an explainer.

The practical consequence: sequencing (A, then B, then A and C together) is easy in Motion Canvas and takes deliberate offsets in Remotion, where you place Sequence components or compute frame ranges. Layout, data-driven UI and reusing existing React components go the other way.

A worked example: a counter ticks up and a bar grows over 3 seconds

Motion Canvas first. This is a sketch built from the patterns on the official docs pages (generators, createRef, createSignal, all, tweening a signal). I did not run it, and import paths have changed between major versions, so check the current docs before pasting:

import { makeScene2D, Rect, Txt } from "@motion-canvas/2d";
import { all, createRef, createSignal } from "@motion-canvas/core";

export default makeScene2D(function* (view) {
  const count = createSignal(0);
  const bar = createRef<Rect>();

  view.add(
    <>
      <Txt fill="white" fontSize={120} text={() => Math.round(count()).toString()} />
      <Rect ref={bar} y={160} height={40} width={0} fill="#3b82f6" />
    </>,
  );

  yield* all(count(100, 3), bar().width(600, 3));
});

The same scene in Remotion, also unrun. It is a 90-frame composition at 30 fps, and extrapolateRight: "clamp" is the option shown in the interpolate() docs for holding the end value:

import { AbsoluteFill, interpolate, useCurrentFrame } from "remotion";

export const CounterBar = () => {
  const frame = useCurrentFrame();
  const opts = { extrapolateRight: "clamp" } as const;
  const count = interpolate(frame, [0, 90], [0, 100], opts);
  const width = interpolate(frame, [0, 90], [0, 600], opts);
  return (
    <AbsoluteFill style={{ background: "#0b0b0f", alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center" }}>
      <div style={{ color: "white", fontSize: 120 }}>{Math.round(count)}</div>
      <div style={{ marginTop: 40, height: 40, width, background: "#3b82f6" }} />
    </AbsoluteFill>
  );
};

// <Composition id="CounterBar" component={CounterBar} width={1920} height={1080} fps={30} durationInFrames={90} />

Look at the shapes. The Motion Canvas version states intent: count to 100 and grow the bar to 600 wide, both over 3 seconds, together. The Remotion version states a mapping: for every frame between 0 and 90, here is the number and the width. Remotion is longer here, but the pattern does not change when the bar becomes a chart, the number becomes a styled code block, or the scene becomes a phone-shaped layout.

Editor and preview

Both ship an editor. Motion Canvas runs its editor at localhost:9000 after npm run serve; it previews the animation and updates when you save a file. Remotion Studio opens with npx remotion studio, lives in the @remotion/cli package, and is described in the docs as allowing fast editing and playback of compositions. I did not benchmark either for hot-reload speed, so I won't rank them. The difference I can state from the docs is the unit being edited: Motion Canvas edits an animation timeline, Remotion Studio plays compositions that are React components.

Output and rendering

This is the clearest difference in output. In the Motion Canvas rendering docs, clicking RENDER saves each frame as an image to the project's output folder, as PNG, JPEG or WebP, and the page suggests converting frames to video with a tool like ffmpeg or importing the sequence into a video editor. The page does not describe a built-in video export, so check the current docs and release notes in case that has changed.

Remotion renders video directly. npx remotion render <composition-id> <output-location> uses the H.264 encoder by default, and --codec accepts h264, h265, av1, vp8, vp9, prores and audio-only codecs such as mp3, aac and wav. Audio follows the same split. In Motion Canvas you import an audio file in project.ts, set the audio property in makeProject, and shift it with audioOffset (seconds); the docs page does not say how audio is exported. In Remotion you place the file in public/ and add an audio component with staticFile(), trimming and volume are props, and the audio ends up in the rendered file.

If your end product is an MP4 for YouTube Shorts, Remotion has fewer steps between code and finished file. If your end product is a frame sequence you will composite elsewhere, Motion Canvas is already there.

Licensing

Motion Canvas: the GitHub API reports an MIT license on the repository (checked November 3, 2026). Remotion is source-available with a two-tier license. The LICENSE.md in the Remotion repository says you are eligible to use it for free if you are an individual, a for-profit organization with up to 3 employees, a non-profit or not-for-profit organization, or evaluating it without yet using it commercially. Larger for-profit organizations need a company license. The file also says the license will change slightly in Remotion 5.0. Read the current terms on Remotion's license page before committing a team. I'm not a lawyer and this is a pointer, not advice.

Maintenance and community

Numbers from the GitHub API and web checks on November 3, 2026:

  • Motion Canvas (motion-canvas/motion-canvas): 19,662 stars, 177 open issues, not archived, MIT. Latest commit July 2, 2026 (a docs domain update). Latest GitHub release: v3.17.2, published December 14, 2024. motioncanvas.io returned HTTP 200.
  • Remotion (remotion-dev/remotion): 70,298 stars, 191 open issues, not archived. Latest commit November 3, 2026. Latest release: v4.0.540, published November 2, 2026.

Note that GitHub's open-issue count includes pull requests, so treat both figures as rough. I am not drawing a conclusion from the dates; they are what a reader can check themselves. If you plan to build a lot on either, read the recent commits and release notes.

Is Motion Canvas still maintained?

As of November 3, 2026, the motion-canvas/motion-canvas repository is not archived, motioncanvas.io responds, the most recent commit was on July 2, 2026, and the latest GitHub release is v3.17.2 from December 14, 2024. Those are the facts I could verify. Check the repository's recent activity yourself for the current picture.

Is Motion Canvas free for commercial use?

The repository carries the MIT license according to the GitHub API, and MIT permits commercial use with the license notice kept. Read the LICENSE file in the version you install, and note that this covers the code, not any fonts, audio or footage you put in a project.

Can I use Motion Canvas with React?

Motion Canvas scenes are written in TSX, so the syntax looks like React, but they are not React components. Scenes are generator functions that build nodes like Txt and Rect, and they render to a canvas, not the DOM. I did not find a documented way to drop an arbitrary React component into a scene, so if you need your existing React components in the video, Remotion is the direct route.

Motion Canvas alternatives if it's not for you

  • Remotion, if you want React components, layout work and a direct MP4 render.
  • Manim, if the content is math or geometry. See our Manim alternatives roundup, and our Remotion vs Manim comparison for the Manim side in detail, including Motion Canvas vs Manim.
  • Tools built on Remotion, if you want a pipeline rather than a framework. A Claude Code workflow is covered in our Claude Code and Remotion post.

Which should you pick?

  • You think in sequences and want an animation-first timeline: Motion Canvas.
  • You think in React components and layout: Remotion.
  • You need a finished MP4 with audio from one command: Remotion. A frame sequence you finish elsewhere is fine: Motion Canvas.
  • You are a for-profit company above 3 employees: read Remotion's company license terms first. Motion Canvas is MIT.
  • You want an LLM to write the scenes: see below.

On agent-friendliness, I have no measurement of which one a model writes correctly more often, and I won't invent one. What I can point to is documentation: Remotion's docs include a section on prompting videos with coding agents and a set of Agent Skills installed with npx skills add remotion-dev/skills, as I confirmed in the Remotion vs Manim post on October 31, 2026. I did not look for an equivalent for Motion Canvas on November 3. Whichever you pick, run the code and look at the frames; generated animation code often needs a pass. Generator-based tweens and signals are also a smaller, newer API surface, and the import-path changes between versions are a place an agent can go wrong.

Where ReelMint fits

ReelMint is built on Remotion. It adds a visual editor for every generated scene and an MCP server at https://studio.reelmint.io/api/mcp that Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Cursor can drive (130+ MCP tools; see /mcp). You bring your own provider keys (BYOK), there is a free tier, and it publishes to YouTube Shorts. Instagram Reels publishing is pending Meta App Review, so I won't promise it. Its strengths are code cards, terminal cards and chart animations for developer Shorts.

It is not the right pick for math or academic animation. There are no equation-morphing primitives. For that, use Manim. And if you want frame-level control of an animation as code, with an animation-first timeline, Motion Canvas or Remotion directly will serve you better than a higher-level tool. For a typical 60 to 90 second reel through the MCP path I measured 45 to 60 minutes elapsed, of which 10 to 20 minutes is hands-on; that is one measurement by the person who built it.

Originally published on reelmint.io.

title: TypeScript `const` Enums Are Deprecated: What to Migrate to and Why the Compiler Team Made the Call
description:
TypeScript const Enums Are Deprecated: What to Migrate to and Why the Compiler Team Made the Call

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

TypeScript const enums promised zero-runtime cost for constant values, but they broke isolated module compilation and caused runtime errors downstream. The compiler team deprecated them not because of theoretical purity, but because they caused production failures when developers mixed const enums with modern build tools like esbuild, swc, and Vite. A const enum in a library's .d.ts file becomes a landmine: the consuming project inlines values at compile time but ships code that expects those enum objects to exist at runtime. When versions drift between compile and runtime dependencies, conditionals take the wrong branch and silent data corruption follows.

The problem diagram shows the failure path:

const enum compilation breaks when compiler cannot see declaration file

The solution eliminates compile-time inlining and removes the dependency on cross-module information:

union types with as const provide type safety without runtime dependencies

TypeScript const enum deprecation warning in compiler output

The migration path depends on whether the enum appears in a library or application code. Libraries must remove const enums entirely because they cannot control how downstream consumers compile their code. Application code can migrate incrementally, starting with high-risk modules that interact with external dependencies.

Key Takeaways

  • Const enums fail in isolated module compilation because the compiler cannot access cross-file information to inline values, causing unresolved imports at runtime.
  • The TypeScript team deprecated const enums to prevent version drift bugs where compile-time values differ from runtime values, leading to wrong conditional branches and data corruption.
  • Union types with as const provide equivalent type safety without runtime objects, making them compatible with modern build tools that compile modules in isolation.
  • Libraries shipping .d.ts files with const enums force downstream consumers to disable isolatedModules, breaking compatibility with esbuild, swc, and other fast compilers.
  • The preserveConstEnums compiler option emits runtime objects but defeats the original zero-cost promise and creates inconsistent behavior between development and production builds.

The Technical Problems With Const Enums

Const enums operate by replacing references with literal values at compile time. When the compiler encounters Direction.Up, it substitutes the numeric literal 0 directly into the emitted JavaScript. This inlining removes the enum object from the output entirely, which sounds efficient until modules compile independently.

The TypeScript documentation on enums explains that const enums "are completely removed during compilation" and "members are inlined at use sites." The removal happens because the compiler treats the enum as a macro expansion rather than a runtime value.

const enum inlining requires cross-module visibility to substitute values

The inlining breaks when the compiler processes files in isolation. Modern build tools compile TypeScript modules independently to maximize parallelism. A module that imports a const enum from another file cannot inline the values because it never reads the declaring file. The import statement stays in the output JavaScript, referencing an enum object that was never emitted.

The failure mode appears when libraries publish ambient const enums in declaration files. A library's .d.ts file declares the const enum shape but provides no implementation. The consuming project's compiler sees the declaration and inlines values based on that snapshot. At runtime, the library's JavaScript code contains no enum object because the const modifier stripped it during the library's build. The consuming code executes with hardcoded values that may not match the library's current version.

Version drift amplifies the problem. A project compiles against version 1.2 of a library, inlining Status.Active = 5. The deployment runtime loads version 1.3 where Status.Active changed to 7. The compiled code still checks if (status === 5) but the library now returns 7 for active status. The conditional silently fails and the application continues executing on the wrong path.

The isolatedModules compiler option exists specifically to catch these situations. When enabled, TypeScript rejects code patterns that only work with whole-program compilation. The documentation states that isolatedModules "is fundamentally incompatible with ambient const enums" because inlining requires seeing the enum definition.

Build tools choose isolated module compilation for speed. The TypeScript 5.0 release notes introduced the verbatimModuleSyntax option to make module semantics explicit and predictable across different compilers. The new option removes import elision and treats all module syntax literally, which makes const enum inlining impossible.

The TypeScript team deprecated const enums because they require whole-program knowledge in an ecosystem moving toward isolated compilation. The tradeoff between zero-cost abstractions and compilation speed tilted decisively toward speed when developers started hitting production failures from version drift.

How Const Enums Break in Isolated Module Compilation

The breakage becomes concrete when examining actual compiler output. A const enum in one file and an import in another produces different JavaScript depending on whether the compiler processes them together or separately.

// constants.ts
export const enum Direction {
  Up = 0,
  Down = 1,
  Left = 2,
  Right = 3,
}

// movement.ts
import { Direction } from "./constants";

export function move(direction: Direction): string {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

When TypeScript compiles both files together, the output for movement.ts replaces enum references with literals:

// movement.js (whole-program compilation)
export function move(direction) {
  switch (direction) {
    case 0: // Direction.Up
      return "moving up";
    case 1: // Direction.Down
      return "moving down";
    case 2: // Direction.Left
      return "moving left";
    case 3: // Direction.Right
      return "moving right";
  }
}

The constants.ts file emits nothing because the const enum disappears entirely. The JavaScript output contains no Direction object and no export statement. This works only because the compiler inlined the values before generating code.

When a build tool compiles movement.ts in isolation, it cannot inline the values because it never reads constants.ts. The output keeps the import statement:

// movement.js (isolated module compilation)
import { Direction } from "./constants";

export function move(direction) {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

At runtime, the JavaScript engine tries to import Direction from constants.js. That file exports nothing because the const enum was stripped during the library's compilation. The import fails with an unresolved module specifier or imports an undefined value, causing the switch statement to match no cases.

Example of runtime error from const enum in isolated compilation

The isolatedModules documentation calls out this specific failure. The compiler option enables a check that rejects const enum imports from external modules. The error message reads: "Cannot access ambient const enums when the '--isolatedModules' flag is provided."

The ambient qualifier matters. An ambient const enum appears in a declaration file without an implementation. Libraries ship .d.ts files containing const enum declarations, expecting consumers to inline the values. The consumer's compiler sees only the declaration and has no way to verify the values match the library's runtime code.

The fix requires either removing the const modifier to emit a runtime object, or migrating to an alternative that works without cross-file inlining. The next sections cover both migration paths and when to use each one.

Migration Path 1: Union Types With as const

Union types combined with the as const assertion replicate const enum type safety without emitting runtime code. The pattern defines an object with as const to create literal types, then extracts a union type from the object's values.

// Before: const enum
const enum Direction {
  Up = 0,
  Down = 1,
  Left = 2,
  Right = 3,
}

// After: union type with as const
const Direction = {
  Up: 0,
  Down: 1,
  Left: 2,
  Right: 3,
} as const;

type Direction = typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction];

The as const assertion tells the compiler to infer the most specific type possible. Without it, TypeScript widens the type to number. With as const, each property gets its exact literal type: 0, 1, 2, 3. The type extraction typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction] produces the union 0 | 1 | 2 | 3.

union type extraction flow from const object to type parameter

Functions that previously accepted the enum type now accept the extracted union type. The type safety remains identical:

function move(direction: Direction): string {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

move(Direction.Up); // type-safe
move(Direction.Down); // type-safe
move(5); // error: Argument of type '5' is not assignable to parameter of type '0 | 1 | 2 | 3'

The TypeScript compiler enforces that callers pass only the valid direction values. The compiled JavaScript contains a runtime object with the direction properties, making it compatible with isolated module compilation:

const Direction = {
  Up: 0,
  Down: 1,
  Left: 2,
  Right: 3,
};

function move(direction) {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

The object exists at runtime, so imports resolve correctly even when modules compile in isolation. The tradeoff is a small runtime cost: the object occupies memory and requires a property access instead of using an immediate literal value. For most applications, the cost disappears in the noise of other object allocations.

String-valued enums migrate the same way:

// Before: string const enum
const enum LogLevel {
  Debug = "DEBUG",
  Info = "INFO",
  Warn = "WARN",
  Error = "ERROR",
}

// After: union type with as const
const LogLevel = {
  Debug: "DEBUG",
  Info: "INFO",
  Warn: "WARN",
  Error: "ERROR",
} as const;

type LogLevel = typeof LogLevel[keyof typeof LogLevel];

The union type becomes "DEBUG" | "INFO" | "WARN" | "ERROR", which the compiler treats as distinct literal types. The TypeScript handbook on enums notes that "an object with as const could suffice" for many enum use cases, and this migration proves the point.

The pattern works in libraries because it requires no special compiler behavior. A library exports the const object and the type, and consumers import both normally. No inlining happens and no cross-file dependencies exist. The module system handles the runtime object like any other export.

Migration Path 2: Plain const Objects

When type safety matters less than convenience, a plain const object without type extraction provides a simpler migration. The object still gets as const to freeze its type, but no union type extraction happens.

// Before: const enum
const enum HttpStatus {
  OK = 200,
  Created = 201,
  BadRequest = 400,
  Unauthorized = 401,
  NotFound = 404,
}

// After: plain const object
const HttpStatus = {
  OK: 200,
  Created: 201,
  BadRequest: 400,
  Unauthorized: 401,
  NotFound: 404,
} as const;

Functions accept number instead of the specific union type:

function handleResponse(status: number): void {
  if (status === HttpStatus.OK) {
    console.log("Success");
  } else if (status === HttpStatus.NotFound) {
    console.log("Resource not found");
  }
}

The compiler allows any number, not just the defined status codes. This loses type safety but matches the original const enum behavior more closely. Const enums with numeric values did not prevent passing arbitrary numbers either, they just provided autocomplete for the defined constants.

plain const object migration removes type extraction step

The JavaScript output includes the object exactly as written:

const HttpStatus = {
  OK: 200,
  Created: 201,
  BadRequest: 400,
  Unauthorized: 401,
  NotFound: 404,
};

function handleResponse(status) {
  if (status === HttpStatus.OK) {
    console.log("Success");
  } else if (status === HttpStatus.NotFound) {
    console.log("Resource not found");
  }
}

This pattern suits internal application code where the team controls all usage sites. The lack of type constraints speeds up refactoring because changing a value requires updating only the object definition, not every function signature that references it.

Libraries should prefer the union type approach. Exporting a plain object without extracted types gives consumers no guidance about valid values. The autocomplete shows the object properties but the type system accepts anything, leading to runtime errors when callers pass invalid values.

The const object approach also handles computed enum values better than union types. Const enums with expressions become cumbersome to migrate to unions:

// Before: const enum with computed values
const enum Permissions {
  None = 0,
  Read = 1 << 0,
  Write = 1 << 1,
  Execute = 1 << 2,
  ReadWrite = Read | Write,
}

// After: plain const object preserves expressions
const Permissions = {
  None: 0,
  Read: 1 << 0,
  Write: 1 << 1,
  Execute: 1 << 2,
  ReadWrite: (1 << 0) | (1 << 1),
} as const;

Extracting a union type here requires computing the expression results manually (1 | 2 | 4 | 3), which defeats the purpose of the named constants. The plain object keeps the expressions readable and maintains the relationship between combined flags.

Const Enums vs Regular Enums vs Modern Alternatives

The three approaches differ in runtime presence, type safety, and compatibility with modern build tools. The table summarizes the key distinctions:

Feature Const Enum Regular Enum Union Type with as const Plain const Object
Runtime object No Yes Yes Yes
Type safety Compile-time only Full Full None
Isolated modules Breaks Works Works Works
Bundle size impact None Small object Small object Small object
Reverse mapping No Yes No No
Library-safe No Yes Yes Conditional

comparison flowchart showing const enum versus modern alternatives

Regular enums emit a runtime object that supports reverse mapping. Numeric enums create a two-way mapping between names and values:

enum Direction {
  Up,
  Down,
  Left,
  Right,
}

console.log(Direction.Up); // 0
console.log(Direction[0]); // "Up"

The compiled JavaScript contains an immediately invoked function expression that builds the bidirectional object:

var Direction;
(function (Direction) {
  Direction[Direction["Up"] = 0] = "Up";
  Direction[Direction["Down"] = 1] = "Down";
  Direction[Direction["Left"] = 2] = "Left";
  Direction[Direction["Right"] = 3] = "Right";
})(Direction || (Direction = {}));

This flexibility comes with a larger bundle footprint. The generated code uses more bytes than a simple object literal. Most applications never use reverse mapping, making the extra code pure overhead.

Union types with as const provide the same compile-time type safety as enums without the reverse mapping machinery. The object literal approach generates minimal JavaScript and works identically across all compilers. The TypeScript 5.0 release notes mention that the verbatimModuleSyntax option makes module semantics predictable, and union types fit that predictability better than enums with their special compilation rules.

Plain const objects sacrifice type safety for simplicity. They work when the codebase treats the values as documentation rather than constraints. API response status codes often fall into this category because external services return arbitrary numbers anyway.

The migration path depends on the enum's role in the codebase. Enums used as discriminated union tags need full type safety and should become union types. Enums used as named constants can become plain objects. Enums with reverse mapping lookups should stay as regular enums.

What to Do With Existing Const Enum Code

Migrating a codebase with existing const enums requires assessing impact before changing code. The first step identifies where const enums appear and whether they cross module boundaries.

migration decision flowchart for const enum replacement strategy

Search the codebase for const enum declarations and catalog their locations. Distinguish between application-internal enums and enums exported from library packages. Internal enums can migrate gradually. Exported enums require immediate attention because downstream consumers may already be hitting compilation failures.

For libraries, the migration path is strict. Remove all const enums from published declaration files. The TypeScript documentation on const enums explains that const enums in .d.ts files create "subtle implications" and "pitfalls" for consumers. The practical implication is that consumers cannot use isolatedModules if they import your const enums.

The migration steps for a library:

  1. Replace const enum declarations with union types using as const
  2. Export both the const object and the extracted type
  3. Update internal code to use the new types
  4. Bump the major version because the change breaks consumers who directly accessed enum values
  5. Document the migration in the changelog

Application code has more flexibility. The preserveConstEnums compiler option provides a temporary bridge. When enabled, the compiler emits runtime objects for const enums instead of removing them entirely. This makes the code compatible with isolated module compilation while preserving the const enum syntax:

// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "preserveConstEnums": true
  }
}

The output JavaScript now includes the enum object:

const Direction = {
  Up: 0,
  Down: 1,
  Left: 2,
  Right: 3,
};

The const enum keyword becomes equivalent to a regular enum in terms of output, but the TypeScript compiler still inlines references during type checking. This creates an inconsistency where development builds inline values but production builds use the runtime object.

The better approach for application code migrates const enums to union types one module at a time. Start with modules that interact with external dependencies or appear in the critical path. These modules cause the most visible failures when const enums break.

The migration preserves type safety by using the union type extraction pattern. Tests catch any mismatches where code passed invalid values that const enums silently accepted. Strict TypeScript configurations with strict enabled surface these issues immediately.

For large codebases, automated refactoring tools can handle the mechanical transformation. A codemod script searches for const enum declarations, generates the equivalent as const object and type extraction, and updates references throughout the codebase. The TypeScript compiler API provides the parsing and type information needed to build such tools.

The investment in migration pays off in build performance and reliability. Codebases that remove const enums can enable isolatedModules and use faster build tools. The reduction in compilation time often measures in seconds for medium-sized projects and minutes for large monorepos.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I still use regular enums without the const modifier?

Yes. Regular enums work correctly with isolated module compilation because they emit runtime objects. The TypeScript compiler team deprecated only const enums due to their specific inlining behavior. Regular enums remain a supported feature with no planned deprecation.

Does preserveConstEnums make const enums safe to use?

No. The preserveConstEnums option emits runtime objects but does not solve the version drift problem. If your library ships .d.ts files with const enums, downstream consumers still inline values at compile time based on your declaration file. The runtime object your library includes may have different values, causing the same silent failures const enums are known for.

Why not just ban const enums with a linter rule?

Linter rules prevent new const enums but do not address existing ones or const enums in dependencies. The TypeScript compiler deprecated const enums to signal that the feature causes real problems and the team will not fix edge cases. Migration to alternatives provides a permanent solution rather than piecemeal prevention.

Will regular enums eventually be deprecated too?

The TypeScript team has not announced plans to deprecate regular enums. The TypeScript handbook still documents enums as a standard feature alongside the as const alternative, giving developers a choice based on their needs. Const enums failed because they broke fundamental module system assumptions, not because enums as a concept are flawed.

How do union types handle bitwise operations like flags?

Union types cannot represent computed values in the type itself, so bitwise flag operations work better with plain const objects. Define the base flags as separate properties and combine them at runtime. The type system sees only the defined properties, not the computed combinations. This limitation makes plain objects more practical than union types for permission flags and similar use cases.

The Future of Enums in TypeScript

The TypeScript compiler team's decision to deprecate const enums reflects a broader shift toward compilation models that prioritize speed and simplicity over optimization tricks. Modern JavaScript bundlers and build tools achieve better performance through parallelization and caching than through aggressive inlining. The zero-runtime-cost promise of const enums mattered more when JavaScript environments were slower and every byte counted.

Union types with as const emerged as the recommended pattern because they align with JavaScript's object literals while providing TypeScript's type safety. The pattern requires no special compiler support and works identically whether the code compiles with tsc, esbuild, swc, or any future compiler. Developers can reason about the code's behavior without understanding const enum inlining rules.

Related posts on TypeScript's evolution cover adjacent deprecation decisions. The TypeScript 6 breaking changes guide discusses other features the compiler team phased out for similar reliability reasons. The TypeScript 6 final JavaScript release explains how new ECMAScript proposals influence TypeScript's feature set. The TypeScript decorators legacy to TC39 migration shows another case where TypeScript deprecated an experimental feature in favor of the standardized alternative.

Const enums served their purpose when build pipelines were simpler and projects rarely mixed compilers. The ecosystem has moved on. The migration to union types or const objects removes a source of subtle bugs and makes TypeScript codebases more portable across different build tools. Teams that complete the migration gain faster build times and fewer production surprises. The const enum deprecation pushes TypeScript toward patterns that scale with modern development workflows rather than fighting against them.

title: Neural Compression over Equivalence Classes: Exact Gauges and Functional Rate-Distortion
description:
arXiv:2611.07233v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural networks admit many parameterizations of the same or nearly the same function, but deployment typically stores whichever parameter vector training happens to produce. We show that this representational freedom can itself be used for compression. Rather than redesigning the codec, we search over exact function-preserving transformations and controlled functional perturbations, using the unchanged physical compressor itself to select cheaper representations. Exact gauge families provide a zero-distortion reference under the strict audit; allowing small functional changes exposes much larger rate-distortion gains. Across SmolLM2 and Qwen3, our method reduces Zstandard-compressed checkpoint size by up to 23.4\%, with similar relative reductions under gzip, Brotli, and ZipNN, establishing trained-network representational freedom as a practical storage resource.

title: FisherDistill: Diffusion Distribution Distillation via Closed-Form Fisher Critics
description:
arXiv:2611.07604v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in diffusion distillation have enabled high-quality image generation in only one or a few network function evaluations (NFEs). Despite their efficiency, aggressively distilled generators often retain a residual distribution gap from their multi-step teachers, motivating recent methods to introduce adversarial refinement with a learned discriminator. In this work, we ask whether such refinement necessarily requires a learned adversarial discriminator. We introduce \textbf{FisherDistill}, a simple alternative based on Fisher linear discriminant analysis. Using intermediate representations from the frozen teacher, we estimate the first- and second-order statistics of real and generated samples and derive a closed-form Fisher direction that maximally separates their feature distributions relative to within-class variation. This direction provides a lightweight refinement signal that complements the original distillation objective without requiring an additional adversarial discriminator or its optimization loop. Across multiple distillation frameworks, our approach consistently improves generation quality over their respective distilled baselines and substantially closes the gap to adversarially refined counterparts. Code: https://bhosalems.github.io/FisherDistill/

title: The Gating Mechanism of KV Cache Eviction
description:
arXiv:2611.07605v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: KV cache eviction must decide which entries carry information that the rest of the cache can no longer supply. A natural way to estimate this is a learnable gate: give each cached entry a gate on its attention weight and train the gate on the model's own objective. The gate belongs inside the normalizing softmax, where suppressing one entry hands its mass to the others rather than discarding it. That same normalizer absorbs any per-query constant, so a constant gate cancels and reproduces the frozen model exactly. Trained on the language-modeling loss the gate stays near a constant score while its loss falls throughout: optimization succeeds, but a frozen backbone was fit for dense attention, so its loss prefers the no-op, and a near-constant score ranks nothing. The no-op is not a floor the gate improves from but what its objective asks for. A second obstacle survives once the gate moves, since the same gradient charges the gate for errors the frozen model already makes, which no reweighting of positions separates out. Much of the machinery in learnable eviction, from sparsity penalties to relaxations of the discrete decision, works around the first obstacle rather than removing it; both are removed by putting dense attention beyond the gate's reach and making the dense model's predictions its target. Under these two conditions capacity is never the missing ingredient: neither a larger scorer, nor explicit access to the past, nor a trainable backbone helps. The same holds for what eviction unavoidably discards, which is recovered by parameter-free centroids read inside the same softmax far better than by any memory read outside it, since the mass they must return is a share of that normalizer and available nowhere else. At 75\% KV cache compression, this gate reaches 90.14 on RULER at 8K and 46.03 on LongBench with Qwen3-8B, 3.72 and 1.36 points below full-cache inference.

title: TriAttention: Unified Sparse Mixed-Precision Attention for Long-Context LLM Inference
description:
arXiv:2611.07256v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparsity and quantization reduce the cost of attention by skipping interactions and lowering the precision of those retained. However, useful interactions differ in their precision requirements: some tolerate low-precision scores while remaining sensitive to removal. We therefore introduce TriAttention, which assigns query-key (QK) tiles to skipping, 4-bit, or 8-bit computation, using 4-bit to retain quantization-tolerant interactions at lower cost. To represent compactly, we encode each head's computation regions with two diagonal-distance boundaries, keeping policy storage independent of context length. Offline calibration then evaluates candidate boundary pairs using normalized projected-output errors and complete-tile execution costs. Using these measurements, a model-wide allocator selects each head's boundaries to minimize calibration error under a shared computation budget. During prefill, the selected boundaries generate precision-grouped traversals for a fused kernel that skips omitted tiles and combines contributions from both QK precisions into one normalized attention output. The quantized keys and values prepared during prefill are then reused in a compressed key-value (KV) cache for decoding, reducing repeated reads of prompt data. Experiments show that TriAttention achieves end-to-end generation speedups of up to 7.88x over the Torch attention and 2.65x over the BF16 baseline. Meanwhile, TriAttention maintains quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks. These results show how a compact retention-and-precision policy translates local sensitivities into attention computation and repeated KV-cache access. The implementation is https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TriAttention.

title: Why Public Wi-Fi Feels Risky and How Encryption Quietly Protects You on It
description:
You sit in a café, connect to the free Wi-Fi, and open your email without a second thought. Millions of people do this every day, and most of them come to no harm. Still, it may be worth asking what actually happens between your device and the outside world once you join a network full of strangers.

A public Wi-Fi network is simply a network that many unknown people share at the same time. The router itself does not check who you are, and it does not keep neighbors from listening in principle. Understanding what can and cannot go wrong may help you make calmer choices, rather than avoiding every hotspot out of fear.

This article explains the risk in plain terms and shows why encryption, a way of scrambling messages so only the right reader can undo it, quietly does most of the protective work.

Simple analogy

Think of a postcard versus a sealed envelope. A postcard can be read by anyone who handles it along the way, while an envelope hides the words inside. Traffic that travels without protection on a shared network behaves like a postcard.

Encryption turns your postcard into an envelope. It scrambles the text using a secret key, which is a piece of information that lets you lock and unlock the message. Other people on the same network may still see envelopes moving back and forth, but they likely cannot read what is written inside.

The comparison also explains why the café itself matters less than people assume. The waiter who carries the envelope cannot open it, and neither can the stranger at the next table. What matters is whether the letter inside was sealed before it left your hands.

Core mechanism

When a website uses HTTPS, your browser and the server agree on a temporary key at the start of each visit. From that moment, the messages travel in scrambled form that only the two ends can read. A person sitting nearby may observe the traffic, yet the content stays unreadable without that key.

The risk on public Wi-Fi comes from two main directions. First, some older sites or apps may still send data without encryption, and those messages can be observed directly. Second, someone with bad intent may trick your device into talking to them instead of the real site, a setup often called a man-in-the-middle attack, where the attacker quietly sits between you and the service.

Modern browsers push back against the second case. They check certificates, which are digital ID cards that prove a site is what it claims to be, and they warn you loudly when something looks off. These checks are not flawless, but they remove most of the easy attacks.

There is a quieter detail worth knowing as well. The name of a free network is set by whoever controls the router, so a look-alike name can appear in your list during busy travel seasons. Your device may connect on its own if it recognizes a familiar name, which suggests that turning off automatic joins is a simple and useful guard.

Real-world example

Security teams think about this problem at company scale, because employees now work from trains, airports, and hotels as a matter of routine. Some vendors build unified office security systems, such as Ping64, to bring data leakage prevention and endpoint management into a single platform. The aim is not to ban remote work, but to keep protection close to the data no matter where people log in from.

Consider a traveler who joins hotel Wi-Fi and opens an old internal tool that still runs without encryption. On a shared network, an eavesdropper may be able to observe parts of that session, including login details in the worst case. With HTTPS in place, the same scene looks very different, and the intercepted traffic reads as meaningless noise.

Limitations and common misconceptions

One common belief is that public Wi-Fi is a trap that no careful person should ever touch. In practice, encrypted connections now cover most everyday activity, so the realistic risk has dropped sharply over the past decade. Another belief is that a VPN makes you anonymous, while it mainly moves the place where your traffic gets decrypted from the café to the VPN provider.

It also helps to remember what encryption does not fix. If you install a fake app, type your password into a phishing page, or share a document with the wrong link, the network was never the weak point. Devices that have not received security updates in years may carry older weaknesses as well, and no hotspot habit can repair that.

There is a middle ground between fear and carelessness. Turning off automatic connection to open networks, paying attention to browser warnings, and preferring your phone’s tethered connection in sensitive moments are small habits that may cover most of the gap.

Closing and references

Public Wi-Fi is less frightening than its reputation suggests, as long as you treat the network itself as untrusted. Encryption carries the real burden of protection, and it works well when you notice and respect the warnings your browser gives you. A few steady habits are likely to matter more than avoiding cafés altogether.

https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/48/r1/final
https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world
https://www.enisa.europa.eu/publications/enisa-threat-landscape-2024

title: Improving Long-Tail Detection via Layout-Instruction Conditioned Diffusion Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2611.07553v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthetic data from diffusion models can improve object detection, but long-tail performance is still limited by scarce rare classes and inflexible conditioning (e.g., text-only or layout-only inputs). In this paper, we propose Tail-SD, a layout-instruction conditioned stable diffusion framework that supports text, layouts, or their hybrid, enabling controllable synthesis from boxes, masks, and/or prompts to better cover the long-tail objects. To train a single model across heterogeneous conditions, we introduce a multi-task cross-attention module and multi-task embedding tokens, improving generation quality and diversity. Extensive experiments on COCO and LVIS demonstrate that diffusion synthesis with hybrid conditioning consistently benefits detection, e.g., on LVIS val, it achieves +4.89% / +5.68% rare Box/Mask AP, highlighting strong potential for addressing long-tail challenges.

title: Modelling Month-End Close: Cut-Off Events, Inventory Snapshots, Adjustment Audit Trails and eTIMS Stock Alignment
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

If you model a food factory's month-end close as a set of events, four objects matter more than the trial balance:

  1. Cut-off events — a timestamp after which receipts, issues, outputs and dispatches belong to the next period.
  2. Inventory snapshots — counts of raw materials, WIP and finished goods by lot, location and status (including QA hold / quarantine / rework).
  3. Adjustment audit trail — every variance with reason code, value and named approver, linked back to a count.
  4. eTIMS stock alignment — invoice and credit-note quantities that reconcile to the same movements.

Kenya Revenue Authority's stock management functionality notice cites section 23A(2)(b) of the Tax Procedures Act, 2015 and expects records of stock received, purchased, sold, transferred, returned, adjusted or otherwise disposed of, aligned with TIMS/eTIMS invoices. The Star (2 Oct 2026) reported manufacturers preparing for a January 2027 rollout; People Daily framed the operational test as reconciling transactions with goods actually held and moved.

Below is the 15-point close I recommend for Kenyan food and agro processors — broader than a stock count — with a close-file template and FAQ. Full references on the canonical post.

What the guidance and the law actually say

KRA stock management for electronic invoicing. On its stock management functionality page, KRA informs taxpayers that they must maintain accurate and up-to-date stock records while invoicing through TIMS/eTIMS, in accordance with section 23A(2)(b) of the Tax Procedures Act, 2015. The records should cover stock that is received, purchased, sold, transferred, returned, adjusted or otherwise disposed of, and they should align with the transactions invoiced through TIMS/eTIMS. KRA links this to correct tax reporting, accurate business records and compliance, and has been running consultative forums with businesses.

Manufacturers and the January 2027 prep window. The Star (2 October 2026) reported that KRA issued a public notice on 7 September 2026 requiring accurate stock records through TIMS/eTIMS, and that preparations point toward a January 2027 rollout. The Kenya Association of Manufacturers has asked for clarity on how the functionality will sit beside existing ERP systems, how conversion of raw materials into finished goods (including wastage, by-products, damaged goods and samples) will be captured, how imports and inter-warehouse transfers will be treated, and what happens during system downtime. KRA's George Obell was quoted saying the initiative targets missing-trader fraud and unfair competition. The same piece notes that eTIMS architecture already includes stock inventory, stock by item, imported items, stock-in and stock-out histories, movements and opening and closing stock.

Accounting for every unit. People Daily (10 October 2026) walks through the basic equation: opening stock plus what came in, minus what went out, should equal what remains. A physical shortfall needs investigation with supporting documents — purchase invoices, sales records, transfer notes, adjustment records and physical counts — not a silent journal. Multi-branch businesses need consistent product codes and transfer records. Electronic invoicing improves visibility; it does not replace physical controls for damage, theft, returns, internal use or transfers.

Five-year retention. Section 23 of Kenya's Tax Procedures Act, 2015 requires a person to keep documents required under a tax law so that tax liability can be readily ascertained, and to retain them for five years from the end of the reporting period they relate to (subject to the exceptions in the Act). KRA's eTIMS FAQ points taxpayers back to that rule. Your month-end close pack belongs in that set. Our eTIMS guide for food and agro manufacturers covers the invoicing side of the same story.

Why month-end close goes wrong in food plants

Factories rarely fail the close because nobody counted anything. They fail because the close is treated as a finance ritual after the fact.

The patterns are familiar. Cut-off was never announced, so GRNs and dispatch notes from the last day of the month land in the next period. Production orders stay open with material issued and nothing received. WIP sits on the floor with no status. Finished goods on QA hold are counted as free stock. Yields are estimated at month-end instead of recorded per batch. Returns and scrap are written off without a named approver. Accruals for power, transport or lab tests are guessed. And when the stock figure still looks wrong, someone posts a balancing adjustment with the reason "month-end".

None of that survives a world in which stock movements and eTIMS invoices are expected to tell one story.

The 15-point month-end close checklist for food processors

Cut-off and freeze

1. Announce a hard cut-off date and time.

Write it down: last receipt, last issue, last production booking and last dispatch that belong to this period. Tell stores, production, QA and dispatch. Anything after the cut-off belongs to next month, even if someone "was in a hurry".

2. Post every open slip before anyone counts.

GRNs, production issues and outputs, transfers, delivery notes and credit notes that belong to the period must be in the system before the count starts. A count against an incomplete ledger invents variances. Use the same discipline as in our stock count reconciliation checklist and supplier intake checklist.

Stock, WIP and finished goods

3. Count raw materials and packaging by lot and location.

Blind counts where practical. Partial bags, open drums and returned packaging get their own lines. Confirm units of measure before you chase a variance.

4. Count work-in-progress with a status, not a guess.

List every open tank, silo, line, vat or pallet of WIP: product, batch or order, quantity, stage and owner. WIP that has no status is stock that will not survive an audit question.

5. Count finished goods separately from free stock that is blocked.

Sellable FG in the warehouse is one figure. Stock on hold, in quarantine, in rework, in the returns bay or awaiting disposal is another. Record status on the sheet, as in our QA hold checklist and rework control checklist.

Quality and production close

6. Clear or formally carry open QA holds.

Every held batch at month-end needs a decision: release, rework, reject or keep on hold with a named owner and a next review date. Held stock must not be counted as available for sale.

7. Close or park every production order.

Orders with material issued and no output, or output with no issues, must be finished, cancelled or explicitly carried with a reason. Open orders are where yields disappear.

8. Reconcile yields and batch costing for the period.

Compare expected recipe yields with actual output, scrap and by-products for closed batches. Investigate outliers before you accept a period cost. See batch costing and yield tracking for agro processors. FEFO and expiry write-offs belong here too: FEFO and batch expiry tracking.

Purchases, sales and eTIMS alignment

9. Match purchases and GRNs to the period.

Every supplier invoice in the period should have a corresponding receipt (or a documented accrual). Every GRN should have a matching invoice or a clear "goods received, invoice pending" line. Quantity and unit mismatches are closed here, not left for next month.

10. Reconcile sales invoices and credit notes with eTIMS.

Confirm that invoices issued for the period were transmitted through TIMS/eTIMS as required, that credit notes are paired, and that quantities on invoices match what left the warehouse. Our eTIMS guide and finished goods dispatch checklist cover the floor side of that match.

11. Close inter-warehouse and inter-branch transfers.

In-transit stock at month-end needs a named sender, receiver and expected arrival. People Daily's multi-branch point applies: goods that left one store must not vanish from both.

Adjustments, accruals and the pack

12. Post returns, scrap and stock adjustments only with named approval.

Every adjustment carries item, lot, location, system quantity, counted quantity, difference, value, reason code and approver. The counter does not approve their own write-off. "Month-end adj" is not a reason. KRA's stock-management notice expects returns, adjustments and disposals to be recorded, not absorbed into silence.

13. Document accruals and period expenses.

Power, water, transport, laboratory tests, casual labour, packaging on order and similar costs that belong to the period get a schedule: amount, basis, owner and supporting document. Guessed accruals become next month's surprise.

14. Assemble the month-end close pack and retain it.

File cut-off notice, posted transaction list, count and recount sheets, WIP and hold registers, production-order close list, yield summary, purchase/GRN match, invoice/eTIMS match, transfer register, approved adjustments, accrual schedule and sign-off page together. Plan to keep them at least five years under section 23 of the Tax Procedures Act, and confirm longer food-safety retention with your quality lead using your food safety records checklist.

15. Get a named sign-off that the period is closed.

Operations and finance both sign that cut-off was observed, counts and holds were reviewed, production was closed or parked, invoices align with movements, and adjustments have approvers. Without that page, the close is a conversation, not a record.

A simple month-end close file

Section What to record
Cut-off Date/time announced; what belongs in / out of the period
Posting completeness Open GRNs, issues, outputs, transfers, dispatches posted before count
RM & packaging count Blind sheets, lots, locations, UoM, recounts
WIP register Order/batch, stage, quantity, owner
FG & blocked stock Sellable vs hold / quarantine / rework / returns / disposal
QA holds Decision, owner, next review date
Production orders Closed, cancelled or carried with reason
Yields & costing Expected vs actual, scrap, by-products, outliers
Purchases / GRNs Match or documented accrual
Sales / eTIMS Invoice list, credit notes, transmission status, qty match to dispatch
Transfers In-transit, sender, receiver, expected arrival
Adjustments Variance, reason code, value, named approver
Accruals Amount, basis, owner, support
Retention Pack filed; retention date (min. five years for tax docs)
Sign-off Operations + finance names, dates

If you cannot point to the pack for last month in under five minutes, the close is not under control.

An illustration

This is an illustrative example, not a real case. A mid-sized juice plant closes October. The accountant's stock report looks tidy. On the floor, three production orders still have concentrate issued and no finished output booked, twelve pallets of a new SKU sit on QA hold but were counted as free stock, and a GRN for sugar delivered on the afternoon of the 31st was left on a clipboard. Finance posts a balancing stock adjustment so the trial balance closes.

Two weeks later the same sugar appears again when the GRN is posted, the held SKU is released and sold, and the open production orders are closed with scrap that was never recorded. November opens with a stock figure nobody trusts. Under KRA's stock-management expectation — records of what was received, sold, adjusted and disposed of, aligned with eTIMS invoices — that tidy October close is exactly the kind of story that does not hold. The fix is not a better journal. It is checks 1–2, 5–7 and 12 done before anyone signs.

How FactoraERP helps

FactoraERP keeps stock by item, lot, location and status, and records receipts, production issues, output and dispatch as they happen, so month-end starts from a live ledger rather than a pile of slips. Blind count sheets, recounts, variance reason codes and approved adjustments link each write-off to a count and a named approver. QC results and holds sit on the same stock: a batch on hold is not available for picking or delivery notes until QA releases it with user, time and results. Recipes can declare primary product, co-product, by-product or waste, and waste quantities can be recorded against production runs, which supports yield and scrap review at period close. See factoraerp.com.

Free download: eTIMS readiness checklist for factories

Kenyan manufacturers increasingly need their operational records, stock records and invoices to tell one consistent story. If you want a free eTIMS readiness checklist for factories, sign up for the FactoraERP Insights newsletter at https://isaacmuthui.substack.com. You will get practical operations notes for food and agro manufacturers. No spam; unsubscribe anytime. For background, see our guide to eTIMS for food and agro manufacturers.

FAQ

What is a month-end close in a food factory?

It is the set of steps that lock a period: cut-off, posting completeness, counts of raw materials, WIP and finished goods, clearance of QA holds and production orders, yield and cost review, purchase and sales/eTIMS matching, approved adjustments, accruals and a signed close pack.

How is this different from a stock count?

A stock count compares physical quantities with the system and posts approved variances. Month-end close includes that work and also closes production, quality holds, purchases, sales/eTIMS alignment, transfers, accruals and retention of the pack.

What does KRA expect on stock records for eTIMS?

KRA's stock-management notice, citing section 23A(2)(b) of the Tax Procedures Act, 2015, expects accurate records of stock received, purchased, sold, transferred, returned, adjusted or otherwise disposed of, aligned with TIMS/eTIMS invoices. Consult your tax adviser for how that applies to your registration and timeline.

When is the eTIMS stock-tracking rollout expected?

Reporting in The Star on 2 October 2026 described preparations for a January 2027 rollout, following a 7 September 2026 public notice and ongoing consultations with manufacturers. Treat dates as reported and confirm current guidance with KRA.

How long should we keep the month-end close pack?

Section 23 of the Tax Procedures Act, 2015 sets a general five-year retention period for documents required under a tax law, with exceptions. Food-safety records may need longer. Confirm with your accountant and quality lead.

Can a small plant run this close on paper?

Yes, if cut-off is written, slips are posted before counting, WIP and holds have registers, adjustments have reason codes and named approvers, and the pack is filed together. Software helps when lots, locations, holds and invoice volumes outgrow paper.

Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd

title: Egocentric Action Recognition with Objects and Vision-Language Affordances
description:
arXiv:2611.07673v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Action recognition, and more specifically egocentric action recognition, is a core task in computer vision, with applications such as monitoring the daily life activities of elderly people and task assistance. Recent methods rely on visual modalities such as RGB video or depth. However, in egocentric video, an action is largely defined by its objects, which these methods rarely model. We propose a method that combines a frozen SlowFast video expert with an attention-based object expert by late fusion. Each object is represented with its affordances, that is, what can be done with it, generated zero-shot by a vision-language model. Since datasets such as MECCANO annotate only the objects involved in each action, evaluating with these boxes tells the model which objects are active. We therefore train on annotated boxes and evaluate the method with detections from the official active-object detector, and with annotated boxes as an upper bound. Without affordances, our fusion reaches 68.4% Top-1 with annotated boxes but 49.0% with detections. About half of this drop comes from non-active detections. To remove them, the same vision-language model generates an interaction affordance that decides whether a hand is manipulating each detected object. On MECCANO, objects raise the Top-1 of the video expert from 44.9% to 49.0%, and the two affordances raise it to 49.9%, above SlowFast and object-aware RGB baselines. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Autonomous AI Agents Systematically Diverge From Human Preferences in Proof Formalization
description:
arXiv:2611.06995v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have ushered in a new age of proof abundance, but helping humans understand these proofs requires new attention to the differences in how AI agents and humans pursue a proof-making task. We present "simulated collaboration", a methodology that allows us to examine two key questions: (1) the relative attention AI agents pay to surface syntax or, conversely, deeper underlying semantics, and (2) how and where AI agent preferences for what to do next diverge from human preferences. On a set of nine major human collaborations in Lean with 4.7M definitions across more than 6K commits, we find that, over the course of proof construction, AI agents (1) are far more strongly drawn than humans to explicitly marked gaps; (2) show a relative aversion to densely connected proof centers and to complex or surprising proof goals; and (3) are relatively attracted to surprising proof bodies, which they tend to regularize toward baseline. Our results highlight important blind spots and potential interventions for future human-AI collaboration in mathematics.
