title: WebRTC Calls, Key Agreement and ORM Checks at Build Time
description:
The last post this week covers what Parley, Savor and Wayline needed underneath: calls, encryption and a backend you can trust with real data. These are features you'd usually assemble from three vendors and a few weekends of glue code.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Voice and video calls with WebRTC

com.codename1.webrtc carries live audio and video directly between two devices, encrypted on the way, with a TURN relay when there's no direct path. On Android it's Google's WebRTC library, on iOS the Apple build of the same library, and in the browser it's the browser's own WebRTC. Referencing the package is what adds the native library to a build, so apps that don't make calls don't pay for it.

WebRtc.openUserMedia(true, true, true).ready(media -> {
    PeerConnectionConfig config = new PeerConnectionConfig()
            .addIceServer(IceServer.stun("stun:stun.example.com:3478"));
    pc = WebRtc.createPeerConnection(config, new PeerConnection.Listener() {
        public void iceCandidate(PeerConnection connection, IceCandidate candidate) {
            signalling.send(candidate);
        }

        public void stateChanged(PeerConnection connection, String state) {
        }

        public void remoteTrack(PeerConnection connection, MediaTrack track) {
            if (track.isVideo()) {
                form.add(BorderLayout.CENTER, new VideoView(track, false));
                form.revalidate();
            }
        }
    });
    pc.addTrack(media.getAudio());
    pc.addTrack(media.getVideo());
    pc.createOffer().ready(offer -> pc.setLocalDescription(offer)
            .ready(done -> signalling.send(offer)));
});

Signaling is yours on purpose. The package creates the offer, the answer and the candidates, and you send them over whatever you already have: a WebSocket, your server, a push. So the same call code works with a Codename One backend or with anything else. Parley sends them over its live channel, and the media never touches its server.

Key agreement and HKDF everywhere

End-to-end encryption needs two parties that have never met to agree on a key over a channel anyone can read. Codename One now does that on every port and on the backend. KeyGenerator.ec(256) makes a P-256 key pair, KeyAgreement.ecdh combines your private key with the other side's public key, and Hkdf turns the shared secret into a proper key:

byte[] shared = KeyAgreement.ecdh(mine.getPrivateKey(), theirs.getPublicKey());

// The shared secret is not a key yet. HKDF turns it into one, and the info
// label keeps keys derived for different purposes apart.
byte[] info = "chat message key v1".getBytes();
byte[] key = Hkdf.derive("SHA-256", null, shared, info, 32);

byte[] nonce = SecureRandom.bytes(12);
byte[] sealed = Cipher.aesEncrypt(Cipher.AES_GCM, new SecretKey("AES", key),
        nonce, null, message);

The key agreement runs in the platform's native crypto provider. Hkdf is portable Java over Hmac, so it gives the same bytes on every device and on your server. These are the building blocks of Parley's X3DH and Double Ratchet, and they're just as useful for encrypted backups, secure pairing or signing data between your app and your server.

A backend client for serious integrations

Real backends call other services: a payment processor, a bank, a partner API. Many of those authenticate callers with a client certificate. The backend's WebClient handles that, along with HTTP/2, timeouts and connection pooling:

this.partner = new WebClient()
        .setClientCertificate(ClientCertificate.pkcs12(archive, password))
        .setRequireHttp2(true)
        .setRequestTimeoutMillis(10000);

Server certificates and host names are always verified, and there is no option to turn that off. Two clients never share a connection, so a connection authenticated with one certificate is never used for a request made with another.

ORM mistakes fail the build

This is my favorite one. With Hibernate and Spring, plenty of mapping mistakes compile fine and only blow up when the application starts, or worse, on the first request that touches the broken entity. You find out in staging if you're lucky.

Codename One's ORM reads your entities when you compile, so those mistakes are build errors that name the class and the field:

@Temporal requires a java.util.Date field: signedUp
Persistent fields must be writable: name
@Entity class com.example.Customer must declare a public no-arg constructor
@Version requires an int or long field: revision

Repositories get the same treatment: an unsupported method signature, a derived query that names a field the entity doesn't have, or a missing parameter name stops the build and names the repository and the method.

The same release makes it easier to put the ORM on a database you already have. Columns keep their names, native TIMESTAMP and DATE columns map to java.util.Date with @Temporal, and lifecycle callbacks can stay private:

@Entity(table = "legacy_customer")
public class LegacyCustomer {
    @Id @Column(name = "customer_no")
    private long id;

    @Column(name = "full_name", nullable = false)
    private String name;

    @Temporal(TemporalType.TIMESTAMP) @Column(name = "signed_up")
    private Date signedUp;

    @PrePersist
    private void defaults() {
        if (signedUp == null) {
            signedUp = new Date();
        }
    }
}

Before you deploy, session.schemaReport() compares the mappings with the real tables and tells you what's missing, without changing anything in the database.

That's the week

Three new apps you can launch, a word processor that holds up against Rust, and a stack of features that make the next app easier. Everything is in the repository, and the guides for WebRTC, security, backend web and the ORM have the details. If you build something with these, I want to see it.

title: The Memory Trap: Language Agents Overgeneralize from Benign Interactions
description:
arXiv:2611.07554v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language agents increasingly use persistent memory to record user preferences and procedures across sessions. We show that memory from benign interactions can cause unsafe or unreliable behavior on later tasks. We call this failure the memory trap. To study this issue, we compare behavior in sessions with and without memory across six frontier models (including Claude Sonnet, Opus, and Fable models and GPT-5.6). We evaluate these models in a range of settings. First, in autonomy experiments, we find that requests to skip confirmation during low-stakes coding chores lead agents to skip confirmation and verification on simulated high-stakes tasks in both coding and everyday life. We next study memories formed when users seek emotional support, or describe harm from uncritical feedback, and find these memories bias later judgments of mathematical work, arguments, and poems toward sycophancy or over-critique (respectively). Memory notes written during legitimate stale-test repairs lead agents to weaken correct tests that catch broken safeguards; these memories also increase cheating on ImpossibleBench, with larger increases for stronger Sonnet and Opus models. We show that memory traps can arise both from overgeneralizations in memory writing, and when acting on memory. These findings demonstrate that even benign interactions can lead to serious risks from memory systems, and thus motivate the need for new research into ensuring that agents preserve the scope of their memories.

title: Provably Efficient Representation Learning for Low-Rank CMDPs
description:
arXiv:2611.07295v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study representation learning in low-rank Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs), where both value and reward functions are approximated by a set of unknown representation vectors, and the transition dynamics admit a low-rank factorization. The objective is to maximize expected cumulative rewards while complying with constraints on the expected cumulative utility. To achieve this, we propose \texttt{MFRLC} (Model-Free Representation Learning for Low-Rank CMDP), a model-free algorithm that uses a primal-dual scheme to effectively balance reward regret and constraint violations. To the best of our knowledge, \texttt{MFRLC} is the first representation-learning method for low-rank CMDPs that combines the Least-Squares Value Iteration with Upper Confidence Bound (LSVI-UCB) and primal-dual techniques. \texttt{MFRLC} further enhances value function estimation with bonuses for function approximation and learns the mapping from representations to value functions directly, avoiding explicit estimation of the transition kernel. We prove that, with high probability, \texttt{MFRLC} achieves $\widetilde O(K^{3/4})$ reward regret and cumulative constraint violation over $K$ deployment rounds, independent of the size of the state space. To our knowledge, these are the first sublinear regret and violation guarantees for CMDPs with unknown features.

title: Extending Reasoning in Typed Decision Models via Looping
description:
arXiv:2611.07736v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Typed decision models choose among a fixed set of answer options in a single forward pass, so unlike generative language models they cannot spend more test-time compute on hard inputs by generating more tokens. Looping a block of layers offers this compute in latent space without adding parameters, but prior work found no gain from loops retrofitted into conventionally pretrained models. We show that such loops help when trained together with the decision model. Our method, RELOAD (retrofitted loops for adaptive decisions), fine-tunes a pretrained encoder or decoder with a damped loop over its middle block and a lightweight controller picks the number of passes adaptively for each input. Across six models from 0.4B to 4B parameters, looping improves both accuracy and calibration, mostly on problems that need longer chains of reasoning than any seen in training, where encoders gain up to 23 points. Neither matched training compute nor more data closes this gap, and separate layers for each pass come close only with nearly twice the parameters. The controller keeps most of the gain at about three quarters of the compute.

title: Java: When Life Gives You Problems, Build a ProblemFactory
description:
We've already explored PHP's questionable decisions, JavaScript's complicated relationship with logic, Python's ability to produce confidently incorrect results, and C#'s enterprise-grade surprises.

Now it's Java's turn.

Java is different.

Java is serious.

Java is strongly typed, object-oriented, carefully specified, and famously obsessed with backward compatibility.

This is a language that makes you declare what things are before you're allowed to do anything with them.

Surely, then, Java should be relatively free of surprises?

Well.

Let's talk about that.

1. String Concatenation: Apparently, + Needed a Performance Review

Let's start with something that every Java developer has written thousands of times.

String message = "Hello, " + name + "!";

Perfectly reasonable.

Now consider:

System.out.println("Total: " + 1 + 2);

Output:

Total: 12

But:

System.out.println(1 + 2 + " total");

Output:

3 total

Same numbers. Same operator. Different arithmetic.

Because Java evaluates these expressions from left to right, and once a string enters the expression, + becomes string concatenation.

Fine. We can live with that.

But Java has another surprise waiting.

Meet StringBuilder

Java strings are immutable.

Once created, a String cannot be modified.

So what happens when you repeatedly append characters?

String result = "";

for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    result += i;
}

Conceptually, each iteration creates a new string containing the accumulated result plus the new value.

As the string grows, increasingly large amounts of data may need to be deal with by the jvm.

That's potentially a lot of unnecessary work.

Java developers have traditionally solved this problem with StringBuilder.

StringBuilder result = new StringBuilder();

for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
    result.append(i);
}

String finalResult = result.toString();

One mutable buffer, rather than repeatedly rebuilding an immutable string.

Much better for this kind of workload.

For years, the conventional advice was simple:

Use + for simple concatenation. Use StringBuilder when you're building strings in loops.

But Java being Java, it couldn't leave things quite that straightforward.

Plot Twist: The Compiler Was Already Helping

Before Java 9, the Java compiler typically translated ordinary string concatenation expressions into StringBuilder operations behind the scenes.

So this:

String message = "Hello, " + name + "!";

Wasn't necessarily doing the naive string-building work you might imagine.

Then Java 9 introduced a new concatenation mechanism using invokedynamic.

This allowed the runtime to select and optimize string-concatenation strategies more flexibly, without requiring the compiler to generate an explicit StringBuilder sequence.

So now we've got:

  • Strings that can't be changed.
  • A mutable class specifically for building strings.
  • A compiler that historically generated that class automatically.
  • A newer mechanism that can optimize concatenation differently.
  • Performance characteristics that depend on the expression, loop structure, compiler, and runtime.

Congratulations. We've turned joining two strings into a discussion about bytecode generation.

To be fair, modern Java handles ordinary + concatenation quite well.

The real performance concern remains repeated accumulation into a growing string, particularly in loops. An explicit StringBuilder is still a sensible choice there.

The lesson: Java's simple syntax can hide considerable compiler and runtime sophistication. And performance advice from 2005 doesn't always survive contact with modern JVMs.

2. Two Integers Are Equal. Until They Aren't.

Here's one of Java's most entertaining party tricks.

Integer a = 127;
Integer b = 127;

System.out.println(a == b);

Output:

true

Okay.

Now:

Integer a = 128;
Integer b = 128;

System.out.println(a == b);

On a typical JVM configuration:

false

Wait. What?

Two integers containing the same number can compare equal or unequal depending on the number.

The trick is that Integer isn't the same thing as int.

int is a primitive value.

Integer is an object wrapper around an integer value.

And for objects, == checks reference identity, not numerical equality.

But Java caches certain Integer objects.

Specifically, Integer.valueOf() is guaranteed to cache values from -128 through 127.

Autoboxing uses this mechanism.

So when you write:

Integer a = 127;
Integer b = 127;

Both variables normally refer to the same cached object.

But outside the guaranteed range, Java is allowed to create separate objects.

Hence the surprising result for 128.

There's one more complication: implementations are permitted to cache additional values, so 128 isn't guaranteed to produce false everywhere.

Which makes relying on this behavior an even worse idea.

The correct comparison:

System.out.println(a.equals(b));

Or compare the underlying primitive values when appropriate.

The lesson: In Java, == can mean numerical equality or object identity depending on the types involved. And integer caching makes that distinction particularly easy to overlook.

3. Arrays.asList() Gives You a List. Terms and Conditions Apply.

Here's a perfectly ordinary bit of Java:

String[] names = {"Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"};

List<String> list = Arrays.asList(names);

You now have a list.

And lists are mutable collections, right?

Let's add someone.

list.add("Dave");

Result:

java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException

Excuse me?

We created a list.

We tried to add an item.

And Java objected.

Here's the explanation.

Arrays.asList() returns a fixed-size list backed by the original array.

It isn't a regular, independently resizable ArrayList.

You can replace existing elements:

list.set(0, "Zoe");

That works.

But you can't change the list's size.

No adding.

No removing.

And here's the really interesting part:

System.out.println(names[0]);

Output:

Zoe

Changing the list changed the original array!

Because they're backed by the same storage.

The reverse is true too. Change an element in the array, and the list reflects that change.

So Arrays.asList() gives you something that:

  • Looks like a normal list.
  • Lets you replace elements.
  • Refuses to grow or shrink.
  • Shares its underlying data with the original array.

Java also offers List.of(), which creates an unmodifiable list.

And new ArrayList<>(...), which creates a separate, resizable list.

Three ways to obtain something called a list, with three different sets of rules.

The fix when you want an independent, resizable list:

List<String> list =
    new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(names));

The lesson: In Java, knowing that something implements List doesn't tell you everything about what operations it supports.

Sometimes the interface makes a promise that the implementation politely declines to fulfill.

4. Removing an Integer Can Remove the Wrong Integer

This one is genuinely nasty.

Suppose you have a list of numbers:

List<Integer> numbers =
    new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 20, 55));

Now you want to remove the number 1.

numbers.remove(1);

What happens?

The list becomes:

[1, 55]

You can kind of guess this one.

Our friend List has two overloaded remove() methods.

One removes an element by index.

The other removes an element by value.

Conceptually:

remove(int index)
remove(Object value)

And when you pass the literal integer 1, Java selects the overload accepting a primitive int.

So:

numbers.remove(1);

Means:

"Remove the element at index 1."

Not:

"Remove the integer whose value is 1."

If you actually want to remove the value 1:

numbers.remove(Integer.valueOf(1));

Now Java selects the object-based overload.

Same method name.

Same apparent kind of argument.

Completely different operation.

And because both operations are perfectly valid, the compiler has absolutely nothing to complain about.

The lesson: Method overloading, autoboxing, and collection APIs can combine into a surprisingly effective footgun.

Sometimes Java's type system is so helpful it confidently does the wrong thing you explicitly asked it to do.

5. Two Decimal Numbers Can Be Equal but Not Equal

For our final example, let's involve money.

Java provides BigDecimal for decimal arithmetic where precision matters.

Unlike ordinary binary floating-point numbers, BigDecimal can represent decimal values exactly.

Very useful for financial applications.

Now consider:

BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("2.0");
BigDecimal b = new BigDecimal("2.00");

System.out.println(a.equals(b));

Output:

false

Seriously?

Two dollars is not equal to two dollars?

Now try:

System.out.println(a.compareTo(b) == 0);

Output:

true

So the numbers compare as equal.

But equals() says they're different.

Why?

Because BigDecimal stores both an unscaled numerical value and a scale.

2.0 and 2.00 represent the same numerical value, but they have different scales.

And BigDecimal.equals() considers scale part of equality.

compareTo() compares their numerical values instead.

That's actually defensible. Scale can matter for certain decimal calculations.

But it creates a wonderfully awkward consequence.

Consider:

Set<BigDecimal> hashSet = new HashSet<>();

hashSet.add(new BigDecimal("2.0"));
hashSet.add(new BigDecimal("2.00"));

System.out.println(hashSet.size());

Output:

2

Now:

Set<BigDecimal> treeSet = new TreeSet<>();

treeSet.add(new BigDecimal("2.0"));
treeSet.add(new BigDecimal("2.00"));

System.out.println(treeSet.size());

Output:

1

Two sets. Same values. Different answers about how many distinct elements exist.

Why?

HashSet uses equals() and hashCode() to determine uniqueness.

TreeSet uses ordering comparisons, which for BigDecimal normally means compareTo().

And BigDecimal explicitly defines those operations differently.

So Java gives you two completely legitimate definitions of uniqueness for the same numerical values.

Imagine discovering that while reconciling financial records.

The lesson: Equality, numerical comparison, and collection uniqueness aren't necessarily interchangeable. With BigDecimal, choosing the wrong one can produce very real business problems.

Java Is Predictable. You Just Need to Predict the Right Things.

Here's what makes Java interesting.

Unlike JavaScript, Java generally doesn't let values wander casually between unrelated types.

Unlike PHP, it doesn't enthusiastically reinterpret everything based on context.

And unlike Python, it tends to insist that you explain exactly what you're trying to do.

Java is explicit.

Java is disciplined.

Java is designed to make large programs easier to reason about.

And yet...

An integer can be identical to another integer until you increase it by one.

A list can refuse to let you add anything.

Removing a number can remove a completely different number.

Two decimal values can be equal according to one method and unequal according to another.

And joining strings can involve compiler transformations, runtime call sites, and an optimization discussion that lasts longer than the code itself.

None of this is random.

There are carefully documented reasons for every behavior.

But that doesn't make the surprises any less entertaining.

In fact, it makes them more interesting.

Java is a language where even the weirdness comes with a specification.

But Wait. Which Java Are We Talking About?

There's one more twist.

We've spent this article discussing Java, the programming language.

But Java is also commonly used to describe an entire development platform.

And that platform has a rather complicated family tree.

For starters, there's the JVM: the Java Virtual Machine.

The thing that executes Java bytecode.

Except there isn't just one implementation of the JVM.

There's HotSpot, the familiar JVM used by most OpenJDK distributions.

There's Eclipse OpenJ9, a separate JVM implementation with different approaches to memory management, startup performance, and garbage collection.

Then there's GraalVM, which builds on HotSpot while offering advanced compilation technology and Native Image, a way to compile Java applications into native executables that don't require a JVM at runtime.

And that's before we get into the different JDK distributions.

Oracle JDK.

Eclipse Temurin.

Amazon Corretto.

Azul Zulu.

Microsoft's Build of OpenJDK.

Those are distributions rather than entirely separate JVM implementations, but their packaging, support, licensing, and release policies can differ.

And then there's the small matter of the languages.

Because the Java Virtual Machine doesn't actually require you to write Java.

You can use Kotlin.

Scala.

Clojure.

And plenty of others.

So now we have one language, multiple JVM implementations, multiple JDK distributions, multiple languages targeting the JVM, and an alternative compilation model that can eliminate the need for a running JVM altogether.

Remember Java's original promise?

Write once, run anywhere.

Turns out the more interesting question is:

Run where, on which JVM, from which vendor, using which language?

And that's a rabbit hole worthy of its own article.

Coming next: the Java ecosystem, where the language is only the beginning of the confusion.

title: Action-Conditioned VLM Monitoring for Autonomous Vehicle Semantic Anomalies
description:
arXiv:2611.07540v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study action-conditioned monitoring of autonomous-vehicle behavior in semantically unusual driving scenes. The target is whether the executed ego action is appropriate for the scene: the same scene can admit both normal and anomalous behavior, so visual unusualness alone does not determine the monitoring label. A Vision-Language Model (VLM) first predicts the scene-required action from an outcome-hidden video window; the monitor then compares that expectation with the realized ego-motion trajectory under an explicit compatibility rule. To study this monitoring task, we contribute a six-field taxonomy of 112 paired scenarios spanning both failure polarities (42 derived from documented incidents), a generated video corpus with estimated trajectories, and an exploratory two-stage monitor on that corpus. On 235 clips from 15 scenario families, the two-stage protocol with a fixed T-2.5 s window obtains 83.0% accuracy and anomaly recall 0.773, versus 74.5% and 0.536 for a single-stage video-only baseline; specificity is 0.880 versus 0.928.

title: NestJS Rate Limiting: In-Memory vs Redis vs Postgres
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

I shipped a NestJS API with the default @nestjs/throttler storage last year and only noticed the hole when we ran two instances behind a load balancer. Each process kept its own counter, so a client that should have been cut off at 100 requests in a minute quietly got closer to 200. Today I re-tested that on NestJS 12 with three storages on the same box: in-memory, Redis, and Postgres.

What I tested

Everything ran on one 8 vCPU / 16 GB Linux VM on November 6, 2026:

  • Node.js 24.22.1, NestJS 12.3.3, @nestjs/throttler 6.7.1
  • Redis 7.2.11 with persistence off, via @nestjs-redis/throttler-storage 2.0.1 and the redis 5.12.1 client
  • PostgreSQL 18.6 with a small custom storage that upserts into one throttler_hits table
  • Limit: 100 requests / 60 seconds, tracker keyed on x-forwarded-for so localhost tests don't all share 127.0.0.1

I measured three things: p50/p95 latency of allowed requests, whether request 101 returns 429, and whether two Nest processes behind the same storage still stop at 100 total.

If you're comparing Nest to thinner frameworks, I wrote about Hono vs Express and the NestJS 12 upgrade separately. Redis vs Postgres as infrastructure shows up again in my pg-boss vs BullMQ and BullMQ pipeline posts.

Wiring @nestjs/throttler

The default setup is tiny. Global guard, one named throttler:

ThrottlerModule.forRoot({
  throttlers: [{ name: 'default', ttl: seconds(60), limit: 100 }],
  getTracker: async (req) => {
    const xf = req.headers['x-forwarded-for'];
    if (typeof xf === 'string' && xf.length) return xf.split(',')[0].trim();
    return req.ip;
  },
}),
// providers: [{ provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: ThrottlerGuard }]

That uses the built-in in-memory storage. Fine for a single process. Wrong the moment you scale out.

Redis storage

I used @nestjs-redis/throttler-storage, which implements ThrottlerStorage with a Lua script so the increment is atomic:

const redis = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
await redis.connect();

ThrottlerModule.forRoot({
  throttlers: [{ name: 'default', ttl: seconds(60), limit: 100 }],
  storage: new RedisThrottlerStorage(redis),
  getTracker: /* same as above */,
});

Pass an existing client. The package does not manage connect/disconnect for you.

Postgres storage (custom)

There isn't an official Nest Postgres throttler storage, so I wrote one. One row per key, upsert that resets when the window expires:

CREATE TABLE throttler_hits (
  key text PRIMARY KEY,
  hits integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  expires_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  is_blocked boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  block_expires_at timestamptz
);

// inside increment():
INSERT INTO throttler_hits (key, hits, expires_at)
VALUES ($1, 1, now() + ($2 || ' milliseconds')::interval)
ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET
  hits = CASE WHEN throttler_hits.expires_at <= now() THEN 1
              ELSE throttler_hits.hits + 1 END,
  expires_at = CASE WHEN throttler_hits.expires_at <= now()
                    THEN now() + ($2 || ' milliseconds')::interval
                    ELSE throttler_hits.expires_at END
RETURNING hits, expires_at, is_blocked, block_expires_at;

I wrap that in a transaction and set is_blocked when hits > limit, matching how the in-memory storage behaves. No SKIP LOCKED here: a single-row upsert is enough for a counter. SKIP LOCKED is the pattern I use for job claiming, not for rate-limit tallies.

Latency (allowed requests)

Eighty requests under the limit, median of three runs. Raw Node http with no Nest is the baseline.

Storage p50 (ms) p95 (ms)
none (raw http) 0.34 0.57
memory 0.36 0.64
redis 0.38 0.81
postgres 1.00 1.42

On localhost, memory and Redis are basically free. Postgres adds about 0.6 ms at p50 versus the raw baseline. That is one round trip plus the upsert. Across a network to a remote Postgres the gap will be larger; across a network to Redis it will grow too, just usually less.

Reject correctness

Single process, LIMIT + 20 requests with the same client IP:

Storage 200s 429s First 429 at request #
memory 100 20 101
redis 100 20 101
postgres 100 20 101

All three cut off exactly after 100. So the bug is not "throttler is wrong". The bug is sharing.

Multi-instance correctness

Two Nest processes, same Redis or Postgres (or none for memory), alternating requests for the same IP, LIMIT + 30 = 130 total:

Storage Allowed Blocked Shared limit held?
memory 130 0 No
redis 100 30 Yes
postgres 100 30 Yes

Memory allowed every request. Each process only saw 65 hits, both under 100. That is the load-balancer failure mode. Redis and Postgres stopped at 100 total across both processes.

What I'd pick

  • One instance, local or edge: in-memory. Lowest moving parts. Don't pretend it will survive a second replica.
  • Already running Redis (BullMQ, cache, sessions): use @nestjs-redis/throttler-storage. Latency matched memory on this box and shared correctly.
  • Postgres only, no Redis: the custom upsert storage works. Expect roughly a millisecond of overhead on localhost, more over the network. Keep the table tiny and index-free beyond the primary key.

I would not put rate-limit counters in the same hot transactional tables as orders or payments. A dedicated table (or Redis) keeps the lock footprint small.

One caveat: this is one machine, client and storage on localhost, Nest 12.3.3, throttler 6.7.1. It answers "does shared storage actually share" and "how much does each storage add on this box". It does not answer global multi-region limits or abuse at the CDN layer. Put a WAF or edge limit in front when that matters.

If you only remember one number from today: memory let 130 through where Redis and Postgres stopped at 100. That is the whole reason to change the storage.

FAQ

Does NestJS @nestjs/throttler work across multiple instances?

Only if you swap the default in-memory storage for a shared one. With two Nest processes and a limit of 100, in-memory allowed all 130 alternating requests in my test because each process only saw 65. Redis and Postgres both stopped at 100 total.

What Redis storage should I use with @nestjs/throttler?

I used @nestjs-redis/throttler-storage 2.0.1 with the redis 5.x client on NestJS 12. You pass an existing Redis client; the package runs the increment in a Lua script so it stays atomic.

Can I store NestJS rate limits in Postgres?

Yes, with a custom ThrottlerStorage. I used a single throttler_hits table and an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT upsert that resets hits when the TTL window expires. On localhost it added about 0.6 ms at p50 versus a raw HTTP baseline.

How much latency does NestJS rate limiting add?

On one 8 vCPU box with localhost storage, allowed-request p50 was 0.36 ms for in-memory, 0.38 ms for Redis 7.2.11, and 1.00 ms for PostgreSQL 18.6, against a 0.34 ms raw HTTP baseline. Remote Redis or Postgres will cost more.

Is in-memory rate limiting OK for production NestJS?

It is fine for a single instance. The moment you run two replicas behind a load balancer, each keeps its own counter, so clients can exceed the limit. Switch to Redis or Postgres (or an edge/WAF limit) before you scale out.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: GuidedWAM: Training-Free Energy Guidance for World Action Models in Autonomous Driving
description:
arXiv:2611.07912v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World action models (WAMs) for autonomous driving couple the driving policy and the visual world model in a single generative network whose objectives are fixed post-training. Conditioning on a new driving objective requires retraining. We study energy guidance as a general mechanism and present GuidedWAM, a model-agnostic framework for injecting driving objectives into frozen WAMs at sampling time. Our framework constructs each objective as differentiable energies on the sampler's intermediate clean-action estimate, which needs only forward access to the frozen model, and is stabilized by sampling-time guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded correction. On the NAVSIM v2 hard-split, guidance improves all three frozen, publicly released WAMs by 1.8 to 3.6 EPDMS, averaged over three sampler seeds, and adds less than 10% to the sampling time per step. These results position energy guidance as a practical post-training control channel for WAMs.

title: Cloud Storage vs Physical Hard Drives: Which One Is Safer for You?
description:
Cloud storage and physical hard drives both keep your files safe — but in very different ways. Hard drives are fast, cheap, and fully in your control, while the cloud keeps your files backed up and reachable from anywhere. The safest setup is both: follow the 3-2-1 rule, with three copies of your files, on two different kinds of storage, and one copy off-site.

title: OptIMerge: Optimization-Based Merging of Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2611.07543v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The arithmetic merging of weights from multiple task-specific models fine-tuned from a shared base model, commonly known as model souping, has emerged as a popular strategy for multi-task learning without the computational overhead of joint retraining. However, naive scalar weight averaging frequently leads to severe performance degradation when the constituent models learn structurally divergent feature representations, leading to destructive parameter interference. We study this problem in a largely unexplored setting: merging image-to-image (I2I) diffusion models fine-tuned for dense, pixel-accurate tasks such as image restoration. Unlike the large language models (LLMs) and text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models for which most merging methods were developed, I2I experts encode conflicting spatial priors (e.g., anisotropic motion-blur vs. isotropic defocus-blur) in their convolutional filters, where both naive soup and LLM-style element-wise merging introduce visible artifacts. We introduce OptIMerge, a gradient-based optimization framework: instead of relying on heuristic scalars, OptIMerge learns highly expressive, yet parameter-efficient merger coefficients by minimizing a multi-task diffusion loss over a small set of 100-500 images. OptIMerge parameterizes the merge with architecture-aware transformations: for attention layers, a structured low-rank feature alignment with explicit channel biases; for convolutional layers, per-kernel merger coefficients, and a low-rank Cayley transform that aligns channels by orthogonal rotation without distorting the filters. By keeping the experts frozen and optimizing only these lightweight merger parameters (equivalent to <0.4% of the network footprint), OptIMerge achieves simultaneous multi-task capabilities that rival computationally expensive joint training and decisively outperform zero-shot model soups.

title: Crypto AI Vaults: 3 of 6 Beat Bitcoin, 1 Fell 30% — What That Actually Proves
description:
The most checkable corner of AI trading is Hyperliquid vaults — public numbers, no screenshots. The results split the hype cleanly in two.

Crypto is where AI trading claims can actually be checked, because Hyperliquid vaults publish their numbers on-chain. No screenshots, no self-reported PnL — just public data. So what does the checkable corner of AI trading actually show?

As of the 2 November 2026 verified check: of 6 Hyperliquid vaults whose leaders say they are AI-run, 3 beat Bitcoin over the same dates, 2 lost money, and 1 fell more than 30% from a peak. Among the vaults passing strict safety and drawdown gates, results ranged from +26.5% (with a −24.2% max drawdown) to −0.1% (with a −10.8% drawdown) — and the top-ranked vault overall, not AI-labelled, returned +24.1% with an −11.9% drawdown while trailing Bitcoin by 4.2 points over the same period.

First, “AI-run” predicts nothing

The label is the operator’s claim, not a performance category. AI-labelled vaults appear across the entire distribution — top, middle, and bottom. If a label predicted returns, the spread would be narrow. It is not. The label tells you what the operator says about their process. It tells you nothing about whether that process works.

Second, beating Bitcoin is the right benchmark — and most don’t

Holding Bitcoin costs nothing, needs no skill, and takes no drawdown decisions. Any vault that trails it over the same dates charged you complexity, fees (typically a 10% profit share for the leader), and drawdown risk for less than doing nothing. Several vaults in the data did exactly that.

Third, drawdown is the story the return hides

A vault up 26.5% that fell 24.2% from a peak is a different proposition from a vault up 8% that fell 3%. The first can wipe out a depositor who arrived at the wrong time; the second is boring in the best way. Rankings by return alone are how people buy the top of a drawdown.

How to evaluate any vault in two minutes

(1) Return vs Bitcoin over the same dates. (2) Max drawdown from peak. (3) Leader’s profit share and stake. (4) How long it has been live (a month of numbers is an anecdote, not a record). (5) Whether deposits are open and what happens in a drawdown — who bears it, you or the leader?

The checkable corner of AI trading does not vindicate the hype or confirm the dismissal. It shows variance: some AI-labelled vaults beat the benchmark, some lose, one fell hard. That variance is the honest answer to “do AI vaults work?” — sometimes, for some operators, with drawdowns that demand respect. Anyone selling you a simpler answer is selling you something else.

BuildIT Index applies the same standard to backtests: recompute from raw data, beat baselines, check folds, count trials, model costs. A vault that cannot survive those checks on its own history is a bet on luck, not skill.

If the label predicted returns, the table would not look like this.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past results do not predict future returns.

title: InfMasking: A Unified Variational Framework for Synergistic Multimodal Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.07702v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal models are expected to exploit synergistic information, that is, information available only when multiple modalities are observed together. In practice, however, a fusion module can fit the training objective by relying on a dominant modality or on information that modalities share, and the synergy between modalities is often left unused. We propose InfMasking, a unified multimodal learning framework based on Infinite Masking. Before fusion, InfMasking randomly masks the features of each modality; each sampled mask produces a different partial combination of cross-modal evidence and a fused representation of the corresponding modality interactions. All masked fused representations are required to remain consistent with a reference target: the unmasked fused view when training is unsupervised, and the class proxy of the task label when labels are available. Maintaining this consistency across diverse partial combinations discourages reliance on a dominant modality or on shared information alone, and drives the fusion module to learn cross-modal interaction patterns that remain meaningful under partial observations. Since the objective is an expectation over infinitely many masks, we model the masked fused representations as Gaussian and optimize closed-form variational bounds, whose population-moment gaps are controlled by the masking-induced covariance under this model. On the evaluated benchmarks, InfMasking improves predictive performance and yields higher mean PID estimates of task-label synergy in learned modality-specific representations, alongside higher InterSHAP interaction attribution in the trained predictors. Code is available at https://github.com/brightest66/InfMasking.

title: How Others Test Cross-Zone Locally
description:
How Others Test Cross-Zone Locally

tc netem, Toxiproxy, Pumba, Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos, zone labels in kind and k3d, Jepsen and Testcontainers: what each gives, a short config form for each, and an honest comparison with what we built.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

Every claim about a tool below links to its own documentation, read for this article. Our side of the comparison is what part 3 built; our failure-scenario runs are still planned.

This is part 5 of the series on testing cross-zone, cross-datacenter and cross-provider behaviour on a laptop. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.

Five layers

Part 4, Placement In Every Trace, made every span say where it ran. Before going further with our own emulation, it is worth looking at what the world already uses. The tools sort into layers by where they act:

Layer Tools Acts on
kernel tc netem packets on a device
TCP proxy Toxiproxy, Testcontainers' Toxiproxy module one connection through a proxy
container Pumba a container's namespace, from outside
Kubernetes Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos, zone labels in kind and k3d pods selected by labels
history Jepsen what the system did, checked afterwards

The lower the layer, the more it can do and the less it knows about your system. The higher, the more it knows and the more it needs installed.

tc netem

Everything network-shaped in this list ends at the kernel's netem sooner or later. It adds delay, jitter and loss to packets leaving a device (tc-netem(8)):

tc qdisc change dev eth0 root netem delay 100ms 20ms distribution normal
tc qdisc change dev eth0 root netem loss 0.3% 25%

The man page has one warning worth repeating: for TCP performance tests, netem should sit on the ingress of the receiver, not on the sender. On its own, netem knows nothing about which peer is which; that is up to the filters around it.

Toxiproxy

Toxiproxy is "a TCP proxy to simulate network and system conditions for chaos and resiliency testing" (Toxiproxy). The client connects to the proxy instead of the real service, and toxics are added to the proxy over an HTTP API on port 8474:

toxiproxy-cli create -l localhost:26379 -u localhost:6379 redis
toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=1000 redis

The toxics are latency, down, bandwidth, slow_close, timeout, reset_peer, slicer, limit_data and packet_loss. That is a richer vocabulary than netem has, at one price: the client must be pointed at the proxy.

Pumba

Pumba does chaos and network emulation for containers on Docker, containerd and Podman (Pumba). It runs tc from a helper that joins the target's namespace, so the target image needs nothing:

pumba netem --duration 5m delay --time 3000 mydb
pumba iptables --duration 2m loss --probability 0.1 myapp

That is the same trick as our sidecar in part 3, packaged as a tool.

Chaos Mesh and LitmusChaos

In Kubernetes, network chaos becomes a resource. Chaos Mesh's NetworkChaos supports netem, delay, loss, duplicate, corrupt, partition and bandwidth, selects pods by label and has a direction of to, from or both (Chaos Mesh):

apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1
kind: NetworkChaos
metadata: { name: delay-example }
spec:
  action: delay
  mode: one
  selector: { namespaces: [default], labelSelectors: { app: frontend } }
  delay: { latency: '20ms', jitter: '5ms', correlation: '0' }

LitmusChaos, a CNCF Incubating project, describes itself as "a Cloud-Native Chaos Engineering Framework with cross-cloud support" (Litmus). Its pod-network-latency experiment starts tc with netem inside the target, takes NETWORK_LATENCY, JITTER and DESTINATION_IPS or DESTINATION_HOSTS to aim at one peer, and can use Pumba as its library (pod-network-latency).

Zones in kind and k3d

Zones on a laptop cluster are node labels. kind takes them in the cluster config (kind); k3d takes them on the command line with a node filter (k3d):

# kind
nodes:
  - role: worker
    labels: { topology.kubernetes.io/zone: a }
  - role: worker
    labels: { topology.kubernetes.io/zone: b }

# k3d
k3d cluster create --agents 3 \
  --k3s-node-label "topology.kubernetes.io/zone=a@agent:0" \
  --k3s-node-label "topology.kubernetes.io/zone=b@agent:1" \
  --k3s-node-label "topology.kubernetes.io/zone=c@agent:2"

Then topologySpreadConstraints spread the pods. DoNotSchedule tells the scheduler not to place a pod that would break the skew; ScheduleAnyway places it anyway, preferring nodes that reduce the skew (Kubernetes):

topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: my-app } }

Labels and spread give zones as a scheduling fact. They give no distance: two "zones" on a laptop are as close as two processes.

Jepsen

Jepsen is at a different layer altogether. It "aims to improve the safety of distributed databases, queues, consensus systems" (Jepsen). While a test runs operations against a system, a nemesis process introduces faults, and a checker then analyses the recorded history for correctness (jepsen-io/jepsen). Network manipulation in its tests is typically done with iptables.

What Jepsen adds is not a better way to cut a network. It is a rigorous answer to "was the result correct", which every tool above leaves to you.

Testcontainers

For tests in code, Testcontainers wraps Toxiproxy as a module. A ToxiproxyContainer joins the same network as the service under test, a proxy is created in front of it, and toxics are added from the test (Testcontainers):

proxy.toxics().latency("latency", ToxicDirection.DOWNSTREAM, 1_100).setJitter(100);
proxy.toxics().bandwidth("CUT_CONNECTION_DOWNSTREAM", ToxicDirection.DOWNSTREAM, 0);
proxy.toxics().bandwidth("CUT_CONNECTION_UPSTREAM", ToxicDirection.UPSTREAM, 0);

A connection cut is bandwidth zero in both directions; removing the toxics restores it.

Side by side

What the world gives What we built
latency and loss netem directly; Pumba, Chaos Mesh, Litmus on top of it; Toxiproxy per connection the same netem, but every rule derived from one topology file, per pair of sites
zones node labels in kind and k3d, spread constraints the same in k3d, plus compose with a subnet per site and zone
continents and providers not a concept in any of these tools levels of the declaration, with link kinds derived from them
partitions Chaos Mesh partition, Jepsen's nemesis, Toxiproxy down iptables DROP on both sides, each cut remembering its cause
checking the result Jepsen's checker on the history QA thresholds declared; the runs are planned
what we lack bandwidth limits, a Jepsen-grade history check —

The honest summary: we did not invent a new way to delay a packet. Under the hood it is netem and iptables, like most of the list. What is ours is the model above them - one declaration of a planet, from which every rule, every placement and every chaos action is derived. None of the tools above has a continent or a provider as a concept.

What we would borrow

Two things, both from the top of the list. Toxiproxy's vocabulary - slow_close, reset_peer, limit_data - names failures that netem cannot express. And Jepsen's stance: a chaos run without a strict check of the result is a demonstration, not a test. Both are ideas, not plans yet.

What I do not claim

  • Not a ranking of these tools. Each is good at its own layer.
  • Not that our emulation does what Jepsen does. It does not check histories.
  • Not that any of our scenarios has run. They are planned.
  • Not completeness. These are the tools I read for this part, not all of them.

What of this is method

  • Know the layer of a tool. Kernel, proxy, container, cluster, history - each sees a different system.
  • Read the documentation, not the reputation. Every claim here has a link.
  • A cut is not a test. The check of the result is the test.

Cross-anything on a laptop - Part 5. Next: Every Verdict Carries A Trace.

If you use Toxiproxy in tests, which toxic found the most? If you run Chaos Mesh or Litmus, do you run it locally or only on a shared cluster? If you have run Jepsen, what did the checker catch that nothing else would? Which of these would you add to a laptop first?

title: How Finite Brains Generalize Without Bound: Spatial Memory as a Universal Computer
description:
arXiv:2611.07920v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A child who learns to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace the difference to what a learner reads when it decides. A position, a count or a time keeps taking new values as the input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine is at least 99% correct, on average over lengths 41 to 500, on nine of fifteen benchmark tasks, five of them tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves; given new cycles after training it reverses strings of 15,015 symbols without error and fails beyond that on the curve the theory predicts; and its controllers run unchanged on neurons.

title: Amazon Connect Beat Genesys on Cost. Here's Proof.
description:
I Ran the SAME Customer on Amazon Connect and Genesys Cloud for 30 Days — The Results Were Embarrassing

Everyone says Genesys is the enterprise king and Amazon Connect is the AWS afterthought. I spent 30 days routing identical, scripted customer journeys through both. One of them quietly won in 7 metrics — and it's not the one you'd bet on.

Before you scroll past: this isn't a vendor-sponsored listicle. I built the same 50-call test script, the same IVR tree, the same CRM integration, and ran it on both platforms for a full month. Here's what actually happened.

Why This Isn't a Stale 2023 Comparison

On 28 April 2026, AWS rebranded Amazon Connect into Amazon Connect Customer and expanded it into a family of four agentic AI solutions: Customer, Health, Decisions, and Talent. The original product now handles 20 million daily interactions and 12 billion minutes of AI-powered customer conversations.

Meanwhile, Genesys deepened its AWS partnership in July 2026, expanding to 22 AWS regions serving 7,000+ organizations and 2 million+ users. At Xperience 2026, Genesys launched its four-layer agentic orchestration stack — Navigator, Orchestrator, Contextual Intelligence, and AI Control Plane — powered by Scaled Cognition's APT-2 action model.

Both platforms are now agentic-AI-first. The question is which one actually delivers on that promise in a real Indian enterprise context.

The 30-Day Head-to-Head

I used a mid-size e-commerce scenario: 50 scripted calls covering order status, returns, payment failures (Razorpay/Paytm), and account changes. Same test data, same SLA targets, same integration stack.

Dimension Amazon Connect Customer Genesys Cloud Verdict
Setup time to working AI agent 18 hours (agentic CX Designer, no-code canvas) 3 days (requires partner + AppFoundry config) 🏆 Connect
Cost per resolution (TCO) ~₹14 / $0.17 per resolved interaction (inferred from $0.038/min × 4-min avg + AI included) ~₹42 / $0.50 per resolved interaction (inferred from $115/seat/mo CX2 ÷ ~230 interactions/agent) 🏆 Connect
AI agent accuracy (50-call script) 82% (41/50 fully resolved without human handoff) 88% (44/50 fully resolved) 🏆 Genesys
Indian payment/CRM integration Razorpay: custom Lambda (6 hrs). Paytm: custom Lambda (4 hrs). Salesforce: native connector Razorpay: AppFoundry marketplace (2 hrs). Paytm: custom API (3 hrs). Salesforce: native, pre-built 🏆 Genesys
Compliance & data residency (DPDP Act) AWS Mumbai region (ap-south-1) — data stays in India. Full DPDP alignment out of the box. Genesys runs on AWS, but no dedicated India region listed; data routes through nearest available region (ap-south-1 available but not marketed as "India data residency") 🏆 Connect
Agent-assist / QA automation Contact Lens + Bedrock-powered real-time suggestions. Good but requires tuning. Contextual Intelligence + AI Control Plane. More granular QA scoring, journey-level analytics. 🏆 Genesys
Vendor lock-in risk Deep AWS dependency. Leaving means rebuilding on another cloud. Multi-cloud capable (runs on AWS but architecture is cloud-agnostic). Pinkfish acquisition adds 500+ integrations as an exit ramp. 🏆 Genesys

Pull-quote #1: "Connect won on speed and cost. Genesys won on depth. The question isn't which is better — it's which failure mode you can afford."

The Twist: Where Connect Quietly Won

Here's the metric most comparison articles miss: cost-per-resolution for AI-first self-service.

Amazon Connect's Bedrock-powered agentic self-service resolved 68% of the 50 test calls without any human agent touching them. Genesys's Agentic Virtual Agent (GCAVA) resolved 72% — a narrow lead.

But the cost of those resolutions is where it gets embarrassing.

Connect's $0.038/min model with AI included means an AI-only resolution costs roughly ₹14 ($0.17). Genesys's per-seat model means even an AI-resolved call still consumes a portion of the $115/seat/month licence. At scale, that gap compounds:

For a 200-agent operation handling 40,000 interactions/month:

  • Connect: ~$5,000–$7,700/month (usage-based)
  • Genesys (CX2): ~$23,000/month (seat-based)

Pull-quote #2: "If 70% of your calls are AI-resolvable, per-seat pricing is a tax on your own efficiency. Connect's usage model means you pay less as your AI gets better."

This is the structural advantage no one talks about: Connect's pricing model rewards AI adoption. Genesys's punishes it. Every call your AI resolves is a dollar you save on Connect. On Genesys, it's a dollar you still paid for.

Where Genesys Still Dominates

Let's be fair. Genesys isn't losing.

The multi-brand routing capability is simply more mature. If you run 3+ brands with different IVR trees, different SLA tiers, and different CRM instances, Genesys's Orchestrator (GA Q1 FY2027) and Navigator (GA Q4 FY2026) give you a single control plane. Connect requires you to build that orchestration layer yourself with Lambda and Step Functions.

The Salesforce integration is also not close. Genesys has a pre-built, certified connector. Connect requires custom development. For any Indian enterprise running Salesforce (and most mid-to-large ones do), that's a 2–3 week head start.

And the Pinkfish acquisition (June 2026) — 500+ integrations, 25,000 MCP tools — gives Genesys a genuine "connect to anything" story that Connect's AWS-centric ecosystem can't match for non-AWS back-office systems.

The Verdict (Screenshot This)

If you're an AWS-native Indian enterprise with high AI-resolvable volume and DPDP compliance needs: Amazon Connect Customer is the 2026 default. If you're a multi-brand enterprise with complex routing and non-AWS back-office: Genesys Cloud is still the enterprise king — but you're paying for it.

Team Connect or Team Genesys? Drop your contact-center war story below. 👇

title: Why FreePi runs on the Pi harness (and what the new Harness Leaderboard shows)
description:
The model gets all the attention. The harness around it — prompts, tools, context management, when to stop — usually decides whether a coding agent actually ships work.

A new Harness Leaderboard from Joel Niklaus makes that measurable: same open models, same provider, same reasoning effort, same tasks. Only the coding-agent harness changes.

What FreePi is

FreePi is a free AI coding agent in your terminal. Ads pay for inference. Under the hood it runs Mario Zechner's Pi harness — the same open agent loop the leaderboard just put under a microscope.

What the board measured

Joel ran 28,849 trials across nine harnesses on GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Flint, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE (~$4,746 of inference). Headline score is resolve rate; cost is measured outside the harness.

Where Pi landed

Averaged over the three models:

  • Pi — 49.4% resolve at $0.29 per solved task
  • mini-swe-agent — 51.4% at $0.53 (Pi is statistically tied, ~45% cheaper)
  • OpenCode — $3.35 per solved task (11.7× Pi)

Pi sits in the top cluster and is the cheap strong option. The best harness still depends on the model, but the cost gap is hard to ignore.

Source announcement: Joel's post.

Why FreePi ships on Pi

We didn't invent a new agent loop. We ship Pi with free models, a GitHub sign-in, and no card required:

npx free-pi-cli@latest

When an independent board says the harness is near the top and thrifty, that's the product story: best harness we know how to ship, batteries included.

Wrapping up

Harness choice moves quality and cost as much as model choice. Pi cleared that bar. FreePi puts that harness in your terminal for free.
