title: SQL Challenge: Extract the Year and Month From a Date
description:
94 SQL Challenge: Can You Extract the Year and Month From a Date?

Imagine your manager asks you to prepare a monthly sales report.

The report should show how much revenue the business generated in each month.

Your "orders" table contains complete dates, such as "2026-01-15".

How would you group these orders month by month?

Let's look at the data.

orders

order_id order_date amount
101 2026-01-05 5000
102 2026-01-15 3000
103 2026-02-10 7000
104 2026-02-20 4000
105 2026-03-12 6000

Your Challenge

Write an SQL query to:

  1. Extract the year from "order_date".
  2. Extract the month from "order_date".
  3. Calculate total sales for each month.
  4. Group the results by year and month.
  5. Sort the results by year and month.

Think before you scroll!

The SQL Solution

SELECT
EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS year,
EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS month,
SUM(amount) AS total_sales
FROM orders
GROUP BY
EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date),
EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)
ORDER BY year, month;

Expected Output

year month total_sales
2026 1 8000
2026 2 11000
2026 3 6000

Why is this useful?

Monthly sales reports are common in real projects.

You can use the same approach to find:

  • Monthly revenue
  • Customer registrations
  • Employee joining trends
  • Monthly order volume
  • Business growth over time

One Important Thing to Remember

Don't group only by month if your table contains data from multiple years.

For example, January 2025 and January 2026 are different reporting periods.

Always include the year along with the month.

Your Turn: Can you write the same query using "YEAR()" and "MONTH()"?

Share your SQL query in the comments. Let's learn together!

SQL #SQLChallenge #DataAnalytics #LearnSQL

title: Towards Generalist Graph-Level Anomaly Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.07706v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) aims to identify graphs that deviate significantly from the majority. While recent advances have achieved competitive performance, existing approaches mainly follow a dataset-specific paradigm, requiring substantial in-domain data and training cost when applied to new application scenarios. This limits their scalability and practicality in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce and diverse domains are continuously emerging. In this paper, we investigate the problem of generalist GLAD, which seeks to learn a single unified model capable of detecting anomalous graphs across multiple domains with minimal supervision on the target data. This problem introduces key challenges, including learning transferable patterns from heterogeneous graph datasets and effective adaptation under limited supervision. To address these challenges, we propose GenGLAD, a generalist GLAD approach that leverages discriminative subgraph extraction as the core mechanism to learn transferable anomaly knowledge and enable efficient adaptation to new domains. Specifically, GenGLAD employs a graph neural network-based discriminative subgraph extraction model to learn the anomaly-discriminative substructures that distinguish anomalous and normal graphs across diverse domains. During the test-time adaptation phase, multi-dimensional discrepancies between the extracted subgraph and multi-level contextual information are calculated to characterize anomalies from multiple perspectives. For efficient adaptation, a lightweight scoring module is introduced to automatically decide the most informative signals, improving robustness against misleading patterns. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves strong performance, superior generalization ability, and improved data efficiency compared to existing methods.

title: Evolutionary Adaptive Neighborhood Learning: A Genetic Algorithm for Instance-Dependent k Optimization in Nearest Neighbor Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.07257v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The number of neighbours k is the central hyperparameter of the k-nearest neighbour (k-NN) classifier and is usually selected globally through cross-validation or evolutionary search. However, the bias-variance trade-off is inherently local: dense and noise-free regions may favour small neighbourhoods, whereas sparse or noisy regions may require larger ones. Since global-k optimization is one-dimensional, replacing exhaustive search with a genetic algorithm offers little computational advantage. We therefore optimize an instance-dependent neighbourhood policy instead. We propose EANK (Evolutionary Adaptive Neighborhood K), which uses a low-dimensional policy to map local neighbourhood descriptors, including density, label entropy, vote margin, and concentration, to an adaptive number of neighbours k(x). A real-coded elitist genetic algorithm optimizes this policy using leave-one-out accuracy with a neighbourhood-smoothness penalty. Precomputed neighbour votes reduce fitness evaluation costs. We investigate theoretical properties of the method, including dominance over global-k solutions on the training criterion, evolutionary convergence, policy regularity, and generalization guarantees. Experiments on synthetic data with spatially heterogeneous structure and twelve public datasets evaluate predictive performance, robustness, and computational cost. Under nested cross-validation, EANK achieves competitive performance relative to tuned global-k baselines and improves upon the default k=5. We also examine the gap between training and test performance to assess the practical value of adaptive neighbourhood selection.

title: Model Vendor Routing Through 2 Admission Gates (When Tenants Pin or Exclude)
description:
Consider a proposed page for a gaming service: a tenant's scoped key has been revoked, but its previously admitted model requests still hold budget reservations. The responder sees refused requests alongside reserved spending, while the routing constraint says to pin a vendor or exclude one. Which decision stopped traffic? This is a design exercise, not an account of a production incident.

Short answer: excluding a provider ages better when the intended rule is that one destination must remain forbidden while other approved destinations can change. Pinning ages better when permission applies to exactly one provider, because adding another destination must require an explicit policy change. Neither rule enforces a tenant's spend ceiling or revokes its key. Put those decisions in separate gates, and record which gate refused the request.

The operational question is narrower than which constraint offers more fallback: when a gaming tenant's key is issued, rotated, or revoked, can the responder explain precisely why traffic stopped, and can the service keep its spending commitment while it stops?

What page fired, and what decision actually failed?

Start with the page.

In this proposed design, the actionable condition is an attempted admission using a revoked tenant credential that the admission service nevertheless accepts. The page should identify the tenant, credential identifier, policy revision, and admission decision, without putting the secret itself into telemetry. A refusal involving a revoked key is evidence that the boundary worked; paging on every such refusal would let stale clients repeatedly summon a responder. OWASP's secrets-management guidance provides the security basis for treating revocation, lifecycle management, and auditing as explicit responsibilities.

There is a different condition that deserves investigation before containment fails: a policy update has been acknowledged, but an admission point still reports an older revision. Instrument that mismatch as a precursor signal. Whether it warrants a page depends on the revocation guarantee the service promises and whether that admission point can still accept traffic; a stale, isolated instance and a stale instance serving tenants have different consequences. No arbitrary universal delay threshold belongs here.

A green dashboard isn't sufficient. An aggregate success rate can combine refusals from invalid credentials, exhausted budgets, and empty candidate sets into a number that offers no safe next action. The responder needs the decision reason from the authority that admitted or refused the request, then a separate account of what happened to work already admitted.

Revocation needs a boundary.

Define that boundary in the service contract: revocation prevents new admissions once the revocation transaction commits at the authoritative admission service. Requests admitted earlier have a separate cancellation and settlement policy. Don't imply that changing a key record reverses a request already sent to a destination.

Should gaming tenants pin a model vendor or exclude one?

Treat routing as a set operation inside an explicit approval boundary. Begin with destinations approved for this tenant and capable of serving the requested model. Pinning intersects that set with one provider identity; exclusion removes the forbidden identity. An empty result means refusal. It must never mean that the router silently drops the constraint and tries whatever remains reachable.

That distinction answers the aging question. With a pin, removing the selected provider makes the candidate set empty until an authorized policy change selects another destination. That is the desired result if permission was specific to that provider. It is an operational burden if the actual requirement was merely to avoid a different destination, because every replacement now requires editing a rule that encoded a stronger restriction than intended.

Exclusion carries the opposite obligation: a newly approved provider can enter the candidate set without changing the exclusion rule. This is useful only if the approval process really authorizes that expansion. An exclusion list against an uncontrolled global roster makes the set of permissible destinations grow through someone else's roster changes. Keep the tenant approval boundary explicit, version it, and apply exclusions within it.

For a gaming tenant, write the decision as a sentence before encoding it: this credential may use approved model destinations except the prohibited provider, or this credential may use only the named provider. Those are different permissions. A temporary traffic incident doesn't justify quietly substituting one for the other.

The trade-off is refused traffic versus breadth of permission. A pin deliberately accepts more occasions for refusal as the roster changes; an exclusion accepts roster flexibility within the approval boundary. Neither is categorically more durable. The durable constraint is the one whose meaning still matches the tenant's permission after a roster update.

Separate credential containment from budget admission

A scoped key should identify a tenant and reference permissions enforced by the service. Rotating it should not create a fresh spending allowance unless that is an explicit account operation. Revoking it should not erase budget reservations or accounting records. Store a credential identifier suitable for auditing alongside lifecycle state, following the secret-handling and access-control principles in the OWASP guidance; the raw secret has no place in a page or a request trace.

Use a hypothetical budget expressed in internal accounting units: the ceiling is 1,000, settled usage is 960, and outstanding reservations total 40. The available amount is zero, even if a usage panel displays only the settled 960. Admitting more work because another provider becomes eligible would violate this proposed accounting rule. This arithmetic illustrates reservation semantics; it isn't a measured workload, a price, or a claim about a provider's billing.

For a strict ceiling, admission needs a defensible upper bound for each request's liability. Reserve that amount atomically against the tenant's shared allowance before dispatch. If no upper bound can be established, the design cannot promise a strict ceiling merely by checking a balance before sending traffic; refuse that class of request or change the promised budget behavior explicitly. A reservation system also needs settlement rules for timeouts and uncertain outcomes, since uncertainty about completion isn't proof that no charge can arrive.

The following Go example illustrates the two decision gates with anonymous provider identities. The snapshot is an input contract, not a storage implementation: credential status and candidate eligibility must come from authoritative policy state, and BudgetReserved must represent an atomic reservation for this admission.

package admission

type Snapshot struct {
    CredentialActive bool
    Approved         map[string]bool
    ModelCompatible  map[string]bool
    Pin              string
    Excluded         map[string]bool
    BudgetReserved   bool
}

func Decide(s Snapshot, provider string) string {
    if !s.CredentialActive {
        return "credential_inactive"
    }
    if !s.Approved[provider] || !s.ModelCompatible[provider] {
        return "destination_ineligible"
    }
    if s.Excluded[provider] {
        return "provider_excluded"
    }
    if s.Pin != "" && s.Pin != provider {
        return "provider_not_pinned"
    }
    if !s.BudgetReserved {
        return "budget_unavailable"
    }
    return "admit"
}

The first gate establishes whether this credential may send this request to this destination. The second establishes whether the tenant can reserve the request's liability. A conflicting pin and exclusion refuses the destination; it never relaxes either condition.

Concurrency is the trap that a small function cannot solve. Checking an active flag, reserving budget elsewhere, and dispatching later leaves a race with revocation. The implementation needs a defined admission commit that orders credential revocation, policy revision, and reservation acceptance; any reservation acquired for an admission that loses that race must be released without dispatch. Document how dispatch and revocation interleave rather than claiming that an ordinary map lookup supplies this guarantee.

Change the evidence before changing the threshold

Replace the undifferentiated refusal counter with bounded reason categories corresponding to the decisions above. Keep tenant identifiers, credential identifiers, policy revisions, and request identifiers in access-controlled audit records rather than making every identifier a metric label. That is a proposed instrumentation design: metrics answer whether a boundary is failing broadly, while the audit trail explains the individual decision. Neither should contain the credential secret.

Record admission separately from dispatch and settlement. If a request was admitted before revocation and settled afterward, the timeline should show that ordering without labeling it a fresh post-revocation admission. If an attempt was refused because its provider was excluded, the record should preserve that reason even while the tenant also happens to have no budget remaining. A deterministic refusal order makes this evidence interpretable, although it doesn't replace investigating all applicable constraints.

Test the boundary that the page claims to defend:

  • Race revocation against admission and verify that no admission commits after the authoritative revocation commit.
  • Submit concurrent requests against the last available budget reservation and check the total reserved liability.
  • Add an approved destination and verify that exclusion permits it while a pin still rejects it.
  • Remove the pinned destination and verify that the result is a refusal.

These are policy tests, not synthetic performance results.

For deployment, evaluate the proposed policy against recorded decision inputs before enabling enforcement, keeping credentials out of the replay data. Have the policy owner review differences in candidate eligibility and refusal reasons. A rollback must preserve revocations and accounting commitments; rolling back application code must not resurrect a credential or restore an earlier balance. This creates coordination work between security, billing, and the routing team, but it also gives the responder a named owner for each decision.

The cost of an eager page

Close the loop with the original alert: an accepted admission using a credential already revoked at the authority is a containment violation under this design's contract. A refused request using that credential is an expected enforcement outcome. Volume alone doesn't turn the latter into the former.

A threshold that pages on every refusal can turn a disconnected game client retrying an old key into repeated interruptions. A threshold that ignores every refusal can hide a legitimate tenant's loss of access after a roster change. Route expected credential refusals to investigation or client-remediation workflows, and assess traffic loss against the service's documented availability objective; preserve a distinct page for a proven admission-boundary violation.

Choose the provider constraint from the permission sentence. Keep the budget ceiling and credential lifecycle independently enforceable. Then make the page report the failed promise, with enough evidence to decide whether to stop admissions, correct a routing policy, or repair a stale client. A responder shouldn't need to guess which of those three jobs a red chart intended.

References

OWASP's Secrets Management Cheat Sheet supports the credential lifecycle, revocation, access-control, and auditing discussion. The routing sets, budget arithmetic, code, and alert conditions above are proposed design rules and explicitly hypothetical examples. The source URL follows under Further reading.

Further reading

  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: KI-Agent zur Fehlerbehebung: So baut man einen Agenten, der Bugs zuerst reproduziert
description:
KI-Agent zur Fehlerbehebung: So baut man einen Agenten, der Bugs zuerst reproduziert

Ein KI-Agent, der Bugs selbstständig behebt, funktioniert nur, wenn er eine Regel befolgt: keine Reproduktion, keine Lösung. Der Agent verwandelt den Bug-Report in einen Test, der aktuell fehlschlägt, patcht den Code auf einem isolierten Branch, führt diesen Test erneut aus – zusammen mit der gesamten Testsuite – und meldet sich erst zurück, wenn alles grün ist. Das Merging übernimmt weiterhin ein Mensch. Kann er den Bug nicht reproduzieren, bleibt er still.

Testen Sie Apidog noch heute

Das DeepSeek-Harness-Team stellte diese Idee am 1. November 2026 einem breiten Publikum vor – in einem Essay zum Design von Super-Agenten. Diese Anleitung macht daraus eine Pipeline, die Sie noch diese Woche bauen können: mit einer Reproduktion, die als API-Test vom Agenten selbst erstellt und im Terminal ausgeführt wird.

Warum „Agent, behebe das“ ohne Repro scheitert

Bittet man einen Coding-Agenten, einen Bug-Report zu beheben, erhält man meist einen souveränen Diff. Ob damit Ihr Bug behoben wird, ein eingebildeter Bug oder gar nichts – das lässt sich nicht erkennen.

Ohne Reproduktionsschritt gehen drei Dinge schief:

  • Der Agent rät die Ursache. Er wählt die plausibelste Zeile anhand der Fehlermeldung und bearbeitet sie.
  • „Behoben“ hat keine Definition. Der einzige Beweis ist die eigene Zusammenfassung des Agenten.
  • Regressionen schleichen sich ein. Ein Patch an einem gemeinsamen Validator kann einen Endpunkt reparieren und vier andere beschädigen.

Ein fehlschlagender Test löst alle drei Probleme: Er verankert den Bug, definiert „fertig“ und bleibt als Regressionstest in Ihrer Suite.

Woher „stillschweigend reproduzieren und beheben“ stammt

In „Exploring Super-agent Design“ beschreibt das DeepSeek-Harness-Team eine Richtlinie aus seiner eigenen Nutzergruppe: Meldet jemand einen Bug, versucht ein Agent, ihn im Hintergrund zu reproduzieren. Er äußert sich erst, wenn es eine bestätigte, einfache Lösung gibt. Andernfalls schweigt er.

Das Essay nennt das spekulative Ausführung und kombiniert es mit zwei Bausteinen, die Sie hier wiederverwenden. Worker erhalten je Aufgabe eine isolierte Session, sämtliche Tools und das stärkste Modell – und berichten an einen Router, statt mit Menschen zu sprechen. Ein Watchdog ist eine separate Session, die prüft, ob jeder Worker Fortschritte macht oder abdriftet.

Ein Vorbehalt: Das Essay beschreibt eine Architektur, keine ausgelieferten DeepSeek-Harness-Features. Teile davon stecken in einem Prototyp-Plugin, dsh-superagent-prototype, das laut den Autoren kein offizielles DeepSeek-Produkt ist. Zum Router-und-Worker-Bild siehe wie man einen Super-Agenten baut.

Die fünfstufige Agent-Pipeline zur Bugbehebung

Ein sich selbst reparierender Agent durchläuft jedes Mal dieselbe Schleife – mit zwei Schranken:

  1. Aufnahme: Bericht, die fehlschlagende Anfrage und die erhaltene Antwort einsammeln.
  2. Reproduzieren: Einen Test schreiben, der aus dem gemeldeten Grund fehlschlägt. Kein fehlgeschlagener Test, keine Lösung.
  3. Beheben: Den Code auf einem isolierten Branch oder Worktree patchen.
  4. Erneut ausführen: Der neue Test muss bestehen, ebenso die bestehende Suite.
  5. Übergeben: Einen Pull Request mit den Nachweisen öffnen – oder schweigen.

Schritt 1: Den Bug-Report aufnehmen

Ihr Agent kann „der Checkout ist wieder kaputt“ nicht reproduzieren. Geben Sie der Aufnahme eine feste Struktur:

Feld Beispiel Warum es wichtig ist
Endpunkt POST /orders Welcher Handler gelesen werden soll
Anfrage Body mit "coupon": null Die exakte Eingabe, die den Fehler ausgelöst hat
Tatsächliche Antwort 500, {"error":"internal"} Was der Test fehlschlagen sehen muss
Erwartete Antwort 201 mit einer Order-id Was der Test behauptet
Umgebung staging Wo die Repro läuft

Fehlen Felder, fragt der Agent einmal nach oder zieht die Anfrage aus den Logs. Error-Bodies, die den RFC-9457-Problem-Details folgen, helfen, weil der Fehlertyp in einer vorhersagbaren Form ankommt.

Schritt 2: Den Bug als fehlschlagenden API-Test reproduzieren

Das ist die Schranke. Der Agent wandelt den Aufnahme-Datensatz in einen Testfall mit zwei Assertions um – den erwarteten Statuscode und ein Feld, das die Antwort enthalten soll – und führt ihn gegen die echte Umgebung aus. Drei Ausgänge sind möglich:

  • Er schlägt aus dem gemeldeten Grund fehl. Sie haben eine Repro. Weiter geht’s.
  • Er besteht. Der Bug ist wie beschrieben nicht reproduzierbar. Loggen und stoppen.
  • Er schlägt aus einem anderen Grund fehl (Auth-Fehler, fehlende Daten, Timeout). Das ist eine defekte Repro, kein bestätigter Bug. Stoppen.

Nur der erste Fall schaltet eine Lösung frei. Das bedeutet „stillschweigend“ in der Praxis: Die anderen beiden erzeugen einen Log-Eintrag für diejenigen, die die Warteschlange prüfen – nicht eine Nachricht im Chat des Nutzers.

Schreiben Sie die Repro als API-Test, nicht als Unit-Test: Der Agent trifft dieselbe Schnittstelle wie der Nutzer, sodass er nicht versehentlich einen anderen Bug reproduziert.

Schritt 3: Den Code in einem isolierten Branch beheben

Sobald die Repro rot ist, erhält der Worker eine eigene Kopie des Codes. Ein git worktree ist die leichtgewichtigste Option: ein zweites Arbeitsverzeichnis auf einem neuen Branch, sodass die Änderungen des Agenten Ihr Checkout nie berühren. Führen Sie den Service daraus aus und verweisen Sie die Testumgebung dorthin.

Halten Sie zwei Einschränkungen streng ein. Die Lösung muss klein sein: Legen Sie ein Limit fest, etwa 3 Dateien oder 50 geänderte Zeilen, und behandeln Sie alles Größere als Meldung für einen Menschen. Und sie muss die Repro zielen: keine Refactorings, Umbenennungen oder Aufräumarbeiten – jede zusätzliche Änderung ist etwas, das Ihr Reviewer prüfen muss.

Schritt 4: Repro und gesamte Suite erneut ausführen

Die zweite Schranke hat zwei Teile. Zuerst führt der Agent denselben Testfall aus Schritt 2 unverändert erneut aus – und er muss bestehen. Hat der Agent die Assertions bearbeitet, um dorthin zu gelangen, scheitert die Lösung; Ihre Pipeline findet das heraus, indem sie die Testdatei vor und nachher vergleicht.

Zweitens muss die bestehende Suite grün bleiben. Eine Lösung, die einen Test grün und drei rot macht, geht zurück zu Schritt 3. Begrenzen Sie die Schleife zeitlich, etwa auf 3 Versuche oder 20 Minuten, dann stoppen und protokollieren, was versucht wurde. Hier beweist der Watchdog seinen Wert: Er kann einen Worker abwürgen, der immer wieder dieselbe Zeile bearbeitet oder in Dateien abdriftet, die die Repro nie berührt hat.

Schritt 5: Nur eine bestätigte, einfache Lösung übergeben

Sind beide Schranken grün, öffnet der Agent einen Pull Request mit Nachweisen, nicht mit einer Erzählung: der Bericht, der fehlgeschlagene Lauf, der Diff und der erfolgreiche Lauf samt Suite-Ergebnissen. Ein Mensch prüft und merged. Geschützte Branches stellen sicher, dass das Token des Agenten zwar Branches pushen, aber nie in main mergen kann. Scheitert eine Schranke, hört der Melder nichts; der Agent schreibt eine Log-Zeile und macht weiter.

Schutzmaßnahmen für einen sich selbst reparierenden KI-Agenten

Errichten Sie diese Zäune, bevor der erste unbeaufsichtigte Lauf startet:

Schutzmaßnahme Einstellung Was sie verhindert
Umfang Max. Dateien und Zeilen pro Lösung Neuschreibungen, die als Lösungen ausgegeben werden
Zeitfenster Max. Versuche und Minuten pro Bug Ausufernde Schleifen, die Tokens verbrennen
Zugangsdaten Nur Staging, keine Produktions-Schlüssel Eine Repro, die echte Orders schreibt
Merge-Rechte Branches pushen, nie mergen Ungeprüfter Code, der main erreicht
Test-Integrität Testdatei vor und nachher vergleichen Auf Erfolg gezäumte Assertions
Schweigen Keine nutzergerichtete Nachricht bei Fehlschlag Lärm und halb bestätigte Behauptungen

Zugangsdaten sind am wichtigsten: Eine Repro trifft die API tatsächlich – nutzen Sie also Staging oder lokale Testdaten.

Ihren Coding-Agenten die Repro mit Apidog CLI erstellen lassen

Schritt 2 ist das Herz der Pipeline – und genau dafür wurde die Apidog CLI gebaut. Ihr Coding-Agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor oder OpenCode) schreibt den Testfall als JSON, legt ihn in Ihrem Apidog-Projekt an und führt ihn im Terminal aus. Sie schreiben nur einen Prompt.

Einmalig einrichten:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog auth login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Dann geben Sie Ihrem Agenten den Bug-Report und diesen [REDACTED PROMPT]
Here is a bug report for POST /orders in Apidog project .
Turn it into an Apidog test case that fails today: assert status 201
and that $.id exists. Run it against staging and confirm it fails for
the reported reason. If it does, fix the handler on a new worktree
branch until the same test passes, run the endpoint's other cases, and
open a PR with both JSON reports. If it doesn't reproduce, stop and log why.


Der Agent baut das Payload nicht aus dem Gedächtnis. Er liest das Schema, findet eine Kategorie, validiert seine Datei und legt den Testfall erst dann an:


bash
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog test-case category --project
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file repro-orders.json
apidog test-case create --project --file repro-orders.json


Die Datei, die er schreibt, sieht so aus (die IDs stammen aus Ihrem Projekt):


json
{
"name": "Repro: POST /orders with null coupon returns 500",
"apiDetailId": 123456,
"categoryId": 1,
"method": "post",
"path": "/orders",
"parameters": {},
"commonParameters": {},
"requestBody": {
"type": "application/json",
"data": "{\"items\":[{\"sku\":\"A-100\",\"qty\":1}],\"coupon\":null}"
},
"postProcessors": [
{ "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
"data": { "name": "status is 201", "subject": "httpCode", "comparison": "equal", "path": "", "value": "201" } },
{ "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
"data": { "name": "order id exists", "subject": "responseJson", "comparison": "exists", "path": "$.id" } }
]
}


Jetzt der rote Lauf, der den Bug beweist:


bash
apidog run --test-case --project -e -r cli,json --out-file repro-before


Der CLI-Reporter zeigt die fehlschlagende Status-Assertion bei einem 500, und `repro-before.json` landet in `apidog-reports/`. Nach der Lösung führt der Agent denselben Befehl mit `--out-file repro-after` aus, und beide Assertions bestehen. Diese beiden Dateien sind die Nachweise im Pull Request. Für Schritt 4 führt er jeden Testfall des Endpunkts aus, damit die Lösung keinen Nachbarn still beschädigen kann:


bash
apidog test-case run --project --endpoint -e -r cli,json




Fügen Sie `--upload-report` hinzu, um den Lauf in der Apidog-App anzuzeigen. Nach dem Merge bleibt der Repro-Testfall als Regressionstest in Ihrem Projekt, und derselbe `apidog run` mit `-r junit` lässt sich in CI einbinden, wie in [Apidog CLI in einer CI/CD-Pipeline ausführen](https://apidog.com/de/blog/apidog-cli-ci-cd-pipeline?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) gezeigt. Weitere Setups finden Sie im [Apidog-CLI-Agenten-Workflow](https://apidog.com/de/blog/apidog-cli-agent-workflow?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) und unter [Apidog CLI in Claude Code](https://apidog.com/de/blog/apidog-cli-in-claude-code?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Apidog Free deckt bis zu 4 Nutzer ab – Sie können also die gesamte Schleife ohne Bezahlplan ausprobieren.

## FAQ

### Kann ein KI-Agent Bugs wirklich ohne Menschen beheben?

Er kann viele einfache Bugs selbstständig reproduzieren, patchen und beweisen – aber er sollte sie nicht mergen. Behalten Sie einen Menschen beim Merging, und lassen Sie den Branch-Schutz das durchsetzen.

### Was, wenn der Agent den Bug nicht reproduzieren kann?

Er stoppt und protokolliert, was er versucht hat. Ein Bug, den er nicht reproduzieren kann, ist eine Lösung, die er nicht bestätigen kann – jeder Patch wäre ein Ratespiel. Ein Mensch ergänzt dann Details im Bericht oder schließt ihn.

### Wie verhindere ich, dass der Agent den Test so bearbeitet, dass er besteht?

Speichern Sie eine Kopie oder einen Hash des Testfalls, sobald er erstmals fehlschlägt, und vergleichen Sie, bevor Sie die Lösung akzeptieren. Halten Sie die Testdatei außerhalb der Pfade, die der Worker bearbeiten darf.

### Brauche ich DeepSeek Harness, um das zu bauen?

Nein. Das Essay beschreibt ein Design, und sein Prototyp-Plugin ist kein offizielles DeepSeek-Produkt. Jeder Coding-Agent, der Shell-Befehle ausführt, funktioniert – auch Claude Code in [GitHub Actions](https://apidog.com/de/blog/claude-code-github-actions?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Sehen Sie sich [an, was DeepSeek Harness ist](https://apidog.com/de/blog/what-is-deepseek-harness?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation), wenn Sie es dort ausprobieren möchten.

title: Automation Testing With Playwright Using JavaScript
description:
Automation testing is a critical part of software development that helps ensure the quality and reliability of your application. Playwright is a robust end-to-end testing framework that enables you to automate browser actions and interactions. This comprehensive guide will walk you through performing automation testing using Playwright in a Next.js application.

Playwright is a JavaScript library that provides a high-level API to automate browsers like Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. It allows you to write browser automation scripts that simulate user interactions, navigation, form submissions, and more. Playwright's unique architecture provides a fast and reliable way to test web applications.

Setting Up a Javascript Project

Before we start writing tests, let's set up a Next.js project:

Create a new Javascript project:

mkdir my-js-project
cd my-js-project
npm init -y

This will create a new directory called my-js-project, navigate into it, and initialize a new Node.js project with default settings.

The -y flag in the npm init -y command is a shorthand for "yes". It automatically answers "yes" to all the prompts that npm init would normally ask you, thereby accepting all the default values for the project setup.

Install the Playwright dependencies:

npm install playwright

Writing Automation Tests with Playwright

Let's create a simple automation test for a javascript application. We want to test the navigation from the home page to a blog post page.

const { chromium } = require('playwright');

describe('Next.js Blog Automation Test', () => {
  let browser;
  let page;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    browser = await chromium.launch();
  });

  beforeEach(async () => {
    page = await browser.newPage();
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    await browser.close();
  });

  it('should navigate to a blog post', async () => {
    await page.goto('http://localhost:3000');
    await page.click('a[href="/blog"]');
    await page.waitForSelector('h1');
    const pageTitle = await page.textContent('h1');
    expect(pageTitle).toContain('Blog Post Title');
  });
});

Let us see the components of the above code in a bit more detail.

When using testing frameworks like Jest, Mocha, Jasmine, or Playwright, the describe block is a fundamental organizational structure that helps group related test cases together. It provides a way to define a logical container for a set of tests with a common context or functionality. The describe block is primarily used to improve your test suite's organization, readability, and maintainability.

The beforeEach function is a part of testing frameworks like Jest and is used to set up a consistent and controlled environment before running each individual test case within a describe block. This is particularly helpful in maintaining a clean state and avoiding interference between test cases.

In testing, it's important to create a controlled environment for each test case to ensure that they run independently and reliably. Sometimes, tests require the same setup steps before execution. Instead of repeating the setup code in every test case, you can use beforeEach to define those common setup actions.

In automated testing, especially when using testing frameworks like Jest, you often encounter lifecycle functions that help you set up and tear down certain conditions before and after tests are run. One important lifecycle function is beforeAll.

The beforeAll function executes a block of code before all the tests within a test suite (also known as a test file or describe block) are run. This block of code typically sets up any common resources or configurations required for all the tests in that suite.

The afterAll function is a part of testing frameworks like Jest, and it is used to perform cleanup tasks or teardown operations after all the test cases within a describe block have been executed. It's the counterpart of the beforeAll function, which is used for setup operations before the test cases.

In testing, there might be scenarios where you need to perform cleanup tasks or reset the environment after all the test cases within a particular test suite have run. afterAll allows you to define these cleanup actions.

Enhancing API Testing with Playwright

Did you know that Playwright, commonly recognized for its powerful browser automation capabilities, can also be utilized for API testing? This versatile tool excels in web application testing and offers robust features to automate and validate API interactions. By leveraging Playwright for API testing, you can streamline your testing processes and ensure your APIs function as expected.

Writing Your First API Test

Let's start with a basic example. We'll test a simple REST API that returns user information.

  1. Start with creating a new file called apiTest.spec.js.

  2. Import Playwright:

const { test, expect } = require('@playwright/test');
  1. Write a Basic Test:

Here's a test that fetches user data from a hypothetical API endpoint.

test('GET user data', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.get('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1');
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
  const userData = await response.json();
  expect(userData.id).toBe(1);
  expect(userData.name).toBe('Leanne Graham');
});

Breaking Down the Test

  • test: Defines a test case.

  • request.get: Sends a GET request to the specified URL.

  • expect: assertions to check if the response meets our expectations.

  • response.status(): Checks the HTTP status code of the response.

  • response.json(): Parses the response body as JSON.

Handling Different HTTP Methods

Playwright supports various HTTP methods. Here are examples of POST, PUT, and DELETE requests.

POST Request:

test('POST create new user', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.post('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users', {
    data: {
      name: 'John Doe',
      username: 'johndoe',
      email: 'johndoe@example.com'
    }
  });
  expect(response.status()).toBe(201);
  const newUser = await response.json();
  expect(newUser.name).toBe('John Doe');
});

PUT Request:

test('PUT update user data', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.put('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1', {
    data: {
      name: 'Jane Doe'
    }
  });
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
  const updatedUser = await response.json();
  expect(updatedUser.name).toBe('Jane Doe');

});

DELETE Request:

test('DELETE user', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.delete('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1');
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
});

Handling Authentication

Many APIs require authentication. Here’s how to handle it in Playwright:

test('GET user data with authentication', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.get('https://api.example.com/protected-resource', {
    headers: {
      'Authorization': `Bearer YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN`
    }
  });
  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
});

Using Fixtures for Setup and Teardown

Fixtures help set up and tear down resources required for your tests. Here's an example:

test.describe('API tests with setup and teardown', () => {
  let userId;

  test.beforeAll(async ({ request }) => {
    const response = await request.post('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users', {
      data: { name: 'Test User' }
    });
    const user = await response.json();
    userId = user.id;
  });

  test.afterAll(async ({ request }) => {
    await request.delete(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/${userId}`);
  });

  test('GET created user data', async ({ request }) => {
    const response = await request.get(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/${userId}`);
    expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
  });
});

Running Your Tests

You can run your Playwright tests using the Playwright Test Runner. Add a script to your package.json:

"scripts": {
  "test": "playwright test"
}

Then, run your tests with:

npm test

Generating Test Depictions

Playwright Test generates reports by default. You can view the test results in the console, but you might want a more detailed report. Playwright provides a built-in HTML report. To enable it, add a playwright.config.js file in your project root:

module.exports = {
  reporter: [
    ['list'],
    ['html', { outputFolder: 'playwright-report', open: 'never' }]
  ],
};

Run your tests again.

After completing the tests, you'll find the HTML report in the playwright-report directory. To open it, run:

npm playwright show-report

This command opens the HTML report in your default browser, providing a detailed view of your test results.

Best Practices for Automation Testing

Here are some best practices to follow when writing automation tests using Playwright in a Next.js application:

  • Isolation: Each test should be independent and not depend on the state of other tests.

  • Use Data Attributes: Use data attributes in your components to make it easier to select elements in your tests.

  • Mock API Calls: Use mocking or stubbing to avoid making actual API requests during tests.

  • Assertions: Use meaningful assertions to verify the expected behavior of your application.

  • Page Objects: Create page objects or helper functions to encapsulate the interactions with specific parts of your application.

Continuous Integration with Playwright

Integrate your Playwright tests into your continuous integration (CI) pipeline. This ensures that your tests are automatically executed whenever you push code changes.

  1. Choose a CI platform like GitHub Actions, Jenkins, or Travis CI.

  2. Configure the CI pipeline to run the Playwright tests using Jest.

Playwright vs. Selenium: A Comparison

Feature Playwright Selenium
Language Support Javascript/TypeScript, Python, C#, Java Java, C#, Python, Ruby, JavaScript, Kotlin
Browser Support Chromium (Chrome, Edge), WebKit (Safari), Firefox Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge, IE, Opera
Installation and Setup Single package installation (includes browser binaries) Separate installations for WebDriver binaries
Speed and Performance Generally faster (uses DevTools Protocol) Slower (uses WebDriver protocol)
Parallel Testing Built-in support for parallel testing Requires additional configuration/tools (e.g., Selenium Grid)
APIs and Features Modern API, auto-wait, network interception, mobile emulation Mature API, similar features but more configuration
Community and Support Growing community, backed by Microsoft Established community, extensive documentation
Cross-Browser Testing Consistent results with the same API for all browsers It is possible but may have inconsistencies
Test Reporting Integrated reporting tools Requires additional tools/libraries (e.g., TestNG, JUnit)
Script Debugging Built-in tools for debugging (e.g., Playwright Inspector) Debugging through language-specific IDE/tools

Conclusion

Automation testing using Playwright in a Next.js application can help you catch bugs and ensure the quality of your software. Following the steps in this guide, you've learned how to set up a Next.js project, write automation tests, and integrate them into your CI pipeline. Remember to continuously update and expand your test suite as your application evolves.

title: English Calibration Erodes Lithuanian in Expert-Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.07654v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Expert pruning compresses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models by removing the experts that a calibration set marks as unimportant. Studies of high-resource languages largely find that English calibration transfers well to other languages. We test this for Lithuanian: we pruned four MoE models with REAP, removing 25% or 50% of the experts with English, Lithuanian or mixed calibration, and evaluated both languages on reading comprehension, translation and language modelling. English calibration does not transfer to Lithuanian: at 25% pruning, English comprehension fell by a median of 1.7 points but Lithuanian by 21.4. The transfer is asymmetric. Lithuanian calibration removed most of the Lithuanian loss and never significantly hurt English comprehension, which was on average 2.5 points better than under English calibration; only English language modeling got slightly worse. Routing suggests why: in the last layers, Lithuanian sends 55-72% of its expert selections to just eight experts, against 19-39% for English, and English calibration removes some of these experts. Compressed models should be calibrated, and evaluated, in every language they must serve.

title: Secure Formal Raising: Protecting the Development of AI through Executable Properties
description:
arXiv:2611.08042v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model raising revisits Turing's developmental view of machine intelligence. Formal Raising (FR) has recently been proposed to complement this view with explicit behavioral properties. This paper extends that proposal to the security of the raising environment. Secure Formal Raising (SFR) models policy integrity, authorization, and confidential data flow using four-valued evidence that preserves unknown and inconsistent assessments. We prove six security invariants and show that they force admission to accept only confirmed evidence. A plain-C reference implementation satisfies the invariants in a bounded exhaustive exploration, which also exposes a confused-deputy gap for tool calls that a provenance requirement closes.

title: Scenario Augmentation for Rare Financial Events via Multimodal Latent Diffusion
description:
arXiv:2611.07282v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Extreme market movements are scarce, heterogeneous, and difficult to learn from imbalanced historical data. We study whether generative augmentation can improve the representation and classification of CVaR-labeled rare financial windows while retaining the complementary structure exposed by different financial representations. Each market window is expressed through three aligned modalities: structured market variables, a spatial image transformation, and a sequence of portfolio returns. Separate variational autoencoders map the modalities to compact latent codes, and a class-conditional diffusion model learns their joint latent distribution. Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) provides a risk-aware definition of rare windows and directs generation toward the minority regime. Across four window lengths on U.S. technology equities, the resulting synthetic samples improve fidelity and support relative to tabular diffusion baselines. An XGBoost classifier trained with real and generated samples attains AUCs of 0.953 - 0.960, exceeding both tabular generators and the corresponding real-only baselines. These results show that multimodal latent generation can provide useful synthetic stress scenarios for data-scarce financial risk models.

title: Octopus: One Brain, Many Branches for Latent-KV Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.06956v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems explore in parallel by spawning sub-agents with isolated context windows, whereas single-agent systems append every search and verification step into one growing trajectory. However, existing multi-agent frameworks duplicate prefix KV caches across branches, exchange findings by re-prefilling text summaries, and flatten or drop cross-branch dependencies during reinforcement learning (RL).
  We introduce Octopus, a single-model multi-agent RL framework in which all threads share one backbone and coordinate over a GPU-resident directed acyclic graph (DAG) of KV states through five primitives (fork, read_thread, wait_threads, rewind, commit). Octopus combines three co-designed mechanisms: (1) Zero-Copy Radix Forking, which spawns branches as $\mathcal{O}(1)$ cursor views over shared physical KV pages; (2) Attention-Only KV Mounting, which mounts a sibling thread's terminal KV blocks directly into full-attention layers while bypassing linear-recurrent states (Gated DeltaNet / Mamba-2), cutting off-task hijacking by $21\times$ ($57.9\% \to 2.7\%$) while retaining $92.2\%$ of full-text mutual information at zero extra KV allocation; and (3) a Packed DAG-GRPO Trainer, which packs all episode branches into one block-sparse attention pass and assigns counterfactual branch credit via leave-one-branch-out marginal rewards.
  Trained end-to-end with GRPO on Qwen3.5-4B over a sparse BM25 corpus, Octopus reaches $49.6\%$ accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus ($+17.5$ points over single-agent GRPO at 143K context and $+12.5$ points over text-summary multi-agent RL) and $51.2\%$ on OpenResearcher, outperforming dense-retrieval agents up to $250\times$ larger while increasing training throughput $3.3\times$ and cutting peak KV memory $2.8\times$.

title: Why Indian D2C Brands Are Ditching Genesys in 2026
description:
I've been a Genesys customer for 4 years. Multi-brand, 340 agents, 12,000 daily interactions. I believed in the platform.

Then the FY27 renewal invoice landed on my desk: ₹1.84 crore. Up 41% year-over-year. And I hadn't added a single new agent.

I didn't sleep that night. By 9 AM the next morning, I'd booked a 2-hour architecture session with my AWS TAM. By the end of 14 days, we were live on Amazon Connect Customer.

Here's the full story — the numbers, the pain, the one thing I genuinely miss.

Why We Were on Genesys (And Why That Made Sense)

We're a D2C fashion brand with 3 sub-brands, each with different IVR flows, different SLA tiers, and a shared Salesforce CRM. In 2022, Genesys was the only platform that handled multi-brand routing natively without us building a custom orchestration layer.

The pitch was clean: one control plane, three brands, zero custom code for routing logic.

For 3 years, that held. Then Genesys started adding "agentic AI" line items to the renewal.

Here's what the FY27 invoice actually broke down to:

Line Item FY26 FY27 Δ
CX2 seats (340) ₹1.02 Cr ₹1.18 Cr +16%
Agentic AI add-on (GCAVA) — ₹2.4 L New
AI Control Plane (QA + Agent Assist) — ₹3.8 L New
Premium support (24×7) ₹1.2 L ₹1.4 L +17%
Total ₹1.14 Cr ₹1.84 Cr +61%

Pull-quote #1: "I didn't buy more agents. I didn't add a brand. I didn't increase volume. The AI features I didn't even turn on yet cost me ₹6.2 L."

That's the part that made me angry. I was being charged for capabilities I hadn't activated. The "agentic AI" line was a per-seat entitlement, not a usage-based charge. Whether my AI resolved 0 calls or 10,000, the cost was identical.

The 14-Day Switch (What Actually Happened)

I'm not going to pretend it was clean. Here's the real timeline:

Day 1–2: AWS TAM session. Mapped our 3 IVR trees to Connect's Contact Flow Builder. Realized our multi-brand routing would need custom Lambda logic — the thing Genesys did natively.

Day 3–5: Built the Lambda orchestration layer. 3 brand-specific routing functions, a shared Salesforce connector (Connect has no native one — this was the painful part), and a Razorpay webhook for payment-failure calls.

Day 6–8: Migrated contact flows. Tested the 50-call script from our QA team. Hit 84% first-contact resolution on Day 8.

Day 9–10: Data migration. Call recordings, agent profiles, historical QA scores. Genesys's export format was a CSV nightmare. Connect's import was cleaner but still 14 hours of manual mapping.

Day 11–12: Parallel run. Both platforms live, 50% traffic each. Monitored CSAT, AHT, and resolution rate in real time.

Day 13: Cut over. Full traffic on Connect.

Day 14: First full week of data.

Pull-quote #2: "The multi-brand routing was the thing I missed most. I built what Genesys gave me out of the box, but it took me 5 days of Lambda code. That's the real cost of 'flexibility' — someone on your team becomes the platform engineer."

The Numbers After 60 Days

Metric Genesys (FY26 baseline) Connect (Day 60) Δ
Monthly platform cost ₹9.5 L ₹3.1 L −67%
Cost per resolution (AI-assisted) ~₹48 ~₹12 −75%
First-contact resolution 79% 84% +5 pts
Average handle time 4m 12s 3m 48s −24s
CSAT (post-call survey) 4.1/5 4.3/5 +0.2
Multi-brand routing complexity Native (0 code) Custom Lambda (~400 lines) ⚠️
Salesforce integration Pre-built connector Custom (Week 1 effort) ⚠️
DPDP data residency Nearest AWS region (not marketed as India) ap-south-1 (Mumbai), explicit ✅

The headline number: ₹6.4 L/month saved. ₹76.8 L/year. That's the entire "agentic AI" line item plus more, gone.

What I Genuinely Miss

I'll be honest about this, because every "I quit Genesys" article that doesn't mention what they lost is a vendor blog post in disguise.

1. Multi-brand routing. Genesys's Orchestrator handled our 3-brand logic in a drag-and-drop canvas. My Lambda code works, but it's a maintenance burden. When we launch a 4th brand, that's another sprint.

2. The Salesforce connector. Genesys's pre-built integration meant zero code for CRM sync. On Connect, I wrote a custom Apex-to-Lambda bridge. It works, but it's mine to fix when Salesforce changes an API field.

3. The vendor relationship. Genesys had a dedicated CSM who knew our account. My AWS TAM is great, but I'm one of 200 accounts in their portfolio.

The Verdict (Screenshot This)

"Genesys sells you a platform. Amazon Connect sells you infrastructure. If your routing is complex and your CRM is Salesforce, you're paying a 3× premium for convenience. If your team can write Lambda and your volume is high, Connect's usage-based model means your AI efficiency literally lowers your bill. Pick the one that matches your engineering reality, not the one with the better demo."

Did you just switch CCaaS platforms? What broke? What surprised you? Drop it below — I read every single one. 👇

title: SKIM: Pruning Large Language Model Agents via Selective Knowledge Informed Masking
description:
arXiv:2611.07558v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed under structured generation, where grammar constraints enforce output format at inference time. Whereas existing compression methods target unconstrained generation, we first identify a fundamental mismatch: under structured generation, grammar constraints reduce the model's output distribution to valid tokens, and the logits matter most at the small set of positions that decide the agent's action. Motivated by this finding, we propose SKIM (Selective Knowledge-Informed Masking), the first pruning and distillation framework for LLM agents under structured generation, with both stages guided by token role. SKIM partitions token positions into context, decision, and format categories, and this partition drives two complementary axes: (1) category-aware pruning saliency scores that preserve parameters most relevant for decision positions; and (2) an on-policy distillation objective that aligns student and teacher on valid tokens, paired with category-aware feature matching. We evaluate SKIM on tool-calling benchmarks and within multi-step agent loops, across multiple model scales and sparsity levels. SKIM consistently improves accuracy over baselines, with its superiority becoming most striking in high-sparsity regimes where conventional methods struggle, demonstrating the potential of category-aware compression for deployment-time grammar-constrained agents.

title: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
description:
arXiv:2611.07653v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space. We introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with organized large-scale exploration. Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and, together with expert-developed skills, supports research decisions. Self-Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents inheriting research context and decision-making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies. We introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, comprising 121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks assessed with expert-defined process rubrics. PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, autonomous investigations generated findings subsequently supported by human-executed experiments. For LpxH, PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site and screened compounds against it, identifying a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding. For JAK1, it prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity. Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self-Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome and identified a new binding target, with the interaction subsequently confirmed experimentally. PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.

title: Fine-Tuning a Transducer for Impaired Speech: Where the Gains Appear and What They Mean for Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2611.07587v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speech recognition still works poorly for many people whose speech is affected by conditions such as ALS, Parkinson's disease, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome or stroke. We took part in the Speech Accessibility Project Challenge 2 (SAPC2) with a public speech recognizer that we fine-tuned on the challenge data. Our best entry scored 7.81% character error rate on Test1, the first of two hidden test sets (official baseline 15.26%). Our live entries ran on CPUs with a combined median latency of about 0.9 seconds at 7.96-8.07% error. On new speakers, fine-tuning reduced errors most for the speakers that an off-the-shelf recognizer finds hardest to understand. Sentences already seen in training had far lower error rates than new ones (2.58% vs 6.42%), a larger difference than being a familiar speaker made. We close with lessons for evaluating such systems.

title: Degree-Equalized View-Graph Selection under Tight Pair Budgets
description:
arXiv:2611.07498v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fully matching all image pairs in Structure-from-Motion is quadratic in the number of images, so practical pipelines pass a budgeted subset to the final matching and reconstruction backend. One-shot selectors score candidates with image retrieval, cheap geometric probes, or a learned prior and finalize B pairs before full matching. Their priorities do not account for the degree already allocated to each image, which can concentrate edges on a few images. Across nine large 1DSfM internet photo collections at B=2N, the coverage top-B selector leaves 54% of covered images with realized degree at most two. Reconstruction can then fail even when the selected graph is nearly connected and almost fully verified. Our training-free greedy rule, Degree-Equalized Allocation (DEAL), exponentially downweights pairs whose endpoints are already well covered. On these collections, DEAL improves the one-shot selector built on the same prior (from 0.776 to 0.929) and matches the mean registered-image ratio of an SfM-supervised edge prior under the shared backend (0.929 vs 0.930), without training. On the largely saturated 38-scene standard benchmark suite, DEAL gives the highest mean among the evaluated training-free selectors (0.875 vs 0.858 one-shot).

title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
description:
Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments.

We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox. Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off.

Persisting state with a drive

Create a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI:

Or from the Sandbox SDK:

In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it.

The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive.

Sharing state across sandboxes

Agents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. If one agent builds a dataset on a drive, other agents can mount read-only copies to analyze the data or generate reports without rebuilding the dataset. They use the shared files as input and save their results separately.

Agents can also fork a drive to explore different approaches independently. Each fork starts with the drive’s contents and provides its own writable workspace. Agents can try different transformations of the dataset in parallel without changing the original or affecting one another. Forks don’t merge back into the original drive.

Forking is generally available.

Get started

Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on all plans.

Drives default to 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, with up to 16 TiB available. See the documentation for configuration, snapshots, and limits, or the changelog for what changed at GA.

title: ArtCrafter: Feed-Forward Generation of Articulated 3D Object with Analytic Joint Derivation
description:
arXiv:2611.07658v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Articulated 3D assets are essential for robotic simulation and training, yet their generation from casual images poses a key challenge: recovering part geometry and kinematics that remain mutually consistent. We present ArtCrafter, a novel feed-forward generative model for controllable generation of articulated 3D objects from a pair of images, one depicting the object in the rest state and the other in the open state. At the core of ArtCrafter is a DiT-based generative model that jointly produces part-level meshes for both articulation states in a single forward pass. Inspired by Slot Attention, its denoising process operates on a $1+2N$ slot layout comprising one shared base slot and $N$ paired rest/open slots, encouraging each pair to bind to the same kinematic part. To ensure geometrically consistent and disjoint part generation, we introduce Triplet Attention to enforce cross-state geometric consistency between paired rest/open slots anchored through the shared base slot, and a repulsion loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rep}}$ on decoded part point clouds to prevent inter-part penetration throughout denoising. Given the resulting paired meshes, URDF joint parameters---type, axis, origin, and range---are derived analytically from the rigid transformation between each rest/open pair, providing an interpretable alternative to learned joint-parameter regression. Extensive experiments on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets demonstrate that ArtCrafter outperforms existing method under the same dual-state setting in geometry quality and articulation precision, while remaining competitive with methods operating under different input settings and paradigms.

title: MammoSeek: A Mammography Agent with selective zooming for grounded reports
description:
arXiv:2611.07188v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Radiologists read a screening mammogram by first forming a global impression of the four views and then selectively magnifying suspicious regions before assigning a BI-RADS assessment. MLLMs, in contrast, see the whole image at a fixed, reduced resolution, which makes sub-millimeter calcifications invisible, and they perform close to chance on mammography. Therefore, we present MammoSeek, a mammography agent that reproduces this reading process. After forming an impression of each breast, the agent performs selective zooming: it decides by itself which detector candidates deserve a closer look and inspects only those on full-resolution views. Guided by a BI-RADS assessment skill, it then assigns a category and generates a localized, lexicon-structured report for each breast; its assessment is combined with image-model scores in a decision layer to decide recall. On an internal (EMBED) and an external (VinDr-Mammo) dataset, \ours reaches exam-level AUCs of 0.824 and 0.818, far above other MLLMs, mammography agent and CNN classifiers. Selective zooming also outperforms both no zooming and forced zooming in localization, structured-report F1 and recall decisions at low cost.

title: FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving
description:
arXiv:2611.07542v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/tree/releases/v0.30.0.

title: BlockLock: Reproducible LLM Inference with Fixed Batch Geometry
description:
arXiv:2611.06977v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reproducible LLM inference requires that a request produces the same output regardless of the other requests in the batch. Existing solutions pay for this in different ways: batch-invariant kernels constrain every operator, and isolating prefill with fixed-shape decode ({our CoRun-style baseline}) gives up shared prefill compute and pads decode. We present BlockLock, which keeps shared batched prefill and pins only the numerical path of the protected request: it fixes the geometry that the request sees, with {two modes: BlockLock-Rows uses fixed-width rows and retains batched decode of all requests; BlockLock-Pack uses terminal-anchored packing with an isolated dummy segment, then extracts the protected request's KV state for target-only decode. Under a stated per-deployment contract, both modes preserve the target's output bitwise when its companions change.} Across five {dense} models (Qwen3-8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B/12B-IT) and three single-GPU deployments (NVIDIA A6000, A100, and H100), we evaluate our approach on both tinyBenchmarks and BFCL{; we also include initial tensor-parallel experiments on two NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Both modes preserve target sequences and Top20-logit bits in the reported tests.} At equal delivered work, {BlockLock-Rows} reduces latency by 53.5--55.0\% and improves throughput by 115.2--122.2\% relative to vLLM Batch-Invariant; compared with batch-invariant kernels, it needs no custom kernel implementations and constrains only the protected requests.

title: Permanent and Transient Representations for Continual Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.07327v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) agents struggle to adapt to new situations while retaining prior knowledge, leading to a stability-plasticity trade-off. One approach to solving this problem is by using complementary learning systems: one for slow, long-term learning and another for quick, transient adaptation. Anand & Precup (2023) instantiated this idea using permanent and transient value functions, but used the same features in both systems. Intuitively, long-term learning should rely more on parametric representations for broad generalization, while transient learning would be best served by non-parametric representations for situation-specific adaptation. In this paper, we explore this idea both theoretically and empirically. By introducing a novel non-parametric approximation for estimating the transient value function in complex tasks, we demonstrate that our method enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic, underscoring the effectiveness of our system-level decomposition.

title: CST-Bench: Benchmarking Counterfactual Spatial Transition Reasoning with Causal Transition On-Policy Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.07541v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing benchmarks mainly focus on static scene understanding. When objects are moved or swapped, models must infer not only spatial relations but also how interventions change the scene state. To address this problem, we introduce CST-Bench, a benchmark for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CST-Bench contains 7,082 examples covering 6 intervention types and 12 transformation operators, with dense causal annotations including intervention sources, affected relations, expected effects, invariant relations, and metric changes. We benchmark general-purpose MLLMs on CST-Bench and further compare post-training strategies on CST-Bench and standard spatial benchmarks. Results show that methods effective for ordinary spatial reasoning can still fail under counterfactual interventions. We further formulate counterfactual spatial reasoning as causal state-transition modeling and propose CT-OPSD, which uses CST-Bench annotations to guide a teacher model in learning counterfactual state transitions and causal reasoning chains. These chains are then distilled into a student model that reasons only from real observations. Overall, experiment results establish CST-Bench as a challenging benchmark and reusable supervision resource for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CT-OPSD further provides an initial demonstration of how its annotations can support model improvement.

title: Closed-Loop Agent Evaluation: Layered Measurement and Self-Calibration
description:
arXiv:2611.07051v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Once an agent is live, teams want to know whether it is doing its job, not just whether it throws errors. Yet most evaluation is one-off: a benchmark run, a look at traces, a single score. Its conclusions neither check themselves nor reach the agent. We propose closed-loop evaluation, an evaluation method for deployed agents. It models evaluation as performance estimation under biased raters and censored outcomes, and it requires every level's conclusion to trace back to atomic data and to be computed by versioned rules. The method covers four levels of analysis (span, trace, conversation and engagement), measures along a spine of Execution, Substance, Trajectory and Results, treats Conduct as a constraint throughout, and uses Provenance and Adjudication components to certify the evidence and the evaluators. Evaluator agents generated by an Agent Factory carry these components, each with a domain knowledge pack and an adapter harness. Two loops close the evaluation: an inner loop audits the evidence, rules and metrics themselves, and an outer loop uses per-component regression checks to drive agent improvement. We also give a pipeline that runs this process automatically. Using the business-analysis agent SharpInsight as a case and porting the method to public conversation data, we show how problems differ across levels and how evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring (ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81; kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63).

description:
Syncing Inventory Across Multiple Shopify Locations Without Overselling

The moment a product sells across more than one location or channel, inventory sync stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the thing standing between you and an oversold order you have to apologize for.

⚡ The Actual Race Condition

Two orders for the last unit arriving within milliseconds of each other, from two different channels, is the scenario that breaks naive sync logic. Whichever system checks available inventory a moment too late sells a unit that's already gone.

🔒 The Reservation Pattern That Fixes It

Inventory needs to be reserved at the moment of checkout initiation, not just decremented after payment succeeds — a short-lived hold that releases automatically if checkout isn't completed within a few minutes. This closes the race window that a simple decrement-on-sale approach leaves open.

📊 Buffer Stock Is a Pragmatic Backstop

Even with good reservation logic, keeping a small safety buffer (2-3 units reported as unavailable before true zero) absorbs sync-delay edge cases across third-party channels that don't support real-time reservation at all, like some marketplace integrations.

Originally published on the KLYX blog.

title: Big Models, Small Gains: Frozen Forecasters as Classifiers on MONSTER
description:
arXiv:2611.06988v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Forecasting foundation models are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for time series classification, but it remains unclear whether their pretrained representations offer an advantage over strong classifiers that do not require pretraining. This raises an important question: do these representations provide useful information beyond what the model architecture alone can capture, particularly when labelled data are scarce? We present a controlled benchmarking of two forecasting models, Reverso and Chronos-Bolt, on six large datasets from the MONSTER benchmark, using 1%, 10%, and 100% of the available training labels. We compare their frozen representations against four established time series classification methods and random-weight versions of the same forecasting models. Our results show that pretraining improves classification accuracy over random-weight counterparts on five of the six datasets, with gains of up to 23 percentage points. However, the frozen representations do not reliably outperform the strongest non-pretrained baseline in any setting: they perform worse in 15 of 17 settings and tie in the remaining two. Further experiments show that restoring amplitude information recovers part of the performance gap, while fine-tuning and forecast-error features do not close it. These findings highlight the importance of strong task specific baselines and random weight controls when evaluating forecasting foundation models for classification. Our code is available at https://github.com/Rachet2006/frozen-forecasters-monster.

title: Test-Time Self-Play: Scaling without a Verifier
description:
arXiv:2611.07367v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time scaling methods spend additional compute at deployment to improve a large language model's performance on a hard target problem. Most methods rely on a verifier that scores candidate solutions for correctness, using it to select among or refine the model's outputs. In many deployment regimes, however, a strong verifier on the target problem is unavailable. We introduce Test-Time Self-Play (TTSP), an approach to test-time scaling using asymmetric self-play without reliance on a verifier. On a difficulty-calibrated subset of LiveCodeBench v6, TTSP is the best-performing method at every verifier strength we evaluate, and the gap to the strongest baseline widens as the verifier weakens; in the no-verifier limit, TTSP yields a 35\% absolute improvement in mean@8. The gains hold across a range of verifier strengths, except when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.
