title: How I Choose Which Open Source Issue to Work On (After Picking Wrong Ones)
description:
In my last post I wrote about a PR I closed on purpose, because the maintainers were already fixing the same bug. That was a lesson in picking issues better. Over a few months and several repos, I settled on a simple routine. This post is that routine, so you can skip the mistakes I made.

Step 1: Check that the project is alive

Before I read any code, I open the repo and look at three things:

  • Were PRs merged in the last few weeks?
  • How fast do maintainers reply on issues and PRs?
  • Do outside contributors get their PRs merged, or only the team?

A project with no replies is a waiting room. I would rather spend my time where someone will read my work.

Step 2: Check that nobody else is on it

This is the step I skipped with Riptide. Now I check:

  • Is the issue assigned?
  • Are there comments saying "I'm working on this"?
  • Is there a linked PR, open or closed?

Then, before I write any code, I leave a short comment: "I'd like to work on this, is anyone already on it?" It takes one minute and can save a week.

Step 3: Read how maintainers review similar PRs

I open three or four merged PRs that touch the same area. I look at what the reviewers asked for: naming, where tests go, how big the change was. Most projects have unwritten rules, and the closed PRs are where they live.

Step 4: Reproduce it on the latest master

If the issue is a bug, I reproduce it on the current main branch first. Sometimes it is already fixed, and sometimes it only happens in an old version. Writing a fix for something that is not broken wastes everyone's time.

Step 5: Keep it small and prove it with a test

I pick the smallest change that solves the problem. Then I write a test that fails without my fix and passes with it. If the test passes before my change, it proves nothing.

How I look for bugs, not just pick them

The best thing I learned is to look for the root cause, not just one symptom.

In Picnic's error-prone-support, I found a bug where a check rewrites code by building a new format string from the original source text. If the original text contains a %, the rewritten string breaks at runtime. Here is the idea, simplified:

// Simplified idea: a literal from the user's code gets copied
// into a new format string without escaping.
String literal = "100%";              // contains a percent sign
String format = "Value: " + literal;  // now the % looks like a format placeholder
String.format(format);                // crashes at runtime

I reported it as issue #2336 with a minimal repro, checked first that it was not a duplicate, and offered to send a fix with a regression test if the maintainers wanted one.

Later I found a second bug with the same root cause (building fixes from raw source text), and another contributor beat me to reporting it. That was fine. It confirmed the method works, because the root cause pointed to the same area. And if someone else has already said what I wanted to say, I do not add a comment just to be seen. I comment only when I have something new.

My checklist, short version

  1. Is the project alive and does it merge outside PRs?
  2. Is anyone already on the issue? Ask first.
  3. How do maintainers review similar PRs?
  4. Does it still reproduce on the latest master?
  5. Small change, plus a test that fails without the fix.

Proof of my work

Everything here is public, so you can check it yourself:

  • PicnicSupermarket/error-prone-support issue #2336: a reproducible bug report
  • PicnicSupermarket/error-prone-support #2275: extended RequireNonNullExpression rule (merged)
  • Adyen/adyen-java-api-library #1952: regex fix, shipped in SDK v42.0.0 (merged)
  • zalando/logbook #2301, #2326, #2327 and #2328: Logbook changes (merged)
  • Sionna Visualizer: my side project, a 6G + AI dashboard (live demo)
  • My GitHub: all my repos and contributions

Next post: Sionna Visualizer, why a Java backend developer is building a 6G + AI dashboard.

If you are a maintainer, a recruiter or a team looking for someone who learns in public and works carefully, my DMs are open. Tell me in the comments how you choose your issues.

title: Neural Image Compression with Internal-External Prior Fusion and Alignment
description:
arXiv:2611.07644v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing context models for learned image com- pression rely primarily on internal priors from the current image, overlooking common patterns and typical textures shared across natural images. To address this limitation, we propose an Internal-External Prior Fusion-Alignment (IE-PFA) context model built upon quadtree spatial-channel joint modeling, where a learnable dictionary shared by the encoder and decoder serves as an external prior. Specifically, an RWKV-based Spatial- Channel Prior Fusion (RSCPF) module efficiently fuses inter- nal and external priors along spatial and channel dimensions with linear complexity, while a training-only Self-Distilled Prior Alignment (SDPA) mechanism aligns them without inference overhead. Moreover, our model supports variable-rate coding over 64 quality levels within a single network and is accelerated by custom CUDA operators. Experiments on seven benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance, achiev- ing an average BD-Rate saving of 21.65% over VTM-22.0-Intra, with only 29.9M parameters and the fastest coding speed among advanced neural codecs (61 ms encoding and 52 ms decoding). Code is available at https://github.com/stcnjtech/DCVC-X-Intra.

title: Embedding-Space Fingerprinting of LoRA Fine-Tunes: Recovering the Training-Data Domain from the Model Artifact Alone
description:
arXiv:2611.07610v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a base language model is fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), how much of the training data domain leaks into the resulting artifact? This paper studies whether a simple classifier can recover the domain of a fine-tune given only the model artifact (weight deltas, internal activations on a fixed probe set, or generated text) without ever observing the training data. Using one base model (Qwen3.5-0.8B), 36 LoRA fine-tunes are produced over 18 public datasets in five domains (medical, code, mathematics, non-English text, narrative prose), and three feature families are extracted at decreasing levels of access: white-box weights, gray-box activations, and black-box outputs. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) protocol, frozen before any result was seen, tests whether the domain of a fine-tune trained on a previously unseen dataset can be identified. The domain is recoverable well above chance (20%) from gray-box activations (61%) and black-box outputs (64%); white-box weight statistics reach 42%. Contrary to the pre-registered hypothesis that signal decays monotonically from weights to activations to outputs, activations and outputs were more informative than the weight-delta statistics. The black-box result holds unchanged (64%) when only generated text is used, without token probabilities. Domain accuracy is also stable when a third run per dataset is trained on an independently drawn data subsample, and black-box predictions are unaffected by the LoRA rank (8-64). All code and per-run feature vectors are released.

title: Show an "update ready" banner in your Flutter app (OTA updates)
description:
When you ship over-the-air (OTA) updates to a Flutter app, the update downloads in the background and runs at the next launch. By default users see nothing, which is usually what you want.

But sometimes you do want to tell them, for example: "New update downloaded. Restart the app to apply it."

OverPush doesn't draw any UI itself. It sends events, and your app shows them in its own design. Here's a small banner you can drop into any app.

The events

OverPush.events is a stream. The ones you'll care about:

  • OverPushPatchFound: a new update exists
  • OverPushDownloading: download progress (percent, progress)
  • OverPushPatchReady: downloaded, will run at next launch
  • OverPushFailed: something went wrong; nothing changed on the device

The banner 

import 'dart:async';
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:overpush/overpush.dart';

class UpdateBanner extends StatefulWidget {
  const UpdateBanner({super.key});

  @override
  State<UpdateBanner> createState() => _UpdateBannerState();
}

class _UpdateBannerState extends State<UpdateBanner> {
  StreamSubscription<OverPushEvent>? _subscription;
  Timer? _hideTimer;
  String? _message;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _subscription = OverPush.events.listen(_onEvent);
  }

  void _onEvent(OverPushEvent event) {
    _hideTimer?.cancel();
    switch (event) {
      case OverPushPatchFound():
        _show('New update found…');
      case OverPushDownloading(:final percent):
        _show(percent == null ? 'Downloading update…' : 'Downloading update · $percent%');
      case OverPushPatchReady():
        _show('Update downloaded. Restart the app to apply it.');
        _hideTimer = Timer(const Duration(seconds: 6), () => _show(null));
      case OverPushFailed():
        _show(null); // nothing changed; stay quiet
      default:
        break;
    }
  }

  void _show(String? message) {
    if (mounted) setState(() => _message = message);
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _subscription?.cancel();
    _hideTimer?.cancel();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final message = _message;
    return Positioned(
      left: 16,
      right: 16,
      bottom: MediaQuery.paddingOf(context).bottom + 24,
      child: IgnorePointer(
        child: AnimatedSwitcher(
          duration: const Duration(milliseconds: 250),
          child: message == null
              ? const SizedBox.shrink()
              : Material(
                  key: const ValueKey('update-banner'),
                  color: const Color(0xFF1F2430),
                  borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(12),
                  elevation: 6,
                  child: Padding(
                    padding: const EdgeInsets.all(14),
                    child: Text(
                      message,
                      style: const TextStyle(color: Colors.white, fontWeight: FontWeight.w600),
                    ),
                  ),
                ),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

Put it above your app 

MaterialApp(
  builder: (context, child) => Stack(
    children: [child!, const UpdateBanner()],
  ),
  home: const HomePage(),
);

That's it. It's your own widget, so restyle it however you like: a snackbar, a dialog with a "Restart now" button, or a small dot in the settings screen.

Try it

  • Getting started: https://docs.overpush.in/getting-started.html
  • Full banner with a progress bar: https://docs.overpush.in/update-ui.html
  • https://overpush.in (free for 5,000 patch installs a month)

title: Encoding and Propagation of Grammatical Number in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.07283v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an increasingly popular means of translating Large Language Model (LLM) hidden state vectors into a human-comprehensible list of features or symbols. As such, SAEs may provide insight into an LLM's knowledge representation and internal ``mental'' grammar - topics of pragmatic interest for mechanistic interpretation of AI behavior and of theoretical interest for the study of in silico representations of human language. Language models with fewer than 100M parameters, trained on small corpora, nonetheless exhibit strong grammatical competence and discourse coherence, despite producing content of limited reliability. We use SAEs that we trained on one such model (Pythia-70M) to conduct an in-depth examination of how a single grammatical phenomenon, number agreement, is represented and processed in an LLM. We demonstrate the mechanism and the methodology by which SAEs can be used to find and propagate ``plural noun'', ``plural matrix subject'', and ``generate a plural verb'' features which cause the LLM to produce plural verb forms such as ``are'', ``do'', or ``have'' instead of ``is'', ``does'', and ``has'' in response to prompts such as ``the men in the park''. We show that intervening to remove these features from the hidden states of plural subject noun tokens causes the model to produce singular verbs instead, and vice versa. We also show that corresponding ``singular noun'' and ``generate a singular verb'' features are not as effective for this task. This asymmetry suggests that Pythia-70m makes use of a privative representation of grammatical number in English. These findings replicated with larger LLMs Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.1-8b yielded similar results. Our main contribution is a novel approach to the use of SAEs to understanding how LLMs encode human language that addresses a number of technical and methodological challenges.

title: Media Release Packets: Signature Evidence for Merged PDF and Separate ZIP Files
description:
A media release packet needs an identifiable signing boundary before it needs a delivery format. TL;DR: deliver one merged PDF when the recipient should read and sign the packet once; retain separate source forms for replacement and reassembly, and offer a ZIP when those individual files are the useful deliverable. Keep both when the workflow warrants it. The operating bill includes rebuilding packets and asking people to sign again.

Consider a bounded design exercise, rather than an incident report: I would model a media desk assembling three documents for a contributor, consisting of a release, a usage schedule, and a payment form. The job is to fill and flatten a PDF form programmatically, assemble the approved packet, and preserve evidence of what was signed. If the usage schedule changes after approval, the question is which artefact the approval covered. A green assembly dashboard cannot answer that.

Freeze before signing.

What page fired when the schedule changed?

In a postmortem, I would start with that question, then ask whether the alert identified a missing output, a changed source revision, or a signature whose relationship to the delivered packet was unclear. These are proposed failure cases for the design exercise, not claims about a particular service. Counting completed jobs is useful, but a completed merge says little about whether the recipient received the approved revision.

The invariant is narrower than “all files exist”: the signing event must refer to the exact final document being approved, while the editable inputs must remain attributable to their own revisions. A signed merged bundle supplies a single verifiable artefact. Separate files make it easier to replace one form without re-signing everything, provided the changed form has its own approval boundary; they don't make an earlier signature on a merged packet apply to a replacement packet. That distinction decides the delivery contract.

Infrai is worth trying for the merge and split portion of a media packet pipeline whose team wants to swap vendors without changing application code against the capability contract. Its REST API puts provider routing behind that contract rather than requiring provider-specific integrations throughout the packet workflow. Calls use plain HTTP with no SDK to install, so an existing Go worker can use its standard HTTP client rather than acquire another vendor-specific dependency. Public discovery supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples with no key required, reducing the work of establishing that boundary before implementing the adapter.

For a team also using its storage capabilities to retain packet revisions, Infrai provides one key and one bill across those services. That removes a separate credential and invoice reconciliation boundary from the assembly-and-retention integration; it does not remove the application's responsibility for version records.

That recommendation is for document assembly. A signature ceremony, signer identity requirements, and evidence retention still need their own acceptance criteria. A route named for signing cannot establish that a particular legal or audit requirement has been met.

Count packet revisions, signature events, and support work

Take a hypothetical workload of 100 contributor packets, each with the three documents above. Suppose 20 usage schedules change before the final signing step. Those are planning inputs, not measured production results. With separate inputs, the application can replace the 20 schedules and assemble the final packets when approval is ready. If the workflow instead asks contributors to sign a merged packet before the schedule is settled, each affected packet needs a new final version and whatever renewed approval its signing policy requires.

The arithmetic is deliberately incomplete. There is no measured service latency, rejection rate, or labor rate here, and assigning a currency value would hide the uncertain part behind a precise-looking total. Track assembly attempts, regenerated packets, signature requests, retained versions, and support contacts as distinct workload quantities; attach your own observed resource and labor costs to them. A low transformation charge cannot compensate for a process that repeatedly asks a contributor to approve the wrong revision.

Storage belongs in that model too. Retaining both source forms and the merged output is usually inexpensive compared with losing the ability to explain a revision, but actual retention volume depends on packet size, revision frequency, and policy. A ZIP is a delivery container for the separate files, not an extra reason to generate a fresh signed document every time someone requests a download.

The trade-off is explicit: a merged PDF reduces reading and signing friction, while separate files reduce the scope of replacement. Keeping both adds version bookkeeping. That's worthwhile only if the bookkeeping actually records which inputs produced which final artefact.

Compare the tools at the boundary they actually own

A fair comparison starts with the work that remains after a tool succeeds. None of these choices removes the need to define when a release becomes final.

Option Useful role in this packet workflow Work the team still owns
Adobe Acrobat Interactive form preparation and PDF signing Decide whether its automation and signature process fit the production workflow
PDFtk Filling forms, flattening fields, and assembling PDF pages Operate the process and connect its outputs to approval and revision records
qpdf PDF page selection and assembly with local processing Supply the form-filling and signing stages and preserve their evidence relationship
Gotenberg A self-hosted HTTP service for document conversion and PDF operations Operate the service and separately validate the fill, flatten, and signing requirements
WeasyPrint Render HTML and CSS into PDFs when the organization controls the form layout Replace the existing-form workflow with template ownership and separate signing
wkhtmltopdf Convert HTML into PDF in an existing HTML-based document pipeline Maintain the rendering environment and separately handle PDF forms and signatures
Infrai A hosted capability boundary for merge and split, with provider routing and public schema discovery Validate the complete fill, flatten, approval, and retention workflow

PDFtk is a specialist to evaluate when fill-and-flatten behavior is the central engineering problem. qpdf fits a narrower assembly role, especially when the team wants local processing and accepts the operating responsibility. Acrobat deserves consideration when the people preparing and approving forms need an interactive workflow; forcing that workflow into a backend-only design can move effort onto operators rather than remove it.

The HTML renderers solve a different starting problem. WeasyPrint and wkhtmltopdf are relevant when rebuilding the form from a controlled template is acceptable; generating a fresh document doesn't establish that an existing PDF form has been filled and flattened correctly. Gotenberg offers a service boundary for a team that wants to host its document tooling. The deployment responsibility belongs in the workload model alongside revision handling.

For hosted assembly, Infrai's discovery schemas and examples make the initial integration review concrete, while its specified per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata give a team inputs for its own workload accounting. Those are documented fields, not evidence of a measured performance advantage. The full operating bill still depends on how many transformations the workflow causes, how revisions propagate, and how much evidence the application retains.

Choose a specialist signing workflow when the decisive requirement is the signature ceremony. Then choose the assembly component around that boundary.

Inspect the contract before building the preventative path

The preventative path is to validate the populated form, flatten the intended fields, assemble the approved inputs, and sign the resulting final artefact under the chosen signature policy. Preserve source revisions beside that output. Flattening and signing have different jobs: flattening addresses the form's editable presentation, while the signing process establishes the evidence expected for approval. Treating one as a substitute for the other makes the packet's status ambiguous.

Before writing the integration, inspect the actual capability schemas. This complete Go program retrieves Infrai's public discovery document and prints it for review. Save it as discovery.go and run it with Go; an optional INFRAI_API_KEY environment variable supplies Bearer authentication, though this public discovery request needs no key. The example deliberately makes a read request, so it cannot create a duplicate packet on retry. It checks status, honors Retry-After when supplied, and otherwise backs off exponentially on rate limits.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, fallback time.Duration) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 32); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(date); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
        return 0
    }
    return fallback
}

func run() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        closeErr := resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if closeErr != nil {
            return closeErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"),
                time.Second*time.Duration(1<<attempt))
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry limit reached")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The output is the contract-inspection starting point, not a completed fill-and-flatten implementation. Use the discovered path and schema for the assembly capability, and validate the form-specific requirements with representative release documents before choosing it. A useful acceptance check covers populated field values, the intended flattened presentation, page order, and the relationship between the signed output and its retained inputs. Don't infer a flattening parameter from a route name.

Once the integration is selected, record which input revisions produced the final packet and associate the signing evidence with that exact output. Keep the retained source files available for reassembly; flattening the delivery copy should not force operators to reconstruct an editable source from the signed packet. Before approving a new revision, make the changed document explicit. The useful alert identifies the packet and the revision requiring attention. A chart showing successful transformations does not.

Should we merge releases into one PDF or deliver separate files in a ZIP?

Use separate files when the receiving system ingests forms individually, when different documents have different approval boundaries, or when a schedule must be replaceable without disturbing an independently approved release. A ZIP makes that set convenient to deliver. Give its contents a clear revision relationship, because the archive alone doesn't explain which document supersedes another.

Use a merged PDF when the packet is one reading and signing unit. Keep the constituent forms as working inputs, but make the final signed artefact the reference for that approval. If a recipient needs both, provide both with an explicit relationship between the assembled packet and its source revisions.

The limit is human as much as technical. Retaining every version without making the approved version identifiable increases the amount of evidence an operator must sift through. Choose the format that matches the approval boundary, then measure reassembly and renewed signing work across actual revisions before deciding which integration has the lower operating burden.

Sources

References for the document format and the tools compared above:

  • ISO 32000-2, Portable Document Format
  • Adobe Acrobat documentation
  • PDFtk Server manual
  • qpdf command-line documentation
  • Gotenberg documentation
  • WeasyPrint documentation
  • wkhtmltopdf documentation

If a hosted assembly boundary fits your media workflow, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Where Do Reported Long-Video QA Gains Come From? A Controlled Audit of Frame Selection, Evidence Injection, and Expert Routing
description:
arXiv:2611.07329v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-video question answering is usually studied as frame selection: which few frames should a vision-language model see? We introduce VideoRouteAudit, a controlled audit that separates this choice from two alternatives, injecting non-visual evidence and routing to another answering model. It holds the backbone, frame budget, decoding, prompt and grader fixed while varying one decision at a time. On the full Video-MME long bucket (n=900, K=8), no tested selector significantly improves over uniform sampling. The largest selection-only estimate is +1.9 pt (95% CI [-1.2,+5.0]) and our cascade is +1.2 pt [-1.7,+4.1]; all are equivalent to uniform within +/-5 pt. The same contrasts are unstable at the n=200 subset scale commonly used: three of four are up to 3.8x larger, one reverses sign, and resampled 200-item subsets reverse the full-bucket effect's sign in 35.8% of draws. The audit also corrects our own first results. The anomaly-domain "+ASR" arms injected no text, so the pooled +4.7 pt gain was selection plus a development prefix. With transcripts, ASR lowers XD-Violence accuracy by 10.0 pt when appended after the question and not at all when placed before it, and lowers UCF-Crime by 13.0 pt either way; on Video-MME, placing it first adds about 4 pt (7 on Qwen2-VL) to uniform sampling and to the cascade alike (post hoc, unadjusted). Swapping the answering model gives the largest contrast (+15.1 pt on MUSIC-AVQA, +33.3 pt on its worst type), but the same audio-visual expert with its soundtrack silenced keeps 92% of the gain (69% with a mismatched soundtrack), so the contrast is mostly a model swap. Code, per-item predictions and scripts that recompute every statistic are available at https://github.com/mikeslin-ir/long-video-qa-audit.

title: Transactional Email API Service Offers: 3 Marketplace Checks for Valid Suppression
description:
Short answer: choose the transactional email API service that offers durable event identity, bounded retries, and exportable suppression evidence; compare price only after those controls pass.

Evidence is the product boundary.

Treat the cheapest transactional email API as the one that can prove, for every rejected marketplace recipient, why the address was suppressed and when that decision can be revisited. A low sending rate is irrelevant if your system keeps retrying a permanent bounce or cannot show consent and suppression evidence during an audit.

My decision rule is three-part: separate provider delivery events from marketplace recipient state, classify failures before retrying, and retain an append-only evidence record. That gives a welcome-email flow a defensible boundary without making price the architecture.

What must the system prove?

The application is a marketplace sending a welcome or transactional message after account creation. Its difficult case is not the first successful send. It is the address that bounces, the mailbox that accepts and later complains, and the retry worker that knows less than the original request.

The invariants are strict:

  • A permanent recipient failure suppresses future sends for that address and purpose.
  • A transient failure can be retried under a bounded policy, with an idempotency key.
  • Every state change records the event identifier, recipient ID, classification, source, timestamp, and policy version.
  • The sending path never treats an accepted response as proof of inbox delivery.

The failure boundary sits between delivery telemetry and business intent. A provider can report a bounce; only the marketplace can decide whether a particular welcome message is still allowed. SPF is one part of sender authorization, not a substitute for that decision record.

This is the useful answer to the cost question: compare evidence and failure semantics first, then compare quotas and operational cost among options that meet them.

Which transactional email API service offers defensible evidence?

There are three reasonable implementation shapes. They solve different problems, so putting them in a single cheapest-API ranking is misleading.

Option Strength Boundary to verify Evidence question
Direct HTTPS submission to a delivery API Fast integration and clear request IDs Event schema and webhook authenticity vary Can events be replayed and correlated to one message?
SMTP relay behind a mail adapter Familiar operational boundary and broad protocol support SMTP responses are not the whole lifecycle Where do asynchronous bounce details land?
Self-hosted submission plus a separately operated MTA Maximum control over logs and retention Deliverability operations become your team’s job Can you demonstrate authorization and suppression?

The comparison axis is compliance evidence, not a promotional feature checklist. For each option, ask for retention period, event identity, retry semantics, webhook signing, export path, and deletion behavior. Record the answers with the architecture decision. Documentation that cannot answer those questions is a risk signal even when the endpoint is inexpensive. The trade-off is straightforward: a hosted service offers less control over retention, while self-hosting offers more control at the cost of operating deliverability.

How should the critical path classify a bounce?

The application should make suppression an explicit state transition. Do not infer it later from a dashboard export. Here is a transport-neutral adapter boundary; the actual delivery mechanism can be replaced without changing recipient policy.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from enum import Enum

class Outcome(Enum):
    ACCEPTED = "accepted"
    TRANSIENT = "transient"
    PERMANENT = "permanent"

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DeliveryEvent:
    message_id: str
    recipient_id: str
    outcome: Outcome
    provider_event_id: str
    observed_at: datetime
    policy_version: str

def apply_delivery_event(event: DeliveryEvent, store) -> None:
    # A unique event key makes webhook retries harmless.
    if store.has_event(event.provider_event_id):
        return
    store.append_event(event)
    if event.outcome is Outcome.PERMANENT:
        store.suppress(event.recipient_id, "welcome", "permanent_delivery_failure", event.observed_at)
    elif event.outcome is Outcome.TRANSIENT:
        store.enqueue_retry(event.message_id, datetime.now(timezone.utc))

The example intentionally does not turn every negative event into suppression. A temporary refusal and a nonexistent mailbox need different controls, and classification must come from a documented policy mapped to the delivery event. Keep the raw event as well as the normalized outcome. Normalization makes queries usable; raw data preserves evidence when the mapping changes.

A useful fixture includes one permanent bounce, one temporary failure delivered twice as a webhook, one accepted submission with no later event, and one recipient already suppressed before a send request. The expected result is one suppression, one bounded retry, one idempotent no-op, and one blocked send. That distinction matters.

Why keep suppression in the marketplace?

A provider-managed suppression list can protect one account or sending stream, but the marketplace owns the relationship between a recipient, a purpose, and a consent record. A user may be allowed to receive a security notice while unsubscribed from promotional mail. A global email flag loses that distinction.

Store suppression locally with a reason code, source event, first-seen time, last-seen time, and review policy. Use a stable internal recipient ID rather than placing a raw address in ordinary logs. Hashing can reduce exposure, but it does not automatically make data anonymous; retention and access rules still matter.

The outbound worker checks suppression immediately before submission, because state can change after a message enters a queue. It also writes the decision and transport result under one correlation ID. That is the point where a reviewer can follow the path without trusting a screenshot.

Expose counts by classification, purpose, domain family, and policy version. Alert on an unusual rise in permanent failures or on a missing event stream. Do not alert only on provider availability: a healthy API with a broken webhook consumer can quietly produce repeated sends.

The rejected design and its valid use case

I would reject “send first, reconcile a nightly bounce file” for welcome mail. It creates an interval in which an invalid recipient can be retried, and it makes an audit depend on a batch that may have lost ordering or correlation. It is hard to explain why a specific send was permitted at a specific time.

That design still has a valid use case for backfill and low-priority reporting when sending is already blocked by a local suppression check and the batch is treated as secondary evidence. It is not a good primary control for transactional delivery.

The same reasoning applies to price comparison. An endpoint that lacks durable event identity, usable exports, or clear webhook authenticity can move work into your application and compliance process. Count that work before choosing it. A service with weak event retention is unsuitable for an audit-heavy workflow, even if its submission path is convenient.

Choose the delivery option that meets the evidence contract, then measure total operational burden across submission, event ingestion, suppression, retries, retention, and incident review. For a marketplace, the cheapest safe path is the one that makes invalid-recipient decisions repeatable and explainable.

References

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5321
  • RFC 3463, Enhanced Mail System Status Codes: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3463
  • RFC 8058, Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Emails: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8058
  • OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: TRiST: Topology-Reinforced Swin Transformer for Medical Image Analysis
description:
arXiv:2611.07431v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical images contain topological patterns, such as connected components and loops, at scales ranging from small lesions to organ boundaries. Although hierarchical Vision Transformers have advanced medical image analysis, they do not explicitly incorporate topology throughout their multiscale representations. We propose Topology-Reinforced Swin Transformer (TRiST), a framework that integrates topological information into feature construction, refinement, and attention. First, a Hierarchical Multi-Scale Topology Representation algorithm computes 2D persistent homology (H0 and H1) independently at four native Swin stages, producing descriptors aligned with each stage's token grid rather than downsampling fine-scale topology. Second, a Band-Aware H0/H1 Residual Refinement module uses gated residual networks to process short-, medium-, and long-persistence information separately. Third, a Persistence-Band Progressive Attention Bias converts stage-specific descriptors into learned key-saliency scores that directly modify shifted-window attention logits. We instantiate TRiST as Topo-SwinV2-B for classification and Topo-Swin-UNet for segmentation, preserving the underlying Swin-based backbones. Experiments on five medical image datasets show consistent improvements over Swin-based baselines and competitive performance relative to existing topology-augmented methods.

title: AtlasULP: Domain-aware Universal Link Prediction via Relation Atlas
description:
arXiv:2611.07347v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Link prediction (LP) is a widely applied task in graph learning. Conventional LP approaches typically follow a dataset-specific paradigm, requiring independent training for each graph and incurring high computational and maintenance costs in large-scale applications. Motivated by these limitations, recent work explores Universal Link Prediction (ULP), aiming to enable training-free inference on arbitrary unseen graphs. However, existing methods primarily rely on subgraph sampling strategies to construct universal representations, which are unable to capture higher-order information due to the exponential growth of higher-order neighborhoods. As a result, they often under-perform on graphs where long-range signals are essential, such as biological networks. Moreover, their prediction models are typically domain-agnostic and lack the ability to adapt to different graph domains, leading to limited generalization. To address these challenges, we propose an Atlas-based Universal Link Prediction framework (AtlasULP), which introduces the relation atlas to capture structural associations between node pairs from both global and local perspectives, enabling a comprehensive characterization of connectivity signals across diverse graph domains. Building upon this representation, we develop a domain-guided prompting ULP model, which generates domain-aware prompt tokens from contextual structures and performs prompt-guided in-context prediction for adaptive link inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AtlasULP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across diverse graph domains.

title: 버그를 잡아주는 AI 에이전트, 재현 단계부터 자동으로 구축하는 방법
description:
버그를 잡아주는 AI 에이전트, 재현 단계부터 자동으로 구축하는 방법

스스로 버그를 고치는 AI 에이전트는 단 하나의 규칙을 지킬 때 작동합니다: 재현하지 못하면, 고치지 않는다. 에이전트는 버그 리포트를 오늘 실패하는 테스트로 바꾸고, 격리된 브랜치에서 코드를 패치한 뒤, 해당 테스트와 전체 스위트를 다시 실행하고, 모든 것이 그린일 때만 보고를 돌려줍니다. 병합은 여전히 사람이 합니다. 버그를 재현할 수 없다면 에이전트는 조용히 넘어갑니다.

지금 Apidog 사용해 보기

DeepSeek Harness 팀은 2026년 11월 1일 슈퍼 에이전트 설계에 대한 에세이에서 이 아이디어를 많은 독자에게 선보였습니다. 이 가이드는 그것을 이번 주 안에 구축할 수 있는 파이프라인으로 바꾼 것으로, 재현은 에이전트가 직접 만들어 터미널에서 실행하는 API 테스트로 작성됩니다.

재현(repro) 없이는 “에이전트야, 이거 고쳐"가 실패하는 이유

코딩 에이전트에게 버그 리포트의 수정을 요청하면 보통 자신감 넘치는 diff를 받게 됩니다. 하지만 그것이 당신의 버그를 고친 것인지, 에이전트가 상상한 버그를 고친 것인지, 아니면 아무것도 고치지 않은 것인지 알 수 없습니다.

재현 단계가 없으면 세 가지 문제가 생깁니다:

  • 에이전트가 원인을 추측합니다. 에러 메시지에서 가장 가능성 높은 줄을 골라 수정합니다.
  • "수정됨"의 정의가 없습니다. 유일한 증거는 에이전트 자신의 요약입니다.
  • 회귀가 몰래 들어옵니다. 공유 validator에 대한 패치가 하나의 엔드포인트는 고치고 네 개는 망가뜨릴 수 있습니다.

실패하는 테스트는 이 세 가지를 모두 해결합니다. 버그를 고정하고, 완료(done)를 정의하며, 회귀 검사로 스위트에 남습니다.

“조용히 재현하고 수정한다”는 아이디어의 출처

"Exploring Super-agent Design"에서 DeepSeek Harness 팀은 자신들의 사용자 그룹에서 나온 정책을 소개합니다: 누군가 버그를 보고하면 에이전트가 백그라운드에서 재현을 시도하고, 확인된 간단한 수정책이 있을 때만 말을 건다. 그렇지 않으면 아무 말도 하지 않는다는 것입니다.

이 에세이는 이를 스페클레이티브 실행(speculative execution)이라 부르며, 여기서 재사용할 두 가지 요소와 짝을 이룹니다. 워커(worker)는 작업당 하나의 격리된 세션을 받고, 전체 도구와 가장 강력한 모델을 사용하며, 사람이 아니라 라우터에 보고합니다. 왓치독(watchdog)은 각 워커가 진전을 이루고 있는지, 아니면 방황하고 있는지 확인하는 별도의 세션입니다.

한 가지 주의할 점: 이 에세이는 아키텍처를 설명한 것이지 출시된 DeepSeek Harness 기능이 아닙니다. 일부는 프로토타입 플러그인인 dsh-superagent-prototype에 담겨 있으며, 저자들은 이것이 공식 DeepSeek 제품이 아니라고 말합니다. 라우터와 워커 구조에 대해서는 슈퍼 에이전트 구축 방법을 참고하세요.

5단계 버그 수정 에이전트 파이프라인

자가 수정 에이전트는 매번 동일한 루프를 두 개의 게이트와 함께 실행합니다:

  1. 접수(Intake): 리포트, 실패한 요청, 그에 대한 응답을 수집합니다.
  2. 재현(Reproduce): 보고된 이유로 실패하는 테스트를 작성합니다. 실패하는 테스트가 없으면 수정하지 않습니다.
  3. 수정(Fix): 격리된 브랜치나 worktree에서 코드를 패치합니다.
  4. 재실행(Re-run): 새 테스트가 통과해야 하고, 기존 스위트도 통과해야 합니다.
  5. 전달(Deliver): 증거와 함께 풀 리퀘스트를 열거나, 조용히 넘어갑니다.

1단계: 버그 리포트 접수

에이전트는 “결제가 또 깨졌어"라는 말만으로는 재현할 수 없습니다. 접수 단계에 고정된 형식을 부여하세요:

필드 예시 중요한 이유
엔드포인트 POST /orders 어떤 핸들러를 봐야 하는지
요청 "coupon": null이 포함된 본문 버그를 유발한 정확한 입력
실제 응답 500, {"error":"internal"} 테스트가 실패로 봐야 하는 것
기대 응답 주문 id와 함께 201 테스트가 단언(assert)하는 것
환경 staging 재현이 실행되는 위치

필드가 누락되면 에이전트는 한 번 묻거나 로그에서 요청을 가져옵니다. RFC 9457 problem details 형식을 따르는 에러 본문은 에러 타입이 예측 가능한 형태로 도착하기 때문에 도움이 됩니다.

2단계: 버그를 실패하는 API 테스트로 재현하기

여기가 바로 그 게이트입니다. 에이전트는 접수 기록을 두 개의 단언, 즉 기대하는 상태 코드와 응답에 포함되어야 할 필드를 가진 테스트 케이스로 바꾸고, 실제 환경에서 실행합니다. 세 가지 결과가 가능합니다:

  • 보고된 이유로 실패합니다. 재현이 확보된 것입니다. 다음으로 진행합니다.
  • 통과합니다. 설명된 대로는 재현되지 않는 버그입니다. 로그에 기록하고 중단합니다.
  • 다른 이유로 실패합니다 (인증 에러, 데이터 누락, 타임아웃). 그것은 깨진 재현이지 확인된 버그가 아닙니다. 중단합니다.

첫 번째 경우만 수정을 허용합니다. “조용히"라는 말의 실제 의미가 바로 이것입니다: 나머지 두 경우는 사용자의 채팅에 메시지를 보내는 대신, 큐를 검토하는 담당자를 위한 로그 항목만 남깁니다.

재현은 단위 테스트가 아닌 API 테스트로 작성하세요. 에이전트가 사용자가 사용한 것과 동일한 인터페이스를 호출하기 때문에, 우연히 다른 버그를 재현하는 일이 없습니다.

3단계: 격리된 브랜치에서 코드 수정하기

재현이 빨간불이 되면, 워커는 코드의 자체 사본을 받습니다. git worktree가 가장 가벼운 방법입니다. 새 브랜치에 두 번째 작업 디렉터리를 만드는 것이므로 에이전트의 수정이 당신의 체크아웃에 절대 영향을 주지 않습니다. 거기서 서비스를 실행하고 테스트 환경이 그곳을 가리키게 하세요.

두 가지 제약을 엄격하게 유지하세요. 수정은 작아야 합니다: 3개 파일 또는 50줄 변경 같은 한도를 정하고, 그보다 큰 것은 사람에게 넘길 보고로 취급합니다. 그리고 수정은 재현을 대상으로 해야 합니다: 리팩터링, 이름 변경, 정리 작업은 금지입니다. 모든 추가 변경은 검토자가 확인해야 할 항목 하나가 되기 때문입니다.

4단계: 재현 테스트와 전체 스위트 재실행하기

두 번째 게이트는 두 부분으로 구성됩니다. 먼저 에이전트는 2단계의 동일한 테스트 케이스를 그대로 다시 실행하며, 반드시 통과해야 합니다. 만약 에이전트가 통과하기 위해 단언을 수정했다면 수정은 실패합니다. 파이프라인이 테스트 파일의 실행 전후 diff를 비교해 이를 잡아냅니다.

둘째, 기존 스위트가 그린을 유지해야 합니다. 하나의 테스트를 그린으로 만들고 세 개를 빨간으로 만드는 수정은 3단계로 되돌아갑니다. 루프에 시간 제한을 두세요. 예를 들어 3회 시도 또는 20분을 넘기면 중단하고 시도한 내용을 기록합니다. 왓치독이 빛을 발하는 순간이 바로 여기입니다. 같은 줄만 계속 수정하거나 재현이 전혀 건드리지 않은 파일로 방황하는 워커를 종료시킬 수 있습니다.

5단계: 확인된 간단한 수정만 전달하기

두 게이트가 모두 그린이면, 에이전트는 이야기가 아니라 증거와 함께 풀 리퀘스트를 엽니다: 리포트, 실패한 실행, diff, 그리고 스위트 결과가 포함된 통과한 실행입니다. 사람이 검토하고 병합합니다. Protected branches를 사용하면 에이전트의 토큰이 브랜치를 푸시할 수는 있지만 main에 병합하는 일은 결코 못하게 됩니다. 어떤 게이트라도 실패하면 보고자는 아무런 소식을 듣지 못합니다. 에이전트는 로그 한 줄을 남기고 다음으로 넘어갑니다.

자가 수정 AI 에이전트를 위한 가드레일

첫 무인 실행 전에 이 울타리들을 세워두세요:

가드레일 설정 방지되는 것
범위 수정당 최대 파일 수와 줄 수 수정으로 둔갑시킨 전면 재작성
시간 제한 버그당 최대 시도 횟수와 시간 토큰을 태우는 무한 루프
자격 증명 staging 전용, 프로덕션 키 금지 실제 주문을 생성하는 재현
병합 권한 브랜치 푸시만, 병합 금지 검토되지 않은 코드가 main에 도달
테스트 무결성 테스트 파일의 실행 전후 diff 비교 통과하기 위해 단언을 수정하는 행위
침묵 실패 시 사용자에게 메시지 없음 소음과 반쯤 확인된 주장

자격 증명이 가장 중요합니다. 재현은 API를 실제로 호출하므로 staging이나 시드된 로컬 데이터를 사용하세요.

Apidog CLI로 코딩 에이전트가 재현을 만들게 하기

2단계가 파이프라인의 핵심이며, 바로 Apidog CLI가 만들어진 목적입니다. 코딩 에이전트(Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode)가 테스트 케이스를 JSON으로 작성하고, Apidog 프로젝트에 생성한 뒤 터미널에서 실행합니다. 당신은 프롬프트 하나만 작성하면 됩니다.

한 번만 설정하세요:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog auth login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

그런 다음 에이전트에게 버그 리포트와 이 프롬프트를 넘기세요:

Here is a bug report for POST /orders in Apidog project <projectId>.
Turn it into an Apidog test case that fails today: assert status 201
and that $.id exists. Run it against staging and confirm it fails for
the reported reason. If it does, fix the handler on a new worktree
branch until the same test passes, run the endpoint's other cases, and
open a PR with both JSON reports. If it doesn't reproduce, stop and log why.

에이전트는 기억에 의존해 페이로드를 만들지 않습니다. 스키마를 읽고, 카테고리를 찾고, 파일을 검증한 후에야 케이스를 생성합니다:

apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog test-case category --project <projectId>
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file repro-orders.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file repro-orders.json

에이전트가 작성하는 파일은 다음과 같습니다 (ID는 프로젝트에서 가져옵니다):

{
  "name": "Repro: POST /orders with null coupon returns 500",
  "apiDetailId": 123456,
  "categoryId": 1,
  "method": "post",
  "path": "/orders",
  "parameters": {},
  "commonParameters": {},
  "requestBody": {
    "type": "application/json",
    "data": "{\"items\":[{\"sku\":\"A-100\",\"qty\":1}],\"coupon\":null}"
  },
  "postProcessors": [
    { "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
      "data": { "name": "status is 201", "subject": "httpCode", "comparison": "equal", "path": "", "value": "201" } },
    { "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
      "data": { "name": "order id exists", "subject": "responseJson", "comparison": "exists", "path": "$.id" } }
  ]
}

이제 버그를 증명하는 빨간 실행입니다:

apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <stagingEnvId> -r cli,json --out-file repro-before

CLI 리포터는 500에서 상태 단언이 실패하는 모습을 보여주고, repro-before.json이 apidog-reports/에 저장됩니다. 수정 후에는 에이전트가 --out-file repro-after로 동일한 명령을 실행하고 두 단언 모두 통과합니다. 이 두 파일이 풀 리퀘스트의 증거입니다. 4단계를 위해 엔드포인트의 모든 케이스를 실행해 수정이 조용히 이웃을 깨뜨리지 못하게 합니다:

apidog test-case run --project <projectId> --endpoint <endpointId> -e <stagingEnvId> -r cli,json

--upload-report를 추가하면 실행 결과를 Apidog 앱에서 볼 수 있습니다. 병합 후에는 재현 케이스가 회귀 테스트로 프로젝트에 남고, -r junit을 붙인 동일한 apidog run이 CI에 그대로 들어갑니다. 자세한 내용은 CI/CD 파이프라인에서 Apidog CLI 실행하기를 참고하세요. 추가 설정은 Apidog CLI 에이전트 워크플로와 Claude Code에서의 Apidog CLI를 확인하세요. Apidog Free는 최대 4명의 사용자까지 지원하므로 유료 플랜 없이 전체 루프를 시도해볼 수 있습니다.

FAQ

AI 에이전트가 정말 사람 없이 버그를 고칠 수 있나요?

많은 간단한 버그를 스스로 재현하고, 패치하고, 증명할 수 있지만 병합까지 해서는 안 됩니다. 병합은 사람이 담당하고, 브랜치 보호로 이를 강제하세요.

에이전트가 버그를 재현하지 못하면 어떻게 되나요?

중단하고 시도한 내용을 기록합니다. 재현할 수 없는 버그는 확인할 수 없는 수정이므로, 어떤 패치든 추측에 불과합니다. 이후 사람이 리포트에 세부 정보를 추가하거나 닫습니다.

에이전트가 테스트를 통과하도록 수정하는 것을 어떻게 막을 수 있나요?

테스트 케이스가 처음 실패했을 때 사본이나 해시를 저장하고, 수정을 수락하기 전에 비교하세요. 테스트 파일을 워커가 수정할 수 있는 경로 밖에 두세요.

이것을 만들려면 DeepSeek Harness가 필요한가요?

아니요. 에세이는 설계를 설명한 것이고, 그 프로토타입 플러그인은 공식 DeepSeek 제품이 아닙니다. 셸 명령을 실행할 수 있는 어떤 코딩 에이전트든 작동합니다. GitHub Actions의 Claude Code를 포함해서요. 거기서 시도해보고 싶다면 DeepSeek Harness란 무엇인가를 참고하세요.

title: Using Transformers for Teaching and Learning via Symbolic Distillation of Neural A-life Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.07254v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural networks controlling behavior of A-life agents can evolve over multiple generations. While effective in making the agents survive, such networks are generally opaque to a human observer. Furthermore, the neural weights cannot be transferred between agents with different neural architectures. Distilling such neural networks into compact symbolic policies can help humans understand agent behavior in A-life. Additionally, it allows the agents to share their knowledge in a compact fashion, improving population-level learning. Distilling a neural policy into a symbolic policy is typically performed by searching the space of symbolic policies to find one that approximates the neural policy. However, even with a domain-specific language the space of policies can be large, necessitating incomplete stochastic search such as genetic algorithms. Yet the distillation remains computationally expensive. We propose to instead use a transformer pre-trained on readily available random percept-action data. Doing so speeds up distillation substantially. We derive the transformer architecture via a neural architecture search. Empirical results compare different distillation methods and the influence of the symbolic space on A-life population dynamics through self-reflection and teaching and learning.

title: CSS Pixels vs Device Pixels: Why "It Looks Fine on My Monitor" Is a Bug Report
description:
Most layout bugs are not bugs. They're mismatches between the viewport we designed on and the viewport someone else is using.

Here's the thing that trips people up: a phone can report a 412 CSS-pixel-wide screen while being physically half the size of your laptop, and a 4K monitor at 200% scaling gives you exactly the same usable width as a 1080p one. Resolution and viewport are not the same number, and treating them as one is where "it works on my machine" comes from.

Three numbers that get confused

Number What it really means Where you see it
Physical resolution Actual pixel count of the panel, e.g. 3840×2160 Product specs, OS display settings
CSS viewport width What window.innerWidth reports after scaling and zoom DevTools device mode, media queries
Device pixel ratio Physical pixels per CSS pixel (1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3) window.devicePixelRatio

A 27" 1440p monitor at 100% gives you roughly 2560 CSS pixels to play with. A 15" laptop at 1920×1080 and 150% scaling gets 1280. A common Android phone gets somewhere around 360–412. Those are three wildly different layouts, and none of them tell you how big the screen physically is.

Why 1920 already equals 4K

Once you account for scaling, a 4K panel at 200% has a 1920×1080 CSS viewport — the same layout budget as a plain 1080p screen. So "we tested on 4K" is not a wider test than "we tested on 1080p". If you want the wide end of the curve you need an ultrawide (3440 or 5120 physical) or a monitor at 100% scaling.

// Print the real numbers of whatever device you're on
console.log({
  cssWidth: window.innerWidth,
  cssHeight: window.innerHeight,
  dpr: window.devicePixelRatio,
  physicalWidth: window.innerWidth * window.devicePixelRatio,
});

Run that on a phone, a laptop and your desk monitor. The spread in cssWidth is usually much smaller than people expect, and the spread in physical size is much larger.

The five profiles that catch the most layout problems

  1. 1366×768 — still common in offices, education and cheap laptops. Catches overflowing navs and fixed-height hero sections.
  2. 1920×1080 at 125–150% scaling — the "high-DPI laptop": effectively 1280–1536 CSS px.
  3. 2560×1440 at 100% — the desktop default; the width most designs are actually drawn for.
  4. 3440×1440 ultrawide — catches max-width-less layouts stretching into unreadable line lengths.
  5. 390×844 (phone) — plus one small Android around 360 px, which is stricter than the iPhone.

That's five checkpoints instead of infinite combinations, and it covers the four scaling regimes plus both extremes of width.

Turning it into a repeatable check

Manual resizing is a good start, but the useful version is deliberate and repeatable:

  • Fix the profile list in the project, not in someone's head, so every release is measured the same way.
  • Record the viewport next to every screenshot in bug reports. A screenshot without a viewport is only half a bug.
  • Compare across profiles: if a heading wraps differently on two screens, that's a layout rule, not a mystery.
  • Watch device pixel ratio when testing text and icons: at DPR 1.5 and 2, hairline borders and 1px icons start to disappear.

If you just need the raw numbers while deciding on a target, Screen Size Comparison compares screen sizes and resolutions side by side — useful for sanity-checking what CSS width a given physical panel will actually give you.

The takeaway

Resolution is a spec sheet number. The viewport is what your CSS sees. Design and test against the viewport, pick five profiles that span the real world, and write the viewport down next to every screenshot — the "works on my monitor" class of bugs mostly disappears on its own.

title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model
description:
arXiv:2611.07265v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $\theta$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.
