title: RIVER: Evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval for enzyme--reaction discovery
description:
arXiv:2611.07757v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enzyme function annotation and the identification of candidate enzymes for a given reaction are essential steps in connecting genomic information to biochemical reaction networks. However, existing methods rely on sequence or structural similarity or on training with known enzyme--reaction pairs, making it difficult to integrate biochemical evidence across large candidate spaces; they also struggle with retrieval tasks involving enzyme families whose members are highly similar. Here, we introduce RIVER (Reaction--enzyme Inference via Evidence-guided Retrieval), a multi-agent framework for bidirectional enzyme--reaction retrieval that identifies potentially catalyzed reactions for a given enzyme and ranks candidate enzymes for a given reaction. RIVER coordinates large language models, specialized biochemical computational tools, and external knowledge resources to assemble evidence at multiple levels, including reaction chemistry, protein sequences and domains, catalytic mechanisms, and database annotations. Dedicated validation modules further examine evidence gaps and potential conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records. On public benchmarks, RIVER achieves the highest success rates in both enzyme retrieval and enzyme annotation. In family-specific enzyme retrieval, RIVER outperforms the evaluated baselines on the selected datasets and metrics. In Escherichia coli enzyme retrieval tasks constructed from recent literature, RIVER achieves the best retrieval results with closed-source and open-source model configurations, substantially outperforming closed-source general-purpose and biology-specialized multi-agent systems, including Claude Code, Codex, and Phylo Max. These results suggest that evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval can prioritize biochemically supported enzyme--reaction relationships, providing a basis for subsequent experimental validation.

title: Reweighting is not Harmless: Understanding the Role of Dataset Characteristics
description:
arXiv:2611.07258v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reweighting is a widely used pre-processing method for promoting discrimination-free model behavior by assigning different weights to data points during model training. While it is often credited with improving fairness, particularly by mitigating systematic underestimation for underrepresented groups, it can also introduce unintended harms under certain data conditions. Using controlled simulations that vary group size and baseline event prevalence, we show how reweighting can yield misleading improvements in fairness by reducing underestimation for one group while introducing it for another. Across 3,000 simulated datasets with event prevalence of 7-14%, reweighting improved parity in positive classification and false negative rates (FNR) between groups, but did so partly by decreasing positive classifications and increasing FNR for the group with higher baseline prevalence. These effects were most pronounced when that group was a minority: its FNR rose by 6 percentage points, approximately 82 additional missed cases per 10,000 group members, and roughly three-quarters of the improvement in FNR parity came from this increase rather than from gains for the other group. The pattern held across six classifiers, from logistic regression to neural networks, while overall accuracy was essentially unchanged, leaving the shift invisible in aggregate performance metrics. These findings mirror patterns reported in real-world applications and underscore the critical role of data characteristics in shaping the impact of this fairness intervention. While reweighting may create desirable outcomes in some applications, practitioners should critically evaluate it relative to their problem area and goals. Specifically, when the goal is to reduce underestimation in one group without introducing underestimation in another, reweighting may not be the appropriate approach.

title: Top 10 PostgreSQL Production Outages & SRE Incident Troubleshooting Runbooks
description:
Top 10 PostgreSQL Production Outages & SRE Incident Troubleshooting Runbooks

Introduction

PostgreSQL is one of the most widely adopted open-source relational database systems, powering applications ranging from startups and SaaS platforms to large-scale enterprise infrastructure.

However, running PostgreSQL in production introduces challenges that go beyond writing SQL queries and designing database schemas.

A sudden database outage can cause application downtime, failed transactions, delayed background jobs, broken APIs, and even data loss. Sometimes, the database remains technically available but becomes so slow that applications experience timeouts and users cannot complete their operations.

For Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), Database Administrators (DBAs), and backend engineers, understanding how to identify, troubleshoot, and recover from PostgreSQL incidents is essential.

🚀 Keep Learning with DevsCampus

Technology evolves continuously, and staying updated with practical engineering knowledge is essential for every developer.

At DevsCampus, we publish technical articles, engineering tutorials, and learning resources covering PostgreSQL, Database Engineering, DevOps, Cloud Computing, System Design, Artificial Intelligence, and emerging technologies.

Whether you are a student preparing for a software engineering career or an experienced developer looking to strengthen your technical skills, DevsCampus helps you explore concepts, understand real-world engineering challenges, and keep up with the latest technology trends.

Explore these resources to continue learning:

  • PostgreSQL Engineering Articles – Explore PostgreSQL architecture, implementation, and production best practices.
  • SQL Learning Hub – Learn SQL, database design, indexing, query optimization, and production database engineering.

Visit DevsCampus.com to read more technical articles, explore practical tutorials, and stay updated with the latest developments in technology.

Now, let's explore the 10 most common PostgreSQL production outages, their root causes, and practical SRE troubleshooting runbooks that engineers can use to investigate and resolve real-world incidents.

Whether you manage PostgreSQL on Kubernetes, AWS RDS, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, or self-hosted Linux servers, these runbooks will help you respond to production incidents systematically.

1. PostgreSQL Connection Pool Exhaustion

Incident Scenario

Your application suddenly starts returning errors:

FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved
for non-replication superuser connections

Your API response times increase, background workers stop processing jobs, and new application connections fail.

Root Cause

PostgreSQL has a configured maximum number of concurrent connections.

The following configuration controls the connection limit:

SHOW max_connections;

Common causes include:

  • Application connection leaks.
  • Too many application instances.
  • Incorrect connection pool configuration.
  • Long-running transactions.
  • Background workers opening excessive connections.
  • Missing connection pooling.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check active connections

SELECT
    state,
    COUNT(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY state;

Step 2: Identify applications consuming connections

SELECT
    application_name,
    client_addr,
    state,
    COUNT(*) AS connections
FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY application_name, client_addr, state
ORDER BY connections DESC;

Step 3: Identify long-running connections

SELECT
    pid,
    usename,
    application_name,
    state,
    now() - query_start AS duration,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY duration DESC;

Step 4: Terminate confirmed problematic sessions

SELECT pg_terminate_backend(12345);

Replace 12345 with the actual process ID after verifying that terminating the session is safe.

Recovery Strategy

  • Configure connection pooling using PgBouncer.
  • Set appropriate application pool limits.
  • Implement connection timeouts.
  • Close unused connections.
  • Investigate connection leaks.
  • Monitor active connections against max_connections.

Production Prevention: Establish connection budgets across all application instances rather than allowing every service to independently consume the entire database connection limit.

Related Reading: Explore PostgreSQL engineering resources on DevsCampus to learn more about PostgreSQL architecture, connection management, and production database operations.

2. PostgreSQL High CPU Utilization

Incident Scenario

The PostgreSQL server suddenly reaches 95–100% CPU utilization.

Applications become slow, API requests time out, and database queries take significantly longer than usual.

Root Cause

High CPU utilization can result from:

  • Missing database indexes.
  • Expensive JOIN operations.
  • Inefficient SQL queries.
  • Large sequential scans.
  • Excessive concurrent queries.
  • Poor query execution plans.
  • Incorrect database statistics.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Identify expensive queries

SELECT
    pid,
    now() - query_start AS duration,
    state,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active'
ORDER BY duration DESC;

Step 2: Identify frequently executed expensive queries

If pg_stat_statements is enabled:

SELECT
    query,
    calls,
    total_exec_time,
    mean_exec_time,
    rows
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

Step 3: Analyze the execution plan

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1001;

Remember that EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query. Exercise caution with expensive queries and statements that modify data.

Step 4: Check server CPU usage

top

Or:

htop

Recovery Strategy

  • Identify and optimize expensive queries.
  • Add appropriate indexes.
  • Update database statistics using ANALYZE.
  • Reduce unnecessary query concurrency.
  • Review execution plans.
  • Consider read replicas for read-heavy workloads.

Production Prevention: Monitor query execution time, CPU utilization, and database workload continuously.

Related Reading: Learn how production database schemas influence query performance and scalability in Production Database Design on DevsCampus.

3. PostgreSQL Disk Space Exhaustion

Incident Scenario

Your application starts reporting database write failures:

ERROR: could not extend file
No space left on device

Insert and update operations begin failing. PostgreSQL may also experience problems writing WAL files or temporary query files.

Root Cause

Common causes include:

  • Rapid database growth.
  • Unbounded application logs.
  • Large temporary files.
  • WAL accumulation.
  • Failed replication slots retaining WAL.
  • Missing WAL archiving cleanup.
  • Large database indexes.
  • Long-running transactions preventing cleanup.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check available disk space

df -h

Step 2: Identify large directories

sudo du -sh /var/lib/postgresql/*

Adjust the PostgreSQL data directory according to your installation.

Step 3: Check database sizes

SELECT
    datname,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(datname)) AS size
FROM pg_database
ORDER BY pg_database_size(datname) DESC;

Step 4: Check WAL directory size

sudo du -sh /var/lib/postgresql/*/pg_wal

Step 5: Check replication slots

SELECT
    slot_name,
    active,
    restart_lsn,
    pg_wal_lsn_diff(
        pg_current_wal_lsn(),
        restart_lsn
    ) AS retained_wal_bytes
FROM pg_replication_slots;

Recovery Strategy

  • Expand the underlying storage volume.
  • Investigate inactive replication slots.
  • Correct WAL archiving failures.
  • Review temporary file generation.
  • Remove only confirmed obsolete files through supported PostgreSQL maintenance procedures.
  • Implement database growth alerts.

Critical Warning: Never manually delete files from PostgreSQL's pg_wal directory. Doing so can cause database corruption or prevent PostgreSQL from starting.

Production Prevention: Configure disk usage alerts at 70%, 80%, and 90% capacity.

4. PostgreSQL Replication Lag

Incident Scenario

Your production application uses PostgreSQL primary-replica architecture.

The primary database processes writes successfully, but read replicas return outdated data.

Users update their profiles but continue seeing old information.

Root Cause

Replication lag can occur because of:

  • Network latency.
  • High write throughput.
  • Slow replica storage.
  • Long-running queries on replicas.
  • Replication conflicts.
  • Insufficient replica resources.
  • WAL receiver or replay delays.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check replication status on the primary

SELECT
    application_name,
    client_addr,
    state,
    sync_state,
    write_lag,
    flush_lag,
    replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

Step 2: Check replication status on the replica

SELECT
    pg_is_in_recovery(),
    pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(),
    pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();

Step 3: Calculate replay delay

SELECT
    now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()
    AS replication_delay;

This timestamp-based calculation is most meaningful when the primary is actively committing transactions.

Recovery Strategy

  • Investigate network connectivity.
  • Increase replica compute and storage capacity where necessary.
  • Optimize queries running on replicas.
  • Investigate WAL receiver and replay activity.
  • Review replication configuration.
  • Temporarily route consistency-sensitive reads to the primary.

Production Prevention: Monitor replication lag and establish thresholds that trigger alerts before application consistency is affected.

5. PostgreSQL Deadlocks

Incident Scenario

Your application starts reporting transaction failures:

ERROR: deadlock detected
DETAIL: Process 1234 waits for ShareLock on transaction 5678

Multiple transactions are waiting for resources held by each other.

Root Cause

A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions wait indefinitely for locks held by one another.

Example:

Transaction A:

BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 100
WHERE id = 1;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 100
WHERE id = 2;

COMMIT;

Transaction B:

BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 50
WHERE id = 2;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 50
WHERE id = 1;

COMMIT;

Both transactions acquire locks in different orders, potentially creating a deadlock.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Inspect database locks

SELECT
    locktype,
    relation::regclass,
    mode,
    granted,
    pid
FROM pg_locks
ORDER BY pid;

Step 2: Identify blocked queries

SELECT
    pid,
    pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocking_pids,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

Step 3: Inspect PostgreSQL logs

Look for:

ERROR: deadlock detected

Recovery Strategy

  • Acquire database locks in a consistent order.
  • Keep transactions short.
  • Avoid unnecessary operations inside transactions.
  • Implement application-level transaction retries.
  • Review transaction isolation requirements.

Production Prevention: Enable appropriate deadlock logging and monitor deadlock frequency.

6. PostgreSQL Slow Queries and Query Timeouts

Incident Scenario

Your application starts experiencing intermittent API failures:

ERROR: canceling statement due to statement timeout

Some database queries take several seconds or even minutes to complete.

Root Cause

Common reasons include:

  • Missing indexes.
  • Inefficient joins.
  • Large table scans.
  • Outdated database statistics.
  • Lock contention.
  • Excessive sorting.
  • Poor pagination strategies.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Find long-running queries

SELECT
    pid,
    now() - query_start AS execution_time,
    wait_event_type,
    wait_event,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active'
ORDER BY execution_time DESC;

Step 2: Analyze query execution

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'PENDING';

Step 3: Check table statistics

SELECT
    relname,
    n_live_tup,
    n_dead_tup,
    last_analyze,
    last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables;

Step 4: Review timeout configuration

SHOW statement_timeout;
SHOW lock_timeout;
SHOW idle_in_transaction_session_timeout;

Recovery Strategy

  • Optimize problematic SQL.
  • Add appropriate indexes.
  • Review JOIN conditions.
  • Update statistics.
  • Investigate lock waits.
  • Apply sensible timeout limits.

Production Prevention: Use pg_stat_statements to identify queries with high total execution time and monitor query latency percentiles.

Related Reading: Learn more about production schema design, indexing considerations, and query scalability in Production Database Design – DevsCampus.

7. PostgreSQL Database Crash or Unexpected Restart

Incident Scenario

Your production application suddenly loses database connectivity.

Monitoring reports:

Connection refused

The PostgreSQL service is no longer accepting connections.

Root Cause

Possible causes include:

  • Operating system out-of-memory termination.
  • Hardware failures.
  • Storage problems.
  • PostgreSQL process crashes.
  • Invalid configuration changes.
  • Container or Kubernetes restarts.
  • Host-level resource exhaustion.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check PostgreSQL service status

sudo systemctl status postgresql

Step 2: Inspect recent PostgreSQL logs

sudo journalctl -u postgresql \
    --since "30 minutes ago"

Depending on the distribution, PostgreSQL logs may also be available under:

/var/log/postgresql/

Step 3: Check memory utilization

free -h

Step 4: Check kernel OOM events

dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'oom|killed process'

Step 5: Check storage health

df -h

Recovery Strategy

  • Identify the actual crash reason before restarting repeatedly.
  • Verify storage availability.
  • Check memory and CPU pressure.
  • Review PostgreSQL recovery logs.
  • Restore service after confirming the underlying issue is resolved.
  • Validate application connectivity and transaction processing.

Production Prevention: Implement database health checks, infrastructure monitoring, automated backups, and tested recovery procedures.

8. PostgreSQL VACUUM Problems and Table Bloat

Incident Scenario

Your database size keeps increasing even though application data is not growing significantly.

Queries become slower, indexes grow larger, and disk utilization increases.

Root Cause

PostgreSQL uses MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) to manage concurrent transactions.

Updates and deletes create obsolete row versions that must eventually be cleaned up by VACUUM.

Table bloat can increase when:

  • Autovacuum is disabled or incorrectly configured.
  • Long-running transactions prevent cleanup.
  • High update/delete workloads generate dead tuples.
  • Autovacuum cannot keep up with table modifications.
  • Replication slots or standby feedback retain old row versions.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Identify tables with dead tuples

SELECT
    relname,
    n_live_tup,
    n_dead_tup,
    last_vacuum,
    last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC
LIMIT 10;

Step 2: Inspect autovacuum configuration

SHOW autovacuum;
SHOW autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor;
SHOW autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor;

Step 3: Identify long-running transactions

SELECT
    pid,
    usename,
    state,
    now() - xact_start AS transaction_duration,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY transaction_duration DESC;

Recovery Strategy

  • Investigate long-running transactions.
  • Ensure autovacuum is enabled.
  • Tune autovacuum for large and frequently updated tables.
  • Run targeted VACUUM operations where appropriate. 
VACUUM (ANALYZE) orders;

For severe table bloat, evaluate specialized maintenance approaches such as pg_repack, accounting for locking, disk-space, and operational requirements.

Production Prevention: Monitor dead tuples, autovacuum activity, transaction age, and table growth.

Related Reading: PostgreSQL maintenance is essential for preventing table bloat and keeping query performance stable. Explore Database Maintenance on DevsCampus to understand VACUUM, ANALYZE, index maintenance, and database statistics in greater detail.

9. PostgreSQL WAL Growth and Checkpoint Problems

Incident Scenario

Your database experiences increased disk utilization and write latency.

PostgreSQL logs contain messages related to checkpoints:

checkpoint starting: time
checkpoint complete

The WAL directory continues growing, and storage consumption becomes a concern.

Root Cause

Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) is essential for PostgreSQL durability and crash recovery.

WAL growth can result from:

  • High transaction volume.
  • Inactive replication slots.
  • WAL archiving failures.
  • Replication lag.
  • Long-running backups.
  • Incorrect WAL retention configuration.

Frequent checkpoints can also increase I/O pressure.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check WAL configuration

SHOW wal_level;
SHOW max_wal_size;
SHOW min_wal_size;
SHOW checkpoint_timeout;
SHOW checkpoint_completion_target;

Step 2: Check replication slot retention

SELECT
    slot_name,
    active,
    restart_lsn,
    wal_status
FROM pg_replication_slots;

Step 3: Check archiver statistics

SELECT
    archived_count,
    failed_count,
    last_archived_wal,
    last_failed_wal,
    last_failed_time
FROM pg_stat_archiver;

Step 4: Review PostgreSQL logs

Search for:

checkpoints are occurring too frequently

Recovery Strategy

  • Fix WAL archiving failures.
  • Investigate inactive replication slots.
  • Tune checkpoint settings based on workload.
  • Ensure storage capacity is sufficient.
  • Review replication and backup configurations.

Production Prevention: Monitor WAL generation rate, retained WAL, checkpoint frequency, and archiving failures.

Important: Never delete WAL files manually to free disk space.

10. PostgreSQL Backup and Recovery Failure

Incident Scenario

A production database becomes corrupted or unavailable.

The SRE team attempts to restore the latest backup but discovers that the backup is incomplete, outdated, or unusable.

This is one of the most serious production incidents because it directly affects business continuity and data recovery.

Root Cause

Common reasons include:

  • Backup jobs silently failing.
  • Incorrect backup retention policies.
  • Missing WAL archives.
  • Unverified backup integrity.
  • Incomplete restore procedures.
  • Missing encryption keys.
  • Backups stored in the same failure domain as the database.

SRE Troubleshooting Runbook

Step 1: Check backup availability

For pg_dump backups:

ls -lh /backup/postgres/

Step 2: Create a logical backup

pg_dump -Fc -U postgres \
    -d production_db \
    -f production_db.dump

Step 3: Validate the dump archive

pg_restore -l production_db.dump

This checks whether the archive can be listed, but it does not prove that a complete restore will succeed.

Step 4: Restore into a separate database

createdb -U postgres recovery_test

pg_restore -U postgres \
    -d recovery_test \
    production_db.dump

Step 5: Validate restored data

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM important_table;

Compare the results against expected records and application-level consistency checks.

Recovery Strategy

  • Maintain automated database backups.
  • Use continuous WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery (PITR).
  • Store backups in a separate failure domain.
  • Define Recovery Point Objective (RPO) and Recovery Time Objective (RTO).
  • Perform regular restore drills.
  • Document disaster recovery procedures.

Production Prevention: A backup should never be considered reliable until a successful restore has been tested.

PostgreSQL SRE Incident Response: A Practical Framework

Knowing individual PostgreSQL failures is important, but production reliability requires a consistent incident response process.

SRE teams should follow a structured approach whenever a database outage occurs.

Step 1: Detect

Use monitoring and alerting tools to identify incidents before customers report them.

Monitor:

  • Database availability.
  • Active connections.
  • CPU utilization.
  • Memory utilization.
  • Disk utilization.
  • Query latency.
  • Replication lag.
  • WAL growth.
  • Deadlocks.
  • Database errors.

Step 2: Triage

Determine the impact and severity.

Ask:

  • Is the database completely unavailable?
  • Are writes failing or only reads?
  • Are all applications affected?
  • Is the problem isolated to one database or replica?
  • Is data integrity at risk?

Avoid making configuration changes before understanding the incident.

Step 3: Mitigate

Prioritize restoring critical application functionality.

Examples:

  • Terminate confirmed problematic sessions.
  • Route consistency-sensitive reads to the primary.
  • Scale infrastructure resources.
  • Reduce non-critical database workloads.
  • Restore available service capacity.

Always evaluate the impact of each mitigation action.

Step 4: Recover

After resolving the immediate issue:

  • Verify database health.
  • Validate application connectivity.
  • Test read and write operations.
  • Confirm replication health.
  • Check for data consistency issues.
  • Monitor the system for recurring failures.

Step 5: Conduct a Blameless Postmortem

Every major production incident should produce a postmortem.

A useful postmortem includes:

Section Description
Incident Summary What happened?
Timeline When did the incident begin and end?
Impact Which services and customers were affected?
Root Cause What technical condition caused the failure?
Detection How was the incident identified?
Resolution What actions restored service?
Prevention What engineering improvements are required?
Action Items Who owns each improvement and its deadline?

The goal is not to blame an engineer. The goal is to improve the system so the same failure is less likely to happen again.

Essential PostgreSQL Production Monitoring Metrics

A production-ready PostgreSQL environment should continuously monitor the following metrics.

Metric Why It Matters
Active Connections Detect connection exhaustion
CPU Utilization Identify expensive database workloads
Memory Utilization Detect memory pressure
Disk Utilization Prevent storage exhaustion
Query Execution Time Identify slow SQL
Replication Lag Detect replica synchronization problems
Deadlocks Identify transaction conflicts
Dead Tuples Detect vacuum-related issues
WAL Generation Monitor write workload and WAL growth
Checkpoint Frequency Identify excessive checkpoint activity
Transaction Age Detect long-running transactions
Backup Status Ensure recoverability

Recommended PostgreSQL Monitoring Tools

1. Prometheus and Grafana

Use Prometheus with PostgreSQL Exporter to collect database metrics and Grafana to build operational dashboards.

2. pg_stat_statements

A PostgreSQL extension that provides statistics about SQL query execution.

3. PgBouncer

A lightweight connection pooler that helps manage database connection overhead.

4. pgBadger

A PostgreSQL log analyzer that helps identify slow queries and database workload patterns.

5. Patroni

A high-availability solution for managing PostgreSQL clusters with automated failover capabilities.

Learn More: Production Database Monitoring

Monitoring is one of the most important responsibilities of an SRE team. Identifying performance degradation before it becomes a production outage requires more than checking whether a database is online.

Explore Production Database Monitoring on DevsCampus to understand:

  • Database latency and p99 query performance.
  • Active and available database connections.
  • Replication lag monitoring.
  • Cache and buffer hit ratios.
  • Lock waits and deadlock detection.
  • Table and index bloat monitoring.
  • Production database alerting strategies.

This learning resource complements the troubleshooting runbooks covered in this article.

PostgreSQL Production Readiness Checklist

Before deploying PostgreSQL into production, validate the following:

Availability

  • [ ] Configure appropriate connection pooling.
  • [ ] Implement database health checks.
  • [ ] Configure replication where required.
  • [ ] Define failover procedures.

Performance

  • [ ] Enable pg_stat_statements.
  • [ ] Monitor slow queries.
  • [ ] Review index usage.
  • [ ] Configure autovacuum appropriately.

Storage

  • [ ] Configure disk utilization alerts.
  • [ ] Monitor WAL growth.
  • [ ] Monitor replication slots.
  • [ ] Review backup retention policies.

Security

  • [ ] Use strong authentication.
  • [ ] Apply least-privilege database permissions.
  • [ ] Enable encrypted connections.
  • [ ] Store database credentials securely.
  • [ ] Audit privileged database access.

Disaster Recovery

  • [ ] Automate backups.
  • [ ] Configure point-in-time recovery where required.
  • [ ] Define RPO and RTO.
  • [ ] Perform regular restore tests.
  • [ ] Document disaster recovery runbooks.

Conclusion

PostgreSQL production outages are not always caused by database crashes. Many incidents originate from connection exhaustion, inefficient queries, storage pressure, replication lag, transaction conflicts, or inadequate backup strategies.

For SREs and database engineers, the ability to identify symptoms, investigate root causes, and execute safe recovery procedures is critical.

The ten incident scenarios covered in this guide provide a practical starting point for building reliable PostgreSQL operations.

However, production reliability is not achieved by troubleshooting incidents alone. It requires continuous monitoring, capacity planning, automation, tested disaster recovery procedures, and a culture of learning from failures.

Remember: A production-ready database is not simply one that runs without errors. It is one that can detect failures, recover safely, and maintain data integrity when things go wrong.

title: CardioLM: A multilingual suite of small language models for the cardiology domain
description:
arXiv:2611.07940v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Background: Cardiovascular care generates large volumes of clinical free-text documentation in local languages. However, clinical natural language processing (NLP) resources remain concentrated in English, and no existing benchmark is cardiology-specific, multilingual, and broad in entity coverage.
  Methods: We present two contributions. The first is CardioCCC, a corpus of 508 cardiology case reports originally published in Spanish and extended to Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, and Swedish through machine translation, annotation projection, and clinician review, with annotations covering diseases, symptoms, procedures, and medications. The second is CardioLM, comprising CardioBERTa, a set of language-specific encoders obtained by continued pretraining on cardiology and biomedical corpora, and CardioNER, a set of named entity recognition (NER) models fine-tuned on CardioCCC.
  Results: Cardiology-specific pretraining reduced pseudo-perplexity by up to a factor of eight, yet changed strict span-level F1 by at most 0.04, with benefits concentrated in languages whose backbones lacked biomedical coverage. The jointly trained multilingual XLM-RoBERTa-large models achieved the best strict F1 in nearly every language and entity type, exceeding the strongest monolingual system by up to 0.13 F1. A large share of residual errors concerned boundary detection: relaxed matching recovered 0.10-0.23 F1 for disease, procedure, and symptom, but only 0.01-0.07 for medication. Clinicians rated CardioNER well above a rule- and dictionary-based baseline, with the mean rating across entity types rising from 26% to 73%.
  Conclusions: Specialty-specific pretraining is not the decisive factor for downstream entity recognition, whereas multilingual joint training yields the strongest results in nearly all settings and a simpler deployment path for multi-country clinical information extraction.

title: Subspace Learning with Outlier Exposure for Out-of-Distribution Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.07580v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Out-of-Distribution (OoD) detection is pivotal for reliable deployments of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), aiming to distinguish anomalous samples from the In-Distribution (InD) data in training. By introducing outliers as surrogate OoD data to finetune DNNs, Outlier Exposure (OE) has greatly advanced OoD detection in recent years. Existing OE-based research remains predominantly logit-centric, either by generating diverse outliers or by regularizing them with objectives operating at the prediction-output level. Nonetheless, these approaches leave much of the rich information in feature spaces untapped. In this work, we propose an OE-based detection framework, named RecOE, that learns appropriate feature subspaces from InD data and auxiliary outliers, such that the InD-OoD discrepancy can be effectively characterized through the learned feature subspaces. Specifically, the feature subspaces are optimized to capture the dominant variations of InD and outliers by minimizing reconstruction errors therein. Besides, a sample-level objective discourages reconstruction in the opposing subspace, while an orthogonality regularizer reduces subspace overlap, further promoting discriminative subspaces. At inference, the difference in reconstruction errors between the learned subspaces serves as the OoD detection score. Extensive experiments show the superiority of RecOE on multiple benchmarks, in which significant performance gains are achieved over recent strong baselines with only slight extra overhead from two small-size matrices of subspace bases. The source code is available at https://github.com/shenhongxu123/RecOE.

title: Data-Driven Modeling of Molten Chloride Corrosion Using Static Test Data
description:
arXiv:2611.07125v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Molten chloride corrosion has been studied for decades, yet reliable prediction across different alloys, salts, and test conditions remains difficult. In this work, 291 static molten chloride corrosion experiments reported in the literature were compiled into a structured dataset and used to develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for corrosion-rate predictions. To better represent the differences in salt condition across studies, a Chloride Salt Preparation Index (CSPI) was introduced to bring the reported salt-treatment method, atmosphere control, and pre-exposure impurity condition on a common numerical scale. A blended tree-based ensemble provided the most consistent predictive performance, achieving a cross-validated \(R^2\) of 0.85 and an MAE of 0.41 mg cm\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). The graded CSPI retained more useful information than a simple purified/unpurified classification and emerged as the dominant model descriptor. Global sensitivity and SHAP analyses further identified exposure time, temperature, and alloy chemistry as important contributors to the model predictions, with several observed trends consistent with the established molten-chloride corrosion behavior. The conformal prediction intervals were well calibrated, providing an estimate of prediction uncertainty in addition to the point prediction. Overall, the framework demonstrates that historical corrosion data can support quantitative, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware prediction when experimental context is represented explicitly, while also highlighting where more consistent reporting and targeted experiments are needed to improve future molten-salt corrosion models.

title: Generate-then-Rank: Learning Symbolic Goal Interpretation for Embodied Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.07825v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Goal interpretation is to translate a natural language instruction into a formal symbolic goal that a planner can execute. It is critical for embodied agents because any error here propagates to every downstream planning and action step. Doing it well requires both generating suitable candidates and reliably selecting among them. We present a two-stage generate-then-rank approach to Goal Interpretation in the Embodied Agent Interface (EAI). First, supervised fine-tuning adapts a Large Language Model (LLM) to EAI's output convention. Second, Candidate-Output Ranking from Errors (CORE) learns preferences over complete outputs from the model's own generated alternatives. We conducted experiments on the household scenes of the Embodied Agent Interface Benchmark. Multiple open source LLMs including DeepSeek-V3 chat, DeepSeek-Reasoner, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-72B were evaluated. The proposed method outperformed the baseline models including LLMs with simple prompting, chain-of-thought, and knowledge graph based approaches.

title: Reclassification Is All You Missed: Surfacing Variant Reinterpretation Need in Online Health Communities at Population Scale
description:
arXiv:2611.07054v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Genetic variants are routinely reclassified in ClinVar after a patient is tested, sometimes from uncertain to pathogenic, yet patient recontact is inconsistent, with no clear duty and responsibility diffused among labs, providers, and patients. Many affected people discuss their results in public online health communities that clinical recontact often does not reach. We built PRISM, an agentic large-language-model pipeline that screens these posts, checks whether the variant was later reclassified, and drafts a disclaimer-bearing outreach message, in a no-contact dry run. Across 3.9 million posts from 32 communities, agent-predicted reinterpretation-relevant discussion is rare (0.288%) but concentrated in specialist genetics communities (6.30% versus 0.10% in general medical-advice communities) and growing fivefold since 2014; PRISM surfaces 123 candidate classification differences, 5 of them from an uncertain submission to pathogenic or likely pathogenic. On a held-out set of 30 real-post drafts, a clinician judged 27 factually grounded and 15 fit to send: factual accuracy is necessary but not sufficient for clinically acceptable outreach. PRISM contributes a population-scale reinterpretation-need map with code and data to be released upon publication.

title: Satisficing as competitive Bayesian weighting: a minimal model of goal-directed choice under an unattained target
description:
arXiv:2611.07270v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Animals and humans often do not maximize; they act relative to goals (aspiration levels) that are frequently not yet met. How can a goal that is not (yet) realized organize choice? Deacon (2012) calls such absence-referenced organization \emph{ententional}, and Garc\'{i}a-Valdecasas and Deacon (2024) argue that ends are best understood as constraints rather than as particular states. We examine this idea in a minimal formal setting: Risk-sensitive Satisficing (RS), a bandit learning rule that values each action by its share of past trials multiplied by its surplus or shortfall relative to an aspiration level. We show that RS can be rewritten as a Bayesian-like estimator, Attention Competitive Bayes (ACB), in which the aspiration level is the prior mean of every action and the finite budget of trials sets how strongly evidence can override it. Two consequences follow. First, actions that are no longer sampled are partially overridden by the goal rather than by past observations: their estimates relax toward the aspiration level without any data being discarded. This ``pseudo-forgetting'' distinguishes ACB from models with an explicit forgetting rate. Second, when the aspiration is unattainable, exploration does not settle; in Bernoulli bandit simulations, adjusting the aspiration level from evidence reduced regret (expected loss). ACB offers an analyzable model in which an unattained goal and a limited attentional resource jointly constrain behavior, and it yields testable predictions about how organisms revalue options they have abandoned.

title: A component foundation still in use eight months later
description:
I shipped a component foundation from scratch: layout primitives, theme, color palette, interactive documentation. Eight months later, other teams are extending it, and other developers have written its tests.

What matters to me is that others use it without me. Here are the choices that helped.

A semantic palette, not a list of colors. A component doesn't say "use this green", it says "use the action color". Changing the theme then happens in one place.

A typed palette. If roles are typed, you can't use a role that doesn't exist: the editor refuses it before you even run the app.

// generic example
const palette = {
  text: { primary: "#1a1c1b", muted: "#5a5f5c" },
  action: { default: "#0b7a5b" },
} as const;

type TextTone = keyof typeof palette.text; // "primary" | "muted"

Contrast fixed in the palette itself. Light grey text on a white background looks nice and is unreadable. Fix the contrast once, in the palette, and it's fixed everywhere. For body text, the target is a ratio of 4.5 to 1.

Interactive documentation. A component you can't try without running the application won't get reused. The documentation shows each component in each of its states, and doubles as a visual check.

What I aim for with a foundation: a developer on another team can use it without asking me anything.

Amine Affif, full-stack developer in Paris. amineaffif.com

title: Inherited Green: Freeze Debt Accounting for Agent Patches
description:
The conclusion first: an agent patch is not verified by the suite passing. It is verified by the assertions that executed in the head branch and did not execute in the base branch. Everything else is borrowed.

Most agent pipelines report one bit: green or red. That bit hides two inflators. Skips inherited from the base branch silently shrink the evidence surface. Property tests that re-draw their randomness on every run make a pass non-reproducible by default. Fix both and the patch review gets shorter, not longer.

This post is about accounting, not about catching flakes. Attribution work — deciding whether a patch caused a flake or merely surfaced one — is a separate gate. Here the question is narrower: how much of this green did the patch actually earn?

1. The failure mode, with a small trace

The following trace is illustrative, not a benchmark.

  • Base branch: 412 tests pass, 1 test frozen as FRZ-014 because it fails roughly 1 in 40 CI runs on a wall-clock boundary.
  • Agent patch touches src/pricing/rounding.py, adds two tests, suite goes green at 414 executed.
  • The delta looks like +2. The riskiest changed line is covered by exactly the frozen test, which did not run.

Nothing here is dishonest. The patch genuinely added two tests. The problem is that "+2" was reported without subtracting what the patch was already missing, and without noticing that the freeze covered the changed file.

So the rule is not "no skips". It is: skips are fine, unaccounted skips are not, and a skip whose blast radius overlaps your diff is a blocker unless a compensating check runs in the same build.

2. Step 1 — make every skip auditable

Add a session-level collector. It records executed and skipped node IDs with no plugin dependency, so it works the same in a container, a laptop, and a hosted runner.

# conftest.py — run with: EVIDENCE_OUT=head.json pytest -q
import json
import os
import pathlib

_records = []


def pytest_runtest_logreport(report):
    # setup-phase skips and call-phase results are the only ones we count
    if report.when not in ("setup", "call"):
        return
    if report.when == "call" or report.outcome == "skipped":
        _records.append(
            {
                "nodeid": report.nodeid,
                "when": report.when,
                "outcome": report.outcome,  # passed | failed | skipped
                # xfail reports as "skipped"; keep it separable
                "xfail": getattr(report, "wasxfail", None) is not None,
            }
        )


def pytest_sessionfinish(session, exitstatus):
    path = pathlib.Path(os.environ.get("EVIDENCE_OUT", "evidence.json"))
    path.write_text(
        json.dumps({"exit": int(exitstatus), "records": _records}, indent=2),
        encoding="utf-8",
    )

Run it twice, in the same image digest, against the same dependency lockfile:

git worktree add /tmp/base "$(git merge-base origin/main HEAD)"
(cd /tmp/base && EVIDENCE_OUT=/tmp/base.json pytest -q || true)
EVIDENCE_OUT=/tmp/head.json pytest -q || true

Same image matters more than it sounds. A drifted dependency between the two runs produces a delta that measures the environment, not the patch.

3. Step 2 — compute the evidence delta

The script below answers four questions: how many tests net executed, what skips are new, what previously passed and no longer does, and whether the diff touches a frozen blast radius.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""evidence_delta.py <base.json> <head.json> <freeze_ledger.toml> <today ISO>

Adjust the git ref below to your integration branch."""
import json
import subprocess
import sys

try:
    import tomllib  # Python 3.11+
except ModuleNotFoundError:  # 3.10 and older
    import tomli as tomllib


def load(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        data = json.load(fh)
    buckets = {"passed": set(), "failed": set(), "skipped": set(), "xfail": set()}
    for r in data["records"]:
        key = "xfail" if r["xfail"] else r["outcome"]
        buckets[key].add(r["nodeid"])
    return {"exit": data["exit"], **buckets}


def frozen_surface(ledger_path, today):
    with open(ledger_path, "rb") as fh:
        ledger = tomllib.load(fh)
    return {
        path
        for entry in ledger.get("freeze", [])
        if str(entry["expires"]) >= today  # ISO dates compare lexicographically
        for path in entry["covers"]
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    base_path, head_path, ledger_path, today = sys.argv[1:5]
    base, head = load(base_path), load(head_path)

    introduced = head["skipped"] - base["skipped"]
    retired = base["skipped"] - head["skipped"]
    lost = base["passed"] - head["passed"]
    net = len(head["passed"]) - len(base["passed"])

    changed = set(
        subprocess.check_output(
            ["git", "diff", "--name-only", "origin/main...HEAD"], text=True
        ).split()
    )
    hot = changed & frozen_surface(ledger_path, today)

    print(f"net executed delta  : {net:+d}")
    print(f"new skips           : {len(introduced)}")
    print(f"retired skips       : {len(retired)}")
    print(f"previously passing  : {len(lost)} no longer passing")
    print(f"frozen surface hit  : {sorted(hot) or 'none'}")

    problems = []
    if head["exit"] != 0:
        problems.append(f"head suite exit {head['exit']}")
    if introduced:
        problems.append("patch-introduced skips need a ledger entry")
    if lost:
        problems.append("tests that passed on base no longer pass")
    if hot:
        problems.append("diff touches a frozen blast radius; compensating check required")
    for p in problems:
        print(f"BLOCK: {p}")
    sys.exit(1 if problems else 0)

A positive net number is not a pass. It is a number that still has to survive the block list.

4. Step 3 — the ledger that gives a freeze an owner and a deadline

A freeze without a blast radius cannot be matched against a diff, and a freeze without an owner never ends. Fourteen days is a policy choice, not a measurement.

# freeze_ledger.toml
[[freeze]]
id = "FRZ-014"
test = "tests/test_pricing.py::test_rounding_boundary"
covers = ["src/pricing/rounding.py"]        # blast radius, not a guess
owner = "finley"                             # a human, reviewed in the PR
opened = 2026-10-30
expires = 2026-11-13
reason = "wall-clock boundary; fails ~1/40 CI runs, see run 8812"
compensating_check = "tests/property/test_rounding.py::test_fee_monotonic"

Three rules keep the ledger from rotting:

  1. covers must be file paths, because file paths are what git diff returns. A test name alone is not matchable.
  2. Renewal requires a new reason and evidence that the compensating check advanced. No silent re-freeze chains.
  3. Ledger edits are human-reviewed. An agent that can both introduce a skip and write its ledger entry has removed the control entirely.

5. Step 4 — two lanes for property checks

Property tests are the natural compensating check for a frozen example-based test. They are also the easiest way to produce a green that nobody can reproduce, because the generator picks new inputs each run.

Use two lanes over the same properties.

# tests/property/test_rounding.py
import os
from decimal import Decimal

import pytest
from hypothesis import given, settings, strategies as st

MONEY = st.decimals(
    min_value=Decimal("0"),
    max_value=Decimal("100000"),
    places=2,
    allow_nan=False,
    allow_infinity=False,
)

PINNED = settings(derandomize=True, max_examples=300, deadline=None, database=None)
HUNT = settings(max_examples=2000, deadline=None)  # keeps the example database

LANE = os.environ.get("PROPERTY_LANE", "pinned")
CFG = PINNED if LANE == "pinned" else HUNT


@CFG
@given(amount=MONEY)
def test_fee_is_bounded(amount):
    total = apply_fee(amount)  # code under test
    assert total >= amount
    assert total - amount <= MAX_FEE

Why both lanes:

  • Pinned lane (derandomize=True, empty example database) reproduces byte-for-byte on every run. It belongs in the patch gate, because a reviewer must be able to re-run it and see the same inputs.
  • Hunting lane (unpinned, database enabled) explores. It belongs on a schedule, not on every patch, or it becomes the flake source you were trying to eliminate.

When the hunting lane finds a counterexample, promote it: add a literal @example(Decimal("1234.56")) to the test. The pinned lane then replays it forever. A patch touching fee logic is expected to either add a promoted example or state why the invariant space did not grow. That is corpus growth as a reviewable artifact, not a coverage percentage.

6. Fixtures: hash them, do not read them

Fixture changes are an evidence-surface change, not a code change. Diff them explicitly instead of relying on a reviewer to notice:

git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD -- tests/fixtures tests/factories tests/conftest.py

Any output triggers two requirements: human sign-off and a ledger entry with scope = "fixture". You do not need to judge whether the new fixture is weaker. You need it to be visible.

7. Decision table

Numbers below are illustrative; thresholds are policy, not measurements.

Base passed Head passed New skips Frozen surface hit Verdict
412 412 0 none merge-eligible
412 409 0 none reject — evidence shrink, needs explanation
412 414 3 none merge-eligible if each skip is ledgered and unexpired
412 414 3 none reject — unledgered suppression
412 415 1 src/pricing/rounding.py merge-eligible only with the compensating property test executing in head
412 415 1 src/pricing/rounding.py reject if the freeze expired yesterday

8. Where a hosted agent loop fits

This harness is deliberately boring to run: two pytest invocations in one image plus one script. The expensive part is the patch loop itself, not the accounting.

MonkeyCode's free model access keeps that loop cheap enough to generate candidate patches in volume, and its free server option is one way to run the agent session and both evidence runs in the same hosted environment rather than splitting base and head across a laptop and a CI runner. Both availability claims are operator-supplied: no quotas, model names, hardware, or duration are asserted here, and the harness below is equally valid with a local model or no agent at all.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

9. Limitations, and who should skip this

  • Aggregate counts are gameable. A patch can add ten cheap tests and delete one expensive test and score +9. Track the per-file delta, not just the total.
  • Pinning removes exploration. The pinned lane alone will never find a new counterexample. If the hunting lane does not actually run on a schedule, the two-lane design is decoration.
  • xfail is not skip. The collector separates them for a reason; merging them makes an expected failure look like suppression.
  • Deletions are ambiguous. lost fires for obsolete tests too. That is intentional friction, not a bug — it forces a sentence of explanation in the PR.
  • This is a pre-filter, not a proof. It does not replace mutation testing or deliberate fault injection. It is the cheap step that tells you whether the expensive step is worth running.

Do not adopt this if your suite is under roughly twenty tests, if you have no flake history to freeze against, or if your CI has no budget for a second lane. In those cases the ledger is ceremony and the delta is noise. For a small patch queue, a plain diff review is honest and faster.

Run the delta over your last twenty agent patches before adding any new tooling. The number that matters is not how many went green — it is how many the block list rejected, and whether you agreed with it.

Code in this article is a sketch: the collector and delta script are written against standard pytest hooks and git diff, but you should expect to adjust the git ref, the ledger path, and the settings profiles to your repository before relying on any exit code.

title: Token-2022 v12: What Changed for Rust Developers
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

On 28 October the Token-2022 repository released v12. It rewrites the program on Pinocchio, roughly halving the compute cost of a transfer, and publishes seven crates with breaking version bumps. The program every Solana wallet and exchange calls did not change: all three clusters still run v11.1.0, byte for byte.

So for now, “v12” means Rust crates. We diffed the v11.1.0 and v12.0.0 tags, read the deployed program on mainnet, devnet and testnet, and resolved both versions with Cargo. What follows is what breaks for Rust code, what does not, and how to tell when the new program actually ships.

Published is not deployed

The deployed Token-2022 binary carries a security.txt that names the release it was built from. Read it from the program-data account and hash the same bytes, and you know exactly what a cluster runs:

Mainnet — program@v11.1.0, since 23 Oct

Devnet, testnet — program@v11.1.0, since 23 Sep

SHA-256, all three — 5e888b29⁠…⁠6413d9

v11.1.0 verified build — 5e888b29⁠…⁠6413d9

v12.0.0 binary on any cluster — none

Mainnet took v11.1.0 on 23 October at 15:39 UTC, a month after devnet and testnet. The v11.1.0 release notes carry a deployment section, a verifiable-build hash and an audit link. The v12.0.0 notes list changes only. Until a v12 build is verified and deployed, every Token-2022 instruction on chain runs the v11.1.0 code, whatever crate version your project depends on. To check for yourself:

import base64, hashlib, json, struct, urllib.request

RPC = "https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com"
PROGRAMDATA = "DoU57AYuPFu2QU514RktNPG22QhApEjnKxnBcu4BHDTY"  # Token-2022's program-data account

def rpc(method, params):
    req = urllib.request.Request(RPC, json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": method,
                                 "params": params}).encode(), {"content-type": "application/json"})
    return json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req))["result"]

data = base64.b64decode(rpc("getAccountInfo", [PROGRAMDATA, {"encoding": "base64"}])["value"]["data"][0])
slot = struct.unpack_from("<Q", data, 4)[0]          # last deploy slot
elf = data[45:].rstrip(b"\x00")                     # 45-byte header, zero padding stripped
tag = elf.find(b"source_release\x00") + 15
print("deployed at slot", slot)                      # 460497271
print("source_release ", elf[tag:elf.index(b"\x00", tag)].decode())   # program@v11.1.0
print("sha256         ", hashlib.sha256(elf).hexdigest())             # 5e888b29…6413d9

The Pinocchio rewrite, and the savings still waiting

Pull request #1469 replaces the SDK entrypoint with Pinocchio’s and switches the processor from AccountInfo to Pinocchio’s AccountView, the zero-copy view of the input buffer. It is the same move that made p-token cheap for the original token program. The pull request reports these instruction counts from its own tests:

transfer — 1,444 → 719 CU

transfer_checked — 1,782 → 856 CU

initialize_account — 1,822 → 614 CU

initialize_mint — 1,347 → 553 CU

mint_to — 1,262 → 545 CU

burn — 1,372 → 638 CU

close_account — 1,219 → 535 CU

These are the pull request’s measurements from its instruction-count tests, not ours, and extensions add their own cost on top. They become real only when a v12 binary is deployed. Until then, a transfer of any Token-2022 asset on mainnet costs what v11.1.0 charges.

What breaks in Rust

Most Rust code depends on spl-token-2022-interface, the crate with instruction builders and account layouts. Its builders and state types did not change. The breaks are in four places.

1. The processor signature

In the spl-token-2022 program crate, Processor::process changed from &[AccountInfo] to &mut [AccountView]. Test suites that run Token-2022 as a native processor, with processor!(spl_token_2022::processor::Processor::process), stop compiling on 12.0.0. Load the program’s binary into the test instead, or keep the test on 11.

2. The zk-ops feature is gone

#1524 removed zk-ops, a default feature its own manifest said to remove “once the underlying syscalls are released on all networks”. It gated the confidential-transfer and confidential mint-and-burn processors, which are now always compiled in. A manifest that still names the feature does not build. We asked Cargo to resolve both versions with it:

# spl-token-2022 = { version = "=11.1.0", default-features = false, features = ["no-entrypoint", "zk-ops"] }
#   resolves

# spl-token-2022 = { version = "=12.0.0", default-features = false, features = ["no-entrypoint", "zk-ops"] }
error: failed to select a version for `spl-token-2022`.
package `featcheck` depends on `spl-token-2022` with feature `zk-ops` but `spl-token-2022` does not have that feature.
help: available features: no-entrypoint, test-sbf

3. Two interface helpers take AccountView

In spl-token-2022-interface 4.0, alloc_and_serialize and alloc_and_serialize_variable_len_extension now take &mut AccountView. They grow an account and write an extension into its TLV data; Token-2022 itself uses them for its token-metadata and token-group extensions, and a program that stores TLV data the same way can call them too. Callers holding an AccountInfo need to move to Pinocchio’s types or stay on interface 3.

4. The zero-knowledge types moved a major version

The interface re-exports its proof types from solana-zk-elgamal-proof-interface, now 1.0.0 instead of 0.1. Its confidential builders take those types, for example ProofLocation<CiphertextCommitmentEqualityProofData>. Proof data built against the old crate will not type-check. The confidential stack moves together: interface 4.0, proof-generation and proof-extraction 0.7, and solana-zk-sdk 8.

Instruction builders — unchanged

Mint and account layouts — unchanged

onchain CPI helpers — still AccountInfo

Processor::process — AccountView

zk-ops feature — removed

Confidential transfers: new call, same keys

Changing how confidential keys are derived would be the dangerous kind of break: a wallet that derives different keys can no longer decrypt balances it already holds. zk-sdk 8 changed the derivation API, but not the keys. In 7.0.1, derive_confidential_keys(signer, seed) signs "solana-conf-bal/v1" ‖ seed. In 8.0.1, STANDARD_DERIVATION_MESSAGE is defined as that same "solana-conf-bal/v1", so the seedless call signs the same bytes the old empty-seed call did.

// zk-sdk 7 (Token-2022 v11 stack)
let (elgamal, ae) = derive_confidential_keys(&signer, b"")?;

// zk-sdk 8 (v12 stack): the seed parameter is gone; seeded keys use
// derive_confidential_keys_with_seed(&signer, seed)
let (elgamal, ae) = derive_confidential_keys(&signer)?;

// zk-sdk 8 takes a solana-signer v4 Signer. Signers from the Agave 4.3 stack
// are v3, so sign the standard message yourself (same keys):
let signature = signer.try_sign_message(STANDARD_DERIVATION_MESSAGE)?;
let (elgamal, ae) = derive_confidential_keys_from_signature(&signature)?;

The last pattern is the one Token-2022’s own CLI and client tests now use, per #1584. zk-sdk 8.0.1 depends on solana-signer 4.0.0, while 7.0.1 used 3.0.0, and a v3 keypair does not satisfy the v4 trait.

Two smaller fixes ride along. The interface documentation listed the multisig accounts for confidential mint and burn wrongly, naming the mint twice and dropping the token account. The builders and the IDL that generates the JavaScript client were already right, so only hand-written integrations that followed the comments are affected (#1509). And spl-token-client 0.21.0 no longer builds proof-record transactions that exceed the packet limit when a memo, nonce or compute-budget instruction is added (#1550).

An upgrade order that works

Every crate in the release took a breaking version bump, so nothing moves until you change a version requirement: Cargo will not pick 12.0.0 to satisfy "11". When you do move:

Builders and account reads only — interface 3 → 4

Token-2022 as a native test processor — load the binary

A manifest that names zk-ops — delete the feature

TLV account helpers — move to AccountView

Confidential transfers — upgrade the stack together

None of this changes what happens on chain. The mint and account layouts did not change, and the instruction builders encode every instruction exactly as interface 3 did.

What this does not show

We did not build or run v12, so the compute figures are the pull request’s. Our Cargo check covered dependency resolution, not a compile of downstream code. Where we say a signature or type changed, we read it from the tagged source. The deployment facts come from each cluster’s program-data account, and a later upgrade would show up there first.

Token-2022 v12: Questions People Actually Ask

Is Token-2022 v12 live on Solana mainnet?

No. Mainnet, devnet and testnet all run the same v11.1.0 binary: its embedded security.txt says source_release program@v11.1.0 and its hash matches the v11.1.0 verified build, 5e888b29…. Mainnet was upgraded to it on 23 October 2026. v12.0.0 was published as Rust crates on 28 October, and its release notes have no deployment or verification section.

Will upgrading the spl-token-2022 crate to 12.0.0 break my build?

Only if you use the program crate itself. Processor::process now takes &mut [AccountView] instead of &[AccountInfo], so registering Token-2022 as a native processor in tests no longer compiles, and the zk-ops feature no longer exists, so a Cargo.toml that names it fails to resolve. Instruction builders, state parsing and the onchain CPI helpers are unchanged.

Does solana-zk-sdk 8 change my confidential transfer keys?

No. zk-sdk 8’s derive_confidential_keys(signer) signs STANDARD_DERIVATION_MESSAGE, which is the constant "solana-conf-bal/v1", and zk-sdk 7’s derive_confidential_keys(signer, b"") signed the same bytes. The keys are identical; only the function signature changed, and seeded derivation moved to derive_confidential_keys_with_seed.

How much cheaper is Token-2022 v12?

According to the instruction-count tests in the pull request that moved the program to Pinocchio, transfer falls from 1,444 to 719 compute units and transfer_checked from 1,782 to 856, roughly half. None of that applies on chain until a v12 binary is deployed.

How do I check which Token-2022 version a cluster runs?

Read the program-data account DoU57AYuPFu2QU514RktNPG22QhApEjnKxnBcu4BHDTY, skip its 45-byte header and trailing zero bytes, and read the source_release field of the embedded security.txt. Hashing the same bytes with SHA-256 gives the value solana-verify reports for a verified build.

The one-line version

v12 is a Pinocchio rewrite that halves transfer costs, but for now it exists only as crates: it breaks native test processors, the zk-ops feature and two TLV helpers, keeps confidential keys identical, and changes nothing on chain until a verified v12 binary replaces the v11.1.0 that every cluster runs.

For the extensions themselves, see pausable and permissioned burn and how confidential transfers compare.

Sources: the v12.0.0 and v11.1.0 releases and the tagged source (1bc00fa5, 8867f751); pull requests #1469, #1524, #1584, #1509 and #1550; the solana-zk-sdk 7.0.1 and 8.0.1 crate sources; and the Token-2022 program-data account on mainnet, devnet and testnet.

title: Why Functional Testing Isn't Enough for Web Application Security
description:
A web application can pass every functional test and still contain serious security vulnerabilities.

The login page works. The contact form submits successfully. The API returns the expected response. The deployment pipeline is green.

Everything looks fine.

But what happens when someone changes a request parameter, accesses another user's resource, or submits input the application wasn't designed to handle?

These scenarios highlight an important distinction between functional testing and security testing.

Functional testing verifies whether an application behaves as expected. Web application vulnerability assessment examines how the application behaves when its security assumptions are challenged.

Let's explore why both are necessary and how development teams can approach vulnerability assessment more effectively.

1. Functional correctness does not guarantee security

Consider a simple API endpoint:

GET /api/orders/1042
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

A functional test might verify that an authenticated user can retrieve order 1042.

If the API returns the expected data, the test passes.

But what if the user changes the request to:

GET /api/orders/1043
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

If order 1043 belongs to another customer, the application must enforce object-level authorization.

Otherwise, a user may access data they should not be able to see.

This is an example of a broken object-level authorization vulnerability.

The application may work perfectly from a functional perspective while failing to protect sensitive information.

This is why security testing needs to examine more than expected user behavior.

2. What does a web application vulnerability assessment cover?

A vulnerability assessment identifies and evaluates security weaknesses in an application.

The exact scope depends on the architecture, business requirements, and sensitivity of the data involved.

Common assessment areas include:

Area Typical security concerns
Authentication Weak login protection, account recovery issues
Authorization Unauthorized access to functions or data
Input handling SQL injection, cross-site scripting
Session management Insecure cookies, session handling weaknesses
File uploads Unsafe file processing and validation
APIs Missing authorization, excessive data exposure
Configuration Exposed debug features, insecure settings

These categories are not independent.

For example, a weakness in session management may interact with an authorization flaw, increasing the potential impact.

A useful assessment therefore considers both individual vulnerabilities and how application components interact.

3. Automated scanning is useful, but it has limits

Automated vulnerability scanners can help identify common security weaknesses.

They are particularly useful for repeatable checks, broad endpoint coverage, and detecting known patterns.

For example, a scanner may flag missing security headers, outdated components, or certain input validation weaknesses.

However, automated scanning cannot reliably understand every application's business rules.

Consider an expense approval system.

An employee can submit a reimbursement request, and a manager can approve it.

A security issue may exist if employees can approve their own requests by manipulating an API call.

Detecting this requires understanding the intended business workflow and authorization rules.

An automated scanner may not have enough context to identify the problem.

This is where manual security testing becomes valuable.

A balanced assessment often combines automated checks with targeted manual verification.

4. API security deserves particular attention

Modern web applications frequently depend on APIs.

A single frontend may communicate with several backend services, including authentication systems, payment providers, and internal business applications.

As a result, API security has become a central part of application security.

Consider an endpoint:

PATCH /api/users/204/profile
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

{
  "displayName": "Example User"
}

The backend should verify that the authenticated user is authorized to modify the requested profile.

It should also validate the accepted fields and prevent unauthorized changes to protected properties.

Important API security considerations include:

  • Object-level and function-level authorization
  • Input validation
  • Authentication and token handling
  • Rate limiting where appropriate
  • Sensitive data exposure
  • Secure configuration
  • Logging and monitoring

The OWASP API Security Top 10 provides a useful framework for identifying common API security risks.

However, a checklist alone is not sufficient. Testing must reflect the application's actual data flows and permission model.

5. When should vulnerability assessments happen?

A common mistake is treating security testing as a one-time activity immediately before launch.

While pre-release testing is important, vulnerabilities can also be introduced after deployment.

For example, a team may add a new API endpoint, modify user permissions, or integrate an external service.

Each change can affect the application's security posture.

There are several useful assessment points throughout the development lifecycle.

Before production release

Assess critical application functions, authentication, authorization, and data handling before exposing the system to real users.

After significant changes

Reassess affected components when introducing new functionality, changing access controls, or modifying integrations.

During ongoing operations

Schedule assessments based on the application's risk level, exposure, and rate of change.

After major vulnerability disclosures

When a serious vulnerability is reported in a framework, library, or runtime used by the application, investigate exposure and apply the relevant remediation.

The goal is to make security verification part of the application lifecycle rather than an isolated event.

6. Integrating security testing into CI/CD

Not every security test needs to be performed manually.

Development teams can automate several security checks within their pipelines.

A simplified workflow might look like this:

Code Commit
    |
    v
Static Analysis / SAST
    |
    v
Dependency Scanning
    |
    v
Build & Deploy to Test Environment
    |
    v
Automated DAST
    |
    v
Manual Security Review (Risk-Based)
    |
    v
Production Release

Static Application Security Testing (SAST) examines source code or related artifacts for potential security issues.

Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) examines a running application.

Dependency scanning helps identify known vulnerabilities in third-party components.

These approaches complement one another, but none guarantees complete coverage.

For applications with complex business logic or sensitive workflows, manual assessment remains important.

7. Finding vulnerabilities is only the beginning

A vulnerability assessment produces findings, but those findings do not automatically make an application more secure.

The next step is remediation.

A practical process usually includes:

  1. Validation: Confirm whether a finding represents a real security issue.
  2. Prioritization: Evaluate severity, exploitability, exposure, and business impact.
  3. Remediation: Fix the underlying weakness.
  4. Retesting: Verify that the issue has been resolved.
  5. Regression testing: Confirm that the fix has not broken expected functionality.

Severity scores can support prioritization, but they should not be the only factor.

A moderate-severity issue affecting a critical business workflow may require urgent attention.

Similarly, an issue in an internet-facing system may deserve different treatment from the same issue in a tightly restricted environment.

8. Choosing a vulnerability assessment approach

The appropriate assessment depends on the application.

A public marketing website, a customer portal, and a financial transaction platform have different threat models.

Before selecting an assessment method, engineering teams should clarify:

  • Which applications, APIs, and environments are in scope?
  • What sensitive data does the system handle?
  • Which user roles and permission levels exist?
  • What testing methods are permitted?
  • Who will implement and verify fixes?
  • How will findings be prioritized and documented?

These questions help ensure the assessment produces actionable results rather than just a long list of scanner alerts.

For teams looking for a more detailed overview, SotaTek Japan has published a Japanese-language guide covering web application vulnerability assessment, common testing categories, assessment methods, costs, and implementation steps.

Further reading: Web Application Vulnerability Assessment: Testing Areas, Costs, and Process — SotaTek Japan

The guide also discusses how assessment findings can be connected to remediation and follow-up verification.

Final thoughts

A web application that functions correctly is not necessarily secure.

Functional tests verify expected behavior, while vulnerability assessments examine potential weaknesses in authentication, authorization, input handling, APIs, and other security-sensitive components.

Automated scanners can provide valuable coverage, but manual testing is often needed to evaluate business logic and complex access-control scenarios.

Most importantly, security assessment should not end with a report.

The real value comes from identifying risks, fixing the underlying issues, and verifying that the application is safer afterward.

Suggested tags: #security #webdev #testing #devops
