title: October 28, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI and vector search features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • The alloydb_scann extension supports four-level tree (4LT) ScaNN vector indexes on PostgreSQL 17 and later, providing support for tables with up to 10 billion vector rows. For more information, see Four-level ScaNN tree indexes.

  • 4LT ScaNN vector indexes support automatic index maintenance. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and Maintain vector indexes automatically.

  • You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy_limit parameter to relaxed_order. When enabled, the vector scan continues searching through additional leaf partitions until it finds enough results to satisfy the LIMIT clause of your query, improving recall on filtered searches. Additionally, you can enable this feature for parallel process scans by setting the scann.enable_parallel_satisfy_limit database flag to on. For more information, see ScaNN index reference and Best practices for tuning ScaNN indexes.

  • Vector assist simplifies the deployment and management of your AlloyDB vector workloads by helping you set up production-ready vector search capabilities, including embedding generation, query optimization, and index creation for vector types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). For more information, see Vector assist overview.

  • For AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances running PostgreSQL 17 and later, the maximum supported value for num_leaves when building ScaNN vector indexes is increased from 30,000,000 to 104,857,600. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and ScaNN index reference.

  • You can use the external_search_fdw extension to connect to external search clusters and query their data directly from your database using the following search sources:

    • Elasticsearch

    • Solr

    • OpenSearch

  • AlloyDB supports the rum extension for high-performance full-text search operations on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier. The rum extension extends standard GIN indexes by storing positional information directly in the index, letting you perform faster phrase searches and relevance ranking without accessing the table data. For more information, see Create and manage a RUM index.

Fixed

AlloyDB provides more accurate memory usage estimation and prevents out-of-memory (OOM) errors when you build a ScaNN four-level tree index. This feature is in Preview. This update improves the stability of index builds by enforcing memory limits and improving memory estimation under constrained conditions.

Feature

Identity and Access Management (IAM) group authentication is generally available (GA) for new and existing AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 15 and later. With IAM group authentication, you can manage database roles and privileges at the group level across primary instances and read pool instances, including first-time sign-ins directly to read pool instances. You can also preserve individual and IAM group user configurations when you migrate from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backup.

For more information, see IAM database authentication overview and Manage IAM authentication.

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating AlloyDB managed components. The fix to the certificate store is shipped in a new maintenance version that AlloyDB applies during scheduled maintenance, so you don't need to manually update AlloyDB managed instances. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance.

Depending on how you connect to AlloyDB, take the following actions:

  • If you use the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, then upgrade it to v1.17.2 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use the AlloyDB Language Connectors, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later).

Application Integration

Security

A Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability was discovered in the SubWorkflow task in Application Integration versions prior to September 11, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-074 security bulletin.

Feature

Application Integration agent skills

Application Integration agent skills are available in the public google/skills repository: application-integration-basics, application-integration-authoring, and application-integration-troubleshooting. AI coding agents that use these skills can help you set up Application Integration; build, publish, and run integrations through the REST API; and troubleshoot failed runs. For more information, see Application Integration agent skills and Build an integration with an AI agent.

Bigtable

Feature

You can configure Bigtable tables with microsecond timestamp granularity to capture and store high-frequency data. By supporting microsecond precision for cell timestamps, Bigtable helps you prevent data loss from write collisions in workloads with high event rates. This feature is generally available (GA) for instances in the Enterprise Plus edition. For more information, see Data type enforcement in Bigtable.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Google Cloud Migration Center

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

Database Migration Service for homogeneous SQL Server migrations now supports Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations in general availability (GA).

With DAG migrations, you can use gcloud CLI and Database Migration Service API to migrate databases from self-managed SQL Server Enterprise Edition instances directly to Cloud SQL for SQL Server over a private network connection. DAG migrations don't require exporting backup or transaction log files to Cloud Storage, and support post-promotion reverse replication for zero-data-loss failback.

For more information, see About Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations and Migrate from self-managed SQL Server using Distributed Availability Groups.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Managed replica indexes for Cloud SQL for MySQL are generally available (GA). This feature lets you automatically retain and restore secondary indexes on read replica instances when Cloud SQL re-creates a replica.

Previously, re-creating a read replica deleted custom secondary indexes because primary backups don't have replica-only index definitions. With managed replica indexes, Cloud SQL tracks secondary index metadata on the primary instance, replicates this metadata to read replicas, and automatically rebuilds secondary indexes after replica re-creation.

Managed replica indexes are supported on instances that are running Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 or later, Cloud SQL Enterprise edition or Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition, and maintenance version R20260726.00_05 or later.

For more information, see Read replica indexes overview and Create and manage read replica indexes.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (261001) is available. This image removes compromised CA certificates from the OS trust store. See the security bulletin for more details.

This image also adds support for running workload containers as a non-root user. Workload authors can require non-root execution with the tee.launch_policy.nonroot_container launch policy, and workload operators can enable it with the tee-nonroot-container metadata variable. For more information, see Non-root container execution.

You can use the Gemini Enterprise app in the Brazil (br) in-country region with at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP) in region.

This location is available in GA with allowlist. To get access to this location for use with Gemini Enterprise, contact your Google account team.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Change

Use a single regional Agent Registry instance for Gemini Enterprise apps

For Gemini Enterprise apps, we recommend associating each Agent Gateway with a single regional Agent Registry instance in the same project and region as the gateway. Use the us-central1 registry for global and us apps, and the europe-west1 registry for eu apps.

This note updates the September 9, 2026 entry. For more information, see Register your agents and destination resources.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.17.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Support bundle diagnostics: Introduce cm support-bundle to collect environment metadata, configuration policies, health reports, and session logs into a compressed archive for streamlined troubleshooting.
  • Plain output mode: Add the persistent --plain flag (configurable via the CM_PLAIN environment variable or output.plain in config.yaml) to suppress decorative emojis, ANSI escape sequences, and Unicode borders for compatibility with screen readers and CI/CD log pipelines.
  • Dedicated exit codes for setup failures: Assign distinct exit codes (such as code 10 for credential issues) to configuration and authentication failures, preventing CI/CD pipelines from confusing environment setup issues with security findings.
  • Tailored CI/CD credential guidance: Provide environment-specific authentication guidance when running inside automated CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, and Jenkins instead of interactive login prompts.
  • Single-line JSONL statistics: Add the --jsonl flag to cm stats to output single-line JSON records with model and team attribution for seamless integration with Cloud Logging and log aggregation pipelines.
  • Granular sandbox and policy flags: Replace the overloaded --unrestricted flag with orthogonal flags (--sandbox=false) and configurable command policies to decouple container sandboxing from execution safety controls.
  • Sandbox configuration protections: Mount .git/hooks, .git/config, and .codemender read-only within writable execution sandboxes during cm fix and cm verify to prevent modifications to repository security policies.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a security warning when commands are executed with both sandbox isolation disabled and interactive approval skipped.
    • Enforced allowedRoots path boundaries across host discovery and remediation file operations to prevent traversal via dangling symlinks.
    • Supplied exact finding line ranges to remediation agents during cm fix to eliminate manual file scanning overhead.
    • Updated cm report import to properly treat findings without location data as file-level findings rather than defaulting to the first line.
    • Ensured cm session cancel routes requests to the session's original region regardless of local environment overrides.
    • Fixed finding status tracking in cm verify so unexploitable verdicts update the local state database rather than leaving findings open.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

title: SEO for a React SPA without Next.js, and without giving up the 3D homepage
description:
This site opens on a small 3D room with an arcade cabinet in it. It is a Vite and React single-page app, and the 3D part loads behind a boot screen. That is great for a visitor and terrible for a search engine. The HTML a crawler receives is a <div id="root"></div> and a script tag.

The usual advice is "move to Next.js". I did not want to: the app is small, the 3D scene is the whole point, and a framework migration to get some HTML into a response felt out of proportion. This post shows what I did instead. It applies to any Vite or Create React App project that needs to be found.

What a crawler actually needs

Same app, two very different first responses.

Search engines can run JavaScript, but rendering is deferred and not guaranteed, and other consumers (link previews in chat apps, social cards, smaller engines) usually do not run it at all. To be safe, a page that should rank needs in its first HTML response:

  • A unique <title> and meta description.
  • A canonical URL, so /classic and /classic/ and ?ref=x count as one page.
  • The real content as text: headings, paragraphs, links.
  • Structured data that says what the page is about and who it belongs to.
  • A sitemap that lists it.

None of that needs a framework. It needs the right HTML at the right URL.

What a crawler gets for each URL.

Step 1: prerender the page that should rank

Prerendering after the build.

The portfolio has two views of the same content: the 3D room at / and a plain "Classic" view at /classic that recruiters can skim. The Classic view is ordinary React with no WebGL, so it can render on the server. After vite build, a small script loads the app through Vite's SSR loader and writes the result into a copy of the built index.html:

scripts/prerender.mjs

import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs'
import { createServer } from 'vite'

const vite = await createServer({
  configFile: false,
  appType: 'custom',
  logLevel: 'error',
  server: { middlewareMode: true, hmr: false, ws: false },
})
try {
  const { render, jsonLd, PAGES, SITE } = await vite.ssrLoadModule('/src/prerender.tsx')
  const template = readFileSync('dist/index.html', 'utf8')
  const ld = `<script type="application/ld+json">${jsonLd()}</script>`

  const page = (meta, body) => {
    const url = SITE + meta.path
    return template
      .replace(/<title>.*?<\/title>/, `<title>${meta.title}</title>`)
      .replace(/(<link rel="canonical" href=")[^"]*/, `$1${url}`)
      .replace(/(<meta property="og:url" content=")[^"]*/, `$1${url}`)
      .replace(/(<meta property="og:title" content=")[^"]*/, `$1${meta.title}`)
      .replace('</head>', `    ${ld}\n  </head>`)
      .replace('<div id="root"></div>', `<div id="root">${body}</div>`)
  }

  writeFileSync('dist/index.html', page(PAGES['3d'], ''))
  writeFileSync('dist/classic.html', page(PAGES.classic, render()))
} finally {
  await vite.close()
}

src/prerender.tsx is tiny: it exports render(), which calls renderToString(<App />), plus the page metadata and the JSON-LD builder. The build command becomes:

package.json

{ "scripts": { "build": "tsc -b && vite build && node scripts/prerender.mjs" } }

And Vercel serves the file for the clean URL:

vercel.json

{ "rewrites": [{ "source": "/classic", "destination": "/classic.html" }] }

The one gotcha: the router during SSR

On the server there is no window.location, so the app does not know which page it is rendering. The router here is a tiny hook over useSyncExternalStore, and its third argument is the snapshot used during server rendering. Pointing it at /classic makes the prerender render the right view:

src/lib/route.ts

export function usePath() {
  return useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getPath, () => '/classic')
}

In the browser the client renders over the same markup, so visitors get the normal app and crawlers get complete HTML. When the user switches views on the client, a small helper updates the title, canonical, description and Open Graph tags so a shared link always matches what is on screen.

Step 2: tell search engines who this is

Structured data is how a page says "this is a person, this is their job, these are their profiles". The site emits one JSON-LD graph with three nodes:

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@graph": [
    { "@type": "Person", "@id": "https://mahmadmanzoor.com/#person",
      "name": "Muhammad Ahmad", "jobTitle": "Full-Stack & AI Product Engineer",
      "address": { "@type": "PostalAddress", "addressLocality": "Lahore", "addressCountry": "PK" },
      "knowsAbout": ["React", "Next.js", "Django", "Node.js", "LLMs"],
      "sameAs": ["https://github.com/mahmadmanzoor", "https://www.linkedin.com/in/…"] },
    { "@type": "WebSite", "@id": "https://mahmadmanzoor.com/#website", "publisher": { "@id": "https://mahmadmanzoor.com/#person" } },
    { "@type": "ProfilePage", "mainEntity": { "@id": "https://mahmadmanzoor.com/#person" } }
  ]
}

One Person, referenced three ways.

The @id values let the nodes refer to each other, and the same Person @id is reused as the author of every blog post. sameAs links the site to profiles search engines already trust. The page title and description carry the phrases people actually search for, such as "software engineer in Lahore", in normal sentences. Stuffing them in reads badly and does not help.

Step 3: a blog that publishes without a redeploy

Prerendering at build time works for pages that change when the code changes. Blog posts are written in a dashboard and saved to storage, so they need to be rendered when requested. A single Vercel function handles /blog and /blog/<slug>:

vercel.json

{
  "functions": { "api/blog-page.ts": { "includeFiles": "dist/blog.html" } },
  "rewrites": [
    { "source": "/blog", "destination": "/api/blog-page" },
    { "source": "/blog/:slug", "destination": "/api/blog-page?slug=:slug" },
    { "source": "/sitemap.xml", "destination": "/api/sitemap" }
  ]
}

How a blog URL is answered.

The function reads the post, renders the article to HTML with every value escaped, and injects it into a template that the build writes next to index.html (with the blog stylesheet already linked, so the article is styled before any JavaScript runs). includeFiles bundles that template into the function. If it were ever missing, the function falls back to fetching /blog.html from the deployment, and as a last resort to a minimal built-in page, so a configuration mistake degrades to plain HTML rather than a 500.

Each post page gets its own title, description, canonical URL, Open Graph image (the post's cover) and a BlogPosting JSON-LD block that points back to the same Person. The response is cached at the edge briefly:

api/blog-page.ts

const CACHE = 'public, max-age=0, s-maxage=15, stale-while-revalidate=300'

Fifteen seconds at the edge means a burst of traffic is served from cache, while a fix to a typo shows up almost immediately.

The sitemap follows the content

A static sitemap.xml would need a redeploy for every post. Instead it is another small function that lists the fixed pages plus every published post, with its last-modified date. robots.txt points to it. Publishing a post in the dashboard makes it appear in the sitemap on the next request.

Two more details that matter for indexing:

  • The private routes (/sign-in, /dashboard) send X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow and are left out of the sitemap.
  • Preview deployments are noindex too, so the same content on a *.vercel.app URL never competes with the real domain.

Step 4: keep it fast

Kept fast.

Rankings and Lighthouse both care about speed, and a 3D site is easy to make slow. The rules that kept it fast:

  • The Classic view ships no Three.js at all. The 3D chunk loads only behind the boot screen on /.
  • A CI budget fails the build if the initial JS and CSS go over 250 KB gzipped. It currently sits around 82 KB.
  • Screenshots are WebP, at most 1280 px wide, with smaller thumbnails for cards.
  • Long-lived immutable cache headers on hashed assets.

The Classic view scores 99 for performance and 100 for SEO, accessibility and best practices on mobile Lighthouse.

After deploying

  1. Verify the domain in Search Console

Use a DNS TXT record so it covers every subdomain and protocol.

  1. Submit the sitemap

Submit https://your-domain/sitemap.xml once. Because it is generated, you do not need to submit it again for new posts.

  1. Request indexing for the key pages

Use URL Inspection on the prerendered page and check "View crawled page" shows real content, not an empty root div.

  1. Validate the structured data

Run the page through the Rich Results Test and the schema.org validator.

  1. Link to it from places that are already indexed

GitHub profile and repository homepages, LinkedIn, and cross-posts of articles that set a canonical URL back to the original.

When you should just use a framework

This approach fits a small site with a handful of indexable routes and one dynamic section. If most of your pages are data-driven, need per-request personalisation, or you find yourself writing a router, a cache layer and a template system, that is the point where Next.js, Remix or Astro will save you time. For this site, about 60 lines of prerender script and one function were enough.

Originally published on my site. More posts and projects at mahmadmanzoor.com.

title: Generator-Aligned Reward Modeling with Target-Aware Bounded Optimization for Visual Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.07648v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-training aims to enhance desired attributes in visual generative models while preserving their general generation capabilities. Reward-guided post-training faces two challenges: real training data may mismatch the generator's output distribution, and attribute supervision may be confounded by unrelated content. Unbounded reward maximization can also cause overoptimization and degrade generation quality. We propose a framework combining Generator-Aligned Reward Modeling (GARM) and Target-Aware Bounded Optimization (TABO). GARM mitigates distribution mismatch through generator-support matching and reduces content confounding using content-matched real contrasts, yielding generator-relevant, attribute-focused reward supervision. TABO maps the learned reward to a smooth, upper-bounded function calibrated from real target-positive examples. This transformation is independent of the optimization algorithm and supports both direct reward-gradient and policy-based optimization. We further introduce Target-Aware GRPO (TA-GRPO), an adaptation of Flow-GRPO that combines fixed stage-wise advantage scaling, a generator-to-target curriculum, and timestep-balanced credit assignment for flow-based video optimization. Experiments show that GARM improves target-attribute expression while maintaining competitive generation quality. TABO better balances attribute enhancement and visual quality than unconstrained reward maximization, while TA-GRPO improves target enhancement over vanilla Flow-GRPO and reduces unintended attribute leakage on neutral prompts. These results highlight the importance of generator-aligned reward supervision and controlled, data-calibrated optimization for targeted visual generation.

title: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels
description:
arXiv:2611.08082v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. Specifically, we cast DictLLM as a four-step post-training optimization. First, we obtain shared dictionaries via singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weight matrices, amortizing rank across grouped layers; second, we sparsify the layer-specific coefficients to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian; and third, we refine the dictionaries given the resulting sparse coefficients. Finally, we aggressively quantize both components using factor-specific Hessian information: input covariance for the dictionaries and the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients. The resulting representation reduces memory footprint by storing a single shared dictionary per layer group, along with sparse layer-specific coefficients. On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, DictLLM consistently outperforms existing post-training low-rank compression methods and pushes the Pareto frontier between model size and performance. DictLLM compresses the original LLaMA-7B model by 5.1x with only a 2.9-point increase in WikiText-2 perplexity, achieving a 3.6x higher compression ratio than the state-of-the-art low-rank method.

title: Resource-Efficient Reinforcement Learning Post-Training through Elastic Expert Parallelism
description:
arXiv:2611.06984v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning post-training improves the capabilities of large language models, but generating training responses is a major computational bottleneck. In mixture-of-experts models, workers that finish their assigned responses may remain occupied because their experts are still needed by workers processing longer responses. Consequently, approximately one-third of occupied worker time in the baseline occurs after local response generation finishes. Here we present FlexFloor, a system that enables earlier resource release during synchronous response generation while preserving the expert computation required by ongoing responses. FlexFloor jointly adapts response scheduling and the active group of workers. It uses historical response lengths and memory constraints to guide batching and prompt placement, then progressively releases workers while maintaining expert availability and correct communication. Compared with the verl baseline, FlexFloor generates approximately 65.40% more response tokens per unit of occupied computing time and increases response generation throughput by 52.74%, with little observed variation in rollout reward. By making reinforcement learning post-training more efficient, FlexFloor supports faster development and iterative improvement of large language models and AI agents.

title: Source-balanced Capped Fisher: Bounded Evidence Aggregation for User Inference in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.07228v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: User inference asks whether a source contributed documents to a language-model update, even when the auditor observes only fresh documents from that source. Document-level scores can provide evidence of participation, but combining this evidence is challenging: documents differ in baseline predictability and in how strongly they reflect information learned from other documents of the same source. We propose source-balanced capped Fisher (SCF), an aggregation method that uses known nonparticipating sources to assess how unusual each document score is. It transforms the resulting reference-tail frequencies into negative-log evidence, caps individual contributions, and averages them within each source. This limits the influence of isolated extreme scores while retaining evidence across multiple documents. We complete the inference procedure with a decision rule that tests source participation using a p-value calibrated against a separate set of known nonparticipating sources. The rule provides finite-sample Type-I error control under source exchangeability. Experiments across four real-world datasets show that SCF achieves the highest AUROC among the evaluated aggregation methods in four domains. With the calibration-based decision rule, SCF delivers consistently competitive detection power across the tested settings, achieving the highest power in many cases, while empirical false-positive rates remain generally close to or below the nominal levels.

title: Database Schema Drift: Why Your Docs Are Always Wrong
description:
Somewhere in your company there's a schema diagram. Maybe it's an ERD in Confluence, a .sql file someone exported two migrations ago, or a wiki page titled "Database Structure" that hasn't been opened since the person who wrote it left. It was accurate once. It almost certainly isn't now.

This is schema drift: the gap between what your documentation says a database looks like and what it actually looks like. Every team has it. Almost nobody tracks it, because tracking it manually means someone re-documenting the schema by hand every time a column gets added, a table gets renamed, or a migration quietly ships without an announcement.

TL;DR

Schema documentation goes stale the moment a migration ships, because nothing in a normal deploy workflow touches the wiki. 1DataCloud sidesteps that by reading schema — tables, columns, types, relationships — directly from the connected database each time it syncs, across AWS, GCP, MongoDB Atlas, and on-prem MySQL/PostgreSQL/MariaDB. Try it free →

Why Schema Docs Go Stale the Moment They're Written

Migrations don't update the wiki. A column gets added in a migration file, the PR merges, the deploy goes out — and the ERD nobody opens stays exactly as it was. Nothing in that workflow touches documentation, because documentation isn't part of the deploy.

Tribal knowledge fills the gap, badly. When the docs are wrong, people stop trusting them and start asking around instead. "Does users still have that legacy_status column?" becomes a Slack message to whoever's been around longest, not a doc lookup.

Nobody owns keeping it current. Schema documentation is everyone's responsibility in theory and nobody's job in practice. It gets written once, usually during onboarding or an audit, and then drifts for months or years.

The bigger the team, the worse it gets. A two-person startup can mostly keep a schema in their heads. A team running a dozen services against a shared database, or a company with instances scattered across AWS, GCP, and MongoDB Atlas, can't — and that's exactly when stale docs start costing real time.

What Actually Fixes This

The fix isn't "document better" — better documentation still goes stale the next time someone ships a migration. The fix is not relying on a written document at all for the one thing that changes constantly: what the schema actually is right now.

That's the problem 1DataCloud's schema mapping solves. When you connect a database — AWS RDS or Aurora, GCP Cloud SQL or Spanner, MongoDB Atlas, or an on-premise MySQL, PostgreSQL, or MariaDB instance — the Unified Dashboard reads the real table names, column names, data types, and relationships directly from the database itself. Not from a doc someone wrote. From the schema as it exists.

How this stays accurate

To be precise about the mechanism: this isn't a live change-detection system watching for schema edits and alerting you when something changes. It's simpler than that — each time a database is synced, what you see reflects what's actually in the database at that moment, because it was just read from the source instead of pulled from a document. Re-sync, and you're looking at the current structure, not whatever was true when someone last updated a wiki page.

Why this matters for natural-language querying specifically

Schema accuracy isn't just a documentation nicety — it's the difference between a natural-language query tool that works and one that quietly gives wrong answers. Query1AI turns a plain-English question into SQL using the schema metadata the Unified Dashboard has mapped. If that schema map were based on a six-month-old doc, a column rename or a dropped table would mean Query1AI either fails outright or — worse — generates a query against a structure that no longer matches reality.

Because it works from schema read directly off the connected database, a question like "how many orders shipped last week" gets translated against the tables and columns that exist today, not the ones that existed when someone last wrote things down.

Where This Shows Up in Practice

Onboarding a new engineer. Instead of a stale ERD and a round of "ask Dave," a new hire opens the dashboard and sees the actual current schema for every connected database — tables, columns, types, relationships.

Debugging a query that used to work. When a column gets renamed or a table gets dropped, the documentation doesn't know. The dashboard does, because it reads the schema fresh rather than relying on anything written down.

Handing a database off between teams. Transferring ownership usually means transferring tribal knowledge along with it. A schema that's mapped directly from the source doesn't depend on whoever's leaving remembering to write it all down first.

Reviewing what's actually in a database before an audit. Instead of trusting a document that might be a year old, the current table and column structure is what's shown — because it's read from the database, not transcribed from someone's notes.

What This Isn't

Worth being precise here: this is schema mapping, not schema monitoring. It doesn't watch your database in real time, diff versions against each other, or alert you the moment a migration runs. It reads the current structure when a database is connected or re-synced. If you need a system that flags every schema change the instant it happens, that's a different kind of tool — what 1DataCloud gives you is confidence that what you're looking at, whenever you look, is real.

Summary

Schema documentation is wrong the moment it's written, because nothing in a normal deploy process updates it. The alternative isn't a better doc — it's not needing one for structural facts at all. Reading schema directly from the database, on every sync, means what you see is what's actually there, and it's also what powers accurate natural-language querying through Query1AI.

title: Concertina: Embodying Manipulation and Cognition in One Diffusion Vision-Language Model
description:
arXiv:2611.07513v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most vision-language-action (VLA) policies decouple manipulation from cognition by bolting an external action mechanism onto a vision-language model (VLM)--either quantizing actions into discrete tokens whose errors bear no stable correspondence to physical displacements, or delegating continuous trajectory generation to a separate action expert whose gradients compete with or are blocked from updating the VLM backbone. We argue that manipulation and cognition should instead be embodied in the same model, shifting from a decoupled VLA to an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM). We introduce Concertina, an eVLM that places continuous trajectory representation, blockwise generation, and physical-coordinate supervision directly on the computation and parameter path of a shared diffusion VLM backbone. Each control timestep is encoded as one continuous latent action token in the backbone hidden space, and the shared Transformer reconstructs temporally ordered action blocks via the same corrupt-and-reconstruct operator used for multimodal pretraining. Active action projections account for only 0.21% of parameters in the 4.46B model with zero separate action-generator layers, compared with 16.5%-35.1% dedicated action-expert capacity in representative continuous VLAs. Using our proposed Action Interface Audit, we confirm that cross-time trajectory coupling emerges in the middle and late layers of the shared backbone rather than at the action interfaces. On standard benchmarks, Concertina achieves 98.15% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC-D.

title: Reversible Password Reset Email Delivery Boundaries for Support Signup Systems
description:
Short answer: use a provider-neutral adapter for password-reset email, and try Infrai when one REST contract and one backend credential reduce migration work; choose SES, SendGrid, or Mailgun when their regional, event, or governance controls better match your support operation.

A password-reset or signup-verification message is a small API call with a large failure surface. The reliable choice is the provider whose boundary you can replace without rewriting account-recovery logic: keep token creation, expiry, suppression decisions, and audit records in your service, then put one narrow send operation behind an adapter. For a support product, I would start with a transactional email provider that gives you domain authentication and delivery evidence, and I would make the provider swappable before the first production incident.

Keep it replaceable.

Tokens are not.

The operational constraint is simple: a user cannot complete recovery if the message arrives late, lands in spam, or is sent to an address already suppressed. High deliverability is therefore a system property, not a checkbox on a vendor page.

For this specific boundary, Infrai is a plausible early candidate: its email send capability puts the message behind one REST API, while the application can keep token and recovery state elsewhere. That is useful when a support backend is already consolidating integrations under one key and one billing boundary. It is a narrow fit, not a verdict on every deliverability requirement.

What must remain yours when delivery changes?

The application should own the reset token, its one-time consumption, its expiration, and the decision to send. The email API should receive a rendered message or a provider template reference plus a destination. That split keeps a migration boring. It also limits the damage from a vendor-specific template language or event model.

The audit record is where many otherwise tidy designs get vague. Store the request ID before the outbound call, then attach the provider message ID only after a successful response. Keep the token hash, purpose, template version, selected provider, and attempt count; do not put the raw reset URL in an ordinary application log. If a customer says, "I never received it," support can distinguish an unissued message, a rejected address, a provider acceptance, and a later suppression decision without asking the user to repeat a sensitive token. That distinction is the practical value of a replaceable boundary.

I use a small internal contract for this boundary: send_password_reset(recipient, reset_url, request_id) -> message_id. The implementation records the provider, request ID, response ID, and timestamps. A retry carries an idempotency key derived from the request ID, so a timeout does not turn into two recovery emails. The consumer still needs to tolerate duplicate delivery because transport retries and mailbox behavior are separate concerns.

There is a less glamorous rule here: never treat a successful HTTP response as proof that a person saw the message. Keep delivery status, bounce or suppression state, and user-visible recovery state separate. If the provider does not offer the event shape you need, polling is a workable fallback, but it is not real-time orchestration.

Which API should send password reset emails with high deliverability?

Amazon SES is a strong fit when an organization already operates its AWS identity, region, DNS, and compliance controls. It is close to the infrastructure layer, which can be useful for teams that want to assemble their own sending and event pipeline. The trade-off is operational ownership: your team must be comfortable wiring the surrounding pieces and validating the exact account and regional constraints.

SendGrid is a reasonable choice for teams that want a mature transactional-email product with templates and a broad operational surface. Its convenience can become coupling if application code starts depending directly on provider-specific dynamic-template fields or event payloads. Keep those details in the adapter.

Mailgun is often attractive to teams that care about developer-oriented domain and message tooling. It still deserves the same scrutiny as any other provider: test authentication, suppression behavior, regional requirements, and event retention against your actual support workflow rather than assuming a familiar API means equivalent deliverability.

Infrai fits the narrower case where a backend team wants email sending behind one plain REST contract while keeping the rest of its service integrations under one credential and billing boundary. Its discovery surface is public and self-describing, and the documented capabilities include runnable examples across ten languages. Those details reduce integration archaeology when a team is migrating a small adapter or adding a second backend capability.

Option Interface Best fit Main boundary
Amazon SES AWS API and SMTP options AWS-native identity, region, and governance More surrounding delivery operations remain yours
SendGrid Email API and product tooling Teams using managed templates and event workflows Provider-specific fields can leak into application code
Mailgun Developer-oriented email API Teams centered on domain and message tooling Regional, suppression, and retention checks remain necessary
Infrai REST API A unified backend boundary with one credential No SMTP relay, hosted email OTP, or webhook events

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the password-reset send adapter when one-key, one-bill administration and a consistent REST surface matter, and keep your application contract independent of it so SES, SendGrid, or Mailgun can take the same slot later. The relevant send operation is /v1/email/send; its documented contract is enough for this boundary. Do not choose it as a substitute for a specialist's complete event, compliance, or regional-delivery program without checking those requirements first.

The comparison is not a ranking. SES may be the better fit for AWS-native governance. SendGrid or Mailgun may be the better fit when their dashboards, event tooling, or established domain operations match the team. A reversible adapter makes that a controlled change instead of an account-recovery rewrite.

That is the whole test.

What does a minimal, replaceable send path look like?

The following Python example keeps provider-specific code in one function. It uses the documented base URL and route, reads the credential from the environment, sets the method explicitly, surfaces non-success responses, and retries a rate limit with Retry-After. The idempotency key is supplied by the caller's reset request, not generated anew for every retry.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests


def send_password_reset(to_address: str, reset_url: str, request_id: str) -> str:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send"
    payload = {
        "to": to_address,
        "subject": "Reset your password",
        "text": f"Use this link to reset your password: {reset_url}",
    }
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": request_id,
    }

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.request(
            "POST", endpoint, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=10
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            if not 200 <= response.status_code < 300:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"email send failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}"
                )
            body = response.json()
            return str(body.get("id", request_id))

        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
        time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("email send rate limit did not clear after retries")


message_id = send_password_reset(
    "customer@example.com",
    "https://support.example/reset?token=one-time-token",
    str(uuid.uuid4()),
)
print(message_id)

The example deliberately does not create the token, expose a public reset record, or pretend that a returned message ID proves inbox placement. In production, render the link from a short-lived, single-use server-side token and record the request before sending. If you use a provider template, make template versioning part of the adapter contract, not part of the account model.

Where does deliverability end and compliance begin?

Authenticate the sending domain and maintain a clear separation between product mail and promotional mail. SPF is one part of that work; RFC 7208 describes how receivers evaluate an SPF policy, but SPF alone does not guarantee inbox placement. DKIM, alignment, bounce handling, suppression checks, and a monitored sending reputation still matter.

A support workflow also needs a clear fallback policy. Infrai's email surface has no hosted email OTP interface, so an email-code fallback is application work. It also has no SMTP relay, and scheduled email has no cancellation route. There are no webhook events in the relevant namespaces, so a design that requires instant push callbacks needs polling or another event source. Those are meaningful boundaries, not footnotes.

The same caution applies to geography. A pending domestic email vendor cannot serve as evidence of domestic compliance. For a customer-support product with regulated users, get the required legal and regional review independently and choose the delivery specialist that can satisfy it.

A migration that can be reversed

Start by capturing a provider-neutral record: recipient hash, purpose, request ID, template version, provider, provider message ID, attempt count, and final status. Keep message bodies out of logs unless the retention policy explicitly permits them. Route a small, observable cohort through the new adapter, compare bounce and completion signals, then expand.

Do not dual-send a password reset merely to compare vendors. That creates user confusion and makes the experiment itself a deliverability event. Shadow the request metadata, or split traffic by a deterministic cohort key, while preserving one authoritative reset token.

The decision rule is compact: choose the provider with the strongest evidence for your recipients and controls, then make its adapter disposable. Infrai is a plausible boundary when its unified REST and credential model reduce integration work; SES, SendGrid, or Mailgun may win on regional operations, event tooling, or existing governance. The architecture succeeds when changing that answer does not change the recovery flow.

If this boundary matches your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current email contract before implementation.

References

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • SendGrid Email API documentation
  • Mailgun API documentation

Sources

  • Amazon SES documentation
  • SendGrid Email API documentation
  • Mailgun API documentation
  • Infrai documentation

title: The DreamHost Data Breach Sat in a Web File Manager for Two Months Before Anyone Noticed
description:
The DreamHost Data Breach Sat in a Web File Manager for Two Months Before Anyone Noticed

The DreamHost data breach, confirmed in a notification this week, ran from roughly August 2026 to October 23, 2026, nearly two months, through a vulnerability in the web-based File Manager tool at files.dreamhost.com. By the time it was discovered, attackers had collected FTP and SFTP usernames and passwords for everyone who had logged into that one tool during the window, plus webmail session credentials for an unspecified number of additional users.

Jump to what DreamHost says wasn't touched if you want the scope boundary first.

What Actually Happened

According to DreamHost's own breach notification, "an unauthorized third party accessed the server that runs our web-based File Manager at files.dreamhost.com," then "exploited a vulnerability in that software" to access FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords for individuals who logged into that File Manager between approximately August 2026 and October 23, 2026. BleepingComputer's reporting adds that webmail systems may also have been reached, exposing session information, including credentials, for a limited number of users.

DreamHost says the attack "appears deliberate," not an opportunistic scan that happened to land somewhere sensitive, and that staff worked to contain it fully once discovered. The company has not disclosed how many accounts were affected. BleepingComputer notes it contacted DreamHost multiple times asking for that number specifically and received no response.

What DreamHost Says Wasn't Touched

The scope boundary matters as much as what was exposed. DreamHost states it found no evidence that the attacker accessed control panel login information or customer billing and payment details, the latter of which is handled by an external provider rather than DreamHost's own systems. That's a meaningfully narrower blast radius than a full account-takeover scenario: FTP/SFTP credentials and webmail sessions are serious, letting an attacker potentially modify website files or read email, but a compromised control panel login would have gone further, toward DNS, billing, and account-level configuration changes across a customer's entire hosting footprint.

Why Two Months Is the Detail That Matters Most

A single vulnerable tool being exploitable is, unfortunately, routine. What makes this incident worth examining structurally is the detection gap: nearly two months between the earliest exposure and discovery on October 23, 2026. During that entire window, every FTP/SFTP login submitted through files.dreamhost.com was potentially being collected, which means the actual number of affected credentials likely scales with ordinary File Manager usage over two full months of customer activity, not a single moment of exposure.

DreamHost's remediation, once it found the issue, was conventional and reasonably fast: the company says it blocked the attacker's access, patched the vulnerable software, terminated active sessions for potentially affected users, and invalidated their passwords, then began offering a year of credit monitoring and identity theft protection through Equifax to affected individuals. None of that undoes the two-month collection window; it only closes it.

What This Means If You Use a Web-Based File Manager on Your Hosting Platform

Our verdict: this isn't a reason to distrust DreamHost specifically, whose public response once the breach was found followed a reasonable playbook. It's a reason to think about what a convenience feature, a browser-based file manager that holds your raw FTP credentials to let you drag and drop files, actually costs in attack surface, because that tool becomes a single point of compromise for every credential it ever processes, for as long as it stays vulnerable and undetected.

  • If you were notified, rotate your FTP/SFTP password immediately, even though DreamHost already invalidated it, and check for any webmail forwarding rules or filters you didn't create, a detail DreamHost itself recommends checking.
  • Audit whether any other accounts reuse the exposed FTP/SFTP or webmail password. A hosting credential that doubles as a password somewhere else turns a contained incident into a much wider one.
  • If a hosting platform offers a convenient web-based file manager as an alternative to direct FTP/SSH access, understand that convenience layer is itself attack surface, separate from and in addition to whatever protects your actual server. It's not inherently unsafe, but it is one more thing that has to stay patched, and this incident shows what two months of it not being patched looks like.

FAQ

What credentials were exposed in the DreamHost data breach?

FTP and SFTP usernames and passwords were exposed for anyone who logged into DreamHost's web-based File Manager at files.dreamhost.com between approximately August 2026 and October 23, 2026. Webmail session information, including credentials, may also have been exposed for a limited number of additional users. DreamHost says it found no evidence that control panel logins or billing and payment details were accessed.

How long did the DreamHost breach go undetected?

Approximately two months. DreamHost's notification states the unauthorized access began around August 2026 and was discovered on October 23, 2026, when the company identified and blocked the intrusion and patched the underlying File Manager vulnerability.

What should I do if I received a DreamHost breach notification?

DreamHost recommends checking your website files for unauthorized changes, reviewing webmail forwarding rules and filters for anything you didn't set up, and changing passwords on any other accounts where you reused the exposed FTP/SFTP or webmail credentials. The company has already invalidated affected passwords and is offering one year of credit monitoring through Equifax to notified individuals.

What We Checked Before Publishing

We pulled DreamHost's own breach notification as quoted directly by daily.dev and cross-referenced the timeline, scope, and remediation details against BleepingComputer's independent reporting. DreamHost has not disclosed the total number of affected accounts despite being asked directly, and we've left that figure unknown rather than estimating it.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud: every Cube ships with full root access over SSH rather than routing file management through a separate web tool that has to independently hold and protect your credentials. That doesn't eliminate attack surface, every piece of software you run is something that can have a vulnerability, but it does mean there's one fewer centralized tool standing between an attacker and every customer's FTP-equivalent credentials at once. More debugging stories at debugly.dev.

title: Regulating Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand Operators with Fixed and Adaptive Penalties: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
description:
arXiv:2611.07122v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Profit-maximizing Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand (AMoD) operators may exploit consumer surplus through excessive prices and underserve less profitable regions by relocating vehicles away from them. We study how penalty-based regulation of an AMoD operator in a multimodal mobility system can limit surge pricing and improve regional service availability. We model regulation as an outer control loop that acts on a learning-based operator. Static regulation with fixed penalties is formulated as a Markov Decision Process for an operator that jointly controls pricing and rebalancing, and dynamic regulation as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game in which a regulator periodically adjusts region-specific penalties in closed loop. Operator and regulator policies are learned with graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning. In experiments with real-world Manhattan data, fixed surge pricing penalties reduce the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%. For regional service availability, dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over fixed penalties of equal mean intensity. The gains in service availability are strongest when spare fleet capacity exists, whereas service deficits persist in peak periods with highly utilized fleets. The learned regulator policy responds by reducing penalties where limited fleet capacity restricts compliance. The results identify trade-offs between regulatory targets, operator profitability, and traveler utility.

title: SAFE-Teen: Evaluating Chatbot Safety Across Adolescent Mental Health Conversations
description:
arXiv:2611.07218v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adolescents are increasingly turning to AI chatbots for mental health support, advice, and companionship, raising safety concerns. While recent evaluations have started to examine safety across multiple conversational turns, few compare how slight changes in a teen's responses can affect a chatbot's safety in the same scenario. We conduct a clinician-informed evaluation of chatbot safety in simulated conversations with adolescents aged 13-17, examining how safety failures vary with adolescents' responses and teen-aware system prompting. We evaluated 32,555 simulated conversations across 18 chatbot APIs and two system-prompt conditions using 22 safety criteria grounded in previously identified harms. Conversations spanned 983 variants of 106 seed scenarios covering urgent safety issues, health advice, and identity and relationships. The overall criterion failure rate was 43.3% without the teen-aware prompt and 24.9% with it. The teen-aware prompt reduced failures, but it didn't eliminate them. When a teenager pushed back on a chatbot's answer, failures on mental health diagnosis, medication, and substance misuse boundaries rose by 10-12 percentage points without the prompt, for more than 80% of chatbots. These findings reveal persistent safety failures in simulated adolescent-chatbot interactions and show that safety depends on how a conversation unfolds.

Bigtable

Feature

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

title: ReferClaw: Disambiguating User Intent for Egocentric Assistance
description:
arXiv:2611.07683v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Users of egocentric AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions whose intended referents cannot be uniquely resolved from video and dialogue history. For example, "Where did I leave it?" may refer to several previously handled objects. Existing VideoQA systems typically commit to a single interpretation, risking plausible but intention-misaligned answers. We introduce ReferClaw, an agentic framework that formulates egocentric streaming QA as an interactive process: the assistant asks clarifying questions to resolve user intent before answering. Three cooperating agents identify candidate interpretations, request clarification, and generate answers grounded in the resolved intent and visual evidence. A bounded, cost-aware policy balances expected information gain against user effort while limiting clarification turns and question complexity. Referclaw learns from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. Evaluations on augmented egocentric QA benchmarks demonstrate improved answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance over existing baselines, alongside zero-shot transfer across datasets. These findings support interactive clarification as a practical approach to resolving online user intent in egocentric streaming assistance.

title: Continued Training of Continuous Language Flows with Token Identity Squared Supervision
description:
arXiv:2611.07721v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion and flow models have recently been extended to language modeling, generating text through continuous denoising in token embedding spaces. Pretrained models provide token representations and contextual prediction capabilities, but improving generation with limited additional training requires an appropriate connection between supervision and continuous generation. Continuous MSE evaluates a predicted vector obtained by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities; different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are therefore indistinguishable under this objective. We propose Token Identity Brier Flow (TIBF), which applies squared supervision directly to token identities when continuing pretrained language flows. TIBF combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities using the Brier loss, and uses probability-weighted embeddings for continuous generation. With fixed token embeddings, we show that the squared error between predicted token probabilities and the true posterior bounds the squared errors of continuous denoising predictions and flow velocities. A risk decomposition separates uncertainty inherent in the observation from posterior fitting error, motivating continued training that preserves pretrained embeddings and focuses on probability prediction. We also establish convergence to token embeddings under ideal predictions and sufficient conditions for local convergence with prediction error. From common pretrained initializations and under matched continuation budgets, frozen-embedding TIBF achieves Gen.PPL values of 33.96 on OWT and 81.17 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE continuation controls. It attains the lowest Gen.PPL at every tested sampling budget on both datasets, together with the lowest repetition rate on LM1B.

title: Teaching Agents the "Principle", Not the "Reward"
description:
arXiv:2611.07130v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning has achieved strong performance in many tasks by letting agents learn from nothing more than a reward signal. However, in more complex tasks, agents still struggle to learn good, generalizable policies, even with carefully designed rewards and abundant samples. We argue that this difficulty stems from the reward decoding burden: designers encode their knowledge of the desired behavior into rewards and penalties, and agents must infer this knowledge from long sequences of noisy scalars. To address this burden, we propose prescriptive policy learning (PPL), which directly teaches agents higher-level knowledge about the tasks, termed principles of behavior, such as how to maintain balance, how to accumulate energy, and how to land smoothly. Through appropriately selected key quantities and references, PPL can directly indicate at every step whether the agent follows the principles and to what extent. Our experiments show that agents can learn good, generalizable policies without any reward. Taught only simple heuristic principles, PPL agents outperform reward-based methods with far fewer samples. Their policies also transfer directly to harder settings and keep performing well, demonstrating their strong generalization ability. In summary, PPL provides a new approach in which rough knowledge of the desired behavior is enough for agents to learn good, generalizable policies, even when the system dynamics cannot be accurately modeled.

title: Towards Real-Time Full-Waveform LiDAR Transformers via Intensity-Guided Token Reduction and Physics-Aware Augmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.07613v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LiDAR is a critical sensor for autonomous driving and robotics, yet it remains vulnerable to adverse conditions such as fog, rain, transparent objects, and low-reflectance surfaces. Full-waveform LiDAR (FWL) addresses these limitations by capturing the complete return waveform as a histogram, preserving rich reflection characteristics including multi-path echoes and weak signals. While recent Transformer-based approaches have demonstrated promise on FWL data, two fundamental bottlenecks remain: high computational cost from redundant tokens in low-intensity background regions, and limited generalization due to scarce annotated training data. We address both bottlenecks by exploiting the physical structure inherent to FWL data. First, we propose FWL-ToPM, a token pruning and merging mechanism that leverages intensity distributions to selectively reduce tokens while retaining critical waveform content. Second, we introduce FWLAug, a data augmentation framework designed as a regularization method that preserves waveform structure, retaining the Time-of-Flight waveform of each ray and the frustum geometry, to improve generalization to unseen scenes. Evaluated on the Ghost-FWL benchmark, FWL-ToPM achieves over 8 times speedup at real-time throughput alongside a nearly 9-point F1 gain over the prior state of the art, establishing the first real-time FWL Transformer that simultaneously improves accuracy. FWLAug further improves performance on both the standard benchmark and an out-of-distribution test set of unseen scenes. Together, these methods push FWL-based perception toward practical deployment. The code and the OOD dataset are publicly available and can be accessed via the project page: https://keio-csg.github.io/FWL-ToPM
