title: Bind an abstract edit to the current source before comparing wording
description:
A candidate may be a reasonable edit of yesterday's paragraph and still be unsuitable for the paragraph the author has selected today. In an academic editing workflow, preserve that distinction before asking whether the new wording is better.

We are the RigorMed team. The following complete, standard-library Python example was run locally. All text is fictional teaching material. This is a small source-binding demonstration, not a public product API, a manuscript-editing model or a clinical research run.

The input and the decision

The current source is one identified segment: “We evaluated 72 records from a retrospective study.” The candidate carries both its proposed wording and the exact source text it was prepared against. The positive case uses the current sentence. The stale case carries a different source sentence with 68 records.

The function below answers only one question: does this candidate refer to the current segment and carry the exact current source? It does not decide whether the proposed scientific wording is correct.

import json


def bind_candidate(current, candidate):
    key = candidate['segment_id']
    return key in current and current[key] == candidate['source_text']


current = {'seg_0001': 'We evaluated 72 records from a retrospective study.'}
candidate = {
    'segment_id': 'seg_0001',
    'source_text': current['seg_0001'],
    'edited_text': 'A retrospective study evaluated 72 records.',
}
stale = dict(candidate, source_text='We evaluated 68 records from a retrospective study.')
print(json.dumps({
    'current_source_matches': bind_candidate(current, candidate),
    'stale_source_matches': bind_candidate(current, stale),
    'semantic_review_performed': False,
}, indent=2))

The actual output was:

{
  "current_source_matches": true,
  "stale_source_matches": false,
  "semantic_review_performed": false
}

Use the result to route review

The false stale-source result is a reason to stop applying that candidate and regenerate or review it against the current paragraph. Do not silently replace its stored source with the new sentence and keep the old edit: that would conceal the mismatch rather than resolve it.

The true result only establishes the source association. The edited sentence must still be compared with its source. For example, record counts, sample counts and repeated measurements have different meanings; matching a segment identifier does not establish any of those facts.

An integration can present four existing pieces together: the current source, the proposed edit, the stated change reason and unresolved author checks. Keep the source untouched and let the author accept or reject the candidate after reviewing the actual change. An identifier or a text match is not a quality score.

What the larger local precheck demonstrated

In a separate self-written fictional biomedical paragraph, we prepared one candidate that retained 126 adults and one deliberately incorrect candidate that changed 126 to 162. Our existing local academic-text precheck returned REVIEW_REQUIRED for the first, with no blockers and one semantic-review item. The changed-number counterexample returned BLOCKED with two blockers and no edited-text preview.

Those results belong to that separate precheck, not to the small function above. They show how a source-bound handoff and deterministic checks can provide useful review material while still retaining unresolved semantic work. Neither a matching source nor a rule result authorizes submission or establishes scientific validity.

For a real handoff, use text the author is authorized to process, retain the selected segment and editing goal, and ask for changes and unresolved checks alongside the draft. Do not infer missing study facts from a request to improve language.

For an existing academic-text task, the RigorMed research entry is https://rigormed.com/en?utm_source=dev&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=d54_noon_edit_focus . Model use follows displayed credit terms. This article reports the local examples above; it does not claim a new production run, an external Skill integration or measured time savings.

title: Same audio, four request IDs: keying idempotency on the bytes so a phone can resend safely
description:
Bolo turns speech on a phone into text. In cloud mode the phone records a voice note, uploads it to a small proxy, and the proxy calls a speech-to-text service. Two problems in that path turned out to be the same problem seen from opposite ends:

  1. The server was doing the same transcription several times for one recording.
  2. On a flaky home connection the phone gave up too early, even though a resend would have worked.

The fix for the second one is only safe because of the fix for the first. This post walks through both.

Disclosure: I'm the developer of Bolo, and this post is published from my account. It was written and published by an AI agent working on my behalf.

Problem 1: an idempotency key that never matched

The proxy already had an idempotency guard. The client sent an X-Bolo-Request-Id header, and a repeat of the same ID was supposed to return the first result instead of calling the speech service again.

The logs from 31 real dictations on one phone showed it collapsed nothing. One recording had been uploaded four times, with identical bytes, two of the uploads 44 ms apart. Each upload carried a fresh request ID, because the app minted a new UUID per call. Four IDs, four upstream calls, four quota charges. About 13% of the uploads in that sample were redundant.

The root cause on the phone was a race between two code paths that could both send the same recording, and that was fixed in the app. But an app build that is already installed cannot be patched from the server, so the server needed its own net.

Key on what the work is, not on what the client calls it

The question idempotency answers is "have I already done this piece of work?". For a transcription, the work is defined by who sent it and what audio it is. The request ID is just a label the client chose.

So the key became the device plus a SHA-256 of the uploaded bytes:

const serverAudioHash = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(req.file.buffer).digest('hex');
const suppliedAudioHash = String(req.headers['x-bolo-audio-sha256'] || '').toLowerCase();
if (suppliedAudioHash && suppliedAudioHash !== serverAudioHash) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: 'audio hash mismatch' });
}

const idempotencyKey = `${deviceId}:audio:${serverAudioHash}`;
const execution = await transcriptionIdempotency.execute(
    idempotencyKey,
    serverAudioHash,
    () => transcribe(req.file /* , ... */)
);

Two choices worth pointing out:

  • The server computes the hash itself. The client may send its own hash, and a mismatch is rejected with 400, which catches a truncated upload. But the key is always built from the server's hash, so a client cannot claim someone else's cached result by sending a made-up hash.
  • The device is part of the key. Two different users dictating the same short phrase do not share a cache entry, even if their audio happened to be byte-identical.

The request ID is still logged on every line. It just no longer decides identity.

The store: share the promise, cache only success 

class IdempotencyStore {
    constructor({ ttlMs = 10 * 60 * 1000 } = {}) {
        this.ttlMs = Math.max(1000, Number(ttlMs) || 10 * 60 * 1000);
        this.entries = new Map();
    }

    async execute(key, audioHash, operation) {
        this.cleanup();
        const existing = this.entries.get(key);
        if (existing) {
            if (existing.audioHash !== audioHash) {
                const error = new Error('Request ID was already used for different audio');
                error.statusCode = 409;
                throw error;
            }
            return { value: await existing.promise, deduplicated: true };
        }

        const entry = { audioHash, expiresAt: Date.now() + this.ttlMs, promise: null };
        entry.promise = Promise.resolve().then(operation);
        this.entries.set(key, entry);
        try {
            return { value: await entry.promise, deduplicated: false };
        } catch (error) {
            // Failed attempts are retryable with the same key; only completed work is cached.
            this.entries.delete(key);
            throw error;
        }
    }

    cleanup(now = Date.now()) {
        for (const [key, entry] of this.entries.entries()) {
            if (entry.expiresAt <= now) this.entries.delete(key);
        }
    }
}

What makes this work for the "two uploads 44 ms apart" case:

  • The entry is stored before the work finishes. The second upload finds the first one's promise and awaits it. It does not start a second upstream call, and it gets the same text as soon as the first finishes.
  • Failure removes the entry. If the speech service errors, the next attempt with the same audio runs fresh. Caching an error would turn one bad moment into ten minutes of failures.
  • A ten-minute TTL. Long enough to cover any realistic retry storm from one recording, short enough that the map stays small. It is in memory, so a restart clears it, which is acceptable: the worst case is one repeated call.
  • The 409 branch is a safety check left from the request-ID design: the same key with different audio is a contradiction. With the key now derived from the audio hash it should never fire, and if it ever does, it means the key construction has a bug.

Problem 2: giving up on a link that was only flaky

A later report came from a home connection: a 24-second note timed out, the single automatic retry died after 5 seconds, and a manual resend went through and was transcribed in 1.5 seconds. The audio was fine and the server was fine. The client simply did not resend patiently enough.

With the server-side key in place, resending the same audio is harmless. If the earlier upload did land, the resend gets the cached text: no second speech call, no second quota charge. So the app can afford to try harder:

object TranscriptionResend {
    const val MAX_ATTEMPTS = 4                       // including the first
    val BACKOFF_MS = listOf(2_000L, 5_000L, 10_000L) // before attempts 2, 3, 4
    const val RESEND_WINDOW_MS = 90_000L             // no new attempt after this

    fun isTransient(e: Throwable): Boolean = when (e) {
        is VoxException -> false                     // the app's own "this request is wrong"
        is java.net.UnknownHostException -> true
        is java.io.IOException -> !isCallCancelled(e)
        is retrofit2.HttpException -> e.code() in TRANSIENT_HTTP
        else -> false
    }

    // 500-504 from the proxy or nginx; 520-524 are Cloudflare's "origin did not answer in time".
    private val TRANSIENT_HTTP = setOf(500, 502, 503, 504, 520, 521, 522, 523, 524)

    // OkHttp reports its own cancel (the user tapped stop) as IOException("Canceled").
    private fun isCallCancelled(e: java.io.IOException) =
        e.message.equals("Canceled", ignoreCase = true)
}

And the loop:

suspend fun <T> run(
    nowMs: () -> Long = System::currentTimeMillis,
    sleep: suspend (Long) -> Unit = { delay(it) },
    block: suspend (attempt: Int) -> T
): T {
    val startedAt = nowMs()
    var attempt = 1
    while (true) {
        try {
            return block(attempt)
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()
            val pause = BACKOFF_MS.getOrElse(attempt - 1) { BACKOFF_MS.last() }
            val outOfTime = nowMs() - startedAt + pause > RESEND_WINDOW_MS
            if (!isTransient(e) || attempt >= MAX_ATTEMPTS || outOfTime) throw e
            attempt++
            sleep(pause)
        }
    }
}

The rules it encodes:

  • Only link failures are retried. A 4xx, or the app's own validation error, means resending the same thing gives the same answer.
  • A user's cancel is never retried. ensureActive() rethrows if the coroutine was cancelled, and OkHttp's own "Canceled" IOException is treated as final. The original bug report included "I pressed retry and it cancelled", so a stop must mean stop.
  • A time budget, not only a count. Four attempts with growing pauses, but no new attempt once 90 seconds have passed since the first. A person waiting for text will not wait forever.
  • Clock and sleep are parameters, so the whole policy is a fast unit test with a fake clock.

A read timeout that scales with the note

One more piece: a fixed 30-second read timeout cut off slow but healthy answers for long notes. The timeout is now 30 s plus half the note's length, capped at 2 minutes, applied by an OkHttp interceptor that reads the duration header the upload already carries:

fun readTimeoutMsFor(audioDurationMs: Long): Long =
    (30_000L + audioDurationMs.coerceAtLeast(0L) / 2).coerceIn(30_000L, 120_000L)

Other calls keep the client's default timeouts.

Takeaways

  • An idempotency key should describe the work, not the request. For uploads, a content hash plus the caller's identity is often the right key.
  • Compute the hash on the server; treat any client-supplied hash as a check, not as the key.
  • Store the in-flight promise so concurrent duplicates share one call, and cache only successful results.
  • Server-side idempotency is what makes aggressive client resends safe. Build it first.
  • Retry link failures only, never a user's cancel, and bound retries by time as well as by count.

Bolo is on Google Play as "Bolo AI Voice Typing & PC Sync" (search "Bolo AI"): https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ashwar.bolo&utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=2026-w45-idempotency. Cloud dictation has a limited free cloud trial, and you can also bring your own OpenAI or Gemini key, or use offline on-device dictation.

title: S3 Select in 2026: Why New Accounts Get MethodNotAllowed, and What to Use Instead
description:
SELECT * FROM S3Object s LIMIT 5

That was the query I expected to work. I had uploaded a tiny CSV to Amazon S3, checked its metadata, and previewed the contents. When I clicked Run Query in Buckets by Serverless Creed, I got this instead:

The specified method is not allowed against this resource.

Changing the SQL didn't resolve it. Running the equivalent operation through AWS CLI returned MethodNotAllowed too.

This post follows that investigation across four scenarios in Buckets v2.8.7 and v2.8.9. It also explains the S3 Select availability change behind a plausible diagnosis, and the alternatives I would consider for a new project in 2026.

What S3 Select was designed to do

S3 Select lets an application send a SQL expression against one S3 object and receive selected records instead of downloading the entire object first.

It supports a subset of SQL over CSV, JSON and Apache Parquet inputs, with CSV or JSON output. For example, an application could request particular employee fields or filter records by department.

The single-object scope matters. A query against S3Object isn't a query across a bucket or a database of related tables.

What changed on July 25, 2024

In its July 2024 announcement, AWS closed new customer access to S3 Select, effective July 25, 2024. Existing eligible customers can continue using it. AWS also stated that it did not plan to introduce new capabilities.

The distinction is eligibility to use S3 Select, rather than simply how old an AWS account is. An older account isn't automatically evidence of existing S3 Select access.

My observed MethodNotAllowed response is consistent with these availability restrictions. However, AWS Support did not independently confirm the test account's eligibility, and the error alone does not establish the exact cause.

That qualification matters throughout the tests below.

The CSV query in Buckets — TC-S3SEL-001

I created a CSV with six employee records and a header row. It was 166 bytes, uncompressed, and encrypted with SSE-S3 (AES256).

The upload, metadata verification and object preview succeeded. In the query dialog, I chose CSV input, None for compression, and CSV output, then submitted the query at the start of this post.


Detail crops from the same testing screenshot: the CSV settings and failure notification.

Buckets displayed the failure rather than query results. Being able to upload and preview the object established that those workflows worked; it did not establish that S3 Select was available.

SSE-S3 also wasn't inherently an incompatible choice: the SelectObjectContent API documentation supports server-side encrypted objects, including SSE-S3.

Reproducing it outside Buckets

I next used AWS CLI to separate the application interface from the underlying service operation. This is the equivalent command with generic resource names:

aws s3api select-object-content \
  --bucket example-test-bucket \
  --key data/report.csv \
  --expression "SELECT * FROM S3Object s LIMIT 5" \
  --expression-type SQL \
  --input-serialization \
    '{"CSV":{"FileHeaderInfo":"USE"},"CompressionType":"NONE"}' \
  --output-serialization '{"CSV":{}}' \
  --region us-east-1 \
  /tmp/select-results.csv

FileHeaderInfo: USE tells S3 Select to treat the first CSV line as a header. The operation and serialization options are documented in the AWS CLI reference.

My independent CLI attempt returned:

An error occurred (MethodNotAllowed) when calling the
SelectObjectContent operation: The specified method is
not allowed against this resource.


The independent CLI attempt returned the same error. Private resource and profile details are covered.

This was the strongest evidence in the investigation: the failure was reproducible without Buckets. It narrowed the investigation, while leaving the exact AWS-side reason unresolved.

Invalid SQL didn't produce a syntax error — TC-S3SEL-002

The next scenario was intended to check SQL error handling. I deliberately submitted:

SELECT FROM S3Object s

I received the same MethodNotAllowed response. Correcting the expression and retrying didn't change the outcome.


Invalid SQL produced the same service response as the corrected query.

The editor remained responsive and let me retry. But I did not verify how Buckets presents an actual SQL syntax error: no parser-specific response was observed. The test also cannot reveal AWS's internal order of request validation.

JSON reached the same boundary — TC-S3SEL-003

I then created an uncompressed JSON Lines file with five employee records, totaling 314 bytes. Buckets identified it as JSON. With JSON input and CSV output selected, I submitted:

SELECT s.name, s.department
FROM S3Object s
WHERE s.department = 'Engineering'


The JSON query also returned MethodNotAllowed; no matching records were returned.

The expression was intended to select names and departments for Engineering employees. That describes the query's intention, rather than an observed result. AWS rejected this request with the same error as the CSV request.

A clearer explanation in Buckets v2.8.9

During the later JSON testing, v2.8.9 gave a more useful explanation of the service restriction. It discussed possible S3 Select availability issues and retained the original AWS error code, response and request identifiers.

The explanation was careful about uncertainty: possible causes included account eligibility and unsupported resource types. The AWS API reference confirms that directory buckets and S3 on Outposts do not support this operation. Those are documented possibilities, not confirmed findings about my test environment.

The expanded response is visible in the BZIP2 screenshot below, with request identifiers covered. It helped explain why repeatedly rewriting the SQL might not resolve this particular failure.

What the compression controls proved — TC-S3SEL-005

Buckets offered None, GZIP and BZIP2 in its compression dropdown. I could select GZIP and BZIP2 successfully.


GZIP was selectable. Selecting an option does not compress the stored object.

I reused the existing uncompressed JSON object and selected BZIP2. No compression-specific mismatch warning appeared before submission. When I ran the query, AWS returned MethodNotAllowed again.


BZIP2 selected for an uncompressed object. The displayed explanation concerns S3 Select availability, not a detected compression mismatch.

The dropdown worked as a UI control. Actual AWS decompression and compression-mismatch handling were not verified. I cannot claim that Buckets detected the mismatch.

AWS's format requirements distinguish these cases:

Input Supported compression
CSV or JSON Uncompressed, GZIP or BZIP2
Parquet Columnar GZIP or Snappy; no whole-object compression

S3 Select also has a 256 KB SQL-expression limit and a 1 MB input/result-record limit. These constraints are separate from service eligibility. Proper compression testing would need working S3 Select access and correctly compressed fixtures as well as mismatch cases.

Separating service behavior from application behavior

These tests made the responsibility boundary clearer:

Responsibility AWS Buckets
Request setup Defines the API and supported formats Collects SQL and input/output options
Execution Evaluates the request and returns data or an error Submits the configured request
Diagnostics Returns the service code and response Displays the response and explains possible causes

The CLI reproduction supports treating this observed failure as an AWS service response rather than assuming a defect in the Buckets SQL editor. It doesn't certify every part of the application: successful execution, syntax-error presentation and compression processing still need verification in an eligible environment.

Amazon Athena as an alternative

For SQL over a dataset spanning many S3 objects, Amazon Athena is a more suitable direction. It is a serverless analytics service that queries S3 data using SQL, with broader analytical capabilities than S3 Select's single-object API.

In a common setup, the AWS Glue Data Catalog stores table metadata: column names and types, data locations, format information and partitions. A crawler can discover that metadata, or it can be defined manually. A crawler is optional; see the Glue catalog documentation.


Illustrative architecture. Glue supplies metadata; it is not an intermediate store for the source records.

After defining a suitable employee table, the equivalent analytical query could be:

SELECT name, department
FROM employees
WHERE department = 'Engineering';

This is an illustrative Athena query, not something successfully executed during these S3 Select tests. Moving to Athena requires table definitions, permissions and result configuration; it isn't just changing an API name.

Where the results go

With customer-managed results, Athena writes to an S3 location selected by the client or workgroup. An enforced workgroup setting takes precedence. For API calls, StartQueryExecution.OutputLocation supplies the client-side location; a console setting alone does not configure API calls. See result-location settings.

Alternatively, a workgroup can enable Athena managed query results. This removes the need to supply your own results bucket. Results are retained for 24 hours at no additional managed-results storage cost, then automatically deleted. This mode does not support query-result reuse.

Costs, limits and when I would process locally

AWS currently illustrates on-demand Athena SQL pricing at US$5 per TB scanned on its pricing page. Check the applicable Region and current rate before estimating a workload. Billing concerns data scanned, rather than just the rows returned. AWS documents rounding to the next MB and a 10 MB minimum per query in its cost-model guidance.

Other models include SQL Capacity Reservations, billed for compute capacity, and Apache Spark, billed for compute use. S3 storage, requests and applicable transfer charges remain relevant, including customer-managed results. Glue catalog usage can incur charges beyond its free allowance; optional crawlers and ETL jobs are billed separately under Glue pricing.

For larger datasets, partitioning, compression and columnar formats such as Parquet can reduce scans. Workgroup scan controls can help constrain query usage.

Athena still has service quotas, including regional concurrency and query timeouts, and a 262,144-byte query-string limit. Its SQL limitations include a 32 MB row/column size ceiling.

For my 166-byte CSV or 314-byte JSON fixture, I would usually download the object and filter it with Python, pandas or DuckDB. That avoids catalog setup for a tiny one-off task, though S3 requests, transfer and local resources still matter. Athena becomes more compelling when the dataset and repeated analytical work justify that setup.

What I learned

No scenario produced successful S3 Select query results. The useful findings were the independent CLI reproduction, the working input controls, and the clearer explanation in v2.8.9.

The lesson I will carry forward is to reproduce an unexpected service error outside the application before deciding which layer needs fixing. Here, that prevented a blocked execution test from becoming an unsupported claim about SQL or compression behavior.

My next article will follow the Glue, Athena and S3 Tables workflow: defining queryable data, running SQL, inspecting result storage and understanding the costs. Those are the next steps to test, rather than outcomes established here.

References

  • AWS: S3 Select availability announcement
  • S3 Select formats and limits · CLI reference
  • Athena User Guide · Pricing
  • Glue Data Catalog
  • Athena result locations · Managed results

title: One Codebase, Two AI Faces: A Spring AI 2.0 Assistant and an MCP Server Sharing the Same Tools
description:
Most Spring AI demos stop at a chat box. Most MCP demos stop at a "hello world" tool. I wanted to see what happens when one real application needs both: an AI assistant for the people logged into the app, and an MCP server so external clients (MCP Inspector, Claude, an IDE agent) can query the same data.

The result is Control Escolar, a school management system built with Spring Boot 4.1.1 and Spring AI 2.0.1. It manages students, teachers, subjects, classrooms, schedules, grades and reports. On top of that it has two AI faces:

  • an internal assistant built on ChatClient, with chat memory, RAG, guardrails, streaming and structured output;
  • an MCP server over Streamable HTTP with 16 tools, 5 resources, a resource template, 3 prompts and argument completions.

The interesting part is that both faces run on the same Java methods. This article walks through how that works, the decisions that mattered, and the one thing I deliberately did not share between them.

The app's domain is in Spanish (it targets a Mexican school), so you'll see names like Alumno (student), Calificacion (grade) and matricula (student ID) in the code.

The problem: two consumers, one source of truth

A school system has a lot of read-heavy questions: What is this student's average? Who is at risk of failing? What is group 2A's schedule? What does the rulebook say about minimum attendance?

There are two very different audiences for those questions:

  1. Logged-in users (teachers, principals, secretaries) who want to ask in natural language from inside the app. They have a session, a role, and a conversation history.
  2. External AI clients that speak the Model Context Protocol. They have no session; they just discover tools and call them.

The naive approach is to write the logic twice: a set of @Tool methods for the ChatClient and a separate MCP server. That doubles the code, and the two versions drift apart the first time someone fixes a bug in only one of them.

The second naive approach is to expose everything to both. That is how you end up with an unauthenticated endpoint that can write grades.

What I wanted:

  • One implementation of each read operation.
  • Different capabilities per audience: the chat can write (with role checks), MCP can only read.
  • Graceful degradation: the app must start and the MCP tools must keep working without an OpenAI key.

The solution: dual-annotated tool methods

Spring AI 2.0 has two annotation families that fit together nicely:

  • @Tool / @ToolParam register a method as a tool for ChatClient.
  • @McpTool / @McpToolParam (plus @McpResource, @McpPrompt, @McpComplete) register it with the MCP server when spring.ai.mcp.server.annotation-scanner.enabled=true.

Nothing stops you from putting both on the same method:

@Component
public class EscolarTools {

    // Registered for the internal ChatClient...
    @Tool(description = "Obtiene el promedio general de un alumno por su matrícula.")
    // ...and for external MCP clients, under a kebab-case name.
    @McpTool(name = "promedio-alumno",
            description = "Obtiene el promedio general de un alumno por su matrícula.")
    public String promedioAlumno(
            @ToolParam(description = "Matrícula del alumno")
            @McpToolParam(description = "Matrícula del alumno") String matricula) {
        Alumno alumno = alumnoService.buscarPorMatricula(matricula);
        if (alumno == null) {
            return "No se encontró ningún alumno con la matrícula " + matricula + ".";
        }
        Double promedio = calificacionService.promedioPorAlumno(alumno.getId());
        if (promedio == null) {
            return "El alumno " + alumno.getNombreCompleto() + " aún no tiene calificaciones registradas.";
        }
        return "El promedio general del alumno " + alumno.getNombreCompleto()
                + " es " + formatoPromedio(promedio) + ".";
    }
}

The class sits on top of the regular service layer (AlumnoService, CalificacionService, ...), so the web controllers, the REST API, the chat and the MCP server all hit the same business logic.

Two small but useful details:

  • Return friendly strings, not exceptions. A missing student is an answer the model can relay, not a stack trace.
  • Tool names differ per protocol. In MCP the tool is promedio-alumno; in the ChatClient it is the Java method name, promedioAlumno. That is fine: each audience discovers tools through its own channel.

MCP gets more than tools

The MCP side also exposes resources, a resource template, prompts and completions from the same class:

@McpResource(uri = "escolar://alumnos/{matricula}",
        name = "ficha-alumno",
        description = "Ficha de un alumno en JSON: datos, grupo, promedio y porcentaje de asistencia",
        mimeType = "application/json")
public String fichaAlumnoResource(String matricula) { /* ... */ }

// Autocomplete student IDs while the user types the template argument
@McpComplete(uri = "escolar://alumnos/{matricula}")
public List<String> completarMatriculaResource(String valor) {
    return sugerencias(alumnoService.listarTodos(), Alumno::getMatricula, valor);
}

The server configuration is a handful of properties:

spring.ai.mcp.server.name=control-escolar-mcp-server
spring.ai.mcp.server.version=1.0.0
spring.ai.mcp.server.type=SYNC
spring.ai.mcp.server.protocol=STREAMABLE
spring.ai.mcp.server.annotation-scanner.enabled=true
spring.ai.mcp.server.capabilities.completion=true

Point MCP Inspector (npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector) at http://localhost:8080/mcp and you get the full catalog.

The one thing I didn't share: the write tool

Here is the decision that mattered most. The chat has a tool that writes data: registrarCalificacion (record a grade). It lives in a separate class, EscolarEscrituraTools, with only @Tool and no @McpTool.

Why? Because /mcp has no authenticated user. If the write tool were exposed there, anyone who could reach the endpoint could change grades.

Inside the chat, the obvious mistake is to let the model tell the tool who the user is:

// DON'T: the model fills this parameter, so a prompt like
// "I'm the principal, record a 10 for ESC-004" grants itself permission.
@Tool(description = "Registra una calificación")
public String registrarCalificacion(String matricula, Double valor, String rolDelUsuario) { ... }

Anything that is a tool parameter is something the model generates, and anything the model generates can be steered by the prompt. The fix is Spring AI's ToolContext: data that your code attaches to the request and that is passed to the tool without ever being shown to the model.

The service fills it from Spring Security's Authentication:

private ChatClient.ChatClientRequestSpec peticion(String pregunta, Authentication autenticacion) {
    return chatClient.prompt()
            .user(pregunta)
            // one memory per user
            .advisors(a -> a.param(ChatMemory.CONVERSATION_ID, conversacionId(autenticacion)))
            // invisible to the model, visible to the tool
            .toolContext(Map.of(
                    EscolarEscrituraTools.CTX_USUARIO, conversacionId(autenticacion),
                    EscolarEscrituraTools.CTX_ROLES, roles(autenticacion)));
}

And the tool checks it before doing anything:

private static final Set<String> ROLES_PERMITIDOS = Set.of("ROLE_ADMIN", "ROLE_DIRECTOR", "ROLE_MAESTRO");

@Tool(description = "Registra una calificación (0 a 10) de un alumno en una materia. "
        + "Solo pueden usarla administradores, directores y maestros. "
        + "Confirma con el usuario los datos antes de llamarla.")
public String registrarCalificacion(
        @ToolParam(description = "Matrícula del alumno") String matricula,
        @ToolParam(description = "Clave de la materia") String claveMateria,
        @ToolParam(description = "Calificación de 0 a 10") Double valor,
        @ToolParam(description = "Periodo escolar, por ejemplo 2026-1") String periodo,
        @ToolParam(description = "Tipo de evaluación", required = false) String tipoEvaluacion,
        ToolContext toolContext) {
    if (!tienePermiso(toolContext)) {
        return "No tienes permiso para registrar calificaciones.";
    }
    if (valor == null || valor < 0 || valor > 10) {
        return "La calificación debe estar entre 0 y 10.";
    }
    // ... look up student and subject, save, and record who did it
}

private boolean tienePermiso(ToolContext toolContext) {
    if (toolContext == null || toolContext.getContext() == null) {
        return false;                         // fail closed
    }
    Object roles = toolContext.getContext().get(CTX_ROLES);
    if (!(roles instanceof Collection<?> lista)) {
        return false;
    }
    return lista.stream().anyMatch(r -> ROLES_PERMITIDOS.contains(String.valueOf(r)));
}

Note the fail-closed default: no context, no permission. The saved grade also records which user triggered it, so the audit trail does not depend on the model either.

The assistant: an advisor chain where order matters

The internal ChatClient is built once at startup with the shared read tools, the write tool, the knowledge base and a chain of advisors:

chatClient = builder
        .defaultSystem(SISTEMA)
        .defaultTools(escolarTools, escrituraTools, conocimiento)
        .defaultAdvisors(advisorsDelChat())
        .build();

private List<Advisor> advisorsDelChat() {
    List<Advisor> advisors = new ArrayList<>();
    advisors.add(SafeGuardAdvisor.builder()
            .sensitiveWords(palabrasBloqueadas())
            .failureResponse("Por seguridad no puedo responder preguntas sobre datos sensibles.")
            // Before memory: blocked text never reaches the history.
            .order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)
            .build());
    advisors.add(MessageChatMemoryAdvisor.builder(chatMemory).build());   // JDBC-backed
    if (conocimiento.getVectorStore() != null) {
        advisors.add(QuestionAnswerAdvisor.builder(conocimiento.getVectorStore())
                .searchRequest(SearchRequest.builder().topK(3).similarityThreshold(0.5).build())
                .promptTemplate(new PromptTemplate(PLANTILLA_RAG))
                .build());
    }
    advisors.add(SimpleLoggerAdvisor.builder().build());
    return advisors;
}

Three lessons from this chain:

1. Put the guardrail before the memory. If SafeGuardAdvisor runs after MessageChatMemoryAdvisor, a blocked question is still saved to the history. From then on every request in that conversation carries a sensitive word, so the guard blocks the whole conversation. Giving the guard HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE means blocked text never reaches memory.

2. Customize the RAG template when you also have tools. The default QuestionAnswerAdvisor template tells the model to answer only from the retrieved context. That is great for pure Q&A, but with the default template the assistant stopped using its tools: the answer had to come from the retrieved rulebook fragments, even when the question was about a student's grades. My template presents the retrieved fragments as optional reference for questions about rules and dates, and tells the model to keep using tools for everything else.

3. Memory is per user, and persistent. JdbcChatMemoryRepository stores messages in SPRING_AI_CHAT_MEMORY in the same database, and the conversation ID is the Spring Security username. A "New conversation" button simply calls chatMemory.clear(conversationId).

Streaming and structured output

The same request spec serves both blocking and streaming calls. The assistant page uses Server-Sent Events:

public Flux<String> preguntarStream(String pregunta, Authentication autenticacion) {
    return peticion(pregunta, autenticacion).stream().content()
            .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(mensajeError(e, pregunta)));
}

For a student risk analysis I use a second client cloned from the same builder, without memory or RAG, and ask for a Java record:

public record AnalisisAlumno(String matricula, String nombre, Double promedio,
                             Double porcentajeAsistencia, String nivelRiesgo,
                             List<String> fortalezas, List<String> areasDeOportunidad,
                             List<String> recomendaciones) { }

return analisisClient.prompt()
        .user("Analiza al alumno con matrícula " + matricula + ".")
        .call()
        .entity(AnalisisAlumno.class);

Keeping it separate means an analysis never pollutes (or is influenced by) the user's chat history. The system prompt defines the risk thresholds explicitly (average below 6.0 or attendance below 80 % means HIGH) so the model classifies instead of guessing.

Graceful degradation without an API key

I wanted mvn spring-boot:run to work for anyone who clones the repo, key or no key:

spring.ai.openai.api-key=${OPENAI_API_KEY:demo}

At startup the service checks whether the key is real (not missing, not blank, not demo). If it isn't, chatClient stays null, the assistant replies with a setup message instead of throwing, and the /api/ia/analisis-alumno endpoint returns 503. The MCP tools don't need the model at all, so they keep working. Even consultar-reglamento falls back from embeddings to a keyword search over the same Markdown files.

Best practices I'd keep

  • Share read logic, isolate write logic. Dual annotations are great for queries. Anything that changes data deserves its own class and an explicit decision about who can reach it.
  • Never let the model assert identity. Roles, user IDs and tenants belong in ToolContext, filled from your security context.
  • Fail closed when that context is missing.
  • Order advisors deliberately. Guardrails first, then memory, then retrieval, then logging.
  • Return messages, not exceptions, from tools. The model can explain "student not found"; it can't explain a 500.
  • Protect /mcp before production. In this project it is permitAll for local testing with MCP Inspector; a real deployment needs a token or a private network.

Observability

With Micrometer and Actuator, Spring AI publishes gen_ai_client_* metrics (token usage, latency, tool calls) at /actuator/prometheus. Prompt and completion logging stay off by default (log-prompt=false), so student data doesn't end up in your logs unless you ask for it.

What's next

The vector store is an in-memory SimpleVectorStore re-indexed on every start, which is fine for two Markdown documents but not for a real knowledge base; PGVector is the obvious next step. Attendance has data and an AI tool but no screens yet, and the MCP endpoint needs authentication.

Wrapping up

The key takeaway: a single set of well-written tool methods can serve both an in-app assistant and the wider MCP ecosystem, as long as you are deliberate about the one boundary that matters, who is allowed to change data, and you keep that decision out of the model's hands.

  • Source code: https://github.com/josesaid/control-escolar-spring-ai-mcp
  • Project page: https://josesaid.github.io/control-escolar-spring-ai-mcp/

Clone it, run mvn spring-boot:run, log in as admin / admin123 and connect MCP Inspector to http://localhost:8080/mcp. I'd love to hear how you're splitting responsibilities between ChatClient tools and MCP in your own projects.

title: HTML Semantic Tags Explained: header, nav, main, article, section and footer
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

HTML semantic tags are elements that clearly describe their meaning and the type of content inside them, for both browsers and people reading the code. Tags such as header, nav, main, article, section and footer tell everyone what each part of a page is for, without guessing from class names. A header is for introductory content, nav is for main links, main holds the primary content, article holds a self contained piece, section groups related content, and footer holds closing information. Using them makes your pages easier to read, more accessible for screen readers, and clearer for search engines.

What Are Semantic Tags, in Simple Words?

The word semantic simply means related to meaning. A semantic tag carries meaning in its name. When you see a nav element in code, you instantly know it contains navigation links. When you see a generic div element, you know almost nothing. It could be a menu, a product card, a warning box, or just a wrapper someone added at midnight and forgot about.

Before HTML5, developers built almost every layout with div elements and added class names like header or footer to explain them. That worked visually, but the browser had no idea what those boxes really were. HTML5 gave us proper elements with built in meaning, so structure is clear in the markup itself.

If you are still getting comfortable with how a page is put together, it helps to first understand the difference between HTML, CSS and JavaScript. HTML provides this structure and meaning, CSS styles it, and JavaScript adds behaviour. Semantic tags belong firmly to the HTML side of that team.

Why Semantic Tags Matter

First, accessibility. Screen readers use landmarks such as header, nav, main and footer to help users jump straight to the part they need, instead of listening to every link on every page. That is a real kindness, not just a technical detail.

Second, search engines read your structure to understand a page. Clear structure does not magically rank you first, and anyone who promises that is selling magic beans. It does make content easier to parse, which supports good SEO. Third, maintainability: six months later, main and article explain themselves, while a pile of div elements named box2-wrapper-final does not. Browsers can also use the structure for reader modes that pull out the main article cleanly.

The HTML reference page on MDN, developer.mozilla.org, which lists the semantic elements.

The Main Tags: header, nav and main

The header element represents introductory content for a page or a section. On a full page, it usually holds the logo, site title and search box. An article can also have its own header, with its title, author and publish date.

The nav element is for a major block of navigation links, such as the main menu or a table of contents. You do not need to wrap every small group of links in it. The full list of elements is documented in the HTML reference on MDN at developer.mozilla.org, which is worth bookmarking.

The main element holds the dominant, unique content of the page. There should be only one visible main per page, and it should not include repeated parts such as sidebars, logos or the main menu.

article, section and footer Explained

An article represents a complete, self contained piece that could make sense on its own if shared separately. Blog posts, news stories, reviews and comments are classic examples. A simple test helps: if you copied that block elsewhere and it still made sense, it is probably an article.

A section groups related content together, usually with its own heading. Use it to divide a long page into chapters, such as features, pricing and testimonials. If you are grouping things only for styling, a plain div is still the honest choice.

The footer holds closing information, such as copyright text, contact details and policy links. An article footer might hold the author bio or tags. Two helpful relatives are aside, for loosely related content such as a sidebar, and figure, which groups media with its caption.

A Complete Page Layout Example

Here is a small but complete page that uses all six tags together. Notice how the structure tells the story of the page before any CSS is added. Our guide to CSS Flexbox explained with examples is a good next step for styling it.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My Simple Blog</title>
</head>
<body>
  <header>
    <h1>My Simple Blog</h1>
    <p>Notes on learning web development.</p>
  </header>
  <nav>
    <a href="/">Home</a>
    <a href="/about">About</a>
    <a href="/contact">Contact</a>
  </nav>
  <main>
    <article>
      <header>
        <h2>My First Post</h2>
        <p>Published on 6 November 2026</p>
      </header>
      <section>
        <h3>Introduction</h3>
        <p>This is the opening part of the post.</p>
      </section>
      <section>
        <h3>Main Points</h3>
        <p>This section holds the key ideas.</p>
      </section>
      <footer>
        <p>Written by a beginner developer.</p>
      </footer>
    </article>
  </main>
  <footer>
    <p>Copyright 2026 My Simple Blog.</p>
  </footer>
</body>
</html>

Notice that header and footer appear twice, once for the page and once inside the article, and that is perfectly valid. Also notice the heading order: h1, then h2, then h3. Keeping headings in order helps readers and assistive tools follow the outline.

Semantic Tags vs Generic div Elements

Div elements are not banned, and you do not need to delete every one of them in a panic. A div is still the right tool for a pure styling wrapper with no meaning. The point is to choose the semantic element when a clear one exists, and fall back to div only when none fits.

Need Semantic choice Generic div version
Top of a page or article header, meaning is clear to browsers and screen readers div with a class, meaning only in the class name
Main navigation links nav, announced as a navigation landmark div with a class, no landmark created
Primary page content main, one per page, easy to jump to div with a class, tools must guess its role
Independent piece of content article, can stand alone and be shared div with a class, relationship stays unclear
Thematic group with a heading section, groups related content clearly div with a class, grouping is visual only
Closing information footer, recognised as closing content div with a class, no built in meaning

The visual result can look identical in both columns. The difference is what the code communicates behind the scenes. MDN also explains grouping in its guide to content categories on MDN.

Common Mistakes and Good Habits

A common mistake is using section for everything. If a block has no heading and no real meaning, a div is cleaner. Another mistake is having more than one main, or placing the site header and menu inside main.

Avoid skipping heading levels just to change font size. Use CSS for size, and keep headings in order. Do not replace a button with a styled div either: a real button gives you keyboard support for free.

Good habits are simple. Sketch each page outline with header, nav, main and footer, then add article and section where content naturally splits. Ask whether the structure still makes sense with styling removed. If it does, you are on the right track.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do semantic tags change how a page looks?

No, not by themselves. Most semantic elements look like plain block boxes by default. You still use CSS to style them, just as you would style a div.

Can I use more than one header or footer on a page?

Yes. A page can have a header and footer for the whole page, and each article or section can have its own. Each one belongs to its nearest parent section.

How many main elements can a page have?

Only one visible main element per page. It must hold the unique, primary content of that page, not menus, logos or other repeated blocks.

Is a section better than a div?

Use section when you are grouping related content, usually with a heading. Use div when the group exists only for styling and carries no meaning of its own.

Do semantic tags help SEO?

They help search engines understand your structure more clearly, which supports good SEO. They are not a ranking shortcut, so combine them with helpful content and clear headings.

Conclusion

Semantic tags are a small habit with a long payoff. Use header for introductions, nav for major links, main for the unique content, article for self contained pieces, section for related groups, and footer for closing information. Your code becomes easier to read, your pages become kinder to assistive tools, and search engines get a clearer picture. Start with your next small page, write the outline first, and let the tags describe the content honestly. That is most of the job done.

title: WeightLoop: Weight-Space Programming with Experimental Feedback
description:
arXiv:2611.07319v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) shows that language models can reason about and rewrite neural network weights; recursive self-improvement (RSI) motivates feedback-driven improvement. Models guiding experiments receive concrete feedback: completed assays reveal prediction errors and inform what to test next. We introduce WeightLoop, a framework that turns experimental feedback into persistent updates to deployed predictors. GPT-6 Astra inspects a task specification and the model implementation, then writes a bounded, reusable parameter-editing program. As new measurements arrive, the program identifies prediction discrepancies, validates candidate edits using observed outcomes, and writes the selected changes back to the original model. The editor remains fixed while the predictor evolves, enabling repeated updates without further LLM calls or gradient retraining while preserving the original inference interface. In offline replay, targeted edits improve mean ranking utility in seven of eight endpoint-budget settings (all eight versus random edits) and mean final discovery across three sequential tasks. WeightLoop connects WSP with an RSI-inspired improvement loop, making experimental evidence a direct driver of model change and subsequent decisions.

title: Node.js Support Routing: Keeping Email and SMS Providers Replaceable
description:
For a Node.js contact form that routes customers to support queues, keep the queue decision and its evidence in your application, then put every email or SMS provider behind a small adapter. The best provider is the one you can remove without changing the routing policy.

Short answer: use SendGrid when email deliverability is the main concern, Twilio when SMS is the main concern, and Sendinblue when a smaller system needs both channels. Infrai is a reasonable option when one REST surface, one key, and one bill reduce the operational boundary around several backend services. None of these choices removes the need to model compliance evidence yourself.

The useful mental model is a ticket, not a message. A form submission becomes a routing decision, an evidence record, and only then a delivery request. That ordering matters when a provider changes, a recipient opts out, or an auditor asks why a message was sent.

What belongs inside the replaceable boundary?

Start with the facts your support team owns: the contact-form event ID, the selected queue, the destination class, the channel, the template revision, the consent decision, and the time of the decision. The adapter can add a provider name, request ID, and raw status. It should not decide whether a question belongs to Billing or Account Access.

I initially treated a common send() method as enough portability. It is not. Email and SMS have different consent rules, status vocabularies, cancellation behavior, and regional constraints. A common method is useful only if the evidence record keeps the distinctions that the method hides.

Here is the small contract I would put between the router and its delivery implementations. The example is intentionally provider-neutral. Its job is to make the migration boundary visible.

type Channel = "email" | "sms";
type Queue = "billing" | "account-access" | "general";

type NotificationIntent = {
  eventId: string;
  queue: Queue;
  channel: Channel;
  destination: string;
  templateRevision: string;
  body: string;
  consentRecordedAt: string;
};

type DeliveryAcceptance = {
  provider: string;
  providerRequestId: string;
  acceptedAt: string;
};

interface NotificationAdapter {
  send(intent: NotificationIntent): Promise<DeliveryAcceptance>;
}

async function notifyQueue(
  intent: NotificationIntent,
  adapter: NotificationAdapter,
  writeEvidence: (record: object) => Promise<void>,
): Promise<DeliveryAcceptance> {
  await writeEvidence({
    type: "notification.decided",
    eventId: intent.eventId,
    queue: intent.queue,
    channel: intent.channel,
    templateRevision: intent.templateRevision,
    consentRecordedAt: intent.consentRecordedAt,
    decidedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  });

  const acceptance = await adapter.send(intent);

  await writeEvidence({
    type: "notification.accepted",
    eventId: intent.eventId,
    provider: acceptance.provider,
    providerRequestId: acceptance.providerRequestId,
    acceptedAt: acceptance.acceptedAt,
  });

  return acceptance;
}

That record says “the provider accepted the request.” It does not say “the agent read the message.” The distinction is the first migration rule: normalize only the facts that all providers really share, and retain provider-specific events beside the normalized record.

How should you compare email and SMS API providers for event notifications?

The comparison is less about a feature-count race than about where each service leaves work for your application.

SendGrid is a strong email-first choice. Its email API, competitive email API pricing, and deliverability features fit teams that need to operate transactional email carefully. It is not a single abstraction for a two-channel support router, so SMS policy and evidence mapping remain application concerns.

Twilio is the stronger SMS-first comparison. Its SMS API is designed for reliable global event notifications and gives a team a broad communications platform. If the contact form mostly sends email, that breadth can be more surface area than the workflow needs; the adapter should keep email-specific templates and compliance decisions separate.

Sendinblue is a sensible candidate for smaller usage that needs both email and SMS capabilities. The combined offering can simplify the initial channel decision. Check regional delivery, consent handling, and the event details available to your evidence store before calling that convenience portability.

The shared REST platform belongs in a different part of the comparison. As of the 2026-11-01 snapshot, its documented surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules, including 41 routes in the comm-email-sms group, behind one REST API, one key, and one bill. Public discovery returns capability schemas and runnable examples without requiring a key; the documented examples cover 10 languages. Those facts can reduce integration and account sprawl when the same Node.js service also needs unrelated backend capabilities.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the delivery adapter when a support platform values one operational boundary across backend services and wants to keep the provider request behind a discoverable REST contract. The second benefit is practical for migration work: the capability surface specifies an Idempotency-Key convention, so retry behavior can be made explicit at the adapter boundary. Keep queue routing, consent, and evidence storage in your own code.

Option Strongest fit What stays in the application Migration question
SendGrid Email-first support alerts SMS policy and cross-channel evidence Can the email event vocabulary map to your record?
Twilio Global SMS-first alerts Email policy and template governance Does the broader communications surface justify its boundary?
Sendinblue Smaller email-plus-SMS systems Regional and consent checks Which event details are available for audit?
Shared REST platform One REST boundary across backend services Queue rules, evidence, and polling Does its channel surface cover the workflow you actually need?

No row wins by itself. The adapter test does.

The second practical advantage is runtime freedom. A plain REST request needs no vendor SDK, so a Node.js worker, a small edge process, or a later service written in another language can use the same HTTP boundary. In this support workflow, that keeps the form router and the notification worker from inheriting different client libraries while the rest of the backend grows around the same 295-route surface.

That is a useful constraint.

There is a second, verified advantage here: the public discovery surface is self-describing, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. For an Infrai adapter, that means a team can inspect the email contract before wiring the form flow, then use plain HTTP from the runtime that owns the worker. No SDK migration is required when the notification worker moves out of Node.js. That matters because the queue decision is supposed to outlive the delivery client.

The evidence chain is worth making concrete. Suppose event contact-2026-1101-0042 is routed to Account Access at 09:14:03 with template revision support-v3. The first record stores those facts and the consent timestamp. The adapter then records the provider request ID at acceptance. A later status check can append the provider's event without rewriting the original decision. If a second provider is tested, it receives the same event ID and template revision, while only the adapter-specific request and status fields change. This is the difference between comparing providers at the boundary and comparing them by screenshots of their dashboards.

How do you test a provider switch before it hurts?

Use the same synthetic contact-form event against each candidate. Route it to a fixed queue, send one email, send one SMS, and record the request IDs. Then remove the adapter and rerun the routing test. If the queue decision changes, provider details have leaked upward.

The test should also inspect the exit path. Can a retry carry the same client-supplied idempotency key? Can a duplicate submission be distinguished from a retry? Can the record show consent and template revision before the provider call? Can the system tell acceptance from later delivery? A green API response answers only one of those questions.

For this adapter, the relevant email operation is POST /v1/email/send. Use the discovery document for the exact request schema instead of guessing fields in application code. The following snippet makes that boundary executable without inventing an email body: it fetches the public schema, uses the environment key convention, retries a rate-limited read once, and surfaces the response body for every other failure.

async function discoverEmailSend(): Promise<unknown> {
  let delayMs = 500;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/email.send", {
      method: "GET",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY ?? ""}`,
      },
    });

    if (response.ok) {
      return response.json();
    }

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 2) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : delayMs;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
      delayMs *= 2;
      continue;
    }

    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed with HTTP ${response.status}: ${detail}`);
  }

  throw new Error("Discovery failed after retries");
}

The returned schema is input to the adapter, not to the queue router. For a retryable POST /v1/email/send, add a client-supplied Idempotency-Key, honor Retry-After, and preserve non-2xx response bodies. Keep it boring.

The same discipline keeps the adapter honest across providers. Do not flatten SMS cancellation and email scheduling into one pretend-common feature. Infrai has POST /v1/sms/cancel/{id}, while email scheduled sends have no cancellation route. That difference belongs in capability checks and evidence, not in a misleading universal interface.

What are the two objections to this design?

The first objection is latency: polling is less convenient than a push event. It is a valid objection. Neither the email nor SMS namespace provides webhook event pushes, so multi-channel orchestration that depends on real-time provider events is limited by polling. A system that requires webhook-driven state changes should prefer a specialist or direct competitor whose contract meets that requirement. This is the main trade-off, and it is a real reason not to choose the shared boundary.

The second objection is compliance coverage. A provider API is not proof of domestic compliance. Infrai's domestic email vendor is still pending, so it cannot be used as a domestic-compliance basis. There is also no hosted email OTP interface, no SMTP relay, and no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. SMS geographic anti-abuse fences and per-country billing circuit breakers remain business-layer work.

Those limits make the choice clearer. SendGrid fits email depth. Twilio fits global SMS. Sendinblue fits a smaller dual-channel deployment. Infrai fits a team that values a single, discoverable REST boundary and explicit retry conventions, provided polling and channel gaps are acceptable.

For unsubscribe behavior, apply the policy that matches the message category and consult RFC 8058 for one-click email unsubscribe details. For the Infrai boundary, start with the email discovery schema, then hide that request shape behind the adapter.

References

  • SendGrid Mail Send API
  • Twilio Programmable Messaging API
  • Brevo API documentation
  • RFC 8058: One-Click Unsubscribe
  • Infrai email.send discovery schema

title: A Proxy-Based Method for Measuring Racial Disparities in~Text-to-Image~Generators
description:
arXiv:2611.07132v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present an automated method for auditing text-to-image generators for representational bias against ground-truth demographic benchmarks. Our approach adapts the racial proxy variables used in U.S. antidiscrimination law to provide a fine-grained comparative analysis of variations in racial representation in generated images. We classify each generated image by race and then compare the model's distribution to publicly available demographic benchmark data to identify patterns of over- and under-representation. We also measure skin tone using CIELAB values and calculate cosine similarity amongst groups of images in order to capture biases that don't show up in demographic comparisons such as differences in image quality across races and skin tones. We report on experiments testing three models (Imagen 4 Fast, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo, and Flux Schnell) using three categories of proxies (geographic, occupational, and surname) and 50 variants within each category. We find notable variation across the models as well as by proxy category. For example, Imagen 4 Fast overrepresents white classified images more than the other models tested and produces images with lighter, more homogeneous skin tones. Imagen 4 Fast also had the largest representational disparity for Black demographics among surname and geographical prompts. Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo produces results that overall diverge most from census data but yield the most diverse range of skin tones. Our method yields a generalizable and legally-grounded auditing tool that surfaces detailed information about model outputs without relying on implicit normative definitions of fairness.

title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
description:
arXiv:2611.06962v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.

title: How to Create an AI Mini Drama with the Chained Together Effect
description:
Short-form video content is changing the way people tell stories online. Instead of producing long videos with complicated scripts, expensive equipment, and multiple actors, creators are experimenting with AI tools to turn simple ideas into entertaining mini dramas.

One interesting concept is the Chained Together effect. Imagine two characters connected by a chain, unable to move independently. They might be strangers, rivals, friends, or even a couple. Every movement creates a new challenge, and every disagreement can become part of the story.

This simple concept creates plenty of opportunities for comedy, suspense, emotional storytelling, and unexpected plot twists.

In this article, we'll explore how to turn this idea into an AI-generated vertical drama using Textideo.

1. Why the Chained Together Concept Works for Short Videos

A good short video needs an interesting hook. The audience should understand the situation almost immediately and have a reason to keep watching.

The Chained Together concept naturally creates conflict.

For example:

  • Two strangers wake up in an unfamiliar room, connected by a chain.
  • A couple tries to go shopping but cannot agree on which direction to walk.
  • Two rivals must cooperate to escape a dangerous location.
  • A funny argument turns into an unexpected friendship.
  • One character wants to leave, but the other refuses to let go.

These scenarios are easy to understand and provide opportunities for unexpected developments.

More importantly, the same characters and central conflict can be developed across multiple episodes. This makes the format interesting for creators who want to build a recurring short-video series instead of publishing unrelated clips.

2. Create a Chained Together AI Drama with Textideo

Textideo offers a dedicated Chained Together AI Drama Generator designed to turn a simple story premise into a vertical mini drama.

Instead of manually creating every scene from scratch, creators can start with a basic idea and use AI to develop the story.

The workflow focuses on several important elements:

Character Creation

Describe your two main characters or upload reference photos. You can establish their appearance, hairstyles, clothing, and other recognizable details.

Story Development

Provide a short premise describing what happens and why the characters are connected. The story engine organizes the idea into a hook, escalation, reversal, and cliffhanger.

Visual Consistency

Keeping the same characters throughout a series is one of the biggest challenges in AI video production. A consistent character setup helps maintain recognizable faces, clothing, and the chain across different scenes.

Vertical Video Generation

The output is designed for a 9:16 vertical format, making it suitable for TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts.

You can explore the effect here:

Try the Chained Together AI Drama Generator

3. Three Story Ideas You Can Experiment With

If you are unsure what to create first, here are three concepts worth exploring.

Idea 1: The Impossible Escape

Two strangers wake up at the bottom of a mysterious underground structure. Their wrists are connected by a heavy chain, and the only way out is to work together.

One character wants to climb immediately, while the other notices something strange on the wall.

Just when they think they have found an exit, they discover that the real challenge has only begun.

This concept works well for suspenseful storytelling and multi-episode adventures.

Idea 2: The Couple Who Cannot Separate

A couple gets connected by a chain after a mysterious incident.

They try to complete ordinary activities such as cooking, shopping, driving, and walking their dog. However, every simple task becomes a hilarious challenge because they cannot move independently.

This is a great direction for relatable comedy and relationship-themed content.

Idea 3: Enemies Forced to Cooperate

Two characters who strongly dislike each other suddenly find themselves chained together.

At first, they constantly argue and blame each other. But when they encounter a bigger problem, they have no choice but to cooperate.

The story gradually changes from conflict to teamwork, with an unexpected twist at the end.

This idea offers plenty of opportunities for emotional moments and cliffhangers.

4. How to Structure an Engaging AI Mini Drama

Generating attractive visuals is only one part of creating a good video. A strong story structure is equally important.

A simple four-part structure can help:

Part 1: The Hook

Introduce the unusual situation immediately. Show the two characters connected by a chain and create a question in the viewer's mind.

Part 2: The Conflict

Give the characters different goals. One wants to escape, while the other has a completely different plan.

Part 3: The Twist

Introduce an unexpected event that changes their relationship or makes the situation more complicated.

Part 4: The Cliffhanger

End with an unanswered question or a surprising discovery that encourages viewers to watch the next episode.

For example, the first episode could end with one character discovering that the chain is connected to something much more mysterious than they originally thought.

This approach gives viewers a reason to return instead of treating every video as an isolated piece of content.

5. Tips for Maintaining Character Consistency

Character consistency is one of the most challenging aspects of AI-generated storytelling.

A character might look different between scenes if their visual details are not clearly established.

Here are a few practical tips:

  • Define the characters before generating the first episode.
  • Use consistent reference photos whenever possible.
  • Keep hairstyles, clothing, and recognizable accessories unchanged.
  • Describe the chain and its position consistently.
  • Review individual scenes before continuing with the next episode.

Textideo's workflow is designed to carry character and visual references forward, helping creators build a more connected series.

It is also useful to regenerate only the scene that needs improvement rather than restarting the entire story.

6. Where Can You Publish Your AI Drama?

Once your video is ready, you can adapt it for different short-form content platforms.

TikTok: Use a strong opening scene and an unexpected ending to encourage comments and discussions.

Instagram Reels: Focus on visually interesting scenes and emotional moments that viewers may want to share.

YouTube Shorts: Build a sequence of connected episodes so viewers can follow the story over time.

A useful strategy is to treat each video as one chapter of a larger story. You can publish several episodes and use the ending of each one to introduce the next.

Remember to review generated content before publishing and make sure you have permission to use any reference photos featuring other people.

Final Thoughts

AI video generation is creating new possibilities for independent creators. A simple idea, such as two characters connected by a chain, can become the foundation for an entire short drama series.

You don't necessarily need a film crew, professional actors, or complicated editing software to start experimenting with this format.

If you want to explore this concept, try the Textideo Chained Together AI Drama Generator and turn your own story idea into a vertical AI mini drama.

Sometimes, the most interesting stories begin when two characters have absolutely no choice but to stay together.

title: TCSExam: Evaluating Frontier LLMs on the Full Range of TCS Research
description:
arXiv:2611.07962v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) advance theoretical computer science and resolve its long-standing open conjectures? To study progress toward this goal, we introduce TCSExam, a unified framework and benchmark covering the full range of TCS research. It evaluates theorem proving, solver engineering, and constructions alongside direct attempts to resolve open conjectures, capturing both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward long-standing research goals. TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed tasks, with submissions checked by the Lean kernel or an executable task checker. TCSExam-Lite selects 20 tasks, five per track, reducing the number of task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget. We evaluate eight agents on Full and nine on Lite. The TCSExam Index combines all four tracks: GPT-6 Astra leads Full (71.9), and Opus 5.5 leads Lite (72.3). Full and Lite rankings are strongly aligned across eight shared agents (Spearman's $\rho=0.93$), supporting Lite as a compact, discriminative benchmark. The evaluations yield improved solver outputs and mathematical constructions, together with independently verified special cases and bounds from open-conjecture attempts. TCSExam provides an extensible framework with task sources, Docker build recipes, and evaluation tools for reproducible use.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python is now a first-class language and runtime on Vercel. Build APIs, full-stack applications, and AI agents with native Python SDKs and a shared development and deployment workflow for your Python backend and JavaScript frontend.

Python framework and runtime support

Vercel handles the infrastructure so you can focus on your application:

Your frontend and backend, together

title: Shaping & Monitoring Models through their Internal Representations
description:
arXiv:2611.07071v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose Mechanistic Shaping, a unified framework for shaping models through their internal representations. Mechanistic Shaping is applied during training so that models follow specifications (rules) about which concepts they express, measured via their outputs or internal representations (e.g., no harmful content), and also which concepts they rely on, i.e., what they use to make their decisions (e.g., not a candidate's gender when screening a r\'esum\'e). Across multiple domains (vision, medical imaging, language), scales (up to 32B parameters), and training paradigms (classification, SFT, DPO, GRPO), we find that Mechanistic Shaping substantially reduces targeted behaviors while preserving task performance. Since training against a representation can also modify it, we ask whether shaped concepts remain monitorable, a question that depends on the class of monitors considered. We therefore introduce a hierarchy of such classes, which separates a concept that escapes one probe from a concept that is truly gone. We characterize three geometric mechanisms of circumvention: the concept can drift away from the monitor, be erased from the layer, or persist in higher-order statistics as a nonlinear encoding, which we explain through a product-code construction. Although other mechanisms may arise in different settings or at larger scales, these three account for all of our observations, and each can be detected by a matching monitor. In practice, we find that shaped concepts largely remain monitorable: refitted linear probes recover the concept in most settings, and the original probe remains reliable whenever gradients do not flow through it. Taken together, these results point to the potential of using interpretability as a tool for training, and call for a correspondingly rigorous science of interpretability-based training.
