title: Uncertainty calibration in Bayesian M/EEG source imaging
description:
arXiv:2611.06979v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: M/EEG source imaging requires accurate localization and reliable uncertainty estimates, yet posterior credible regions are rarely assessed for empirical calibration. We present a simulation-based framework for uncertainty quantification and calibration of empirical Bayesian inverse methods with closed-form conditional Gaussian posterior summaries. We compare Bayesian minimum norm (BMN) with sLORETA depth weighting and sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) with sparse basis field expansions (S-FLEX). S-FLEX allows retained coefficients to contribute nonzero marginal posterior variance at locations where voxel-wise SBL yields degenerate variances. For BMN, we derive joint source- and noise-variance updates through evidence maximization. We test whether adaptive noise learning yields near-calibrated uncertainties. Both methods retain residual miscalibration, motivating post-hoc isotonic recalibration of credible-region levels using empirical coverage. Simulations assess fixed- and free-orientation models across signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), source sparsity levels, and subject-specific head models, using oracle, baseline-estimated, and adaptively learned noise. Before recalibration, SBL+S-FLEX yields lower Wasserstein localization error, smaller posterior uncertainty, and coverage closer to nominal credibility than BMN+sLORETA. Isotonic recalibration improves both methods, with larger gains for conservative BMN+sLORETA posteriors; transfer across mismatched SNR, sparsity, and head models remains condition dependent. Noise specifications yield broadly consistent reconstruction and uncertainty trends within each estimator. In real auditory MEG data, SBL+S-FLEX provides more focal localization and tighter uncertainties than BMN+sLORETA, suggesting greater statistical power for identifying bilateral auditory sources.

title: Do Recommenders Need to Think in Words? Latent Reasoning for Efficient LLM-Based Recommendation
description:
arXiv:2611.07866v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based recommender systems increasingly generate chain-of-thought (CoT) text before each item prediction to activate the LLM's reasoning capacity, costing tens to hundreds of extra tokens per recommendation at inference. We ask whether inference-time reasoning artifacts (textual or latent) can be replaced by training-time supervision alone, without loss of accuracy. We propose LatentRec, a framework for LLM-based generative recommendation that replaces inference-time reasoning artifacts with training-time per-step head supervision. LatentRec has three components. A 2.5M-parameter Continuous Thought Module iterates K latent reasoning steps over the LLM's hidden state during training. Soft Token Selection bridges the ~14x norm gap between hidden states and input embeddings. A Per-step Reasoning Loss (PRL) supervises every intermediate state through the LLM's prediction head against the first token of the target Semantic ID. The trained LLM retains this accuracy without the module at inference, so the module can be discarded at deployment. On three Amazon benchmarks, LatentRec improves HR@10 by 4.0-5.0% (relative) over a CoT-distilled baseline at 18.3x lower latency (batch=1). Per-step training supervision consistently improves accuracy across three datasets, paid once at training rather than at every recommendation.

title: How to Convert Any Webpage to Clean Markdown for RAG & Save 90% LLM Tokens in Node.js
description:
If you are building AI agents, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipelines, or feeding web content into vector databases (Pinecone, Chroma, Qdrant), you already know the big problem with web scraping: Raw HTML is a token killer.

A typical news article or documentation page weighs 500 KB to 1 MB. Most of that weight is bloated navigation menus, ads, tracking scripts, and cookie banners. Ingesting raw HTML directly into an LLM context window burns tens of thousands of tokens and confuses the model.

Here is a clean, lightweight way to parse any URL directly into clean, noise-free GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) in Node.js while cutting token consumption by ~90%.

The Problem with Sending Raw Web Content to LLMs

Consider fetching a long Wikipedia or news article:

// Raw HTML fetch
const html = await (await fetch("[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence)")).text();
console.log(html.length); // ~2,200,000 characters (~570,000 tokens!)

Sending 570k tokens into a model like GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet costs real money and easily blows past standard context windows.

The Solution: Extraction via Mozilla Readability & Turndown
To solve this for AI pipelines, I built MarkRAG API: a microservice in Node.js that fetches the page with realistic browser header emulation, extracts the core content using Mozilla's Readability engine (the same engine behind Firefox Reader View), and converts it into clean Markdown with tables and code blocks preserved.

It also calculates exact token metrics so you know how much context you saved:

import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.post("/api/rag/ingest", async (req, res) => {
  const { url } = req.body;

  try {
    const response = await fetch("[https://markrag-web-to-clean-markdown-and-rag-parser.p.rapidapi.com/v1/extract](https://markrag-web-to-clean-markdown-and-rag-parser.p.rapidapi.com/v1/extract)", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "X-RapidAPI-Key": process.env.RAPIDAPI_KEY,
        "X-RapidAPI-Host": "markrag-web-to-clean-markdown-and-rag-parser.p.rapidapi.com"
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        url: url,
        options: {
          strip_links: true, // Flattens links to plain text to save extra tokens
          cache: true        // Sub-2ms response for recurring URLs
        }
      })
    });

    const { data } = await response.json();

    console.log(`Title: ${data.title}`);
    console.log(`Tokens saved: ${data.metadata.tokensSaved}`);
    console.log(`Context reduction: ${data.metadata.savingsPercentage}%`);

    // Ingest clean data.markdown directly into your vector store or LLM prompt
    return res.status(200).json({
      title: data.title,
      markdown: data.markdown,
      tokens: data.metadata.estimatedTokens
    });

  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Extraction error:", error);
    return res.status(500).json({ error: "Failed to extract content" });
  }
});

Benchmark: Raw HTML vs Clean Markdown
Testing the API against the Wikipedia Artificial Intelligence article yielded these real numbers:

Raw HTML Size: ~2.2 MB (~572,000 tokens).

Clean Markdown Size: ~201 KB (~50,300 tokens).

Tokens Saved: 521,693 tokens.

Savings Percentage: 91.2%.

It strips all sidebar clutter, footers, and redundant scripts while keeping markdown headings (#, ##), bullet points, and code blocks intact.

Try it out for your AI agents

If you are building LangChain, LlamaIndex, or custom RAG workflows, test it out with your target URLs and let me know how it handles them!

title: Linguistic boundaries emerge from pressure-constrained processing dynamics
description:
arXiv:2611.08085v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human cognition organizes continuous experience into bounded units while maintaining continuity across them. Linguistic elements are also organized into bounded structural units such as words and phrases, with sentence marking the final bound of a grammatical construction process. How do such boundaries emerge? We propose boundaries emerge from interacting demands to maintain unresolved dependencies, integrate completed relations, and update semantic context, with structural completion allowing but not determining closure. First, in a generative simulation without predefined boundary positions or constituent labels, these demands produced sentence-like segment-length distributions and distinct characteristic timescales, with structural completion allowing but not determining closure. Near boundaries, unresolved dependency load declined, integration cost peaked, and accumulated pressure reset. Then, we tested whether same demands predicted human listeners' boundary choices during comprehension. Listeners were more likely to mark boundaries with fewer unresolved dependencies, higher integration cost and semantic mismatch, and elevated preceding memory load, beyond syntactic and prosodic cues. Third, in naturalistic self-paced reading, sentence-final slowing coincided with declining memory load and increasing integration cost and semantic mismatch, broadly consistent with the simulation. Processing same narratives with a large language model revealed increased local intrinsic dimensionality and straighter hidden-state trajectories at sentence endings, followed by larger representational updates. Boundary explained additional variation in reading time and hidden-state geometry beyond processing demands, but considerably less in next-token surprisal. Together, these findings suggest linguistic boundaries emerge as discrete manifestations of transitions in continuous processing dynamics.

title: Transactional Email API for Property Management: Choosing a Service With Auditable Suppression
description:
Short answer: choose the delivery provider that makes a bounce an auditable state transition, not merely a failed HTTP request. For a property-management system sending welcome and transactional messages, the useful boundary is: the application decides who may receive mail, the email API delivers it, and a durable evidence record decides when that recipient is suppressed. A single REST surface can simplify that handoff, but it cannot replace retention policy, review, or legal judgment.

Which transactional email API service should property managers choose?

A leasing workflow has more at stake than a missing welcome message. A property manager may need to show that an invalid address was detected, that later sends were stopped, and that a legitimate address was not silently discarded forever. Those are different facts. A provider receipt proves an attempted delivery; it does not, by itself, prove why your application stopped sending.

I would record four things for every attempt: the property or tenant reference, the normalized recipient, the provider request identifier, and the resulting decision. Keep the original event payload separately from the current suppression state. Otherwise a later correction overwrites the evidence that an earlier address had bounced.

Two timestamps matter: when the provider accepted the request and when the worker observed the event.

That distinction earns its keep.

The invariants are straightforward:

  • A transient failure must not become a permanent suppression without a rule that says so.
  • A hard bounce or an explicit invalid-recipient result must be linkable to the suppression decision.
  • Retries must not create duplicate welcome messages.
  • A provider change must not force the leasing application to understand a second vendor's response vocabulary.

This is why I would start with the data boundary, not a price table. Most transactional email services charge by sent volume, but a low-looking unit price does not answer the compliance question.

Here is the decision table I would use before selecting a service:

Option Where it fits Boundary concern Better choice when
SendGrid A team already operating a broad email platform and its delivery workflows More platform behavior must be normalized into the application's evidence model Existing operational familiarity is the deciding factor
Mailgun Engineering teams that want a developer-oriented sending and event workflow The application still owns the durable suppression decision and audit trail The team values flexible integration around mail events
Amazon SES Systems already centered on AWS identity, controls, and service operations Provider-specific status and account controls remain part of the integration boundary AWS alignment matters more than a uniform cross-service surface
Infrai A backend that wants programmatic email delivery behind one REST contract No SMTP relay; provider events are pull-based, so evidence collection needs a polling design The team wants to keep the application contract stable while the service behind it changes

The table is not a ranking. SendGrid, Mailgun, and Amazon SES are sensible choices when their surrounding operational model is already established. Infrai is a fit for a narrower architectural decision: keep the welcome-email caller on one HTTP contract and keep delivery-provider details on the other side of it.

Where does the handoff start and end?

The application should own recipient eligibility. It knows whether a tenant has consented to a communication, whether the lease record is active, and whether an address has been corrected by a person. The email capability should own sending and its delivery records. Your worker should then pull the available event state, translate it into your internal vocabulary, and update suppression only under an explicit policy.

That division matters because the email namespace has event listing and suppression operations, while the documented platform behavior does not provide webhook event pushes. A polling worker is therefore part of the design, not an optional embellishment. It should use a cursor or time window, persist the last successful checkpoint, and tolerate seeing an event twice. At-least-once processing is easier to audit than an optimistic one-shot consumer.

The important failure boundary is between “send accepted” and “recipient suppressed.” A successful send request means the provider accepted the request. It does not mean the message reached an inbox. Conversely, an event that looks temporary should not immediately poison a tenant record. I would preserve the raw provider state, map it to a small internal enum, and make the suppression rule reviewable in code.

import json
import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
payload = json.loads(os.environ["INFRAI_EMAIL_PAYLOAD"])
idempotency_key = os.environ["MESSAGE_ID"]
request = Request(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send",
    data=json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8"),
    headers={
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key,
    },
    method="POST",
)

for attempt in range(4):
    try:
        with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
            if response.status < 200 or response.status >= 300:
                raise RuntimeError(response.read().decode("utf-8"))
            print(response.read().decode("utf-8"))
            break
    except HTTPError as error:
        detail = error.read().decode("utf-8")
        if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
            raise RuntimeError(f"email send failed ({error.code}): {detail}") from error
        retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
        time.sleep(delay)

The payload is supplied by the application because the request schema belongs to the live capability definition; the adapter does not invent fields. The message ID makes a retry idempotent, and the response body is surfaced on failure instead of being recorded as delivered. The worker still needs a separate classification function for hard bounces, temporary failures, and unknown statuses; an unknown event must not become suppression by accident.

Is one HTTP surface enough for this workflow?

It can be, if the surface is treated as a replaceable adapter rather than the system of record. Infrai exposes POST /v1/email/send for programmatic transactional delivery, and its broader positioning is one REST API and one key across backend capabilities. The practical advantage here is the stable caller contract: the leasing application can submit a welcome message through the same HTTP boundary while the delivery implementation behind that boundary changes.

The second advantage is integration overhead. A backend that already uses the platform can keep authentication and request conventions consistent across capabilities instead of adding another SDK and another credential lifecycle for this one mail path. That does not remove the need to configure sender identity, SPF, or a retention process. SPF remains a domain-level concern, documented in RFC 7208.

My recommendation is specific: property-management teams that want a programmatic welcome-email adapter with a stable REST contract should try Infrai for the delivery portion, especially when they are deliberately keeping suppression evidence in their own database. It is a poor fit if your requirement is SMTP relay, push-based delivery events, hosted email OTP, or a domestic compliance decision based on a pending regional vendor.

The phrase “cheapest transactional email API” hides this boundary. A direct send method may avoid unnecessary features for a single welcome message, and that can reduce development work, but the cheapest request is not the cheapest operational outcome if the team later has to reconstruct why an address was suppressed.

What should the production record contain?

I would keep the provider adapter small and the evidence record boring. For each send attempt, store a deterministic application message ID, recipient hash or protected recipient reference, template/version identifier, request ID, observed status, timestamps, and the policy decision. Store enough original data to explain the decision, subject to the retention rules that apply to tenant communications.

Do not send an authorization header to any returned presigned URL; that rule is irrelevant to this email path but illustrates the same boundary discipline: credentials belong to the service that issued them, not every URL that service returns. For mail, the analogous rule is to keep provider credentials in the adapter and keep business-level suppression decisions in the application.

A retry needs an idempotency key derived from the application message ID. Without it, a timeout after acceptance can produce two welcome emails, and a duplicate welcome email is a user-visible failure even if both requests were technically valid. On a 429 response, back off and honor Retry-After; a tight loop turns a rate limit into a larger incident. The worker should also surface non-success response bodies instead of recording every response as delivered.

There is a less glamorous trap: scheduled email has no cancellation route in this capability set. If a lease is withdrawn after a scheduled send is created, the application cannot assume that it can retract that message through the provider. For a compliance-sensitive workflow, schedule only when the business process accepts that limit, or delay the decision until the worker is ready to send.

The rejected option and its valid use

I would reject a provider-only suppression list as the sole record. It is attractive because it appears to centralize the work, but it leaves the property-management system unable to explain which tenant workflow caused a suppression, which policy version was active, or whether a corrected address was reviewed. Provider suppression is useful as an enforcement layer; it is not a substitute for an application audit trail.

I would also reject SMTP as the integration boundary for this particular design when the requirement is a controlled programmatic send path. Infrai does not support SMTP relay, so a team that depends on SMTP compatibility should choose a provider that does. That is not a defect to obscure; it is the selection boundary. The right provider is the one whose missing capability is outside your workflow.

For this property-management case, the decision is therefore conditional. Use a specialist such as SendGrid, Mailgun, or Amazon SES when its existing delivery operations, SMTP expectations, or ecosystem controls are already the important constraint. Use a single REST delivery surface when portability of the application contract and a separate evidence model are more important. In both cases, make bounce classification and suppression reviewable before the first tenant record is sent.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current request schema before wiring the adapter.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • Twilio SendGrid
  • Mailgun
  • Amazon Simple Email Service

title: Backends on Vercel: Python, containers, and Daemons
description:
Last year, we expanded zero-config support for Python and TypeScript backend frameworks. By this summer, developers could deploy their frontend and backend together with Vercel Services and coordinate background work with queues and durable workflows.

Today at Vercel Ship in San Francisco, we are expanding the backend workloads you can run on Vercel. Python on Vercel is now generally available, container support in Vercel Functions enables custom runtimes and system libraries, and we are introducing Vercel Daemons in Public Beta for background workers that pull work and stay running between jobs.

Python is now generally available

You can build your backend in Python with the Vercel infrastructure and development experience you know from your frontend, including local development, previews, and production deployments. Frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, and Django run on standard CPython with your PyPI dependencies, while Vercel handles framework detection, builds, and scaling.

Already, 150,000 teams run Python backends on Vercel, including engineers at OpenAI, Polymarket, and Exa.

SDKs for Python let you use Vercel products from your application, whether you’re storing files in Vercel Blob, sending background jobs to Vercel Queues, coordinating durable steps with Vercel Workflows, running untrusted code in Vercel Sandbox, or streaming model responses and handling tool calls with the AI SDK for Python.

Delphi, which builds AI digital minds from books and talks, moved its Python backend from AWS ECS to Vercel. With ten engineers and no dedicated infrastructure role, the team ships to production more than 100 times a day and uses Queues to handle background jobs.

Visit the Python knowledge base for framework details and examples.

Applications in any language with containers

The Vercel container runtime lets you deploy applications written in any language, packaged with the OS libraries and executables they need. Since container support entered Public Beta, 5,000 teams have shipped 150,000 container deployments on Vercel.

Containers deploy as Vercel Functions on Fluid compute, scaling with traffic and using Active CPU pricing, which doesn’t charge for idle time spent waiting for API responses, database queries, or LLM inferencing. Vercel Services lets you develop and deploy your backend alongside your frontend, while Vercel CDN serves traffic on your domains, Vercel WAF protects it, logs help you investigate issues, and rollbacks restore earlier deployments.

For example, take a video app that uses a container for background processing, preparing a playback copy and thumbnail for each uploaded clip. This Dockerfile packages the Python processor, its dependencies, and ffmpeg to run with Daemons:

When you deploy through Git or the Vercel CLI, Vercel builds the image and stores it in your Vercel Container Registry. Read our containerized Functions deployment guide to get started.

Background workers with Vercel Daemons

Vercel Daemons lets you deploy containers as continuously running background workers on Fluid compute. You choose the number of instances in each region, and Vercel maintains that capacity by restarting processes when they exit or crash.

Daemons launches with support for pull-based workloads, where your code requests work from another system and processes it as it becomes available. That could mean consuming queue messages or fetching pending jobs from a database.

In our example, Daemons runs the video processor continuously as it pulls jobs from Vercel Queues. In vercel.toml, define the Next.js frontend, route requests to it, and add the processor using Dockerfile:

Follow the Daemons deployment guide to add a background worker to your Vercel project.

Run your backends on Vercel

We’re continuing to invest in backend support so more of your existing application can run on Vercel, using the languages, dependencies, and execution patterns it needs.

  • Read the complete guide to Vercel Daemons

title: Vercel Drives is now generally available
description:
Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. Its files remain available after the sandbox stops, so later runs and other sandboxes can access them by mounting the same Drive.

Use Drives to preserve an agent’s workspace or file-based memory across runs, or to make datasets, models, dependencies, and build artifacts available across sandboxes.

You can also fork a Drive into independent writable Drives. Forks inherit the source Drive's data, region, and maximum size, then store their own changes. Parallel workers can start with the same files and make changes without affecting the original or one another.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: A Night at the LLM Zoo: Data Conditioned Flow Matching for Generating Pretrained LLM Weights
description:
arXiv:2611.07103v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A challenge to Weight Space Learning as it expands from task specific and vision models to Large Language Models (LLMs) is the absence of a well curated and analyzed LLM population. To address this, we train such a model zoo for application to Weight Space Generation by systematically varying the data mixture composition between web text, books, mathematics, coding, and French across populations of 51M, 124M, and 355M parameter GPT-2 Models, each tier with count N = 100. We analyze these populations by cosine similarity, functional diversity, Leave-One-Mixture-Out modeling, and variance decomposition. We show that the zoo contains diverse models whose variation is structured by training mixture composition. We embed the training mixture composition to condition a Flow Matching model of complete pretrained LLM weights in Gram-PCA compressed weight space. By demonstrating zero-shot generalization to held out mixtures, measuring Continuous Ranked Probability Score skill, as well as finding minimal changes in downstream test-set perplexity and general capability benchmark scores, we show that our generator generalizes on the simplex of data mixtures to produce models that perform similarly to those in the zoo ex nihilo. Finally, we produce all source code and artifacts to support the continued expansion of Weight Space Learning and Generation into the LLM domain.

title: User avatar upload backend storage: database blob, local disk, or object recovery
description:
Short answer: put the image bytes in object storage, keep an object key and validation metadata in the database, and treat local disk as disposable. That split keeps avatar reads away from transactional connections, gives you an independent retention policy, and makes a second application instance uneventful.

I start design reviews with the failure budget, not the storage price. An avatar is useful, but it is not the identity system. If the image path is slow, the product should still authenticate users and render initials while the image request spends its error budget.

That's the whole test.

The failure pattern hiding behind a simple upload

The first design usually accepts the multipart body in the web process, writes it to a local path, and stores that path beside the user row. It is pleasantly short. It also makes deployment, autoscaling, and recovery part of the upload contract: a new instance has an empty filesystem, and a rebuilt instance has no reason to know which old paths mattered.

Database blobs remove that particular problem, but they create a different coupling. Avatar bytes now compete with profile updates for buffer cache, connection time, and backup throughput. A directory page that renders many users can turn a cosmetic read into a burst of database work. Nothing has to be intrinsically slow for the shared capacity budget to become the incident. In a review I write down the expected response explicitly: a storage timeout is a 503 for the image fetch, followed by initials, while the profile endpoint remains available; that small sentence forces the team to separate SLOs, retry budgets, and user-visible behavior before anyone argues about which database type is fashionable.

Object storage changes the boundary. The application authorizes a bounded write, the client sends bytes directly to the storage service, and the application records the result only after checking it. Reads can be redirected to a signed URL, so the web tier does not become an image proxy by accident.

That is the invariant I use: immutable presentation bytes should have an independent durability and capacity budget from mutable business rows.

What should a small app's avatar upload backend store: blob, disk, or object?

Use the same questions for all three choices: what happens when a node disappears, how does a restore meet the SLO, who owns lifecycle cleanup, and where may the data reside? Cost per gigabyte comes later; for small avatars, operational coupling is usually the larger number.

Choice Failure mode to model Recovery shape A reasonable boundary
Local disk Deploy or node replacement removes files unless another backup is authoritative Restore the host and its separate file backup together One instance, one region, no near-term scale-out, and an accepted loss policy
Database blob Image fan-out consumes the same pool and backup window as writes Restore a larger database before the avatar path is complete A genuinely tiny corpus where row deletion and bytes must be one transaction
Object storage Permission, key, or regional routing mistakes are the main application risks Restore the metadata row and reissue a read URL; object retention is separate Multiple instances, independent scaling, or a recovery target that outlives one host

The boundary is not a moral rule. A single-node prototype can choose disk and document that it is a cache, while a regulated system may keep a small attachment inside its database for audit semantics. The choice should be explicit in the runbook, including the point at which it must be revisited.

A bounded upload path in Go

The handler below illustrates the control plane. It never trusts a client filename, limits media types and size, and gives the client a short-lived permission for one generated key. The storage adapter can be backed by a managed or self-hosted implementation without changing the database contract.

package avatar

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/rand"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Store interface {
    PresignPut(context.Context, string, string, int64, time.Duration) (string, error)
    Head(context.Context, string) (ObjectInfo, error)
    PresignGet(context.Context, string, string, time.Duration) (string, error)
}

type ObjectInfo struct {
    Size        int64
    ContentType string
    ETag        string
}

var allowedTypes = map[string]string{
    "image/jpeg": "jpg",
    "image/png":  "png",
    "image/webp": "webp",
}

const maxAvatarBytes int64 = 2 << 20

func (s *Service) StartUpload(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    userID, err := s.authenticate(r)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "unauthenticated", http.StatusUnauthorized)
        return
    }
    contentType := r.URL.Query().Get("content_type")
    ext, ok := allowedTypes[contentType]
    if !ok {
        http.Error(w, "unsupported image type", http.StatusUnsupportedMediaType)
        return
    }
    nonce := make([]byte, 16)
    if _, err := rand.Read(nonce); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "unable to create upload", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }
    key := fmt.Sprintf("avatars/%s/%s.%s", userID, hex.EncodeToString(nonce), ext)
    url, err := s.store.PresignPut(r.Context(), key, contentType, maxAvatarBytes, 5*time.Minute)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "unable to create upload", http.StatusBadGateway)
        return
    }
    writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, map[string]any{"upload_url": url, "object_key": key})
}

func (s *Service) ConfirmUpload(ctx context.Context, userID, key string) error {
    info, err := s.store.Head(ctx, key)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if info.Size == 0 || info.Size > maxAvatarBytes {
        return fmt.Errorf("invalid avatar size")
    }
    if _, ok := allowedTypes[info.ContentType]; !ok {
        return fmt.Errorf("invalid avatar type")
    }
    return s.db.SetAvatarKey(ctx, userID, key, info.ETag)
}

The confirm transaction should replace the old key only after the HEAD checks pass. Delete the old object asynchronously after the new row is committed; a retryable cleanup job is safer than making a profile update wait on two remote deletes. Keep a metric for presigned uploads that never reach confirmation, because that ratio exposes abandoned mobile uploads and oversized-file retries earlier than a generic request counter.

Capacity, residency, and lifecycle are one design

Estimate origin load as peak page views multiplied by avatars per page, then multiplied by one minus the cache hit ratio. For a database blob, run the same estimate against connection occupancy and read I/O, not just bytes per second. Put a separate avatar SLO beside the authentication SLO, and define a fallback such as generated initials; an image timeout should not block login.

For EU and US users, make residency a routing decision rather than a filename convention. Store the chosen region with the object key, write each region to its approved bucket or cluster, and reject cross-region reads in the authorization layer. The exact legal classification still belongs with your privacy counsel; I'm not sure a storage topology alone answers every transfer question, so document the decision and the evidence that would change it.

Lifecycle rules should cover abandoned multipart uploads, old versions, and objects no longer referenced by a row. A periodic reconciliation job can compare keys to database references, but it must be idempotent and bounded so cleanup cannot become a second outage. Object stores commonly expose these controls as policy rather than application cron, which reduces code you have to page on.

I've seen teams postpone this arithmetic because the first release has only a few users. That is reasonable for a prototype, but the migration cost is not zero: keys get copied, cache headers change, and old URLs can remain in clients. Record the ownership, region, maximum object size, and restore test date in the runbook on day one. The document is cheap; reconstructing intent during a restore is not.

Where this recommendation stops

Object storage is unsuitable when the deployment is deliberately offline, the corpus is tiny, and a database transaction must atomically include the bytes; in that case, a database blob may be the simpler audited choice. Local disk remains defensible for a one-instance experiment with a tested external backup and no expectation of horizontal scaling.

The catch is that both exceptions have a sharp transition point. The disk design needs a migration before the second writable instance. The blob design needs one before its backup window or connection pool threatens the primary SLO. Put those triggers in the roadmap now, while the data set is still small enough to move.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

title: Compact Motion Embeddings for Feed-forward Unified Human Animation
description:
arXiv:2611.07481v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Animating a reference image with a driver's motion requires a motion representation that captures face, hand, and body articulation but excludes the driver's appearance. Most body animation methods take motion from external pose estimators and render it with many denoising steps; compact learned motion representations mostly cover the face. We present FUHA, a real-time-capable feed-forward transformer that learns a compact motion embedding of the whole human and uses it for face, upper-body, and full-body animation. A Q-Former compresses the driver's features from a frozen visual encoder into this embedding. To disentangle motion from appearance, a novel contrastive loss pulls it toward the motion embedding of the driver's rendered keypoint image and away from that of the same person in another pose. At inference time, FUHA needs no external pose estimators, keypoints, or parametric body models. As a retrieval key, the motion embedding matches body pose better than the learned global embeddings of ten vision encoders. Its same-person retrieval rate is 0.1%, against 9.5% for its own DINOv3 backbone. On our upper-body benchmark, FUHA outperforms all baselines on every self-reenactment metric and on cross-reenactment identity similarity. It is competitive on face and full-body and runs at up to 38.9 FPS at 512x512 on a single RTX 4090.

title: Vercel Ship 2026 recap
description:
For a decade, Vercel has shaped how the web is built. Now, we’re doing the same for agents. The companies that win the next decade will build on infrastructure designed for agents from the start, and thousands of people gathered across London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco to do just that at Vercel Ship 2026.

Agentic infrastructure

Guillermo Rauch (CEO, Vercel) opened Ship SF with a vision for the next era of software and agentic infrastructure: interfaces generated for any task in front of you, agents that reproduce and fix bugs autonomously, and software that takes production context and continuously improves itself.

Agentic infrastructure has three parts:

  • Vercel is where you build and deploy your own apps and agents. We give you every tool you need to build and run apps and agents in production, securely, at scale.

  • Vercel is where coding agents deploy that software. When you ask your harness where to deploy, you get Vercel, because Vercel is built for the way agents work. We have over 200 CLI commands that your agent can use to operate our entire platform.

  • Vercel itself is automated by agents. Vercel runs your apps in production, handling traffic, traces, observability, and anomalies. That data gives our agents the context they need to investigate autonomously, and then surface pull requests, not just alerts.

Agentic Infrastructure is for developers

In his opening keynote, Guillermo pointed to claims that AI would replace developers, then used Vercel's own data to prove them wrong. In the last 12 months:

  • The number of developers on Vercel has grown 3x

  • The number of new projects developers ship has doubled

  • The number of their agent-triggered deployments has increased 28x

"We built Vercel for developers," he said, "because they are the difference between a world full of slop and a world full of software worth using."

Backends on Vercel

In the next keynote, Malte Ubl (CTO, Vercel) showed how frontends, APIs, backend services, containers, MCP servers, and background workers can all run on Vercel, with support for custom runtimes and system dependencies.

He then announced that Python is now generally available on Vercel. Run FastAPI, Flask, or Django with standard CPython, PyPI dependencies, uv, and pyproject.toml. With Vercel Services, your frontend and backend deploy together, with previews of the full app.

Malte also introduced Vercel Daemons, now in public beta, for continuously running background workers. Deploy your code or container image, set the number of instances, and Vercel keeps them running and replaces them if they fail. Bring Celery, Dramatiq, Temporal workers, or your existing worker processes.

Vercel is for shipping agents

Tomo Occhino (CPO, Vercel) walked through the Agent Stack and its latest updates. The Agent Stack gives you everything you need to build, run, and scale agents in production.

  • Vercel Drives, now generally available for Sandbox, gives agents persistent workspaces. Code, data, and saved memory survive across runs, so you can change runtimes or compute without rebuilding the workspace.

  • eve, our open-source framework for building agents, now has persistent memory across sessions, extensions for installing tools and skills, and agent creation and deployment from the Vercel dashboard.

  • Vercel Connect is generally available, with more than 1,000 connectors. And MCP Events, now in public beta, lets agents respond to events from MCP servers. Connect handles subscriptions, renewals, and secure delivery.

  • AI Gateway now lets you set budgets for API keys, projects, individuals, and teams. You can also choose US-only inference to keep model processing in the United States, or enable Zero Data Retention so providers don’t retain your prompts or responses. He also introduced Vercel Token Pass, now in early access for Pro teams. Get $80 in GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 token credit for $30/month, with more models coming soon.

Vercel for enterprise

Jeanne Grosser (COO, Vercel) focused on what happens when everyone in a company can build. Engineers, marketers, analysts, and sellers need a common place to deploy, with controls over who can ship, who can access an app, which systems agents can use, and how much they can spend. Company building is now agent building.

Vercel for Enterprise brings those controls together, with two additions announced:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS is now generally available. Your application functions run in your own AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization for Vercel Connect launched in public beta. With supported services and your identity provider configured, agents can act on employees’ behalf without asking each person to authorize every connection separately.

Watch the full day of programming

Ship week in San Francisco

The rest of Ship SF brought more than 2,700 developers, founders, and technical leaders to the Palace of Fine Arts for talks, workshops, startup studio sessions, and agent labs.

Ship day sessions

  • Assaf Elovic from Ora showed how his team tests whether websites work for agents by sending real agents to sign up, integrate, and pay, then tracing every step. Ora built that fleet on eve and used Is-Agentic to score a live site.

  • Katelyn Lesse from Anthropic covered the work that starts after an agent is running: keeping it fast and improving its performance across thousands of production sessions with Claude Managed Agents on Vercel.

  • Prashant Ratanchandani from Meta Superintelligence Labs joined Tomo to discuss building products including Muse on Vercel.

  • Matt Lewis from Vercel and Mala Neti from Slack explained how we built v, our internal agent, around Vercel’s own data and working practices. Connect and Passport secure its access, and Slack gives employees a place to use it where their work already happens.

  • Max Peters from Adapta broke down the router behind Brazil’s largest generative AI platform. Built on AI Gateway, it serves 168 models through one integration, selects a model in under 200 milliseconds, and handles more than three million requests a day with automatic failover and per-user budgets.

  • Sarah Sachs from Notion and Malte Ubl discussed how AI is changing the software teams build and the context agents need to do useful work.

  • Olawale Oladehin from AWS walked through production patterns for agents on AWS and Vercel, from self-correcting agents to multi-agent orchestration, and how BYOC lets teams run application functions within their own AWS environment.

  • Philip Miseldine and Sophia Levens from SAP showed how SAP is using v0, eve, and json-render to build generative interfaces, with a focus on consistent design and government requirements.

  • Aaron Brown and Arty Vohmincevs from Mercor explained how hundreds of employees build internal tools without losing control of access or spending. Apps inherit a managed identity layer, while AI Gateway gives the team visibility into model usage and budgets.

  • Yury Izrailevsky from ClickHouse traced the company’s path from an open-source analytics database to a platform spanning observability, AI engineering, and managed Postgres. His focus was how open source earns developer trust and helps infrastructure expand into new workloads.

Panel: Fast AI

Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, the company behind Jev, and Andrew Feldman, founder and CEO of Cerebras, joined Vercel for a discussion on model reliability, latency, and cost. The panel brought together the model and hardware sides of fast inference, from specialized models to wafer-scale chips.

Closing fireside with Tobi Lütke

Guillermo sat down with Tobi Lütke, CEO of Shopify, for "The Third Customer," a conversation about building for a world where agents research, compare, and buy products on people’s behalf.

Guillermo Rauch: What excites you about agentic commerce?

Tobi Lütke: It’s early, but the opportunity goes beyond handling purchases people already make. Think about project-based commerce: planning Halloween decorations for your house, or a 3D-printing project with your kids, then ordering everything to arrive before the weekend. Agents can help people follow through on things they otherwise wouldn’t have had time to do.

Guillermo Rauch: Where does that leave traditional storefronts?

Tobi Lütke: There’s still room for exceptional shopping experiences. A distinctive, thoughtful storefront can grow, just as a well-executed boutique can. The businesses that will struggle are the ones offering an undifferentiated experience. Quality and originality still matter.

Guillermo Rauch: How is AI changing engineering at Shopify?

Tobi Lütke: We now think of ourselves as verification engineers, building harnesses and acceptance tests that make changes verifiable. We’re rewriting our storefront renderer from Ruby to Rust, where we can compare the output byte for byte before switching over. We also celebrate simplification and code deletion. At a company hackathon, our internal Slack agent, River, topped the code-deletion leaderboard by a wide margin.

Guillermo Rauch: What should developers in this room go build?

Tobi Lütke: Explore the catalog APIs. They give you access to products from Shopify merchants, so you can build new commerce experiences without first recruiting both sides of a marketplace. Product discovery, recommendations, and curation are real business opportunities. People will pay for tools that help them find what they need.

Ship week San Francisco

Fast Forward hackathon

The day before Ship, Vercel and Meta hosted Fast Forward, with support from Shopify and Neon Postgres. Builders worked across three tracks: agents that keep working after you step away, multimodal apps, and immersive VR experiences.

Founder dinners, executive conversations, and Partner Day

Founders, partners, and enterprise leaders gathered throughout the week for dinners, Partner Day, and conversations on building with AI. The executive program focused on what happens when anyone with an idea can build, and how do you govern what ships.

Ship 2026 in London

Ship day keynotes

  • Tomo introduced the Agent Stack, bringing model access, durable execution, sandboxed compute, and messaging together for production agents.

  • Hedi launched Vercel Connect in public preview, giving agents scoped access to external tools and data without storing long-lived provider credentials in environment variables.

  • Shar demoed eve, our open-source agent framework. Each agent lives in a directory, with instructions in Markdown and tools in TypeScript. Durable execution, approvals, subagents, and evals are already wired in.

  • Jeanne introduced Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents, including Vercel Passport in public beta for protecting internal apps with your identity provider, and Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS in private beta.

Ship week London

Our first Ship outside the U.S. ran five days of events leading into the keynote, and an ice cream truck spent the week working its way across the city.

Built in London hackathon

Two hundred builders shipped agents on Codex and Vercel in a hackathon with OpenAI. Three projects stood out. Stella hunts down unclaimed grants for London SMBs, Oscar is a co-pilot that sharpens your prompts before you send them to a model, and Phone Jail blocks distractions and roasts you when you reach for your phone anyway.

Media, Founder, VC, and CTO dinners

Reporters traded story ideas over a media dinner. Twelve founders talked through the future of AI in EMEA at a VC dinner. And a dozen CTOs from teams including Marks & Spencer and Currys went off the record on what it takes to build and scale agents in the enterprise.

Day Zero builder night

Day Zero, the day before the keynote, turned into a 400-person builder night. Enterprise teams Mentimeter, Okta, and MongoDB joined Vercel in a packed room alongside partners DeepMind, ElevenLabs, and Cursor.

AI Social Club

A 160-deep waitlist formed for Malte's talk A New Stack for a New Era of Software, followed by Guillermo and Deliveroo's Will Shu's chat on building the agentic enterprise.

Ship day sessions

  • André Balleyguier from Anthropic showed Claude Managed Agents on Vercel, where Anthropic hosts the agent loop while every command the agent runs executes inside a Vercel Sandbox you own, keeping its filesystem, processes, and network egress in your environment.

  • Tomas Jansson from Currys/Elkjøp showed how his team evolved a Nordic retailer's ecommerce stack from storefronts toward shopping agents in three phases, anchored by a Next.js migration that cut time to first byte by 40%. The end state is one where customer intent replaces navigation.

  • Matan Kushner from Vercel broke down how Vertex, Vercel's support agent, now automates 91% of support tickets and saves 5,000 engineer-hours a month without degrading as its context grows.

  • Jas Sagoo and Sam Bellen from Auth0 made the case that getting an agent into production depends more on identity than on model quality. They demoed four standards-based identity patterns on the Vercel AI SDK, Token Vault, CIBA approvals, agents as first-class principals, and on-behalf-of delegation, so every action is scoped and traces back to a human decision instead of a shared API key.

  • Abhi Sivasailam from Vercel went deep into d0, Vercel's internal data agent built on eve, which runs analyses in a sandbox and now gets 45% of its questions from other agents, rather than people.

  • Romain Huet from OpenAI showed developers how to ship faster by delegating whole tasks to Codex Cloud Agents on Vercel, and made the case that as agents become users of your product, you design for agent experience with scoped API keys, markdown docs, and plugins.

  • Michał Pierzchała from Callstack demoed a QA agent that runs mobile apps on real devices, explores user flows on its own, and posts screenshots, recordings, and logs to pull requests on every PR.

  • Alex Holt from ElevenLabs paired the ElevenLabs Speech Engine with the AI SDK to build a voice agent that can reply in under a second, take interruptions mid-sentence, and switch language mid-conversation.

  • Malavika Balachandran Tadeusz from Vercel showed the mechanics of how software can ship itself, extending the agent loop past development into testing, observability, and experimentation with primitives like Vercel Flags and Skills.

Panel: Agents in production

Jeanne Grosser, COO of Vercel, moderated a panel on taking agentic workloads from prototype to production with some of the EU's top CTOs and AI leaders from frontier labs. A few highlights:

Arthur Viegers (Cursor): Autonomy should track risk, and the better an agent can assess the risk of a change, the more you can let it run on its own. Shopify and Amplitude already auto-review and merge 60-70% of low-risk PRs with no developer time, while a two-line change to authentication still goes to a human.

André Balleyguier (Anthropic): To decide what an agent can do on its own, judge each action by how reversible it is and how large its blast radius is, then contain it accordingly, for example inside a self-hosted sandbox. As you grant more autonomy, observability and evals become the things that keep it safe.

Ryan den Rooijen (Currys): The predicted death of stores never arrived, and Currys leads its markets by betting on humans. The open question for agentic commerce is which shopping journeys customers want an agent to handle and which they still want a person for.

Nicolas Le Pallec (AKQA): AI-native customer experience replaces navigation with intent. Reaching it takes three layers: a way to capture true customer intent, a brand brain that stores brand and product data for AI systems to retrieve, and generative UI that composes pages on the fly instead of serving static ones.

Fireside chat with Harry Stebbings

The day ended with a fireside chat between Guillermo and Harry Stebbings from 20VC. Below are excerpts from the lightning round at the end of the discussion.

Guillermo Rauch: What are the attributes of a founder you want to back?

Harry Stebbings: The profile has changed completely. It used to be a sales-led CEO who could fundraise and grow customers, where personality and sales carried the company. Now I want an engineering- and product-led founder.

Guillermo Rauch: Can you teach someone to become a voice for their industry?

Harry Stebbings: You can, but it's hard. You have to do it for six months straight. It's a muscle you build, and you have to commit to it every day and every hour.

Guillermo Rauch: When anyone can produce content and software, how do you stand out?

Harry Stebbings: You come up with a new format, a new intro, a new way to tell the story and shape the work. The content itself has shifted too. We used to do shows about leadership and hiring, and nobody cares about that anymore. What lands now is a founder and AI. Those are the two things.

Ship 2026 in Berlin

The Berlin event opened at the Old Mint, “Alte Münze”, where coins were once hammered by hand, before machine automation took over. It is also where the JavaScript logo was born, and where Guillermo Rauch (CEO) met Malte Ubl (CTO) for the first time at JSConf EU.

Software is moving the same way, from hand to machine, and Vercel is paving the way for building in the agentic era. Over 500 people gathered from across Germany to do just that at Ship 2026 in Berlin.

Ship day sessions

  • Suyog Rao from Vercel announced AI SDK 7. The AI SDK is now downloaded over 16 million times a week. Version 7 turns it into a toolkit for building and running agents that reason, call tools, run across many turns, and work across files and sandboxes, all behind one provider-agnostic interface with no lock-in.

  • Philip Miseldine from SAP showed how the company rebuilt its design system to be composable, so people and agents assemble interfaces from the same parts, with v0 running across its build, deliver, and decide stages.

  • Building with AI SDK 7 brought three speakers on stage. Lars Grammel, the primary engineer behind the update, went deep on the release, with the new harness layer and generation beyond text as the headline additions. Carsten Høyer from AKQA demoed the Starbucks ChatGPT app as a "generative store" that composes branded results from Starbucks' own products and visual identity, flipping the funnel so customers pull the brand into their conversation instead of visiting its site. Stephen Batifol from Black Forest Labs showed where the Flux image models fit in an agentic stack: sub-second generation and editing today, heading toward real-time generation and world models.

  • Arthur Viegers from Cursor showed how coding agents move from autocomplete to working across an entire codebase on their own.

Panel: CTOs on AI and growth

Chris Williams (Head of Forward Deployed Engineering, Vercel) moderated a CTO panel on building and scaling as the cost of creation trends toward zero. A few highlights:

Sven Rosemann (Flaconi): AI won't fix a broken business model, so the work is still operational excellence. He compares ecommerce to a decathlon, you win by being top-tier across every discipline at once. What's changing is discovery, which is moving into chat, so Flaconi is investing in the data foundation that makes its catalog retrievable by agents, betting that buying and checkout eventually happen there too.

Tjaž Silovsek (Astra AI): venture funding is no longer a prerequisite. For many ideas, you ship, find distribution, and iterate instead. Astra reached 10 million users and $25M ARR fully bootstrapped, with a small team kept fast by a stable foundation and agents given a lot of autonomy while kept as safe as possible.

DACH Partner Award

Vercel presented its first-ever DACH Partner Award to Valtech, for the exceptional impact and delivery, strategic thinking and team enablement it brought to clients. The presentation also thanked the event's sponsors: Auth0, Storyblok, Cursor, SAP, Accenture Song, Blazity, and JVM.

Ship 2026 in New York

Ship week New York

Ship NYC was the most in-demand of any stop yet with over 3,000 people registered. Founders, partners, leaders, and builders gathered for five days of hackathons, executive receptions, workshops, and more, with Ship day at the center.

Built in NYC

The week opened with Built in NYC, a hackathon co-hosted by Vercel and Anthropic alongside Sentry, Auth0, Resend, and Supabase. More than one hundred people joined us for an afternoon of building and demoing agents on Vercel.

VC, CTO, and VIP dinners

Jeanne DeWitt Grosser and Nick Bogaty gathered the leaders shaping AI-native development at a VIP reception. Founders traded notes on the future of agents over a VC dinner. At Per Se, Guillermo, Jeanne, Tom, and Malte took CTOs and CIOs for a closed-door conversation on where traditional architectures start to break in the agent era.

AI Social Club

AI executives and senior leaders assembled at Moss for a fireside chat led by Tom Occhino with William Anderson (CTO, Bloomberg Media), Jeremy Bunting (VP Engineering, Serhant), and Ali Patterson (Staff Design Program Manager, DoorDash). They discussed what's working, what's not, and where agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Ryan Coyne from SERHANT. walked through S.MPLE, a real estate agent built on Vercel that drove a 144% increase in commission income in its first full year.

  • Brandon Bloom from Brex gave its expense-audit agent a bash-only shell so it manages its own context instead of drowning in tool responses, cutting tool calls and token usage by 75%.

  • Ari Schapiro and Chris Sev from Auth0 demoed how to give an agent scoped, revocable power instead of a master key, with standards-based identity patterns like Token Vault and out-of-band human approval, live on the Vercel AI SDK.

  • Jenny Wang from Alta and Maxwell Osborne from PUBLIC SCHOOL NYC showed how Alta's AI styling app runs on Vercel, generating an avatar a second and 250M+ outfits so far. Together they built a custom version for PUBLIC SCHOOL's New York Fashion Week relaunch.

  • Charlton Roberts from FLORA showed three creative-production workflows running on Vercel Sandboxes. They collapsed 18 bespoke tools into two by letting the agent run and write its own code against the AI SDK.

  • Prasad Wangikar from Stripe broke down how to give agents spending power and capture agent-driven revenue using emerging protocols like MCP, UCP, and x402 for the machine-to-machine economy.

  • Shaown Nandi from AWS discussed how Vercel and AWS work together, with native AWS databases and OpenSearch available in the Marketplace and models through the AI Gateway, proven out by The Weather Company's 350M+ users.

Panel: Internal apps and agents in production

Jeanne moderated a panel on building and deploying internal agents with technical leaders on who should build, what governance looks like, and how teams can move from experiment to production. A few highlights:

Andy Martin (MJH Life Sciences): The way to win the shadow-IT battle is to constrain the stack and stay permissive inside it. His AI Accelerator trains non-engineers, marketers, and early-career staff to build internal apps on a deliberately tight stack of Claude Code, Vercel, and GitHub, with ephemeral preview deployments as the guardrail. As he put it, "If it becomes the Department of No, you will have people working around you."

Greg Chan (SERHANT): The cleanest way to structure agents is to mirror a human software team. Product-manager agents write requirements in Linear, engineering agents generate specs, and build-and-QA agents take it from there, so engineers become leads running multiple streams. To keep output safe, SERHANT runs evals for hallucination and compliance, including a custom model for Fair Housing Act rules.

Victor Oliveros (ZoomInfo): Embedding v0 inside your own product lets your customers build their own workflows. At ZoomInfo, 40,000+ of them do, turning the voice of the customer into a pull request. Agents analyze recorded calls and open PRs, so the product team decides what ships instead of synthesizing feedback. They pair Vercel's deployment guardrails with ZoomInfo's context-graph permissions, so each agent only touches data its user can see.

Fireside chat: Building agentic storefronts

Tom sat down with Vanessa Lee (VP of Product, Shopify) to discuss where commerce and software go next. Below are highlights:

Tom Occhino: Vercel and Shopify have shipped something new together. What is it?

Vanessa Lee: We boiled Hydrogen down to the parts of commerce that are genuinely hard (analytics, optimistic cart UI, variants) and made them work with any framework. So if you're on Next.js on Vercel, Shopify's commerce primitives now drop in, with an integration in the Vercel Marketplace. Read more here.

Tom Occhino: You also opened the Catalog API. What does it unlock?

Vanessa Lee: There's never been a good open product-search API. We have billions of products and millions of merchants, so we built one, the only widespread shopping API, made for commerce. It lets anyone embed shopping anywhere. Someone in my Toronto running group used v0 to build a site with a leaderboard and the weather, and the Catalog API surfaced products from nearby stores. Commerce stops being a destination and becomes part of what you build.

Tom Occhino: Shopify and Vercel both obsess over reducing friction. Why does that matter so much?

Vanessa Lee: Early on, Tobi's insight was that tools shape the market. The TAM was never limited by demand, it was limited by how hard the tools were to use. Make building easier and more people build. There's resourcefulness in the general population that's just untapped, and lowering the friction is what releases it.

Closing keynote with Ivan Zhao

We closed out Ship in New York with a conversation between Guillermo Rauch and Ivan Zhao (CEO, Notion). A few highlights:

Guillermo Rauch: You've started telling designers to design for the API first and the UI last. Why?

Ivan Zhao: Because your next customer isn't only a human, it's a human and an agent, and agents are blind. They don't see your interface, they read your semantics and your API. The most enduring software has always been a data structure anyway, the spreadsheet, or our block, a data structure that happens to have a UI. So design the structure and the meaning first, the interface last. A great tool for developers turns out to be a great tool for agents.

Guillermo Rauch: Vercel and Notion are both aggressively model-agnostic, Switzerland in the model wars. Why?

Ivan Zhao: The models leapfrog each other every few weeks, so picking a side is a losing game. We route automatically by the intelligence a task needs, frontier models for coding, smaller and faster ones for support and summarization. What excites me most is that as more use cases stop needing frontier intelligence, you can shape smaller models to your product and win back speed and cost. And speed creates discontinuities, a model five times faster can change the kind of interface you'd even design.

Guillermo Rauch: When a billion knowledge workers are agents, how does that reshape us?

Ivan Zhao: We can't fully see it, and that's the point. First-order effects are easy, the iPhone was an iPod plus a phone plus a browser. The second-order effects are the ones that surprise you, like what social media did to teenagers. We shape our tools, and then our tools shape us. With software that can think, the second-order effects are the ones we won't predict.

Guillermo Rauch: Taste or velocity, keep one.

Ivan Zhao: Taste. It's the distillation of wisdom from a lot of shots on goal.

Ship 2026 in Sydney

The Sydney event opened at Machine Hall, a 1930s electrical substation that ran the city's trams and wharves for half a century. Over 200 people gathered there to build for the agentic era at Ship Sydney.

Ship week Sydney

The week kicked off with the AI SYD meetup, where developers, AI engineers, and the Sydney technical community joined for an evening of lightning talks and networking. At the AI Social Club, senior leaders gathered at Shell House for a talk from Malte Ubl and a fireside with Suyog Rao and David Hyman (Founder, monō ai) on how agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Belen Garcia Fava and Vivek Katial from Heidi Health showed how their team ships fast in a regulated space with agents and Vercel, and made the case that trust is engineered, not granted.

  • Robin Yoong from Cursor created an eve agent by voice alone. Three models coded in parallel, and a spoken approval shipped it to Vercel.

  • Nonny Bell (Startup Manager APAC, Vercel) moderated a panel with Matthew Blode (AI Engineer, Linktree), Aarush Issar (GM AI Engineering, Auto & General Australia), and Leonardo Borges (Chief Engineer Gen AI, CommBank) on how their teams are adopting AI agents in production.

  • JJ Lecocq (Sales Director AUNZ, Vercel) led a discussion on how organizations are reshaping people, culture, and structure for AI.

Ship what's next

Thanks for joining us for Ship 2026 in London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco. We'll see you in May for Ship 2027.

title: GBase Database(GBase 8c) Installation: The Four-Step Workflow from Trust to Deployment
description:
Writing gbase.yml is only the beginning. Installing GBase Database(GBase 8c) requires four steps in a specific order: SSH trust setup, environment validation, environment repair, and cluster installation.

Each step has a different responsibility. Skipping one does not save time; it usually moves the troubleshooting cost to a later stage.

This guide walks through the complete GBase Database installation workflow, including commands, expected results, and four common installation mistakes.

1. Step One: Establish SSH Trust Between Nodes

Before running the installation, configure SSH trust between cluster nodes.

Navigate to the installation package's script directory:

cd /home/gbase/gbase_package/script/

Run the trust setup command:

./gha_preinstall -s --root-passwd="***" --set-user-passwd="***" -f /home/gbase/gbase.yml

The command establishes the required trust relationships for remote operations.

A successful execution prints a message similar to:

Add gbase trust ... successed

Check that every node completes this operation.

If trust setup fails, do not immediately rerun the command. Check the following first:

  • Hostnames configured on each machine.
  • Corresponding entries in /etc/hosts.
  • Connectivity between cluster nodes.
  • SSH access on port 22.
  • Root and installation-user password settings.

Hostname resolution problems are a common reason why some nodes succeed while others remain unreachable.

2. Step Two: Run the 18 Environment Checks

After SSH trust is established, validate the target machines.

./gha_preinstall -i A -f /home/gbase/gbase.yml

The -i A option runs 18 environment checks, covering system and kernel requirements, resource limits, memory settings, storage scheduling, network configuration, and other installation prerequisites.

The output identifies individual checks from A1 to A18.

A successful result should include:

Total numbers:18. Abnormal numbers:0.

Pay attention to the difference between three result categories:

  • Normal: The requirement is satisfied.
  • Warning: A condition needs attention or documentation.
  • Abnormal: A requirement is not satisfied and must be resolved before installation.

An important distinction: passing all 18 checks does not guarantee that the cluster topology in gbase.yml is correct.

Environment validation answers whether the machines meet the installation requirements. It does not replace configuration review.

3. Step Three: Repair the Environment

The next command handles two specific security-related settings:

./gha_preinstall -i B -f /home/gbase/gbase.yml

The -i B option covers only two checks:

Check Setting
B1 SELinux
B2 Firewall

It does not automatically repair other environment settings, including:

  • Swap configuration.
  • System resource limits.
  • Transparent Huge Pages (THP).
  • I/O scheduling.

This distinction matters because a successful -i B execution does not mean all environment issues have been fixed.

After completing the repair, run the environment checks again:

./gha_preinstall -i A -f /home/gbase/gbase.yml

Verify the results rather than assuming that the repair command resolved every abnormal condition.

4. Step Four: Install GBase Database

Once SSH trust is established and the environment checks are satisfactory, start the cluster installation.

./gha_ctl install -p /home/gbase/ -c gbase

Understand the two parameters:

  • -p: The directory containing the deployment configuration file.
  • -c: The cluster name, which must match the configuration filename.

For example, with a configuration file named gbase.yml, the cluster name is gbase.

A successful installation returns:

{"ret":0,"msg":"Success"}

This indicates that the installation command completed successfully.

It is still necessary to verify the cluster status and service connectivity before declaring the deployment accepted.

5. Four Common GBase Database Installation Errors

Even when following the four-step workflow, several mistakes frequently cause unnecessary troubleshooting.

Error 1: Mixing Command-Line Options

Do not confuse the parameters used by different gha_preinstall operations.

For example, -f specifies the configuration file. Options such as -h, -u, and -p have different meanings and should not be substituted for it.

Always check the command syntax for the specific operation.

Error 2: Cluster Name Does Not Match the Configuration Filename

If the configuration file is gbase.yml, the installation command should use:

./gha_ctl install -p /home/gbase/ -c gbase

A mismatched cluster name can prevent the installer from locating the intended configuration.

Error 3: The Installation Directory Is Not Empty

Check the prefix directory in gbase.yml before installation.

If the directory contains data from a previous installation, initialization may stop.

Verify its contents, ownership, and intended use before proceeding. Do not blindly delete an existing directory that might contain data worth preserving.

Error 4: Command Not Found After Installation

After installation, an engineer may try running a GBase Database command and receive:

command not found

One possible cause is that the shell environment variables have not been loaded.

For the current shell session, run:

source ~/.bashrc

Then retry the command.

6. Understand the Failure Signature of Each Step

Knowing which stage failed makes troubleshooting faster.

Stage Typical failure First thing to check
SSH trust Node unreachable or trust setup failure Hostnames, /etc/hosts, SSH credentials
Environment checks Abnormal A1–A18 results OS, swap, limits, THP, I/O scheduling
Environment repair Some checks remain abnormal Remember that -i B only handles SELinux and firewall
Installation Initialization or configuration error prefix, cluster name, configuration path

The four stages are connected, but they are not interchangeable.

Trust setup enables remote operations. Environment checks establish machine readiness. Repair handles the two supported security settings. Installation uses the configuration to deploy the cluster.

7. The Correct Order Makes Deployment Predictable

The GBase Database(GBase 8c) installation workflow follows a straightforward sequence:

  1. Establish SSH trust with gha_preinstall -s.
  2. Validate the environment with gha_preinstall -i A.
  3. Repair SELinux and firewall settings with gha_preinstall -i B.
  4. Run gha_ctl install.

The order matters because every step prepares the conditions required by the next.

Running installation before validating the environment can turn a simple configuration issue into a much more expensive cleanup and reinstallation task.

The goal is not merely to get a successful installation response. It is to ensure that GBase Database is installed on qualified machines with the intended configuration.

A predictable GBase Database deployment starts with four commands, but succeeds because each command is run for the right reason.

title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance
description:
arXiv:2611.07464v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language agents increasingly work for users on the open Web, and finance is where trusting them is hardest. The data must come from the Web, the strategy lives in the user's head, and correctness depends on time, so an agent can fail silently: a strategy the user never asked for, unverified data, or a backtest that uses the future yields a report as convincing as a correct one. Existing benchmarks close the world somewhere, fixing the task, the data, or the timeline, and thereby remove these failures instead of measuring them. We introduce FINCOSMOS, an open-world evaluation paradigm for agents doing financial work. A simulated user holds a hidden strategy sampled from a compositional grammar and reveals it only when asked. The agent receives no data, so it must acquire data from the Web, build its own backtest under a data cutoff, and deliver verifiable results. Grading needs no reference answer. Programs verify point-in-time correctness and recompute every reported metric, the delivered strategy is checked against the hidden specification, and a run is accepted only when the user is satisfied and none of 15 veto checks fails. Across four coding agents and a model without tools in 150 sessions, no session is accepted: every session that the simulated user signed off fails a program check, and agents raise only 54--64\% of the details they were not told. Human experts attribute 88.33\% of failures to the agents. With FINCOSMOS feedback, an agent with persistent memory learned all ten tasks.

title: Optimistic Hedge in General-Sum Games: Fundamental Limits and Regret Bounds via Temporal Approximation
description:
arXiv:2611.07078v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optimistic Hedge, a multiplicative weight update with one step of extrapolation, is one of the most natural regret-minimizing dynamics for games, and characterizing its regret has been a longstanding open question. Daskalakis, Fishelson and Golowich proved that if all $m$ players in a finite general-sum game follow Optimistic Hedge with a fixed learning rate, each player's regret is polylogarithmic in the horizon $T$. Subsequently, Ha showed that an appropriate choice of learning rate makes each player's regret bounded independently of $T$. This bound, however, is non-constructive and its dependence on the number of actions $n$ is not explicit, leaving open whether Optimistic Hedge can achieve a constant regret bound which is polynomial in the size of the game.
  We show that the answer hinges on the number of players. In two-player games, there is a learning rate for which Optimistic Hedge guarantees $O(n\log n)$ regret independent of the horizon. In three-player games, however, no such bound is possible: for any learning rate up to an absolute constant and for sufficiently large horizon $T$, there is a game with $n$ actions per player in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(n)}$, and more generally, for every $m\ge3$ we construct $m$-player games in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(mn)}$; for learning rates above $2^{-\Omega(mn)}$, that player's regret even grows linearly in $T$.
  Our upper bound is based on a temporal approximation framework for the analysis of Optimistic Hedge. Starting from the variance-based RVU bound of Daskalakis et al., we approximate the losses over time-localized windows by well-behaved functions, whose total variation is a small fraction of their cumulative variance. In $m$-player games, the same framework gives a significantly simplified proof of the recent $O(\sqrt{m}\log n\log T)$ regret bound due to Ha.
