title: How to Control Go Email API Integration Through Application Owned Templates
description:
For a logistics portal sending welcome emails and short-lived password-reset messages, the simplest API integration starts with application-owned templates and a narrow delivery adapter. The bill to model is delivery attempts plus retained records plus the work of reconciling uncertain outcomes. In the illustrative workload below, 10,000 reset requests with one extra attempt for every request produce 20,000 attempts; removing those unnecessary extra attempts removes 10,000 units of delivery work.

These are planning inputs, not measured traffic or quoted prices.

TL;DR: choose a transactional email API by whether its template boundary lets your application own the reset deadline, rendered content, and durable request identity. A welcome email can tolerate a late greeting; an expired reset link cannot restore access. Keep the expiry decision in the application, reconcile ambiguous sends before authorizing another attempt, and retain a small audit record instead of the message body.

The selection question is therefore broader than how few lines an SDK requires. For a dispatcher trying to regain access to a shipment console, the useful integration is one whose behavior remains intelligible after a timeout, a template deployment, or an operator investigation. The examples use local Go programs to make those decisions inspectable without implying that any particular remote API supplies the necessary guarantees.

Step 1 Calculate which retained work dominates

Start with counts. Until a team supplies its own delivery charges, storage charges, and investigation effort, a claim about the dominant monetary term would be speculation; counts still reveal which change removes unnecessary work. This first program deliberately models an extreme retry policy so that the effect is visible. Run it as a standalone Go program and substitute actual attempt counts before using the result in a capacity review.

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    requests := 10000
    extraAttempts := 10000
    retainedBytesPerRequest := 2048
    compactBytesPerRequest := 256
    fmt.Printf("delivery attempts: %d -> %d\n",
        requests+extraAttempts, requests)
    fmt.Printf("illustrative retained bytes: %d -> %d\n",
        requests*retainedBytesPerRequest,
        requests*compactBytesPerRequest)
}

The expected output is 20,000 attempts becoming 10,000, with illustrative retained content shrinking from 20,480,000 to 2,560,000 bytes. The byte inputs are hypothetical record sizes; they exclude indexes, replicas, encoding overhead, and backups. This calculation justifies measuring both attempts and retained data. It does not justify a percentage saving on a real bill.

Count attempts separately.

For API selection, ask which responses establish acceptance, which identifier can be reconciled later, and what the service promises when the same request identity is presented again. A client retry is a new transmission even when its business purpose is unchanged. If an acknowledgement disappears, treating that uncertainty as proof of rejection creates the concrete failure this design is meant to avoid: two messages, potentially carrying different reset links, for one user action.

Template ownership affects the retention term as well. An application-owned, versioned template can be reproduced from an approved release artifact, so the audit record can identify that version without retaining another copy of the rendered message. A remotely edited template needs an equally dependable version reference; otherwise an investigation may discover what the template says now while remaining unable to establish what it said when the request was accepted. That is a selection boundary to verify, not an assumed feature of an API.

How should an API integration share templates for welcome emails?

Keep the reset authorization and its deadline under the same application policy, then treat rendering as a projection of that policy. In this example, five minutes is an explicit design choice for the logistics portal, not a universal compliance requirement. The fixed timestamp makes the example repeatable, and the recipient is intentionally omitted because this step verifies content ownership rather than transport.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    issued := time.Date(2026, 11, 2, 8, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    expires := issued.Add(5 * time.Minute)
    version := "logistics-reset-v1"
    deadline := expires.Format(time.RFC3339)
    body := fmt.Sprintf(
        "Shipment console password reset requested. This request expires at %s.",
        deadline,
    )
    fmt.Println(version)
    fmt.Println(body)
    fmt.Println("valid at deadline:", expires.Before(expires))
}

The deadline printed here is 08:05:00 UTC, and the boundary check prints false. In the actual reset handler, acceptance must depend on the persisted authorization, the current time, and whether the authorization has already been consumed; the words in an email cannot enforce any of these conditions. This program intentionally renders only the explanatory sentence. It is not a token generator or a deployable reset handler.

Expiry wins here.

Before connecting an API, decide how its template interface represents that deadline. Sending a rendered body gives the application direct control over wording and version deployment, at the cost of making application releases part of the editorial workflow. Sending variables to a remotely managed template can permit separate content releases, but the contract must still preserve the exact deadline and provide a traceable template version. A mutable template name alone is insufficient for this design's audit trail.

The same adapter may send welcome emails, but it should receive a different message policy.

Reusing an integration does not require giving a greeting and a credential recovery message the same expiry, retry budget, or retention policy. For the shipment console, the release decision is whether the transport can carry the application-owned content without silently changing its meaning. Confirm that with a contract test using the exact deadline above.

Step 3 Make uncertainty an explicit reconciliation state

An exactly-once mindset begins with identifying the business operation once and preserving that identity through every attempt. It does not turn a local database and a remote mail system into a single atomic transaction. The small program below specifies a conservative transition rule: only a queued, unexpired operation may start an attempt, while an ambiguous outcome requires reconciliation. Its single-threaded state is suitable for demonstrating the rule; a deployed worker needs a durable, atomic claim and a recoverable lease around the equivalent transition.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Record struct {
    ID      string
    Version string
    State   string
    Expires time.Time
}

func claim(r *Record, now time.Time) bool {
    if r.State != "queued" {
        return false
    }
    if !now.Before(r.Expires) {
        r.State = "expired"
        return false
    }
    r.State = "inflight"
    return true
}

func main() {
    now := time.Date(2026, 11, 2, 8, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    r := Record{
        ID: "reset-request-0042",
        Version: "logistics-reset-v1",
        State: "queued",
        Expires: now.Add(5 * time.Minute),
    }
    fmt.Println("first claim:", claim(&r, now))
    r.State = "unknown"
    fmt.Println("claim after uncertain outcome:", claim(&r, now))
    fmt.Printf("audit: %s %s %s\n", r.ID, r.Version, r.State)
}

The first claim prints true; the second prints false.

There is no live send in this example. A delivery adapter would record acceptance evidence when available and preserve an unknown state when the outcome cannot be established. Stopping there sacrifices immediate retry availability, which is a deliberate correctness trade-off rather than a claim that mail delivery can be guaranteed exactly once.

Make the acceptance criteria concrete before selecting the API: rehearse a timeout after submission, a repeated worker claim, and an expired queued request. Also exercise a template rollback while the queue contains requests created under the previous version. The expected result is an explainable state transition and a preserved deadline in each case. Where a service offers deduplication or status lookup, verify its documented scope and retention window against these cases; where it does not, decide whether unresolved outcomes can remain unresolved until the reset request expires.

The deployment needs metrics for attempt count, unknown outcomes, queue age, expired-before-send requests, and reconciliation backlog. Keep record identifiers in restricted audit storage rather than making them metric labels, and keep reset secrets out of logs.

These controls do not establish compliance certification.

Sender authentication is a separate acceptance check. RFC 7208 defines SPF authorization of sending hosts for the MAIL FROM and HELO identities; it does not establish that a reset authorization is valid, that the message reached an inbox, or that the application retained suitable evidence. A sending-domain review therefore belongs beside the delivery contract review, with neither used as a substitute for the other.

Stop retaining the message body

After those tests pass, define a retention schedule for each record type with the responsible security and legal reviewers. No universal number of retention days follows from SPF, and neither a template version nor an acceptance identifier establishes that a recipient read a message. Preserve those distinctions in support tooling so that a delivery investigation cannot accidentally become a false assertion about account access.

For the logistics reset flow, the proposed compact record contains the request identity, template version, issue and expiry timestamps, transition history, and available transport correlation evidence. Give that record its own access and deletion rules. Keep the reset authorization separately, with the lifecycle required to enforce expiry and one-time consumption; deleting an email body must never delete the state that prevents authorization reuse.

The release choice follows from template ownership: accept an API boundary only when the team can explain which version was rendered, which deadline was enforced, and what evidence remains after an uncertain attempt. A short SDK example is useful after those questions have answers.

Deliberately stop retaining rendered bodies and reset links in delivery logs. That reduces the retained sensitive material, but the operational cost is real: after a wording dispute or a suspected rendering defect, investigators may have the approved template version and state history without an exact copy of the recipient's message. If exact reconstruction is required, resolve that requirement before deployment and budget for the additional protected evidence. Do not retain secrets by accident merely because debugging is easier.

References

The numerical workload, five-minute deadline, record sizes, and transition rules above are explicit illustrative design inputs. They are not external measurements or legal retention requirements. The protocol claim about sender authorization is grounded in the specification listed below.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF), especially its identity and authorization scope: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208

title: Segment What It Can Draw: Querying a Text-to-Image Generator with Its Own Images for Skin Lesion Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.07061v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Skin lesion segmentation without annotated masks requires the target to be specified through other cues. Existing approaches rely on dermoscopy-specific rules, annotation-derived model priors, or user-selected regions. A general text-to-image diffusion transformer offers a text interface to the target, but its concept-word attention is unreliable on dermoscopy images: in the model's attention-output space, the word-derived skin-to-lesion direction is poorly aligned with the direction separating real skin from real lesions. We show that the direction derived from generated healthy-skin and lesion images is substantially better aligned. Based on this finding, we propose GENIQ, a training-free method that constructs initial skin and lesion prototypes from generated images and refines them using the most skin-like and lesion-like patches from unlabelled dermoscopy images. It scores test patches along the refined direction and applies a gated threshold to suppress contextual spill-over around small lesions. Without inference-time annotations or additional models, GENIQ achieves Dice scores of 0.85-0.88 on three dermoscopy test sets. It outperforms zero-shot and word-based attention methods on all three sets, and a hand-designed dermoscopy pipeline in Dice and IoU on two.

title: A Survey of Nonlinear Filtering Methods for Data Assimilation and Recent Advances in Generative AI-Enabled Score Filters
description:
arXiv:2611.07160v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many real-world applications, such as numerical weather prediction or wildfire tracking, involve modeling highly nonlinear dynamical systems that are chaotic and influenced by various sources of uncertainty. To improve model prediction accuracy and reduce such uncertainties, data assimilation (DA) combines the dynamical model with partial, noisy observations to estimate the evolution of the system's state. Doing so depends on solving the optimal filtering problem: computing the conditional distribution of a hidden state given a sequence of observations. Classical approaches fail along three distinct axes: Kalman-based methods assume Gaussian posteriors and produce biased estimates under nonlinear observation operators; particle-based methods represent distributions with weighted samples and collapse in high dimensions due to the curse of dimensionality; and kernel-based methods move beyond discrete particle representations but cannot maintain their density approximation affordably as dimension grows. The Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) avoids all three constraints by encoding the filtering density in a score function and approximating that score with a training-free Monte Carlo estimator, enabling stable filtering in high-dimensional, chaotic systems. This survey traces EnSF's mathematical foundations, establishes it as the state of the art for non-Gaussian, high-dimensional filtering, and examines fourteen extensions that expand its operational reach. Twelve of the fourteen extensions preserve this training-free Monte Carlo estimator at the core of the update, with only two departing from it to achieve planetary-scale deployment.

title: Adaptive Semantic Branching: Disagreement-Localized Cross-Trajectory Regeneration for Reasoning Candidate Expansion
description:
arXiv:2611.07918v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning trajectories generated for the same problem often arrive at conflicting answers. These disagreements reveal alternative intermediate decisions that can be reused to explore new solutions. We introduce Adaptive Semantic Branching (ASB), a training-free inference procedure that turns cross-trajectory disagreement into targeted candidate generation. ASB first groups independently sampled trajectories by extracted final answer, selects a representative from each group, and aligns their reasoning steps with a monotonic dynamic program. A persistent-divergence objective identifies the point at which initially similar reasoning paths develop different continuations. For each selected directed pair, ASB retains the source trajectory's textual prefix, extracts a short reasoning window from a competing donor trajectory, and generates a fresh solution conditioned on both. A diversity-aware policy allocates up to three additional generations according to the answer-cluster structure. In a 500-problem MATH evaluation with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, ASB increases oracle candidate coverage from 445/500 (89.0%) with seven initial samples to 455/500 (91.0%), recovering correct candidates for 10 of the 55 initially uncovered problems. The method uses 576 additional generation calls across the evaluation set, averaging 8.152 calls per problem. We provide a precise specification of the branching operator, alignment objective, generation policy, and experimental configuration.

title: Expanding the Quality-Coverage Frontier with Competitive Flow Matching
description:
arXiv:2611.07055v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Flow matching (FM) generators often face a quality-coverage tradeoff. Inference-time techniques such as classifier-free guidance raise quality, but at the cost of coverage. We hypothesize this limitation stems from a basic property of the objective: an intermediate noisy image could correspond to many clean images, yet the model can only predict a single velocity, at best averaging over the multiple possibilities. To mitigate this, we introduce competition among predictions during training. We achieve this by augmenting the predictor with a randomly drawn low-dimensional conditioning code $z$. For each training example, we sample $K$ values of $z$ to produce $K$ candidate velocities that compete to explain the target, and apply the loss only to the best-matching candidate. This winner-take-all objective allows different modes to shape different predictions, rather than being averaged into a single compromise. Furthermore, this term naturally enables a new form of guidance, auxiliary conditioning scaling, which complements traditional guidance methods. Together, these two guidance mechanisms show that our method substantially improves the quality-coverage frontier. We validate on ImageNet-256, using two different testbeds, SiT and RAEv2. Given less than 3% of the original SiT pretraining compute for post-training, at the 67% Recall point, our method reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 19.22 to 5.91. On RAEv2, at the 70% Recall point, it reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 16.83 to 3.18.

title: Password Reset Emails: API Sending for High Deliverability and Compliance Evidence
description:
Short answer: For password reset emails and high-deliverability verification sending, use the /v1/email/send API when its region, retention, and processor terms satisfy your compliance review.

An e-commerce signup email has two jobs that are easy to confuse: get a verification link to the buyer, and leave enough evidence to explain what happened later. The second job changes the API decision.

Use /v1/email/send for the single transactional send, but keep consent, token generation, expiry, and compliance records in your own system. A delivery API can move the message; it cannot, by itself, prove the region where every processor handled the data, how long message content was retained, or that a deletion request reached every downstream system. For a password-reset flow, the same boundary applies.

Infrai fits this narrow part of the workflow when one REST boundary, one key, and one bill across backend services are operationally useful. Its public discovery surface also exposes capability metadata and runnable examples without a key, which makes the integration inventory easier to inspect before a compliance review.

Should this API handle password reset emails and verification sending?

The answer is yes only when the provider boundary is acceptable. Here is a minimal Python client that sends an application-owned JSON payload, retries a rate limit with Retry-After, and supplies an idempotency key. It deliberately leaves message fields in INFRAI_EMAIL_PAYLOAD, because the route's verified existence does not make an undocumented request schema safe to invent.

import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request


api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
payload = os.environ["INFRAI_EMAIL_PAYLOAD"].encode("utf-8")
request = urllib.request.Request(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send",
    data=payload,
    method="POST",
    headers={
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": os.environ["INFRAI_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY"],
    },
)


for attempt in range(4):
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
            if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                raise RuntimeError(f"send failed: HTTP {response.status}")
            print(json.loads(response.read()))
            break
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
        if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            raise RuntimeError(f"send failed: HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
        delay = int(error.headers.get("Retry-After", "0"))
        time.sleep(delay if delay > 0 else 2**attempt)

Keep the idempotency key stable for the same internal event. A new key on every retry can turn a transient delivery problem into duplicate recovery mail.

What evidence must the signup flow produce?

Start with the evidence model, not the vendor feature list. For each verification request, record an internal event ID, account ID, purpose, template version, creation time, expiry time, and the provider request ID returned by the send operation. Store the recipient as a protected identifier or a keyed digest where the investigation does not require the raw address. The link token belongs in a separate short-lived store; putting it into a general-purpose audit record creates a needless credential-retention problem.

This is a trade-off, not a checklist. A longer retention window makes support investigations easier, while a shorter one reduces the blast radius of an exported event table. Decide the window from your policy and document it. Do not infer it from an API's default behavior.

The region question is similarly precise: where is the application data stored, where is the message content processed, and where are delivery and abuse-prevention logs retained? Those are different locations and often different processors. SPF is part of sender authorization, not proof of regional processing or deletion; RFC 7208 describes the former boundary clearly.

Which boundary belongs to the sending API?

A useful design divides responsibility into three layers. Your application owns the account event, token lifecycle, consent record, and deletion workflow. The sending service owns the accepted request and its delivery pipeline under its published processor and retention terms. Your compliance process owns the evidence that connects those layers without copying the entire message body into an audit system.

That division also exposes limits that marketing pages tend to blur. The email capability has no hosted email OTP interface, so a fallback code flow needs to be built by the application. It has no SMTP relay. Event retrieval is pull-based rather than webhook-driven, which means a polling job must reconcile provider events with your internal event ID; real-time orchestration should not be assumed. Scheduled email has a scheduled_at field, but there is no email cancellation route, so do not make cancellation a promise in the user experience.

For a domestic compliance decision, do not treat a pending Tencent email vendor as evidence that domestic processing is available. Ask for the actual region and processor commitments that apply to the account and route you will use. If those commitments are mandatory, the specialist provider remains the safer choice until the paperwork is explicit.

Why do the obvious provider comparisons miss the real risk?

SendGrid, Mailgun, and Postmark are credible products to evaluate, but they answer different parts of the question. SendGrid is a broad transactional and marketing email platform, so it can suit teams that want one larger email program. Mailgun is often evaluated by engineering teams that care about programmatic sending and operational controls. Postmark is positioned around transactional delivery, which makes it a natural comparison for verification and reset messages. None of those labels, by themselves, establishes a region, retention period, deletion propagation rule, or processor contract for your exact account.

The comparison should therefore be explicit:

Option Reason to evaluate Evidence boundary to verify
SendGrid Broad email program and mature sending surface Which data is retained for transactional messages, and which processors handle it?
Mailgun Developer-oriented sending and domain operations Can your required region and deletion request path be documented for the selected service?
Postmark Transactional-message focus What delivery, bounce, and abuse logs remain after message deletion?
Infrai One REST API, one key, and one bill across backend services Which region, retention, and processor terms apply to the email route and its vendors?

The last row is where Infrai can be useful, but the distinction matters. Its unified surface removes key and invoice sprawl when the same backend also uses other capabilities, and its public discovery surface exposes capability metadata and runnable examples without a key. That reduces integration inventory. It does not turn a multi-provider delivery chain into a single legal processor, and it does not supply a domestic compliance guarantee.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the single verification or password-reset send when your team wants one REST boundary and one operational account across backend services, provided your compliance review accepts the email route's documented region and processor terms. Choose SendGrid, Mailgun, or Postmark instead when their specialist controls or contract language meet a requirement that the unified layer cannot satisfy.

A small rollout with a hard stop

Ship the flow in stages. First, generate and expire the token inside the application. Second, version the template and write the internal audit event before calling the sender. Third, send through /v1/email/send and persist the provider request ID without storing the token in the provider-facing audit record. Finally, poll for events and reconcile them to the internal event ID. Treat every poll result as evidence to normalize, not as a replacement for your own audit trail.

Before production, make the compliance review answer five questions in writing: the processing regions, each relevant processor, message and event retention, deletion propagation, and the owner of the fallback OTP flow. If one answer is “we will find out after launch,” the rollout is not ready.

The practical answer is narrower than “which API has the highest deliverability.” Choose the sender whose deliverability controls and evidence boundary fit the account workflow. For a unified backend boundary, start with the email API documentation and verify the contractual details before committing the data path.

Sources

References:

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • SendGrid Email API
  • Mailgun API documentation
  • Postmark developer documentation
  • Infrai documentation

title: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.07461v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. We introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that equip a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), a harness engineering framework that builds each task's harness from a library of such primitives. HEELO composes the primitives a task needs into a task-specific graph, verifies the result against evidence from the environment, revises the primitives a failure implicates, and admits new or improved primitives after validation. We instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built for one kind of task, and evaluate them on more than twenty benchmarks. Dev-Primitives raise Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 37.3% under Codex to 55.5% on the same backbone, Harness Primitives composed per task raise Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, Tool Primitives raise ToolBench pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, and Navigation Primitives raise GAIA-Text-103 accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. On the 46 real-world tasks of our heelo.dev platform, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex complete 9 each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through our MCP server, with 1.9$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ less time and 1.55$\times$ lower cost per completed task.

title: RepoDNA v1.5.0 Is Here: Local History Controls, Reviewed Exports, and Clearer CI Impact
description:
RepoDNA v1.5.0 Is Here: Local History Controls, Reviewed Exports, and Clearer CI Impact

RepoDNA v1.5.0 is now available as a stable release!

RepoDNA is an open-source, local-first repository intelligence tool that helps developers understand codebases through architecture, dependencies, Git history, quality signals, and evidence-backed findings.

This release focuses on control, reviewability, and correctness.

1. Delete saved analysis history safely

Version 1.5.0 introduces confirmed deletion of individual saved analyses or an entire repository's stored analysis history.

You can clean up locally stored analysis records without deleting your original repository or source code.

2. Preview findings before exporting

RepoDNA now provides a local preview and explicit confirmation before exporting selected findings as CSV, JSON, or Markdown.

This helps developers review what they are about to share.

Note: Previewing does not automatically detect or redact secrets. Always review sensitive information before sharing exports.

3. Understand CI impact more clearly

CI baseline comparisons now include additional context such as before-and-after module ownership, file paths, and dependency information.

These improvements help developers investigate changes and understand their architectural impact.

4. More reliable comparisons

RepoDNA v1.5.0 improves deterministic handling of repeated findings and ambiguous duplicate paths.

The goal is to produce more consistent, reproducible comparisons.

5. Improved release reliability

The release includes stronger dependency and packaging checks.

Windows executable metadata also displays RepoDNA as the company instead of GitHub.

Try RepoDNA v1.5.0

https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/releases/tag/v1.5.0

RepoDNA is available across Windows, macOS, Linux, and the web, with platform-dependent features.

What's next?

RepoDNA will continue evolving to make repository analysis more useful, explainable, and reliable.

Feedback, bug reports, suggestions, and open-source contributions are welcome.

title: Adapting LLM Judges to Observed Human Annotation Policy through Soft Prompt Tuning
description:
arXiv:2611.07126v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly employed as automated judges for evaluating chatbot responses. While proprietary models can achieve high agreement with human annotators, they remain costly and difficult to deploy in practical settings. Lightweight open-source LLM judges provide an attractive alternative but typically exhibit lower agreement with human ratings. In this paper, we investigate whether soft prompt tuning can align open-source LLM judges more closely with human annotation policy. We train soft prompts on the FairBotBench benchmark and evaluate the adapted judges across the dimensions of bias, toxicity, and personalization. Our findings demonstrate that hybrid soft-prompt tuning, which combines textual prompts with learned continuous prompt embeddings, consistently improves agreement with human annotations over the corresponding untuned baselines. For Qwen 3.5 9B, the adapted judges surpass both hosted reference judges across all three evaluation dimensions.

title: This WebM Says It Has Alpha. Why Is It Still Opaque?
description:
B and C open on the same shot. There’s a man in headphones, a black rectangle behind him, and no sign of the blue checkerboard underneath. Both files report ALPHA_MODE=1. One stays opaque. The other reveals the checkerboard for about 83 milliseconds.

All three clips come from the same BGRemover demo. A keeps the cutout. B and C are test files made from it. The checkerboard is behind each decoded frame so you can see where the alpha lets it through.

All three files give the same answer 

ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 \
  -show_entries stream=codec_name,pix_fmt:stream_tags=alpha_mode \
  -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 C.webm

FFprobe 8.0.1 reported this for A, B and C.

codec_name=vp9
pix_fmt=yuv420p
TAG:ALPHA_MODE=1

ALPHA_MODE=1 describes what the track signals. A frame can still have an alpha plane filled with 255, which makes the entire picture opaque. The yuv420p line is easy to misread here too. All three files exposed an alpha plane when decoded with libvpx.

The decoder changes what you can inspect 

ffmpeg -c:v libvpx-vp9 -i A.webm -vf alphaextract -frames:v 1 alpha.png

On the test build, omitting -c:v libvpx-vp9 gave Requested planes not available on A. Put it before -i to select the input decoder. The PNG that comes out shows the alpha plane in grayscale. Black is transparent and white is opaque. FFmpeg filter reference

The flash is on frame 14

File Alpha tag First frame passes? Frames that pass
A 1 Yes 24 / 24
B 1 No 0 / 24
C 1 No 1 / 24

Frame 14 of C starts about 1.08 seconds in. Checking at 0, 0.5, 1 and 1.5 seconds skips it entirely. If you paused B and C at the start and inspected the alpha plane, both would look solid white.

Recreate the test

Save the demo as source.webm. The commands below take two seconds at 12 fps. B sets alpha to 255 throughout. C does the same except at index 13, which is frame 14 when counting from one. Download the demo WebM

Commands to build A, B and C (Bash)

encode() {
  ffmpeg -v error -c:v libvpx-vp9 -i source.webm -map 0:v:0 \
    -vf "fps=12,scale=640:360,format=rgba,$2" -frames:v 24 -an \
    -c:v libvpx-vp9 -lossless 1 -auto-alt-ref 0 "$1.webm"
}

encode A "format=yuva420p"
encode B "lutrgb=a=maxval,format=yuva420p"
encode C "lutrgb=a=maxval:enable='not(eq(n,13))',format=yuva420p"

To count passing frames, the script checks for both a visible subject and room for a background to show through. On the same frame, at least 1% of pixels must have alpha below 245 and at least 1% must have alpha above 10. It measures a 320 × 180 nearest-neighbor copy of the alpha plane. That’s enough to catch a solid rectangle in this test. For a one-pixel fringe, inspect the mask at full resolution.

Python script to scan every decoded frame

import subprocess
import sys

if len(sys.argv) != 2:
    raise SystemExit('Usage: python scan-alpha.py INPUT.webm')

# One byte per pixel after alphaextract and a fixed scale.
frame_bytes = 320 * 180
cmd = [
    'ffmpeg', '-nostdin', '-v', 'error', '-c:v', 'libvpx-vp9',
    '-i', sys.argv[1], '-map', '0:v:0',
    '-vf', 'alphaextract,scale=320:180:flags=neighbor',
    '-fps_mode', 'passthrough', '-c:v', 'rawvideo', '-threads:v', '1',
    '-pix_fmt', 'gray', '-f', 'rawvideo', 'pipe:1',
]

frames = mixed = 0
examples = []
with subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdout=subprocess.PIPE) as proc:
    while frame := proc.stdout.read(frame_bytes):
        if len(frame) != frame_bytes:
            raise SystemExit('Incomplete decoded frame')
        frames += 1
        clear = sum(a < 245 for a in frame)
        visible = sum(a > 10 for a in frame)
        if clear * 100 >= frame_bytes and visible * 100 >= frame_bytes:
            mixed += 1
            if len(examples) < 5:
                examples.append(frames)
    if proc.wait() != 0 or frames == 0:
        raise SystemExit('No usable alpha scan; check the decoder and input')

print(f'{mixed}/{frames} frames pass; first passing frame numbers: {examples}')

Save it as scan-alpha.py and run python scan-alpha.py C.webm. The test run returned 1/24 frames pass; first passing frame numbers: [14]. You’ll need Python 3.8+ and an FFmpeg build with the libvpx VP9 encoder and decoder.

If a cutout should stay usable for the whole shot, check every frame. If the last few frames are supposed to cover the screen, restrict that check to the part of the clip that will be composited.

The source cutout was made using BGRemover’s video tool. Try the video background remover

For a CI check that samples a few frames with Node.js, see the FFmpeg and CI walkthrough.

If a two-second overlay goes opaque for one frame in the middle, would you fail the build or ship it with a warning?

The prose was drafted and rewritten with AI. Original stock footage is from Mixkit. Bearded announcer, close up

title: Vercel for Enterprise
description:
AI adoption in the enterprise is growing rapidly, and expanding beyond engineering users.

In the last three months, token usage by enterprise companies on AI Gateway has quadrupled, and OpenAI recently reported that from August 2025 to June 2026, non-developer Codex users grew 189x.

Our customers call these builders citizen developers. They know their part of the business better than anyone else, and with AI they can create the software they need to ship work faster and deliver better customer experiences.

Building has never been easier, but that also means that control and governance have never been harder. Employees are using AI tools whether they are approved or not, and if a citizen developer vibe codes a login page incorrectly, private data can reach the public internet.

Enterprise leaders have to figure out how to let everyone build, without giving up security or control.

Enterprise Apps and Agents

We built Enterprise Apps and Agents to solve these challenges at Vercel, and in June, we made it available to our customers. Enterprise Apps and Agents is a central control plane for governing every builder, app, agent, token, and dollar.

Today, we are expanding the platform:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) on AWS is generally available, giving you the full Vercel developer experience, while keeping compute and data inside your AWS boundary.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization through Vercel Connect is launching in public beta, giving agents the ability to access connected services on behalf of employees through your IdP.

A single control plane for governing enterprise AI

Enterprise Apps and Agents gives you a single deployment destination for both engineers and citizen developers, with central governance over access, providers, models, data retention, token budgets, integrations, and policies, managed through your existing IdP.

Vercel centralizes AI governance so that company policies can be applied consistently across control domains.

Control domain

Vercel controls

Deployment governance

Enterprise Managed Users and RBAC

Access governance

Vercel Passport, Deployment Protection, and Vercel Firewall

Integration and data governance

Vercel Connect and Enterprise-Managed Authorization

Model and token governance

AI Gateway, including US-only inference and budget controls

Apps and agents run on the same infrastructure that powers billions of production deployments, and Vercel gives you a single place for observability and security monitoring across every project, through analytics, audit logs, and the Security Dashboard.

Secure Compute provides private connectivity to enterprise systems, while BYOC on AWS lets your application functions run in your own AWS account under your permissions and network controls.

Deployment governance

Citizen developers and engineers use different tools. A marketer might use ChatGPT to build a landing page, an analyst might use Claude Code to run queries and build a report, and an engineer might use Codex, OpenCode, or fx.

No matter the harness, Vercel gives you a single deployment target, and connects to your existing IdP, so you can control who creates deployments.

How Klaviyo's built a secure internal app platform

Before Vercel, shipping a simple internal app at Klaviyo took two weeks of chasing IT, opening tickets for engineering, and following up with the platform team. They built an internal app-building platform on top of Enterprise Apps and Agents, and now anyone in the company can deploy an idea in three minutes. In their first two weeks on Vercel, 512 employees deployed 356 apps.

Access governance

Controlling who can deploy doesn't protect the apps, agents, and data that make it into production.

On Vercel, you can configure every deployment to be private by default, and with Vercel Passport, you can require employees to authenticate through your IdP before they can access internal apps.

Integration and data governance

Agents are only useful when they can access your systems and data, but that often means using long-standing environment varibles with wide-ranging permissions to your CRM, databases, Slack, and other systems.

Vercel Connect implements connectors with scoped access, and mints tokens for each agent task, meaning agents only access the specific context they need for the job. And now, with Enterprise-Managed Authorization, when employees sign into Vercel through your IdP, agents can use connected services automatically, without a separate authorization prompt.

Connect also integrates with Passport, so individual employee permissions also apply at the integration and data layer. If someone can't see data in a source system, they can't access it through an app or agent either.

Model and token governance

The average enterprise company using Vercel AI Gateway routes across 17 different models. Without a model router, that would require integrating with multiple separate providers, spreading API keys and budget management across platforms.

AI Gateway gives you access to hundreds of models through a single API, with no markup on cost, and Zero Data Retention keeps your data from being stored or trained on. You can also elect to route through US-only providers to maintain compliance.

How Mercor manages model governance at scale

Mercor connects AI labs with subject-matter experts who help train and evaluate models. Their engineers need access to hundreds of models to enable that work, but before migrating to Vercel, access was spread across direct integrations and third-party routers, making stolen credentials a huge risk, and token spend impossible to manage.

They moved their model routing to AI Gateway, and now engineers can access hundreds of models with a single, expiring secret, and they can set budgets per person or project.

In their first 10 days on AI Gateway, they processed 63 billion tokens without hitting any rate limits.

Centralized visibility and security

Vercel Observability gives you a single view for app and agent telemetry across every project, so you can easily manage performance and troubleshoot problems for both internal tools and customer-facing products.

The Security Dashboard flags risks across your team and apps, including missing MFA, unprotected preview deployments, long-lived credentials, and framework vulnerabilities. Each finding links to the settings needed to fix it.

Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS

BYOC on AWS is generally available. With BYOC, application functions execute in your AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

Meta Superintelligence Labs runs on Vercel via BYOC, giving its AI teams the ability to test and deploy ideas quickly, inside their own AWS environment. Leaders at Meta said that in their first week on Vercel, they shipped a month worth of work.

From idea to global scale on one platform

Vercel let's everyone in your company build safely, and makes it easy for engineers to ship the best ideas at global scale, all on a single platform.

That is how we built Vertex, our customer support agent. We were previously using a vendor, but it couldn't answer all of our customers questions. When our support team built agents and skills to cover the gaps and increase our responses times, and we realized they had laid the foundation for the experience we wanted to deliver directly to our customers.

Our GTM engineering team took that foundation and made it production ready with evals and model failover.

Today, Vertex handles 91% of our customer support cases autonomously, processing thousands of tickets a week, and it runs on the same platform where the idea started.

Ship your best ideas, securely

Contact sales to learn more about enterprise governance on Vercel and get a custom demo of the platform.

title: Docraft: Turn Pasted AI Responses into Word, PDF and HTML Files, Locally in Your Browser
description:
AI chats are great at producing structured text, but getting that text into a clean, shareable document is still a chore. Docraft is a Chrome extension that turns a pasted AI response into an editable Word file, a styled PDF, or a standalone HTML page in a couple of clicks.

Everything runs locally in your browser. There's no server, no account, no analytics, and no AI API behind it.

GitHub: https://github.com/abmdevx/docraft

What it does

Paste your text into the popup, optionally set a title, and export. When you need more control, open the full workspace.

  • Compact popup for fast paste-and-export
  • Full workspace with an editor, a live document preview, and document settings
  • Three export formats: Word (.docx), PDF, and HTML
  • Markdown-aware parsing that detects headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, code blocks, quotes, links, and inline formatting
  • Light and dark documents: a white page, or a near-black page with white text, for Word and PDF output
  • Document controls: font, size, page size, orientation, margins, title, and page numbers
  • Optional table of contents in all three formats
  • Multi-paste ZIP batches: add several responses, choose a format for each, and download them together
  • Math in PDFs: KaTeX renders supported LaTeX formulas as crisp images

Privacy by design

People paste a lot of sensitive text into AI tools, so the extension asks for as little as possible:

  • Only the storage permission is required
  • clipboardRead is optional and requested only when you use the Paste action
  • No host permissions at all
  • Pasted content isn't saved unless you enable "Remember my draft"
  • Pasted HTML is treated as literal text and is never rendered with innerHTML
  • Only validated http, https, mailto, and tel links become active

Tech stack

  • React + TypeScript for the popup and workspace UIs
  • Tailwind CSS for styling and Vite for building
  • Chrome Manifest V3
  • A Markdown parser feeding separate Word, PDF, and HTML exporters
  • Automated tests for the parser, the exporters, and the UI
  • The open-source Carlito font embedded so PDFs match Calibri's metrics

Known limitations

  • PDF fonts cover Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and many symbols. CJK and complex scripts such as Arabic or Indic scripts may not render fully, and Docraft warns you after export when characters are unsupported.
  • Preview page breaks are estimates.
  • Landscape mode is manual, and wide tables are scaled with smaller type.

Try it

Docraft installs from source for now:

git clone https://github.com/abmdevx/docraft.git
cd docraft
npm install
npm run build

Then open chrome://extensions, enable Developer mode, choose Load unpacked, and select the generated dist/ folder.

It's MIT licensed, so feedback, issues, and stars are all welcome: https://github.com/abmdevx/docraft

What would you want from a tool like this? Let me know in the comments.

title: 메타의 150억 달러 채권 발행, 580억 달러 주문 몰린 날 내 퀘스트 헤드셋 속에서 일어난 일: 약시(Lazy Eye) 아빠가 쓴 Amblyotube 90일 개발자 일지, 이안 시차(Dichoptic) 렌더링…
description:
메타의 150억 달러 채권 발행, 580억 달러 주문 몰린 날 내 퀘스트 헤드셋 속에서 일어난 일: 약시(Lazy Eye) 아빠가 쓴 Amblyotube 90일 개발자 일지, 이안 시차(Dichoptic) 렌더링 파이프라인·MFBF 샤프너·마젠타 포커스 큐·웨지 오클루전·로그마(LogMAR) 자동 캘리브레이션·AR 패스스루 모드·오프라인 카탈로그·핸드 트래킹까지, 기술 스택과 UX가 어떻게 '순응도(Adherence)'를 잡았는지, 그리고 13세 아이와 나를 어떻게 바꾸었는지.

그날 아침, 뉴스 피드에 메타가 150억 달러 규모의 채권을 발행했고 580억 달러 주문이 몰렸다는 헤드라인이 떴다. 내 손에는 퀘스트 3 헤드셋이 있었고, 책상 위에는 13살 딸아이의 약시 치료용 앱 Amblyotube가 켜져 있었다. 개발자이자 아빠로서, 나는 이 두 세계가 어떻게 충돌하는지 직접 지켜보기로 했다.

1. 아키텍처: 이안 시차(Dichoptic) 렌더링 파이프라인

Amblyotube의 핵심은 이안 시차 렌더링이다. Unity URP 기반으로 두 개의 카메라를 각각 왼쪽/오른쪽 눈에 매핑하고, 셰이더에서 MFBF(Multi‑Frequency Band‑Filter) 샤프너를 적용해 고대비 에지를 강조한다. 코드 조각은 대략 다음과 같다.

// DichopticRendering.cs
void OnRenderImage(RenderTexture src, RenderTexture dest) {
    var left  = GetEyeTexture(Eye.Left);
    var right = GetEyeTexture(Eye.Right);
    // MFBF sharpen
    left  = ApplyMFBF(left);
    right = ApplyMFBF(right);
    // Magenta focus cue
    left  = ApplyMagentaCue(left);
    right = ApplyMagentaCue(right);
    Graphics.Blit(left,  dest, 0, 0);
    Graphics.Blit(right, dest, 0, 1);
}

이 파이프라인은 프레임당 2 ms 이하의 오버헤드만 추가한다(Quest 3의 Adreno 650에서 측정). 덕분에 90 fps 유지가 가능하고, 배터리 소모도 3 % 이내로 억제된다.

2. UX 설계: 마젠타 포커스 큐·웨지 오클루전·LogMAR 자동 캘리브레이션

  • 마젠타 포커스 큐: 약시 눈에만 마젠타 컬러 오버레이를 띄워 주의력을 유도한다. 색상 공간 변환은 sRGB → Linear → Oculus Quest 색보정 LUT를 거쳐 적용된다.
  • 웨지 오클루전: 시야 각도 30° 내외의 삼각형 마스크로 건강한 눈을 부분 차단, 억제된 눈의 입력을 강제한다. 마스크는 런타임에 Compute Shader로 생성돼 프레임 드랍 없이 동적 조정이 가능하다.
  • LogMAR 자동 캘리브레이션: 앱 시작 시 5‑포인트 시력 검사를 수행, 결과를 LogMAR 스케일로 변환해 이후 난이도(대비, 크기, 노출 시간)를 실시간으로 스케줄링한다. 알고리즘은 단순 선형 회귀지만, 온디바이스 TensorFlow Lite 모델로 0.2 초 만에 수렴한다.

이 세 가지가 결합되면서 순응도(Adherence) 지표가 90일 동안 78 % → 94 %로 상승했다(내부 텔레메트리, 익명화).

3. AR 패스스루·오프라인 카탈로그·핸드 트래킹

  • AR 패스스루 모드: Quest 3의 컬러 패스스루 카메라를 활용, 실제 책상 위에 가상의 훈련 블록을 띄운다. 깊이 맵은 Depth API로 받아와 셰이더에서 오클루전 처리를 한다.
  • 오프라인 카탈로그: 120 개 이상의 훈련 시나리오를 Addressable Asset System으로 번들링, 초기 다운로드 후 완전 오프라인 실행 가능하다. 압축률 2.3×, 로드 타임 < 1 초.
  • 핸드 트래킹: 컨트롤러 없이 손가락 제스처로 난이도 조절·일시정지·리플레이를 수행. Hand Tracking SDK v2의 Joint Pose 데이터를 필터링해 30 fps 안정적 입력을 보장.

4. 90일, 아빠와 딸의 데이터

주차 평균 세션(분) 완료율 LogMAR 변화
1‑2 12 62 % +0.12
3‑4 18 78 % +0.08
5‑8 24 91 % +0.04
9‑12 28 94 % +0.02

딸아이는 처음엔 헤드셋을 벗으려 했다. 마젠타 큐가 눈에 띄게 보이자 "이건 내 눈에만 보이는 마법 같아"라고 말했고, 웨지 오클루전이 점차 좁아지면서 "이제 내 눈이 더 잘 보여"라고 웃는다. 나는 로그를 보며 프레임 타임, 배터리, 열을 모니터링했고, 필요할 때마다 MFBF 강도를 0.3→0.5로 올렸다. 개발자 로그에서 Debug.Log($"MFBF:{intensity} Adherence:{adherence}") 한 줄이 매일 밤 내 마음을 달랬다.

5. 회고: 기술이 사람한테 닿을 때

채권 발행 뉴스가 터진 날, 나는 퀘스트 헤드셋 속에서 메타의 자본과 내 딸의 시력이 같은 파이프라인을 타고 흐르는 걸 느꼈다. 거대한 자금이 하드웨어 스펙을 밀어올리고, 그 스펙이 실시간 이안 렌더링, 온디바이스 ML, 핸드 트래킹 같은 개발자 도구로 돌아와, 결국 한 가정의 일상에 순응도 94 %라는 숫자로 남는다.

코드 한 줄, 셰이더 한 줄, 텔레메트리 한 줄이 모여 아이의 눈을 바꾸고, 아빠의 밤을 바꾼다. 기술 블로그에 올릴 만한 벤치마크도, 개인 일기에 쓸 만한 감동도, 모두 같은 리포지토리 안에 있다.

title: HyFlash: A Prefix-Memory Prior for On-Device Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.07263v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parallel block drafting accelerates speculative decoding by predicting multiple future positions in a single backbone pass, but on-device deployment constrains both drafter capacity and context storage. Under tight memory budgets, drafters must model long-range dependencies and fine-grained draft-position interactions without the growing KV-cache overhead of full-context attention. We propose HyFlash, a compact parallel drafter that introduces a prefix-memory prior to separate long-range context modeling from fine-grained draft-position interactions with limited capacity. Local attention captures recent context and draft-position interactions, while recurrent memory compresses historical target features into fixed-size states. This inductive bias enables effective local and long-range modeling with bounded draft-side memory. Experiments show that HyFlash achieves higher acceptance than full-context attention with substantially less KV storage and with larger gains for shallow drafters and long contexts.

title: Different Corpora, Different Skills? A Paired Study of Small Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.07812v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Small language models are often trained under tight data budgets, where the choice of pretraining corpus may matter as much as model size or training recipe. We compare two contrasting corpora at matched 10-million- and 37-million-word budgets: the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and the BabyLM 2026 strict pretraining corpus. For each corpus, we train teacher models, distilled 58-million-parameter Baby-Llama students, and no-distillation student ablations, using the same model families, training recipes, and evaluation protocol across corpora. Across BLiMP, BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, Entity Tracking, and COMPS, the corpora produce different skill profiles rather than a single quality ranking. BabyLM 2026 is consistently stronger on linguistic acceptability benchmarks, while Britannica is often stronger on Entity Tracking, a synthetic state-tracking task. The contrast appears across teacher and student models and at both budgets, with the cleanest cross-seed replication in the distilled student comparison. Targeted controls show that the central contrast persists after matching training exposure and at a longer diagnostic context; direct teacher ensembling also does not reproduce the 10M Britannica student's Entity Tracking behavior. Entity Tracking magnitudes nevertheless remain sensitive to training dynamics. For this corpus pair, corpus choice can therefore produce different relative skill profiles at small scale, motivating multi-benchmark evaluation when comparing pretraining data.

title: CoGenRec: A Unified Generative Framework for Complementary Vision Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.07665v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Capturing scenes with extreme motion and high dynamic range is fundamentally constrained by trade-offs among temporal resolution, spatial detail, signal-to-noise ratio, and dynamic range under practical bandwidth, power, and quantum-efficiency limits. Conventional frame-based cameras therefore suffer from temporal undersampling, exposure-induced motion blur, and sensor saturation. The Complementary Vision Sensor (CVS) addresses these limitations by decomposing visual information across two complementary pathways, a spatially dense, temporally sparse, long-exposure RGB pathway and a temporally dense, spatially sparse, short-exposure patiotemporal difference pathway. Their complementary measurements provide appearance, structural, and motion cues across a wide dynamic range that enable reconstruction beyond conventional imaging. We present CoGenRec, a complementarity-driven generative reconstruction framework that unifies video deblurring, high-temporal-resolution frame interpolation, and HDR fusion. CoGenRec encodes complementary measurements into multi-scale spatiotemporal features using exposure-aware appearance modeling and bidirectional temporal propagation. These features constrain a video diffusion model and are injected into the VAE decoder to recover fine structures lost during latent-space compression, combining the scene fidelity of physical measurements with the appearance recovery capabilities of learned video priors. On SportsSloMo-CVS, CoGenRec improves PSNR over the strongest general-purpose baseline by 4.40 dB for deblurring, 3.89 dB for frame interpolation, and 5.04 dB for HDR fusion, respectively. It also achieves strong perceptual quality on 129 unseen scenes captured with real CVS. These results establish a unified approach to advance high-quality reconstruction under challenging motion and illumination conditions. Project page: https://cogenrec.github.io/.

title: Perceptual Distortion for Overfitted Video Coding: Sliced Matching in Space, Error Alignment in Time
description:
arXiv:2611.07148v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent works in neural video coding have increasingly been trading off perceptual quality against reconstruction fidelity at a fixed bitrate. Wasserstein Distortion (WD) offers a principled approach to balancing these objectives by relaxing spatial correspondences in feature matching, enabling lightweight overfitted image codecs to compete with computationally intensive generative decoders. Extending vanilla WD to video, however, presents two challenges: its independent Gaussian approximation limits the expressiveness of feature distribution matching, while unconstrained texture resampling across frames introduces temporal inconsistencies. We address these challenges by distinguishing between the correspondences that can be relaxed and those that must be preserved. Spatially, we introduce a local sliced Wasserstein distortion (SWD) that matches empirical feature distributions through one-dimensional optimal transport, capturing cross-channel dependencies without enforcing exact spatial alignment. Temporally, we employ a novel flow residual that constrains coding errors along motion trajectories, preserving temporal consistency without imposing additional reconstruction fidelity constraints. Evaluated on UVG and HEVC Class B with the overfitted codec COOL-CHIC, our framework achieves BD-rate reductions of 9.2% in DISTS and 3.0% in LPIPS relative to frame-wise WD, averaged over test sequences, while lowering tOF by 10.2% at matched rate.
