title: Grace Periods Are a Product Decision Wearing a Billing Costume
description:
Somewhere in your billing settings sits a number most teams chose once and forgot: how long a subscriber keeps access after a payment fails. Three days, seven days, until the next attempt — whatever it is, that number is doing product work. It decides how forgiving your service feels at the exact moment a customer is most likely to be embarrassed, confused, or quietly broke. Treating the grace period as a billing default rather than a designed experience is how good products end up feeling like debt collectors.

What the grace period is really for

A failed payment is usually not a refusal. Balances refill, cards get replaced, banks unblock. The grace period exists to hold the relationship open while those ordinary repairs happen — to say, in product behaviour rather than in an email, that the account is valued more than the timing of one charge. Cut it too short and you convert temporary problems into permanent churn, then pay acquisition costs to replace people who never wanted to leave. Stretch it too long and a different problem grows: a tail of non-paying accounts consuming support and capacity while the recovery effort loses its urgency.

The right length is therefore an empirical question about your own file. How do your recoveries distribute across the days after a failure? Most subscription businesses find a steep early curve — the majority of eventual recoveries land inside the first week — and a long flat tail. Your grace period should cover the steep part generously and treat the tail as a decision, not a default.

Design the days, not just the length

What happens during grace matters as much as how long it lasts. A subscriber in grace should meet honesty without alarm: the product keeps working, a calm notice explains the payment issue, and updating the card takes one tap rather than a password reset expedition. Escalation should be sequenced — gentle at first, clearer as the window closes, and always specific about the date access actually ends. Vague warnings teach people to ignore warnings; a true date teaches them to act.

Developers building this flow will find the mechanics — attempt scheduling inside the window, access states, the moment of final closure — easier to get right once the policy is written down. A plain-language reference on subscription grace periods covers the common patterns and the trade-offs each length creates, including the special cases of annual plans, where a blunt short grace period can destroy a year of goodwill over one stale card.

The metric that keeps it honest

Review the policy quarterly with one number: of the subscribers who entered grace, what share returned to good standing, and how long did the median recovery take? If the share is high and the median is short, your window is probably longer than it needs to be and costing little — leave it. If recoveries bunch at the very end of the window, your messaging is arriving late, not your grace ending early. The policy, the attempts, and the emails are one system; adjusting any one of them in isolation is how grace periods quietly stop working.

Swipe Again builds that system as one piece for subscription businesses — retries timed inside the window, messages sequenced against it, and the recovery measured against the whole failed pool. However you assemble it, write the policy down, date it, and revisit it like the product decision it is. Your subscribers will feel the difference on their worst billing day, which is exactly when feelings decide renewals.

title: Which MCP servers can actually deploy infrastructure, not just read it? Five compared
description:
If you want an AI agent to deploy and run infrastructure through MCP, five hosted MCP servers can do real write work today: Vercel, Render, Railway, Netlify and Eyevinn Open Source Cloud (OSC). They differ in what the agent can create, whether it can tear things down again, and what is actually running underneath when it does.

Every row below comes from each platform's own MCP documentation, read on 6 November 2026. Tool lists change month to month, so treat the table as a dated snapshot.

What is the difference between an MCP server that reads and one that deploys?

A read-only server lets your agent look: list projects, fetch logs, search documentation. Most cloud MCP servers started there.

A deploying server lets the agent change things. It can create a database, ship your code to a public URL, set environment variables, restart a service and delete what it made. That needs more trust, so check which write actions a server exposes before you connect it to an agent that acts with your credentials.

Which hosting platforms have an MCP server that can deploy?

Platform Remote endpoint What the agent can create or change Tear down from chat?
Vercel https://mcp.vercel.com (OAuth) Deploy code to a new or existing project (deploy_to_vercel, announced July 2026). Tool categories for projects, environment variables, domains and storage. Not stated on the pages we read
Render https://mcp.render.com/mcp (OAuth or API key) Web services, static sites, cron jobs, Render Postgres and Key Value instances. Trigger deploys, update environment variables. No. Render's docs send other changes and deletions to the Dashboard or REST API
Railway https://mcp.railway.com (OAuth, or through the Railway CLI) Create projects, redeploy, accept staged changes. The local server (railway mcp local) adds services, variables, domains and volumes. Yes, on the local server, with a preview and an explicit confirm
Netlify https://mcp.netlify.com/mcp Create, manage and deploy projects. Environment variables and secrets, forms, extensions. Not stated in the README
OSC https://mcp.osaas.io/mcp (OAuth, or a personal access token) Any of the 198 open-source services in the catalog, databases (PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Valkey, CouchDB, ClickHouse), your own app from a GitHub repository, backups, config changes, restarts. Yes, behind a confirmation step

How should I read that table?

Vercel, Netlify and Render are at their best when what you deploy is a web app or a frontend with a managed database beside it. That is what those platforms are built around, and their MCP servers expose it well. Vercel's server added code deploys this summer, so older articles that call it read-only are out of date.

Render is explicit about its limits. Its MCP server does not support every configuration option at creation, and it leaves scaling changes and deletions to the dashboard and API. That is a defensible safety choice, and it is better to know it up front than to discover it mid-task.

Railway splits its tools in two. The hosted server is the default and the narrower one. The local server, run through the CLI, can create and remove services, volumes and domains, and Railway marks destructive actions so that clients ask before acting.

What does the OSC MCP server do that the others do not?

Two things, and both come from what OSC is rather than from the MCP layer.

The first is the catalog. OSC runs managed open-source services, and the MCP server can create any of them. When we checked today there were 198 published, from PostgreSQL and MinIO object storage to Keycloak for user logins and Uptime Kuma for monitoring, plus a long tail of media tools. Your agent is not limited to a web app and a database. If the project needs full-text search, a message queue or a video transcoder, it is the same create-service-instance call.

The second is what runs underneath. Every catalog service runs the unmodified upstream open-source container. A PostgreSQL instance on OSC speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, MinIO speaks S3 and Keycloak speaks OIDC, with no proprietary OSC API between your app and the service. If you leave, you run the same image on another cloud or your own servers and point your app at it. We wrote up that exit as a script in The Exit Test. This matters more when an agent makes the choices, because nobody stopped to read the exit terms.

The services your agent creates on OSC run in Stockholm, on Swedish-owned infrastructure.

Where OSC is the wrong pick: if your project is mostly a frontend and you want the preview-deploy-per-pull-request workflow, the platforms built around that workflow will fit better.

How do I connect the OSC MCP server to Claude Code?

You need an OSC account. The free Basic plan is enough to try it and asks for no card. Then run one command:

claude mcp add --transport http osc https://mcp.osaas.io/mcp

Start Claude Code and type /mcp. A browser window opens, you sign in, pick the workspace the tools should act on and approve. The server implements OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, so there is no key to paste. Claude Desktop, Codex and ChatGPT use the same browser sign-in.

How do I connect it to Cursor?

Create a personal access token in the OSC console under Settings, API, and add this to .cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "osc": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.osaas.io/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer <personal-access-token>"
      }
    }
  }
}

Keep that file out of git, since the token acts as you.

What can an agent actually do once it is connected?

Three prompts that work, and the tools the agent picks for them:

Create a Postgres database called appdb and give me the internal connection string.

This is create-database with type: postgres. Credentials are generated for you, and the database is internal-only by default, so apps in the same workspace reach it over internal DNS without exposing it to the internet.

Deploy github.com/me/my-api as an app and connect it to appdb.

create-my-app builds the repository (Node.js, Python, Go, .NET, PHP or WebAssembly) and gives it a stable HTTPS URL, and wait-for-app-ready reports when it is live. The app has to listen on port 8080.

Back up appdb, then show me everything I have running.

That is create-backup and list-my-services. The agent sees your own workspace, not a generic catalog, so it can manage what already exists.

Deleting is deliberately slower. delete-service-instance first returns a confirmation token and acts only on a second, confirmed call, so an agent that mistakes "stop" for "delete" does not remove a database on the first try.

Can I use my existing Claude subscription instead of buying platform credits?

Yes. The MCP server is a connector, so the AI runs on whatever Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor plan you already pay for. OSC tokens pay for running services, not for prompts, and you are never billed per prompt or for an AI mistake.

What does OSC cost?

Basic is free, with 100 tokens granted once and no card. Personal is 15 EUR a month excluding VAT and adds 40 tokens a day. A single running service typically uses 10 to 100 tokens a day, so size the plan against what you keep running rather than what you try once. Paid plans bill from day one, there is no trial on any plan, and you can cancel any time. Custom domains start at the Professional plan.

Which one should I pick?

Pick by the job, not by the protocol. If the agent's job is to ship a frontend, use the platform you would have picked without MCP. If the job is to assemble a backend out of open-source pieces and keep the option to take every one of them with you, try OSC: create a free account, run the one command above and ask your agent for a database.

Setup for VS Code, Windsurf, Codex and ChatGPT is on the OSC MCP page. A longer walkthrough: The MCP server that provisions a full backend your AI agent can deploy, and you can walk away.

If a platform's tools have changed since 6 November 2026, tell us in the comments and we will update the table.

title: NuGet Source Mapping Closes a Dependency Confusion Gap
description:
NuGet Source Mapping Closes a Dependency Confusion Gap

Package restore is a security decision made thousands of times in a large .NET build. NuGet normally searches every configured source for a package. If a public feed and a private feed can both supply the same package ID, the result depends on source order and content rather than an explicit policy. Package Source Mapping lets a project state which source may satisfy each package pattern.

How source selection becomes a trust issue

Microsoft describes Package Source Mapping as a supply-chain control for projects that mix public and private feeds. With mapping enabled, NuGet filters the configured sources per package during restore, install, and update. The mapping is written under packageSourceMapping, with a source key and one or more package patterns beneath it.

The important design point is that the repository owns the rule. A machine-level feed can be convenient, but a mapping that exists only on one developer laptop does not protect CI or another workstation. Keep the authoritative mapping in the repository-level NuGet.config, then use <clear /> where inherited sources or mappings should not leak into the build.

<packageSourceMapping>
  <clear />
  <packageSource key="company-private">
    <package pattern="Company.*" />
    <package pattern="Internal.Project.*" />
  </packageSource>
  <packageSource key="nuget.org">
    <package pattern="Microsoft.*" />
    <package pattern="System.*" />
  </packageSource>
</packageSourceMapping>

The exact patterns must match the organization's namespace. A broad public fallback can recreate the ambiguity the mapping was meant to remove. Transitive packages also need coverage. Microsoft's guidance recommends listing transitive dependencies, for example with dotnet list package --include-transitive, before freezing the source map.

Test the failure path

A mapping is only useful if an unexpected source selection fails the build. Introduce a test package ID that exists only in the private feed, then verify a clean restore on a runner that has both feeds configured. Repeat with a package that should come from the public feed. Review warnings and the effective configuration, not just the final obj directory.

The control has a documented gap. Microsoft states that Package Source Mapping currently applies to package downloads during restore, install, and update. Some metadata operations, including dotnet package add, dotnet list package, and Package Manager UI browse and update lookups, still send package IDs to all configured sources at the time of the documentation. Teams that treat package names or internal identifiers as confidential should account for that behavior separately.

Operational checks

Store feed credentials in a secret system rather than in a repository file. Review who can publish to the private feed, because source mapping selects an endpoint but does not prove that its contents are trustworthy. Pair the mapping with package signing or trusted signer policy, lock files, vulnerability review, and a controlled process for adding new package prefixes.

During incident response, export the effective NuGet configuration from the exact build environment. Compare source keys, patterns, inherited files, and environment-specific overrides. Then inspect restored package hashes and provenance. The mapping is a useful allowlist for source selection, not a replacement for artifact identity.

References

  • Microsoft Learn: Package Source Mapping
  • Microsoft Learn: nuget.config file reference

title: Open weight takes 71.5% of tokens and 23% of spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — October 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from July, August, and September.

October 2026 summary

  • Open-weight models now process more than seven in ten gateway tokens and account for nearly one in four dollars. Their share of spend has more than quadrupled since June.

  • September’s gateway spend was about 13 times December’s, while the average price per token was 47% lower. Almost one in three teams changed their most-used lab in September, an index record.

  • Nearly 70% of September’s gateway spend on Chinese models went through US-based providers, up from less than 10% in December.

  • Jev was the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history, reaching 35% of paid teams in its first two weeks, but it accounted for just 0.27% of gateway spend over that same period. Opus 5.5 took more than one in ten gateway dollars in its own first two weeks, the largest spend share of any September model launch.

Frontier spend up 900%, spend share down 22%

In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time. The money is now following. Open weight’s share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September.

Open weight's growth is coming from both ends of its price range, and it mirrors the wider gateway. The cheapest models drive token growth, while the expensive models drive spend.

Led by Kimi K3, models priced at least four times the open-weight average cost per token accounted for about two-thirds of the increase in open-weight spend.

In contrast, DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash alone processed nearly half of all September tokens but took just 2.6% of spend. Its price per token was about a fifth of the open-weight average.

Customers are increasing budgets on both sides of the market. Since December, spend on frontier models has grown tenfold; spend on open-weight models has grown more than seventyfold.

In September, 68% of teams that put more money into open-weight models did the same for closed-weight models. And more than two in five teams already paying for frontier models spent more on them than in August, the highest share this year.

Spending on the frontier is still growing, but spending on alternatives is growing faster. A company can spend more with a frontier lab while relying on it for fewer workloads, so the lab gets more money, but a smaller part of the customer’s business.

AI spend increases 13x while the cost per token halves

Market share is changing hands inside a market that is getting much bigger and cheaper.

September's gateway spend was about 13 times December's, an increase of 1,180%, while the average price per token fell 47%. The median paid customer active in both December and September more than doubled its spend.

Teams are spending more, but labs have to keep winning their business. In September, nearly one in two teams changed their most-used model. And almost one in three changed their most-used lab, an index record.

Even teams with lower token volumes use a wide mix of models. Since December, teams that processed at least 10 million tokens over that period used an average of 15 different models. The average rose to 26 for teams processing at least 100 million tokens, and 42 for those processing at least a billion.

The model is becoming a replaceable part of a much larger investment. Companies can continuously improve their AI products and workflows while changing which models power them. They can spend more on AI without becoming more dependent on any one lab.

Chinese models are big business for American providers

More than two-thirds of September’s gateway spend on Chinese-origin models went to US-based providers, up from less than a tenth in December. The Chinese lab builds the model; the American provider runs it and sells access.

DeepSeek’s models processed 58% of all gateway tokens for 6.6% of spend. More than four in five of those tokens were served by DeepSeek itself, yet two in five dollars spent on its models went through US-based providers.

Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based lab behind Kimi, accounted for 3.6% of gateway tokens and 13.2% of spend in September. US-based providers served nine in ten of those tokens.

Z.ai, also based in Beijing and the creator of GLM, accounted for 7.2% of all tokens and 4.5% of spend. US-based providers served seven in ten.

Customers can use Chinese models through access sold by American providers. For teams that put more money into Chinese models in September, an average of 53% of their spending on those models went through US-based providers and 41% through China-based ones.

The same Chinese model can compete with US-based models while generating revenue for US-based providers.

September model launch scorecard: Jev, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6

Whether a model launch is successful depends on what you measure: how broadly it’s tried, how much usage and spend it receives, or what share of its initial users return. We ranked every model launch in September with at least two weeks of data by these metrics; the tables show the top ten for each. The full scorecard is at the end of the report.

Jev is the most-adopted and most-called model

In its first two weeks, Jev reached more than a third of paid teams, nearly double the reach of Sonnet 5.5 in second place. This is the fastest adoption of any model in AI Gateway history.

Jev also received the most requests of any model in September, even though it launched halfway through the month. Of the teams that tried Jev in week one, 55.6% returned in week two, the fifth-highest retention rate.

Jev is a decision model. Compared with typical language-model requests, a Jev request is faster, cheaper and uses a fraction of the tokens. So although its adoption was fast and broad, it accounted for just 1% of the month’s tokens and 0.15% of spend.

In September, Jev quickly became a popular model for production while remaining a tiny part of the inference bill.

Opus 5.5 takes more than one in ten gateway dollars

The launch that received the most dollars was Opus 5.5, with more than twice the share of any other September launch, followed by GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash.

Opus 5.5 caught on quickly, with almost nine in ten dollars coming from teams already using Opus 5. Existing customers were trying the new release while the wider Opus family was losing market share.

Across all versions, Opus accounted for almost a third of gateway dollars in September, down from one in two in August. Anthropic’s overall share fell below half of total gateway spend for the first time, dropping from 63.7% to 43.9%.

Luna brought users back; Astra brought spend

GPT-6 Luna reached nearly three out of every twenty paid teams in its first two weeks, in third place behind Jev and Sonnet 5.5. But its return rate was the highest of the month; almost two-thirds of the teams that tried it in its first week came back in the second.

GPT-6 Astra reached a smaller audience but took more budget. In its first two weeks, it accounted for about one in twenty gateway dollars; Luna accounted for less than one in a hundred. Luna reached almost three times as many teams while Astra captured more than five times the share of spend.

OpenAI is attracting more customers with Luna, but capturing far more money with Astra, even though fewer teams use it.

Full September scorecard

Previous AI Gateway Production Index reports

  • May 2026

  • June 2026

  • July 2026

  • August 2026

  • September 2026

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through September 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, a broader definition than in earlier reports.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million paid tokens in both months. “Most-used” is measured by paid tokens.

  • Provider location means company headquarters.

  • Launch metrics cover external paid teams during each model’s first 14 days. Reach uses paid teams active from the start of the launch month through the data cutoff. Spend share uses total paid gateway spending during the model’s window. Return rate is the share of first-week teams that used it again in week two.

  • Model counts cover December–September, with each version counted separately. Team-size thresholds use total input and output tokens over that period.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: {\tau}-bench-LILT: Evaluating Conversational Agents on Realistic Multilingual Tool-Use Tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.07203v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Frontier evaluations of tool-using conversational agents are conducted almost exclusively in English, leaving a critical gap for organizations deploying agents in other languages and regions. We present ${\tau}$-bench-LILT, a multilingual extension of ${\tau^3}$-bench covering German, Korean, Turkish, and Farsi in the airline, retail, telecom, and banking domains. We natively localize every layer of the benchmark: customer databases are populated with culturally appropriate records, user-simulator prompts are refined iteratively through contrastive annotation by native-language experts, and tasks are updated according to the localized database and to reflect realistic tasks in the target region. Evaluation across eight agent models shows the largest drops compared to English in the Korean and Farsi retail domains, by up to 61 points in pass^4. Code and data released at https://github.com/lilt/tau-bench-lilt.

title: Building Better Social Media Content with AI: Exploring ViralMeme.ai
description:
Memes are more than just funny pictures on the internet. They have become an important part of online communication, social media marketing, and digital content creation. A simple image, short video, or humorous caption can quickly spread across communities and become a recognizable internet trend.

For developers, creators, and digital marketers, one interesting challenge is finding a way to combine AI technology with internet culture. How can we discover trending memes, understand why they become popular, and use AI to create our own versions?

In this article, we'll explore how AI-powered meme discovery and generation tools can make this process easier, using ViralMeme.ai as an example.

1. Understanding the Evolution of Internet Memes

Internet memes evolve constantly. Some begin with a popular social media video, while others come from gaming communities, celebrity moments, movies, or everyday situations.

The interesting thing about memes is how quickly people adapt them. One original image can inspire thousands of variations, each with a different caption, character, or humorous situation.

For content creators, keeping up with these trends can be time-consuming. You need to discover new formats, understand their original context, and decide whether they are still relevant.

This is where meme discovery platforms become useful.

ViralMeme.ai is a platform designed to help users explore popular internet memes, understand their meanings and origins, and find creative ways to remake them.

2. Discover Trending Memes with ViralMeme.ai

Instead of spending hours browsing different social media platforms, creators can use a dedicated meme discovery page to explore popular formats.

ViralMeme.ai provides a collection of trending and established memes, with individual explanations covering:

  • What each meme means.
  • Where the original trend came from.
  • How people use the meme online.
  • Whether the trend is currently rising, peaking, or declining.

This information is useful because understanding the context behind a meme is just as important as creating the content itself.

You can explore the collection here:

Explore Popular Memes on ViralMeme.ai

For developers and marketers, this kind of organized information can also provide inspiration for content research, trend analysis, and creative experiments.

3. From Meme Templates to AI-Generated Content

One of the most interesting developments in AI content creation is the ability to transform ordinary photos into creative visual content.

Traditional meme generators mainly focus on adding text to existing images. AI-powered tools take this concept further by allowing users to experiment with different visual transformations.

ViralMeme.ai offers several creative options.

Meme Caption Editor

Users can choose a meme format, customize the text, preview the result, and download a finished image. The caption editor is free and does not require an account.

AI Image Generation

For supported templates, users can upload their own photos and generate new meme-inspired images.

AI Video Generation

Some templates also support short AI-generated videos, making it possible to experiment with more dynamic content for social media.

Not every meme supports AI generation, and the available outputs and credit requirements depend on the selected template.

You can explore these features through the ViralMeme.ai Meme Maker.

4. A Practical AI Meme Creation Workflow

For developers and creators who want to experiment with AI-powered content, here is a simple workflow:

Step 1: Research a Trend

Start by exploring popular memes and identifying formats that match your audience.

Step 2: Understand the Context

Read about the meme's origin and meaning. This helps avoid using a popular format incorrectly.

Step 3: Choose a Creative Template

Find a suitable meme template based on the type of content you want to create.

Step 4: Customize Your Content

Add your own captions, upload a photo, or experiment with an available AI image or video generator.

Step 5: Review and Share

Check the final result, make any necessary adjustments, and download your content for your preferred social media platform.

This workflow can help reduce the time spent searching for inspiration and make content experimentation more accessible.

5. Why AI Meme Generators Are Interesting for Developers

AI meme generation is an interesting example of how artificial intelligence can be applied to everyday creative activities.

It combines several areas of technology:

  • Image processing and visual transformation.
  • Generative AI models.
  • Template-based content creation.
  • User-friendly editing interfaces.
  • Trend discovery and content organization.

From a product development perspective, combining these capabilities creates a more complete creative experience than offering a simple image generator alone.

It also demonstrates how specialized AI applications can make advanced technology accessible to users who do not have professional design or video editing skills.

6. Final Thoughts

AI is changing the way people discover, create, and share digital content. Meme creation is a simple but interesting example of this transformation.

By combining meme discovery, contextual information, customizable templates, and AI-powered image and video generation, creators have more opportunities to experiment with internet culture.

If you enjoy exploring internet trends or want to experiment with AI-generated social media content, take a look at ViralMeme.ai.

It is a useful starting point for discovering popular memes and turning creative ideas into shareable content.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use.

Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases.

Our goals for Python on Vercel

Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications. We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions:

  • Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async/await, and context managers.

  • A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together.

  • Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on.

The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run.

Deploying Python applications on Vercel

We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv, and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN.

For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them.

For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies.

Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure

A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language:

These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application.

Start building with Python on Vercel

Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services.

To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code.

The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN.

Here’s how the main parts connect:

  • Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files.

  • Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel.

  • Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading.

  • Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow.

The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application.

Investing in the Python community

Last December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work.

At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026.

We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next.

We also published PEP 827, which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking.

What’s next for Python on Vercel

We’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work.

Resources

title: Fractional physics-informed neural networks to model social media virality
description:
arXiv:2611.07215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing models of social media virality either prescribe the functional form of engagement growth or assume a fixed mechanism by which past activity influences future engagement. We present a fractional physics-informed neural network that learns both the temporal memory and nonlinear growth dynamics of social media engagement, using symbolic regression to translate the learned dynamics into interpretable equations. Synthetic experiments at the deployment resolution of 24 hourly observations demonstrate that the fractional order and reaction law can be jointly recovered from clean data. Under observation noise, however, the standard pointwise physics residual drives the fractional order toward its lower bound through a scale artifact. We address this failure using a fully whitened residual that propagates observation noise through the fractional operator. Applying the framework to 348 posts from X (formerly Twitter), we find that a single-window model estimates strongly memory-dependent dynamics but fails to accurately reconstruct held-out trajectories. Partitioning the 24-hour window into four teacher-forced segments substantially improves performance, yielding segment-specific fractional orders that increase from 0.23 to 0.99 and interpretable growth laws for each phase. The segmented model reconstructs 64% of held-out trajectories within a mean squared error of 0.01, compared with 44% for the strongest of nine classical baselines. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of fractional physics-informed equation discovery to uncover interpretable engagement dynamics while highlighting the importance of noise-aware estimation and temporal segmentation.

title: CORE: Coarse-to-Fine Search with Context Management for Deep Research
description:
arXiv:2611.07859v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent's context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE, a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus-CM), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

title: Batch-Conditioned Semantic Anchors for Robust Transductive Adaptation of Vision--Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.06993v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transductive adaptation improves vision-language models at test time by refining predictions on an unlabeled batch, but current methods face a key trade-off. Aggressive approaches exploit batch structure but can drift when batches are sparse, have prior shift, or cover little of the label space. Conservative methods better preserve CLIP text semantics, but fixed semantic references can under-adapt even when the batch provides strong corrective evidence. We propose JPTA (Joint Prior and Transport Adaptation), a prior-aware framework that casts transductive VLM adaptation as batch-conditioned semantic reference estimation. Instead of treating CLIP text prototypes as fixed priors or freely replaceable, JPTA views them as semantic references that shift toward image-side batch structure only under calibrated evidence. It estimates batch priors and soft image-side prototypes to form transported semantic references whose impact is scaled by batch reliability. Across standard benchmarks, low effective-class regimes, all-class evaluation, and online streams, JPTA consistently outperforms TransCLIP and StatA, with the largest gains on sparse and prior-shifted batches. Anchor-drift, active-support, and absent-class-mass diagnostics show that JPTA fixes effective-class mismatch without unconstrained transductive drift, indicating that robust transductive VLM adaptation should recalibrate semantic references using reliable batch evidence rather than choose between unrestricted transduction and fixed prototypes. Code is available at https://github.com/MR-Sherif/JPTA.git.

title: Georeferenced Cross-View 3D Reconstruction from Ground and Satellite Images
description:
arXiv:2611.07575v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Georeferenced 3D reconstruction from ground images requires recovering not only the local scene geometry, but also localizing every camera center and 3D point in a geographic coordinate frame. Existing cross-view geo-localization methods are able to estimate the GPS coordinate of a single ground camera, but do not reconstruct dense 3D geometry, while recent feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction models predict point maps and camera poses only in a local coordinate frame. We introduce X-VGGT, a feed-forward cross-view geometry transformer that unifies these tasks by jointly processing a set of ground-level images and a georeferenced satellite image to predict ground-view camera poses, dense 3D point maps, and a scene-level transform parameterized by gravity, scale, yaw and translation. This transform projects the local reconstruction into the satellite plane, resulting in the geo-registration of all ground images with the georeferenced satellite image. We further propose an evaluation protocol for this joint task and show that, across multiple cross-view datasets, X-VGGT produces accurate georeferenced reconstructions and outperforms prior cross-view geo-localization and multi-view 3D reconstruction models.

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: I Compared Two Runs Across Two Days Without Checking Which Model Served Them
description:
Two runs, forty-eight hours apart, and a latency drop big enough that I started writing the summary before the second log had finished flushing. Then I printed the one metadata column I had been ignoring since day one. Is that a measurement bug, or is it a discipline bug wearing a lab coat?

This is another entry in a small series where I break my own tooling over two days and write down the damage while it still stings. The target this time was a prompt-variance probe I wanted to run on free capacity, because requesting a budget line takes longer than building the thing.

The Setup: One Question, Two Unnamed Unknowns

The question was narrow. After I rewrote a system prompt, did identical inputs produce identical outputs more often than before? That is a variance question, not a leaderboard question, and it needs volume rather than expensive tokens.

I used MonkeyCode's free model access and its free server option so the loop could run without a spend approval, which is the entire reason day two existed at all. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The availability claims are the operator's; everything about the harness below is mine to defend or retract.

Before writing a line of code I listed the unknowns I was not measuring, and both of them came back to bite me within the window:

  1. Which model revision actually served each request, and whether that stayed constant.
  2. How long a long-running process survives on shared, free compute before something reclaims it.

Neither is exotic. Both are the kind of thing you only notice when you decide you want to publish a number.

Day 1: The Harness That Saved Me From Myself

I refused to write a benchmark first. I wrote a logger, because a benchmark without raw rows is a story I am telling myself. Every request appends one JSON line, and nothing is aggregated until the log is closed.

# probe.py
import hashlib, json, time
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime, timezone

LOG = Path('runs/probe.jsonl')
LOG.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

def fp(obj) -> str:
    blob = json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True).encode('utf-8')
    return hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest()[:12]

def probe(client, prompt: str, run_id: str, repeat: int) -> dict:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    resp = client.chat(prompt=prompt, temperature=0, seed=7)
    record = {
        'run_id': run_id,
        'repeat': repeat,
        'prompt_fp': fp({'p': prompt}),
        'text_fp': fp({'t': resp.text}),
        'model_field': resp.meta.get('model'),
        'revision_field': resp.meta.get('revision') or resp.meta.get('system_fingerprint'),
        'tokens_in': resp.usage.get('input_tokens'),
        'tokens_out': resp.usage.get('output_tokens'),
        'latency_ms': round((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, 1),
        'utc': datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    }
    with LOG.open('a', encoding='utf-8') as fh:
        fh.write(json.dumps(record) + '\n')
    return record

Two details are load-bearing and easy to skip. The text_fp field hashes the raw output text so I can count distinct answers instead of eyeballing them, and revision_field reads whatever identifier the vendor echoes back, which differs per SDK. If your client library exposes no such field, that absence is itself a finding you should write down.

The probe loop is deliberately boring: one prompt, twenty repeats, fixed temperature and seed, append-only log. Boring loops are the only ones I trust after 5pm.

mkdir -p runs
python probe.py --run day1 --repeats 20

Day 2: The Log Disagreed With My Summary

I reran the same command the next morning, changed one file, and ran the analyzer before reading any average. The first line it printed was a refusal, not a p50.

# analyze.py
import json, statistics
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

rows = [json.loads(l) for l in Path('runs/probe.jsonl').read_text().splitlines() if l.strip()]
by_key = defaultdict(list)
for r in rows:
    by_key[(r['run_id'], r['model_field'], r['revision_field'])].append(r)

for key, rs in by_key.items():
    lat = sorted(r['latency_ms'] for r in rs)
    p95 = lat[max(0, int(len(lat) * 0.95) - 1)]
    outs = {r['text_fp'] for r in rs}
    print(f'{key} n={len(rs)} p50={statistics.median(lat)}ms p95={p95}ms distinct_outputs={len(outs)}')

revs = {(r['model_field'], r['revision_field']) for r in rows}
if len(revs) > 1:
    raise SystemExit(f'STOP: {len(revs)} revisions in one log; do not compare across them')

That guard is the whole lesson. My day-one rows and day-two rows were grouped under different revision identifiers, which means the two "runs" were different systems wearing the same prompt. The numbers I was about to quote described a change of supplier, not a change of my prompt.

What the dry run prints

The digits below come from a stubbed client that fabricates responses, so read the shape and ignore the values. Real logs from your own endpoint should replace them before any claim leaves your draft folder.

('day1', 'stub-model', 'rev-a') n=20 p50=812.0ms p95=1490.0ms distinct_outputs=1
('day2', 'stub-model', 'rev-b') n=20 p50=604.5ms p95=1102.0ms distinct_outputs=3
STOP: 2 revisions in one log; do not compare across them

The distinct_outputs column matters more than the milliseconds, honestly. One stable answer on day one and three different answers on day two is a variance signal, and a variance signal that arrives alongside an identifier change is not attributable to my prompt.

The Second Break: Free Compute Does Not Owe You Continuity

Somewhere in the middle of the run my process stopped existing, and I only know that because the log ended mid-batch rather than at repeat twenty. Shared or free capacity is not a contract, so the fix is not a longer timeout; the fix is a job that can be picked up.

The runner below is at-least-once by design, which is fine here because the probe is read-only. Every finished item is flushed with os.fsync so an abrupt stop loses at most the item in flight, and the resume path skips anything already marked ok.

# runner.py
import json, os
from pathlib import Path

STATE = Path('runs/state.jsonl')

def load_done() -> set:
    if not STATE.exists():
        return set()
    done = set()
    for line in STATE.read_text().splitlines():
        if line.strip():
            rec = json.loads(line)
            if rec.get('status') == 'ok':
                done.add(rec['item_id'])
    return done

def append_state(item_id: str, status: str, **extra) -> None:
    line = json.dumps({'item_id': item_id, 'status': status, **extra}) + '\n'
    with STATE.open('a', encoding='utf-8') as fh:
        fh.write(line)
        fh.flush()
        os.fsync(fh.fileno())

def run(items, handler) -> None:
    done = load_done()
    for item in items:
        if item['id'] in done:
            continue
        try:
            append_state(item['id'], 'ok', result=handler(item))
        except Exception as exc:
            append_state(item['id'], 'error', error=repr(exc))

Restarting is then just the same command, and the log tells you how much was real work versus replay:

python runner.py --queue runs/queue.jsonl
wc -l runs/state.jsonl

The Decision Table I Now Keep in the Repo

After two days of this I wrote down when pinning matters, because I will absolutely forget by next quarter. The table is short on purpose.

Situation Verify revision identifier? Rerun both sides? Note
Same-day prompt iteration Record only No Compare within one revision bucket
Comparing two calendar days Mandatory Yes, if identifiers differ Never quote across buckets
Changing temperature or seed Record only Yes The setting is part of the treatment
Latency claims Record only Yes Measure client-side, include queue time
Any shared or free compute Record only Depends Assume interruption, checkpoint every item
Publishing a number Mandatory Yes Include the raw log or drop the claim

What I Would Repeat, and What I Would Not

What I would repeat without hesitation: the JSONL-first habit, the analyzer that exits non-zero instead of printing a misleading mean, and the fsync on state writes. Each of those cost me maybe fifteen minutes and saved a day.

What I would not repeat: starting the probe before deciding what a valid comparison even looks like. I recorded the model identifier from the very first request and still did not put a guard on it until the second day, which is a genuinely embarrassing order of operations.

Finally, the boring one. I should have run the full loop end to end against two synthetic items before spending any window on real work. If you cannot resume from a killed process in under a minute of wall time, you are not ready to start a multi-day run on capacity you do not control.

Limitations, and Who Should Skip This

This workflow is honest but narrow, so please do not over-read it.

  • Latency numbers from shared free compute are not an SLO. They describe a noisy shared path on one afternoon, and nothing more.
  • Determinism claims need a seed you actually control. If your endpoint ignores the seed, count distinct outputs and stop pretending you have reproducibility.
  • Skip this entirely if you need audited benchmarks. Pinned hardware, a fixed revision, and a signed methodology are a different project with a different budget.
  • Skip it if your product is intentionally nondeterministic. A variance probe on a creative-writing assistant measures the product, not your prompt.
  • Do not use it to compare vendors. Two logs from two providers will almost never share a revision namespace, and the comparison will be meaningless in exactly the way mine was.

If you want to try the two-day loop before asking anyone for a budget, MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option were enough for me to get the harness running, and I would start with the raw JSONL log rather than the summary table. Just add the revision guard before the first request, not after the first surprise.

title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
description:
OpenEvidence on Vercel

  • Serves 650,000 doctors with medical search

  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidence helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supported more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported that more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with the Next.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel builds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can roll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled Fluid compute for its functions on Vercel, and Micah described the result alongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With Active CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own Vercel project with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

About OpenEvidence: OpenEvidence helps healthcare professionals find medical evidence at the point of care, with answers sourced, cited, and grounded in peer-reviewed literature. Physicians use it daily across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers in the United States. Its mission is to help doctors save lives and improve patient care. Learn more at openevidence.com.

title: building a markdown editor with a live preview
description:
Back in my early days, I assumed a markdown editor was a serious project. A parser, a preview pane, keeping the two in sync, all of it felt like a weekend at least. Then I built one and the whole thing turned out to be a textarea, a library, and about 80 lines. Here is the shape of it.

Try it: type on the left, watch the right
Try it live on nayemalam.com.

The shape of it

Two panes, one piece of state. The textarea holds the raw markdown in a useState, and the preview is just a function of that state. Type a character, the state updates, the preview re-renders. There is no syncing logic to write, because there is only one source of truth and two views of it.

Rendering the markdown

Writing your own parser is a fun exercise and a terrible idea for a real editor. The react-markdown library does the parsing, and it builds React elements instead of an HTML string. That is the whole trick: there is no HTML string anywhere, so there is no dangerouslySetInnerHTML and nothing to sanitize. Raw HTML in the input is ignored by default, and React escapes the text for you.

terminal

npm install react-markdown

MarkdownEditor.jsx

import { useState, useMemo } from 'react';
import Markdown from 'react-markdown';

export default function MarkdownEditor() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('# Hello\n\nType here, watch it render.');
  const preview = useMemo(() => <Markdown>{text}</Markdown>, [text]);

  return (
    <div className="flex h-[600px]">
      <textarea
        value={text}
        onChange={(e) => setText(e.target.value)}
        className="w-1/2 p-4 font-mono"
      />
      <div className="w-1/2 overflow-auto p-4">
        {preview}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

The safety here is not a step you add, it is the default. A script tag typed into the editor shows up as text on the page, it never runs. The old way, parsing to an HTML string and injecting it, needed a sanitizer for exactly this reason. This way does not.

Making it feel realtime

Every keystroke updates the state, so the preview updates on every keystroke. That is the whole trick, and it is fast enough for any doc a person actually types. The one thing worth adding is useMemo around the preview, so a long doc only re-parses when the text changes, not on every render.

The nice touch: synced scrolling

A preview that does not follow you is only half an editor. Ten lines fix it: when the textarea scrolls, work out how far down it is as a ratio, and set the preview to the same ratio.

sync-scroll.js

const editorRef = useRef(null);
const previewRef = useRef(null);

const syncScroll = () => {
  const editor = editorRef.current;
  const preview = previewRef.current;
  const ratio = editor.scrollTop / (editor.scrollHeight - editor.clientHeight);
  preview.scrollTop = ratio * (preview.scrollHeight - preview.clientHeight);
};

// textarea: ref={editorRef} onScroll={syncScroll}
// preview:  ref={previewRef}

On a phone

Two panes side by side do not fit a phone, so the layout stacks: editor on top, preview below, with flex-col md:flex-row and the panes going from full width to half. Same component, same state, the CSS does the work.

So, what have I learnt?

  • The editor is not the hard part. The parser is a library, the layout is flexbox, the state is one string.
  • Render markdown to elements, not to an HTML string. That is what makes the whole thing safe by default, no sanitizer needed.
  • The preview is just a function of the state. One source of truth, two views.
  • useMemo matters once the doc gets long. Parsing on every render is fine at 20 lines, sluggish at 2000.
  • Syncing the scroll is ten lines, and it is what makes the whole thing feel finished.

Originally posted on nayemalam.com/blog.

title: How a Daily Silver Benchmark Is Computed (And Why Unit Conversion Is the Hard Part)
description:
A daily metal "rate" looks like one number on a page. Under the hood it is a small data pipeline, and in my experience most of the bugs are not in the fetch step. They are in the units.

This is a purely methodological note. I am not quoting any live prices, tax rates or dealer margins here, because those change and are exactly the parts people copy-paste without checking.

Start from one fixing, not from a scraped list

The cleanest design is to pick a single authoritative wholesale fixing for a defined fineness, in a defined unit, for a defined trading day. Everything else on the page is derived from that one value.

If you instead scrape several "silver price today" widgets and average them, you have silently mixed:

  • different fineness assumptions,
  • different units (per gram vs per 10 grams vs per kilogram),
  • wholesale versus retail quotes,
  • and different as-of dates.

You cannot reconcile those after the fact. Pick one input, document it, and derive.

The conversion table is the real schema

Once the base is fixed, the derived numbers are arithmetic. A useful mental model is to treat every published figure as a row with four columns: unit, fineness, quote type, as-of date.

For a base expressed per kilogram of 999 fine metal:

Published unit Divisor from the base
per 100 grams 10
per 10 grams 100
per gram 1000
per tola 1000 / grams-per-tola

Two traps worth writing tests for:

  1. Fineness is a multiplier, not a new source. 925 and 999 describe the metal content of an object, not a different market price. Applying the fineness fraction to a number that is already retail-quoted double counts it.
  2. Making charges are not part of the metal. A jewellery bill contains a craftsmanship component that resale usually does not return. If you fold that into a "price per gram" and then compare it with a wholesale fixing, the comparison is meaningless.

So the invariant to assert in code is boring but effective: per_kg == per_g * 1000 == per_10g * 100, and every derived row must carry the same as-of date as its source.

Why a retail quote never equals the benchmark

Readers often treat the difference as an error. It is not. A retail quote can legitimately include a dealer premium, a making charge, applicable tax, and a buyback policy that prices the same object differently on the way out. A benchmark is a reference for the metal content, not a price you can transact at.

That distinction belongs in the UI, not in a footnote. The most useful thing a price page can show is the basis of each number it prints: what unit, what fineness, what quote type, what date.

Data quality problems that actually bite

  • Trading day vs calendar day. A fixing published on Monday may be Friday's session after a holiday. Store both the publication date and the reference date.
  • AM vs PM sessions. Some sources publish more than one fixing per day. If you pick one, record which one; if you switch, you have silently changed the series.
  • Time zones. "Today" in the source's locale is not "today" for the reader. Normalise to a single zone before generating slugs or filenames.
  • Caching and staleness. A cached HTML widget can look perfectly valid and be a day old. Persist the fetched timestamp next to the value, and refuse to render if it is older than your threshold.
  • Anti-bot responses. A 403 is not a missing price. Treat "blocked" as a distinct state from "no data", because retrying a blocked fetch with a different parser will not help.
  • Silent unit changes upstream. If a source switches from per-kilogram to per-10-grams, an unconverted pipeline will happily publish a number 100× too small. Assert plausible ranges.

A small validation checklist

  • One documented base source, one fineness, one unit, one as-of date.
  • Derived values recomputed from the base, never re-scraped.
  • Unit-consistency assertions in the build step.
  • Explicit separation of benchmark, spot-derived conversion, and retail quote.
  • Reference date displayed next to every table, not just in the page footer.
  • A visible "no current data" state instead of a stale number.

None of this is glamorous, but it is the difference between a page that survives an audit and one that quietly publishes the wrong number for weeks.

Wrapping up

If you maintain any kind of daily price or rate page, the highest-value work is almost never adding another source. It is making the units, the fineness and the as-of date impossible to misunderstand — for the reader and for your own future self.

General methodology notes, not financial, tax or purchase advice. Rules and costs change; verify against primary source documents before relying on any figure.

Further reading

If you want to see these ideas applied to a live data page, the data methodology page for India's daily silver benchmark documents the base source, reference dates and unit conversions, and the per-gram, 10-gram and 1kg explainer shows the arithmetic without any live rate assumptions.

title: Meta-Frieren: Beyond Single Level Online Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.07169v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study a two-stage online optimization problem: at each round, a meta-learner first selects an agent-environment pair, then the chosen agent interacts with the environment, and receives a reward. We introduce Meta-Frieren, a general framework for maximizing cumulative reward in this setting. Our analysis yields a simple UCB-style criterion for meta-level selection and recovers prior guarantees as special cases while extending them to broader settings. We instantiate Meta-Frieren with GP-UCB under Bayesian and frequentist assumptions. We also derive, to our knowledge, the first high-probability regret bound for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling, specialize it to finite and parametric function classes, and integrate it into Meta-Frieren. Experiments support our theoretical results and demonstrate that Meta-Frieren can be successfully applied to hyperparameter optimization across multiple model classes.

title: Stochastic Dynamics of Generative AI: From Autoregressive Models to Interacting LLM Networks and Neural SDEs
description:
arXiv:2611.07065v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper develops a stochastic dynamical-systems perspective on three classes of generative AI models. First, we formulate large language models (LLMs) as high-dimensional nonlinear autoregressive models with attention-based dependencies. This formulation connects pretraining by conditional maximum likelihood to sequential token generation and provides a probabilistic interpretation of LLM operation. Second, we consider networks of interacting LLMs and characterize their collective behavior through mean-field ordinary differential equations. These dynamics provide a framework for understanding emergent preferential attachment and persistent structural biases, including type-dependent glass-ceiling effects. Third, we consider neural stochastic differential equations (SDEs) as continuous-time generative models for stochastic trajectories, including those observed at irregular time intervals. We discuss their training with particular emphasis on Wiener-space cubature methods based on rough-path analysis as an efficient alternative to Monte Carlo estimation. Together, the three settings address probabilistic prediction, information exchange and emergent behavior in interacting networks, and path-space generative modeling.
