title: Go Property Alerts: 3 Evidence Checks for Email and SMS APIs
description:
Choose the notification channel whose recipient eligibility you can reconstruct after a failure. For a property-management startup comparing an email API with an SMS API for event alerts, that means accounting for bounce handling, suppression, and evidence review before comparing dispatch charges.

TL;DR: Keep routine email alerts subject to a destination-specific suppression check; authorize SMS through a separate eligibility decision. Before resuming notifications after an address correction, require 3 checks: the failure belongs to the original destination, the correction identifies a new destination version, and any independent restriction still applies. Record the evidence behind each decision. A successful API call cannot establish those facts.

This decision record proposes a Go implementation for maintenance notices and rent-account events. Its decision axis is compliance evidence, examined through reconciliation: an operator should be able to reproduce why a destination was suppressed, why a corrected address became eligible, and why an email failure did or did not produce a text message. These are design requirements, not claims about a deployed system. The FTC's CAN-SPAM guide supplies the US email-purpose boundary; SMTP specifications supply delivery-status distinctions. Neither establishes that a property notice satisfies a jurisdiction's service requirements.

Should email API failures trigger SMS alerts for property events?

An address correction is a new decision, not an instruction to erase the old bounce. Consider illustrative records for property P-204, tenancy T-73, and maintenance event M-108: email destination version 2 receives a confirmed invalid-mailbox report, while a resident subsequently supplies destination version 3. A later replay of the report for version 2 should remain visible without suppressing version 3. Conversely, changing the address must not silently erase a separately recorded opt-out. These identifiers and versions describe a proposed test fixture, not customer data or measured results.

Keep the history.

SMTP enhanced status codes distinguish success, persistent transient failure, and permanent failure through the first component of the code; RFC 3463 also separates address status from policy and other failure subjects. The permanent-failure class alone is insufficient evidence that a mailbox does not exist. A policy rejection needs its own classification. Suppressing every address associated with a permanent response can turn a delivery-policy problem into a growing population of incorrectly excluded residents.

For this design, the bounce consumer records the authenticated source, correlated message, original destination version, classification, and policy revision. The send decision records the version it evaluated. Reconciliation then asks a precise question: did the authorization use the destination and restrictions that were current at that point in the recorded ordering?

That question is narrower than delivery success. It is also answerable.

The FTC guide makes another distinction relevant to property notices: commercial messages and transactional or relationship messages have different treatment, and mixed content requires a primary-purpose assessment. Calling a maintenance template “transactional” in code does not complete that assessment. Keep the reviewed message purpose with the template revision so that a later promotional edit cannot inherit an unexplained eligibility decision. The cited guidance concerns email; SMS permission and legally sufficient property notice require separate applicable authority and review.

Invariants: reconstruct decisions without rewriting the ledger

The proposed system treats notification evidence like a journal alongside the business ledger. A rent-account adjustment has its own authoritative record; its notification can fail without reversing the adjustment, and notification acceptance must not mutate the account balance. Linking the two records makes reconciliation possible while preserving their different meanings. An evidence journal supports auditability, but its existence alone is not a claim of regulatory compliance. Three invariants govern the journal. First, a delivery report may affect only the account and destination version established by its correlated outbound attempt. Second, committing a report receipt must also commit its classification and resulting suppression transition, or commit none of them. Third, a correction must retain the historical restriction and explicitly identify which destination version the new eligibility decision covers. Opt-outs and invalid-address restrictions remain separately identifiable because an address correction is evidence about address validity, not evidence that every other restriction has ended.

The exactly-once mindset belongs at that local transition boundary. It does not extend automatically to remote delivery.

There are two failure boundaries to document. An unmatched or unauthenticated report cannot authorize a suppression update; retain it for investigation through a controlled evidence process. A send timeout, meanwhile, can leave the external result unknown: the remote system might have accepted the request before the local caller lost the response. Preserve that uncertainty in the attempt record and reconcile against documented delivery evidence before deciding on another attempt. A retry decision needs a reason of its own.

Ordering matters too. Suppression updates and send authorization must share a serialization rule in the storage implementation: if suppression commits first, a subsequent authorization must observe it. If authorization precedes the bounce, the audit trail should show that ordering. A worker that checks eligibility, waits in a queue, and sends much later without another check has created a gap between its evidence and its action; the design must define where authorization occurs and what changes invalidate it.

Compare policies by the evidence they leave behind

The following alternatives concern the same property workflow. They compare operating policies rather than commercial products, so the choice turns on the required alert outcome and the work needed to explain it.

Policy Evidence required Treatment of an invalid email address Operational trade-off
Email for routine eligible notices Message purpose, destination version, current restrictions Suppress the affected version and retain the report One channel to reconcile, with unresolved notices requiring an explicit follow-up process
Independently authorized SMS for urgent alerts Phone eligibility, alert urgency, applicable permission decision Preserve email suppression independently A second result stream and permission workflow to maintain
Conditional SMS escalation after email failure Both channel decisions plus the qualifying failure Keep the email failure and SMS attempt linked but distinct More branching and reconciliation, justified only by the escalation requirement

For the startup asking which API is most cost-effective, these obligations belong in the evaluation alongside dispatch charges: callback maintenance, investigation of unmatched reports, retries, evidence retention, and support work when a resident disputes a notice. No unit-price comparison resolves an unexplained eligibility transition. Select the smallest channel policy that meets the actual alert requirement and whose evidence the team can operate.

The trade-off is deliberate: independent SMS authorization adds work, but it prevents an email diagnostic from being mistaken for permission to contact a phone number. Urgency can justify designing an escalation path. It cannot supply the missing recipient evidence.

Go critical path: commit a replay-safe suppression decision

The critical path starts after source authentication, message correlation, and classification have established a confirmed invalid email destination. The code defines a storage contract rather than a provider integration; its receipt key is scoped to the authenticated account and source, while its destination version comes from the correlated attempt. Those are distinct identities.

package notifications

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
)

type ReportKey struct {
    Account, Source, ID string
}

type Destination struct {
    Account, Tenancy string
    Version int64
}

type InvalidEmail struct {
    Key ReportKey
    Target Destination
    MessageID, EvidenceRef, PolicyRevision string
}

type Tx interface {
    // Claim enforces uniqueness within the enclosing transaction.
    Claim(context.Context, ReportKey) (bool, error)
    AppendInvalidEmail(context.Context, InvalidEmail) error
    // SuppressEmail is idempotent for the same destination version.
    SuppressEmail(context.Context, Destination) error
}

type Store interface {
    // Within commits all writes together or rolls them all back.
    Within(context.Context, func(Tx) error) error
}

func ApplyInvalidEmail(ctx context.Context, db Store, r InvalidEmail) error {
    if r.Key.Account == "" || r.Key.Source == "" || r.Key.ID == "" ||
        r.Target.Account != r.Key.Account || r.Target.Tenancy == "" ||
        r.Target.Version < 1 || r.MessageID == "" ||
        r.EvidenceRef == "" || r.PolicyRevision == "" {
        return errors.New("incomplete or inconsistent email evidence")
    }
    return db.Within(ctx, func(tx Tx) error {
        fresh, err := tx.Claim(ctx, r.Key)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if !fresh {
            return nil
        }
        if err := tx.AppendInvalidEmail(ctx, r); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return tx.SuppressEmail(ctx, r.Target)
    })
}

The important implementation work sits behind Within and Claim: concurrent consumers must not both commit a fresh claim for the same scoped report. The claim, evidence append, and suppression update need database-enforced atomicity and uniqueness. The interface cannot provide those properties by itself. An existing receipt must represent a committed transition; a rolled-back claim must remain retryable, and a competing uncommitted claim must be resolved by the storage implementation rather than treated as completed work.

There is a concrete crash trap here. If the consumer commits its receipt in one transaction and suppression in another, a crash between them can leave the replay marked complete while the invalid address remains eligible. A transaction spanning all three writes removes that local partial result. Different reports for the same destination can still append separate evidence while the suppression operation remains idempotent.

This path deliberately grants no eligibility to a corrected address and sends no SMS. Both actions need separate decisions. A correction workflow can refer to the earlier suppression while establishing the replacement version; an SMS workflow can refer to the email outcome while checking its own destination and restrictions. Keeping these contracts small makes it easier to inspect which evidence authorizes each state transition.

Rejected option: resume every channel after an address correction

Clearing all restrictions when a resident edits an email address is rejected because the edit supplies evidence about one destination. It does not explain why a historical opt-out should disappear or why a phone number should become eligible. A valid narrower use case is releasing an invalid-address restriction for a corrected destination after the configured verification and eligibility review, with the release recorded as a new decision. Historical reports stay attached to their original version.

Before deployment, exercise the fixture through a small replay matrix: duplicate report, concurrent duplicate, rollback after claim, old-version report after correction, and email failure with an ineligible SMS destination. The expected outcomes should include both the current restriction and the journal entries. Test send authorization racing with suppression as a storage-level property; sequential handler tests cannot establish the ordering guarantee.

Deploy classification-policy changes with a recorded revision and review their effect before allowing them to change eligibility. For observability, track unmatched evidence, unresolved send outcomes, replayed receipts, and time between a report's receipt and its committed suppression. These are proposed operational signals, not measured service targets. Assign an owner to unresolved records so that collecting evidence does not become a substitute for resolving it.

Retention also needs a purpose and a limit. Restrict access to recipient details, use controlled evidence references, and determine retention requirements through the applicable compliance review rather than assuming an indefinite archive is required by the email guidance. Reconciliation needs enough evidence to explain a decision; copying full message bodies into every log expands the review burden without necessarily improving that explanation.

For property alerts, the decisive result is an explainable next action: suppress the invalid destination, evaluate a corrected one under its own version, or escalate through an independently eligible channel. That is the evidence a startup must be able to maintain whichever delivery API it chooses.

References

  • FTC, CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business: https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/can-spam-act-compliance-guide-business
  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, including reply-code classes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321.html
  • RFC 3463, Enhanced Mail System Status Codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3463.html
  • RFC 3464, An Extensible Message Format for Delivery Status Notifications: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3464.html

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.26

We've released version 6.26 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Scheduled callback for IVR overcapacity

Scheduled callback is now available as an overcapacity deflection option for IVR queues. When a queue is over capacity, callers can choose to schedule a callback. Google Cloud CCaaS then hands the call to your configured virtual agent, which books the callback through the Callback call API. Administrators choose the virtual agent, an optional greeting, and the data parameters to pass at the global or queue level. Reporting shows whether each caller submitted a callback or left without one.

Administrators: You can configure scheduled callback for overcapacity deflection globally at Settings > Call > Overcapacity Deflection, or per queue at Settings > Queue > IVR (Interactive Voice Response) > Edit / View > [QUEUE] > Overcapacity Deflection > Configure.

For more information, see Overcapacity deflection per-queue and Callback call API.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Salesforce: PKCE and refresh token rotation support

You can now connect Google Cloud CCaaS to Salesforce apps that require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and refresh token rotation. Salesforce turns both settings on automatically for newly created connected apps and external client apps. Google Cloud CCaaS uses PKCE when authorizing Salesforce administrator and agent connections. It also saves replacement refresh tokens returned by Salesforce, keeping connections working across subsequent token refreshes. Salesforce apps that don't use these settings keep working as before. This update adds no new configuration steps in Google Cloud CCaaS.

For more information, see Salesforce integration guide.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Branded caller ID label was truncated in the Outbound Number selector when the agent application language was set to French Canadian.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls experienced significant delays in connecting after being assigned to an agent.

  • Fixed an issue where whisper announcements played more than once and the call panel was slow to load in the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce case creation was delayed until the end of a call for inbound callers without a matching contact record.

  • Fixed an issue where callbacks to Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish landline numbers were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix, causing the calls to fail.

  • Fixed an issue where merged call recordings incorrectly reported only the duration of the first segment in the Calls API.

  • Salesforce account linking now completes only in the browser that started it. An authorization link opened in another browser or an incognito window is refused and can't be reused afterwards, and an administrator's Link New User action must be finished by the same signed-in administrator. Android and iOS agent apps link as before. This behavior is off by default and can be enabled per instance.

  • Fixed an issue that affected call connection stability during active calls for instances using Agent Assist.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent callback calls incorrectly required manual acceptance even when queues were configured for Auto-Answer.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx and Twilio virtual agent calls remained stuck in a connected state for an extended period if the carrier didn't send a terminal status callback.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS replies to auto-dismissed chats were incorrectly recorded as an agent timeout instead of an end-user timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where the Unanswered Transferred Call Expiration setting wasn't enforced for calls parked in an overcapacity deflection state.

  • Fixed an issue that affected connection stability and prevented calls from being accurately recorded as end-user hangups when callers hung up while waiting in a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing the queue service level field.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were disconnected when an agent finished their wrap-up following a queue transfer to a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls escalated from a virtual agent to a human agent reported inaccurate call-level queue and wait durations in reporting and data exports.

  • Fixed an issue where unrecorded voicemails incorrectly created Salesforce cases even when the Create CRM records for abandoned calls setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where activating a new language in the CCaaS portal caused the Languages & Messages page to crash or display an infinite loading spinner.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata files were duplicated across different day folders in external storage when re-uploads occurred after midnight.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became permanently stuck in a queued status without reaching a terminal state.

  • Fixed an issue where active agents were incorrectly signed out due to inactivity because the system didn't recognize activity outside the embedded call panel.

  • Fixed an issue where a permanent loading spinner appeared in the agent desktop top bar for instances with the email channel disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound keypad (DTMF) entries didn't reach the virtual agent during periods of stream instability or reconnection.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing required parameters.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls involving a virtual agent didn't record an end time and duration when deflected to an overcapacity queue.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings weren't fetched or saved when CRM ticket creation failed.

  • Fixed an issue where after-hours phone deflections didn't appear in the Deflections dashboard if the outbound dial timed out or failed.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled phone number obfuscation caused degraded performance for live calls.

  • Fixed an issue where CRM ticket assignees weren't consistently updated following an agent's pickup of a chat.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became stuck in a queued state after a caller selected a callback during a cold transfer to a specific agent.

  • Fixed an issue where Smart Disposition suggestions weren't pre-selected on the wrap-up screen, causing the disposition field to remain empty after a call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were incorrectly routed to agents even when the minimum available agent floor wasn't met.

  • Fixed an issue where cold transfers to a direct agent extension didn't trigger overcapacity deflection, leaving callers on hold until they disconnected.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent replies were cut off or silenced when using bidirectional streaming with barge-in disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where JSON chat transcripts in external storage contained unredacted message text even when the setting to store unredacted transcripts was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where the Keep Waiting label in the overcapacity deflection screen displayed an inconsistent font style compared to other menu options.

title: The JPA Field That Turns a Silent Lost Update Into a 409
description:
Originally published on my blog — read it there with the full context, code and updates.

Two people open the same post. Both edit it. Both save. One of the saves
disappears without a trace — no error, no warning, and the API answered
HTTP 200 for both of them.

That is the lost update problem, and it is the quietest data-loss bug in
read-modify-write APIs. I hit it while building my Spring Boot reference
service — a Spring Boot 3.5.16 (Java 21) REST API where editors create and
update posts from a browser page. The fix turned out to be one @Version
field on the JPA entity, one field on the request contract, and one
exception that the API layer maps to HTTP 409 Conflict. This post traces
that path through the actual code.

The problem: an edit that vanishes with no one to blame

Why does one editor's change disappear when two people save the same
record?

Follow the timeline. Editor A and editor B both fetch the same post.
A saves first: the row is updated and the API answers 200. B saves a
moment later: the row is updated again, this time over A's text, and
the API answers 200 again. Every request succeeded; every response told
its caller that their save is the state of the record. A's edit is
simply gone, and neither client has any way to know.

The failure is silent because it is normal read-modify-write behaviour,
not an anomaly. That is exactly why the bug survives in real systems, and
why it is worth fixing properly in something meant to demonstrate
engineering judgement.

What I tried first, and why it failed

My first sketch of the update flow was the obvious one: GET the record,
edit it, PUT it back with the new title and body and nothing else.

GET  /api/posts/{id}    # read the record
PUT  /api/posts/{id}    # write it back with a new title and body

The server loads the row, applies the update, and returns 200. It has no
way to notice that the row moved underneath the client between the GET
and the PUT — the read and the write are two unrelated requests, and
nothing in the contract connects them. The last write wins, and both
writers are told they succeeded.

A 200 is worse than an error here. An error at least tells the losing
client that something happened and gives them a reason to look. A 200
tells both clients that their save is the current state of the record,
which is a lie for one of them. The losing edit now exists nowhere — not
on screen, not in the database — and because the client believes it
saved, nobody goes looking for the data.

The fix: a @version field, a contract, and a conflict

The fix is five small parts, all of them in the reference service's source.

1. The entity carries a version column 

@Entity
@Table(name = "posts", indexes = @Index(name = "idx_posts_title", columnList = "title"))
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
public class Post {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    @UuidGenerator
    private UUID id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 160)
    private String title;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 10_000)
    private String body;

    @Version
    private long version;
    // ...
}

@Version tells Hibernate to treat version as an optimistic lock. Every
UPDATE it generates becomes conditional:

UPDATE posts
SET title = ?, body = ?, version = version + 1, ...
WHERE id = ? AND version = ?

If the row's version no longer matches the value the statement was built
with, zero rows change and Hibernate rejects the flush instead of quietly
overwriting. The entity never bumps the counter by hand — the update
method only touches title and body; the version moves with the write
itself.

2. The version is part of the API contract

A lock is useless if the client cannot take part in it, so the version
travels through the API in both directions. The response record exposes
it:

public record PostResponse(UUID id, long authorId, String title, String body,
                           long version, Instant createdAt, Instant updatedAt) {
}

and the update request requires it back:

public record UpdatePostRequest(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 160) String title,
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 10_000) String body,
        @NotNull @Min(0) Long version) {
}

The learning note next to UpdatePostRequest says it plainly: "the
expected version is part of the update contract, making optimistic
locking visible to clients."

3. The service checks it inside the transaction that owns the write 

@CachePut(cacheNames = "posts", key = "#postId")
@Transactional
public PostResponse updatePost(UUID postId, UpdatePostRequest request) {
    Post post = postRepository.findById(postId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new PostNotFoundException(postId));
    if (post.getVersion() != request.version()) {
        throw new PostVersionConflictException(postId);
    }
    post.update(request.title().trim(), request.body().trim());
    return PostResponse.from(postRepository.saveAndFlush(post));
}

The load, the comparison and the save all happen inside one
@Transactional method, and that is the part that makes the check
honest: the version is compared against the row as it stands at write
time, not against a snapshot from an earlier request. If the read and
the write lived in different transactions, the check would compare
against a version the row has already left behind, and the whole scheme
would be theatre. The learning note on PostService names the rule:
"service methods centralize transaction boundaries, cache coherence, and
optimistic-locking rules." The service also runs with
spring.jpa.open-in-view: false, so no lingering session serves a stale
entity across requests — the row is re-read inside the writing
transaction.

The explicit check catches stale requests deterministically. The
@Version column still matters underneath: if another commit slips in
between the check and the flush, the conditional UPDATE affects zero
rows and Hibernate refuses the write anyway.

4. The handler maps the exception to a 409

The exception itself carries the message a client can act on:

public class PostVersionConflictException extends RuntimeException {

    public PostVersionConflictException(UUID postId) {
        super("Post %s has changed; fetch it again before retrying".formatted(postId));
    }
}

and the error boundary turns it into the right HTTP answer:

@ExceptionHandler({PostVersionConflictException.class, ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class})
ProblemDetail handleConflict(RuntimeException exception) {
    return problem(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "POST_VERSION_CONFLICT", exception.getMessage());
}

HttpStatus.CONFLICT is HTTP 409, and the response is a problem document
— a type URI, a stable machine code (POST_VERSION_CONFLICT) and a
human-readable detail. Mapping both our explicit exception and Spring Data JPA's ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException (thrown when Hibernate detects a race condition) guarantees that concurrent write collisions always return 409 rather than an unhandled 500. The service enables the framework's problem-details
support in its configuration (spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled: true),
so validation and every other error ride the same shape.

5. The whole path, end to end 

stale PUT /api/posts/{id}
  -> PostService.updatePost re-reads the row inside its transaction
  -> post.getVersion() != request.version()
  -> PostVersionConflictException: "fetch it again before retrying"
  -> ApiExceptionHandler.handleConflict
  -> HTTP 409, ProblemDetail with code POST_VERSION_CONFLICT
  -> the client knows its premise was stale

One @Version field, one version in the request contract, one
exception, one handler method. Nothing on the controller changed —
updatePost still looks like an ordinary PUT.

Why a conflict is the correct answer, not a retry

When two editors produce two different versions of the same record, the
server cannot know which intent is the one meant. Both saves are
legitimate from their authors' point of view, and replaying the stale
write just replays the same data loss.

The honest verdict is HTTP's own definition of 409: the request conflicts
with the current state of the resource, and the client is told exactly
how to resolve it — "fetch it again before retrying". The losing client
re-reads the record, sees the other writer's change, and a human decides
what to keep. The silent overwrite becomes a visible decision point,
which is the entire purpose of the exercise.

What the rest of the reference service proves

The version field is one layer of a small system, and the rest of it is
verifiable the same way — every row below is a class or a config file in
the repository, not a claim:

Layer What it does Where it lives
Caching Bounded Caffeine cache on single-post reads (max 500, TTL 10 min, both from config); @Cacheable on read, @CachePut on update, @CacheEvict on delete; GET /api/showcase/cache exposes requests, hits, misses and hit rate CacheConfig, CacheProperties, ShowcaseMetricsController
Security Stateless HTTP Basic with BCrypt; pages and read APIs are public, every mutation needs the EDITOR role; local defaults are a throwaway demo-editor/changeit account overridable via env vars SecurityConfig, application.yml
Errors Request records validate at the boundary; one @RestControllerAdvice returns consistent problem documents with machine codes — POST_NOT_FOUND (404), POST_VERSION_CONFLICT (409), VALIDATION_FAILED (400) with a field-error map CreatePostRequest, UpdatePostRequest, ApiExceptionHandler
Configuration Local profile runs an in-memory H2 database in PostgreSQL mode with ddl-auto: update and seeded sample posts; prod selects PostgreSQL, takes every credential from APP_* env vars and sets ddl-auto: validate application.yml, application-prod.yml
Tests One @SpringBootTest suite asserts the rendered Thymeleaf pages, unauthenticated 401s versus editor 201s, the VALIDATION_FAILED problem response, public search, and cache hits after repeated reads DemoApplicationIntegrationTest

Hardening This Pattern for Production Rollout

Two things change the moment this pattern moves to production. The project
README says both, and they are worth repeating as my own judgement.

First, schema management. I would add Flyway or Liquibase migrations
before ever setting ddl-auto to validate. The local development profile
uses update, which is convenient on a scratch database and dangerous as
a habit — production schema should be versioned code, not a side effect
of startup.

Second, secrets. The local editor account is intentionally a non-secret
demo account with default credentials. For anything real, I would keep
credentials in a managed secret store and refuse to boot without them,
instead of falling back to a default. The prod profile already takes
every credential from environment variables with no committed secrets —
that is the shape I would keep, minus the fallbacks.

The result

A stale update now returns HTTP 409 with code POST_VERSION_CONFLICT
instead of a 200 that silently discards the other writer's change. The
loss can no longer happen quietly: the failure is loud, actionable —
"fetch it again before retrying" — and the integration test suite asserts
the access and validation behaviour end to end.

The whole fix is one annotation on one field, plus plumbing that makes
the version part of the contract. If a record can be read by two people
at the same time, that field is the difference between a lost edit and a
conflict both clients can see.

I build Java/Spring back ends and full-stack web applications — REST APIs
with JPA, optimistic locking, caching, validation and integration tests,
from the browser page down to the database. If you have a form or a field
where edits keep quietly disappearing, tell me about it:
WhatsApp ·
me@hoelee.com ·
hoelee.com.

I write about self-hosted infrastructure, DevOps and the failures behind them at blog.hoelee.com.

title: Vercel and Shopify make agents first-class shoppers
description:
Agents already shop on the web, but they often use pages and tools originally built for people and search engines. Building a better shopping experience for agents means treating them as first-class shoppers, with product information they can read directly and tools designed for agents to shop.

Today, Vercel Shop, our open source Next.js storefront template for Shopify, is generally available. Teams can launch storefronts optimized for how people, search engines, and agents interact with them.

Vercel Shop is built on Shopify’s Hydrogen SDK. The SDK gives teams access to the store’s product catalog, cart and order management, payments, and checkout to build custom storefronts. Earlier this year, Vercel and Shopify announced plans to rebuild Hydrogen to work across JavaScript frameworks. Today, the rebuilt SDK is generally available.

Give agents the information and tools they need

Vercel Shop makes product pages available as machine-readable content, including price, availability, and options. The same product URL can serve a visual page to people or product information that agents can read without interpreting the page’s layout. The template also includes structured data embedded in pages and sitemaps to help search and answer engines discover and understand the products.

Shopify co-developed the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), which gives agents a standard way to search a store’s catalog, read product details, check availability, build a cart, and get a checkout link. Vercel Shop makes these capabilities discoverable at the merchant’s own domain, so agents can use MCP to search products and build carts without navigating the site.

Customize the experience for all customers

Vercel Shop brings the store’s product catalog, cart, and checkout together with a Next.js storefront, product information and shopping tools for agents, and a shopping assistant powered by eve. The storefront and assistant live in the same codebase, so teams can customize the store’s design and how the assistant helps shoppers.

Skills included in the template guide coding agents through setup, customization, and template updates. Teams can create an experience where shoppers browse product pages or ask the assistant to find products and add them to their cart. Both share the same cart, so shoppers keep what they’ve added as they move between experiences.

Storefronts built with Shopify and Vercel

Today, we launched our merch store at vercel.store with limited-edition drops. It’s built on Vercel Shop. The store’s shopping agent helps shoppers find products, add them to their cart, and continue to checkout.

Shopify, Next.js, and Vercel already power storefronts for brands including AG1, Bombas, and PAIGE. When PAIGE re-architected its ecommerce platform, it saw a 22% increase in revenue and a 76% increase in conversion over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, with no downtime.

title: PostgREST .or() Breaks Silently on a Comma
description:
The short version

Interpolating a raw search term into a PostgREST .or() filter via a template literal breaks the filter grammar on a reserved character like a comma. On top of that, supabase-js doesn't throw on a transport or PostgREST failure — it represents it as a {data: null, error} return value — so the moment the caller reads .data ?? [], a broken filter that turns data into null gets treated as an empty array with no exception and no log. Global search's contacts query broke exactly this way. The fix was to split name and email into separate parameterized .ilike() calls and merge the results in JS.

The state it could become

The subject is global search in kimiteras-portal — the source behind both search and the command palette. It queries companies, contacts, projects, contracts, schools, tasks, and documents in one Promise.all round trip. Contacts alone need to match on both name and email, and before the fix it was written like this:

supabase
  .from("contacts")
  .select("id, name, email, company_id, school_id")
  .or(`name.ilike.${like},email.ilike.${like}`)
  .limit(5),

like is the search term formatted into %...%, and wildcard characters (%, _, \) were escaped. What wasn't escaped was the delimiter .or() itself uses: the comma. The result was handled the same way as every other category:

for (const c of contacts.data ?? [])
  hits.push({
    type: "Contact",
    label: c.email ? `${c.name} (${c.email})` : c.name,
    ...
  });

The first argument to .or() is a PostgREST-specific grammar string, name.ilike.<value>,email.ilike.<value>, where a comma is interpreted as a condition separator. If the search term itself contains a comma — someone typing a "Last, First" style name, or pasting a name straight off a business card — the generated string splits into extra conditions for every comma in it, and PostgREST can no longer parse it as a valid filter.

Why

What made this worse was how the failure surfaced. supabase-js query methods are designed not to reject their promise — a transport error and a PostgREST error response are both represented as the same {data, error} shape. This code read only contacts.data ?? [] and didn't even destructure error. When the broken filter made PostgREST return an error, data simply became null, no exception was thrown, and ?? [] quietly treated it as a valid "zero contacts matched" result. Every other category — companies, projects, contracts — still matched fine, so the UI just looked like "a slightly thin result set," with no way to notice that the contacts category alone was vanishing for specific search terms.

Fixing it

Name and email were split into separate parameterized .ilike() queries, with the results merged and deduplicated in JS.

// Query name and email separately with parameterized .ilike and merge in JS. Interpolating
// raw input into .or() lets a reserved PostgREST character like a comma break the filter
// grammar, silently dropping the contacts category (e.g. q="Last, First"). .ilike binds its
// value as a parameter, so reserved characters are safe.
supabase
  .from("contacts")
  .select("id, name, email, company_id, school_id")
  .ilike("name", like)
  .limit(5),
supabase
  .from("contacts")
  .select("id, name, email, company_id, school_id")
  .ilike("email", like)
  .limit(5),

.ilike() binds its second argument as a parameter, so a value containing a comma or . — reserved PostgREST characters — doesn't break the filter grammar itself. Because a name match and an email match can return the same contact twice, the merge side uses a Set to push each ID into hits only once.

const seenContact = new Set<string>();
for (const c of [...(contactsByName.data ?? []), ...(contactsByEmail.data ?? [])]) {
  if (seenContact.has(c.id)) continue; // dedupe a contact matched on both name and email
  seenContact.add(c.id);
  hits.push({ ... });
}

To prevent a repeat, a static-guard test now bans raw interpolation into .or() outright:

it("does not interpolate the search query raw into PostgREST .or() filter grammar (injection prevention)", () => {
  expect(src).not.toContain(".or(`");
  expect(src).not.toContain("ilike.${");
});

Because the test inspects the source string directly, CI fails the moment anyone reintroduces a template literal into .or() for the same reason, no matter why.

The lesson

?? [] is a common idiom for "a safe default when there's no value," but combined with a client like supabase-js that represents failure with the same shape as success, it erases the distinction between "zero rows matched" and "the query itself failed." Here the trigger was a different bug — raw interpolation into .or() — but the underlying danger is shared by every call site that reads data without checking error. In a design that bundles several categories into one request via Promise.all, the category that fails is the one that goes quietly missing, and the fact that every other category returns normally is exactly what makes the gap hard to notice.

Originally published at tech.rebounder.jp.

title: Every keyboard is a mechanical keyboard with Klicky
description:
Somewhere under your keycaps lives Klicky. It is curious, a little mischievous, and very pleased that keyboards make sounds. One click catches its attention. A steady run of typing gives it a rhythm to follow. When you take a break, it curls up and enjoys the quiet too.

The software behind that little creature is a Rust utility that gives ordinary typing a mechanical-keyboard voice. Ten sound packs, a volume control, and a small presence in your desktop. Most of the time, that is all you need to think about.

Building it sent me considerably further down the stack.

I just wanted it on my own machine

I first saw somebody using Sauhard Gupta’s original Klicky project on their Mac. I liked it and wanted to use it myself. There was one small problem: I was running Omarchy on Arch Linux.

So I did what an engineer with some time on their hands does. I took the repo and started moulding it to work on my setup.

First Omarchy. Then Linux more broadly. Then Windows. I kept adding to it, and it kept growing.

The original macOS project already had good foundations: a Rust daemon, decoded sound caching, local socket commands and KeyEcho-compatible packs. Those are Sauhard’s contributions. My work grew around Linux input, audio buffering, normalization, desktop integration and packaging, followed by the Windows implementation and further macOS lifecycle work.

I had found something I enjoyed and wanted it to fit the machine I actually used.

A voice ready before you press a key

The obvious version of a keyboard-sound app is easy to describe: receive a keypress, find a sound, play it.

The important detail is when each piece of work happens.

Opening a file, decoding OGG audio and creating an output stream are things I don’t want between a keypress and its click. Klicky prepares the sounds when a pack loads. Each pack has one sound.ogg recording and a config.json map that identifies the slices for individual keys.

Loading decodes the recording into PCM samples, prepares the slices, normalizes quiet ones and keeps them in shared buffers. A keypress then selects prepared audio for the already-running mixer. Several key sounds can overlap, so a new click does not have to wait for the previous one to finish.

A small part of that preparation solved another very audible problem: some packs were much quieter than others. The normalization uses an 85% peak target and caps amplification at 6×. Here is the gain decision from the sound loader:

let gain = (TARGET_PEAK / peak).clamp(1.0, MAX_NORMALIZATION_GAIN);
if gain == 1.0 {
    return;
}

The function handles silent slices before this step. The lower bound leaves already-loud samples alone; the upper bound prevents an extremely quiet recording from getting an enormous boost. The useful architectural choice is that this work happens during preparation, rather than on every keypress.

The code was fast. The sound still felt late.

An early Linux run recorded an average callback-to-mixer dispatch of 0.241 ms across 55 keypresses, with a p95 of 0.56 ms. That was a useful clue: the input handler was already handing sounds over quickly.

Further along the path, the audio device had negotiated a buffer of 1,102 frames at 44.1 kHz. That works out to roughly 25 ms. A fast hand-off was feeding a much larger buffer.

After the move to Rodio 0.22 and a smaller fixed-buffer request, the tested PipeWire route negotiated 256 frames, about 5.8 ms. The audible lag was gone or clearly reduced in that hardware check, and the stream stayed clean during normal typing.

These bars show calculated buffer durations. The dispatch figures describe the separate input-to-mixer step. Recorded environment and results.

The Unix output setup tries 256 frames, then 512, then 1,024, then a device-selected fallback. Small buffers help responsiveness, but the application still needs to open a working stream on the user’s device.

I carried the same debugging habit into Windows: inspect the actual output route, then sit down and type. Laptop speakers felt near-immediate and comfortable. AirPods had a noticeable delay. That was a useful reminder to include the device in the investigation instead of endlessly optimizing the quickest part of the program.

Three desktops, three native edges

The part that translates a physical keyboard into events depends on the operating system.

Platform Input Desktop integration
Linux evdev, below Wayland and X11 systemd user service; Omarchy controls
macOS Native event taps launchd and a menu bar helper
Windows Passive Raw Input on a dedicated thread Native tray app and console client

Linux responds to initial key-down events and ignores releases and held-key repeats. Windows maintains repeat state per device. The adapters turn those platform events into the key names used by the packs.

The sound data can be shared without making every operating system use an identical lifecycle. Linux and macOS keep their persistent Rodio output. Windows retains the Rodio mixer but uses a Windows-specific CPAL renderer and audio supervisor, including recovery when the output device changes.

That separation let the Windows work grow without replacing an audio path that already worked on Linux and macOS. The shared part earns its place through actual common behaviour: pack definitions, decoding, slices and prepared audio.

A tiny tray menu can still get in the way

A background utility needs more than a quick key handler. It also needs to stay pleasant while someone changes a sound pack, adjusts the volume or asks it to quit.

On Windows, pack preparation and persistence run away from the input and audio callbacks. The tray submits controls asynchronously. A pack change is prepared and saved before it becomes active, rather than making the typing path wait for a file decode.

The queues and active playback are bounded. During audio recovery, obsolete events are discarded so reconnecting a device does not play a burst of old typing. A second launch is supposed to find the existing owner instead of starting another engine with another tray icon.

Some of the most useful feedback was much less abstract: “the volume didn’t change,” “there are two tray icons,” and “some keys went quiet.” Those reports sent the investigation through process ownership, control state and aggregate input/audio diagnostics. The diagnostics can distinguish dropped or stale events without storing typed text.

The intermittent missing-sound report remains open while I collect recurrence evidence. A later typing check did not reproduce it; the aggregate diagnostics are there to help catch the next occurrence.

Leave room for a little personality

I wanted the project to feel like the thing that made me want it in the first place: a small, enjoyable addition to an ordinary day at the keyboard.

Klicky gives that feeling somewhere to live. The sound packs are its different voices. The illustrations suggest a little world under the keys. It is pleased when the typing gets going, and perfectly content when it stops.

The actual controls remain familiar: choose a pack, set the volume, pause, resume, quit. The character can make the project welcoming while the settings still say exactly what they do.

Where it is now

The current downloads are Linux v0.4.0 packages, a macOS source installation and a separate Windows 11 x64 development preview. The native Windows app and tray controls are implemented; final package/recovery and broader release qualification remain part of the work toward the next feature release.

You can meet Klicky and listen to its ten sound packs, explore the Rust source, browse the available releases, or read the architecture guide. There is also a longer Klicky case study on my portfolio, alongside my other projects.

What began as “I want those clicks on my laptop” has involved input APIs, audio scheduling, concurrency, process ownership and packaging. The interaction on the other end is still wonderfully small: press a key, and Klicky answers.

If you’ve built a tool where a tiny delay changed how it felt, I’d be interested to hear where the time turned out to be hiding.

Related reading: Native edges: principles for native apps with a shared core, by Pedro Piñera Buendía, is a useful companion discussion of shared logic and native platform boundaries.

Drafted with AI assistance from my development work and project notes.

title: How Do AI Agents Waste Your Money?
description:
arXiv:2611.07238v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents may consume massive tokens across a wide range of tasks, but how many of those tokens are really necessary? Although prior work has shown that agents can incur unexpectedly high token costs, we still lack a systematic way to identify and measure token waste. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for measuring token waste across heterogeneous agent systems. Our framework records and normalizes complete agent trajectories, identifies removable spans using an LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaJ), and maps the identified text spans back to the original trajectory for token-level measurement. We validate the identified waste through direct interventions by removing marked spans, resuming agent execution, and measuring changes in task outcomes and subsequent actions. In online pruning experiments, we remove 41-46% of the model's reasoning while largely preserving task performance across two distinct agent benchmarks. Using this framework, we analyze agents across multiple settings. Our analysis shows that token waste has a system-level structure that aggregate token usage alone cannot reveal. First, waste varies more across tasks and agent settings than across models. Second, reasoning and visible execution can exhibit different waste patterns. Third, different harnesses can introduce distinct sources of inefficiency even under the same model and task. Overall, our framework transforms token waste into an actionable optimization signal, enabling researchers and practitioners to train more efficient models, design better reasoning strategies, and optimize agent harnesses toward reducing unnecessary computation rather than merely reducing token usage.

title: Frontend vs Backend Development: What's the Difference?
description:
Introduction

Have you ever visited a website, clicked a button, submitted a form, or logged into an account?

Every time you interact with a website, different technologies work together behind the scenes to make everything function properly.

Have you ever wondered how the visual parts of a website are created? Or how your login information is processed and stored?

This is where frontend and backend development come into the picture.

Frontend and backend development are two important parts of modern web development. Although they have different responsibilities, they work together to create complete web applications.

In this article, we will explore what frontend and backend development are, their differences, popular technologies, and how they work together.

1. What Is Frontend Development?

Frontend development is the process of building the visual and interactive parts of a website or web application that users can see and interact with.

It focuses on creating a good user experience through layouts, buttons, forms, navigation menus, images, and other interface elements.

For example, when you open an online shopping website, everything you see on the screen, such as product images, search bars, shopping carts, and navigation menus, belongs to the frontend.

Main Responsibilities of a Frontend Developer

A frontend developer is responsible for:

  • Creating website layouts and user interfaces.
  • Developing responsive designs for mobile, tablet, and desktop devices.
  • Implementing interactive features.
  • Connecting frontend applications with backend APIs.
  • Improving website performance and accessibility.
  • Ensuring a consistent user experience.

Popular Frontend Technologies

HTML (HyperText Markup Language)

HTML provides the structure and content of a web page.

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)

CSS controls the appearance of a website, including colors, layouts, spacing, and typography.

JavaScript

JavaScript adds interactive functionality to websites, such as dropdown menus, form validation, and dynamic content.

Popular Frontend Frameworks and Libraries

  • React: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces.
  • Angular: A TypeScript-based framework for developing web applications.
  • Vue.js: A progressive JavaScript framework.
  • Next.js: A React framework for building modern web applications.

These technologies help developers build scalable and maintainable frontend applications.

2. What Is Backend Development?

Backend development is the process of building the server-side components of a web application.

Unlike frontend development, backend functionality usually runs behind the scenes and is not directly visible to users.

It handles application logic, database operations, authentication, authorization, API development, and communication between different system components.

For example, when you log into an online shopping website, the backend verifies your login credentials and retrieves the relevant account information from the database.

Main Responsibilities of a Backend Developer

A backend developer is responsible for:

  • Developing server-side application logic.
  • Designing and managing databases.
  • Creating and maintaining REST APIs.
  • Implementing authentication and authorization.
  • Handling business logic and data processing.
  • Improving application security and performance.
  • Managing server-side errors and integrations.

Popular Backend Programming Languages

Java

Widely used for enterprise applications and backend development, especially with Spring Boot.

JavaScript / TypeScript

Used for server-side development with Node.js and frameworks such as Express.js and NestJS.

Python

Commonly used for backend development, automation, and data-related applications.

C#

Used for building enterprise applications and APIs with ASP.NET Core.

PHP

A popular server-side language used in web development.

Popular Backend Frameworks

  • Spring Boot: A Java framework for developing backend applications.
  • Express.js: A lightweight Node.js web framework.
  • NestJS: A framework for building scalable Node.js applications.
  • ASP.NET Core: A framework for building modern web applications and APIs.
  • Laravel: A PHP framework for web application development.

3. Frontend vs Backend: Key Differences

Although frontend and backend development work together, their responsibilities are different.

Feature Frontend Backend
Main purpose User interface Server-side functionality
Runs mainly on Browser Server
User visibility Directly visible Mostly behind the scenes
Main focus User experience Business logic and data
Languages HTML, CSS, JavaScript Java, Python, C#, PHP
Frameworks React, Angular, Vue Spring Boot, Express, Laravel
Database access Through backend APIs Direct database operations
Examples Buttons, forms, layouts Login, payment, data processing

Both are essential for building complete and functional web applications.

4. How Do Frontend and Backend Work Together?

Let's understand this using a simple example: a user login system.

Imagine that you are visiting a website and entering your email address and password.

Here is what happens:

Step 1: User Interaction (Frontend)

The user enters their email address and password into a login form and clicks the Login button.

Step 2: Sending a Request

The frontend sends the login information to the backend through an HTTP request, usually using an API.

Step 3: Backend Processing

The backend receives the request and validates the submitted information.

Step 4: Database Communication

The backend retrieves the relevant user record from the database and verifies the password securely.

Step 5: Sending a Response

The backend returns an appropriate response to the frontend.

Step 6: Displaying the Result

The frontend displays the result to the user. If authentication succeeds, the user may be redirected to their dashboard.

This is a simple example of how frontend and backend components communicate to provide a complete user experience.

5. What Is Full Stack Development?

Full stack development involves working with both frontend and backend technologies to build complete web applications.

A full stack developer understands how the user interface, server-side logic, APIs, and databases work together.

For example, a full stack developer might use:

  • Frontend: React or Angular.
  • Backend: Node.js, Spring Boot, or ASP.NET Core.
  • Database: MySQL, PostgreSQL, or MongoDB.
  • Version Control: Git and GitHub.

Full stack developers can work across different layers of an application, although they may still specialize in certain areas.

6. Which Should You Learn First?

If you are a beginner, choosing between frontend and backend development can feel confusing.

Here are some suggestions.

Start with Frontend Development If:

  • You enjoy designing user interfaces.
  • You like working with visual elements.
  • You want to see the results of your code directly.
  • You are interested in website design and user experience.

A good starting roadmap:

  1. HTML fundamentals.
  2. CSS and responsive design.
  3. JavaScript fundamentals.
  4. DOM manipulation.
  5. React or Angular.
  6. API integration.

Start with Backend Development If:

  • You enjoy problem-solving and logical thinking.
  • You are interested in databases and server-side programming.
  • You want to understand how applications process information.
  • You enjoy designing application architecture.

A good starting roadmap:

  1. Learn a programming language such as Java, JavaScript, or Python.
  2. Understand Object-Oriented Programming.
  3. Learn SQL and database fundamentals.
  4. Understand HTTP and REST APIs.
  5. Explore a backend framework.
  6. Learn authentication, security, and testing.

You do not need to master everything immediately. Focus on the fundamentals and build practical projects as you learn.

7. Conclusion

Frontend and backend development are two essential parts of modern web application development.

Frontend development focuses on what users see and interact with, while backend development handles the application logic, data processing, and server-side operations.

Both work together to create reliable, secure, and user-friendly applications.

Whether you choose frontend, backend, or full stack development, understanding how these technologies work together will help you become a better software developer.

Keep exploring, keep experimenting, and continue building your skills.

Thanks for reading The Dev Journal!

Learn. Build. Improve.

What's next? Explore how REST APIs connect frontend applications with backend services.

title: Matriarchy Classics: A Computational Approach to Swap Only Gendered Words in Classic Novels
description:
arXiv:2611.07134v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper proposes a trustworthy computational method to gender-swap public domain novels, with programmatic guarantees that only gendered words are inverted and all other words are left unchanged. This may seem like a simple task, but both large language models and naive rule-based methods fail to complete it. The proposed method includes a custom whitespace-preserving tokenizer, gender-swap mappings across plural and possessive forms, pronoun handling, and a character renaming strategy. It shortens the time required to gender-swap a novel from weeks of manual labor to minutes. The method is demonstrated on two public-domain novels. Pride and Prejudice is transported to matriarchal Regency England, where inheritance flows through daughters, mothers rule the household, and a frantic Mr. Bennet is determined to secure advantageous marriages for his sons. The Great Gatsby pivots to a matriarchal Jazz Age where newly-rich Ms. Gatsbee throws lavish parties in the hopes of reuniting with her lost love, David, who is now married to the violent Thelma Buchanan. Gender-swapped novels could serve as useful tools to investigate the gender biases of readers, authors, societies, and AI systems.

title: A LangGraph SQL agent that only sees the tables it needs
description:
Most text-to-SQL agents paste the whole schema into every prompt. On a real database, most of it is tables the question never touches, and you pay for them on every call.

I added a small LangGraph example to schemagate that does it differently. It has four nodes:

  1. select_schema: SchemagateRetriever picks the few tables the question needs. This step runs offline, with no model call.
  2. write_sql: the model writes one SELECT using only those tables.
  3. run_sql: the agent runs the query. If it fails, the error goes back to the model once.
  4. answer: the model answers in one sentence from the returned rows.

On the bundled 42-table demo database:

Question Schema tokens sent
Which customers owe us money? 489 vs 2,199 (78% fewer)
How many orders did each carrier ship? 706 vs 2,199 (68% fewer)
Which products are below their reorder level, and in which warehouse? 563 vs 2,199 (74% fewer)

All three answers were correct with Claude Haiku. On databases with 50+ tables the saving reaches about 91%. The selection also respects roles: a table the caller can't read never appears in the prompt.

pip install langchain-schemagate langgraph langchain-anthropic tiktoken
python examples/langgraph_sql_agent.py

To use your own database, swap demo_catalog() for Catalog().bootstrap("postgresql://...").

schemagate is #1 on the BIRD Mini-Dev leaderboard (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL), is listed in LangChain's official retriever integrations, and is Apache-2.0.

Example: examples/langgraph_sql_agent.py

title: Automated Feedback to Peer Tutors Increases Their Talk Moves and Learner Reasoning but Not the Balance of Talk
description:
arXiv:2611.07072v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated feedback on classroom discourse improves instruction in professional and online teaching contexts, and recent work suggests that delivering similar feedback to learners may strengthen these effects by sharing responsibility for participation. Whether this holds in small-group volunteer tutoring has not been tested. We present results from a randomized controlled trial across two four-week SAT mathematics bootcamps on the Schoolhouse.world platform, involving 1,030 volunteer tutors, 7,443 learners and 6,508 recorded sessions. Tutors were randomly assigned to receive no feedback, automated feedback on their own discourse, or that feedback together with participation feedback delivered to their learners under one of two motivational framings. Feedback to tutors increased eliciting of learner ideas, uptake of learner contributions, and learner reasoning by 8-15%, and the pattern replicated across both bootcamps. However, tutor talk time, which averaged 91.5% in the control group, did not change in any condition, and learner-facing feedback did not further change discourse. Interviews with 17 tutors indicate that they adopted the moves the feedback recommended but were limited by learners who did not respond. Interviews with 13 learners suggest why the learner-facing feedback had little effect: it reported a group-level rather than a learner-level statistic, some learners preferred to listen, and learner-to-learner interaction was rare in these sessions. Automated feedback can change how tutors invite learner thinking, but shifting how much learners talk likely requires changes beyond feedback.

title: Server-Side Sparse Assignment for Federated Mixture-of-Experts
description:
arXiv:2611.07093v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly recognized for their remarkable capabilities; federated learning (FL) offers a promising framework for collaboratively fine-tuning LLMs on edge devices while achieving data privacy. However, edge devices are inherently heterogeneous: clients may exhibit diverse data distributions and resource constraints, including limited memory and computation budgets. Recent federated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address these challenges by using sparse expert activation or partial expert loading. However, existing partial-expert methods rely on heuristic full-pool observations or prioritize system-wide load balance, without guarantees for recovering client-specific relevant experts from partial observations. We propose $S^3$-MoE, a server-side sparse expert assignment framework that estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments through an exploit--explore mechanism. We also establish relevance-estimation error and exact Top-$K$ recovery guarantees. Experiments using a CNN-based MoE on CIFAR-100 show that $S^3$-MoE recovers task-dependent client--expert preferences and reduces conflicts caused by correlated expert selection across clients. Compared with Full-20 FedAvg, which gives each client access to all 20 experts for local Top-5 routing, $S^3$-MoE achieves 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy while loading only $5$ experts per client.

title: Node.js Daily Email Report Webhook Processing with Bounded Media Queues
description:
Short answer: use a cron trigger to call a public Node.js webhook, enqueue the daily report, and let an idempotent worker send the email within the pool's rate limit.

A media digest has a deadline, but the worker pool has a ceiling. That constraint changes the design: schedule a public Node.js webhook, put one bounded job on a queue per report slice, and let an idempotent worker send the email. The cron request should start the handoff, not spend its runtime generating and delivering every message.

The useful measure is revenue per hour of engineering time. I want a system I can ship weekly and still understand when a report is late. The scheduler and the mailer can share one API key and one base URL in Infrai, while the application keeps the important boundary: cron triggers work, a worker owns retries, and email delivery is a separate step.

How should Node.js handle daily email report webhook processing?

Suppose the report contains a media site's daily article and engagement slices. A pool of workers can process only so many slices at once. If the cron handler loops over every recipient, a slow upstream call holds the webhook open, a retry can repeat completed sends, and the next run competes with the first. A 900-second cron execution limit makes that a poor place for long work.

The first decision is therefore operational, not vendor-specific: use a short webhook as an admission point. It validates the report date, creates or publishes bounded jobs, and returns. The queue consumer does the slow work. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer must make the send operation idempotent; FIFO deduplication is only a five-minute window, not a substitute for a durable application key.

That boundary is the product.

I would use a stable key such as media-digest:2026-10-30:audience-42. Store that key with the report-send record in the application database. On a retry, the worker checks the record before sending and records completion after the provider accepts the message. The exact transaction boundary depends on the mail provider, but the principle does not: never treat a delivery attempt as proof that the job ran only once.

The failure I design around is an ordinary one: the worker accepts a message, the email request reaches the provider, and the process dies before it acknowledges the queue item. The queue quite correctly delivers the item again. Without the report-send record, the second attempt can produce a duplicate digest; with an idempotency key, the worker can recognize the completed business operation and acknowledge the redelivery. This is why I do not put the email call in the cron handler. The handler has no useful place to coordinate a slow send, a retry-after response, a process restart, and a second scheduled run. The queue gives the work a durable boundary, but the application still supplies the business identity. That small bit of database state is cheaper to reason about than pretending a transport retry is a transaction.

Keep it bounded.

The smallest working handoff

Here is the part I want to keep boring. The public webhook receives a cron-triggered request, enqueues one report job, and uses the same credential and base URL for the queue and email capability. The example keeps the long operation out of cron and bounds the worker batch so a rate-limited pool can drain between attempts.

import express from "express";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const queueName = "media-daily-digest";

if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function publishReport(body: unknown) {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/queue/publish`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Infrai ${response.status}: ${detail}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

app.post("/webhooks/daily-media-report", async (request, response) => {
  const reportDate = String(request.body.reportDate ?? "");
  if (!/^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$/.test(reportDate)) {
    response.status(400).json({ error: "reportDate must be YYYY-MM-DD" });
    return;
  }

  const idempotencyKey = `media-digest:${reportDate}`;
  try {
    await publishReport({
      queue: queueName,
      message: { reportDate, idempotencyKey },
      idempotency_key: idempotencyKey,
    });
    response.status(202).json({ accepted: true, idempotencyKey });
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("daily report enqueue failed", error);
    response.status(502).json({ error: "queue handoff failed" });
  }
});

app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000));

The cron configuration points at this public HTTPS endpoint, and the scheduled trigger calls the cron trigger route. The cron itself has a timeout at or below 900 seconds; in this design it should finish in seconds because it only starts the handoff. The worker consumes the queue, applies the same idempotency key to its database record, and then calls the email batch-send capability with the report output. Both calls use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY against https://api.infrai.cc/v1.

That is the seam that matters. A scheduler output becomes a queue message, and the queue message becomes the input to email sending. One key removes a second credential injection into the worker. It also leaves one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. That last trade-off is real.

Which tool fits the retry boundary?

Inngest is a credible choice when the main abstraction is an event-driven function with managed retries and a developer-friendly workflow. It becomes less attractive here if the key requirement is explicitly draining a bounded worker pool while keeping queue semantics and mail delivery under one credential boundary; the application still has to define its send idempotency.

Temporal is stronger when the problem is a durable, multi-step workflow with timers, compensation, and long-lived state. This media digest does not need DAG orchestration or a join primitive. Choosing Temporal for a single scheduled enqueue would buy machinery that I would then have to operate and explain.

BullMQ is a practical Node.js queue when Redis is already part of the stack. It gives a familiar worker model, but the scheduler, queue, and email provider remain separate integrations. That can be exactly right for a team that already owns Redis. For a solo SaaS, every extra credential, dashboard, and failure mode consumes shipping time.

Resend belongs in the comparison as the email specialist, not as a scheduler or worker pool. An Inngest-or-cron plus Resend stack would mean two signups, two credential sets, and glue code for the handoff, deduplication, and delivery monitoring. Infrai's fit is narrower and concrete: try it when the scheduler, queue, and email call should share one REST boundary and one key, while your application remains responsible for idempotency.

The specialist wins at its boundary. I would choose Temporal for a genuine long-running workflow, BullMQ when Redis operations are already cheap for the team, or a mail specialist when email-specific controls matter more than a unified backend surface. Infrai is not a replacement for workflow orchestration, fan-out joins, or replayable Kafka-style history.

Option Handoff shape Best fit Boundary
Infrai One REST key for cron, queue, and email A small service with one worker boundary No DAG, join, or replayable multi-consumer history
Inngest Event-driven functions with managed retries Function-oriented event workflows The app still owns send idempotency
Temporal Durable workflow execution Long-lived steps and compensation Heavy for a single enqueue
BullMQ + Resend Redis queue plus email specialist Teams already operating Redis Separate credentials and integration glue

What I would change at scale

At first, one queue message can describe a report slice and its recipient group. As volume grows, I would cap the worker's in-flight sends, add exponential backoff for HTTP 429 responses, and honor Retry-After rather than retrying in a tight loop. I would keep the retry decision in the worker, where the idempotency record is visible.

The limits shape the design: delayed messages cannot exceed seven days, message bodies cannot exceed 256 KB, retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledging removes the message. There is no native debounce or throttle, so rate control belongs in the consumer and in the job partitioning. A paused cron does not backfill missed triggers, and run output keeps only the first 4 KB; external application logs should carry the report date, idempotency key, queue result, and email result.

The operating bill is more than a unit price. It includes the time spent reconciling credentials, investigating a missed webhook, and recovering a duplicate send. A single REST API can reduce that integration surface, but it cannot make an at-least-once consumer magically exactly once. I would ship this boundary when the reduced glue is worth one vendor dependency, then revisit it when the report becomes a real workflow.

If this boundary matches your system, start with the cron-to-queue guide and verify the live request schema before wiring the worker.

Sources

  • MDN: 429 Too Many Requests
  • Inngest documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Resend documentation
  • Infrai: why scheduled email should enqueue jobs

title: Follow the Policy, Fail the Benchmark: Auditing and Revising Policy-Based Decision Benchmarks
description:
arXiv:2611.07042v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Policy-based decision benchmarks evaluate whether systems apply written rules to financial and operational cases. Yet a rule-following response can be marked wrong when the benchmark misstates the required decision. We audit nine public policy-based decision benchmarks through source tracing, program execution, and controlled checks. We find unsupported targets, reference errors that survive replay or propagate as solved steps, and evaluators that reject acceptable answers or credit incomplete decisions. To measure the scoring impact, we rescore unchanged model responses. On the 96 LegalBench SARA numeric cases, correcting the scorer raises acceptance by more than 80 percentage points for each of three models, without changing references or responses. In RuleArena Tax, restoring a required zero floor changes 27 of 300 references and narrows an observed model gap. A controlled federal-exemption task with explicit ownership and eligibility assumptions also shows that errors in supplied intermediate answers can affect final decisions. We present BAR (Benchmark Audit and Revision), a versioned collection of audit evidence and revisions for reevaluation.
