title: Acoustic Anomaly Detection for Early Identification of Drill Jamming
description:
arXiv:2611.07356v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In the context of Industry 4.0, predictive maintenance is essential to minimize unplanned downtime and ensure operational safety. In machining processes, drill jamming is a critical failure that compromises both workpiece quality and tool integrity. This work proposes an acoustic anomaly detection system using ultrasonic sensors to identify pre-failure patterns in Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining. We release a public dataset of time- and frequency-domain acoustic features from 17 drills, and benchmark semi-supervised autoencoder-based normality modelling against supervised XGBoost classification using Leave-One-Drill-Out validation. The results demonstrate that the Autoencoder is highly effective for industrial safety, achieving a Recall of 1.00 and a consolidated F1-score of 0.81. Furthermore, the threshold-independent analysis shows that the Autoencoder better separates normal and pre-failure acoustic patterns, achieving a consolidated AUC of 0.8294, compared with 0.7559 for the supervised model under inter-tool covariate shift. In contrast, the supervised XGBoost achieved an average F1-score of 0.55 and failed to detect failures in some of the evaluated drills. The findings highlight that the ultrasonic spectrum provides a reliable window for identifying incipient mechanical instabilities, and the AE model offers a robust safety envelope by anticipating all jamming events across the tested drill bits.

title: How to Customize a Website Theme Without Rebuilding It
description:
Changing a website theme does not necessarily mean rebuilding every page. A focused adjustment to colors, typography, or a component can be enough—provided you know where the change belongs and how it will behave when the theme is updated.

This guide describes a practical workflow for choosing a customization method, testing it, and keeping an escape route. The examples are illustrative; settings and supported extension mechanisms differ by theme and platform.

Define the problem before choosing a tool

Replace a broad brief such as “refresh the design” with a testable need: “make the booking link easier to find and improve the service cards on narrow screens.” List the affected page types and the behavior that must remain intact.

For each proposed change, ask:

  • Is it a site-wide style change or a change to one component?
  • Does it alter appearance only, or does it change behavior?
  • Where will the change live, and will an update overwrite it?
  • How will you verify the result and roll it back?

A button color and a checkout flow have different risks. Deep structural changes, unsupported integrations, or inaccessible navigation may justify reassessing the theme rather than adding layers of overrides.

Create a safe starting point

Record the active theme and version, relevant extensions, custom files, and the deployment method. Inventory representative routes: homepage, service page, article, search, form, cart, and checkout as applicable. Save the current settings before changing them.

Back up the files and database, and make sure the team knows how to restore them. A “backup complete” message alone does not prove recovery works; test restoration in an isolated environment. Confirm whether uploaded images and form data are included.

Work on a staging copy where possible. Protect it from public access and indexing with mechanisms suitable for your infrastructure. Use test transactions and test notifications, and avoid exposing copies of personal data. Agree on the reviewer, release window, and rollback method before making changes.

Choose the least invasive supported method

Theme settings

Start with the installed theme's documentation and settings. Some themes expose controls for colors, fonts, spacing, logos, or page blocks. Check whether the specific change is supported and survives an update.

One color setting can affect buttons, links, errors, and keyboard focus. Review its effects across different page templates, not just the homepage. Record the original values so that the change can be reversed.

Custom styles and extensions

If a setting is missing, find the supported location for custom CSS. Depending on the system, that might be a dedicated custom-style area, an extension mechanism, or an inherited theme. In WordPress, a child theme can be appropriate for certain changes; verify the approach against the parent theme and its type.

Editing distributed theme files directly can make updates overwrite your work. Keep changes in a maintainable location and document the reason for each override. Avoid copying an entire template to change a single line when a supported extension point is available.

Template and behavior changes

A block editor may allow some layout changes without code. If a template override is needed, understand how the theme resolves it and how the override will be compared with later upstream updates. A copied template can miss future accessibility or security fixes unless the team reviews changes deliberately.

Forms, interactive components, and checkout behavior deserve particular care. A visually identical button can depend on JavaScript, form state, or server-side processing. Test the complete user action with an appropriate developer rather than judging by appearance alone.

Example: make a card link more visible

Suppose a service page uses cards and the link inside each card is hard to notice. First check the theme's controls. If an override is needed, inspect the actual element and determine where the project loads custom CSS.

The following example uses a fictional class. It will do nothing unless your markup has that class and the stylesheet is loaded:

:root {
  --service-link-color: #174b70;
}

.service-card__link {
  color: var(--service-link-color);
  text-decoration: underline;
}

.service-card__link:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

Replace the selector with one confirmed in your project and use the supported customization location. The result depends on the CSS cascade, stylesheet order, and the existing theme. If a rule is overridden, inspect the computed styles instead of applying !important everywhere.

Check the link against its actual background, including hover and keyboard focus. Test long labels and narrow viewports. Underlining helps distinguish the link without relying on color alone, but the sample does not guarantee accessibility for your page.

Review typography, color, and imagery

When changing fonts, verify the characters and weights used by the actual content, the license, and the fallback when the font is unavailable. Test headings of different lengths, navigation, form labels, and body text. A font that looks good in a short heading may fail on long paragraphs or missing character sets.

Measure text contrast against the actual backgrounds, including images and component states. Check focus indicators and error messages. Don't assume a single successful check on the homepage covers every template.

For images, inspect where each asset is used, the expected aspect ratio, crop behavior, and file size. Use meaningful alternative text for informative images and an empty alternative where an image is genuinely decorative. Check the important subject remains visible at different viewport widths.

Make updates and rollback manageable

Keep a small change log: the reason, affected component, storage location, reviewer, and reversal steps. If the project uses version control, make changes in understandable commits and keep deployment configuration alongside the relevant code.

Test theme and extension updates on staging with the customizations in place. If you copied templates, compare them with the updated originals before release. Repeat critical scenarios, then decide whether the update is ready. Avoid treating “never update” as a maintenance plan; outdated components also need attention.

Don't install random snippets or archives without reviewing their origin and effect. Code can change permissions, data flows, or rendering behavior. Server-side modifications should be handled and tested by someone who understands the existing application.

Know when to reconsider the theme

A targeted override remains useful while the team understands it and can test its consequences. If every requirement demands another copied template, conflicting scripts, or a separate mobile fix, compare the ongoing cost with changing the theme or building a new one.

List each requirement, its supported method, the work needed, the testing approach, and the person who will maintain it. Include content migration, integrations, accessibility, ongoing updates, and rollback in the decision—not just the first release.

Release checklist

  1. The goal is specific and the smallest sufficient change is selected.
  2. Backups and restoration are verified; staging and rollback are ready.
  3. Changes live in supported locations and their purpose is documented.
  4. Representative pages, long content, viewport sizes, and keyboard navigation are tested.
  5. Forms, search, and purchases are tested safely where applicable.
  6. Contrast, focus, font fallbacks, and image crops are checked on real content.
  7. Theme updates are tested with customizations on a copy.
  8. Critical journeys and error logs are checked again after release.

Start with one well-defined change, test the whole journey, and expand the scope only when the evidence calls for it.

title: Testing an AI Code Reviewer Against Real GitHub Pull Requests
description:
Building an AI code reviewer is one thing. Trusting it with real pull requests is another.

I've been developing CodeGuard AI, a self-hosted AI-powered GitHub PR reviewer built with Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.

Instead of relying only on sample code and happy-path demonstrations, I've been testing it against deliberately created GitHub pull requests with different bugs, test scenarios, and edge cases.

What I've been testing

So far, the test lab has covered scenarios across several areas:

  1. Test execution and validation

Passing test suites

Genuine assertion failures

Test execution timeouts

Builds that succeed without executing tests

Unreadable test-result evidence

  1. Bug detection

Unsafe Optional.get() usage

Null input handling

Incorrect discount calculations

Boundary-value errors

Incorrect implementations hidden behind passing tests

  1. False-positive resistance

Safe Optional.orElse() usage

Correct discount calculations

Valid test assertions

Harmless code that should not trigger unnecessary findings

  1. Test-quality analysis

Missing regression tests

Missing edge-case coverage

Whether tests actually validate changed behavior

Some interesting findings

A few results have been particularly useful:

CodeGuard correctly identified a genuine failing assertion and showed the expected versus actual values.

It detected an incorrect discount calculation even though the existing test passed.

It correctly classified a timed-out test execution as TIMED_OUT.

It avoided flagging valid Optional.orElse() usage.

It identified missing regression coverage without claiming that the production implementation contained a confirmed bug.

However, testing also exposed areas that need improvement.

For example, some failing test scenarios received a warning instead of a blocking merge recommendation. In another scenario, test execution was unverified while the merge decision was still marked as safe.

These are exactly the kinds of inconsistencies I want to uncover before calling the product reliable.

What I'm learning

An AI code reviewer should not simply produce more findings.

It should:

Distinguish real bugs from false positives.

Understand whether tests actually executed.

Separate verified evidence from AI inference.

Avoid suggesting fixes that weaken valid tests.

Make merge recommendations consistent with verification results.

A green build does not automatically mean the tests passed. And a suggested fix is not necessarily a correct fix.



What's next?

I'm working through a 100-scenario validation plan.

The next focus areas include repository context, regression detection, team policies, suggested-patch validation, review consistency, and merge decisions.

I'm documenting the failures alongside the successful results because both matter.

CodeGuard AI is available as a source-code product for developers interested in exploring the implementation.

I'd especially like feedback from developers who maintain CI/CD pipelines or GitHub PR review workflows:

What should an AI code reviewer absolutely verify before recommending that a pull request is safe to merge?

Built with Java 21, Spring Boot 3, GitHub integration, and AI provider support.
Explore CodeGuard AI and get the source code here: https://javacoder716.gumroad.com/l/codeguard-ai?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=codeguard_testing_100

title: Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign, Auditable, and Deterministic Capability Execution for Logical Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.07652v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current autonomous logical systems rely on a fragile assumption: that language models should dynamically write code, guess API payloads, and memorize operational constraints through prompt engineering. In practice, this burns massive context windows, inflates API bills, and produces brittle agents that fail unpredictably in production.
  In this work, we present Skillware, an open architectural framework and capability registry that formally separates what an agent wants to do from how that task is executed. Instead of prompting models with loose text instructions or markdown files baptized as 'skills', Skillware equips them with modular, versioned software capability bundles. Much like skill hotkeys in video games that execute deterministically under fixed world rules, each bundle combines a typed JSON input contract, deterministic Python code, task directives, bundled datasets, and automated unit tests. In-process adapters translate these capabilities into native tool declarations for any model, from frontier cloud APIs to local open-weight runtimes with zero network latency.
  Evaluating 23 frontier and open-weight models across 368 benchmark conditions, we show that small local models (3B to 8B parameters) equipped with Skillware consistently outperform unequipped frontier models on complex multi-step workflows. They cut token usage by up to 84.8%, slash inference costs by up to 97.3%, and eliminate parameter errors entirely. True agent reliability does not come from larger models or longer prompts, but from equipping logical systems with verified, deterministic software.
  Finally, we articulate the trajectory of capability bundles across an invariant continuum of information processing systems: from digital logical systems today, to IoT, drones, and embodied robotics tomorrow, establishing a foundation for auditable, real-time capability execution.

title: KG-Neighbor: Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Construction for Embedding Visualization
description:
arXiv:2611.07246v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In embedding visualizations, nearby instances are interpreted as semantically related, although neighborhoods derived from input embeddings may not reflect content relationships. Neighborhood-based dimensionality reduction (DR) methods can propagate this limitation by optimizing layouts from embedding-based neighborhood graphs. We propose Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Graph Construction (KGN), which represents relational knowledge derived from each instance as a set of knowledge graph (KG) triples. It uses the degree of triple sharing as pairwise semantic evidence to adjust embedding distances and reconstruct the top-k neighborhood graph; neither KG extraction nor neighborhood construction uses class labels. We also introduce IDProfile (IDP), which interprets residual mismatches by independently assessing whether the source content supports the assigned class label and the neighborhood-majority class. Across eight text and image dataset-encoder conditions, we characterize KGN over the full guidance-strength sweep and four KG similarity measures. Across this sweep, the maximum NMI and LT_2D each exceed the corresponding kNN baseline in all eight conditions, with the largest gains reaching 0.68 and 1.35, respectively. The gains and the extent of neighborhood reconfiguration vary across conditions and are larger under encoder conditions with lower kNN baseline scores. The IDP analysis shows that the largest reductions are concentrated in Placement Issue candidates, whereas Label Issue and Unresolved Case instances account for a larger share of the remaining review set. These results indicate that KGN can narrow the evaluated gap between embedding-based neighborhoods and content-supported semantic relations, while IDP shows that a residual mismatch should not automatically be interpreted as a projection failure.

description:

Announcement

On October 22, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-7).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
573663408 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the ingress gateway to patch security vulnerabilities.
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
568535165 Skip main_task_wait_time and nio_task_wait_time metrics for the first 12 Prometheus scrapes during Message Processor startup warmup.
573602919 Fix generated OpenAPI specs' servers[] to carry the Apigee envgroup hostname instead of the backend target host.
562964081 The sgpUserIntentMatchingMode verdict-log field is now always present, including on dry-run policy records, and shows the mode used for the evaluation, including when sgpUserIntentMatching isn't set (CONSTRAINTS_AND_INTENT, or INTENT_ONLY when no policies match the tool call).
524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.
572025634 Responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact instead of returning a corrupted body.
549078690 If no SGP policy is attributed for a denial, a customer sees the generic fallback message. This fix short-circuits to show the rationale instead when no matched policy has a configured denial message.
492041991 VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken now set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables only from the LLM operation(s) that matched the request; they are no longer set from unmatched LLM operations or for requests that match no LLM operation.
567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.
567244615 Semantic Governance no longer evaluates a request or response with a field it cannot read when a tool call is involved. It records verdict ERROR naming the field, with status MODEL_ERROR. The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.
560272924 Added continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming support for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Model Armor policies now honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: with it set, Model Armor callouts bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic. Streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
158204922 VerifyJWT now rejects a JWT whose header contains "b64":false, with fault steps.jwt.InvalidToken, as RFC 7797 section 7 requires. Previously, such a token could be accepted if KnownHeaders listed b64, IgnoreCriticalHeaders was true, or the header had no crit.
158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.
158204922 VerifyJWS verifies RFC 7797 unencoded-payload JWS (b64:false), attached or detached. b64 in crit no longer needs a KnownHeaders entry. VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.
575439485 JavaCallout policies that run remotely (per-contract offload) can now pass every value type allowed by the GCP-2025-023 setVariable restriction between policies (collections, maps, arrays, primitive wrappers including Character, Date, BigDecimal, UUID, java.time, atomics, JDK enums, Optional), with their types preserved, instead of failing with steps.remotepolicy.NonSerializableVariable.
575439485 Remotely executed (per-contract offload) JavaCallout policies with continueOnError="true" now continue the flow when the callout faults, instead of returning HTTP 500.
567244901 In enforce mode, Semantic Governance now blocks a tool call when the governance check cannot be completed, instead of letting it through.
573622417 Fixed an issue where istio-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571679067 removes old version of ApigeeTelemetry CRD.
571378258 The Apigee Redis container is now built from the Valkey engine (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) at version 8.1.10. Wire protocol is unchanged (RESP2) and the redis-server/redis-cli binary names are preserved.

title: What a tiny Django ticket taught me about open source
description:
Hi, I'm Stephen, a Djangonaut contributing to Django core. This was my second ticket, and it looked tiny: a one-line capitalization bug in makemessages. It turned into a lesson in code review, minimal diffs, and a lot of git 😂.

Here is the story.

The bug: a helpful message that gives wrong advice

Django's makemessages command extracts translatable strings into .po files, one folder per locale. If you pass a locale that doesn't exist, it tries to help by suggesting a valid one.

Here is what happened when you typed a script-based locale like Simplified Chinese:

$ python manage.py makemessages --locale zh-hans
invalid locale zh-hans, did you mean zh_HAns?

zh-hans is invalid because Django expects an underscore. But the suggestion, zh_HAns, is also invalid. The correct locale is zh_Hans.

The bug was reported on the Django forum and filed as ticket #36642.

Why it happened

Locales come in several shapes:

Locale Parts
de language
pt_BR language + region (2 letters)
en_001 language + numeric region
zh_Hans language + script (4 letters)
nl_NL-x-informal language + region + private use

The suggestion code split the input into a language and "everything after the separator", then assumed that part was a country code and uppercased its first two characters:

territory = (
    locale_parts["territory"][:2].upper()
    + locale_parts["territory"][2:]
)

That is right for pl_pl → pl_PL. For hans it gives HA + ns, which is HAns. The code was written for one locale shape and silently applied to all of them.

One constraint shaped everything: any fix had to leave validation alone. en_001 was valid before, and a fix that broke it would trade one bug for another.

Test first

Django's workflow is to write the test, watch it fail, then fix. My regression test copied the structure of the neighbouring test_invalid_locale_lower_country:

def test_invalid_locale_mixed_case_script(self):
    out = StringIO()
    management.call_command(
        "makemessages", locale=["zh-hans"], stdout=out, verbosity=1
    )
    self.assertIn("invalid locale zh-hans, did you mean zh_Hans?", out.getvalue())
    self.assertNotIn("processing locale zh-hans", out.getvalue())
    self.assertIs(Path("locale/zh-hans/LC_MESSAGES/django.po").exists(), False)

Before the fix, it failed exactly as the ticket described:

AssertionError: 'invalid locale zh-hans, did you mean zh_Hans?' not found in
'invalid locale zh-hans, did you mean zh_HAns?\n'

[Add your failing-test screenshot here]

The fix, three versions

Version 1: the first PR

My first PR looked locales up in Django's LANG_INFO dictionary. It fixed zh-hans, but en_001 stopped being recognized as valid. The reviewer, Jacob Walls, caught that regression. I left is_valid_locale() alone and changed only how the suggestion is formatted.

Version 2: format each subtag by type 

def format_subtag(m):
    subtag = m.group()
    if len(subtag) == 4:  # script, e.g. Hans
        return subtag.title()
    if len(subtag) == 2:  # region, e.g. CN
        return subtag.upper()
    return subtag

territory = re.sub(r"[a-zA-Z]+", format_subtag, territory) + x + private

Private-use parts like -x-informal were split off first with partition("-x-") so they stayed untouched.

Review: "Why special-case length 4?"

Jacob pointed out that another Chinese locale, zh-yue, has a three-letter subtag. A rule built on "scripts are 4 letters" was a guess. Only the 2-letter case needs upper(), so the helper and re.sub could go.

Version 3: the simple rule

Jacob suggested a simpler approach that handles only the 2-letter case. I made the change:

# Two-letter subtags are region codes (e.g. GB), which
# are uppercased. Others, such as scripts (e.g. Hans),
# are title-cased.
if len(territory) == 2:
    territory = territory.upper()
else:
    territory = territory.title()
proposed_locale = f"{language}_{territory}" + x + private
Input Suggestion
zh-hans zh_Hans
pl_pl pl_PL
en-001 en_001
nl-nl-x-informal nl_NL-x-informal

He also suggested .title() over slicing, and asked for a comment explaining why 2-letter strings are special. Both made the code easier for the next reader.

What I chose not to solve

zh_hans_cn still suggests zh_Hans_cn, which is invalid. Fixing it means deciding which subtag is a script, a region, or a variant, and without a length rule, that is guessing. Jacob said that coming back with "I explored it, but it's too error-prone" would also move the PR forward. Knowing when to stop was part of the fix.

The messy middle

The code took an afternoon. The git around it took longer 😂.

  • Old base: my branch was built on old code, so the diff against main listed hundreds of files. I backed it up with git branch backup, ran git reset --hard upstream/main, and re-applied only my changes by hand.
  • A file I overwrote: test_extraction.py had been replaced with an older copy, which reverted unrelated tests and triggered flake8 errors on lines I never touched. git diff revealed it.
  • Push rejected as "stale info": --force-with-lease had no record of the remote branch. git ls-remote --heads origin showed what was actually there.
  • Wrong remote: I once pointed upstream at my own fork instead of django/django.
  • A push that never landed: GitHub looked unchanged. Comparing git log with git log origin/<branch> showed the push had not gone through.
  • The PR bot: it failed my PR on an "Incomplete Checklist" because the boxes had lost their - [x] syntax when I copied the description.

Lessons for first-time contributors

  1. Keep diffs minimal. Reviewers notice whitespace and cosmetic changes.
  2. Verify, don't assume. Check git diff --stat, git log and the remote after every big step.
  3. Back up before destructive commands.
  4. Specific test names beat docstrings.
  5. Reviewers can give you a way out.
  6. Expect the workflow to take longer than the code.
  7. A small ticket is the best way to learn the whole process.

Thank you to Jacob Walls and Tim Schilling for the patient reviews.

Links

  • Trac ticket: https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/36642
  • Pull request: https://github.com/django/django/pull/19984
  • Django contributing guide: https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/dev/internals/contributing/

title: du और Finder एक ही फ़ोल्डर का अलग-अलग साइज़ क्यों दिखाते हैं
description:
किसी फ़ोल्डर पर du -sh चलाएँ और उसे Finder के साइज़ से मिलाएँ, तो दोनों अक्सर अलग निकलते हैं, कभी-कभी कई गीगाबाइट का फ़र्क़। दोनों में से कोई ग़लत नहीं है। वे अलग सवालों का जवाब देते हैं: फ़ाइलें कितनी लंबी हैं, और वे डिस्क की कितनी जगह घेरती हैं। डिस्क भर जाने पर सिर्फ़ दूसरा सवाल मायने रखता है, और उसे सही निकालने के लिए सिर्फ़ st_size जोड़ना काफ़ी नहीं है।

नीचे के नियम osFoundry डेस्कटॉप ऐप की Disk स्क्रीन फ़ॉलो करती है। उसका स्कैनर std::fs के ऊपर एक छोटा Rust फ़ंक्शन है, और वही लॉजिक करीब 40 लाइन के Python में आ जाता है। सारे नंबर 4 KB एलोकेशन ब्लॉक वाले APFS वॉल्यूम पर एक टेस्ट फ़ोल्डर से लिए गए हैं।

बाइट नहीं, ब्लॉक गिनें

st_size फ़ाइल की लंबाई है। st_blocks वह संख्या है जितनी 512-बाइट की इकाइयाँ फ़ाइल सिस्टम ने उस फ़ाइल को दी हैं, चाहे वॉल्यूम का असली ब्लॉक साइज़ कुछ भी हो। ऐप का स्कैनर डिफ़ॉल्ट रूप से दूसरे वाले का इस्तेमाल करता है:

fn allocated_bytes(meta: &fs::Metadata, apparent: bool) -> u64 {
    if apparent {
        return meta.len();
    }
    #[cfg(unix)]
    {
        use std::os::unix::fs::MetadataExt;
        meta.blocks().saturating_mul(512)
    }
    #[cfg(not(unix))]
    {
        meta.len()
    }
}

टेस्ट फ़ोल्डर की तीन फ़ाइलें बताती हैं कि क्यों:

फ़ाइल st_size st_blocks × 512
small.txt (2 बाइट का टेक्स्ट) 2 4,096
sparse.img (1 GiB तक ट्रंकेट की गई, कभी लिखी नहीं गई) 1,073,741,824 0
big.bin (200 MiB डेटा) 209,715,200 209,715,200

छोटी-सी फ़ाइल भी एक पूरा ब्लॉक घेरती है, इसलिए 100,000 छोटी फ़ाइलों वाला फ़ोल्डर डिस्क पर अपनी बाइट-गिनती से कई सौ मेगाबाइट बड़ा होता है। स्पार्स फ़ाइल इसका उलटा है: VM डिस्क, डेटाबेस फ़ाइलें और कुछ डाउनलोड बड़ी लंबाई रिज़र्व कर लेते हैं और ब्लॉक सिर्फ़ उन हिस्सों के लिए लेते हैं जिनमें कुछ लिखा गया है। macOS का du ब्लॉक गिनता है; du -A उसकी जगह apparent साइज़ दिखाता है। ऐप का Apparent size बॉक्स यही स्विच करता है।

लिंक फ़ॉलो न करें, वॉल्यूम से बाहर न जाएँ

जो स्कैनर सिम्बॉलिक लिंक फ़ॉलो करता है, वह एक ही फ़ोल्डर को दो बार गिन सकता है, या अपने ही पैरेंट की ओर इशारा करने वाले लिंक पर हमेशा घूमता रह सकता है। जो माउंट की हुई ड्राइव में घुस जाए, वह किसी दूसरी डिस्क की फ़ाइलें इस डिस्क के टोटल में जोड़ देता है। ऐप हर एंट्री को symlink_metadata से पढ़ता है, जो लिंक का वर्णन करता है, उसके टार्गेट का नहीं, और डिवाइस ID की तुलना उस फ़ोल्डर से करता है जहाँ से स्कैन शुरू हुआ था:

if child_meta.file_type().is_symlink() || !same_device(root_meta, &child_meta) {
    continue;
}

same_device st_dev की तुलना करता है, जो du -x या find -xdev वाली ही जाँच है।

हार्ड लिंक और क्लोन

हार्ड लिंक एक ही फ़ाइल के कई नाम होते हैं। टेस्ट फ़ोल्डर में ln big.bin hard.bin के बाद ls -l दो 200 MiB की फ़ाइलें दिखाता है, लेकिन du डेटा को एक ही बार गिनता है, क्योंकि st_nlink 1 से ऊपर होने पर वह हर देखे हुए (st_dev, st_ino) जोड़े को याद रखता है। ब्लॉक जोड़ने वाले हर स्कैनर को यही करना चाहिए। HFS+ डिस्क पर Time Machine बैकअप और कुछ पैकेज मैनेजर हार्ड लिंक पर काफ़ी निर्भर हैं।

APFS क्लोन ज़्यादा मुश्किल हैं। cp -c big.bin clone.bin (या Finder में Duplicate) एक दूसरी फ़ाइल बनाता है जो मूल फ़ाइल के ब्लॉक तब तक साझा करती है जब तक दोनों में से कोई बदल न जाए। हर फ़ाइल का अपना inode, अपना st_blocks और लिंक काउंट 1 होता है, इसलिए du इस जोड़ी के लिए 400 MiB गिनता है। df से पहले और बाद में नापने पर क्लोन ने फ़्री स्पेस में 0 KB लिया, जबकि उसी फ़ाइल की सामान्य cp ने 204,984 KB लिया। कोई POSIX फ़ील्ड इस साझेदारी को नहीं दिखाता, इसलिए ब्लॉक-आधारित टोटल यह ज़्यादा बताता है कि क्लोन डिलीट करने से कितनी जगह वापस मिलेगी। डुप्लिकेट प्रोजेक्ट या फ़ोटो लाइब्रेरी से भरे फ़ोल्डरों के लिए पहले और बाद में df देखना ही अकेली भरोसेमंद जाँच है।

Python वर्शन

यही नियम, सिर्फ़ स्टैंडर्ड लाइब्रेरी के साथ:

import os
import stat
import sys

def usage(root):
    root_dev = os.lstat(root).st_dev
    seen = set()
    allocated = apparent = 0
    skipped = 0
    stack = [root]
    while stack:
        path = stack.pop()
        try:
            entries = list(os.scandir(path))
        except OSError:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        for e in entries:
            try:
                st = e.stat(follow_symlinks=False)
            except OSError:
                skipped += 1
                continue
            if stat.S_ISLNK(st.st_mode) or st.st_dev != root_dev:
                continue
            if stat.S_ISDIR(st.st_mode):
                stack.append(e.path)
                continue
            if st.st_nlink > 1:
                key = (st.st_dev, st.st_ino)
                if key in seen:
                    continue
                seen.add(key)
            allocated += st.st_blocks * 512
            apparent += st.st_size
    return allocated, apparent, skipped

if __name__ == "__main__":
    alloc, appar, skipped = usage(sys.argv[1])
    print(f"on disk  {alloc / 2**30:8.2f} GiB")
    print(f"apparent {appar / 2**30:8.2f} GiB")
    if skipped:
        print(f"skipped  {skipped} unreadable entries")

टेस्ट फ़ोल्डर पर यह डिस्क पर 0.39 GiB और apparent 1.39 GiB छापता है, जो du -sk (409,604 KB) और du -sAk से मेल खाता है। 14 GiB के सोर्स ट्री पर यह du -sk से दशमलव के दो अंकों तक मिलता है। स्किप की गई एंट्रियों की गिनती रखें: macOS में प्राइवेसी परमिशन से सुरक्षित फ़ोल्डर (Mail, Messages, Safari) Full Disk Access के बिना नहीं पढ़े जा सकते, और जो टोटल उन्हें चुपचाप छोड़ दे वह असल से ज़्यादा पूरा दिखता है।

ऐप नतीजे को इतना छोटा रखता है कि उसे बनाया जा सके। हर फ़ोल्डर अपने 36 सबसे बड़े चाइल्ड रखता है और बाक़ी सब एक ही "Other items" नोड में जुड़ जाते हैं, इसलिए हज़ार पैकेज वाला node_modules फ़ोल्डर खोलने पर 36 बॉक्स और बाक़ी सबके लिए एक और बॉक्स दिखता है, हज़ार पतली पट्टियाँ नहीं।

सुरक्षित तरीक़े से डिलीट करना

डिस्क टूल का असली जोखिम डिलीट वाले कदम में है। ऐप आइटम को unlink करने की जगह trash क्रेट से सिस्टम Trash में भेजता है, और कुछ भी हिलाने से पहले हर पाथ की जाँच करता है:

if !target.starts_with(&root) || target == root || home.as_ref() == Some(&target) {
    return Err("Cannot move a scan root or home folder to Trash".into());
}
if mount_points
    .iter()
    .any(|mount| target == *mount || target.parent() == Some(mount.as_path()))
{
    return Err("Cannot move a volume or its top-level items to Trash".into());
}

पाथ पहले कैनोनिकलाइज़ किए जाते हैं, ताकि .. या कोई सिम्बॉलिक लिंक स्कैन किए गए फ़ोल्डर के बाहर का टार्गेट न घुसा सके। ऐसा चयन भी रिजेक्ट होता है जिसमें एक मार्क किया हुआ फ़ोल्डर दूसरे को समेटे हो, क्योंकि पैरेंट के Trash में जाते ही चाइल्ड का पाथ ख़त्म हो जाता है और बैच बीच में फ़ेल हो जाएगा।

डेस्कटॉप ऐप osFoundry डाउनलोड पेज से मुफ़्त है।

title: Goal-Branching LaCAM: Temporary Goals as Search Branches in Dense Multi-Agent Pathfinding
description:
arXiv:2611.07528v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LaCAM is a search-based solver for multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF) that runs a depth-first search over joint configurations, using PIBT to generate successors and lazily adding single-agent constraints to explore alternatives. Although LaCAM is complete, it can struggle on dense, corridor-heavy instances because extracting blocking agents from deadlocks requires coordinated moves of several agents, often away from their goals, which PIBT's greedy one-step successors rarely propose and which LaCAM can only reach by enumerating constraints one agent at a time. This paper proposes Goal-Branching, where blocking agents are given temporary goals, each tried as an additional branch of LaCAM's search. We examine random and corridor-aware rules for choosing these temporary goals and show that completeness is preserved for any such rule. On dense instances (60-90% of free cells occupied) of three maze and room maps, Goal-Branching solves 89% of instances against 44% for LaCAM*, and, on instances both solve, it finds a first solution 10-14x faster on maze-32-32-2 and room-32-32-4, and nearly 200x faster in median time at 75% density on room-32-32-4. Solution cost increases by 15-22% on instances both solve, while on open maps and the full MovingAI benchmark its solutions cost no more than those of LaCAM* and it is at most 3% slower.

title: Solana CPI Overhead: From 90-Byte Accounts to 4-Byte Indices
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

Every cross-program invocation on Solana starts with the calling program copying information the runtime already has. For each account it forwards, the program builds an account meta and an account info, then hands both arrays to a syscall that reads them back. SIMD-0670 proposes to replace all of that with a 4-byte index.

SIMD-0670, merged on 24 October with status Review, adds sol_invoke_signed_v2 next to today’s invoke. To see what it saves, we wrote a small Pinocchio program that prepares the same CPI both ways and ran it in solana-sbpf, the virtual machine Agave runs programs in, counting every instruction up to the syscall. The v2 path costs about a third as much per account, falls to a constant 17 to 20 compute units when the account list is fixed, and avoids a stack limit that today’s path hits before its own documented maximum.

Where the 90 bytes come from

A program receives its accounts as a serialized buffer and, to call another program, has to describe the accounts it forwards twice. The Rust interface takes an AccountMeta per account, a 32-byte address plus two flags, and an account info; the proposal counts 34 and 56 bytes for them. The C interface, which Pinocchio uses, replaces the address with a pointer, so its meta is 16 bytes with padding, and its account info is 56:

Rust ABI, as the proposal counts it — 34 + 56 = 90 bytes

C ABI (Pinocchio): meta + CpiAccount — 16 + 56 = 72 bytes

SIMD-0670: CpiAccount — 4 bytes

The new record is an index into the caller’s own instruction accounts plus the two flags. The runtime already holds those accounts, so it looks them up instead of reading copies:

#[repr(C)]
pub struct CpiAccount {
    pub account_index: u16, // index in the current instruction
    pub is_writable: u8,
    pub is_signer: u8,
}

pub fn sol_invoke_signed_v2(instruction_addr: u64, signers_seeds_addr: u64, signers_seeds_len: u64);

One naming trap: Pinocchio’s CPI module, solana-instruction-view, already has a type called CpiAccount. That one is the 56-byte account info. The proposal’s CpiAccount is the 4-byte record.

What preparing a CPI costs, measured

Our test program forwards N accounts to a callee in four ways: Pinocchio 0.11.2’s stack path (invoke_signed_with_bounds), its heap path for larger calls, v2 descriptors filled from the account flags, and a v2 descriptor list fixed at compile time. We built it with platform-tools v1.57 and ran it in solana-sbpf 0.26.0, configured as Agave configures it, with inputs serialized the way Agave serializes them. A stub syscall records the instruction count when the program reaches the CPI, and the count for reaching any syscall with the same accounts is subtracted. One executed instruction is one compute unit.

8 accounts: v1 · v2 · v2 fixed — 529 · 171 · 17 CU

16 accounts — 1,011 · 316 · 18 CU

32 accounts — 1,969 · 606 · 20 CU

56 accounts, v1 stack — 3,411 CU

64 accounts: v1 heap · v2 · v2 fixed — 4,319 · 1,179 · 17 CU

128 accounts — 8,543 · 2,332 · 18 CU

254 accounts: v2 · v2 fixed — 4,602 · 20 CU

Today’s path costs about 60 compute units per account on the stack and about 66 on the heap. The v2 path, filling each descriptor from the account’s flags, costs about 18. When a program always forwards the same accounts, the descriptor list can live in read-only data, and the cost stops depending on the number of accounts at all.

The proposal’s own benchmark, a Pinocchio program calling a program that logs how many accounts it received, reports different absolute numbers: from 1,376 to 1,174 compute units at 8 accounts, and from 2,813 to 1,267 at 64. The shape is the same. Today’s path grows with every account. The proposed one barely moves.

The stack limit comes before the documented one

A Solana program function gets a 4 KiB stack frame. Pinocchio allows up to 64 accounts on its stack path, which is 3,584 bytes of 56-byte account infos. Its CPI helpers are #[inline(always)], though, so that array lands in the caller’s frame next to the caller’s own 16-byte metas:

56 accounts, v1 stack — runs

60 accounts, frame estimate — 4,416 bytes, crashes

64 accounts, frame estimate — 4,672 bytes, crashes

254 accounts, v2 descriptors — 1,016 bytes

cargo-build-sbf prints a frame-overflow error for the 60- and 64-account versions but still produces the binary. At run time both stop with an access violation in the stack frame. A program that needs more accounts moves to the heap path, which allocates 72 bytes per account: 9,216 bytes of the default 32 KiB heap at 128 accounts, Pinocchio’s ceiling. With v2 the whole list of 254 accounts fits in about a quarter of one frame.

What the proposal leaves unchanged

Only the program’s side gets cheaper. The runtime still translates every account, applies the same privilege checks and charges the same compute: the proposal keeps the per-account charge at 34 bytes, because the runtime reads the same information either way. Old programs keep working, since today’s syscall is not changed or removed.

Indices also mean a program can only forward accounts that are already in its own instruction. That is true of today’s invoke as well, which needs an account info the program can only get from its input, so nothing a program could do before is lost.

Where it stands

The proposal is merged with status Review. Agave’s implementation was open as #15979 at the time of writing, and a new syscall also needs a feature gate before mainnet programs can call it. Program libraries will need a v2 path of their own; our test declared the syscall by hand. For a busy program the saving adds up: compute units are what priority fees are priced against, and a router that forwards dozens of accounts on every call pays the per-account cost every time.

What this does not show

We measured the program’s preparation only. The syscalls were stubs, so the runtime’s CPI work and the callee are not included. The numbers are for one program built with one toolchain. Other code, including Anchor’s, will differ, though not in shape. The v2 syscall was not running anywhere we could test, so we checked that our descriptors matched the proposal’s layout rather than that a runtime accepted them.

CPI Overhead: Questions People Actually Ask

What does SIMD-0670 change about Solana CPIs?

It proposes a second invoke syscall, sol_invoke_signed_v2, that describes each account passed to a cross-program invocation with a 4-byte record: the account’s index in the caller’s own instruction plus writable and signer flags. Today a program passes two records per account, an account meta and an account info: 90 bytes through the Rust interface by the proposal’s count, 72 through the C interface Pinocchio uses. The runtime’s CPI logic and its compute charge stay the same; only the program-side preparation shrinks.

How many compute units does SIMD-0670 save?

In our measurement inside Solana’s VM, preparing a CPI the way Pinocchio does today costs about 60 compute units per forwarded account (529 for 8 accounts, 1,969 for 32). Filling v2 descriptors from the accounts costs about 18 per account (171 and 606), and a descriptor list fixed at compile time costs 17 to 20 regardless of size. The runtime’s own CPI charge is not included and does not change.

What is the maximum number of accounts a Solana CPI can forward from the stack?

With Pinocchio 0.11.2’s stack path, our test program ran with 56 forwarded accounts and failed with a stack access violation at 60 and 64. Each account costs 72 bytes of the 4 KiB stack frame, and Pinocchio inlines its account array into the caller. With SIMD-0670’s 4-byte descriptors, 254 accounts take 1,016 bytes.

Is sol_invoke_signed_v2 available on mainnet?

No. SIMD-0670 was merged on 24 October 2026 with status Review, and Agave’s implementation was an open pull request at the time of writing. Like every new syscall it needs a feature gate before programs can call it on mainnet.

Does sol_invoke_signed_v2 change CPI security?

The proposal says the security surface is identical: the runtime applies the same privilege checks and compute metering, and it still charges as if each account were 34 bytes. A program can only reference accounts that are already in its own instruction, which is also true of today’s invoke.

The one-line version

SIMD-0670 lets a program forward an account to a CPI with a 4-byte index instead of 72 to 90 bytes of copies, cutting preparation from about 60 compute units per account to about 18, or to a constant 20 for a fixed list, and keeping 254 accounts inside one stack frame.

Pinocchio itself is the library behind p-token, where the same idea of not copying what the runtime already has made the token program several times cheaper.

Sources: SIMD-0670 at commit c9ec366a; Agave #15979; Pinocchio 0.11.2 and solana-instruction-view 2.1.0; solana-sbpf 0.26.0. Measurements are from our own test program and harness.

title: When Verification Is Not Agreement: Cross-Agent LLM-to-Dafny Formalization
description:
arXiv:2611.07073v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A verified Dafny postcondition certifies that a formula holds, but it does not guarantee that the result was reached through genuine independent reasoning. We introduce a cross-agent formalization protocol where a Specifier model translates clinical trial criteria into a Dafny predicate, and an Implementer model writes an operational method checked against it. A same-model control establishes that even with no capability gap, independent re-extraction from identical text agrees only 59.3% of the time. Evaluating four model configurations on 96 clinical trial documents, we find that agreement is highly sensitive to how model capability is allocated across the two roles: the GPT-4.1-nano/GPT-4.1-mini configuration achieves 53.0% agreement when the stronger model is the Implementer, but only 14.3% when the roles are reversed. The strongest tested configuration, GPT-5.6-luna/GPT-5.4-mini, improves agreement to 34.4% but remains below the same-model baseline and is dominated by direct contradiction (42.7%). We also detect a critical verification artifact in which a weaker Implementer satisfies the postcondition by invoking the Specifier's predicate directly; after structural auditing, corrected agreement falls from 14.3% to 13.2%. Our results show that verification success alone is insufficient evidence of independent cross-agent agreement, and that model capability does not guarantee agreement when formalizing the same source independently.

title: Align Before Aggregation: Basis-Consistent Federated LoRA under Heterogeneous Ranks
description:
arXiv:2611.07598v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) under heterogeneous client capacities is increasingly important, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with heterogeneous ranks makes it practical. Existing server-side aggregators compose local matrix updates $\Delta W_i$ from client-specific LoRA factors $(A_i,B_i)$ before aggregating them. Although these matrix updates lie in the same weight space $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and can be averaged directly, the LoRA factors that generate them may expressed client-specific local basis. In the typical compose--aggregate--factorize--dispatch loop, this basis inconsistency can make the rank-$r_i$ reference prefix dispatched to lower-rank clients unstable after server-side refactorization. In this work, we propose \textbf{FedAbA}, a basis-consistent federated LoRA aggregation framework for heterogeneous ranks. FedAbA first extracts each client's local basis, aligns it to the corresponding prefix of the global reference basis, and constructs a basis-consistent reconstruction of each local matrix update before aggregation. It then aggregates these reconstructions with weights that combine client data size and consistency score, followed by exact coefficient-space SVD refactorization and gauge fixing before rank-prefix dispatch. Our theoretical analysis clarifies the role of basis consistency and supports the proposed consistency-aware aggregation mechanism. Extensive experiments show that FedAbA outperforms representative federated LoRA baselines, with the largest gains under the strongest rank heterogeneity.

title: Integrating Learned Priors through Prior-Space Reparameterization for Physically Based Inverse Rendering
description:
arXiv:2611.07573v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physically based inverse rendering decomposes appearance into materials and illumination, an ambiguous problem for which learned material predictions provide useful prior information. Most existing methods incorporate these cues through auxiliary regularization losses, which alter the optimization objective and require balancing their influence against photometric fitting. We propose a prior-guided material reparameterization that uses the predicted feature relationships to restrict the optimization space while leaving the objective unchanged. We fuse multi-view material predictions onto a mesh and construct a permutohedral lattice in the resulting prior feature space. Surface points with similar predictions share material variables, which are optimized jointly with geometry and illumination using a purely photometric objective. Experiments with two learned predictors on three synthetic benchmarks and Stanford-ORB demonstrate improved material decomposition and relighting. Our method improves relighting PSNR by 1.5-2.5 dB over the strongest evaluated mesh-based baseline on Synthetic4Relight and TensoIR-Synthetic, and outperforms a regularization loss using the same prior in controlled comparisons. We further show that our reparameterization pools noisy photometric gradients, producing updates that are more consistent across sampled views. This consistency enables a shortened joint optimization schedule that takes less than a minute while retaining relighting quality above all evaluated baselines on TensoIR-Synthetic.

title: Jev is the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history
description:
Within 24 hours of launching on AI Gateway, Jev from TypeSafe AI reached more than twice as many paid teams as any previous model launch, making it the fastest-adopted model in gateway history.

Jev passed every other comparison model in its first twelve hours and continued to widen its lead for the rest of the day. By hour 24, nearly 13% of paid teams were using it. That's 2x the GPT-5.6 family and more than 6x Fable 5.1's share.

Jev’s launch shows how quickly a specialized model can find a place in production. Its first-day adoption was unmatched among recent launches; the next test is whether that early adoption lasts.

About Jev

Jev was introduced on September 15 as a probabilistic decision model designed to support structured decision-making within software. An application sends it context and a set of questions. Jev evaluates those questions in parallel and returns typed choices, scores, or true-or-false answers, along with probabilities.

Unlike the text produced by a general-purpose language model, Jev’s answers come in a format the code can use directly. Developers can use it to:

  • choose an agent’s next tool or subagent

  • decide whether a workflow should continue, retry, ask the user, or stop

  • score urgency or risk before taking an action

  • verify model outputs, enforce guardrails, or send uncertain cases for human review

In its own workflow evaluations, TypeSafe AI reports that Jev was up to 194 times faster and 445 times cheaper than language models.

See the September AI Gateway Production Index for more model usage data, or try Jev through AI Gateway and build with the AI SDK.

title: Loopback Transformer: Towards a Unified View of Residual Looped Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.07226v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how the results of repeated computation are reused. We take the depth-memory view of residual connections and analyze which representation is stored after each block application and how later reads weight it. A full block output contains both its input and its new update, so weighting that output also reweights the history already carried by the input. Reading individual updates instead, with the shared stack's input kept on a separate path, gives separate controls over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. The Loopback Transformer implements these controls: geometric decay sets the total update weight and supplies a recency prior, and attention learns how to allocate that weight. On ClimbMix, Loopback reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters (excluding token embeddings and the output head) at reference scales from 191M to 3B, with training tokens and executed depth matched. It also has higher mean accuracy over thirteen downstream tasks at 1.4B and 3B. At 191M, 374M, and 778M, it has the lowest validation loss and the highest thirteen-task mean among the standard Transformer and seven looped residual designs.

title: Interactive Backdoor Attacks in LLM-Based Proactive Dialogue Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.06969v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based proactive dialogue systems provide goal-directed support through sustained interaction. Fine-tuning their underlying models on externally supplied dialogue data introduces backdoor risks. Existing LLM backdoor studies primarily focus on eliciting an attacker-specified response upon trigger activation. We present an interactive backdoor attack framework that uses training-data poisoning to steer post-trigger, multi-turn interactions toward an attacker-specified objective. Poisoned fine-tuning dialogues implant a trigger-conditioned guidance-policy bias that ordinary user utterances can activate, without deployment-time prompt modification or further attacker intervention. Specifically, we instantiate three complementary attacks under progressively expanded post-trigger interaction settings: (1) Direct Attack, which targets an immediate response deviation upon trigger activation, retaining the conventional trigger--response setting; (2) Constrained Progressive Attack, which progressively advances the attack objective along a predefined multi-turn trajectory; and (3) Unconstrained Progressive Attack, which extends target-directed steering to open-ended interactions with varied user continuations. Using psychological counseling as a representative setting, experiments on two LLM backbones and two dialogue datasets show that all three attacks effectively achieve their objectives under their respective interaction settings while largely preserving normal utility. Separate defense evaluations show that the tested training-data filters retain nearly all poisoned dialogues, while three post-admission baselines leave substantial residual attack-specific success.

title: Axis-LoRA: Probing and Adapting Embedding Models for Personal-Memory Retrieval
description:
arXiv:2611.07820v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly asked questions about a user's personal experiences, retrieval must distinguish memories by time, place, person, and event. Current personal-memory pipelines rely on frozen dense embedding models to embed memories for retrieval, but we find that these models do not capture the four axes well. Swapping a memory's date or place barely shifts its embedding, and a trained projection on top of the frozen embedding does not recover the missing signal. The problem lives inside the model, where each axis is encoded by a distinct attention-head pattern. Guided by these findings, we propose Axis-LoRA, a per-axis adapter that places four LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them via a per-query gate. Across three standard embedding models evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo, Axis-LoRA improves 4-benchmark mean R@10 by $+1.28$ to $+1.56$~pp while training only a small fraction of the base parameters on a small axis-counterfactual training set. Code is available at https://github.com/dohoonkim-ai/axis-lora.

title: ChatGPT Can’t Backtest: Why “AI” Trading Bots With 10-Year Backtests Are Fiction
description:
A bot that needs live ChatGPT calls cannot have a 2019 backtest — ChatGPT didn't exist. That single fact exposes most “AI EAs” on the market.

Here is a fact that eliminates most “AI trading bots” on the market in one sentence: a bot whose decisions require live calls to a language model cannot be backtested — because the model did not exist for most of the backtest window.

ChatGPT launched in 2022. A product showing you a flawless 2019 backtest for its “ChatGPT-powered” bot is showing you fiction — or, more charitably, a conventional strategy with AI branding. Real AI decisions require live API connectivity, cost money per call, and take seconds per decision (roughly 3–7 seconds end to end in published breakdowns). You cannot retroactively generate historical decisions from a model that did not exist, and you cannot backtest a system whose response times and model versions change underneath you. GPT-5 thinks differently from GPT-4. A backtest run on one is not evidence about the other.

The five red flags that expose fake AI EAs

Perfect long backtests. Five to ten years of flawless “AI-optimised” results. If the AI did not exist for those years, the backtest is not AI. Period.

No live record. No public wallet, no vault, no exchange-verified account. Only screenshots — which can be cropped from a cherry-picked window.

Hidden recovery systems. “Our AI intelligently scales positions for optimal recovery” is usually a martingale system doubling down on losses, described in softer words.

Annualised short windows. A good fortnight dressed as a triple-digit APR. Always ask: over what window, in what market, net of what fees?

No losing months shown. Every real trading record has losing months. A record without them is a curated exhibit, not a record.

How to validate a real AI trading system, then?

Forward testing. Since backtesting is impossible for genuine LLM-driven bots, the only honest validation is: demo for at least 30 days, then small live capital, with every trade logged and every cost counted. If a vendor refuses forward testing and offers only a backtest, that refusal is the answer.

The broader lesson applies to every trading claim, AI or not: recompute from raw data, beat the baselines, demand the trial count, check the folds. A claim that cannot survive those checks is marketing, whatever technology word is printed on it.

BuildIT Index applies that standard to any prediction file: recompute accuracy, beat baselines, check folds, count trials, return a verdict with an exit code.

If a vendor refuses forward testing and offers only a backtest, that refusal is the answer.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past results do not predict future returns.

title: NestJS 12.2: Why validationError.target Is Now undefined
description:
A NestJS app upgrades from @nestjs/core 12.1 to 12.2 — npm i @nestjs/core@latest @nestjs/common@latest, nothing else touched. The test suite stays green. In production, an audit log that has recorded every failed signup for months — the field that failed, the message, and the full payload the user actually submitted — starts writing submittedPayload: undefined on every single entry. No exception, no crash, no warning in the logs. The validation itself still works exactly as before: bad input still gets rejected with a 400. Only the forensic trail disappeared.

This is written against @nestjs/core 12.2.0 (verified 2026-10-20 via npm view @nestjs/core dist-tags and the official v12.2.0 release notes; 12.0.0 shipped 2026-08-27, and the 11.x line remains on the legacy npm tag at 11.2.7). The change described here — validationError.target defaulting to false — is listed by name in that release's "new defaults and behaviour changes" section, not inferred from a diff. It applies to the class-validator-based ValidationPipe only; it does not touch the newer StandardSchemaValidationPipe covered in an earlier episode of this series.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain exactly what target, value, and property each mean on a class-validator ValidationError, and which of them NestJS's own built-in exceptionFactory actually uses
  • State precisely why @nestjs/core 12.2 changed validationError.target's default to false, in the maintainers' own words
  • Fix a custom exceptionFactory that silently breaks on the upgrade, without just disabling the new default
  • Restore the pre-12.2 behavior deliberately, globally or per pipe, when you genuinely need it
  • Place this change correctly on the request lifecycle's pipes stage, and rule out the two other places it could be confused for a bug

Who this is for

You've registered a ValidationPipe — global or scoped — against class-validator DTOs at least once, and ideally you've written or read a custom exceptionFactory. If you haven't read this series' NestJS request lifecycle episode, it maps exactly where a pipe runs relative to guards, interceptors, and filters — useful background, but this article stands on its own.

Table of contents

  • The problem: an exceptionFactory that used to work
  • The mental model: target, value, and property are three different things
  • Stage 1: why 12.2 changed the default
  • Stage 2: fixing the broken exceptionFactory
  • Stage 3: restoring the old behavior on purpose
  • Stage 4: the quieter 12.2 changes riding along
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

The problem: an exceptionFactory that used to work

Here's the pipe registration behind the audit log in the intro, unchanged across the upgrade:

// main.ts
app.useGlobalPipes(
  new ValidationPipe({
    exceptionFactory: (errors) => {
      const first = errors[0];
      auditLog.record({
        field: first.property,
        message: Object.values(first.constraints ?? {})[0],
        // this line is what broke — quietly
        submittedPayload: first.target,
      });
      return new BadRequestException(errors);
    },
  }),
);

Before 12.2, first.target was the whole object class-validator had just validated — the full DTO instance built from the request body, every field included, whether it passed or failed. That made it an easy, if slightly lazy, way to log "here's exactly what the user sent" next to the one field that failed. After 12.2, with nothing else in the application touched, first.target is undefined. submittedPayload: undefined is syntactically valid, so nothing throws — the audit log entry is just worse than it was.

The mental model: target, value, and property are three different things

The mental model: a class-validator ValidationError is a small record for one failing property, and it can carry up to four separate pieces of information about that failure — and only one of them changed in 12.2:

  1. property — the name of the field that failed, e.g. "email". Always present. Unaffected by this change.
  2. constraints — a map of rule name to human-readable message, e.g. { isEmail: "email must be an email" }. Always present. Unaffected.
  3. value — the actual value that was submitted for that one field, e.g. "not-an-email". This is scoped to the failing property alone. Unaffected by the 12.2 change.
  4. target — not the field's value, but the entire object being validated, with every property, whether it passed or failed. This is the one @nestjs/core 12.2 now suppresses by default.

That distinction is the whole article: value tells you what was wrong with the one field that failed; target repeats the complete request body on every single error in the array. A DTO with three failing fields used to produce three ValidationError objects, each one carrying a full copy of the same object. NestJS's own source comment on the change states the reasoning plainly: "the target of an error is the whole object it was found in, so an exception factory that sends the errors would repeat that object." Repeating it isn't just noisy — it's also how a request body with a password field, a token, or any other sensitive value ends up duplicated into every validation error a naive exceptionFactory forwards to a client or a log.

Stage 1: why 12.2 changed the default

Before @nestjs/core 12.2, ValidationPipe didn't configure validationError for you at all — it passed your validatorOptions straight through to class-validator's validate(), and class-validator's own long-standing default includes target. Since 12.2, ValidationPipe.transform() builds that option itself, and your own setting — if you have one — wins:

// @nestjs/common's ValidationPipe, from 12.2.0 onward (simplified)
const errors = await validate(object, {
  ...this.validatorOptions,
  validationError: {
    target: false, // the new default
    ...this.validatorOptions.validationError, // your setting, if any, overrides it
  },
});

Key concept: this is a default you can always override, not a removed feature. If you never touch validationError, you now get target: false. If you explicitly configure validationError: { target: true } on your ValidationPipe, that object sits on top of the spread above and wins, on every version from 12.2 onward.

Stage 2: fixing the broken exceptionFactory

The honest fix usually isn't restoring target — it's noticing that target was the wrong tool for the job. The audit log wanted "what did the user submit," and that's exactly what value already gives you, scoped to the field that actually failed, with no risk of dragging unrelated fields (passwords, tokens) along for the ride:

app.useGlobalPipes(
  new ValidationPipe({
    exceptionFactory: (errors) => {
      const first = errors[0];
      auditLog.record({
        field: first.property,
        message: Object.values(first.constraints ?? {})[0],
        submittedValue: first.value, // scoped to this field — works on every 12.x
      });
      return new BadRequestException(errors);
    },
  }),
);

Key concept: value was never touched by the 12.2 change, on any version. If your exceptionFactory only needs to know what the failing field contained, switching from target to value fixes the bug today and keeps working on whatever the default does next.

If you genuinely need the whole object — reconstructing the full attempted request for a support ticket, say — read on.

Stage 3: restoring the old behavior on purpose

When the full object really is the requirement, say so explicitly instead of relying on an implicit default that already changed once:

app.useGlobalPipes(
  new ValidationPipe({
    validationError: { target: true }, // explicit — survives future default changes
    exceptionFactory: (errors) => {
      const first = errors[0];
      auditLog.record({
        field: first.property,
        message: Object.values(first.constraints ?? {})[0],
        submittedPayload: first.target, // present again, on purpose
      });
      return new BadRequestException(errors);
    },
  }),
);

Key concept: this is scoped to wherever you construct that particular ValidationPipe. A global pipe with validationError: { target: true } restores the old behavior app-wide; a route-scoped @UsePipes(new ValidationPipe({ validationError: { target: true } })) restores it only there, leaving the global pipe on the new, leaner default.

Stage 4: the quieter 12.2 changes riding along

target isn't the only ValidationPipe default the same release changed. Two more are worth knowing before you assume a 400 you're suddenly seeing is a bug in your code:

new ValidationPipe({
  // New in 12.2 — caps how long the combined message string can get.
  // Past this, extra messages are replaced with one "omitted" entry.
  maxErrorMessagesLength: 1_000_000, // this is already the default
});

The other: sending an array or a bare primitive where a validated class is expected now gets a 400 instead of silently passing an unvalidated value through. If a route's DTO is CreateUserDto and the body arrives as [1, 2, 3] or the string "oops", 12.2 rejects it at the pipe instead of letting it reach the handler shaped nothing like the DTO. Both changes ship in the same release and share the same spirit as the target default: stop assuming more than class-validator was actually asked to check.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • The built-in exceptionFactory was never affected. @nestjs/common's own default error formatter — the one ValidationPipe uses when you don't pass your own — only ever reads property and constraints to build its message array. If you've never written a custom exceptionFactory, this entire change is invisible to you.
  • Nested DTOs still carry children, not a nested target. A failure on address.zip produces a ValidationError with children: [{ property: 'address', children: [{ property: 'zip', ... }] }]; target suppression applies at every level of that tree the same way.
  • This is specific to class-validator's ValidationPipe. StandardSchemaValidationPipe (covered in an earlier episode) validates with a Standard Schema library's own ~standard.validate(), which has no target concept at all — nothing here applies to it.
  • A pipe constructed before you set the option doesn't retroactively pick it up. validationError is read once, in the constructor's resolved options — set it when you call new ValidationPipe({ ... }), not after.
  • Logging error.target to the console for local debugging is still fine. The change doesn't remove the data from the validation run itself — it only removes it from what reaches exceptionFactory by default. console.log statements inside your own services that build the object from the raw request body are unaffected either way.

Best practices

  • Default to error.value, not error.target, in any exceptionFactory you write. It's scoped to the one field that failed, was never affected by this change, and can't accidentally leak an unrelated sensitive field.
  • Never echo the full submitted payload back to the client in an error response, with or without this default — a validation error is exactly the response an attacker can use to fingerprint which fields your DTO expects.
  • Set validationError: { target: true } explicitly, and only, where you've confirmed you need it — an internal audit log or a support tool, never a response body a client sees.
  • Audit every custom exceptionFactory in the codebase before upgrading to 12.2, the same way you'd check for any other breaking default: grep -rn "exceptionFactory" src/ and look for .target on the result.
  • Pin the behavior you rely on, not the default. The target: true default existed for years and still changed once; writing it explicitly means the next default change can't surprise you again.

FAQ

Does this break validation itself, or just error reporting?

Just error reporting. Validation still runs exactly the same way, and the HTTP response code and the fact that invalid requests get rejected are unchanged. Only what a custom exceptionFactory can read off each error changed.

Will my app silently stop validating anything after this upgrade?

No. target being undefined has nothing to do with whether validation ran — it only affects what one specific field on the resulting error object contains.

Does error.value ever get suppressed the same way?

No. The 12.2 release notes and the pipe's own source only change the target default; value — the specific field's submitted value — is untouched on every 12.x version.

Is this in the official migration guide, or just the release notes?

It's listed in the v12.2.0 release notes under that release's own "new defaults and behaviour changes," since it's a minor-version default change rather than a major-version breaking change requiring a migration guide entry.

Can I set validationError.target per route instead of globally?

Yes — pass the option to a ValidationPipe instance scoped with @UsePipes() on a controller or a single handler, the same way any other ValidationPipe option can be scoped.

Cheat sheet

Task Code Notes
Check if your code is affected grep -rn "exceptionFactory" src/ Only custom factories reading .target are affected
Fix forward (recommended) Read error.value instead of error.target Scoped to the failing field; unaffected by this change
Restore old behavior, globally new ValidationPipe({ validationError: { target: true } }) Register once, in main.ts
Restore old behavior, one route @UsePipes(new ValidationPipe({ validationError: { target: true } })) Leaves the global pipe on the new default
Confirm the built-in factory is unaffected Don't pass exceptionFactory at all The default formatter only ever used property + constraints
target vs value target = whole submitted object · value = one field's value Only target changed its default in 12.2
Other 12.2 ValidationPipe defaults maxErrorMessagesLength (new), array/primitive → 400 (new) Same release, same "stop assuming more than was checked" theme 
// main.ts — explicit, upgrade-proof configuration
app.useGlobalPipes(
  new ValidationPipe({
    // Only set this if something genuinely needs the whole submitted object.
    // validationError: { target: true },
    exceptionFactory: (errors) => {
      const first = errors[0];
      return new BadRequestException({
        field: first.property,
        message: Object.values(first.constraints ?? {})[0],
        submittedValue: first.value, // not first.target
      });
    },
  }),
);

Key takeaways

  • @nestjs/core 12.2 defaults validationError.target to false on ValidationPipe — a deliberate change, documented in the v12.2.0 release notes, not a regression.
  • target is the entire validated object; value is the one failing field's value. Only target's default changed; value never moves.
  • NestJS's own built-in exceptionFactory never read target — this only bites a hand-written one, which is exactly why it fails silently instead of at boot.
  • Fix forward by reading error.value, or restore the old behavior deliberately with validationError: { target: true }, globally or per route.
  • This lives entirely in the pipes stage of the request lifecycle — guards, interceptors, and filters are untouched by it.

Ending

The bug in the intro was never really about NestJS removing something — it was about a default quietly doing less work on an app's behalf than it used to, in a way that compiles, ships, and only shows up as a slightly worse log entry months later. That's the same shape of risk every implicit default carries: it's free until the day it changes, and the fix is almost always the same one — write down what you actually need (error.value, not "whatever target happens to contain") instead of leaning on whatever the framework currently hands you.

Has a NestJS minor-version upgrade ever changed behavior you didn't know you were depending on? Drop it in the comments.
