title: Reproducing, disclosing, and fixing the libheif vulnerability with Hacktron and the maintainers
description:
In August 2026, Hacktron reported what looked like a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Next.js image optimization. Their investigation found that the vulnerable code was not in Next.js itself, but upstream in libheif, an AVIF image decoder used by Next.js, ImageMagick, WordPress, sharp, and much of the web.

Shortly after Hacktron notified us, we worked with them to reproduce the RCE against a current Next.js build and disclose it to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. We then deployed a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and started working with the maintainers on a fix.

The dependency chain

Next.js image optimization lets applications resize and optimize images through the <Image> component (next/image). For AVIF images, the image-processing dependency chain is as follows:

  • <Image> invokes /_next/image,

  • /_next/image calls sharp

  • sharp calls libvips

  • libvips uses libheif to decode the image

That meant the vulnerable code was not in Next.js, but it was still reachable through Next.js image optimization. A malicious AVIF image sent to the image optimization endpoint would invoke libheif through sharp and libvips.

As such, one obvious mitigation was to disable AVIF optimization in Next.js. Malicious AVIF images would then stop at the image optimization endpoint instead of being passed through sharp and libvips to libheif. The exploit would not propagate upstream.

However, only mitigating Next.js, without an upstream fix, posed a disclosure problem.

Disclosing the vulnerability and coordinating the upstream fix

After we worked with Hacktron to successfully reproduce the issue, we rolled out a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and reached out to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif to disclose the vulnerability and begin working on a fix.

Here is the timeline:

  • August 11-12: Hacktron reported the issue to Vercel; Hacktron and Vercel reproduced the RCE with a working proof of concept.

  • August 13: Vercel applied a platform mitigation through its Image Optimization Service.

  • August 19: The Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and began coordination across sharp, libvips, and libheif.

  • August 24: Next.js informed its security partners.

  • August 25: Next.js published a security release that disabled AVIF optimization.

The Vercel security team contacted the maintainers of sharp and libvips by email, and opened coordination with libheif through a GitHub Security Advisory. Hacktron had also submitted vulnerability and exploit details to libheif. On August 19, the Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and aligned on the path forward across sharp, libvips, and libheif. The libheif maintainer continued remediation through Hacktron’s GitHub Security Advisory.

On August 24, Next.js informed its security partners of the libheif vulnerability and its impact on Next.js (partner notifications are a routine part of Next.js’ security release process).

On August 25, six days after the August 19 meeting, the libheif maintainer released v1.23.2, which remediated the RCE.

Vercel and Next.js mitigations

Securing Vercel and its customers was straightforward: all Next.js image optimization requests on Vercel go through a central Image Optimization Service. Therefore, we disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in that central service. Any incoming AVIF images were not passed to libheif for decoding and RCE was not possible on Vercel.

Protecting self-hosted applications required a Next.js release. On August 25, Next.js published a security release that had originally been planned to address a separate issue. After coordinating an upstream fix, we bundled the AVIF mitigation into that release and shipped it a day earlier than planned. The release disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in Next.js; given that the patched libheif release was still propagating downstream, this was the most timely option. We also published a security advisory to communicate the issue’s severity.

Our commitment to making the web more secure

The volume of OSS vulnerabilities discovered continues to increase, and the numbers are overwhelming:

  • In 2026, the CVE program has published more than 35,000 CVEs.

  • Private vulnerability reports on GitHub grew from 500 per week in January to 3,000 per week in May.

  • GitHub also reported 1,560 reviewed advisories in May 2026, the highest monthly volume in the advisory database’s history.

As LLMs accelerate vulnerability research, we expect to see more upstream vulnerabilities like the libheif RCE surface across the OSS ecosystem. There have been a higher number of Next.js security releases in recent months, and we expect that trend to continue as we mitigate new vulnerabilities that both we and the research community uncover.

We are committed to proactively finding vulnerabilities before attackers, responsibly disclosing everything we find, and collaborating with researchers and maintainers on fixes.

Credit

Thanks to Hacktron for responsibly disclosing the AVIF vulnerability, working with us to reproduce the issue, and coordinating with the upstream maintainers through remediation.

We also want to thank the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. Their work on the upstream fix made coordinated remediation possible across the image processing dependency chain.

We work with a talented set of researchers to secure Next.js and other open source frameworks through Vercel's Open Source Bug Bounty. Anyone interested in contributing to the security of eligible frameworks is encouraged to participate there.

References

  • Next.js August 2026 security release

  • Upstream libheif advisory

  • Vercel security release changelog

  • Just a rumor of a bug is enough to find a security exploit

title: What Happens When Your Team Adds Azure to AWS and GCP
description:
It usually starts with one reason.

A new enterprise client requires Azure. Or the company gets acquired by a Microsoft shop. Or the data team wants Azure OpenAI Service. Or legal requires a specific Azure region for data residency. Whatever the trigger — it's never "let's add Azure because we wanted three clouds."

But the result is always the same: you now have a third cloud, and the operational complexity doesn't just add — it multiplies.

I've seen this happen at multiple companies — teams that had a reasonably clean AWS + GCP setup suddenly find themselves managing three credential models, three consoles, three billing dashboards, and databases spread across providers that have no awareness of each other.

Here's what actually happens, and what you can do about it.

The Azure Credential Model Is Different

AWS uses IAM roles and access keys. GCP uses service accounts with JSON key files. Azure uses something called service principals — identities registered in Azure Active Directory (now called Microsoft Entra ID) with roles assigned at the subscription or resource group level.

If your team already has muscle memory for aws configure and GCP service account JSON files, Azure will feel unfamiliar at first.

A minimal setup for database management looks like this:

# Create a service principal with Reader role on a resource group
az ad sp create-for-rbac \
  --name "1datacloud-reader" \
  --role Reader \
  --scopes /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<rg-name>

This gives you a clientId, clientSecret, tenantId, and subscriptionId — four values you'll need to authenticate against Azure APIs.

Compared to a GCP service account (one JSON file) or AWS IAM (access key + secret), it's more moving parts. And it's completely separate from the mental model your team already uses for the other two clouds.

The Azure Database Landscape

Before you can manage Azure databases, you need to know what Azure calls them.

Azure SQL Database — Microsoft's managed relational service. Similar to AWS RDS for SQL Server, but Azure-native. Good performance, tight Active Directory integration, T-SQL.

Azure Database for PostgreSQL — Flexible Server — Managed PostgreSQL. This is the one that matters most if your team is already on PostgreSQL on RDS or Cloud SQL. Flexible Server is the current generation (the old Single Server was deprecated in 2025).

Azure Database for MySQL — Flexible Server — Same generation shift. If you're migrating from RDS MySQL, this is the target.

Azure Cosmos DB — A globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database. Supports multiple APIs: SQL (document), MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table. If your team uses DynamoDB on AWS, Cosmos DB is the Azure equivalent in terms of positioning.

Azure SQL Managed Instance — A deployment option that gives you a full SQL Server engine (including SQL Server Agent, cross-database queries, linked servers) rather than the PaaS-scoped Azure SQL Database. Useful for migrations from on-prem SQL Server.

Azure Synapse Analytics — Azure's answer to BigQuery and Redshift. Distributed SQL at scale, integrated with Azure Data Lake.

That's six different service types, each with its own API surface, pricing model, and management interface — before you've written a single query.

What Breaks First

1. Nobody knows what's running

With AWS and GCP, at least your team knows which console to open. With Azure added, there are now resources in Resource Manager that the DevOps team created, resources in the old Classic deployment model that nobody touches, and resources across multiple subscriptions that were set up at different times for different reasons.

Azure has resource groups as an organizing layer, but if your team didn't enforce naming conventions and resource group discipline from day one, you'll spend a lot of time clicking around the portal to understand what exists.

2. Schema awareness disappears

When a new database gets spun up on Azure — say, a PostgreSQL Flexible Server for a new product — it often happens outside the normal provisioning process. Someone clicks through the portal. It doesn't get added to the inventory spreadsheet. The team doesn't know its schema until someone asks "where does this data live?"

This is the same problem that exists on AWS and GCP, but Azure makes it worse because it's the new unknown. Your AWS and GCP databases are at least in the mental model of the team. The Azure ones aren't yet.

3. Credential rotation gets complicated

Now you have three sets of credentials to rotate on a schedule:

  • AWS: IAM access keys (or instance profiles if you're doing this right)
  • GCP: service account JSON keys
  • Azure: service principal secrets (which have an expiry date and will stop working when they expire)

Azure service principal secrets expire — the default is 1 year. If you don't have rotation automation in place, you'll get a failed deployment or a broken integration six months from now, traced back to an expired credential nobody remembered to rotate.

4. Monitoring is fragmented

Azure Monitor is its own ecosystem, completely separate from CloudWatch and Cloud Monitoring (GCP). Each provider has its own metrics, its own alerting primitives, its own cost of learning. Teams that didn't have unified observability before will feel this most acutely.

The Multi-Cloud Inventory Problem, Revisited

If you were managing AWS and GCP and already felt like you lacked a complete picture of your databases, adding Azure makes that problem structurally harder.

Every provider has native tooling that shows you that provider's resources only. No cross-cloud view exists unless you build it or use a tool designed for this.

With three providers, the options are:

  • Three console tabs always open
  • A custom aggregation script that you maintain (and that breaks when any provider updates its API)
  • A unified tool that connects to all three and maintains the view automatically

What Good Multi-Cloud Database Management Looks Like

The goal isn't to eliminate Azure's complexity — that complexity reflects real engineering tradeoffs. The goal is to not re-solve the same "where are my databases?" problem every time you add a provider.

A good multi-cloud database management setup:

  1. Connects to each provider once using that provider's native credential model (IAM for AWS, service account for GCP, service principal for Azure)
  2. Auto-discovers all instances across accounts, subscriptions, and projects — without you clicking through consoles
  3. Maintains schema metadata so you know not just that an instance exists, but what tables and columns are inside it
  4. Requires no agents or infrastructure changes — purely API-based, read-only by default

This is what 1DataCloud does. AWS, GCP, and MongoDB Atlas are fully supported today. Azure support is in active development — SQL Database, Cosmos DB, and PostgreSQL Flexible Server are coming. If you want to be notified when Azure goes live, sign up for the free tier and you'll get early access.

Practical Steps for Your Next 30 Days

If your team just added Azure (or is about to), here's a pragmatic checklist to avoid the worst outcomes:

Week 1 — Inventory what exists:

  • List all Azure subscriptions your organization has
  • List all resource groups with "sql", "db", "postgres", "mysql", "cosmos" in the name
  • For each: note engine type, region, size, who owns it

Week 2 — Tighten credential hygiene:

  • Create service principals with Reader role (not Contributor) for monitoring/inventory access
  • Set explicit expiry reminders for all Azure service principal secrets
  • Document where the credentials are stored (Key Vault, secrets manager, etc.)

Week 3 — Connect schema metadata:

  • For each database with real production data: connect and document the top-level schema (database names, table count)
  • Flag any instances that are publicly accessible (Azure portal → Networking → Public access)

Week 4 — Unify the view:

  • Either add Azure to your existing inventory tool, or start using a tool that handles all three providers together
  • Set a calendar reminder to verify the inventory is still accurate in 90 days

The Bigger Picture

Adding Azure isn't a mistake — for many teams it's the right call. Enterprise integrations, Microsoft ecosystem dependencies, data residency requirements, specific services like Azure OpenAI — these are real reasons.

But adding a cloud provider without a plan for managing what you deploy there is how you end up with databases nobody tracks, credentials that expire in production, and schema documentation that's six months out of date.

The teams that handle multi-cloud well aren't the ones that avoided complexity. They're the ones that decided early on how they were going to keep a complete picture of what they have.

Is your team running Azure alongside AWS or GCP? What's been the hardest part to manage? I'm particularly curious about organizations that migrated workloads TO Azure from another cloud — the other direction is less common.

Abd Alrhman Alloush is the Founder & CEO of 1DataCloud — a unified dashboard for managing and querying databases across AWS, GCP, and MongoDB Atlas, with Azure support in development.

title: Cloud Architecture Review: Step-by-Step Planning Guide
description:
Meta title: Cloud Architecture Review Planning Guide: Step-by-Step

Meta description: Follow this cloud architecture review planning guide to assess security, reliability, performance, and cost, prioritize risks, and implement improvements.

A cloud architecture review is most useful when it answers a practical question: Can this workload meet its business, security, performance, reliability, and cost requirements with its current design?

The review should do more than identify technical weaknesses. It should help teams decide which risks matter, what needs to change, who is responsible, and how improvements will be verified.

This cloud architecture review planning guide explains how to prepare for a review, assess the architecture, prioritize findings, and turn recommendations into an implementation plan. It applies to new cloud projects, existing workloads, cloud migrations, and hybrid or multi-cloud environments.

The need for structured reviews is becoming more significant as cloud-native infrastructure expands. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation’s January 2026 report, based on its 2025 annual survey, found that 82% of organizations using containers run Kubernetes in production. That adoption makes architecture decisions about resilience, security, observability, and operational complexity increasingly important.

1. What Is a Cloud Architecture Review?

A cloud architecture review is a structured assessment of a cloud-based workload’s design, infrastructure, security controls, operational practices, and ability to meet defined business requirements.

It examines how components work together, where dependencies create risk, and whether the architecture is suitable for its expected workload and operating conditions.

A review typically covers six areas:

  • Operational excellence: Deployment processes, monitoring, incident response, and operational ownership.
  • Security: Identity and access management, data protection, network security, and compliance.
  • Reliability: Availability, fault tolerance, backup, disaster recovery, and recovery objectives.
  • Performance: Resource sizing, latency, throughput, and scalability.
  • Cost optimization: Resource utilization, unnecessary spending, and cost visibility.
  • Sustainability: Efficient resource consumption and environmental impact.

These areas align closely with the major pillars of the AWS and Google Cloud Well-Architected Frameworks. Google Cloud also includes sustainability as a core pillar.

A review is not necessarily a formal audit or a complete redesign. Its purpose is to identify meaningful gaps and guide improvements based on the workload’s actual requirements. AWS describes the review as a lightweight, blame-free conversation rather than an audit, with the outcome being prioritized actions that improve the workload. docs.aws.amazon

2. Cloud Architecture Review Planning Steps

2.1 Define the review’s scope and objectives

Before examining infrastructure, establish what the review needs to accomplish.

A review of an entire cloud environment is different from an assessment of a single application, database, or migration project. An unclear scope can lead to broad discussions without actionable conclusions.

Document:

  • The workload, application, or cloud environment being reviewed.
  • Cloud providers, regions, and deployment models involved.
  • Business-critical services and their dependencies.
  • Known technical issues or recent incidents.
  • Regulatory, security, and data residency requirements.
  • The decisions the review is expected to inform.

Define specific objectives wherever possible. For example:

  • Determine whether the application can meet its availability target.
  • Assess whether the current design supports expected traffic growth.
  • Identify security gaps before production deployment.
  • Investigate rising infrastructure costs.
  • Validate whether a proposed migration architecture is operationally viable.

Practical output: A short review charter defining scope, objectives, stakeholders, and expected deliverables.

2.2 Gather architecture documentation and operational evidence

A review should be based on the architecture that actually exists, not only on its original design documents.

Collect the information needed to understand both the intended and deployed environment.

Information required What to examine
Architecture diagrams Application components, network boundaries, data flows, and dependencies
Infrastructure inventory Compute, storage, databases, containers, and managed services
Configuration Network rules, identity permissions, encryption, and resource settings
Operational records Incidents, alerts, deployment history, and maintenance procedures
Performance data Utilization, latency, throughput, and capacity trends
Financial data Cloud bills, cost allocation, resource utilization, and spending patterns
Recovery documentation Backup schedules, recovery objectives, and disaster recovery procedures

Use infrastructure-as-code repositories, cloud configuration exports, monitoring dashboards, and deployment records to validate documentation.

One important distinction: an architecture diagram shows intended relationships, while configuration and operational evidence show what is actually running. Both are necessary.

2.3 Assess the architecture against relevant frameworks

Once the evidence is available, evaluate the workload across the review areas.

You do not need to create an entirely new assessment methodology. Established frameworks provide structured questions and recommendations.

  • AWS Well-Architected Framework: Evaluates workloads across six pillars and encourages constructive reviews focused on architectural decisions and improvement opportunities.
  • Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework: Provides guidance on operational excellence, security, reliability, performance, cost, and sustainability.
  • Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework: Organizes recommendations around reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence, and performance efficiency.

These frameworks offer useful starting points, but their recommendations should be interpreted in the context of the workload rather than applied mechanically.

For each review area, ask questions such as:

Review area Questions to investigate
Security Are identities, permissions, secrets, and network access appropriately controlled?
Reliability What happens if a region, service, or database becomes unavailable?
Performance Can the architecture handle peak demand without excessive latency?
Operations Can teams detect, diagnose, and resolve incidents effectively?
Cost Are resources appropriately sized and continuously monitored?
Sustainability Can resource consumption be reduced without compromising requirements?

Record evidence alongside each finding. A statement such as “security needs improvement” is too vague to guide implementation. Specify the affected component, the observed weakness, and its potential impact.

2.4 Identify architectural risks and prioritize findings

Not every issue deserves immediate attention. A review becomes valuable when it distinguishes urgent risks from longer-term optimization opportunities.

Classify findings according to:

  • Business impact: What happens if the issue remains unresolved?
  • Likelihood: How probable is the failure or unwanted outcome?
  • Exposure: Is the issue affecting production, sensitive data, or critical services?
  • Implementation effort: How difficult and expensive is remediation?
  • Dependencies: Must another technical or organizational change happen first?

A practical prioritization model is:

Priority When to use it Example findings
Critical Immediate attention Exposed credentials, missing recovery capability for a critical workload, or a serious production security weakness
High Near-term remediation Capacity limitations, inadequate monitoring, or a single point of failure affecting important services
Medium Planned improvement Inefficient resource allocation, inconsistent configuration, or manual operational processes
Low Backlog or ongoing optimization Documentation gaps, minor configuration improvements, or opportunities to simplify architecture

This classification is an internal planning aid, not a universal risk-scoring standard. A medium technical issue may become critical if it affects a regulated workload or a business-critical service.

2.5 Develop the implementation plan

The next stage of the cloud architecture review implementation process is converting findings into specific, owned actions.

For each recommendation, document:

  • The issue and supporting evidence.
  • The proposed architectural or operational change.
  • Expected business and technical benefits.
  • Implementation effort and dependencies.
  • Responsible owner and target date.
  • Risks introduced by the change.
  • Validation criteria and success measures.

For example:

Finding Recommended action Validation
Database is a single point of failure Introduce an appropriate high-availability configuration Test failover and recovery behavior
Excessive permissions Apply least-privilege access policies Review permissions and test required workflows
Unpredictable cloud spending Introduce tagging, budgets, and resource monitoring Compare cost trends and allocation coverage
Limited incident visibility Improve logging, metrics, and alerting Run an incident simulation and verify detection

Avoid turning every recommendation into a separate project. Group related changes into workstreams, such as security remediation, reliability improvements, cost optimization, and operational maturity.

2.6 Validate changes and schedule follow-up reviews

Implementation is not complete when a configuration change is deployed. Teams need to verify that the change solved the original problem without creating another one.

Validation may involve:

  • Load and performance testing.
  • Failover and disaster recovery exercises.
  • Security configuration reviews.
  • Access-control testing.
  • Cost comparisons before and after optimization.
  • Monitoring and alert verification.

Microsoft’s Azure Well-Architected Review guidance recommends integrating assessment recommendations into workload planning, prioritizing implementation, and monitoring improvements. It also suggests recurring reviews for existing workloads, with a cadence such as every four months as one example.

AWS similarly recommends reviewing architectures at important lifecycle milestones, including early design, before launch, and after significant architectural changes. docs.aws.amazon

The result should be a continuous improvement cycle rather than a document that becomes outdated after the review meeting.

3. Cloud Architecture Review Examples

The review process varies depending on the workload. The following examples show how teams can apply the planning steps to common situations.

3.1 Reviewing a cloud migration

A company plans to move an existing business application from on-premises infrastructure to a public cloud.

The review should examine:

  • Application dependencies and compatibility.
  • Network connectivity between environments.
  • Data migration and integrity requirements.
  • Identity management and access controls.
  • Availability and disaster recovery requirements.
  • Expected cloud operating costs.

Possible outcome: The team identifies a database dependency that requires modernization before migration. Instead of moving the entire application immediately, it creates a phased migration plan with database validation as an initial milestone.

3.2 Reviewing a growing SaaS application

A SaaS platform experiences increasing user traffic and occasional performance degradation.

The review examines application scaling, database capacity, caching, load balancing, observability, and infrastructure costs.

Possible outcome: The team identifies database connection limits and inefficient resource allocation as the main constraints. It prioritizes connection management and capacity adjustments before considering a more extensive architecture redesign.

3.3 Reviewing a security-sensitive workload

A financial services application stores sensitive customer information and operates across multiple cloud services.

The review focuses on identity permissions, encryption, network segmentation, audit logging, data residency, backup protection, and incident response.

Possible outcome: The team identifies excessive service permissions and insufficient recovery testing. It prioritizes least-privilege access and a documented recovery exercise before introducing lower-risk performance optimizations.

These examples demonstrate an important principle: the review should be driven by workload requirements, not by a predetermined preference for particular cloud services or architectural patterns.

4. Who Should Participate in a Cloud Architecture Review?

A useful review requires input from the people who design, operate, secure, and depend on the workload.

Role Primary responsibility
Cloud architect Evaluates architecture, integration, and design decisions
DevOps/platform engineer Reviews deployment, automation, and infrastructure operations
Security specialist Assesses security controls, access, and compliance
Site reliability engineer Examines availability, monitoring, and recovery
FinOps or finance representative Evaluates spending, allocation, and cost controls
Product or business owner Confirms business priorities and acceptable risk

Not every review requires a large committee. A focused assessment of a small application may only need an architect, engineer, security representative, and workload owner.

For broader technology planning, teams can also explore the Heloix technology and business ecosystem as a starting point for understanding the wider business context in which technology decisions are made.

5. Frequently Asked Questions

5.1 How often should a cloud architecture review be conducted?

Review architecture during initial design, before major production launches, and after significant changes such as migrations, infrastructure redesigns, or security incidents. Existing workloads should also undergo periodic reviews. The appropriate frequency depends on workload criticality, change rate, and risk. docs.aws.amazon

5.2 What is the difference between a cloud architecture review and a cloud security assessment?

A cloud architecture review evaluates the overall design, including security, reliability, performance, cost, and operations. A cloud security assessment focuses specifically on security risks, vulnerabilities, identity controls, data protection, and compliance. Security is therefore one important part of a broader architecture review.

5.3 Which framework should teams use for a cloud architecture review?

Choose a framework based on the cloud environment and review objectives. AWS Well-Architected, Google Cloud Well-Architected, and Microsoft Azure Well-Architected are useful starting points. Multi-cloud teams can combine relevant principles while maintaining a consistent internal assessment process.

5.4 What documents are needed before a cloud architecture review?

Prepare architecture diagrams, infrastructure inventories, configuration records, access policies, monitoring data, incident reports, cloud cost information, and backup and disaster recovery documentation. The exact evidence required depends on the workload.

5.5 What should a cloud architecture review report include?

A useful report should include the review scope, architecture overview, assessment findings, supporting evidence, risk classifications, recommended actions, responsible owners, target dates, and validation criteria. It should also identify unresolved risks and decisions requiring management approval.

6. Conclusion

A well-planned cloud architecture review gives teams a structured way to understand whether their infrastructure supports current business requirements and future growth.

The process begins with clear objectives and reliable evidence, moves through framework-based assessment and risk prioritization, and ends with an implementation plan that has measurable outcomes and accountable owners.

Most importantly, a review should not be treated as a one-time approval exercise. Cloud workloads change as applications evolve, traffic increases, security requirements shift, and services are introduced or retired. Regular reviews help teams identify architectural weaknesses before they become expensive operational problems.

title: WeLM-Image: A Unified Image Generation Model towards Visual Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2611.07392v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present \textbf{WeLM-Image}, a unified image foundation model that integrates multimodal understanding into text-to-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and multi-reference synthesis. Designed for single-GPU deployment in WeChat's large-scale consumer applications, the model processes text, reference images, and target latents as one interleaved sequence. A Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone combines shared attention with independent understanding and generation parameters to limit optimization interference. Equipping each path with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) modules provides sparse capacity, with 31.7B stored parameters and approximately 5.4B generation parameters activated per target latent token. A generation-oriented data engine combines a knowledge-grounded visual vocabulary with large-scale visual clustering to balance semantic coverage and editing tasks, while training-time evaluation guides iterative data refinement. Bilingual annotations and verified editing supervision support progressive training up to native 1.5K resolution. We optimize generation and editing separately with rubric- and checklist-based rewards, then consolidate the specialized policies through noise-aware on-policy distillation. In the reported overall comparisons, the 1536-resolution model ranks first among the evaluated open-source models on PRISM-Bench, Qwen-Image-Bench, and UnicBench. MeanFlow-based few-step distillation yields WeLM-Image-Turbo, which generates a $1024\times1024$ image in 4.98\,s on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU using eight guidance-free steps.

title: Don't lazy-load the image people see first (Web HIG tip #15)
description:
Open your home page or a product page on a phone, on a slow connection. The headline and buttons show up, but the big hero image stays blank for a beat longer than everything else. Look at its markup and you'll often find loading="lazy", added to every <img> on the site by a template, a plugin, or a well-meant "lazy-load all images" change.

Web HIG tip #15 (Quick #84): Lazy-load below-the-fold media; never lazy-load the LCP candidate.

Why it matters

Lazy loading is a trade: the browser waits to fetch an image until it's close to the viewport. That's a win for images further down the page, and a loss for the one people see first:

  • Images far below the fold that nobody scrolls to never download, which saves data and leaves bandwidth for what's on screen
  • A lazy image's fetch can't start until the browser has laid out the page and worked out where the image sits, so a lazy hero image starts downloading later than it would have otherwise
  • The LCP candidate is usually the biggest image or text block in the first view. When it arrives late, the page looks unfinished, and Largest Contentful Paint gets worse
  • If the image URL only exists in JavaScript, for example a data-src that a script swaps in, the browser can't find it in the HTML at all until that script runs

The full HIG covers the image side of this in §2.1, Document Fundamentals, under responsive images: lazy-load non-critical images where appropriate, and avoid lazy-loading the LCP candidate and other immediately needed content. The LCP candidate SHOULD be discoverable early and MAY use fetchpriority="high" when appropriate. Quick #84 is Quick-only guidance, with no rule ID of its own. It pairs with Quick #83, which asks every image to declare its dimensions or aspect ratio, and with Quick #82's LCP target of 2.5 s or less.

The rule of thumb

Ask: will this image be on screen before anyone scrolls? If yes, don't lazy-load it.

This page looks fine on a fast laptop, but the hero waits for layout and for a script before it even starts downloading:

<!-- Hero: the LCP candidate, hidden from the browser until JS runs -->
<img class="lazy" data-src="https://example.com/img/hero.jpg" alt="">

<!-- Further down the page -->
<img src="https://example.com/img/team.jpg" alt="The team at the spring meetup">

Load the hero early and lazy-load what's further down:

<!-- Hero: a real src in the HTML, high priority, not lazy -->
<img src="https://example.com/img/hero.jpg"
     width="1200" height="600"
     fetchpriority="high"
     alt="A reader using the app on a phone">

<!-- Further down the page -->
<img src="https://example.com/img/team.jpg"
     width="800" height="533"
     loading="lazy"
     alt="The team at the spring meetup">

The page looks the same. The difference is when each image starts downloading.

Do this instead

  • Leave loading off the LCP image (the default is eager), give it a real src or srcset in the HTML, and consider fetchpriority="high". Browsers that don't support fetchpriority ignore it
  • Add loading="lazy" to images and iframes that sit well below the first view: long article bodies, comment sections, footers, embedded maps and video players
  • For a <video> further down the page, use preload="none" (or "metadata") and a poster image. loading="lazy" on <video> is newly specified but only some browsers support it so far, so treat it as a bonus, not the fix
  • In a carousel or gallery, load the first slide eagerly and lazy-load the rest
  • Give lazy images width and height (or a CSS aspect-ratio) so the page doesn't jump when they arrive
  • If the hero is a CSS background-image, the browser only finds it after the CSS has loaded. Use an <img> instead, or add <link rel="preload" as="image"> for it
  • The LCP element can be different on a phone and on a desktop. Check both layouts before you decide which images stay eager

Quick check for your app

Open your main pages (say, example.com and example.com/products) at a phone width and at a desktop width. In the browser's developer tools, find the LCP element in a performance recording, then check its markup: no loading="lazy", and a URL that's in the HTML rather than added by a script. Scroll down and watch the network panel: images further down should only start loading as you get near them. A tool can flag a lazy-loaded LCP image in a single lab run, but only checking the real LCP element on your own pages, at the widths people use, shows which image needs to load first.

The Web HIG is an open set of guidelines for how the web should behave, not a component library. Design systems define how it looks. The Web HIG defines how it behaves.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/frozonfreak/webhig/discussions/32
  • Hashnode: https://thewebhig.hashnode.dev/dont-lazy-load-the-image-people-see-first-web-hig-tip-15
  • Dev.to: https://dev.to/frozonfreak/dont-lazy-load-the-image-people-see-first-web-hig-tip-15-38k3
  • Bluesky: https://bsky.app/profile/sastha.bsky.social/post/3mzmmnfubak2p

title: Rethinking Data Selection: The Importance of Coverage over Difficulty in LLM Fine-Tuning
description:
arXiv:2611.07323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Selecting high-quality training data can reduce computation cost for LLM fine-tuning. Prior work on data selection developed a variety of difficulty-based scores, motivated by the intuition that harder examples are more informative. While effective for smaller classification models, we find that such methods often fail to outperform random selection for LLM fine-tuning. Our analysis reveals that random selection performs better because it is more representative of the underlying input space---i.e., has better coverage. To validate the importance of coverage, we implement a simple clustering-based selection method which selects data that is more representative of the underlying input distribution. On a set of diverse single-domain tasks, this method yields performance at or above that of random selection. On the diverse, multi-domain T\"{u}lu 3 mixture, where random sampling no longer guarantees a balanced subset, our method outperforms all methods. Overall, our results indicate that prioritizing coverage over difficulty leads to more effective data selection for LLM fine-tuning.

title: O$^2$PD: Overlap-Gated On-Policy Distillation on Reliable Prefix
description:
arXiv:2611.07731v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) supplies dense token-level supervision by aligning a student to the teacher's next-token distribution on its own generated rollouts. Existing works mostly implement top-$k$ OPD, applying reverse Kullback-Leibler ($\RKL$) divergence between the teacher's and the student's renormalized distributions over teacher top-$k$ support. However, the teacher scores student-generated rollouts that are inherently off-policy for itself, leaving the reliability of its next-token guidance unclear. Restricting the divergence to the teacher top-$k$ support also discards the remaining mass outside that support. These gaps leave two questions implicit: 1) which tokens to align, and 2) how to align those tokens. To answer these questions, we propose Overlap-gated On-Policy Distillation (O$^{2}$PD). As for 1), we quantitatively analyze the reliability of teacher supervision and find that alignment on the student's trajectory prefix is more reliable than alignment on the full context. Therefore, our O$^{2}$PD is applied only to the 20\% prefix tokens of each student rollout. As for 2), we theoretically characterize two problems of top-$k$ OPD: the \emph{Teacher-support Uncovering} and the \emph{Dominant-Mode Mismatch}. Based on these analyses, we propose two support strategies: the \emph{Reset Support} strategy attaches a reset atom to every token, pooling mass outside the teacher top-$k$, and the \emph{Support Convergence} strategy converges the support to the already aligned intersection. Our O$^{2}$PD employs the designed overlap-gated $\alpha$-divergence to interpolate between mode-covering and mode-seeking for per-token alignment, where the overlap is used as a gate to switch the support and adaptively modulate $\alpha$.

title: Cloud Security Posture Assessment: Finding Misconfigurations Before Attackers Do
description:
Understand cloud security posture assessment, how misconfigurations arise, and how to keep posture healthy over time.

Many cloud breaches do not involve clever exploits. They involve something left open: a storage container with public access, a database with no password, an overly generous role. A cloud security posture assessment is designed to find exactly this kind of problem and show how your settings compare with good practice.

What “posture” means

Security posture is the overall state of your defenses at a point in time. In the cloud, much of it comes down to configuration: how services are set up, who can access them, what is logged, and how data is protected. Because configuration can be changed in minutes, posture can shift just as quickly.

Why misconfigurations are so common

Several factors combine:

Speed. Teams deploy fast and may skip reviews.
Complexity. Providers offer hundreds of services, each with its own settings.
Defaults. Some defaults favor convenience over security.
Decentralization. Many teams have the ability to create resources.
Human error. A single checkbox can change exposure.
Temporary changes. A rule opened for testing never gets closed.

None of these indicate negligence. They are natural side effects of flexible platforms.

What a posture assessment looks at

The review compares live settings with benchmarks and internal standards. Typical areas:

Storage and database access permissions.
Encryption settings and key policies.
Network rules and public exposure.
Identity configuration and privileged roles.
Logging and monitoring status.
Patch and image status for compute.
Account-level settings, such as organization policies.

Benchmarks and standards

Assessors rarely invent criteria from scratch. Common references include CIS Benchmarks, provider best-practice guides, and regulatory control sets. Using recognized baselines makes results defensible and comparable across time.

Point-in-time versus continuous

A one-time assessment reveals the current state. It is valuable for establishing a baseline and finding serious issues quickly. But posture drifts. Continuous monitoring uses automated tools to check configurations repeatedly and alert when something changes.

A balanced approach often works best:

Run a full assessment to understand the baseline.
Fix high-risk issues.
Implement continuous checks for the most important rules.
Repeat deeper reviews periodically.

Reading the results sensibly

Posture tools can produce large numbers of findings. Not all are equally important. Prioritize using these questions:

Is the resource exposed to the internet?
Does it hold sensitive data?
Could the issue be combined with others to form an attack path?
Is there a simple fix?

A medium-severity issue on a public system holding customer data may deserve attention before a high-severity issue on an isolated sandbox.

Attack paths and combined risk

Individual misconfigurations are one thing. Combined, they can be more serious. For example, a publicly reachable virtual machine, running with an overly privileged role, in a network that can reach a sensitive database, forms a path. Good assessments highlight these chains instead of listing issues in isolation.

Reducing drift through guardrails

Prevention beats cleanup. Practical guardrails include:

Organization-level policies that block risky settings, such as public storage.
Infrastructure-as-code with automated checks before deployment.
Approved templates for common services.
Limited permissions to create or change high-risk resources.
Alerts when critical settings change.

Ownership

Findings stall when no one owns them. Tag resources with owners and teams so that issues can be routed quickly. Track fix times and share simple metrics, such as the number of open high-risk findings and average time to resolve.

Exceptions

Sometimes a risky setting is intentional, such as a public website bucket. Record these as documented exceptions with an owner, a reason, and a review date. This keeps reports clean and prevents repeated debate.

Measuring progress

Useful posture metrics include:

Percentage of resources compliant with the baseline.
Number of public-facing resources, and how many are justified.
Share of accounts with logging enabled.
Time to remediate critical findings.
Count of recurring issues, which signals a process gap.

Closing perspective

Posture is not a score to chase for its own sake. It is a practical view of how exposed you are right now. Regular assessment, sensible guardrails, and clear ownership keep small configuration errors from becoming large incidents.

title: Berrypicking still beats the single answer for search, even in the world of AI
description:
In 1989 Marcia Bates showed that people search by gathering, shifting, and revising as they go. Her ideas explain what AI still misses and what is still relevant from research done 47 years ago.

Much of what product teams are learning about artificial intelligence search, an information scientist wrote down before the web existed. Marcia J. Bates spent her career at UCLA studying how people search and her 1989 paper, The Design of Browsing and Berrypicking Techniques for the Online Search Interface, argued that real searches wander, change shape, and collect value in pieces.

She aimed it at library databases that assumed one query and one best result; AI turns this on its head.

The chat box makes the same assumption, only faster.

Bates is still relevant in the age of artificial intelligence, arguably more than ever. Large language models changed what a system can answer but they didn’t change how a person goes about asking, which still means starting vague, learning while reading, and changing direction midway.

I had the pleasure of meeting her at the IA Summit in Chicago in 2018 — she most politely asked if we could have lunch and I brought a few others. It became a great conversation where I still learned concepts that I apply today, and they are incredibility relevant to what we’re doing with AI back when my company was only applying machine learning.

I’ve used her concepts to frame search and artificial intelligence summarization in legal tech software. Anyone designing search or summarization should be thanking her.

Five of her ideas hold up, each tied to a decision you’re making now.

Support Evolving Searches

Bates built the berrypicking paper as an attack on the classic retrieval model, which treats a search as one query matched once against a database to produce one best set of results.

Her objection fit in one line: “typical search queries are not static, but rather evolve.”

People begin with one reference or a narrow slice of a bigger topic, read what comes back, and let each find reshape the question.

She named the bit-at-a-time collecting after picking huckleberries scattered through a forest. Marti Hearst later made the model a standard reference for interface designers in Models of the Information Seeking Process.

The need itself shifts as the person learns, and that separates berrypicking from search methods that look similar from the outside:

  • Known-item lookup. You know what you want, such as a fact or a file, and one query finds it or doesn’t. You can accomplish this usually in a single term.
  • Iterative refinement. You rephrase to hit a fixed target, the job Gerard Salton’s relevance feedback automated. The words change, but the need doesn’t.
  • Browsing. You glimpse, sample, and pick within one place. Bates treated it as one move inside a larger search, not the same thing.
  • Berrypicking. The need evolves, and the answer arrives in pieces from many sources rather than as one final set.

That last difference is why a successful search is so hard to define:

  • The classic model let researchers score one result set for precision and recall.
  • A berrypicking search has no single set to score, and Bates called knowing when to stop one of the fundamental problems of search strategy.
  • A thumbs-up on one chat answer measures the last berry, not the picking.

Sometimes what matters most is what isn’t found.

An empty patch tells a berrypicker something, whether it’s no earlier case on point, no conflicting clause in a contract, or no research on a question. A system that always produces a confident answer hides that signal, because it never lets the absence show.

The chat window rewards the user who already knows exactly what they want, which is the user who needs the least help.

Language models repeat the classic assumption.

In LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation, a 2025 study of more than 200,000 simulated conversations, every top model tested did worse when a task arrived in pieces, with an average drop of 39 percent across six tasks. The models guessed early and didn’t recover.

The design job is to support the person whose question is still forming. Show what has shifted since the first prompt, and let people revise early assumptions without starting over.

Bates even sketched the tooling in 1989: a temporary store where searchers could flag findings as they went.

Expose Search Tactics

A decade earlier, Bates published Information Search Tactics, which won her field’s best paper award the following year. A tactic, in her definition, is a move made to further a search.

She named 29 of them in four groups, including these:

  • Check. Compare the current search against the original request.
  • Pinpoint. Narrow to the most precise terms.
  • Parallel. Broaden with synonyms and related terms.
  • Trace. Mine what you’ve already found for new terms.
  • Record. Track the trails you followed and the ones you meant to revisit.

Her premise was that naming a tactic makes it easier to reach for. Reference librarians used many of these moves without names, which left beginners no easy way to learn them.

The web repeated the problem.

People had to learn to search like Google, stripping questions down to two or three keywords and adding quotes or a minus sign when results went wrong. They’re doing the same with chat now, working out by trial and error which phrasings get a useful answer.

A blank prompt box ships with none of them, so people improvise.

Nielsen Norman Group documented one improvisation in Accordion Editing and Apple Picking: Early Generative-AI User Behaviors.

Users copied part of an earlier response into a new prompt by hand, because the interface gave them no other way to point at it. It’s berrypicking with copy and paste as the only tool.

That’s a search behavior, because chat and search are closer than they look. In both, a person puts a need into words, the system matches it against stored information, and the person judges what comes back and tries again.

Retrieval-augmented assistants run a search behind the scenes and summarize the results, so the biggest difference is the shape of the reply: a list of links in one, a paragraph in the other.

Everything Bates learned about searching also applies to chatting in spades.

Missing controls matter most for experts, who read a bad result set as a clue rather than a verdict. They tighten, exclude, widen, and re-sort in small passes until the set matches what they meant, and they decide when it’s done. In Investigating the Querying and Browsing Behavior of Advanced Search Engine Users, Ryen White and Dan Morris found marked differences between people who used query operators and those who didn’t, in how they queried, clicked, browsed, and fared.

Faceted search is the interface version of those moves.

In a study reported in Hearst’s chapter Integrating Navigation with Search, 91 percent of 32 art history students preferred a faceted image interface to a plain one, even though it was slower.

A chat reply hides exactly those facets and filters, when most of Bates’s 29 tactics could become buttons nobody has to phrase.

Choose the Automation Level

In 1990, Bates asked the question every agent team is now answering under deadline: Where Should the Person Stop and the Information Search Interface Start? Her answer was a scale.

  • At level 0 the system offers no help.
  • Level 1 explains possible moves
  • Level 2 carries them out on command
  • Level 3 watches the search and suggests next steps
  • Level 4 runs the whole search, either explaining its choices or just returning results.

In product terms, the levels are easy to spot:

  • Level 1 is a help panel that lists search operators
  • Level 2 is a filter that runs when you click it
  • Level 3 is a “did you mean” correction or a suggested follow-up question.
  • Level 4 is the research agent that disappears for several minutes and comes back with a finished report.

She argued that research had fixated on level 4, while many searchers wanted the speed of automation and control of strategy. Jakob Nielsen called generative tools AI: First New UI Paradigm in 60 Years in 2023, describing a reversal of the locus of control in which users state the outcome and the computer picks the method.

Bates had mapped that reversal decades earlier, and put most of the useful ground short of the far edge.

Most AI products jump straight to level 4 and call the result an agent. That’s not right.

Skipping the middle skips the levels where trust gets built. People defer to the machine even when it’s wrong, which I document in the Automation Bias entry on UX Guidelines, a reference site I maintain. Pick the level per task, and let people move the dial.

Fix the Content Layers

Her 2002 paper The Cascade of Interactions in the Digital Library Interface lists the layers under any search experience: infrastructure, content, metadata, indexing, and the search engine, with the interface and the person at the top.

Decisions at each layer ripple upward, and good interface design can’t rescue weak choices further down.

Swap “digital library” for “retrieval-augmented assistant” and little changes. Above the model is the chat window your team keeps polishing. Below it are document stores, chunking rules, and permissions someone set up years ago for another purpose. Good metadata is what sets context for the model, telling it what a document is, who it applies to, and whether it’s still current. The demo runs on 20 clean documents, and production meets a decade of duplicate policies and unlabeled drafts.

A semantic layer goes a step further.

It defines what terms mean and how they relate, so “customer,” “client,” and “account holder” resolve to the same thing, and the model works from shared definitions instead of guessing.

Bates proposed something close to this in 1986: a cluster thesaurus that gathered every variant of a concept under one entry, so a search on any term could reach them all.

A fluent answer built on a bad index is still a bad answer.

Gartner predicted in Lack of AI-Ready Data Puts AI Projects at Risk, a February 2025 release, that through 2026 organizations will abandon 60 percent of artificial intelligence projects that lack ready data. That’s a forecast, but the same release reported that 63 percent of organizations lacked the right data practices or weren’t sure they had them.

This is the uncomfortable part for designers. The quality of a search result, or of a generative answer, is the user experience, and no polish around it makes up for a weak one.

Your influence has to reach down the cascade into labeling and indexing, and Bates argued the specialists for every layer had to design together.

Design for Browsing

Bates returned to browsing in 2007 with What Is Browsing — Really? A Model Drawing From Behavioural Science Research. Browsing, she argued, is a series of glimpses: you take in a field of view, select something, examine it, then keep it or drop it, and repeat.

She traced it to the exploratory behavior animals use to find food and shelter, which is why nobody needs to be taught how.

Similarly, I’ve been through 65 airports, partly to see how cities tell people where things are. The good terminals let you take in the whole hall at once, spot the sign you need, and change course without asking anyone. That’s the opposite of waiting at the information desk for one answer.

Generative search is quietly moving people toward the desk.

Pew Research Center tracked the browsing of 900 U.S. adults in March 2025 and reported that Google Users Are Less Likely to Click on Links When an AI Summary Appears in the Results. Visits with a summary led to a result click 8 percent of the time, against 15 percent without one, and sessions ended outright on 26 percent of summary pages versus 16 percent elsewhere.

Some of that is the summary doing its job. Some is a person who never glimpsed the source they didn’t know to ask for. So keep the scene around the answer, with neighboring sources and related threads, so the glimpse still has somewhere to land.

Conclusion

None of these ideas came from studying artificial intelligence. They came from watching people in libraries, card catalogs, and early online databases, and that’s exactly why they hold.

The technology between a person and the information keeps changing. The person mostly doesn’t.

Read together, Bates’s five ideas make one argument. Search is something people do over time, using moves they choose, at a level of control they want, on top of layers they never see. Their eyes do more of the work than any query. Every piece of that is a design decision, and most current products make it by default.

She also left what I’d call the berrypicking test for any assistant on your roadmap. Does it expect the question to change, or punish the change? Does it name the moves, or make people invent them? Can the person choose how much the system decides, and does anyone own the content underneath? Is there still room to look around?

The single answer is impressive. It’s also the classic model she spent decades arguing against, with better grammar. The teams that do best with this generation of tools will design for the berrypicker, the searcher whose question hasn’t settled yet.

Action Items

  • Show question history. Keep a visible summary of what the person has asked so far, and let them edit an earlier question without starting a new chat.
  • Add refine controls. Put buttons for narrowing, excluding, broadening, and checking against the original request next to every answer, so nobody has to phrase those moves as a prompt.
  • Set automation per task. Decide which tasks the system only suggests on and which it can run by itself, and give people a setting to change that.
  • Fix metadata first. Tag documents with type, owner, date, and status, define shared terms in a semantic layer, and show the sources behind every answer, including when nothing relevant was found.

Resources

  • Information and the Information Professions, Selected Works of Marcia J. Bates, volume I (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Her essays on what information is, including “Fundamental Forms of Information” and “The Invisible Substrate of Information Science.”
  • Information Searching Theory and Practice, Selected Works, volume II (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Collects “Information Search Tactics” and “What Is Browsing — Really?” along with her work on search techniques.
  • Information Users and Information System Design, Selected Works, volume III (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Includes the berrypicking paper and her 1990 paper on how much a search system should do for the person.
  • Understanding Information Retrieval Systems: Management, Types, and Standards (Auerbach Publications, 2012). A reference volume she edited on how retrieval systems are managed, the main types, and the standards behind them.
  • Marcia J. Bates Home Page. Her UCLA page, with free copies of many of the papers cited in this piece.

Berrypicking still beats the single answer for search, even in the world of AI was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.22

We've released version 6.22 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

For more information, see Chat transcripts and chat history.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

For more information, see Campaign management.

title: Building an Embeddable, Zero-Dependency DevTools Panel for React & Next.js
description:
Debugging network requests and browser storage during development often forces you to constantly switch context—toggling native browser DevTools, sifting through noisy logs, or relying on heavy browser extensions that don't travel with your repository.

To solve this, I built React Dev Companion: an embeddable, zero-dependency developer tools panel designed specifically for React and Next.js applications.

🎯 Why React Dev Companion?

Most debugging tools fall into two categories:

  1. Full-blown Browser Extensions: Requires every developer on the team (and QA testers) to install specific extensions.
  2. Heavy External Panels: Adds bloated dependencies to your project bundle.

React Dev Companion runs directly inside your application during development, giving you instant client-side inspection without bundle bloat.

Key Capabilities

  • ⚡ Real-Time Network Interception: Intercepts outgoing window.fetch calls, logging HTTP methods, target URLs, and response statuses live.
  • 💾 Multi-Store Storage Inspector: View, inject, and delete keys across localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies from a single unified panel.
  • 📦 Zero Dependencies: Ultra-lightweight footprint engineered for zero impact on application performance.
  • 🌐 Framework-Agnostic Support: Works out of the box with React SPAs (Vite, CRA) and Next.js (App Router / Client Components).

🛠️ How It Works Under the Hood

1. Non-Invasive window.fetch Interception

Rather than requiring wrapper functions around your HTTP client, React Dev Companion safely wraps window.fetch upon mounting. It streams response metrics to an isolated state container without altering original request promises or application flow:

const originalFetch = window.fetch;

window.fetch = async (...args) => {
  const [resource, config] = args;
  const method = config?.method || 'GET';
  const url = typeof resource === 'string' ? resource : resource.url;

  try {
    const response = await originalFetch(...args);
    notifyDevTools({ url, method, status: response.status });
    return response;
  } catch (error) {
    notifyDevTools({ url, method, status: 500 });
    throw error;
  }
};

2. Unified Storage Management

Browser APIs handle storage types inconsistently (localStorage vs string parsing for document.cookie). The Storage Inspector abstracts key management, enabling instant state invalidations and seamless standard cookie expiration handling.

🚀 Quick Start Guide

Installation

Install via npm, yarn, or pnpm:

npm install react-dev-companion

Next.js (App Router) Integration

Load the companion component conditionally in your root layout so it only runs during development:

'use client';

import { DevCompanion } from 'react-dev-companion';

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        {children}
        {process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development' && <DevCompanion />}
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

Vite / React SPA Integration 

import React from 'react';
import { DevCompanion } from 'react-dev-companion';

export function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <MainContent />
      {import.meta.env.DEV && <DevCompanion position="bottom-right" />}
    </div>
  );
}

🏭 Built with Modern Engineering Standards

React Dev Companion was built from day one following open-source best practices:

  • CI/CD Pipeline: Fully automated via GitHub Actions (Node 22).
  • Strict Commit Standards: Conventional Commits enforced via Husky & Commitlint.
  • Type Safety: Written 100% in TypeScript with strict mode enabled.

💬 Let's Build Together! (Call to Action)

This project is fully open-source and ready for community feedback!

  • ⭐ Star the repo on GitHub: Kickz1nn/react-dev-companion
  • 🤝 Want to contribute? Check out our CONTRIBUTING.md and grab a good first issue!
  • 💬 Feedback: What features or tabs would you like to see next? (e.g., React Query status inspector, Console log collector, or Performance timers?) Let me know in the comments below!

title: Automated Video-to-QA Pipeline: End-to-End Question Generation and Verification Using Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.07755v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The exponential growth of educational and informational video content on platforms like YouTube presents a challenge for efficient knowledge retrieval and assessment. This paper proposes an end-to-end automated pipeline for extracting structured summaries and generating high-fidelity Question-Answer (QA) pairs from video streams. The framework integrates a cascade of state-of-the-art models: audio extraction is handled via FFmpeg, followed by automatic speech recognition (ASR) using Whisper (A library in Python) to generate accurate transcripts. Due to the token constraints of Large Language Models (LLMs), transcripts are segmented and summarized using Facebook's BART. A key innovation of this work is a Self-Verification and Fine-Tuning Loop. We utilize meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8BInstruct to generate candidate QA pairs from transcript chunks, which are then fed back into the model to rigorously assess their relevance and importance. Only verified, high-quality pairs are retained to construct a synthetic dataset. This dataset is subsequently used to fine-tune the Llama model using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), resulting in a specialized model capable of generating domain-aligned assessment questions. This approach demonstrates a scalable method for creating self-improving educational tools without the need for manual data annotation. The proposed model can be downloaded from Kaggle with all the codes from GitHub.

title: JWT Authentication Explained: A Token You Can Verify Without a Database
description:
Ayesha manages a small online shop. Each morning she checks yesterday's paid orders and marks parcels ready to ship. Her dashboard talks to a small Node.js API, and every request has to answer one question first: is this really Ayesha? The usual answer is a session stored on the server, but that means a database lookup on every request, and it breaks when the API grows a second server. A JSON Web Token, a JWT, answers the same question without the lookup. The token carries who the caller is, and the server checks the token's signature instead of asking a database. This post builds that check with nothing but Node.js built-in crypto, and shows where it breaks if you use it carelessly.

What I would check before using it

My judgement, from building small APIs for years, is this: a JWT is the right call when several services need to check who is calling without sharing a database, and the wrong call when you need to cancel access instantly. The first check is revocation. A token stays valid until it expires, and there is no way to cancel it early, so a stolen token keeps working until its expiry time passes. The honest fix is a short lifetime, fifteen minutes to an hour. If you need a logout button that works everywhere at once, use sessions, because a JWT on its own cannot do that.

The second check is what goes inside the token. The payload is only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone who gets the token can read it. Keep it to an id, a name, and a role, and never put a password or anything else sensitive in there.

The third check is the secret. The whole scheme rests on one secret string that signs every token. It must be long and random, it must live in an environment variable rather than in the code, and every service that verifies tokens must use the same one. A short secret such as "secret" can be guessed offline by trying candidates against a captured token.

The fourth check is size. The token travels on every request, usually in an Authorization header, so keep the payload small.

The verdict, in short: use a JWT for short-lived access tokens in this shop API, with a one-hour expiry and a payload holding only an id, a name, and a role. Do not use it where instant logout matters.

A worked example that is not a toy

The worked example is the shop's login flow. Ayesha logs in, the API issues a token that says she is user-1042, a shop manager, valid for one hour. Her dashboard then sends that token with every request, and the API verifies it before returning any orders. The token has three parts, separated by dots: a header saying which algorithm signed it, a payload with the claims, and a signature. Both functions below were run with Node.js built-in crypto only, no packages installed.

const crypto = require('node:crypto');

const SECRET = 'demo-secret-do-not-use-in-production';

function base64url(input) {
  return Buffer.from(input).toString('base64url');
}

function signToken(payload, secret) {
  const header = { alg: 'HS256', typ: 'JWT' };
  const encodedHeader = base64url(JSON.stringify(header));
  const encodedPayload = base64url(JSON.stringify(payload));
  const data = encodedHeader + '.' + encodedPayload;
  const signature = crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(data).digest('base64url');
  return data + '.' + signature;
}

function verifyToken(token, secret) {
  const parts = token.split('.');
  if (parts.length !== 3) throw new Error('malformed token: expected three parts');
  const [encodedHeader, encodedPayload, signature] = parts;
  const data = encodedHeader + '.' + encodedPayload;
  const expected = crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(data).digest();
  const actual = Buffer.from(signature, 'base64url');
  if (actual.length !== expected.length || !crypto.timingSafeEqual(actual, expected)) {
    throw new Error('invalid signature');
  }
  const payload = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(encodedPayload, 'base64url').toString('utf8'));
  if (payload.exp && Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) > payload.exp) {
    throw new Error('token expired');
  }
  return payload;
}

Issuing the token at login and verifying it on the next request gave this real output:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJ1c2VyLTEwNDIiLCJuYW1lIjoiQXllc2hhIiwicm9sZSI6InNob3AtbWFuYWdlciIsImlhdCI6MTc5MzkxMjI4NywiZXhwIjoxNzkzOTE1ODg3fQ.BW4Av2PoMZMpM82x_3g4F7VNWODbf4u2z9t4hZig8f8
Decoded payload: {"sub":"user-1042","name":"Ayesha","role":"shop-manager","iat":1793912287,"exp":1793915887}
Access granted for Ayesha (role: shop-manager)

The header and payload are readable once decoded; the signature is what makes the token trustworthy. The iat and exp numbers are seconds since 1 January 1970, from the real run, so yours will differ.

Now the part the tidy tutorials skip: something goes wrong. A curious user copies the token, changes one character in the payload, and sends the edited token back. The signature was computed over the original payload, so it no longer matches the edited one, and the check refuses it:

Rejected: invalid signature

That is the whole security of the scheme in one line. The signature covers the header and the payload together, so any change to either part breaks it. The same check also catches a token verified with the wrong secret, which fails with the same message, and an expired token, which fails differently:

Rejected: token expired

The fix is already in the function above, and it is a matter of order: verify the signature first, then read the payload, then check the expiry before trusting anything it says. A version of the check that skips the expiry test is worse than useless, because it looks secure while accepting tokens that should be dead. Running the expired token through such a version proved it:

Accepted anyway: {"sub":"user-1042","name":"Ayesha","role":"shop-manager","iat":1793905087,"exp":1793908687}

The token had expired an hour before the check, and the careless verifier let it through. The lesson is that a JWT is not a magic string. It is a signature plus an expiry date, and both have to be checked every time.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

1. Trusting the payload before verifying the signature. The payload is only base64url encoded, so anyone can decode it without the secret. If your code reads the role from the payload without checking the signature, an attacker can set the role to "admin" in their own token. The fix: verify the signature first, then read the payload.

2. Using plain base64 instead of base64url. Node's Buffer.toString('base64') produces +, /, and = padding, which break inside a URL or a header, and encoding the same payload with plain base64 gave a string ending in ==. The fix is to use the base64url encoding for tokens.

3. Skipping the expiry check. A verifier that never looks at exp accepts tokens forever, as the run above showed. The fix is the exp comparison in the function above, run on every request.

4. A weak secret, or a different secret in each service. Verifying the real token with a different secret failed with "invalid signature", which is also what happens when two services drift apart. Worse, a short secret such as "secret" can be guessed offline against a captured token. The fix is one long random secret, at least 32 characters, in an environment variable, shared by every service that verifies tokens.

Where this leaves you

A JWT is a signature check, not encryption. The signature proves nobody changed the token, and the expiry date limits how long a stolen one stays useful. Keep tokens short-lived, keep payloads small and free of secrets, and keep the signing secret long, random, and out of the code. The test is simple. Take the token from the run above, change one character, and watch it get rejected, then check that your own verifier also rejects an expired token. The next step is to move the secret into an environment variable, add a login route that issues the token, and put the verify function in front of the orders route.

Further reading

  • RFC 7519, JSON Web Token (JWT)
  • RFC 8725, JSON Web Token Best Current Practices
  • Node.js crypto documentation

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/jwt-authentication-explained-token-you.html
