title: Who Should Know What? Empirical Information Design for Multi-Agent LLM Economies
description:
arXiv:2611.07667v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The performance of multi-agent LLM systems depends not only on the capabilities of the underlying models but also on information-sharing policies, which govern what information each agent observes and at what level of detail. But does providing AI agents with more detailed information always improve collective outcomes, or can transparency paradoxically degrade efficiency? To investigate this, we introduce empirical information design, an experimental framework that systematically compares disclosure policies across economic markets populated by LLM agents, while holding interaction rules and models fixed. We evaluate ten frontier LLMs in multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining, and double auctions, using ground-truth utilities to decouple identified opportunities from realized outcomes. We find that finer information disclosure yields highly model-dependent results. In trade, revealing exact valuations rather than ordinal preference rankings reduces realized gains for GPT-6 Sol (from 98% to 91% of maximum) yet increases them for Claude Sonnet 5 (from 72% to 86%). In bargaining, exact information leads Grok 4.7 to produce less balanced agreements, whereas Claude Opus 5.5 divides gains symmetrically. In double auctions, full disclosure inflates price demands, triggering market breakdown and lowering welfare for Gemini 3.1 Pro (97% to 78%), Claude Opus 5.5 (94% to 64%), and Grok 4.7 (97% to 62%). Overall, these results suggest that model selection and information design must be co-optimized, as LLMs vary in how their strategic responses to information impact system objectives.

title: Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
description:
Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Web Answer is a managed tool that returns a synthesized, grounded, cited answer to a natural-language question in a single call, so agent builders can attach it to an agent and get back a finished answer grounded in current web sources, without building and maintaining their own search, retrieve, synthesis, and citation pipeline. 

Web Answer builds on Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which launched in June, extending it from "find the web content" to "return the finished answer," a capability customers have been asking for. With Web Answer, your agent sends a question and receives a synthesized cited answer in one tool call. Web Answer works like an agent; it plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has gathered enough evidence to answer. You stay in control of the boundaries, with domain include, deny lists and publish-date filters that scope where it looks. It attaches as a target on an AgentCore Gateway and is called over MCP, authenticated with IAM, with zero data egress. 

Web Answer is available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, with per-tool call pricing. 

To learn more about Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, see Web Answer’s documentation page and Web Answer’s website. For Region availability, see the AWS Region table.

title: FreePath: Neural Mean Free Path for Image Dehazing
description:
arXiv:2611.07398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Single image dehazing requires recovering scene radiance from visual responses that are weakened and veiled by participating media. Existing methods either invert explicit scattering variables, which can be unstable under complex scenes, or learn direct restoration mappings, which often discard the physical organization of haze formation. We present \emph{FreePath}, a neural mean free path framework for image dehazing. Instead of estimating atmospheric parameters, FreePath represents dehazing as feature space path state restoration, inspired by the expected distance a visual response can propagate before interacting with haze. Within a residual encoder and decoder, the Mean Free Path Residual Block learns path and collision fields to guide haze constrained correction, while FreePath State Conservation Integration preserves restored path states during deep feature aggregation. Experiments on paired CDD-11 haze images and real RTTS scenes show that FreePath consistently improves full reference fidelity, no reference perceptual quality, and visual faithfulness over representative dehazing baselines.

title: SteelAgent: LLM-Orchestrated, Physics-Informed Steel Property Prediction with Audited Generalization and Calibrated Uncertainty
description:
arXiv:2611.06953v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Steel property models can perform well on random test splits even when they extrapolate poorly to unfamiliar alloys. SteelAgent couples metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design. We examine how the choice of held-out unit changes the conclusions drawn from SteelBench tensile-strength evaluations. For gradient boosting, pooled out-of-fold $R^2$ fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when steel families were held out. Empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals ranged from 91.0% under random splitting to 37.6% on held-out sources. The effect of physics-derived features depended on the evaluation. They increased gradient-boosting $R^2$ by 0.2534 in a 17-family holdout analysis and decreased it by 0.358 in a separate four-grade laboratory analysis. We report group-level errors and a synthetic regression experiment illustrating how calibration can deteriorate on held-out groups. These results motivate reporting the evaluation population alongside a property estimate or compliance score.

title: MetricTrail: Revisiting the Power of Metric Depth and Local Optimization for Long-Sequence Streaming 3D Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.07555v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present MetricTrail, a streaming system for accurate camera motion estimation and dense reconstruction from long monocular videos. To keep inference efficient over long sequences, we revisit DPVO's sparse local estimator. We find that single-image metric depth substantially improves its trajectory accuracy, without retraining the correspondence network or enlarging the optimization window. Metric predictions initialize patch depths and remain as soft constraints during optimization. We further improve correspondence estimation through learned adapters that augment matching features and recurrent context with frozen DINOv3 representations. The correspondence estimator and adapters are trained on diverse short clips without additional long-sequence training. This modular design also allows the depth provider to be independently upgraded and supports supplied camera intrinsics and calibrated stereo observations without retraining. Under the reported RGB-only protocols, MetricTrail achieves the lowest average trajectory error among evaluated methods on KITTI, Oxford Spires, and VBR. Pairing the estimated poses with single-image depth predictions also produces strong dense reconstruction on indoor and outdoor benchmarks and coherent reconstructions of in-the-wild videos. With supplied intrinsics, the system processes KITTI-02 at 12.70 FPS with 3.21 GB peak GPU memory.

title: The Daily Drawdown Trap: Why One Bad Morning Ends Your Prop Challenge
description:
You can be net profitable for two weeks and still fail a prop challenge. Not because your strategy broke. Because one bad morning breached the daily cap — and the challenge does not care about your two good weeks.

The rule most traders misunderstand

FTMO's daily drawdown limit is 5%, calculated from the highest equity point of the day. That “highest equity point” clause is the trap: intraday peaks count against you. If your account peaks 3% up in the morning and then falls 5% from that peak, you have breached the daily limit even though you are only 2% down on the day. Many traders learn this clause only when it eliminates them.

The math that makes it inevitable at normal risk sizes

Risk 2.5% per trade and two consecutive losses end your challenge. Risk 2% and three losers in a row does it. With typical win rates of 45–55%, losing streaks of two, three, and four are not rare events — they are routine occurrences across any meaningful sample of trades. Data from prop-firm analyses puts daily-drawdown breaches behind roughly 70–79% of all evaluation failures. The challenge is not filtering for bad traders. It is filtering for traders whose position sizing cannot survive their own normal losing streaks.

What passers actually do

They risk 0.5–1% per trade — even when the rules allow two or three times that. At 1% risk, a four-loss streak costs 4% and stays inside the daily cap. At 0.5%, it costs 2%. The difference between passing and failing is rarely strategy quality. It is whether a normal bad morning is survivable.

How to survive it (before you pay)

Backtest against the exact rules — daily cap from intraday peaks, total cap, profit target, minimum days — not just for profit.

Size positions so that your worst normal losing streak (not your average streak, your worst) stays inside the daily cap.

Set a personal daily stop below the firm's cap — stop trading at 3% down, not 5%. The buffer is the difference between a bad day and a failed challenge.

Validate the strategy first: recompute from raw predictions, beat the baselines, check walk-forward folds. A strategy that cannot survive its own rules on paper will not survive them with a fee attached.

The daily drawdown trap is not unfair. It is the product: firms sell evaluations, and the evaluation is designed to filter. Knowing the filter exists — and sizing for it — is the entire game. Most traders pay to discover it. You just read it for free.

BuildIT Index runs that validation mechanically: recompute accuracy, beat baselines, check walk-forward folds, model costs, count trials, return a verdict with an exit code. The same standard applies to prop challenge strategies.

Most traders pay to discover the filter. You just read it for free.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past results do not predict future returns.

title: Evaluating Token Probabilities as Confidence Estimators in Human Behavior Simulations: A Case Study in Luxembourgish Next Like Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.07735v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, their operational validity is typically assessed through accuracy alone, implicitly treating human behavior as deterministic. We argue that on noisy digital trace data, a model's performance depends not only on predicting the correct outcome but on its calibration. We present a case study testing whether the token probabilities of open-weight LLMs can serve as confidence estimates in a Next Like Prediction task: predicting how a user of the Luxembourgish news platform RTL.lu rates a comment, conditioned on their prior interactions. Evaluating Ministral 3 (3B, 8B), we find that, with in-context learning only, the tested models are overconfident and are outperformed on accuracy and calibration by a simple statistical baseline. Accuracy and calibration do not move together: scaling from 3B to 8B improves accuracy while degrading calibration, and longer behavioral histories raise accuracy while confidence declines. Task-specific supervised fine-tuning acts as an effective calibration intervention, reducing Expected Calibration Error from 0.2 to 0.006 while improving accuracy from 0.536 to 0.758. We conclude that confidence estimation should be evaluated alongside accuracy to improve validity when using LLM-based agents.

title: SD-LoRA: Training-Time Structural Distillation into LoRA for Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2611.07063v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Few-shot adaptation of vision-language models must balance two competing goals: learning fine-grained visual distinctions from very limited supervision and preserving the efficiency that makes frozen CLIP-like models attractive for deployment. Existing lightweight adaptation methods, including prompt tuning, LoRA, and cache-based adapters, typically supervise global image embeddings and therefore underuse token-level structure. Conversely, structure-aware methods exploit local evidence but often introduce additional inference-time computation. We propose SD-LoRA, a structural distillation framework that uses token-level graph reasoning only during training and transfers its effects into a lightweight LoRA-adapted CLIP model. During training, a heterogeneous graph teacher models patch-patch, global-local, and visual-text relations over high-resolution ViT tokens. Rather than retaining this graph at test time, SD-LoRA transfers its structural bias into the shared CLIP-LoRA backbone through implicit distillation and Prototype Predictive Alignment, which aligns graph-conditioned representations with support-derived class prototypes. At inference, the graph teacher is discarded; prediction requires only a single CLIP-LoRA forward pass and a cache-based classifier. Across 11 few-shot benchmarks, SD-LoRA improves over a strong CLIP-LoRA baseline by 2.4/1.8/3.0/2.4/2.0 percentage points in the 1/2/4/8/16-shot settings, respectively, without additional graph computation at test time. Results on base-to-novel generalization, cross-dataset transfer, out-of-distribution robustness, and calibration further show that training-time structural supervision improves both accuracy and transfer reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/MR-Sherif/SD-LoRA.git.

title: The Black Friday VPS Illusion: What an 85% Renewal Hike Actually Costs You
description:
Every November, developers rush to grab Black Friday VPS discounts to host their personal projects, Docker containers, databases, and staging environments.

Headline banners shout "Up to 80% OFF!" and "$6.49/month!".

Before you swipe your card and commit to a 24-month or 48-month contract, let's look past the marketing red tags and calculate the real engineering budget.

1. Two Bills for the Exact Same Server

Take Hostinger’s Black Friday lineup as a prime case study. When you browse the landing page, the entry plan (KVM 1) is displayed at $6.49/month. But open the fine print for renewal terms, and the exact same instance jumps to $11.99/month.

Those are two completely different billing phases of a single machine. Here is the breakdown across the tiers based on late-2026 pricing:

Plan Specs Black Friday Promo Rate Standard Renewal Rate Price Hike
KVM 1 1 vCPU / 4GB RAM / 50GB NVMe $6.49 / mo $11.99 / mo +85%
KVM 2 2 vCPU / 8GB RAM / 100GB NVMe $8.99 / mo $14.99 / mo +67%
KVM 4 4 vCPU / 16GB RAM / 200GB NVMe $12.99 / mo $28.99 / mo +123%
KVM 8 8 vCPU / 32GB RAM / 400GB NVMe $25.99 / mo $49.99 / mo +92%

Notice that wide spread: KVM 4 experiences a staggering 123% jump upon renewal. That is more than double the price overnight for the exact same compute instance.

2. "Monthly Average" Isn't What Leaves Your Bank Account

The "$12.99/mo" rate shown on promotional pages is an amortized monthly average. To lock that price in, you must pay for 24 months upfront.

When you look at the four-year lifecycle of hosting a continuous production app, the math looks very different:

Plan First 24 Months (Promo) Next 24 Months (Renewal) 4-Year Total Out-of-Pocket True 4-Year Monthly Avg
KVM 1 ~$155.76 ~$287.76 ~$443.52 $9.24 / mo
KVM 4 ~$311.76 ~$695.76 ~$1,007.52 $20.99 / mo

For KVM 4, the true four-year baseline is $20.99/month — over 60% higher than the promotional number displayed on the sales banner.

3. Four Hidden Hosting Traps to Audit Before Buying

Beyond the renewal rate, discount hosting models rely on several behavioral friction points:

Trap A: The Prepayment Lock-in Risk

If you pay ~$312 upfront for 24 months, but your side-project or startup pivots after 6 months, hosting companies rarely issue prorated refunds for unused multi-year terms. The migration friction alone often forces teams to stay and eat the renewal hike.

Trap B: Powered-Off Instances Incur 100% Cost

Unlike AWS EC2 or DigitalOcean Droplets where shutting down an unreserved instance releases compute, multi-year fixed-term VPS providers charge you whether your Linux instance is booted or powered off. The RAM allocation, disk block, and dedicated IPv4 address remain allocated to your tenant.

Trap C: Backup and Snapshot Add-ons

Automated snapshot backups are frequently treated as paid add-ons rather than defaults. Adding daily snapshots at $2–$5/month can quietly add 20%–50% to an entry-level bill.

Trap D: Traffic Throttling vs Overage Charges

Budget providers often handle bandwidth limits in one of two unpleasant ways:

  1. Hard cutoff or sudden $0.02/GB overage invoices.
  2. Silent throttling down to a virtually unusable 10 Mbps until the billing cycle resets.

4. The Pre-Checkout Verification Checklist

Before you enter your payment details this Black Friday, run this 60-second audit:
[ ] 1. Have you multiplied the renewal monthly rate by 12 or 24 to know Year 3/4 costs?
[ ] 2. Are automatic snapshots and automated backups included, or are they billed separately?
[ ] 3. What happens if your server exceeds its monthly bandwidth allocation?
[ ] 4. Does the provider allow exporting disk images or automated snapshots if you migrate?
[ ] 5. What is the exact refund window (typically 14 to 30 calendar days)?

Summary: How to Choose Wisely

If you are validating a new project with an uncertain lifespan, hourly billing providers (like Vultr, DigitalOcean, or Hetzner Cloud) where you can destroy instances anytime often deliver a lower total risk profile than a 2-year upfront commitment.

If you know your application will run for 3+ years, multi-year plans are genuinely economical — provided you budget for the renewal price from Day 1.

This article is part of our independent hosting benchmark series. You can read the full interactive pricing comparison and live benchmarks across 20+ cloud providers on VPSRankings.

title: Building a Deterministic Market-Data Replay Engine for Backtesting on QuestDB
description:
The first backtest I ever trusted turned out to be a liar. It showed a Sharpe north of 3, a drawdown curve that looked like a staircase going one direction, and fills so clean I should have known. The strategy bought when a signal fired and sold a few seconds later, and in the backtest it always sold at a price that existed only after the decision was made. I had joined my trades to a quote table on timestamp equality, and because my quote snapshots were sampled a hair later than my signal, every single fill borrowed a price from a moment that hadn't happened yet. The future was leaking in through a JOIN clause.

That bug cost me a weekend and a lot of embarrassment, and it taught me the thing that most people building strategy code never internalize: a backtest is a simulation of what you knew at each instant, and the hardest part is not the strategy logic, it's refusing to let the engine know anything it couldn't have known. This post is how I built a replay engine that enforces that discipline — on top of QuestDB, with a Spring Boot harness, using real captured order-book data instead of toy CSVs.

Why timestamp-equality joins lie to you

Market data does not arrive on a clock. A trade prints at 09:31:04.218734, the top-of-book quote that preceded it was set at 09:31:04.102881, and the next quote update lands at 09:31:04.251002. If you want to know the prevailing quote at the moment of the trade, you need the most recent quote at or before the trade's timestamp. Not the closest. Not the next one. The last one that already existed.

A naive JOIN ON trades.ts = quotes.ts almost never matches, so people "fix" it by rounding timestamps to the nearest second or by matching whichever quote sits closest in time, before or after. Rounding destroys ordering inside the second — exactly where equities microstructure lives. Matching the nearest quote regardless of direction quietly lets a quote that printed after the trade attach itself to that trade, so your fill prices are built from information the market hadn't produced yet. Both tricks flatter the equity curve, and you only find out how much when the strategy meets a live spread and the edge isn't there.

The operation I actually want is a temporal, backward-looking join, and in QuestDB it's spelled ASOF JOIN. Given a trade on the left, it reaches back to the latest quote whose timestamp hasn't passed the trade's timestamp — the quote that was standing when the trade printed, never a later one. That single "at or before" rule is the entire point-in-time guarantee, written as a join instead of as a page of defensive application code.

The capture pipeline underneath

Before any replay, you need data you trust. I run a live depth-capture service that ingests top-of-book (mbp-1) and trade events for a nine-name basket — AAPL, MSFT, NVDA, AMZN, TSLA, META, SPY, QQQ, and AMD — straight into QuestDB over the InfluxDB line protocol. The ingestion path writes nothing it didn't receive: no enrichment, no derived columns, no spread or mid computed at write time. It records exactly what came off the wire, with the exchange timestamp kept as the designated timestamp, plus a separate ingestion timestamp so I can measure capture latency afterward without tangling it up with event time.

On a normal session those nine names generate between 28 and 41 million rows, the bulk of it quote churn in SPY and NVDA. The reason I keep ingest_ts as its own column rather than trusting wall-clock-at-read is that it lets me answer a concrete question later: subtracting ts from ingest_ts across a full day, my median capture lag sits around 1.1 ms with a p99 near 6 ms — the socket-read-to-WAL-commit cost, nothing exotic. That number matters because it becomes the floor for the order latency I simulate.

The table that matters looks like this:

CREATE TABLE market_events (
    ts            TIMESTAMP,      -- exchange/event time, designated
    ingest_ts     TIMESTAMP,      -- when our capture wrote it
    symbol        SYMBOL CAPACITY 4096 CACHE,
    event_type    SYMBOL,         -- 'quote' or 'trade'
    bid_px        DOUBLE,
    bid_sz        LONG,
    ask_px        DOUBLE,
    ask_sz        LONG,
    trade_px      DOUBLE,
    trade_sz      LONG,
    seq           LONG            -- exchange sequence number
) TIMESTAMP(ts) PARTITION BY HOUR WAL;

Two choices on that table pay off repeatedly. The first is PARTITION BY HOUR. The 09:30–10:00 open is a different animal from the 12:00 lull — the opening hour alone can hold a quarter of the day's rows — and hour partitions let a replay of just the auction touch a handful of physical chunks instead of dragging the whole day off disk. I didn't take that on faith. On one AAPL session, a single-symbol trade-plus-quote scan over the 09:30–10:30 window ran in 0.6 s against PARTITION BY HOUR versus 2.9 s when I rebuilt the same table as PARTITION BY DAY and forced it to prune inside one giant daily partition. The second choice is carrying seq, the exchange sequence number: when two events land on an identical nanosecond stamp — which happens far more than you'd hope, especially during bursts — seq gives me a total order to break the tie. Determinism dies the instant two same-timestamp events can replay in different orders across two runs.

Partitions older than seven days get converted to QuestDB's Parquet tier (ALTER TABLE market_events CONVERT PARTITION TO PARQUET WHERE ts < dateadd('d', -7, now()), driven on a nightly cron). The trade is real and measurable: on my box a native QuestDB partition for a busy session sits around 2.1 GB, and the Parquet-converted version of the same partition lands near 430 MB — roughly a 5x reduction thanks to columnar compression on the heavily repeated symbol and side data. The cost shows up on first touch: a cold scan of a converted partition runs about 3–4x slower than the native one (the 0.6 s scan above becomes roughly 2.2 s cold, then warms back down once the OS page cache is primed). For replaying history I'll take that trade every day — I'm bounded by correctness, not by milliseconds. You can read more about how I think about storage and ingestion trade-offs in my projects.

Expressing point-in-time correctness in SQL

Here is the query at the heart of the whole engine. I take every trade in a session and attach the top-of-book quote that was prevailing at the instant each trade printed:

SELECT
    t.ts,
    t.symbol,
    t.trade_px,
    t.trade_sz,
    q.bid_px,
    q.ask_px,
    q.bid_sz,
    q.ask_sz,
    (q.ask_px - q.bid_px)                         AS spread,
    (q.bid_px + q.ask_px) / 2.0                   AS mid
FROM (
    SELECT * FROM market_events
    WHERE event_type = 'trade'
      AND symbol = 'AAPL'
      AND ts IN '2026-10-15'
) t
ASOF JOIN (
    SELECT * FROM market_events
    WHERE event_type = 'quote'
      AND symbol = 'AAPL'
      AND ts IN '2026-10-15'
) q;

The ASOF JOIN guarantees q is the newest quote whose ts is <= t.ts, so no future quote can glue itself to a trade. The strategy I'd fooled myself with was a dumb mean-reversion scalp on AAPL: when the last trade printed more than two spreads below the trailing 30-second VWAP, buy one lot, exit after 5 seconds or a half-cent of profit, whichever came first — tested over the 2026-09 to 2026-10 sessions in the capture. Under the old ts = ts equality join (which, because my quote snapshots were stamped a touch later than trades, kept handing the exit the next quote) it showed a Sharpe around 3.1. Re-run with ASOF semantics and a fill model that pays the prevailing ask on entry and bid on exit, the same strategy printed a Sharpe of 0.4. The 3.1 was the equality join leaking the exit quote backward; the 0.4 was the strategy's actual, unglamorous edge. Painful, but honest.

One subtlety is easy to trip over: the join only behaves if both sides are already in timestamp order. QuestDB gets you that for free on a timestamp-partitioned table, and crucially it does not check the ordering — feed it unsorted input and it returns a confidently wrong answer instead of an error. Worse, dropping an ORDER BY into an ASOF subquery can strip the designated-timestamp property off the intermediate result and break the join quietly. So I keep ASOF subqueries to plain WHERE filters and never re-sort inside them.

Streaming a day in event-time order

The SQL gives me correctness within a single joined view, but a replay engine has to do more than answer one query. It has to walk the entire session forward, one event at a time, in the exact order those events occurred, and hand each one to a strategy that is only allowed to see the past. That's the Spring Boot harness.

The core abstraction is an event stream pulled from QuestDB over a cursor instead of being loaded into memory. Forty-odd million rows won't sit comfortably in heap, and — the part that matters more — the moment a full day lives in a List, some well-meaning strategy author will index into it and read ahead. A cursor only moves forward, so the lookahead temptation never even exists. The data arrives one event at a time and is gone once consumed.

@Component
public class MarketEventReplayer {

    private final DataSource questDb;

    public MarketEventReplayer(DataSource questDb) {
        this.questDb = questDb;
    }

    /**
     * Streams every event for a session in strict event-time order.
     * seq is the tiebreaker so two events sharing a nanosecond
     * timestamp always replay in the same order across runs.
     */
    public void replay(LocalDate session, String symbol, EventSink sink) {
        String sql = """
            SELECT ts, event_type, bid_px, ask_px, bid_sz, ask_sz,
                   trade_px, trade_sz, seq
            FROM market_events
            WHERE symbol = ? AND ts IN ?
            ORDER BY ts, seq
            """;

        try (Connection c = questDb.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(sql)) {

            ps.setString(1, symbol);
            ps.setString(2, session.toString());
            ps.setFetchSize(10_000);            // keep the cursor streaming

            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                while (rs.next()) {
                    sink.onEvent(MarketEvent.from(rs));
                }
            }
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new ReplayException("replay failed for " + symbol
                + " on " + session, e);
        }
    }
}

The ORDER BY ts, seq is the determinism contract. Two runs over the same partition produce byte-identical event sequences. The setFetchSize keeps the JDBC driver from trying to haul the whole result set across at once; events trickle through as the strategy consumes them.

The strategy harness that cannot see the future

A strategy, in my framework, is an object that reacts to events and emits orders. The critical design rule is that the harness never passes a strategy anything but the current event and whatever state the strategy has already accumulated from past events. There is no getNextQuote(), no lookahead buffer, no "peek" method anywhere in the interface. The absence is the feature.

public interface Strategy {
    /** Called once per event, in strict event-time order. */
    List<Order> onEvent(MarketEvent event, BookState book);
}

public final class BookState {
    private double bidPx, askPx;
    private long   bidSz, askSz;
    private long   asOfNanos;   // event time of the last update applied

    void applyQuote(MarketEvent e) {
        this.bidPx = e.bidPx();
        this.askPx = e.askPx();
        this.bidSz = e.bidSz();
        this.askSz = e.askSz();
        this.asOfNanos = e.tsNanos();
    }

    public double mid() {
        return (bidPx + askPx) / 2.0;
    }

    public double spreadBps() {
        double m = mid();
        return m == 0 ? 0 : (askPx - bidPx) / m * 10_000.0;
    }

    public long asOfNanos() {
        return asOfNanos;
    }
}

BookState is the only market context a strategy gets, and it only ever reflects quotes that have already been replayed. When a trade event arrives, the book still shows the quote state from before that trade, which is exactly what the strategy would have seen live. The asOfNanos field is my paranoia made visible — if a fill simulator ever tries to use a price whose timestamp is ahead of the current event, I can assert against it and blow up the run rather than quietly bank a fantasy profit.

Deterministic fills, not optimistic ones

The other place backtests lie is the fill model. Assuming you always get filled at the mid, or that your market order executes at the quote you saw rather than the quote that exists when the order actually reaches the book, manufactures returns from nothing. My fill simulator takes the opposite stance: a market buy pays the ask that is prevailing when the order lands, after a configurable latency, and it eats through available size if the order is large.

@Component
public class FillSimulator {

    private final Duration orderLatency;   // decision -> book arrival

    public FillSimulator(ReplayProperties props) {
        this.orderLatency = props.getOrderLatency();  // e.g. 900 microseconds
    }

    public Fill simulate(Order order, BookState bookAtArrival) {
        long arrivalNanos = order.decisionNanos()
            + orderLatency.toNanos();

        // The book passed in is the state as of arrivalNanos, resolved
        // by the engine via ASOF semantics -- never the decision-time book.
        if (bookAtArrival.asOfNanos() > arrivalNanos) {
            throw new LookaheadException(
                "fill used quote from the future: book asOf="
                + bookAtArrival.asOfNanos() + " arrival=" + arrivalNanos);
        }

        double fillPx = switch (order.side()) {
            case BUY  -> bookAtArrival.askPx();
            case SELL -> bookAtArrival.bidPx();
        };

        long available = order.side() == Side.BUY
            ? bookAtArrival.askSz()
            : bookAtArrival.bidSz();

        long filledQty = Math.min(order.qty(), available);
        return new Fill(order.id(), fillPx, filledQty, arrivalNanos);
    }
}

The latency parameter is where a backtest earns or loses its credibility. Set it to zero and you're claiming your order teleports to the exchange, which is a claim no real system can make. I calibrate it against the capture latency I measured earlier — the gap between ingest_ts and ts in the raw table gives me a sober sense of how far behind the live world I actually operate. The LookaheadException is not decoration; it has fired during development and caught a bug where I resolved the arrival-time book with a closest-match instead of an as-of match. That exception has saved me from publishing nonsense twice. The habits here are close cousins of the ones I wrote about in transactional outbox and idempotent consumers — in both worlds, correctness means refusing to let the system act on information it shouldn't have or process the same thing twice.

Wiring it together with Spring configuration

The pieces assemble into a runnable backtest through ordinary Spring wiring. I keep the replay parameters in a typed properties class so a backtest is fully described by its configuration — same config, same data, same result, every time.

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "replay")
public record ReplayProperties(
        LocalDate session,
        List<String> symbols,
        Duration orderLatency,
        boolean strictLookaheadChecks) {
}

@Service
public class BacktestRunner {

    private final MarketEventReplayer replayer;
    private final FillSimulator fills;
    private final ReplayProperties props;

    public BacktestRunner(MarketEventReplayer replayer,
                          FillSimulator fills,
                          ReplayProperties props) {
        this.replayer = replayer;
        this.fills = fills;
        this.props = props;
    }

    public BacktestResult run(Strategy strategy) {
        LedgerSink ledger = new LedgerSink(fills, strategy);
        for (String symbol : props.symbols()) {
            replayer.replay(props.session(), symbol, ledger);
        }
        return ledger.settle();
    }
}

Because BacktestResult is a pure function of ReplayProperties plus the strategy code plus the immutable QuestDB partition, two runs are reproducible to the cent. When a colleague says "I can't reproduce your numbers," the first thing I check is whether they're pointed at a partition that got rewritten — which is why I treat replayed partitions as append-only and never backfill a session after it has been used in a published result.

What the production reality actually costs

A few things I did not expect when I started. First, the single biggest performance lever was not JVM tuning, it was QuestDB partitioning granularity combined with fetch size — getting the cursor to stream rather than buffer turned a nine-minute replay into forty seconds. Second, SYMBOL columns in QuestDB are interned and cheap to filter, so per-symbol replay scans are far faster than the generic string-column intuition suggests. Third, the Parquet tier is genuinely fine for backtesting even though it is slower per scan — I am not latency-sensitive when replaying history, I am correctness-sensitive, and correctness is a property of the data and the joins, not the storage tier.

The discipline that matters most has nothing to do with any of the tooling. It is the willingness to make your engine throw an exception the instant it touches information from the future, and to keep that check on in production rather than switching it off because it's inconvenient. Every optimistic assumption you let slide — fills at the mid, zero latency, closest-quote joins — is a small loan against reality that gets called in the moment you trade live. I would rather have a backtest that reports a boring 0.4 Sharpe I can trust than a glamorous 3 that evaporates on contact. If you want to talk through the capture side or the strategy harness, reach me through my contact page, and there's more on the systems I've built across trading and fintech in my experience.

Go instrument your fill model with a lookahead assertion this week, point it at one real session, and watch what your "winning" strategy does when it can no longer see tomorrow's prices.

title: Compositional Unalignment: Auditing Safety in Large Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.07216v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are vulnerable to compositional harm: an image and a prompt that are benign in isolation become harmful through the model's cross-modal reasoning. Recent alignment methods report strong scores on compositional safety benchmarks, but an LLM judge only measures observed behavior and cannot reveal how robustly safety is integrated into the model. We argue that un-alignment provides a complementary audit of alignment robustness. We first show that minimal supervised fine-tuning reaches an LLM-judge score comparable to a multi-stage reinforcement-learning pipeline, so similar benchmark scores cannot establish robustness by themselves. We then show that recognition and refusal of compositional harm are decoupled: nine standard direction-finding methods detect compositional harm with up to AUC=0.99, yet ablating the recovered directions either leaves refusal intact or destroys model coherence. We therefore propose CMaG, a training-free un-alignment method for compositional safety. CMaG measures refusal intention with a refusal-versus-compliance log-probability margin, takes its gradient with respect to mid-layer activations, and contrasts it against partially benign pairs to isolate the cross-modal interaction term. A single backward pass over 80 examples yields a direction along which steering monotonically converts refusal into compliance. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.5-7B, CMaG reduces compositional safety scores by up to 65 points while over 98% of outputs remain coherent, outperforming gradient-based baselines; the direction also transfers to text-explicit harm and un-aligns models hardened by defensive training. Compositional safety can thus appear behaviorally strong while remaining fragile to targeted internal intervention. Warning: this paper contains unsafe model outputs, including references to self-harm.

title: Expand seed keywords into hundreds of Google and YouTube autocomplete ideas, grouped by intent
description:
Autocomplete is the cheapest keyword research there is: it shows what people actually type, in their own words, ranked by how often Google sees them. The manual version is typing "coffee maker a", "coffee maker b" and so on into a search box and copying what drops down. The scripted version runs every letter, digit and question word against Google and YouTube, for each market you sell in, and hands you a deduplicated list.

This post turns a few seeds into a content plan grouped by intent, then compares the autocomplete scrapers on the Apify Store using the prices their Store pages listed at the time of writing.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Google Autocomplete Scraper. It's a paid tool (prices below). Check each Store page before you buy: prices change.

How the expansion works

For each seed, source (Google Search, YouTube) and market (country and language), the tool asks autocomplete for the seed plus every modifier in expansions:

  • alphabet: seed + a to z and 0 to 9, 36 queries.
  • questions: how, what, why, which, can and other question words + seed, in English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese or Italian, following the market's language.
  • prepositions: for, with, without, near, vs, or and similar words, which is where comparison and use-case phrases come from.

Each unique phrase is one row: keyword, seed, source, country, language, the modifier and query that produced it, its position in the suggestion box, and intents (question, commercial, local, comparison) tagged by word rules. A phrase that repeats in the same source and market is dropped and not charged. depth: 2 expands the results once more for long-tail phrases.

Seeds to a content plan 

pip install apify-client

import csv
import os
from collections import defaultdict

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/google-autocomplete-scraper").call(
    run_input={
        "keywords": ["coffee maker", "espresso machine"],
        "sources": ["google", "youtube"],
        "expansions": ["alphabet", "questions", "prepositions"],
        "countries": ["us", "ca"],
        "languages": ["en"],
        "maxResults": 2000,
    }
)
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

groups = defaultdict(dict)
for r in rows:
    for intent in r["intents"] or ["other"]:
        best = groups[intent].get(r["keyword"])
        if best is None or r["position"] < best["position"]:
            groups[intent][r["keyword"]] = r

with open("content_plan.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["intent", "keyword", "seed", "sources", "best_position"])
    for intent, kws in sorted(groups.items()):
        for kw, r in sorted(kws.items(), key=lambda x: x[1]["position"]):
            srcs = sorted({x["source"] for x in rows if x["keyword"] == kw})
            w.writerow([intent, kw, r["seed"], "+".join(srcs), r["position"]])

for intent, kws in sorted(groups.items()):
    print(f"{intent}: {len(kws)} keywords")

How to read the groups:

  • question: one FAQ entry or one article each. "how coffee maker works" is a headline as it stands.
  • comparison: "espresso machine vs ..." phrases are buyer's guides and comparison pages.
  • commercial: best, cheap, price, deal, review phrases are close to purchase; product and category pages.
  • local: "near me", "nearby" and "open now" phrases mean a store finder or a local landing page.
  • Found on Google and YouTube (sources = google+youtube): a topic worth both a written page and a video.

For a second language, add it to languages (for example ["en", "fr"] with "countries": ["ca"]): the question and preposition modifiers switch to that language, so French Canadian searchers get French modifiers, not English ones.

Autocomplete scrapers on the Apify Store compared

Prices per 1,000 keywords from each Store page at the time of writing:

Bronze $0.35 $0.90 $0.50

YouTube autocomplete yes no (Google only) no (Google only)
A to Z modifiers yes yes yes
Question and preposition modifiers 6 languages English question words English question words
Several countries and languages in one run yes no (one each) yes
Intent tags yes not stated not stated
Duplicates dropped and not charged yes not stated not stated

Where each wins: automation-lab has the most users of the three and the longest track record. memo23 is close on price on the free plan. The Aurelix tool is the cheapest of the three on every plan, and the only one of the three that reads YouTube autocomplete, uses question and preposition modifiers in six languages and tags each phrase by intent.

Limits

  • No search volume, CPC or difficulty. Autocomplete gives phrases and their order only. To compare how much interest a few shortlisted phrases get, and how it moves over time and by region, use Google Trends on the shortlist.
  • At most 10 suggestions per query, so a seed yields at most about 60 queries' worth per source and market at depth 1.
  • Suggestions are personalised by location and change over time; the country setting localises them, but they can differ slightly from what a signed-in user sees.
  • Intent tags come from word rules, not a model, so rare phrasings can be missed or mis-tagged.
  • At most 20 country and language combinations per run, and depth at most 2.
  • Google can throttle datacenter IPs; the run then stops early with the keywords collected so far.

Cost

At the time of writing the Store page lists $0.45 per 1,000 keywords on Apify's free plan and $0.35 per 1,000 on paid plans, plus $0.0005 per run. Only unique keywords are charged, and a seed with no suggestions of its own is not expanded, so a typo costs only the start fee. Apify's free plan includes $5 of credit a month, about 11,000 keywords.
