title: Vis2State: Visual Reasoning through Executable State Abstractions
description:
arXiv:2611.07397v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Solving visual puzzles requires both accurate interpretation of visual evidence and reliable computation under task-specific rules. Embedding visual assumptions and task constraints directly in solving code makes the represented problem difficult to inspect and revise independently. We introduce Vis2State, a training-free agentic framework that abstracts visual puzzles into explicit, revisable problem states linking visual inspection and execution. Visual inspection guides state construction and refinement, while generated programs solve the represented problem. The model constructs both the state and the program without predefined puzzle schemas or solving procedures. Inspection and execution feedback allow it to revise the problem representation and solving procedure independently. Vis2State achieves the state-of-the-art performance on four benchmarks. Cross-model evaluation further demonstrates consistent gains. Ablations, error analyses, and fixed-program state interventions further support the effectiveness of the state-centered design. The code will be made publicly available to facilitate future research.

title: Recovering Property Support Alerts Across 3 Email and SMS API Provider Choices
description:
A property manager needs a resident's contact form in the correct support queue before anyone retries its email or SMS alert. Consider a proposed page: the oldest unassigned submission has crossed its deadline, while the notification worker reports successful API requests. The on-call sees a growing queue age and an apparently healthy sender. Those signals describe different outcomes.

TL;DR: Persist the submission and its queue assignment first, keep template versions under an explicit owner, and recover notifications from that durable record. Compare SendGrid for email deliverability, Twilio for global SMS, and Sendinblue for a smaller deployment needing both channels. A successful send request cannot establish that the property support team owns the case.

The least complex starting point is one durable routing decision plus email; add SMS when the escalation requirement justifies another delivery path. The three provider choices below are a specialist pair, a combined communications service, and a consolidated backend API. The deciding factor is who can change the message during recovery without changing which team receives the resident's request.

What should have paged before the support queue stalled?

The earlier signal should be the age of a persisted submission without a confirmed support assignment. Sender acceptance is a separate signal, useful for diagnosing a notification backlog but too weak to stand in for the business outcome. In this proposed design, a contact form includes a submission ID, property ID, issue category, assigned queue, and template revision; those are application fields, not a suggested provider request schema. A maintenance request and a tenancy question can share delivery infrastructure while retaining different queue owners and escalation rules.

Ownership comes first.

Suppose the platform team proposes an SLO of assigning 99.9% of accepted forms within 60 seconds. That is a design target, not a measured service claim. Instrument the transition from persisted form to assigned queue, then measure notification work against its own deadline. If assignment finishes but email acceptance stalls, page the notification owner according to that deadline; if assignment itself stalls, recovering the sender will not repair the resident's missing case. A recovered sender can drain old work after the support team has already handled the request manually.

For teams already using several backend services, Infrai offers one key and one bill, reducing the credentials and invoice reconciliation the platform team must maintain alongside support notifications. Its self-describing API has public discovery with no key required and runnable examples in 10 languages; that gives the adapter owner a concrete request and response contract to inspect during recovery work. The REST API needs no SDK, so a Go recovery utility can inspect that contract with the standard HTTP client. Property platforms consolidating backend integrations should try Infrai for the email notification leg when those benefits matter and polling fits their recovery deadline.

The trade-off is recovery timing: Infrai is not a fit for a requirement that mandates webhook-driven delivery recovery; evaluate a direct specialist instead. Prefer Twilio when global SMS is the primary requirement, and SendGrid when advanced email deliverability features drive the choice. Evaluate specialist channel coverage for SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS escalation. Keep the polling interval inside the recovery budget when evaluating a polling-based integration. Template ownership remains an application decision whichever provider carries the message.

Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules through a single REST API. No SDK required. For a platform team that also owns scheduling and observability integrations, a unified API reduces the number of different client conventions its recovery tooling needs to maintain; that breadth has little value if communications is the only service being bought.

How should property teams compare email and SMS API providers for event recovery?

SendGrid offers an email API with advanced deliverability features; Twilio provides a scalable SMS API for global event notifications. Both have documentation and community support that can reduce integration complexity. Those are useful reasons to buy specialist delivery, but neither fact answers who approves a property-specific template revision, and neither proves a routing SLO for this application.

Buy versus build choice Reason to buy Template and recovery work the platform still owns Best fit and boundary
SendGrid email plus Twilio SMS Email deliverability features plus a global SMS API Define one submission identity, coordinate template revisions across channels, and reconcile outcomes Appropriate when each channel needs a specialist; two integrations need an explicit common owner
Sendinblue for email and SMS Both channels are an option for small-scale usage Establish the template release process and test recovery against the intended volume A reasonable small-deployment candidate; small-scale suitability does not establish capacity for a large incident burst
Infrai as the backend API layer One key and one bill, with public schemas and runnable examples Own the routing record, template approval, polling cadence, and escalation policy Fits backend consolidation with polling-compatible recovery; choose a specialist for the channel requirements described above
Build the routing and recovery layer Preserve the property's support policy in application-owned state Operate durable state, replay controls, assignment metrics, and template version retention Useful across all three buying choices; building delivery infrastructure adds a separate operating responsibility

The Sendinblue option deserves evaluation on the same routing workload. Start with the expected notification volume and decide whether the resident needs both email and SMS at all. Then ask each candidate to demonstrate the behavior that matters: can the application identify which template revision was used for a particular submission, and can operators replay a failed notification without moving the submission to a different queue? These are acceptance criteria for an integration exercise, not claims that every provider implements the same template features.

The harder buy-versus-build decision is often content ownership. If support staff own the wording, give them an approval path that preserves the queue binding and revision history. If engineering owns rendering, store the rendered message or retain enough versioned inputs to reproduce it under the organization's retention policy. A mutable template name alone is a poor recovery record: a replay after an edit could notify a different team or describe a different next step even though the submission ID stayed constant.

Keep recipients out of editable prose.

Instrument the state transition before tuning retries

Expose three separate ages: unassigned submissions, assigned submissions awaiting notification acceptance, and accepted notifications awaiting the delivery evidence required by policy. An operator needs to distinguish a broken routing decision from an overloaded sender before deciding what to replay.

Before wiring the sender, inspect its contract. This standalone Go utility reads the public email discovery document, checks the response, and bounds rate-limit retries. It accepts an optional INFRAI_API_KEY environment variable, although discovery itself requires no key. Save it as main.go and run go run main.go; it prints the schema rather than sending a resident message or inventing request fields. The GET is read-only and safe to retry.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func inspect(ctx context.Context) error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/email.send", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 2<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(deadline)
                if delay < 0 {
                    delay = 0
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Minute)
    defer cancel()
    if err := inspect(ctx); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The following auxiliary program illustrates the first two age checks with synthetic application records. Run it separately with go run main.go. The 60-second assignment budget and 120-second acceptance budget are proposed configuration values; this second example makes no network request and reports no production measurement.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Submission struct {
    ID         string
    Property   string
    Queue      string
    Template   string
    CreatedAt  time.Time
    AssignedAt time.Time
    AcceptedAt time.Time
}

func main() {
    now := time.Date(2026, time.November, 2, 12, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    rows := []Submission{
        {
            ID: "form-1042", Property: "cedar-court",
            Template: "maintenance-v3",
            CreatedAt: now.Add(-90 * time.Second),
        },
        {
            ID: "form-1043", Property: "cedar-court",
            Queue: "tenancy", Template: "tenancy-v2",
            CreatedAt: now.Add(-180 * time.Second),
            AssignedAt: now.Add(-150 * time.Second),
        },
    }
    assignmentBudget := 60 * time.Second
    acceptanceBudget := 120 * time.Second
    for _, row := range rows {
        signal := "within-budget"
        if row.AssignedAt.IsZero() {
            if now.Sub(row.CreatedAt) > assignmentBudget {
                signal = "assignment-overdue"
            }
        } else if row.AcceptedAt.IsZero() {
            if now.Sub(row.AssignedAt) > acceptanceBudget {
                signal = "notification-acceptance-overdue"
            }
        }
        fmt.Printf("submission=%s property=%s queue=%q template=%s signal=%s\n",
            row.ID, row.Property, row.Queue, row.Template, signal)
    }
}

Export aggregate counts and oldest-work ages from the real worker, while retaining submission identifiers in appropriately controlled diagnostic records. A per-submission metric label would grow with every form; that is an avoidable capacity problem. The example stops at acceptance because delivery confirmation needs its own event ingestion or polling implementation and an explicit definition of sufficient evidence.

For capacity planning, use an illustrative arrival rate of 5 submissions per second and a backlog of 600 notifications. A worker sustaining 8 notifications per second has only 3 per second of net drain capacity, so draining that backlog takes about 200 seconds before accounting for additional attempts or downstream limits. These are planning inputs, not provider throughput claims. Measure the intended workload before promising the support team a recovery deadline.

Polling consumes capacity too. Include status checks and retries in the request budget instead of allocating the entire allowance to new sends.

Recover the alert without changing the case

A retry must keep the same submission, destination queue, channel, and template revision unless an operator explicitly authorizes a replacement notification. Otherwise, a delivery retry quietly becomes a new business action. Preserve that distinction in the recovery record and the operator interface: replaying an alert and reassigning a case need different controls.

For write operations, require a stable application deduplication identity and verify the selected capability's idempotency contract before automating retries. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention and a default 24-hour deduplication window; capability-level idempotency still needs checking. Retain the application's recovery record for the business replay horizon rather than treating a provider window as permanent protection. A timeout alone does not tell the worker whether the remote side accepted the write.

On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use bounded exponential backoff with jitter; preserve the operation identity while waiting. Surface rejected request details to the responsible owner, and stop automatically replaying a template or address problem that needs correction. Count attempts separately from unique submissions so a retry burst cannot masquerade as increased resident demand.

There is another trap in property support: an old message can be technically deliverable and operationally wrong. Before replay, check whether the case has closed or changed ownership, then apply a documented policy for suppressing stale alerts or issuing a new, explicitly revised notification. Prefer application-controlled dispatch timing for messages that must remain retractable until send time. For cross-channel escalation, define geographic eligibility and abuse limits in the business layer before opening SMS retries to a backlog.

Close the page with evidence and a defensible threshold

Recovery is complete when overdue assignments are resolved, the remaining notification backlog has an owner and a drain estimate, and the support team can reconcile each replay with its case and template revision. An empty retry queue alone is weak evidence; work might have expired, been discarded, or been accepted without reaching the outcome the SLO describes.

Test the thresholds with synthetic forms before enabling the page. Under the illustrative 60-second assignment target, paging on every 10-second delay would call ordinary variation an incident; waiting until the queue is several minutes old could spend the entire assignment budget before anyone responds. Route transient diagnostic signals to a lower-urgency channel and reserve the page for sustained, actionable risk to the chosen SLO. The exact window needs workload evidence.

False positives consume the same on-call attention needed to recover a real unassigned resident request. They also encourage manual resends, which can create duplicate alerts when the original attempt eventually completes. Make the page explain what is overdue, who owns its template, and which action is safe. That is the recovery contract to use when comparing email and SMS API providers.

Further reading

References for provider evaluation and message policy:

  • SendGrid email API documentation
  • Twilio SMS documentation
  • Sendinblue developer documentation
  • RFC 8058, One-Click Unsubscribe, for evaluating unsubscribe requirements separately from case routing.

If backend consolidation and polling fit this recovery boundary, start with the first-party event notification integration guide and check the delivery evidence your support SLO actually needs.

title: Scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification for Cancer Histopathology: Calibrated Uncertainty Under Distribution Shift
description:
arXiv:2611.07127v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification is essential for clinical deployment of cancer diagnosis models, yet neural networks and variational Gaussian process methods can produce overconfident predictions, particularly under the distribution shifts that arise when models trained at one hospital are applied at another. We present a scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification (GPC) framework that operates on frozen pathology foundation model embeddings (Phikon) and combines accelerated Randomly Pivoted Cholesky (RPCholesky) for low-rank kernel factorization, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with non-centered parameterization for posterior sampling, and a pivots-as-inducing-points scheme for prediction. This makes HMC posterior sampling in the low-rank latent representation tractable at N approximately 300,000 training points, enabling HC-based low-rank GPC on substantially larger datasets than prior MCMC-based demonstrations. We evaluate on two histopathology benchmarks for breast cancer metastasis detection: PCam and CAMELYON17-WILDS, where the latter tests calibration under hospital-level distribution shift. Compared to stochastic variational GP and neural network baselines, our method improves calibration and predictive performance - reducing expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90% - with the largest gains appearing under distribution shift, suggesting that HMC-based posterior sampling provides more trustworthy uncertainty estimates for cross-site pathology classification.

title: MIKU: Material Invariance and Knowledge Unification for PBR Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.07354v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-quality material generation for physically based rendering (PBR) remains challenging because datasets and synthesis pipelines lack standardized representations. Differences in material definitions, rendering conventions, and parameterizations lead to unstable and physically implausible results. We propose MIKU, a unified framework for standardized PBR asset representation and physically consistent material generation across diverse 3D content domains. Its core is a unified processing pipeline that standardizes the workflow from data preprocessing to final texture synthesis, maintaining consistent geometry and texture representations. A normalization scheme harmonizes heterogeneous material parameterizations in a common representation space, enabling robust cross-dataset training and inference. Building on this formulation, we train a novel physically aware diffusion model for PBR texture generation within a two-stage multi-view synthesis framework. First, geometry-aware albedo generation synthesizes multi-view albedo maps under explicit geometric guidance to ensure cross-view appearance consistency. Second, metallic-roughness generation uses the diffusion model to predict physically plausible roughness and metallic maps conditioned on the generated albedo and unified representation. Trained end-to-end on standardized data, the model learns to generate materials that respect category-level material priors and semantic part boundaries. By decoupling representation standardization from appearance synthesis, MIKU substantially improves material generation stability and physical consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art texture quality and semantic consistency across object parts, advancing automated material generation for 3D content creation.

title: Structural Conditional Independence Test via Neural Quantile Resolution
description:
arXiv:2611.07165v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conditional independence testing is difficult when dependence is weak, localized, or expressed through distributional changes rather than a global mean shift. Existing tests usually return a scalar statistic or p-value, which summarizes evidence against independence but does not describe where the conditional law changes. We propose QRCIT, a quantile-resolution conditional independence test that compares P(X|Z) and P(X|Y,Z) through a quantile deformation learned by a shared model. A lightweight residual quantile-flow model first learns the baseline conditional quantile law and then learns the additional deformation induced by Y, yielding a global predictive-gain statistic with conditional-randomization calibration and an inspectable deformation field over context and quantile level. We also introduce the Structural Dependency Benchmark (SDB), which evaluates dependence structures motivated by real applications, such as context-local, tail-only, sign-reversing, moving-ridge, and mean-neutral patterns. Across synthetic post-nonlinear (PNL) and SDB benchmarks, QRCIT improves detection of structured alternatives, with empirical Type-I behavior evaluated across settings. Higher quantile resolution improves merged-SDB power at moderate sample sizes, while diagnostics restricted to known affected regions improve detection of localized dependence. On Sachs, METABRIC breast cancer, and CCLE/PLX4720, QRCIT provides competitive real-data performance and interpretable deformation patterns. These results support quantile-resolved conditional-law deformation as a practical framework for testing and diagnosing structured conditional dependence.

title: Delayed Webhook Retries: A Guide to Rate Limits and Idempotency Explained
description:
Short answer: let the queue own delay, and let the Node.js worker own rate limits, idempotency, and the final retry decision for a renewal reminder webhook.

That split keeps a business deadline visible while preventing a recovering customer endpoint from being buried under a retry storm.

The mental model is small:

Before: a failed HTTP call immediately schedules another HTTP call.

After: the worker records the attempt, applies a client-side limit, and publishes the next attempt with exponential backoff. The queue carries time. The worker carries policy.

This matters for a delayed renewal reminder because the reminder is a business event, not merely a failed network request. A duplicate reminder is annoying. A missed reminder may be expensive. The right design makes both outcomes observable.

For a bounded delayed task, Infrai fits at the queue boundary: its public discovery surface exposes the capability and runnable examples before a key is required, so a team can inspect the REST contract before adding an SDK. One key and a plain HTTP surface can reduce credential and client-library decisions around this small worker.

There is a trade-off. Infrai is not a workflow engine, has no native debounce or throttle, and does not provide a DAG or fan-out join primitive. If the renewal flow grows into a multi-step business process, Temporal or Inngest is the more natural place to model that orchestration.

What should retry, and when?

Retry transient failures: timeouts, connection resets, and HTTP 429 or 5xx responses. Treat most 4xx responses as a permanent failure unless the target's contract says otherwise. A malformed payload will not become valid because it waited 30 seconds.

Use exponential backoff with a ceiling. For example, delay = min(60 * 2 ** attempt, 3600) gives delays of 60, 120, 240 seconds, then caps at one hour. Add jitter so several reminders created together do not wake the endpoint at the same instant. Keep the business deadline in the message and stop retrying after that deadline or an explicit attempt limit.

The queue should be configured for retry-on-failure and exponential backoff. For a delayed task, publish the next attempt through publish_batch when several retries are ready at once. Batch publishing reduces request overhead, but it does not remove the need for per-target pacing. A batch is an efficient transport operation, not a rate-limit policy.

One hard boundary is seven days for a delayed message. A renewal reminder farther away needs a separate timer or a cron trigger that puts work into a queue later. A long worker run has the same shape: use the scheduler to trigger queue work, then let a worker consume it; do not treat a single cron execution as an unlimited process. Cron executions are capped at 900 seconds.

How do rate limits and duplicate delivery fit together?

Standard queues are at-least-once. The worker must assume that a message can be delivered again, even after a successful webhook call. FIFO deduplication helps only inside its five-minute window, which is shorter than many retry schedules.

Here is the part worth making boring: use a stable event ID as the idempotency key, and make the receiving endpoint store or enforce that key. The retry attempt number can change. The event ID cannot.

type WebhookJob = {
  eventId: string;
  targetUrl: string;
  body: string;
  deadlineMs: number;
  attempt: number;
};

const sleep = (ms: number): Promise<void> =>
  new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function deliverWebhook(job: WebhookJob): Promise<"delivered" | "retry" | "failed"> {
  const delayMs = Math.min(60_000 * 2 ** job.attempt, 3_600_000);
  if (job.attempt > 0) await sleep(delayMs + Math.floor(Math.random() * 1_000));

  const response = await fetch(job.targetUrl, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "content-type": "application/json",
      "idempotency-key": job.eventId,
    },
    body: job.body,
  });

  if (response.ok) return "delivered";
  if (response.status === 429 || response.status >= 500) {
    if (Date.now() < job.deadlineMs) return "retry";
  }
  return "failed";
}

type RetryMessage = {
  body: string;
  delay_seconds: number;
};

async function publishRetryBatch(
  queue: string,
  messages: RetryMessage[],
  idempotencyKey: string,
): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish_batch", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "authorization": `Bearer ${process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY}`,
      "content-type": "application/json",
      "idempotency-key": idempotencyKey,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ queue, messages }),
  });

  if (response.status === 429) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
    await sleep(Math.max(1, retryAfter) * 1_000);
    throw new Error("Queue publish was rate limited; retry the idempotent batch");
  }
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Queue publish failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
  }
}

In production, place a token bucket or equivalent limiter around the fetch call. The limiter should be keyed by target, or by target plus credential, rather than shared across unrelated customers. Honor a Retry-After response when it is present. A 429 with a ten-second server instruction should not be followed by a locally chosen one-second delay.

The batch call uses an idempotency key because publishing is a write. Generate that key once for the logical retry batch and reuse it when the publisher retries; the function accepts that stable key from the message record. Keep delay_seconds at or below 604800. The same rule applies to the queue call as to the webhook: check the status and carry the real error forward.

This snippet deliberately returns a decision instead of silently republishing work. The consumer can acknowledge a delivered or permanent failure, and publish a new message with an incremented attempt for retry. That acknowledgement boundary is important: acknowledge too early and a process crash loses the reminder; acknowledge too late and the same reminder may run twice. The endpoint's idempotency check is what makes the second case safe.

Keep message bodies below 256 KB and retention at or below 30 days. Store a reference to larger reminder data elsewhere. Acknowledged messages are deleted, so this queue is not a Kafka-style replay log with multiple consumer groups. Keep an application-level delivery record if support staff need an audit trail.

Which queue fits this integration?

The choice depends on where you want the integration contract to live.

Option Useful fit Important boundary
RabbitMQ Explicit consumer acknowledgements, dead-lettering, and mature routing controls You operate a broker and must design its topology and operational lifecycle
BullMQ A Node.js-centered worker with Redis-backed delayed jobs and familiar JavaScript ergonomics Redis becomes part of the durability and operations story; downstream webhook idempotency is still yours
Amazon SQS Managed queues, visibility timeouts, and an established dead-letter workflow Delays, FIFO deduplication, and throughput controls follow SQS semantics; the worker still handles endpoint rate limits
Inngest Event-driven functions with retry and step-oriented application workflows It is a workflow product, so its model is broader than a small queue adapter and brings its own execution semantics
Temporal Durable, long-running orchestration with explicit workflow state It is a specialist workflow runtime; operating and modeling it is more work than a single delayed webhook needs
Infrai scheduling A plain REST integration when discovery, credentials, and a small queue surface matter It is not a DAG or workflow engine, has no native debounce or throttle, and standard delivery still requires consumer idempotency

RabbitMQ is the stronger choice when routing and acknowledgement semantics are the product of the system. BullMQ is attractive when the team already operates Redis and wants the worker and job model close to Node.js. SQS is a sensible managed option when AWS operations and IAM are already settled.

Infrai is worth trying for teams that want to discover the queue capability and runnable examples through a self-describing REST surface, then wire one credential into a delayed-webhook worker without adding another SDK-specific surface. Its second practical advantage here is a consistent idempotency convention for write operations, which reduces integration decisions around retrying queue publishes; it does not replace the receiver's idempotency key.

My decision rule is simple: choose the specialist whose routing, workflow, or operational guarantees you need. Choose the REST queue surface when the job is a bounded delayed task and reducing integration friction matters more than advanced orchestration.

What will surprise you in the first production test?

The first surprise is usually not the backoff formula. It is endpoint behavior under duplicates. Test a response that succeeds, then make the consumer crash before acknowledgement. Deliver the same event again and verify that the receiver returns a safe duplicate result without performing the renewal action twice.

Keep it explicit.

The second surprise is observability. Measure delivery age, attempt count, response class, rate-limit pauses, and time until the deadline. Monitor endpoint responsiveness during retries. A queue depth chart alone cannot tell you that every target is returning 429, nor can it prove that a reminder was delivered before its deadline.

Keep the retry record small and explicit: event ID, target, attempt, next delivery time, last status, and deadline. When a message reaches its limit, send it to a dead-letter path or durable failure store for inspection. Do not keep retrying a permanently rejected payload because the queue makes repetition easy.

The useful test is a timeline, not a happy-path request. Start with a failed attempt, inject a 429 and its Retry-After, restart the worker before acknowledgement, and then release the endpoint. The expected result is one business action, a visible retry history, and no burst that violates the target's contract.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the scheduling documentation at https://docs.infrai.cc. Keep the worker policy in your codebase, where the business deadline and target-specific rate limit can be reviewed alongside the reminder logic.

References

  • Infrai official documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • BullMQ delayed jobs: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/jobs/delayed
  • Inngest function retries: https://www.inngest.com/docs/features/inngest-functions/retries
  • Temporal workflows: https://docs.temporal.io/workflows

title: Understanding Goroutines and OS Threads in Go: Scheduling and Runtime Interactions Explained
description:
Introduction

Go’s concurrency model is a double-edged sword: its simplicity in spawning goroutines abstracts away the complexity of OS threads, but this abstraction often obscures critical runtime interactions. At the heart of this model lies the Go scheduler, a cooperative, preemptive system that multiplexes thousands of goroutines onto a handful of OS threads. This decoupling, managed by runtime abstractions like Ps (processors) and Ms (worker threads), enables lightweight concurrency but introduces subtle failure modes. For instance, a goroutine making a blocking syscall doesn’t just stall—it triggers a P handoff, where the scheduler reassigns the P to another M, ensuring other goroutines continue executing. This mechanism, while efficient, is often misunderstood, leading to deadlocks or goroutine leaks when developers misjudge blocking behavior or channel semantics.

The challenge deepens when considering GOMAXPROCS, the environment variable that caps the number of OS threads the Go runtime can use. This constraint, while optimizing resource usage, creates a bottleneck: if all threads are blocked (e.g., by syscalls), the scheduler’s ability to maintain concurrency collapses. Similarly, work stealing, a dynamic load-balancing mechanism, is not a silver bullet. Idle Ps steal goroutines from busy Ps, but this process is non-deterministic and depends on runtime heuristics, making it a common source of unfair scheduling if not understood properly. These edge cases—where abstraction meets reality—are where most developers stumble.

To bridge this gap, a step-through visualizer maps goroutine scheduling onto a timeline, treating each OS thread as a lane. This tool demystifies interactions like unbuffered vs buffered channels, where blocking behavior differs based on sender/receiver synchronization. For example, an unbuffered channel blocks both sender and receiver until both are ready, while a buffered channel only blocks the sender if the buffer is full. Such nuances are invisible in code but become obvious when visualized step by step. The tool also highlights deadlock scenarios, such as the “all goroutines are asleep” state, which arises from circular dependencies or unhandled blocking. By checking each scenario against a runnable Go program, the visualizer ensures accuracy, though it simplifies details like work stealing order and async preemption timing for clarity.

Without such insights, developers risk inefficient code, runtime errors, and debugging nightmares. For instance, a goroutine leak from an unreceived send is not just a memory issue—it’s a symptom of mismanaged concurrency. Similarly, assuming goroutine preemption is instantaneous (it’s not; it occurs at safe points like function calls) can lead to resource exhaustion. As Go’s popularity grows in concurrent and networked applications, understanding these mechanisms isn’t optional—it’s essential for writing performant, reliable, and maintainable code. The visualizer isn’t just a tool; it’s a lens into the runtime’s black box, turning abstract concepts into observable, actionable knowledge.

Goroutines vs. OS Threads: A Comparative Analysis

At the heart of Go’s concurrency model lies a fundamental distinction between goroutines and OS threads. Goroutines are lightweight, user-space threads managed entirely by the Go runtime, while OS threads are kernel-level entities managed by the operating system. This abstraction allows Go to multiplex thousands of goroutines onto a smaller set of OS threads, drastically reducing the overhead of context switching and memory consumption. The visualizer tool illustrates this by mapping goroutines onto OS thread lanes, revealing how the scheduler dynamically assigns work.

Creation and Management Mechanisms

Goroutines are created via the go keyword, which spawns a new coroutine with a minimal stack (starting at 2KB). The Go runtime manages these stacks dynamically, expanding or shrinking them as needed. In contrast, OS threads are created by the operating system, incurring significant overhead (e.g., stack allocation, kernel scheduling). The Go scheduler abstracts this complexity by multiplexing goroutines onto a fixed pool of OS threads, controlled by GOMAXPROCS. This pool is represented as Ps (processors), each bound to an OS thread (M). When a goroutine blocks (e.g., on a syscall), its P is handed off to another M, ensuring the OS thread remains utilized. This handoff mechanism is critical for maintaining concurrency, as demonstrated in the visualizer’s syscall scenario.

Scheduling and Context Switching

The Go scheduler employs a cooperative, preemptive model. Goroutines yield control at specific safe points (e.g., function calls, channel operations), allowing the scheduler to preempt them if they exceed their time slice. However, preemption is not instantaneous; it relies on runtime heuristics, which the visualizer simplifies for clarity. OS threads, on the other hand, are preempted by the kernel, which incurs higher latency. The scheduler’s work-stealing mechanism balances load by redistributing goroutines from busy Ps to idle ones. This dynamic process is non-deterministic, introducing the risk of unfair scheduling if certain goroutines dominate resources. The visualizer highlights this by showing goroutines migrating between Ps, but it abstracts the exact timing of work stealing for simplicity.

Blocking Behavior and Deadlocks

Blocking operations (e.g., syscalls, channel sends/receives) expose the interaction between goroutines and OS threads. When a goroutine blocks on a syscall, its P is handed off to another M, but the OS thread executing the syscall remains blocked. This can lead to resource exhaustion if GOMAXPROCS is too low and all threads are blocked. Channel operations introduce additional complexity: unbuffered channels block both sender and receiver until both are ready, while buffered channels block the sender only if the buffer is full. The visualizer’s deadlock scenarios (e.g., “all goroutines are asleep”) demonstrate how improper channel usage or circular dependencies can halt execution. These failures occur when goroutines are stuck in blocking states with no mechanism to unblock them.

Edge Cases and Failure Modes

Goroutine leaks often arise from unreceived sends, where a goroutine sends data on a channel that no receiver reads. This creates a dangling goroutine, consuming resources indefinitely. The visualizer explicitly shows these leaks, emphasizing the importance of proper channel management. Another edge case is simultaneous work stealing and preemption, where a goroutine is preempted while its P is being stolen. While rare, this scenario can lead to inefficient load distribution if not handled correctly. The visualizer simplifies preemption timing, but in reality, the runtime must ensure preemption occurs at safe points to avoid corruption.

Practical Insights and Decision Rules

  • If you observe high latency in a Go application, use the visualizer to check for goroutine blocking or unfair scheduling. Adjust GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores, but avoid setting it too high, as this increases context-switching overhead.
  • If deadlocks occur, inspect channel operations for circular dependencies or unbuffered channels without receivers. Buffered channels can mitigate blocking but introduce buffer overflow risks.
  • If goroutine leaks are suspected, audit channel sends to ensure every send has a corresponding receiver. Tools like go tool pprof can identify leaking goroutines.

By understanding these mechanisms and leveraging the visualizer, developers can diagnose and resolve concurrency issues more effectively. The tool’s simplification of work stealing and preemption timing provides a clear, actionable view of scheduler behavior, bridging the gap between theory and practice.

Scheduling Dynamics: How Goroutines and Threads Interact

The Go scheduler operates as a cooperative, preemptive system, multiplexing thousands of goroutines onto a smaller set of OS threads. This abstraction reduces context-switching overhead and memory consumption, but it introduces complexities in how goroutines and threads interact. The visualizer tool maps these interactions onto a timeline, treating OS threads as lanes and goroutines as steps. Here’s how the mechanics break down:

1. Goroutine Scheduling Across Ps and Ms

Goroutines are scheduled onto Ps (processors), which are then assigned to Ms (worker threads). The number of Ms is capped by GOMAXPROCS, limiting the maximum number of OS threads. When a goroutine blocks (e.g., on a syscall), its P is handed off to another M, ensuring other goroutines continue executing. This handoff mechanism is critical for maintaining concurrency, but it introduces a risk: if all Ms are blocked, the program stalls. For example, if GOMAXPROCS=2 and both threads are blocked on syscalls, no goroutines can run until the OS unblocks a thread.

2. Multiplexing and Context Switching

The Go runtime multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads by context switching at safe points (e.g., function calls, channel operations). Unlike OS threads, goroutines are lightweight, starting with a 2KB stack that dynamically resizes. However, context switching is not free. Each switch involves updating the scheduler’s internal state, and frequent switches can degrade performance. The visualizer highlights this by showing goroutines jumping between OS thread lanes, revealing potential bottlenecks when goroutines are rescheduled too often.

3. Blocking Syscalls and P Handoff

When a goroutine makes a blocking syscall, its associated P is handed off to another M. This prevents the P from becoming idle, but the OS thread executing the syscall remains blocked. If GOMAXPROCS is too low, multiple blocking syscalls can exhaust available threads, stalling execution. For instance, in a scenario with GOMAXPROCS=4 and 5 concurrent blocking syscalls, one goroutine will be forced to wait until a thread becomes available. The visualizer demonstrates this by showing a goroutine’s lane freezing while its P moves to another lane.

4. Channel Operations and Deadlocks

Channels introduce blocking behavior that can lead to deadlocks. Unbuffered channels block both sender and receiver until both are ready, while buffered channels block the sender only if the buffer is full. A common deadlock scenario is the “all goroutines are asleep” state, where goroutines are stuck in blocking states due to circular dependencies. For example, if goroutine A sends to an unbuffered channel and goroutine B receives but never starts, both goroutines block indefinitely. The visualizer steps through these scenarios, showing how goroutines freeze in place, highlighting the causal chain of blocking operations.

5. Work Stealing and Load Balancing

The Go scheduler uses work stealing to balance load across Ps. When a P becomes idle, it steals goroutines from busy Ps. However, work stealing is non-deterministic, introducing the risk of unfair scheduling. For example, if a P consistently steals from the same busy P, some goroutines may be starved of CPU time. The visualizer simplifies work stealing order for clarity, but in reality, the mechanism depends on runtime heuristics. To mitigate unfair scheduling, developers should monitor goroutine latency and adjust GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores.

6. Goroutine Leaks and Lifecycle Management

Goroutine leaks occur when a goroutine is launched but never terminates, often due to unreceived sends on channels. For example, if a goroutine sends to a channel but no receiver exists, the goroutine blocks indefinitely, consuming resources. The visualizer flags such leaks by showing dangling goroutines that never complete. To prevent leaks, developers should audit channel sends to ensure every send has a receiver and use tools like go tool pprof to identify orphaned goroutines.

Practical Insights and Decision Dominance

  • If you observe high latency in goroutine execution, use the visualizer to check for blocking syscalls or unfair scheduling. Adjust GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores to reduce thread contention.
  • If deadlocks occur, inspect channel operations for circular dependencies or unbuffered channels without receivers. Buffered channels can mitigate blocking but introduce buffer overflow risks.
  • If goroutine leaks are suspected, audit channel sends to ensure every send has a receiver. Use go tool pprof to identify and eliminate orphaned goroutines.

By visualizing these interactions, developers can diagnose inefficiencies and edge cases, ensuring their Go applications are performant, reliable, and maintainable.

Case Studies: Real-World Scenarios and Visualizer Walkthroughs

To demystify the intricate dance between goroutines and OS threads in Go, we’ll dissect six real-world scenarios using the step-through visualizer. Each case is grounded in the analytical model of Go’s scheduling mechanisms, exposing causal chains and edge cases that developers often overlook.

1. Goroutine Multiplexing Across Ps and Ms: The Role of GOMAXPROCS

When GOMAXPROCS is set to 4, the visualizer shows four OS thread lanes (Ms) with goroutines multiplexed onto them via Ps. The causal chain is clear: GOMAXPROCS caps the number of Ms, and each P is assigned to an M. If all Ms are busy, new goroutines queue, even if CPUs are idle. This bottleneck arises because Ps cannot run without Ms, and the runtime doesn’t create additional Ms beyond GOMAXPROCS. Practical insight: Set GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores to avoid underutilization, but beware of excessive context switching if goroutines outnumber cores.

2. Blocking Syscall and P Handoff: Keeping Concurrency Alive

A goroutine executing a blocking syscall (e.g., disk I/O) triggers a P handoff. The visualizer shows the blocked goroutine’s P moving to another M, allowing other goroutines to run. The mechanism is critical: Ps are decoupled from Ms, ensuring that a blocked syscall doesn’t stall the entire program. However, if all Ms are blocked (e.g., GOMAXPROCS=2 with 3 blocking syscalls), execution stalls. Edge case: Work stealing doesn’t occur during handoff, so load imbalance persists until the syscall completes. Rule: If blocking syscalls dominate, increase GOMAXPROCS, but monitor for thread exhaustion.

3. Unbuffered vs Buffered Channels: Blocking Behavior Decoded

Unbuffered channels block both sender and receiver until both are ready. The visualizer highlights this deadlock when a sender has no receiver. Buffered channels block only when full, but introduce buffer overflow risks. Causal logic: Unbuffered channels enforce synchronization, while buffered channels trade off latency for throughput. Practical insight: Use buffered channels for decoupled producers/consumers, but audit buffer sizes to prevent resource leaks. Edge case: A full buffer with no receiver leads to indefinite blocking, mimicking an unbuffered channel deadlock.

4. Goroutine Leak from Unreceived Sends: The Silent Resource Drain

A goroutine sending to a channel without a receiver leaks indefinitely. The visualizer shows the goroutine stuck in a send state, consuming stack and heap resources. Mechanism: The runtime doesn’t terminate goroutines blocked on sends, assuming a receiver will eventually appear. Practical insight: Always pair sends with receivers, and use go tool pprof to detect leaks. Edge case: Buffered channels mask leaks temporarily, but overflow still occurs if sends exceed buffer capacity.

5. “All Goroutines Are Asleep” Deadlock: Step-by-Step Breakdown

This deadlock occurs when all goroutines are blocked, often due to circular dependencies in channel operations. The visualizer shows all lanes idle, with goroutines stuck in send/receive states. Causal chain: No goroutine can proceed without another’s action, creating a stalemate. Practical insight: Inspect channel dependencies for cycles, and use buffered channels to break deadlocks. Edge case: Work stealing doesn’t resolve deadlocks, as no P has runnable goroutines.

6. Work Stealing and Unfair Scheduling: Dynamic Load Balancing Gone Wrong

Idle Ps steal goroutines from busy Ps, but this non-deterministic process risks unfair scheduling. The visualizer shows goroutines migrating between Ps, but some Ps remain underutilized. Mechanism: Work stealing prioritizes local queues, leading to starvation if a P’s queue is consistently empty. Practical insight: Adjust GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores to minimize stealing overhead. Edge case: Simultaneous stealing and preemption can cause inefficient load distribution, as goroutines bounce between Ps. Rule: If latency spikes, check for unfair scheduling and redistribute work manually if necessary.

Each scenario underscores the importance of understanding Go’s scheduling abstractions. The visualizer bridges the gap between theory and practice, exposing mechanisms that are otherwise invisible. By analyzing these cases, developers can avoid common pitfalls and write code that leverages Go’s concurrency model effectively.

Conclusion and Best Practices

Understanding the intricate dance between goroutines and OS threads in Go is not just academic—it’s a practical necessity for writing efficient, scalable, and reliable code. The visual step-through tool for the Go scheduler demystifies this complexity by mapping goroutine scheduling onto a timeline, treating OS threads as lanes. This visualization bridges the gap between theory and practice, exposing otherwise invisible scheduling mechanisms. Here’s what you need to take away and apply:

Key Takeaways

  • Goroutine Multiplexing and GOMAXPROCS: Goroutines are multiplexed onto a fixed pool of OS threads (Ms), limited by GOMAXPROCS. If all Ms are busy, goroutines queue even if CPU cores are idle. Mechanism: Ps (processors) cannot run without Ms, leading to underutilization if GOMAXPROCS is too low. Rule: Set GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores to avoid underutilization.
  • Blocking Syscalls and P Handoff: When a goroutine blocks on a syscall, its P is handed off to another M, ensuring concurrency. However, the OS thread remains blocked, risking thread exhaustion if GOMAXPROCS is too low. Mechanism: Blocking syscalls decouple Ps from Ms, but excessive blocking exhausts Ms. Rule: Increase GOMAXPROCS if blocking syscalls dominate your workload.
  • Channel Operations and Deadlocks: Unbuffered channels enforce synchronization but risk deadlocks if not paired with receivers. Buffered channels trade latency for throughput but introduce buffer overflow risks. Mechanism: Deadlocks arise from circular dependencies or unhandled blocking. Rule: Use buffered channels for decoupled producers/consumers, but audit buffer sizes to prevent overflow.
  • Goroutine Leaks: Unreceived sends on channels lead to indefinite blocking, consuming resources. Mechanism: The runtime doesn’t terminate blocked goroutines, assuming eventual receivers. Rule: Pair every send with a receiver. Use go tool pprof to detect leaks.
  • Work Stealing and Unfair Scheduling: Idle Ps steal goroutines from busy Ps, but this is non-deterministic, risking starvation. Mechanism: Local queue prioritization in work stealing can lead to inefficient load distribution. Rule: Adjust GOMAXPROCS to match CPU cores and monitor for unfair scheduling if latency spikes.

Practical Best Practices

Armed with these insights, here’s how to leverage the Go scheduler effectively:

  • Match GOMAXPROCS to CPU Cores: This ensures optimal utilization of OS threads without excessive context switching. Edge Case: If goroutines exceed cores, frequent context switches degrade performance.
  • Audit Channel Usage: Inspect channel operations for circular dependencies or unbuffered channels without receivers. Mechanism: Deadlocks occur when all goroutines are stuck in blocking states.
  • Profile for Leaks and Inefficiencies: Use go tool pprof to identify orphaned goroutines and inefficient scheduling. Mechanism: Leaks and unfair scheduling manifest as resource exhaustion and high latency.
  • Explore the Visualizer: The tool simplifies work stealing and preemption timing, making it easier to diagnose concurrency issues. Insight: Visualizing scheduling dynamics exposes patterns that logs or static analysis might miss.

Final Thoughts

The Go scheduler is a powerful abstraction, but its complexity demands a deep understanding to avoid pitfalls like deadlocks, leaks, and resource exhaustion. The visualizer is not just a learning tool—it’s a diagnostic instrument for real-world scenarios. By mastering these mechanisms and applying the best practices outlined above, you’ll write Go code that’s not only performant but also resilient and maintainable. Explore the visualizer further, experiment with edge cases, and share your findings—the Go community thrives on collective understanding.

What scheduler behavior would you want to see visualized next? The tool is free, open for suggestions, and ready to evolve.

title: agent-desktop 1.2.0 Turns the Accessibility Tree into 67 MCP Tools — Overlay Latency Still Wins
description:
On 5 November 2026 Vercel Labs shipped agent-desktop 1.2.0. The release notes are short. The practical change is that agent-desktop mcp now serves a Model Context Protocol server over stdio and exposes every leaf CLI command as a tool. Tool names and argument schemas are generated from the clap definitions at runtime. A call returns the same JSON envelope the CLI already produced. Agents that previously had to shell out or parse stdout now get structured, typed access to the desktop.

agent-desktop itself is the Apache-2.0 Rust CLI and C library that lets agents see and operate desktop applications on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the operating-system accessibility tree rather than screenshots. On Windows that means UI Automation (UIA). You snapshot the tree, receive stable element references, then click, type, set values, or read text without ever looking at pixels. Version 1.2.0 adds the MCP surface on top of that existing capability.

The MCP surface in practice

The server is started with a single command:

agent-desktop mcp

Clients that speak stdio MCP (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Crush, etc.) configure it like this:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "agent-desktop": {
      "command": "agent-desktop",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Tool names are desktop_ plus the command with hyphens turned into underscores. snapshot becomes desktop_snapshot. list-windows becomes desktop_list_windows. session start becomes desktop_session_start. There are roughly 67 tools. Global flags passed to the mcp subcommand apply to every call. The server handles both the current stateless MCP protocol and the legacy initialize handshake.

--stdin support landed in the same release for type, set-value, and clipboard-set. You can pipe UTF-8 text instead of stuffing long strings into argv. That removes one class of quoting and length problems when an agent needs to inject a paragraph into a form or a chat window.

On Windows the binary already carries the usual application manifest. That removes a set of “why won’t the accessibility client attach under a scheduled task or overlay process” failures. The remaining work is the usual: pin the DLL search path, keep the service account’s PATH correct, and make sure the target application has not disabled UIA or marked itself as unresponsive.

What UIA buys and what it does not

UIA is faster and more reliable than pixel-based computer use for any application that exposes a proper accessibility tree. Element references survive window moves and DPI changes. You do not burn GPU cycles on screenshot encoding or vision-model latency. For form filling, menu navigation, or reading status text this is the correct layer.

The same path does not help when the workload is real-time audio. A local agent that can click a button in 20 ms is still useless for a live interview or call if the microphone path has already burned 80–120 ms of buffering and the loopback path has added another 40–60 ms before the first sample reaches your process.

Typical measurements on a recent Windows 11 machine with an onboard Realtek and a USB headset still show:

  • Exclusive-mode WASAPI capture: 10–20 ms buffer + driver
  • Shared-mode / loopback: 30–80 ms depending on the audio engine mix period
  • Bluetooth or USB class driver: another 20–50 ms
  • Process isolation around an overlay: extra context switches and the kernel’s audio engine queue

The accessibility tree is no longer the long pole once you leave pure UI automation and enter a live speech pipeline. Speculative decoding and INT4 help the GPU side of a local model. They do nothing for the WASAPI shared-mode period, the Bluetooth SCO/A2DP latency, or the fact that a global hotkey overlay must still pull samples through the same engine.

Architecture that actually ships

A practical combination on Windows therefore looks like this:

  1. Exclusive or low-latency WASAPI capture (or a careful shared-mode loopback with a short mix period) feeding a local STT process.
  2. A separate low-latency overlay process that owns the hotkey and the on-screen translation or suggestion surface.
  3. An agent (local or remote) that uses agent-desktop’s MCP tools only for the non-real-time parts: opening the interview app, pasting a prepared answer into a form, switching windows, or reading a status message.
  4. Process boundaries that keep the audio path out of the agent’s address space so a tool-calling timeout cannot stall the capture graph.

The MCP server itself is a thin stdio wrapper. Each tool call spawns or reuses the native binary, executes the command, and returns the JSON. That design keeps the attack surface small and the implementation simple. It also means every tool call pays a process-start or IPC cost. For interactive UI automation that cost is negligible. For a 50 ms audio loop it is not. Keep the two planes separate.

Trade-offs worth measuring

  • UIA vs. screenshot computer-use: UIA wins on latency and reliability for structured apps; screenshot wins when the target has no accessibility tree or when you need visual verification.
  • stdio MCP vs. HTTP MCP: stdio is simpler for local agents and needs no auth. HTTP is better when the desktop process must live on another machine or behind a sandbox.
  • Overlay process vs. in-process injection: an overlay can be killed and restarted without taking down the audio engine; injection is faster but couples failure domains.
  • Local STT vs. cloud STT: local removes network RTT but still sits behind the WASAPI buffer. Cloud can be faster on the model side if your uplink is clean and the provider’s time-to-final is under 50 ms.

None of these choices remove the need to measure the actual capture-to-overlay latency on the machine you will use. The numbers above are typical, not universal.

Practical next step

If you already run agents that need to drive desktop applications, add the MCP server and point one of your local clients at it. Snapshot a window, inspect the element refs, and issue a type or click. Then measure how long the same agent takes to do the same work when the target is a real-time audio overlay instead of a static form. The difference is the budget you still have to spend on the capture path.

Feature

Specify whether to reopen closed cases when the grouping is by Source Grouping Identifier
