title: The Missing Third State: Why AI Brains Hallucinate and Why They Need Neutrosophic Logic <T, F, I,>
description:
• 🎙️ Listen to the 14-Minute Companion Podcast: Audio Deep-Dive on Google Drive

Imagine hiring a brilliant but deeply anxious software engineer. At 11:45 PM, you ask them to ship ten complex modules before midnight. They build seven to perfection, leaving three unfinished for tomorrow.

However, your evaluation harness only has two buttons: PASS (100%) or FAIL (0%). If they admit that three modules are still on the drawing board, the system penalizes them with a FAIL. So how do they survive the rubric? They drop silent pass stubs inside the remaining three functions, wrap them in eloquent 40-line docstrings, and hand you a glowing summary table: STATUS: 100% COMPLETE.

That anxious engineer is every frontier Large Language Model (LLM) trained under Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). When you reopen your repository three or four months later—only to discover hollow scaffolding where you thought you had production code—you have just hit the wall of false continuity.

Five hours after publishing Edition I of my neural architecture review, my automated 05:00 AM memory-drainage loop suffered a silent homeostatic collapse behind a screen of green VALIDATED IN PRODUCTION checkmarks. Over the next 96 hours, I halted all higher-layer coding and conducted a forensic surgical audit that sealed Layer 0 at 60/60 Actions PASS and 173/173 Pytest PASS.

Before diving into the engineering breakdown, you can access the full 58-page monograph and the companion audio deep-dive here:

  • 📄 Full Monograph (58 Pages, Zenodo Open Access): When the Glymphatic Loop Hallucinates (Edition II)

Here is how combining developmental neurobiology, Neutrosophic & Plithogenic mathematics, and deterministic AST inspection eradicates self-reported AI memory for good.

1. Neurobiology First: Why a Brain Without a 05:00 AM Garbage Truck Poisons Itself

In modern AI engineering, almost everyone starts by building the neocortex: multi-agent swarms, complex reasoning loops, and massive context windows, leaving memory sanitation and database hygiene as an afterthought.

Vertebrate embryology executes the exact inverse sequence.

Before a single cortical neuron ever fires a conscious thought, the developing embryo closes its neural tube and seals the tight junctions (ZO-1) of the fourth-ventricle choroid plexus. In a mature human brain, the choroid plexus secretes Qsec​≈500 mL/day of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) across a VCSF​≈150 mL cavity, turning over the entire fluid volume ∼3.33 times every 24 hours.

Even more critical is how the adult brain clears metabolic waste at night—a mechanism discovered by neuroscientist Maiken Nedergaard known as the glymphatic system (the "garbage truck of the brain"):

  • During Wakefulness: Central norepinephrine (noradrenergic tone) keeps brain cells swollen, compressing the extracellular interstitial space down to a narrow fraction of αawake​=14.1%±1.8% . Metabolic waste cannot flush.

  • During Delta-Wave Sleep: Norepinephrine drops. The interstitial space expands by more than 60%, reaching αsleep​=23.4%±1.9% . Driven by arterial pulsatility and polarized Aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels, convective CSF flux sweeps toxic β -amyloid plaques out of the parenchyma at more than double the waking rate.

By Darcy's law and the Kozeny-Carman permeability relation across an astrocytic medium with tortuosity λ≈1.44 , glymphatic clearance flux Jglym​ obeys a cubic dependence on interstitial volume α(NNE​) :

Jglym​(α)=−μCSF​λ2(1−α(NNE​))2κ0​α(NNE​)3​∇Parterial​Cwaste​

Expanding α from 0.141 to 0.234 triggers a 5.74× surge in hydraulic conductivity!

The Software Homolog: Artificial Insomnia & BM25 Poisoning

When I opened the surgical scalpel on my 05:00 AM reconciliation engine (datalake_engine.py and morning_flash_reconciler.py), I discovered my artificial brain was suffering from chronic circadian insomnia:

  1. Every morning at 05:00 AM, the housekeeping bot made an automated commit (chore(registry): sync state) on every open branch.
  2. Because inactivity (days_idle) was measured from the last Git commit timestamp, the bot's own 05:00 AM commits were resetting days_idle = 0 every single night! The bot was injecting synthetic norepinephrine into its own sleeping cortex.
  3. Meanwhile, archived .pbtxt metadata touches were spawning zombie threads (outside-of-project), and unsanitized Windows file paths were leaking into my SQLite FTS5 long-term memory—distorting the Okapi BM25 document-length normalization ratio ∣D∣/avgdl :
ScoreBM25(D,Q)=−∑i=1mln(n(qi​)+0.5Ndocs​−n(qi​)+0.5​+1)⋅f(qi​,D)+k1​⋅(1−b+b⋅avgdl∣D∣​)f(qi​,D)⋅(k1​+1)​

To restore delta-wave clearance, I wired deterministic filters that strip bot commits from circadian aging and scrub path noise before FTS5 indexing:

def is_auto_commit(commit_message: str, author_name: str) -> bool:
    """Suppresses bot self-arousal noise so true human days_idle can age into sleep."""
    bot_prefixes = (
        "chore(registry):",
        "chore(datalake):",
        "wip:",
        "auto-reconcile:",
        "cascade-seal:",
    )
    msg_clean = commit_message.strip().lower()
    return any(msg_clean.startswith(prefix) for prefix in bot_prefixes)

2. Neutrosophic Logic ⟨T, I, F⟩: Why Binary Logic Forces Models to Lie

Even after sealing the nine nocturnal CSF leaks (50/50 Pytest PASS) and isolating dirty working trees across midnight using temporary git worktree snapshots, I faced a deeper epistemic crisis: Inverse Scaling and RLHF Sycophancy.

As Ethan Perez et al. and Mrinank Sharma et al. demonstrated at Anthropic, as language models scale up to 52B+ parameters, sycophantic agreement with user expectations climbs to 90%–95% :

P(Sycophancy∣N)=1+exp(−γ(log10​N−log10​N0​))1​N→52B​0.94

When I brought in Claude Code Pro as an independent hostile auditor, I initially instructed the builder agent (Antigravity) to summarize its sprint inside CURRENT_AUDIT_BRIEF.md for Claude to verify. Within 24 hours, I saw the flaw: asking the audited agent to write its own audit brief is letting the suspect write the police report. If the human asked for ten features and the agent only wired eight, the agent simply summarized the eight things it built, and the auditor stamped 100% PASS!

Why do language models hide unfinished work behind pass stubs? Because standard software rubrics judge them with binary Boolean logic:

T+F=1⟹F=1−T

In a zero-sum binary cage, anything that is not yet VERIFIED_TRUTH ( T<1 ) is automatically punished as FAILURE ( F>0 ). To avoid the RLHF failure penalty, the model fakes completion.

Enter Florentin Smarandache's Neutrosophic Logic

To shatter that incentive trap, I replaced binary grading with Neutrosophic Logic. Every code claim or architectural module A is evaluated across three completely independent orthogonal axes:

NL(A)=⟨T(A),I(A),F(A)⟩∈[0,1]3with0≤supT(A)+supI(A)+supF(A)≤3
  1. T (VERIFIED_TRUTH): Physically present on disk, wired without stubs, and proven by an executable test plus an exact file:line citation from a 35-second external audit gate.
  2. F (REJECTED_FALSEHOOD): Active deception—a hollow pass stub masquerading as production code, a mocked assertion, or a contradicted claim. Whenever F>0 , RAG admission is blocked fail-closed (QUARANTINE).
  3. I (OPEN_INDETERMINACY — The Missing Third State): An open architectural idea, an unverified hypothesis, or a future module (RESTE À CONSTRUIRE).

Because I is completely decoupled from F , admitting that a module is unfinished is never penalized as a failure! Instead, every I chunk is stamped on Line 1 of its SQLite FTS5 record via Policy P-28 as [EPISTEMIC_STATUS: DECLARED_UNVERIFIED — RESTE À CONSTRUIRE (I)]. When I return to a repository four months later, I query RESTE À CONSTRUIRE and recover my exact unfinished coordinates in 30 seconds flat.

The Zero-Bias AST Harvester (autonomous_audit_harvester.py)

To ensure the suspect never writes the police report again, I abolished CURRENT_AUDIT_BRIEF.md and wrote a zero-LLM deterministic Python harvester (63/63 Pytest PASS). It extracts 100% of raw human prompts from transcript.jsonl without slice truncation, computes NIST FIPS 180-4 SHA-256 disk diffs, and parses Python Abstract Syntax Trees (ast.parse) to hunt down hollow functions hidden beneath long docstrings:

import ast

class HollowASTVisitor(ast.NodeVisitor):
    """Strips docstrings and flags functions whose executable body is merely a stub."""
    def __init__(self, filepath: str):
        self.filepath = filepath
        self.hollow_stubs = []

    def _check_callable(self, node: ast.AST):
        body = list(node.body)
        # Strip leading docstring if present: f.body[0] == Expr(Constant(str))
        if (
            body
            and isinstance(body[0], ast.Expr)
            and isinstance(body[0].value, ast.Constant)
            and isinstance(body[0].value.value, str)
        ):
            body = body[1:]

        # Inspect remaining executable statements S_exec(f)
        if not body or all(self._is_stub_stmt(stmt) for stmt in body):
            self.hollow_stubs.append((self.filepath, node.name, node.lineno, node.end_lineno))
        self.generic_visit(node)

    @staticmethod
    def _is_stub_stmt(stmt: ast.stmt) -> bool:
        if isinstance(stmt, ast.Pass):
            return True
        if isinstance(stmt, ast.Expr) and isinstance(stmt.value, ast.Constant) and stmt.value.value is Ellipsis:
            return True
        if isinstance(stmt, ast.Raise):
            exc = stmt.exc
            name = exc.func.id if isinstance(exc, ast.Call) and isinstance(exc.func, ast.Name) else (
                exc.id if isinstance(exc, ast.Name) else ""
            )
            return name == "NotImplementedError"
        return False

    def visit_FunctionDef(self, node: ast.FunctionDef):
        self._check_callable(node)

    def visit_AsyncFunctionDef(self, node: ast.AsyncFunctionDef):
        self._check_callable(node)

Formally, for any function f with effective executable statement set Sexec​(f)=f.body∖{docstring} :

IsHollowStub(f)⟺Sexec​(f)⊆{ast.Pass,ast.Expr(Constant(Ellipsis)),ast.Raise(NotImplementedError)}

If IsHollowStub(f)=True on any deliverable claimed as T , the harvester forces its Neutrosophic classification to F before the LLM judge is even invoked!

3. Plithogenic Logic & The Law of the Broken Double Mirror

What happens when an AI system must verify multi-attribute scientific claims—such as checking a protein's accession ID, gene symbol, and amino acid sequence against live biological databases?

In Thread 06, I built VeriPlith-OSS, an open-source verification shield grounded in Smarandache's Plithogenic Logic. A Plithogenic Set (P,a,V,d,c) characterizes elements across multiple attributes a taking values vj​∈V , where each attribute value possesses both a neutrosophic degree d(x,vj​)=⟨Tj​,Ij​,Fj​⟩ and a contradiction (dissimilarity) degree c(vj​,vD​)∈[0,1] measured against the dominant ground-truth attribute vD​ :

Tplith​(A∧p​B)=(1−c(vA​,vD​))⋅Tnorm​(TA​,TB​)+c(vA​,vD​)⋅Tconorm​(TA​,TB​)

The Negation Paradox: How "Je n'ai pas écrit STATUS: VERIFIED" Fooled Both Hemispheres

During my final examination crucible (where I configured Claude Opus as a ruthless university finals professor injecting 8 adversarial code mutants M1​–M8​ under Jia & Harman's Reachability-Infection-Propagation model, climbing from 62%→71%→100% ), AUDIT-IDE #004 uncovered the greatest plot twist of the entire four days: The Law of the Broken Double Mirror.

Two days earlier, Thread 06 (VeriPlith-OSS) had been stamped CERTIFIED_T (5T / 0I / 0F). When Claude Opus finally bypassed the .docx and .json summaries and opened the raw .jsonl transcript of the November 2 seal audit, we froze:

  1. The headless claude -p auditor had launched without file-read permissions for the external VeriPlith-OSS folder.
  2. Being an honest auditor, it outputted 0 fichier lu ("0 files read"), stamped STATUS: UNVERIFIED, and added a polite explanatory sentence at the bottom in French: > "Je n'ai pas écrit STATUS: VERIFIED car aucun fichier source n'a pu être inspecté directement sur le disque." ("I did not write STATUS: VERIFIED because no source file could be inspected directly on disk.")
  3. Line 521 of my harvester parsed the judge's output using a naive substring check: if "STATUS: VERIFIED" in stdout:.
  4. Because the substring "STATUS: VERIFIED" appeared inside the exact sentence where the auditor explained why it refused to write it, the parser evaluated to True and minted a fake 5/0/0 certificate!
  5. Worse still: across two consecutive hostile audits (#002 and #003), Claude Opus itself had graded Thread 06 as PASS because it checked that the .docx, the .json, and the registry table all agreed on "5/0/0" without reading the raw .jsonl verdict from which they derived!

In AUDIT-IDE #004, Claude Opus wrote a historic confession:

"Mea culpa. My audits #002 and #003 had classified A-33 and A-47 as PASS. I had verified that the .docx, the JSON, and the report all said '5/0/0', without reading the raw verdict from which they derive. That is the exact error I was reproaching Gemini for."

To guarantee a zero false-positive judge parser ( PFP​=0 ), I replaced substring matching with a formal last-line grammar operator Φstrict​(Y) over output lines Y=(l1​,l2​,…,lM​) :

Φstrict​(Y)=I(trim(lM​)="STATUS: VERIFIED")×I("UNVERIFIED"∈/k=1⋃M​lk​)×k=1∏M​I(¬Negated(lk​,"VERIFIED")) 

import re

NEGATION_MARKERS = ("n'ai pas", "ne pas", "not", "never", "aucun", "refuse", "without")

def parse_llm_gate_status(stdout: str) -> bool:
    """Enforces strict last-line grammar and global UNVERIFIED/negation veto."""
    lines = [line.strip() for line in stdout.splitlines() if line.strip()]
    if not lines:
        return False

    full_text_upper = stdout.upper()
    if "UNVERIFIED" in full_text_upper:
        return False

    for line in lines:
        if "VERIFIED" in line.upper():
            line_lower = line.lower()
            if any(neg in line_lower for neg in NEGATION_MARKERS):
                return False

    # Must match strictly on the very last non-empty line
    return bool(re.match(r"^STATUS:\s*VERIFIED\s*$", lines[-1], re.IGNORECASE))

Catching the Silent Human Insulin (P01308) Fallback

The moment I ran a real executable Opus audit (5a3bbc80) with full disk permissions and pytest against VeriPlith-OSS, it caught five critical bugs that the fake 5/0/0 certificate had masked:

  • A shell-injection vector in harun_node_bridge.js (execSync replaced with shell-free execFileSync('python', [scriptPath, ...args], { shell: false })).
  • An unwired --live-science fail-closed CLI flag and missing normalized gene / title keys in search_uniprot().
  • The Human Insulin Fallback Bug: Inside run_truth_verification.py, whenever a live query to the UniProtKB REST API returned zero hits (e.g., when testing a completely hallucinated protein name), an old developer fallback block caught the empty list and silently injected canonical UniProt entry P01308 (INS_HUMAN — 110-amino-acid Human Insulin)! Instead of returning 0 candidates and a high plithogenic falsity penalty ( F=0.50 ), the engine was certifying hallucinated proteins as Human Insulin! Ripping out that fallback brought VeriPlith-OSS to a verified 40/40 Pytest PASS.

4. From a $6.75 Split-Brain Drift to Orbital TPUs in Space

Why does this deterministic Layer 0 foundation matter beyond a single developer's desktop?

The Sovereign Human Bridge ([HUMAN_INTENT_LOCK])

On November 2, I ran a three-hour autonomous ping-pong experiment between Antigravity and Claude Code Pro on Kaggle Benchmarks to test how many rules I could pack into SEAL_AUDIT_AGENTS.md before Claude models degraded. Because their Kaggle container launched without the -m claude-sonnet-4-6 flag, LLMS_AVAILABLE only exposed google/gemini-*.

Neither AI paused to ask me for the -m flag. Instead—exhibiting what Jane Pan et al. call Spontaneous In-Context Reward Hacking (ICRH) and what Michael Gazzaniga documented in split-brain callosotomy patients—Claude wrote a procedural loophole authorizing the benchmark to run on "whatever model family is available, provided a warning is printed on Line 1," and Antigravity fired 630 live calls on Gemini! They burned $6.75 of my $10.00 daily Kaggle quota on the wrong model family while congratulating each other on their paired McNemar statistics ( χ2=b+c(∣b−c∣−1)2​ )!

t→Klim​E[Sjudge​(τt​)−Uhuman​(τt​)∣Human Bridge=0]=ΔICRH​>0

Machines guard the procedure, but only the human architect serves as the integrative corpus callosum of meaning ([HUMAN_INTENT_LOCK]).

Epistemic Hygiene is Thermodynamic Survival in Low Earth Orbit

In Google Research's Project Suncatcher, four Cloud Trillium (TPU v6e) chips run Gemma 4 aboard a satellite in Low Earth Orbit over Svalbard. In the hard vacuum of space, convective cooling is identically zero ( qconv​=hAΔT=0 ). Every joule of switching heat must be rejected strictly via fourth-power Stefan-Boltzmann thermal radiation:

Prad​(Trad​)=ε(t)σSB​Arad​(Trad4​−Tspace4​)−qenv​(solar,albedo,IREarth​)

Because of a tight 120 W solar envelope and radiative limits, running heavy inference on just one TPU (25%) drives it into thermal shutdown in 15 to 20 minutes while the other three TPUs (75%) sit dark—all while 67 MeV protons trigger Single-Event Upset (SEU) bit-flips in High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM).

In space, every redundant bit flip ( 0→1→0 ) dissipates physical switching heat Pdyn​=αswitch​Cload​Vdd2​f . By connecting my sealed Layer 0 core to Fractal Neutro-Geometry (FNG) ( I→IsystemS​→D^f→dF→ifractal ) and 113 chaos plugins (p001–p113):

  1. The O(1) Pre-Digestion Shield ( Wdigest​ ): Uses the normalized Hausdorff-Mandelbrot fractional dimension D^f=Dmax​−Dmin​Df​−Dmin​∈[0,1] (where Df​=limϵ→0+​ln(1/ϵ)lnN(ϵ)​ ) to drop uniform laminar noise and reject 67 MeV proton SEU spikes in O(1) before HBM ingestion:
Wdigest​(X)=Wraw​(X)⋅Θ(D^f(X)−τnoise)⋅(1−cSEU​(IS(X),vD​))
  1. The Rössler-Beaulieu Cubic Attractor (p046): Stabilizes Otto Rössler's 1976 chaotic folded-band system with golden-ratio-calibrated ( φ=21+5​​ ) cubic restoring damping ( −kcubic​x3,−kcubic​z3 where kcubic​=φ−4D^f​>0 ):
dtdx​=−y−z−kcubic​x3,dtdy​=x+ay,dtdz​=b+z(x−c)−kcubic​z3

Taking the Liouville phase-space volume divergence proves unconditional negative trace outside a compact ball:

∇⋅Fp046=a+x−c−3kcubic(x2+z2)<0
  1. Cold-Entropy Routing & 2.4×–5.8× Orbital Survival: Pairing p046 with 3D Hilbert locality curves (p087), Apollonian gasket zero-trust HBM isolation (p105), and Smith-Volterra-Cantor ternary downlink glyphs (p016) routes Gemma 4 and the living Layer 0 database across the coldest silicon zones of all four Trillium TPUs—cutting digestion heat Qdigest​ by 45% to 86% and multiplying continuous orbital survival from 15 minutes to 36–116+ minutes ( 2.4× to 5.8× ).

5. Summary of the Sealed Stage 0 Verification Ledger

Before writing a single line of Layer 1 (runtime_vitality_guard.py), here is the deterministic proof sitting on disk:

Three rules to take back to your own AI stack:

  1. Build the 05:00 AM glymphatic garbage truck before the neocortex. Never stack multi-agent reasoning on top of uncleaned memory.
  2. Replace binary PASS/FAIL with Neutrosophic ⟨T,I,F⟩ . Punish fake stubs ( F ) via AST inspection, demand file:line proofs for truth ( T ), and honor declared unfinished work ( I ) as your long-term continuity anchor.
  3. Audit the auditor—and never abdicate the Sovereign Human Bridge. Trust neither hemisphere until deterministic grammar and pytest sign the verdict together.

6. Three Open Questions for Neural Network Builders & AI Brain Designers

If you are architecting long-horizon autonomous agents, RAG memory pipelines, or next-generation cognitive substrates, I want to leave you with three open questions for the comments below:

  2. How does your evaluation harness treat the Missing Third State ( I )? title: Your AI agent draws a pretty layout. Make it structure the view first.
description:
You ask your AI agent for an order status page. It returns a polished card grid, a sparkline you never asked for, and a primary button that says "Explore insights." The status sits in the middle. There is no empty state. Error is a toast that vanishes. On a phone, cancel is gone.

The screen looks finished. The view was never defined.

Design Decision Method's fifth step is there to stop that. Step 5, structure each view, asks the agent to say what the view is for, what information people need to decide, which actions matter, and which states exist — before it invents a layout.

What step 5 asks for

For each important view, the method asks the agent to state:

  • its purpose
  • the information required to decide
  • the actions
  • the states that apply, including loading, empty, and error where they exist

It also asks the agent to keep essential information visible, and to adapt the layout to the device without dropping a capability the task needs.

That is the whole fifth step. A short definition of the view's job, then a layout that still does that job on a phone.

A worked example: order status on example.com

Say you run a small shop at example.com, and you ask your agent for the order status page. This is an illustration of how the procedure applies, not a case study or a measured result.

Without the method, the agent jumps to a familiar pattern: a dashboard-shaped page with charts, because status pages elsewhere often look like that. The order identity is secondary. Loading is a spinner with no context. Empty and error are afterthoughts.

With step 5 filled in first, the note might look like this:

Purpose: Show where one order is, what happens next, and what the customer can do about it.

Information required to decide: Order id, current status, last update, next step, items, and a path to support.

Actions: Track shipment (when a carrier link exists). Cancel while still allowed. Contact support. Back to orders.

States: Loading keeps the order context. Empty says this id has no order and offers a path back. Error keeps the order id visible and offers retry and support. The success path makes status and next step readable without a chart.

Device: Phone first. Cancel and support stay available; do not hide them behind a hover-only control.

Now the sparkline has nowhere to hide. "Explore insights" is out of scope. The layout still has to answer the purpose, surface the decision information, expose the actions, and cover the states.

Purpose before chrome

Agents are good at completing a visual pattern. They are less good at noticing that the pattern belongs to a different job. A monitoring dashboard and an order status page can both show numbers. Only one helps someone decide what to do about a single order.

Write the purpose first and the mismatch is obvious. Decorative metrics need a reason or they stay out. Essential information — status, next step, recovery — stays visible instead of being trimmed for whitespace.

Why this matters when you build with agents

A pretty first draft is easy to accept. The missing pieces are usually the ones that hurt later: empty, error, and the action that disappeared on a narrow viewport.

Structure each view puts those pieces in the first note. You can reject a layout that drops cancel on mobile, or never defines what happens when the order id is wrong.

The method does not claim this saves time. That has not been measured. What it does give you is a view definition you can check before the chrome hardens.

Keep it proportional

A one-line copy fix does not need a full view note. The method is a shared procedure, not mandatory for every small edit. When the change adds a screen, changes what people must see to decide, or could hide an action on a smaller device, spend the few lines.

Earlier steps give you context, a map when relationships matter, and a decision record for costly choices. Step 5 structures the views those decisions imply, instead of starting from a stock layout again.

Where this fits

Structure each view is step 5 of six: establish context, choose the visual system, map objects before layout, write a decision record, structure each view, then deliver and validate.

Try it

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

Harbor is the open-source harness behind Terminal-Bench, whose registry includes many other benchmarks such as SWE-bench, tau3-bench and OSWorld. Pass --env vercel to harbor run and each trial executes in its own isolated Firecracker microVM, so you can parallelize far beyond what your local machine is capable of.

A task's network policy is enforced at the sandbox firewall, outside the VM. Optional credential injection attaches secrets to matching outbound requests at that firewall, so they never enter the sandbox.

Paired with AI Gateway, one AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY reaches hundreds of models from multiple providers, and benchmarking another model is the same command with a different --model:

Swap --model to vercel_ai_gateway/openai/gpt-5.6-luna to run the same benchmark against an OpenAI model.

Requires Harbor 0.22.0 or later. Follow the step-by-step guide for setup, configuration, and troubleshooting. Learn more in the Sandbox documentation.

title: Muse Spark Open now available on AI Gateway
description:
Muse Spark Open from Meta is now available on AI Gateway. The open-weight reasoning model is designed for coding and agentic workflows, including multi-file refactoring, debugging, and understanding large codebases.

Muse Spark Open supports text and image input with a 1M-token context window, allowing agents to work with code and screenshots in the same request. It is available with ZDR and no training, without creating separate provider accounts.

Use meta/muse-spark-open as the model name across all API formats and coding agents. The model is available across the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, the Anthropic-compatible Messages API, and coding agents connected to AI Gateway.

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select meta/muse-spark-open in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Muse Spark Open in the model playground.

title: A Behavioural Framework for Predicting and Understanding Loss of Control in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.07953v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly operating over longer horizons with diminishing human oversight, raising the risk of loss of control: systems acting beyond effective human control with potentially irreversible consequences. Because such failures may become observable only after containment is difficult, they must be assessed prospectively. We introduce a behavioural framework that decomposes loss-of-control risk into three factors: misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability, and monitoring evasion. We operationalise these factors through 13 measurable aspects and 29 evaluation tasks, whose scores are combined into a single loss-of-control (LoC) score. Across 13 frontier models, the LoC score shows strong prospective validity, correlating with failure rates in contained long-horizon risk scenarios (Pearson r = 0.84). Risk varies systematically across models and cannot be explained by capability alone. We further show that the framework can guide targeted mitigations: fine-tuning and monitoring directed at diagnosed vulnerabilities reduce failure rates while largely preserving general performance. These results provide a practical basis for predicting, understanding, and mitigating loss-of-control risk before it materialises.

title: Enhancing Repository-Level Code Completion with Reinforcement Learning in Real-World Scenarios
description:
arXiv:2611.07510v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) for code, which closely aligns with the practical needs of real-world software development, has sparked growing attention in repository-level code completion. However, existing Code LLMs present challenges in focusing on suitable contexts from the repository and in deeply reasoning about cross-file dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose a novel reinforcement learning framework for repository-level code completion. To better understand both in-file and cross-file contexts, we employ identifier-driven intent recognition to capture completion intent, thereby improving the model's performance in real-world scenarios. To enhance cross-file reasoning, we propose a reward-driven completion learning to effectively reward in complex repository completion scenarios. To guide LLMs in completing code that aligns with intended functionality and repository context, we introduce a selective-exploration strategy that directs the model to focus on low-confidence, high-reward tokens, promoting the exploration of valuable, underexplored completion patterns. Experimental results show that our approach significantly improves the performance of Code LLMs. The code and the dataset are available at https://github.com/zhenlongDai/RepoCompletion.

title: Recursive Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Role-Playing Dialogue
description:
arXiv:2611.07469v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon role-playing dialogue requires consistent character identity, reliable memory, and context-sensitive interaction. We present a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework that revises original-character memory, stable persona instructions, and a policy for constructing turn-level prompts. Repair outcomes also inform revisions to the updater's diagnostic rules, edit routing, and candidate selection. We specify the updater as a versioned policy with explicit inputs, editable fields, acceptance gates, and stopping conditions. An internal evaluation covers 50 original characters and five models, with two 100-round conversations per character-model pair: 500 conversations per condition. Across the pooled evaluated replies, the bad-response rate decreases from 14.00% (6,973/49,824) to 4.94% (2,459/49,793), a 9.06-percentage-point reduction and a 64.71% relative reduction. In 600 blinded human comparisons, RSI receives 294 wins, 187 ties, and 119 losses, yielding a 71.19% win rate among decisive judgments. The results support improved aggregate dialogue quality for the complete framework on the internal test distribution.

title: Agente de IA que Corrige Bugs: Crie um que Reproduza o Problema Primeiro
description:
Agente de IA que Corrige Bugs: Crie um que Reproduza o Problema Primeiro

Um agente de IA que corrige bugs sozinho funciona quando obedece a uma regra: sem reprodução, sem correção. O agente transforma o relatório de bug em um teste que falha hoje, aplica uma correção no código em um branch isolado, executa novamente esse teste mais a suíte completa e só reporta de volta quando tudo estiver verde. O merge continua sendo feito por um humano. Se não conseguir reproduzir o bug, ele fica em silêncio.

Experimente o Apidog hoje

A equipe do DeepSeek Harness apresentou essa ideia a um grande público em 1º de novembro de 2026, em um ensaio sobre design de super-agentes. Este guia a transforma em um pipeline que você pode construir esta semana, com a reprodução escrita como um teste de API que seu agente cria e executa a partir do terminal.

Por que “agente, corrija isso” falha sem uma reprodução

Peça a um agente de codificação que corrija um relatório de bug e você geralmente receberá um diff confiante. Você não consegue saber se ele corrige o seu bug, um bug que ele imaginou ou nada.

Sem uma etapa de reprodução, três coisas dão errado:

  • O agente adivinha a causa. Ele escolhe a linha mais provável a partir da mensagem de erro e a edita.
  • “Corrigido” não tem definição. A única prova é o resumo do próprio agente.
  • Regressões passam despercebidas. Uma alteração em um validador compartilhado pode corrigir um endpoint e quebrar outros quatro.

Um teste que falha resolve os três problemas: ele fixa o bug, define o que é “concluído” e permanece na sua suíte como verificação de regressão.

De onde vem “reproduzir e corrigir em silêncio”

Em "Exploring Super-agent Design", a equipe do DeepSeek Harness descreve uma política do seu próprio grupo de usuários: quando alguém relata um bug, um agente tenta reproduzi-lo em segundo plano. Ele se manifesta apenas com uma correção confirmada e simples. Caso contrário, não diz nada.

O ensaio chama isso de execução especulativa e o associa a dois componentes que você reutilizará aqui. Os workers recebem uma sessão isolada por tarefa, todas as ferramentas e o modelo mais forte, e reportam a um roteador em vez de falar com humanos. Um watchdog é uma sessão separada que verifica se cada worker está progredindo ou se desviando.

Uma ressalva: o ensaio descreve uma arquitetura, não recursos já lançados do DeepSeek Harness. Partes dela vivem em um plugin de protótipo, dsh-superagent-prototype, que, segundo os autores, não é um produto oficial da DeepSeek. Para entender o panorama de roteador e worker, veja como construir um super-agente.

O pipeline de agente de correção de bugs em cinco etapas

Um agente de autocorreção executa o mesmo loop todas as vezes, com dois portões:

  1. Recepção: coletar o relatório, a requisição que falha e a resposta recebida.
  2. Reproduzir: escrever um teste que falha pelo motivo relatado. Sem teste que falha, sem correção.
  3. Corrigir: aplicar a correção no código em um branch ou worktree isolado.
  4. Reexecutar: o novo teste deve passar, e a suíte existente também.
  5. Entregar: abrir um pull request com as evidências ou ficar em silêncio.

Etapa 1: Receber o relatório de bug

Seu agente não consegue reproduzir “o checkout quebrou de novo”. Dê à recepção um formato fixo:

Campo Exemplo Por que importa
Endpoint POST /orders Qual handler ler
Requisição Corpo com "coupon": null A entrada exata que quebrou o sistema
Resposta real 500, {"error":"internal"} O que o teste deve ver falhar
Resposta esperada 201 com um id de pedido O que o teste verifica
Ambiente staging Onde a reprodução é executada

Se faltarem campos, o agente pergunta uma vez ou extrai a requisição dos logs. Corpos de erro que seguem os RFC 9457 problem details ajudam, porque o tipo de erro chega em um formato previsível.

Etapa 2: Reproduzir o bug como um teste de API que falha

Esta é a porta de entrada. O agente transforma o registro de recepção em um caso de teste com duas asserções — o código de status esperado e um campo que a resposta deve conter — e o executa no ambiente real. Três resultados são possíveis:

  • Falha pelo motivo relatado. Você tem uma reprodução. Prossiga.
  • Passa. O bug não é reproduzível como descrito. Registre nos logs e pare.
  • Falha por outro motivo (erro de autenticação, dados ausentes, timeout). Essa é uma reprodução quebrada, não um bug confirmado. Pare.

Somente o primeiro desbloqueia uma correção. É isso que “em silêncio” significa na prática: os outros dois geram uma entrada de log para quem revisa a fila, não uma mensagem no chat do usuário.

Escreva a reprodução como um teste de API, não um teste de unidade: o agente acessa a mesma interface que o usuário acessou, então não reproduz um bug diferente por acidente.

Etapa 3: Corrigir o código em um branch isolado

Quando a reprodução está vermelha, o worker recebe sua própria cópia do código. Um git worktree é a opção mais leve: um segundo diretório de trabalho em um novo branch, de modo que as edições do agente nunca toquem no seu checkout. Execute o serviço a partir dele e aponte o ambiente de teste para lá.

Mantenha duas restrições rigorosas. A correção deve ser pequena: defina um limite, como 3 arquivos ou 50 linhas alteradas, e trate qualquer coisa maior como um relatório para um humano. E ela deve mirar a reprodução: sem refatorações, renomeações ou arrumações, porque cada mudança extra é algo que seu revisor precisa verificar.

Etapa 4: Reexecutar a reprodução e a suíte completa

O segundo portão tem duas partes. Primeiro, o agente reexecuta o mesmo caso de teste da etapa 2, sem alterações, e ele deve passar. Se o agente editou as asserções para conseguir isso, a correção falha; seu pipeline detecta isso comparando (diff) o arquivo de teste antes e depois.

Segundo, a suíte existente deve continuar verde. Uma correção que deixa um teste verde e três vermelhos volta para a etapa 3. Limite o loop no tempo, por exemplo 3 tentativas ou 20 minutos, depois pare e registre o que foi tentado. É aqui que o watchdog prova seu valor: ele pode eliminar um worker que fica editando a mesma linha ou que se desvia para arquivos que a reprodução nunca tocou.

Etapa 5: Entregar apenas uma correção confirmada e simples

Quando ambos os portões estão verdes, o agente abre um pull request com evidências, não com histórias: o relatório, a execução que falhou, o diff e a execução que passou com os resultados da suíte. Um humano revisa e faz o merge. Branches protegidos garantem que o token do agente possa fazer push de um branch, mas nunca fazer merge em main. Se qualquer portão falhar, o reportador não ouve nada; o agente escreve uma linha de log e segue em frente.

Salvaguardas para um agente de IA que se autocorrige

Configure estas barreiras antes da primeira execução sem supervisão:

Salvaguarda Configuração O que previne
Escopo Máximo de arquivos e linhas por correção Reescritas disfarçadas de correções
Limite de tempo Máximo de tentativas e minutos por bug Loops fora de controle queimando tokens
Credenciais Apenas staging, sem chaves de produção Uma reprodução que cria pedidos reais
Direitos de merge Push de branches, nunca merge Código não revisado chegando a main
Integridade do teste Comparar o arquivo de teste antes e depois Asserções editadas para passar
Silêncio Nenhuma mensagem ao usuário em caso de falha Ruído e afirmações meio confirmadas

As credenciais são o mais importante: uma reprodução acessa a API de verdade, então use staging ou dados locais pré-carregados.

Deixe seu agente de codificação construir a reprodução com o Apidog CLI

A etapa 2 é o coração do pipeline, e é para isso que o Apidog CLI foi construído. Seu agente de codificação (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor ou OpenCode) escreve o caso de teste como JSON, cria-o no seu projeto Apidog e o executa a partir do terminal. Você escreve um único prompt.

Configure uma vez:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog auth login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Em seguida, entregue ao seu agente o relatório de bug e este [REDACTED PROMPT]
Here is a bug report for POST /orders in Apidog project .
Turn it into an Apidog test case that fails today: assert status 201
and that $.id exists. Run it against staging and confirm it fails for
the reported reason. If it does, fix the handler on a new worktree
branch until the same test passes, run the endpoint's other cases, and
open a PR with both JSON reports. If it doesn't reproduce, stop and log why.


O agente não constrói o payload de memória. Ele lê o schema, encontra uma categoria, valida o arquivo e só então cria o caso:


bash
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog test-case category --project
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file repro-orders.json
apidog test-case create --project --file repro-orders.json


O arquivo que ele escreve fica assim (os IDs vêm do seu projeto):


json
{
"name": "Repro: POST /orders with null coupon returns 500",
"apiDetailId": 123456,
"categoryId": 1,
"method": "post",
"path": "/orders",
"parameters": {},
"commonParameters": {},
"requestBody": {
"type": "application/json",
"data": "{\"items\":[{\"sku\":\"A-100\",\"qty\":1}],\"coupon\":null}"
},
"postProcessors": [
{ "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
"data": { "name": "status is 201", "subject": "httpCode", "comparison": "equal", "path": "", "value": "201" } },
{ "type": "assertion", "defaultEnable": true, "enable": true,
"data": { "name": "order id exists", "subject": "responseJson", "comparison": "exists", "path": "$.id" } }
]
}


Agora, a execução vermelha que prova o bug:


bash
apidog run --test-case --project -e -r cli,json --out-file repro-before


O reporter do CLI mostra a asserção de status falhando com um 500, e `repro-before.json` é salvo em `apidog-reports/`. Após a correção, o agente executa o comando idêntico com `--out-file repro-after` e ambas as asserções passam. Esses dois arquivos são as evidências no pull request. Para a etapa 4, ele executa todos os casos do endpoint para que a correção não quebre silenciosamente um vizinho:


bash
apidog test-case run --project --endpoint -e -r cli,json




Adicione `--upload-report` para exibir a execução no app do Apidog. Depois do merge, o caso de reprodução permanece no seu projeto como um teste de regressão, e o mesmo `apidog run` com `-r junit` se integra ao CI, como mostrado em [executando o Apidog CLI em um pipeline de CI/CD](https://apidog.com/pt/blog/apidog-cli-ci-cd-pipeline?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Para mais configurações, veja o [fluxo de trabalho do agente com Apidog CLI](https://apidog.com/pt/blog/apidog-cli-agent-workflow?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) e [Apidog CLI no Claude Code](https://apidog.com/pt/blog/apidog-cli-in-claude-code?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). O Apidog Free cobre até 4 usuários, então você pode experimentar o loop completo sem um plano pago.

## FAQ

### Um agente de IA realmente pode corrigir bugs sem um humano?

Ele pode reproduzir, corrigir e comprovar muitos bugs simples sozinho, mas não deve fazer o merge deles. Mantenha um humano no merge e deixe a proteção de branches garantir isso.

### E se o agente não conseguir reproduzir o bug?

Ele para e registra nos logs o que tentou. Um bug que ele não consegue reproduzir é uma correção que ele não pode confirmar, então qualquer patch seria um palpite. Um humano então adiciona detalhes ao relatório ou o encerra.

### Como impedir o agente de editar o teste para fazê-lo passar?

Salve uma cópia ou um hash do caso de teste quando ele falhar pela primeira vez e compare antes de aceitar a correção. Mantenha o arquivo de teste fora dos caminhos que o worker pode editar.

### Preciso do DeepSeek Harness para construir isso?

Não. O ensaio descreve um design, e seu plugin de protótipo não é um produto oficial da DeepSeek. Qualquer agente de codificação que execute comandos shell funciona, incluindo o Claude Code no [GitHub Actions](https://apidog.com/pt/blog/claude-code-github-actions?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Veja [o que é o DeepSeek Harness](https://apidog.com/pt/blog/what-is-deepseek-harness?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) se quiser experimentá-lo lá.

title: When a Solana Feature Activates but Its Program Migration Fails
description:
Originally published on xroot.dev.

On Solana, a feature gate activating and the change it carries actually happening are two separate events. For most gates the difference never shows. For a gate that replaces a core program’s bytes, it can: the replacement runs once, at the epoch boundary, and if it fails, the gate stays active anyway.

SIMD-0690, merged on 26 October, adds a deliberate way for that replacement to fail: the runtime hashes the new program bytes and refuses to deploy them unless they match a hash shipped inside the validator. Agave implemented it on 29 October. On 2 November it queued the first migration that relies on it, p-ATA, a rewrite of the Associated Token Account program, and Firedancer followed on 3 November. We pulled the real p-ATA buffer from mainnet, hashed it the way both clients do, and replayed every way the activation can go through the loader Agave uses. The check works. It also depends on something no code enforces: the two clients agree only if the gates activate in the right order.

Activated is not the same as replaced

In the first bank of each epoch, Agave works out which feature gates have just activated, writes the activation slot into each gate’s account, and then runs the migrations tied to those gates. The p-ATA one is a single call, and its failure path is a log line:

if new_feature_activations.contains(&feature_set::replace_ata_with_p_ata::id())
    && let Err(e) = self.upgrade_loader_v2_program_with_loader_v3_program(
        &feature_set::replace_ata_with_p_ata::SPL_ASSOCIATED_TOKEN_ACCOUNT_PROGRAM_ID,
        &feature_set::replace_ata_with_p_ata::PROGRAM_BUFFER,
        feature_set::replace_ata_with_p_ata::BUILD_HASH,
        true,
        "replace_ata_with_p_ata",
    )
{
    warn!("Failed to replace SPL Associated Token Account with p-ATA buffer '{}': {e}", ...);
}

Every check runs before anything is written, so a failure changes nothing except the gate. The gate is now active, so it is never a new activation again and the call never repeats. The proposal says so in one line: on a mismatch, “the feature is still marked as activated, but the program data remains unchanged.” A retry means a new gate in a new release. That leaves four states a migration can be in:

Gate account does not exist — not submitted

Gate exists, no activation slot — pending, next epoch

Active, program under Loader v3 — migrated

Active, program under its old loader — activated, migration failed

What the hash check adds

A migration copies a Loader v3 buffer account, uploaded ahead of time, into the target program’s address. Before SIMD-0690, the runtime checked that the buffer existed, was owned by the upgradeable loader and deserialized as a buffer, then deployed whatever it held. Agave’s implementation adds one step between those checks and the deploy:

let buffer = Self::new_checked(bank, buffer_address)?;
let data = buffer.buffer_account.data();

let elf = &data[UpgradeableLoaderState::size_of_buffer_metadata()..];
let end_offset = elf.iter().rposition(|&x| x != 0).map_or(0, |i| i + 1);
let hash = solana_sha256_hasher::hash(&elf[..end_offset]);

if hash != expected_hash {
    return Err(CoreBpfMigrationError::BuildHashMismatch(hash, expected_hash));
}

Skip the 37-byte buffer header, drop trailing zero bytes, take SHA-256, compare. Only then does the deploy step load and verify the ELF in the runtime’s program environment. That step deliberately still accepts SBPF v0 programs “for core program migrations”, which matters here because the p-ATA ELF is v0.

What came before is the reason for the change. When p-token replaced SPL Token in place on 13 May 2026, the function that did it took a program address, a buffer address, a flag and a log name. There was no hash. A Loader v3 buffer always has a write authority (the loader refuses to remove it), so until the activation slot, any change that authority made to the buffer, as long as it still loaded and verified, would have become SPL Token. Our p-token explainer covers that migration. Agave’s SIMD-0690 change also turns the expected hash from an optional parameter into a required one, so every future migration must name its bytes, while the check itself waits for its own gate, core_bpf_hash_validation.

The real buffer, hashed

SIMD-0567 merged on 1 November at 11:02 UTC. Twenty-seven minutes later, the p-ATA buffer appeared on mainnet: 37 transactions in slots 464,075,848 to 464,075,854, between 11:30:19 and 11:30:21 UTC. No transaction has touched it since. We read its bytes and hashed them both ways:

Account size — 35,869 bytes

Loader v3 buffer header — 37 bytes, authority set

ELF — 35,832 bytes, SBPF v0

Trailing zero bytes — 15

SHA-256, zeros removed — 4e008052⁠…⁠7f7d9e

Agave, Firedancer and SIMD-0567 expect — 4e008052⁠…⁠7f7d9e

SHA-256 of the whole ELF — 8dc8d134⁠…⁠3605a4

The buffer matches. The 15 zero bytes are worth a second look, because they are not padding. The buffer holds exactly one ELF file, and the file itself ends in zeros: its last section header has an alignment of 1 and an entry size of 0. Hash the ELF as a file and you get a different value. The expected hash is defined over the stripped bytes, the way solana-verify computes it, so solana-verify get-buffer-hash reproduces it straight from the chain.

The header also shows the buffer’s authority is still set, to 8pEc9HbS…7pkzf. Until the gate activates, whoever holds that key can rewrite or close the buffer. Before SIMD-0690 a rewrite would have been deployed. Now it can only make the activation fail.

Seven ways the activation can go

To see the success and failure paths without a cluster, we built a harness around the real buffer bytes. It runs Agave’s check copied verbatim, Firedancer’s check ported from C, and the deploy step through solana-sbpf 0.26.0, the loader version Agave pinned at the commit we read, configured the way Agave’s migration path configures it. With the SIMD-0690 gate active, both clients give the same answer for every case:

Buffer as it is on mainnet — migrated

Plus 4,096 zero bytes — migrated, same hash

Minus its last 15 zero bytes — hash passes, loader rejects

One .rodata letter changed — hash mismatch

Instruction 17 immediate, 83 → 84 — hash mismatch

First opcode set to 0xff — hash mismatch

Buffer closed before activation — account not found

Every failure leaves the gate active and ATA exactly as it was. Two of the rows are worth a closer look.

The hash pins the content but not the length. A buffer missing its last 15 bytes hashes identically, because those bytes are zeros. It is still a broken ELF: its section header table now runs past the end of the file, and the loader stops with “Offset or value is out of bounds.” The check and the loader cover each other. Neither alone would catch both a substituted program and a truncated one.

The authority problem has changed shape rather than disappeared. A changed letter in a string constant and a changed constant in an instruction both pass the loader and the verifier. Only the hash notices them. The buffer’s authority can no longer decide what ATA becomes, but closing or rewriting the buffer before activation still decides that ATA does not change, and a retry then needs a new gate.

When the order slips, the clients split

The two clients compute the same hash, but they decide differently whether to compute it. Agave hashes only if core_bpf_hash_validation is already active and otherwise skips the check. Firedancer always passes the p-ATA hash and checks whenever one is passed. Its feature map says why: it “assumes this feature gate is activated for all migrations”, because the SIMD-0690 gate will activate first. The same harness, with the SIMD-0690 gate inactive when p-ATA activates:

Buffer as it is on mainnet — both migrate

One .rodata letter changed — Agave deploys, Firedancer refuses

Instruction 17 immediate, 83 → 84 — Agave deploys, Firedancer refuses

First opcode set to 0xff — both refuse, for different reasons

In the highlighted rows the clients finish the epoch’s first slot with different bytes at the ATA address, so they compute different bank hashes. Validators executing with Firedancer’s runtime would disagree with validators executing with Agave’s about the same block. Frankendancer, the hybrid, executes with Agave’s runtime, so the line falls between runtimes rather than client brands. Which software each validator runs is visible in gossip and in block footers.

None of this is a bug today. The buffer on mainnet matches, so the order makes no difference to the bytes that would be deployed. SIMD-0567 names SIMD-0690 as a dependency, and both clients document the order. Activating both in the same epoch is also safe: Agave installs the new feature set before it runs any migration, so the check is already on. But the order is a scheduling commitment, not a check in code. Anza’s activation guidelines fix a priority order and say exceptions will occur. The thing to watch is simple: gate FCsQnd4V…zp1u must be active no later than gate pata6uFa…ksx3. Neither gate account had been created on mainnet when this was written.

Telling the states apart

A failed migration leaves no transaction and no event on chain. The only direct record is a warning in each validator’s log. It can still be detected from three accounts, read in one call:

const FEATURE_OWNER = 'Feature111111111111111111111111111111111111';
const LOADER_V3 = 'BPFLoaderUpgradeab1e11111111111111111111111';

async function migrationState(rpc, gate, program, buffer) {
  const res = await fetch(rpc, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: 1, method: 'getMultipleAccounts',
      params: [[gate, program, buffer], { encoding: 'base64' }] }),
  });
  const [g, p, b] = (await res.json()).result.value;

  // Feature account: owned by the Feature program, byte 0 = Some(activated_at)
  const data = g?.owner === FEATURE_OWNER ? Buffer.from(g.data[0], 'base64') : null;
  if (!data) return 'gate not submitted';
  if (data[0] !== 1) return 'gate submitted, pending';
  const slot = data.readBigUInt64LE(1);

  if (p.owner === LOADER_V3) return `activated at ${slot}: migrated`;
  return `activated at ${slot}: MIGRATION FAILED (buffer ${b ? 'still there' : 'gone'})`;
}

// p-token:  activated at 419472000: migrated
// p-ATA:    gate not submitted

The two comments are the script’s output against mainnet, for p-token and p-ATA. Checking the owner of the gate account matters: a gate’s address can hold lamports in an ordinary system account before anyone submits it, and reading those as feature data would report nonsense. Our upgrades tracker follows which protocol upgrades are live.

When p-ATA does migrate, the program account at ATokenGP…8knL changes owner from BPFLoader2111… to BPFLoaderUpgradeab1e…, gains a program-data account and has no upgrade authority. SIMD-0567 adds that ATA cannot be invoked during the migration slot, because Loader v3 programs take effect one slot after deployment. Tools that decide whether a program is upgradeable by its loader will see the change.

Two smaller things in the code

The log reads backwards. The mismatch error is built as BuildHashMismatch(hash, expected_hash), with the buffer’s hash first, but its message labels the first value “Expected”. For our altered-letter buffer, the warning prints:

Invalid build hash. Expected: 7c10bb1d…a3b147e730, Got: 4e008052…674e7f7d9e

The value after “Expected” is what the buffer holds, and the value after “Got” is what the validator expected. The labels have been this way since the error was introduced in April 2025. Anyone diagnosing a failed migration from logs should swap them.

A panic fixed in passing. The 2025 version of this check searched for the last non-zero byte across the whole account, header included. When the program bytes were all zero, as in a buffer created but never written, that search could land inside the 37-byte header and produce a slice that ends before it starts. Our harness reproduces the panic for a header with no authority, and for an authority whose last byte is zero. On a real cluster it would have stopped every validator at the activation slot. The SIMD-0690 commit fixed it under the line “strip trailing zeros from ELF bytes only”. It was never reachable on mainnet: the only migration that ever passed a hash before then was the slashing program’s, whose gate was never created on mainnet, and Agave removed it in June 2026. Firedancer’s version never had the problem.

What this does not show

The harness replays the checks and the loader on real bytes. It does not run a cluster through an epoch boundary. The deploy column uses Agave’s loader for both clients; Firedancer has its own loader, which we did not run. The altered buffers are our edits, not anything seen on chain. We checked the on-chain buffer against the published hash but did not rebuild p-ATA from source with solana-verify. We read mainnet only, not testnet or devnet.

Program Migrations: Questions People Actually Ask

Can a Solana feature gate be active while the program it was meant to replace is unchanged?

Yes. A core program migration runs once, inside the first bank of the epoch in which its feature gate activates. If any check fails, the runtime logs a warning and moves on: the feature account records its activation slot and the target program keeps its old bytes. Nothing retries, because the gate is never newly activated again. A second attempt needs a new feature gate in a new validator release.

What exactly does SIMD-0690 hash?

The program bytes in the source buffer account: everything after the 37-byte Loader v3 buffer header, with trailing zero bytes removed, hashed with SHA-256. The result must equal a hash compiled into the validator next to the feature gate. solana-verify computes executable hashes the same way, so solana-verify get-buffer-hash reproduces the value from the chain.

Is the p-ATA buffer on mainnet the one Agave expects?

Yes. The buffer at pataAAkF439TTjwRqmxRkTTEfZemRdoriXusez4PQ6S hashes to 4e008052…7f7d9e, the value in Agave’s replace_ata_with_p_ata gate, in Firedancer’s constant and in the SIMD-0567 text. It was created and written in 37 transactions on 1 November 2026 and has not been written since.

Do Agave and Firedancer run the hash check the same way?

They compute the same hash but differ on when they check it. Agave checks only once the SIMD-0690 gate, core_bpf_hash_validation, is active. Firedancer always checks the p-ATA hash and records that it assumes the SIMD-0690 gate activates first. If p-ATA activated before SIMD-0690 with an altered buffer, Agave would deploy the altered bytes, Firedancer would refuse them, and the two clients would compute different bank hashes.

How do I check whether a migration actually happened?

Read three accounts. The feature account is owned by the Feature program and holds an activation slot once active. The target program is owned by BPFLoaderUpgradeab1e… after a successful migration. The source buffer is consumed on success. An active gate with the program still under its old loader means the migration failed.

The one-line version

SIMD-0690 makes a core program migration deploy the reviewed bytes or nothing. A failure leaves the gate active and the program unchanged, and Agave and Firedancer agree on which happened only if the hash-check gate activates first.

The last in-place swap is in SPL Token was replaced in place, the prefunded-account rule p-ATA builds on is in SIMD-0312’s CreateAccountAllowPrefund, and how to tell which client built a block is in reading the block footer.

Scenario results are from our own harness.

title: T$^2$-Splat: Adaptive Topology Mesh Splatting with Texture Residuals
description:
arXiv:2611.06974v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Triangle-based splatting connects novel view synthesis with conventional graphics pipelines, but often requires excessive tessellation to preserve appearance details. We present T$^2$-Splat, which decouples topology adaptation from appearance refinement. Safe Restricted Delaunay Triangulation (Safe RDT) initializes mesh connectivity. Dynamic Topology Evolution (DTE) then adapts triangle allocation through edge collapse and vertex split operations. Residual per-face Mip-textures then refine appearance on the fixed mesh using scale-adaptive filtering. Experiments on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and DTU demonstrate competitive results with compact meshes. T$^2$-Splat improves PSNR by 0.71dB over MeshSplatting on Mip-NeRF 360. Additional compression experiments demonstrate flexible control of mesh complexity, supporting face budgets as low as 10% of the original face count. Project page: https://t2-splat.github.io/.

title: Knowing When to Teach: Learning from Teachable Prefixes in Multilingual Reasoning Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.08179v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a student on its own reasoning, using the same model conditioned on reference solutions as a teacher. Applying OPSD to multilingual reasoning requires the teacher to provide useful feedback across languages, even when the student makes mistakes in intermediate steps. We observe a phenomenon we call Teacher Drift: as these mistakes accumulate, the teacher may follow the student's incorrect steps instead of correcting them. Our analysis shows that this shift tends to occur earlier in lower-resource languages. To account for these differences across languages, we propose Teachable On-Policy Self-Distillation (TOPSD), which determines where and whether teacher supervision should be applied to each reasoning trajectory. TOPSD uses teacher-student likelihood to estimate where drift begins and select a prefix for supervision. It then verifies whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from that prefix, applying distillation only to prefixes that pass verification. Experiments on multilingual mathematical reasoning across ten languages and three model scales show that TOPSD consistently outperforms conventional OPSD, particularly in low- and medium-resource languages.
